additional_notes: Used when you start a relative clause describing a man/person: „ein/der Kerl, der …“ (= “a/the guy who …”). „Kerl“ is informal (like “guy” or sometimes “dude”) and can sound a bit rough depending on context. The relative pronoun „der“ refers back to „Kerl“ (masculine nominative).
target_language_example: Das ist der Kerl, der immer zu spät kommt.
native_language_example: That’s the guy who is always late.

additional_notes: „mögen“ means “to like” or “to be fond of.” It’s usually followed by the thing/person liked in the accusative (e.g., „Kinder mögen Eis.“). In the present tense: ich mag, du magst, er/sie/es mag, wir mögen, ihr mögt, sie/Sie mögen.
target_language_example: Kinder mögen oft Süßigkeiten.
native_language_example: Children often like sweets (candy).

additional_notes: Used to describe a general fact or the state/quality/location of children. **Kinder** = children (plural). **sind** is the plural form of **sein** (to be) used with **wir/ihr/sie** and plural nouns: *Kinder sind…* / *Eure Kinder sind…*. Common with adjectives (*fröhlich, laut, süß*) or places (*im Garten*).
target_language_example: Kinder sind manchmal sehr müde.
native_language_example: Children are sometimes very tired.

additional_notes: Used for the activity/skill of playing the piano. Often appears with modal verbs like können (can), wollen (want), or würden gern (would like), and after verbs of perception like hören/sehen: Ich höre ihn Klavier spielen (I hear him play the piano).
target_language_example: Meine Schwester kann sehr gut Klavier spielen.
native_language_example: My sister can play the piano very well.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like anfangen/beginnen (to start), aufhören (to stop), and lernen (to learn): „anfangen, Klavier zu spielen“, „aufhören, Klavier zu spielen“. Here „zu spielen“ is the infinitive ("to play") used after certain verbs (often in the pattern „Verb + zu + Infinitiv“).
target_language_example: Ich versuche, Klavier zu spielen, aber es ist nicht leicht.
native_language_example: I'm trying to play the piano, but it's not easy.

meaning: contact with; (to) get in touch with.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like haben/halten (to have/keep contact), verlieren (to lose contact), abbrechen (to cut off contact), or aufnehmen/aufnehmen zu (to make contact / get in touch). Often followed by a person or group in the dative: Kontakt zu Tom / zu meinen Eltern. With aufnehmen, it commonly means reaching out: Kontakt zu dir aufnehmen = to contact you.
target_language_example: Ich habe wieder Kontakt zu meiner Schwester.
native_language_example: I’m back in contact with my sister.

meaning: “Chin up!” / “Keep your head up!” (Don’t be discouraged.)
additional_notes: A common encouraging phrase used to comfort someone who’s sad, worried, or has made a mistake. It’s an elliptical imperative (short for something like “Halt den Kopf hoch”). Often used alone (“Kopf hoch!”) or followed by a reason/plan: “Kopf hoch, wir schaffen das.”
target_language_example: Kopf hoch, das wird schon wieder.
native_language_example: Chin up, it’ll be okay again.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **backen** (“to bake”) in the **Perfekt** (past tense): **(jmd.) hat/habe ... Kuchen gebacken**. **gebacken** is the past participle; you can change the number: **einen Kuchen / drei Kuchen gebacken**. In questions: **Hast du den Kuchen gebacken?**
target_language_example: Ich habe gestern einen Schokoladenkuchen gebacken.
native_language_example: I baked a chocolate cake yesterday.

additional_notes: Usually used with a possessive pronoun: „mein Leben lang“, „dein Leben lang“, „sein/ihr Leben lang“ = “all my/your/his/her life.” It expresses duration (how long something lasts) and is similar to „ein Leben lang“ (“a lifetime”). Common word order is: pronoun + Leben + lang.
target_language_example: Ich werde das mein Leben lang nicht vergessen.
native_language_example: I will never forget that as long as I live.

meaning: life and death; an extremely serious matter (everything is at stake).
additional_notes: Used in phrases like „(Es geht) um Leben und Tod“ or „ein Kampf wie um Leben und Tod“ to emphasize that a situation feels as serious as a life-or-death struggle (often figurative, not always literally about dying).
target_language_example: In den Bergen kann schlechtes Wetter schnell zu einer Frage von Leben und Tod werden.
native_language_example: In the mountains, bad weather can quickly become a matter of life and death.

additional_notes: Uses the verb „werden“ (to become) with a noun: „[job] werden“. Often used to talk about career plans or wishes. With „wollen“: „Ich will Lehrer werden.“ With „sollen“ in the past (Konjunktiv II): „Ich hätte Lehrer werden sollen.“ = “I should have become a teacher.”
target_language_example: Sie möchte später Lehrer werden.
native_language_example: She would like to become a teacher later.

meaning: to feel sorry (for someone); to pity someone; (also) to regret / be sorry about something.
additional_notes: Common patterns: (1) „jdm. Leid tun“ = to feel sorry for someone / to pity someone: „Er tut mir Leid.“ (2) „etwas wird jdm. Leid tun“ = someone will regret something: „Es wird dir Leid tun.“ (often used as a warning: “You’ll be sorry.”). Note spelling/capitalization: „Leid“ is a noun and is capitalized; the verb is „tun“ and is conjugated (tut, tat, hat … getan).
target_language_example: Geh raus, oder es wird dir Leid tun.
native_language_example: Get out, or you'll be sorry.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a group of people described by what they do or are like. After „Leute“ you often add a relative clause with „die“ + verb at the end: „Leute, die hier arbeiten, …“. You can also use it without an article („Leute, die …“) for a general statement, or with an article („die Leute, die …“) for specific people.
target_language_example: Leute, die viel reisen, haben oft interessante Geschichten.
native_language_example: People who travel a lot often have interesting stories.

additional_notes: Used as a short command to switch the light(s) off. Often said without a verb (instead of the full sentence: „Mach das Licht aus.“ / „Schalten Sie das Licht aus.“). Can also be used as a question („Licht aus?“) to suggest/confirm turning the lights off.
target_language_example: Es ist schon spät—Licht aus, bitte.
native_language_example: It’s already late—lights out, please.

additional_notes: A fixed phrase for falling in love immediately when you first see someone. Often used with "Es war ..." or "an ... glauben" (to believe in), and sometimes with "mit" + person: "Mit David war es Liebe auf den ersten Blick."
target_language_example: Ich glaube nicht an Liebe auf den ersten Blick, aber ich habe mich sofort in sie verliebt.
native_language_example: I don’t believe in love at first sight, but I fell in love with her immediately.

additional_notes: Used to start a statement/idea about love. "Liebe" is a noun and is always capitalized in German; "ist" is the 3rd person singular of "sein" (to be). Often followed by an adjective or noun phrase (e.g., "Liebe ist möglich." / "Love is possible.").
target_language_example: Liebe ist kompliziert.
native_language_example: Love is complicated.

meaning: “(to) feel like … with me” / “(to) want to … with me”.
additional_notes: Used in invitations, usually in the pattern: „Hast du Lust, mit mir … zu + infinitive?“ (informal) or „Hätten Sie Lust, mit mir … zu + infinitive?“ (polite). It’s a friendly way to ask if someone is up for doing something together. Note: German „Lust“ often means “desire/feel like,” and is a false friend with English “lust.”
target_language_example: Hast du Lust, mit mir einen Kaffee trinken zu gehen?
native_language_example: Do you feel like getting a coffee with me?

meaning: feel like going for a walk.
additional_notes: Used with (Lust) haben: „Ich habe Lust auf …“ = “I feel like …”. In questions, it’s a friendly way to invite someone: „Hast/Hättest du Lust auf …?“ (“Do/Would you feel like …?”). Formal: „Hätten Sie Lust auf …?“; informal: „Hättest du Lust auf …?“ / plural „Hättet ihr Lust auf …?“.
target_language_example: Hast du Lust auf einen Spaziergang nach dem Abendessen?
native_language_example: Do you feel like going for a walk after dinner?

additional_notes: A formal/neutral noun phrase. Typically used with genitive: "die Lösung des Problems" = "the solution of the problem" → in natural English: "solution to the problem". Often appears after prepositions like "bei" (in/with), "für" (for), or with verbs like "suchen nach" (to look for).
target_language_example: Wir brauchen schnell eine Lösung des Problems.
native_language_example: We quickly need a solution to the problem.

additional_notes: Common loanword in German. Often used with verbs like **Make-up tragen** (to wear makeup) and **Make-up anhaben** (to have makeup on). You’ll also see it in compounds like **Make-up-Proben** (makeup samples).
target_language_example: Ich trage heute kaum Make-up.
native_language_example: I’m wearing hardly any makeup today.

meaning: "Mom, I…" (starting a sentence while addressing your mom).
additional_notes: Used when speaking directly to your mother, often said by children. In writing, you usually put a comma after the form of address: "Mama, ich …". "Mama" is more informal/affectionate than "Mutter".
target_language_example: Mama, ich brauche Hilfe.
native_language_example: Mom, I need help.

additional_notes: A familiar, often childlike way to refer to one’s parents. Adults may also use it affectionately, but in more neutral/formal contexts you’ll often hear "meine Eltern" (“my parents”). Can be used both when talking to your parents and when talking about them.
target_language_example: Mama und Papa kommen heute Abend zu Besuch.
native_language_example: Mom and dad are coming to visit tonight.

additional_notes: Used with a noun in the dative case: **Mangel an + Dativ** (e.g., *ein Mangel an Erfahrung*). Often appears in more formal contexts to describe missing qualities or insufficient supplies.
target_language_example: Man muss seinen Mangel an Erfahrung berücksichtigen.
native_language_example: You have to take his lack of experience into account.

additional_notes: Used when you add more information about a specific man with a relative clause: „der Mann, den …“. The comma is required before the relative pronoun. „den“ is the accusative masculine relative pronoun (he is the object in the relative clause), e.g. „der Mann, den ich kenne“ = “the man (that) I know.”
target_language_example: Das ist der Mann, den ich gestern im Park getroffen habe.
native_language_example: That is the man (who/that) I met in the park yesterday.

additional_notes: Used when a relative clause describes which man you mean. The comma comes before the relative pronoun „der“: „ein Mann, der …“ = “a man who …”; „der Mann, der …“ = “the man who …”. In other cases, the pronoun can change with grammar (e.g., „dem Mann, der …“ = “the man to whom …”).
target_language_example: Das ist der Mann, der mir geholfen hat.
native_language_example: That is the man who helped me.

additional_notes: Used with the verb „ändern“: „seine/ihre/deine Meinung ändern“ = to change one’s mind/opinion about a decision or plan. Often used in the perfect tense: „Ich habe meine Meinung geändert.“
target_language_example: Tut mir leid, ich habe meine Meinung geändert und komme doch nicht mit.
native_language_example: Sorry, I changed my mind and I’m not coming after all.

meaning: to change your mind / to change your opinion.
additional_notes: Usually used with a possessive: „seine/ihre/deine Meinung ändern“. The infinitive phrase „(die/eine) Meinung zu ändern“ is commonly used after verbs like „versuchen“, „schaffen“, „bereit sein“ or in fixed expressions like „nicht leicht/schwer, die Meinung zu ändern“.
target_language_example: Es ist nicht leicht, seine Meinung zu ändern.
native_language_example: It’s not easy to change your mind.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause that describes or identifies a group of people. “Die” changes with case/number (e.g., Menschen, denen … / Menschen, die …). Often used after words like "die Menschen" or "einer der Menschen".
target_language_example: Ich mag Menschen, die ehrlich sind.
native_language_example: I like people who are honest.

additional_notes: Used to make general statements about people. "Menschen" is plural, so the verb is plural: "haben" (not "hat"). Often followed by a noun (e.g., "Angst", "ein großes Gehirn", "kein Benehmen").
target_language_example: Menschen haben unterschiedliche Meinungen.
native_language_example: People have different opinions.

additional_notes: Used with a number to say how tall/high something is: „X Meter hoch“. Common with measurements of buildings, walls, snow, waves, etc. The number changes: „einen Meter hoch“, „drei Meter hoch“, „hundert Meter hoch“, etc.
target_language_example: Der Zaun ist zwei Meter hoch.
native_language_example: The fence is two meters high.

meaning: (to have/feel) pity for; to feel sorry for.
additional_notes: Usually used with the verb "haben": "Mitleid mit jemandem haben" (= to feel sorry for someone). "mit" takes the dative case: "mit mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/ihnen". Common in requests like "Hab/Habt Mitleid mit mir!"
target_language_example: Bitte hab Mitleid mit ihm.
native_language_example: Please have pity on him / please feel sorry for him.

additional_notes: Used with a number or quantity word to say how long something lasts: „drei Monate lang“, „ein paar Monate lang“. It’s an adverbial expression of duration and often goes with the simple past or present (e.g., „Ich war …“, „Ich lag …“, „Er spart …“).
target_language_example: Wir haben vier Monate lang auf die Lieferung gewartet.
native_language_example: We waited for the delivery for four months.

additional_notes: Common infinitive phrase used to describe the activity of listening to music. Often appears in hobby/activity lists (e.g., „lesen, Musik hören“) and with modal verbs: „Ich möchte Musik hören“ (I want to listen to music), „Wir können Musik hören“ (we can listen to music). Typical question: „Was für Musik hören Sie/du gern?“ (What kind of music do you like listening to?).
target_language_example: Mein Hobby ist Musik hören.
native_language_example: My hobby is listening to music.

meaning: to encourage someone; to give someone courage.
additional_notes: Usually used with a person in the dative: „jemandem Mut machen“ = to encourage someone (literally: to make courage for someone). Common when someone is nervous, scared, or unsure: „Mach dir Mut“ / „Ich will dir Mut machen.“
target_language_example: Ich will dir Mut machen: Du schaffst das!
native_language_example: I want to encourage you: You can do it!

additional_notes: Used when you add extra information about a specific girl: „ein/das Mädchen, das …“. Even though a girl is female, the noun „das Mädchen“ is grammatically neuter, so the relative pronoun is often „das“ (not „die“). The verb in the relative clause usually goes at the end: „das … kam/sitzt/sprechen kann“.
target_language_example: Das ist das Mädchen, das neben mir wohnt.
native_language_example: That’s the girl who lives next to me.

additional_notes: A neutral, general phrase used to refer to people of both genders together. Often used in formal writing or speeches (e.g., talking about a group, society, or a workforce).
target_language_example: In diesem Kurs lernen Männer und Frauen gemeinsam Deutsch.
native_language_example: In this course, men and women learn German together.

additional_notes: Used to state someone’s or something’s name. Very common in introductions: “Mein Name ist …” = “My name is …”. With “der”: “Der Name ist …” = “The name is …”. In fixed expressions it can appear as part of a larger meaning, e.g. “Der Name ist mir entfallen.” = “I’ve forgotten the name / The name has slipped my mind.”
target_language_example: Mein Name ist Alex.
native_language_example: My name is Alex.

meaning: "number one"; the best/top-ranked, or the first one.
additional_notes: Used for rankings ("die Nummer eins" = the top/best in a competition or category). It can also be used as a label or call sign for a person/object (like "Number One, take over"), and in family contexts to mean the first child (e.g., "Sohn Nummer eins" = first son).
target_language_example: Unser Team will dieses Jahr die Nummer eins werden.
native_language_example: Our team wants to become number one this year.

additional_notes: A common pairing in shopping and food contexts, especially at the supermarket or market. "Obst" = fruit, "Gemüse" = vegetables; often used as a category or department (e.g., im Supermarkt).
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte Obst und Gemüse für heute Abend einkaufen?
native_language_example: Can you please buy fruit and vegetables for tonight?

meaning: “place where” (a place in which something is/ happens).
additional_notes: Used to describe a specific place and add a relative clause with information about it. Often seen as „der Ort, wo …“ or „einen Ort, wo …“. In more formal German, you may also hear/see „Ort, an dem …“ instead of „Ort, wo …“.
target_language_example: Kennst du einen Ort, wo man hier gut Kaffee trinken kann?
native_language_example: Do you know a place where you can get good coffee around here?

additional_notes: Used with numbers and quantities: "ein Paar Schuhe" (one pair), "drei Paar Schuhe" (three pairs). After numbers, German often keeps "Paar" in the singular: "drei Paar Schuhe" (also possible: "drei Paare Schuhe" but less common). In questions you’ll often see "welches Paar Schuhe …?" = "which pair of shoes …?".
target_language_example: Ich brauche ein neues Paar Schuhe für den Winter.
native_language_example: I need a new pair of shoes for the winter.

additional_notes: Used when you stop working/doing an activity for a short time to rest. Commonly appears as "eine Pause machen" or "eine kleine Pause machen". You can ask about timing with "Wann wirst du Pause machen?" or suggest it with "Du solltest (mal) Pause machen."
target_language_example: Ich finde, du solltest Pause machen.
native_language_example: I think you should take a break.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has been unlucky, often with a blunt or unsympathetic tone (like “Tough luck!”). Literally “had bad luck” (Pech = bad luck, gehabt = had). You can use it about yourself or someone else: „Ich habe Pech gehabt.“ / „Er hat Pech gehabt.“
target_language_example: Tut mir leid, aber du hast Pech gehabt.
native_language_example: Sorry, but tough luck.

meaning: to have bad luck; to be unlucky; to be out of luck.
additional_notes: Common everyday phrase used when something unfortunate happens to you. In the present tense it’s typically used as „Ich habe Pech“ / „Du hast Pech“. In the past, Germans often say „Pech gehabt“ (literally: ‘had bad luck’). You can intensify it with „richtig“, „total“: „Ich habe total Pech.“
target_language_example: Ich will heute ins Schwimmbad, aber ich habe Pech haben: Es regnet den ganzen Tag.
native_language_example: I want to go to the swimming pool today, but I have bad luck: it’s raining all day.

additional_notes: Used when you add information about a specific person. Since **Person** is grammatically feminine, the relative pronoun is often **die** (e.g., *die Person, die…*). In other cases you’ll see other forms like **der/dem/den/deren** depending on gender/case (e.g., *die Person, der ich vertraue* = “the person (to) whom I trust”).
target_language_example: Das ist die Person, die mir immer hilft.
native_language_example: That’s the person who always helps me.

meaning: a backup plan; an alternative plan.
additional_notes: Used when the first plan ("Plan A") might fail, or when you need another option. Often said with "Es gibt (k)einen Plan B" (There is/isn't a Plan B) or asked as "Und was ist Plan B?" (So what’s Plan B?).
target_language_example: Wenn das Restaurant voll ist, haben wir einen Plan B.
native_language_example: If the restaurant is full, we have a backup plan.

meaning: to need space; to take up space.
additional_notes: Used when something (or someone) requires physical room (e.g., furniture, luggage, parking). Common in phrases like „Wir brauchen mehr Platz.“ (we need more space) or „Das wird viel Platz brauchen.“ (that will take up a lot of space).
target_language_example: Der Kinderwagen wird viel Platz brauchen im Auto.
native_language_example: The stroller will take up a lot of space in the car.

meaning: 'space/room for' (enough capacity or an available spot for someone/something).
additional_notes: Used with an object to say there is (or isn’t) space/capacity for something: "Platz für + Akkusativ" (e.g., Platz für alle). It can mean physical space (bags, dessert) or an available spot/opportunity (a reserved seat; no room for tourists in these jobs). Common verbs: "Platz für ... haben" (to have room for), "Platz für ... schaffen" (to make room for), "einen Platz für ... reservieren" (to reserve a spot for).
target_language_example: Kannst du noch etwas Platz für meinen Rucksack machen?
native_language_example: Can you make a bit of room for my backpack?

meaning: to have space/room; to have a free seat/spot.
additional_notes: Used to say that there is enough room for someone/something. Very common in questions like „Hast du noch Platz?“ (Do you still have room?) or statements like „Hier haben wir Platz.“ You conjugate only „haben“: ich habe, du hast, er/sie/es hat, wir haben, ihr habt, sie/Sie haben.
target_language_example: Haben wir im Auto noch Platz haben für zwei Koffer?
native_language_example: Do we still have space in the car for two suitcases?

meaning: to make room (for someone/something); to move aside.
additional_notes: Used when you need more space, often with a dative pronoun: „Mach mir bitte Platz.“ You can also say what it’s for with „für“: „Platz machen fürs Bett.“ As an imperative, it can be a direct command: „Platz machen!“ or more polite: „Würdet ihr mir etwas Platz machen?“
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, könnten Sie bitte kurz Platz machen?
native_language_example: Excuse me, could you please make room for a moment?

meaning: to take a seat; to sit down (polite).
additional_notes: Commonly used as a polite invitation or instruction, especially in service or formal situations (doctor’s office, meetings, restaurants). Often appears in imperative form: „Nehmen Sie Platz.“ / „Bitte nehmen Sie Platz.“ More casual alternatives: „Setz dich (bitte).“ / „Setzen wir uns.“
target_language_example: Bitte nehmen Sie Platz, der Arzt kommt gleich.
native_language_example: Please take a seat; the doctor will be here shortly.

additional_notes: A very common food word in German (often just called „Pommes“). Used in restaurants when ordering a side dish: „Pommes frites dazu?“ = “French fries with that / as a side?”
target_language_example: Ich nehme einen Burger mit Pommes frites, bitte.
native_language_example: I’ll have a burger with French fries, please.

meaning: to ride a bike; to cycle.
additional_notes: Common verb phrase with the noun "Rad" (bike): "Rad fahren" / "Ich fahre Rad" = "to ride a bike / to cycle." You can also say "Fahrrad fahren" (same meaning, a bit more explicit). In writing, "Rad" is capitalized because it’s a noun.
target_language_example: Ich gehe jeden Morgen Rad fahren.
native_language_example: I go cycling every morning.

additional_notes: Used with a possessive pronoun or name in the genitive: meinen/deinen/euren/Ihren/seinen Rat befolgen (“follow my/your/your (pl.)/your (formal)/his advice”). Common in more formal or written German; in everyday speech you also hear „einen Rat annehmen“ (accept advice).
target_language_example: Ich sollte deinen Rat befolgen und früher ins Bett gehen.
native_language_example: I should follow your advice and go to bed earlier.

additional_notes: Most commonly means “to be right” in opinions or arguments: „Du hast Recht.“ / „Sie haben Recht.“. With „das Recht haben + zu …“ it means “to have the right to …” (a legal or moral right): „Er sollte das Recht haben, selbst zu entscheiden.“
target_language_example: Ich denke, du könntest Recht haben.
native_language_example: I think you might be right.

additional_notes: Used with a destination: „eine Reise nach + Stadt/Land“. With cities you usually don’t add an article (z.B. „nach Berlin“). With some places you use an article and then often switch to „in“ + accusative (z.B. „eine Reise in die USA / in die Schweiz“ rather than „nach die USA/Schweiz“).
target_language_example: Nächste Woche mache ich eine Reise nach Berlin.
native_language_example: Next week I’m taking a trip to Berlin.

additional_notes: Used with an object: ein Risiko / dieses Risiko. Common with müssen (have to), wollen (want to), sollen (should), or würde (would). Often means doing something even though there could be negative consequences.
target_language_example: Ich will kein Risiko eingehen.
native_language_example: I don’t want to take any risks.

additional_notes: This is an infinitive phrase with „zu“ (…„to“ do something). It’s often used after verbs like „empfehlen“ (recommend), „versuchen“ (try), or expressions like „Es fällt mir schwer, …“ (I find it hard to …). With a specific novel, you’ll often see an article: „einen Roman zu lesen“ (a novel) / „den Roman zu lesen“ (the novel). Note: German „Roman“ means „novel“ (not „Roman“ as in ancient Roman).
target_language_example: Ich habe keine Zeit, einen Roman zu lesen.
native_language_example: I don’t have time to read a novel.

meaning: to stay calm; to keep your cool.
additional_notes: Used as advice or an instruction, especially in stressful or urgent situations. Very common as an imperative: „Ruhe bewahren!“ You can also use it with „müssen“/„sollten“: „Wir müssen Ruhe bewahren.“
target_language_example: Bitte Ruhe bewahren und langsam sprechen.
native_language_example: Please stay calm and speak slowly.

meaning: to leave (someone/something) alone; to let (someone) be; to stop bothering (someone/something).
additional_notes: Most commonly used as "jdn/etw in Ruhe lassen" = "leave someone/something alone" / "leave someone/something in peace." Frequently appears in the imperative: "Lass mich in Ruhe!" You can also use it for not touching or messing with something: "Lass das in Ruhe."
target_language_example: Bitte Ruhe lassen.
native_language_example: Please leave it alone / Please don’t disturb.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the activity of playing the board game chess. Common in questions and invitations (e.g., „Kannst du …?“ / „Willst du …?“).
target_language_example: Willst du Schach spielen?
native_language_example: Do you want to play chess?

meaning: to go ice skating; to ice-skate.
additional_notes: Used for the activity/sport of ice skating. Often used with verbs like „gehen“ (to go) or „können“ (to be able to): „Wir gehen Schlittschuh laufen.“ / „Ich kann Schlittschuh laufen.“ (Without “gehen”, it can still mean “to ice-skate” in general.)
target_language_example: Im Winter gehen wir oft Schlittschuh laufen.
native_language_example: In winter, we often go ice skating.

additional_notes: Used with "mit" + dative to say who you broke up with: "mit Tom Schluss gemacht". Most often in the perfect tense: "Ich habe Schluss gemacht." / "Hast du Schluss gemacht?" It refers to ending a relationship, not just finishing an activity.
target_language_example: Warum hast du mit ihm Schluss gemacht?
native_language_example: Why did you break up with him?

meaning: to stop/finish (for now); also: to break up (end a relationship).
additional_notes: Used in two common ways: (1) to end an activity/work for the day: „Wollen wir für heute Schluss machen?“ = “Shall we call it a day?” (2) to end a romantic relationship, usually with „mit + Dativ“: „mit jemandem Schluss machen“ = “to break up with someone.” Often used with time words like „jetzt“ (now).
target_language_example: Ich muss jetzt Schluss machen.
native_language_example: I have to stop now.

additional_notes: From the verb **finden** (“to find”). Often appears in the **Perfekt** tense with **haben**: *Ich habe den Schlüssel gefunden.* It can also be used as a short label/notice (e.g., in a lost-and-found context): *Schlüssel gefunden!* Use **den Schlüssel** for one key and **die Schlüssel** for multiple keys.
target_language_example: Ich habe den Schlüssel gefunden!
native_language_example: I found the key!

additional_notes: Used when talking about missing keys, often in questions or statements. You can use it with a possessive pronoun: „meinen Schlüssel verloren“ (lost my key), „meine Schlüssel verloren“ (lost my keys). Common in the perfect tense: „Ich habe … verloren“ / „Hast du … verloren?“
target_language_example: Ich habe meinen Schlüssel verloren—kannst du mir aufmachen?
native_language_example: I lost my key—can you open the door for me?

additional_notes: This is the formal imperative of **schreiben** used with **Sie** (e.g., in instructions, forms, or polite requests). It’s addressed to one person (or used as the polite form in general). It can take a direct object (e.g., *Schreiben Sie Ihren Namen.*) and is often combined with separable-prefix verbs like **mitschreiben** (*Schreiben Sie das bitte mit.* = “Write that down too / take notes.”) or **aufschreiben** (*Schreiben Sie mir das auf.* = “Write that down for me.”).
target_language_example: Schreiben Sie bitte Ihre E-Mail-Adresse hier.
native_language_example: Please write your email address here.

meaning: step by step; gradually, one step at a time.
additional_notes: Used to say you should do or explain something in a slow, orderly sequence. Often with verbs like lernen (learn), erklären/erzählen (explain/tell), vorgehen (proceed). It can describe learning, instructions, or how something happens over time.
target_language_example: Wir lösen das Problem Schritt für Schritt.
native_language_example: We'll solve the problem step by step.

additional_notes: Used with the separable verb "ausziehen" (to take off clothes/shoes): "(die) Schuhe ausziehen". In speech you may hear shortened forms like "Ich zieh mir die Schuhe aus." The opposite is "Schuhe anziehen" (to put shoes on).
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte die Schuhe ausziehen?
native_language_example: Can you please take off your shoes?

additional_notes: Past action with "kaufen" (to buy). Often used with a form of "haben" (e.g., "ich habe", "du hast", "Sie haben") to form the present perfect: "Ich habe Schuhe gekauft" = "I bought/have bought shoes." You can add details like "ein Paar" (a pair), "neue" (new), or say where: "… im Laden / online".
target_language_example: Ich habe gestern neue Schuhe gekauft.
native_language_example: I bought new shoes yesterday.

additional_notes: Usually used with an indirect object (dative) and the noun **die Schuld**: **jemandem die Schuld geben** = “to blame someone.” You can add **für + Akkusativ** to specify the reason: **jemandem die Schuld für etwas geben**. Related: **Schuld haben** = “to be at fault / to be guilty.”
target_language_example: Warum willst du mir die Schuld geben?
native_language_example: Why do you want to blame me?

meaning: to be to blame; to be at fault.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is responsible for a mistake/problem/accident. Often with a situation using „an + Dativ“: „Er hat Schuld an dem Unfall.“ You can also use it with „daran“: „Du hast daran Schuld“ (= it’s your fault). Common question: „Wer hat Schuld?“ (= Who is to blame?).
target_language_example: Ich habe Schuld an dem Fehler.
native_language_example: It’s my fault for the mistake.

meaning: to catch on; to set a trend and be copied by others.
additional_notes: Used when an idea, method, or behavior becomes popular and other people start doing the same; often appears in the idiomatic phrasing „Das macht Schule“. Here it’s given in the exact word order „Schule machen“.
target_language_example: Die neue Art zu arbeiten wird in vielen Firmen Schule machen.
native_language_example: The new way of working will catch on in many companies.

additional_notes: Most often used in the fixed phrase „etwas in Schutt und Asche legen“ = to destroy something completely (to raze it, reduce it to rubble). It’s a dramatic/literary-sounding expression and is common in war or revenge contexts.
target_language_example: Der Brand hat das Haus in Schutt und Asche gelegt.
native_language_example: The fire reduced the house to rubble and ashes.

meaning: to be lucky; to have good luck.
additional_notes: Common, fairly informal idiom meaning you got lucky (often unexpectedly), e.g., you avoided a problem or something worked out in your favor. Often used in the perfect tense as "Schwein gehabt" (e.g., "Du hast aber Schwein gehabt!") even though the base idiom is "Schwein haben".
target_language_example: Wir haben Schwein haben und noch den letzten Zug erwischt.
native_language_example: We were lucky and still caught the last train.

additional_notes: Used to report that you heard shots being fired (often in a police/witness context). You’ll see it with or without an article: **Schüsse** (some shots) vs. **die Schüsse** (the specific shots everyone is talking about). It’s typically used with **haben** in the perfect: **Ich habe Schüsse gehört.** In reported speech it often appears in the subjunctive: **Er sagte, er habe Schüsse gehört.**
target_language_example: Ich habe gestern Abend Schüsse gehört.
native_language_example: I heard gunshots last night.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the genre in movies, books, etc. In German it’s often written with a hyphen (Science-Fiction) and can be used in compounds like Science-Fiction-Film / Science-Fiction-Roman. You can also say: „Ich mag Science-Fiction.“
target_language_example: Ich lese gern Science-Fiction-Bücher.
native_language_example: I like reading sci-fi books.

additional_notes: Used with the verb „begehen“ (past participle: „begangen“) to talk about suicide, often in news or formal contexts: „Er/Sie hat Selbstmord begangen.“ In everyday German, many people also say „sich das Leben nehmen“ (to take one’s own life).
target_language_example: Laut der Polizei hat er Selbstmord begangen.
native_language_example: According to the police, he committed suicide.

additional_notes: A common, direct way to talk about having sex, typically meaning sexual intercourse. It’s fairly explicit; in more polite or softer contexts people may prefer alternatives like „miteinander schlafen“ or „Sex miteinander haben“.
target_language_example: Glaubst du, wir werden Sex haben?
native_language_example: Do you think we’ll have sex?

meaning: Formal pattern: “(… you …), that you …” — polite address with a verb + comma + "dass" clause whose subject is again "Sie".
additional_notes: Used when addressing someone formally ("Sie") and then adding a subordinate clause introduced by "dass" (“that”). The first "Sie" is the object of the main-clause verb (e.g., bitten/entschuldigen/fragen/hoffen/glauben/leugnen), and the second "Sie" is the subject inside the "dass" clause. In the "dass" clause, the conjugated verb typically goes to the end (verb-final word order).
target_language_example: Entschuldigen Sie, dass Sie warten mussten!
native_language_example: Sorry that you had to wait!

meaning: a formal way to say “(you) … that I …” (a polite verb + a dass-clause).
additional_notes: This isn’t a fixed phrase by itself, but a common pattern: **[Verb] Sie, dass ich …**. **Sie** is formal “you” (to one person) and **dass ich …** means “that I …”. It’s often used after polite imperatives like **Entschuldigen Sie, dass ich …** (“Sorry that I …”), but also with other verbs, e.g. **Vergessen Sie, dass ich …** (“Forget that I …”) or **Wollten Sie, dass ich …?** (“Did you want me to …?”).
target_language_example: Entschuldigen Sie, dass ich zu spät bin.
native_language_example: Sorry that I’m late.

additional_notes: Used when speaking politely/formally to one person (or more) you don’t address as “du”. In instructions and imperatives you often see both together, e.g. “Wiegen Sie Ihr Gepäck” (“Weigh your luggage”). Both are capitalized in this meaning: Sie/Ihr. (Lowercase sie/ihr usually refers to “she/they” and “her/their”.)
target_language_example: Bitte zeigen Sie Ihr Ticket.
native_language_example: Please show your ticket.

additional_notes: Used in formal/polite speech: **Sie** = “you” (formal), and **Ihre** = “your” (formal). **Ihre** changes form depending on the noun’s gender/case (e.g., *Ihr, Ihre, Ihren, Ihrem, Ihres*). Note: **Ihre** can also mean “her/their” in other contexts, but with **Sie** it’s typically “your.”
target_language_example: Haben Sie Ihre Schlüssel dabei?
native_language_example: Do you have your keys with you?

additional_notes: Used when speaking politely to one person (or sometimes to a group). "Sie" is the formal form of "you" and is always capitalized, as is the possessive "Ihr-/Ihr(e)". "Ihren" is a declined form meaning "your" in the accusative masculine/neuter (e.g., Ihren Wagen = your car, Ihren Sohn = your son). Word order often looks like: Sie + verb + Ihren + noun.
target_language_example: Können Sie Ihren Ausweis bitte zeigen?
native_language_example: Could you please show your ID?

additional_notes: Used in polite requests/commands in the pattern: **Verb + Sie + das + bitte** (e.g., *Behalten/Schreiben/Ziehen Sie das bitte ...*). **Sie** is the formal 'you' (to one person or a group). **das** refers to 'it/that' (something understood from context).
target_language_example: Öffnen Sie das bitte.
native_language_example: Please open that.

additional_notes: Used with the formal pronoun “Sie” (for strangers, customers, officials, etc.). Often appears in subordinate clauses where the verb goes to the end, e.g. “wenn Sie das tun …” (“if you do that …”) or “dass Sie das tun” (“that you do that”). In a main clause you’d more commonly say “Sie tun das.”
target_language_example: Wenn Sie das tun, bekommen Sie eine Fehlermeldung.
native_language_example: If you do that, you’ll get an error message.

meaning: "you" (formal) + "the" (masculine accusative: den), often in polite instructions or questions.
additional_notes: "Sie" is the polite/formal form of "you" used with strangers, customers, or in official contexts. "den" is the accusative form of "der" (= “the”) for masculine nouns (e.g., den Satz, den Bahnhof, den Rechner). This combination is very common in commands with an implied "please" (imperative) like "Korrigieren Sie den …" or in questions like "Mussten Sie den …?".
target_language_example: Öffnen Sie den Brief bitte erst zu Hause.
native_language_example: Please open the letter only at home.

meaning: “you … then/actually …?” (adds emphasis in a polite question).
additional_notes: Used with the modal particle „denn“ in questions addressed to „Sie“ (formal “you”). It doesn’t change the basic meaning, but adds a tone like surprise, impatience, curiosity, or “come on—really?”. In English it’s often left untranslated or rendered with “then”, “actually”, “so”, or “really”. (Not to be confused with „denn“ meaning “because” in statements.)
target_language_example: Wie heißen Sie denn?
native_language_example: So what’s your name, then? / What’s your name again?

additional_notes: This is not a fixed expression; it’s a very common sequence in formal German (Sie-form). **Sie** is the polite "you" used with strangers, customers, older people, etc. **die** is the definite article for **feminine singular** or **plural** nouns, and in these examples it’s in the **accusative** (direct object) after a verb or in a question/command: *Schließen Sie die Tür.* / *Wie fanden Sie die Gedichte?* Word order often stays verb-first in polite commands and questions: **Verb + Sie + (object)**.
target_language_example: Können Sie die Rechnung bitte unterschreiben?
native_language_example: Could you please sign the invoice?

meaning: Formal “you” + *doch* (modal particle) expressing emphasis, reminder, mild contradiction, or an expectation that the other person agrees/has done something; often felt as “you do … (after all),” “surely you …,” or “come on, you …”.
additional_notes: *Sie* is the formal “you.” *Doch* is a very common German modal particle with no single fixed English translation. In patterns like **“Verb + Sie doch …”** it can (a) gently urge or prompt (*Kommen Sie doch rein.* = “Do come in.”), (b) signal the speaker expects confirmation (*Das werden Sie doch wissen?* = “You do know that, right?”), or (c) contradict an assumption (*Ich kenn Sie doch überhaupt nicht!* = “But I don’t know you at all!”).
target_language_example: Die werden Sie doch haben?
native_language_example: You do have them, right?

additional_notes:
Not a fixed phrase on its own—it's the combination of the formal pronoun **Sie** (“you”) and **es** (“it”). You often see it in:
- **Imperatives (commands)**: *Behalten/Bewahren/Überlassen Sie es …* (“Keep/Store/Leave it …”).
- **Questions with past tense**: *Hielten Sie es für klug …?* (“Did you consider it wise …?”).
- **Common verb patterns**: **für klug halten** (to consider wise), **es lernen** (learn it / learn the lesson).
Word order depends on the verb, but **Sie** stays the polite form (capitalized) and **es** is the object (“it”).
target_language_example: Bitte schicken Sie es mir per E-Mail.
native_language_example: Please send it to me by email.

additional_notes: Used in polite/formal questions with the pronoun "Sie" (you) and "gerne" (“gladly/with pleasure”) to ask whether someone enjoys doing an activity. Word order: verb first in questions ("Gehen Sie gerne …?"). For an answer, you can say: "Ja, (sehr) gerne." / "Nein, nicht so gerne."
target_language_example: Kochen Sie gerne?
native_language_example: Do you like to cook?

additional_notes: Used in polite questions addressing one person (Sie) about plans later today. Word order varies: e.g., "Gehen Sie heute Abend ...?". Note spelling: "heute Abend" is often capitalized (noun).
target_language_example: Was machen Sie heute Abend?
native_language_example: What are you doing this evening?

meaning: “you here” (formal), used to talk about you being in this place.
additional_notes: Usually appears in questions like „Was machen Sie hier?“ or „Warum sind Sie hier?“ to ask why someone is here, what they’re doing here, or whether they’re staying/working/studying here. „Sie“ is the polite/formal “you” (for strangers, customers, officials). In speech, it often has emphasis: “*You* here?”
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, arbeiten Sie hier?
native_language_example: Excuse me, do you work here?

additional_notes: Not a fixed phrase—just two pronouns often used together in formal speech: **Sie** is the polite form of “you” (for one or more people), and **ihm** means “to him” (dative), used with verbs like *helfen* (to help), *sagen* (to tell), *geben* (to give). In sentences, **ihm** often comes before a direct object: *Ich gebe **ihm** das Buch.*
target_language_example: Können Sie ihm bitte helfen?
native_language_example: Can you please help him?

additional_notes: Used when speaking politely/formally to one person (Sie) and referring to a male person as the object of the verb (ihn = “him”). Often appears with verbs like kennen, lieben, untersuchen, korrigieren: "Kannten Sie ihn?" = “Did you know him?”
target_language_example: Haben Sie ihn gesehen?
native_language_example: Have you seen him?

additional_notes: "in letzter Zeit" means “lately / recently” and is often used in questions about how things have been going over the past days/weeks. "Sie" is the formal “you” (used with strangers, customers, patients, etc.), so the verb is also in the formal form: "Bekommen/Schlafen/Stehen Sie …?". Word order is flexible: "Bekommen Sie in letzter Zeit …?" or "In letzter Zeit bekommen Sie …?".
target_language_example: Haben Sie in letzter Zeit viel gearbeitet?
native_language_example: Have you been working a lot lately?

meaning: “to meet you” / “to get to know you” (formal).
additional_notes: Used with the formal pronoun "Sie" when meeting someone for the first time, often in polite phrases like "(Es hat mich gefreut,) Sie kennenzulernen" or "Schön/Nett, Sie kennenzulernen." The verb is "kennenlernen" (to get to know/meet), here in the infinitive form "kennenzulernen" after phrases like "sich freuen" (to be pleased) or "kaum erwarten" (can’t wait).
target_language_example: Es freut mich sehr, Sie kennenzulernen.
native_language_example: I’m very pleased to meet you.

additional_notes: Not a fixed phrase by itself—it's just the formal pronoun "Sie" (you) with the object pronoun "mich" (me). You’ll see it in polite requests/commands and statements, usually with a verb: "Besuchen Sie mich" (Visit me), "Nennen Sie mich …" (Call me …), "Rufen Sie mich an" (Call me). In questions/commands, the verb often comes first: "Rufen Sie mich an!"
target_language_example: Können Sie mich bitte morgen anrufen?
native_language_example: Could you please call me tomorrow?

meaning: (Formal) “Don’t … me.” (used with a verb in commands/requests).
additional_notes: This is part of a formal imperative (Sie-form). Pattern: **Verb + Sie + mich + nicht** (e.g., *Töten Sie mich nicht.* = “Don’t kill me.”). **Sie** here means “you” (formal), **mich** = “me”, **nicht** negates the verb. Word order is typical for commands: the verb comes first. You can replace **mich** with another object pronoun (e.g., *uns, ihn, sie*).
target_language_example: Bitte helfen Sie mir, aber rufen Sie mich nicht an.
native_language_example: Please help me, but don’t call me.

additional_notes: Not a fixed phrase by itself. It’s the formal/polite “Sie” (you) used with “mir” (me/to me, dative). You’ll often see it in polite requests or statements with a verb in between, e.g. “Bitte helfen Sie mir.” (Please help me.) “Mir” is used for the indirect object (“to/for me”), not the direct object (“mich” = me).
target_language_example: Können Sie mir bitte sagen, wo der Bahnhof ist?
native_language_example: Could you please tell me where the train station is?

meaning: “… me/for me, please” (polite/formal request with Sie).
additional_notes: Used in formal commands/requests: verb (imperative) + „Sie“ + „mir“ + „bitte“. „Sie“ is the formal “you”, „mir“ = “to me/for me”, „bitte“ = “please”. Very common with verbs like helfen, schicken/senden, schreiben, geben, zeigen: „Helfen Sie mir bitte.“ / „Schicken Sie mir bitte …“
target_language_example: Können Sie mir bitte den Weg zum Bahnhof zeigen?
native_language_example: Could you please show me the way to the train station?

additional_notes: "Sie" is the formal/polite "you" (used with strangers, customers, officials, etc.). "nicht" negates the verb phrase: e.g. "Zögern Sie nicht" = "don’t hesitate", "Das dürfen Sie nicht!" = "You mustn’t do that!". Word order depends on the verb, but in commands it’s often "Verb + Sie + nicht" ("Machen Sie nicht..." / "Trödeln Sie nicht").
target_language_example: Bitte warten Sie nicht auf mich.
native_language_example: Please don't wait for me.

additional_notes: Used with reflexive verbs in the polite/formal form (Sie = “you”). Many German verbs require a reflexive pronoun: sich. In imperatives you often see the pattern “Verb + Sie sich …” (e.g., “Benehmen Sie sich.” = “Behave yourself / behave.”). In questions/statements it can also appear as “Sie sind sich sicher …” = “you are sure …”. Here, “sich” is usually not emphasis (“yourself!”) but just required by the verb.
target_language_example: Fühlen Sie sich heute besser?
native_language_example: Do you feel better today?

additional_notes: This is a very common pattern in formal German when the verb is reflexive (verb + sich). You’ll see it in commands and advice: “Mischen Sie sich nicht ein.” (“Don’t get involved.”), “Rühren Sie sich nicht!” (“Don’t move!”), or in sentences like “damit Sie sich nicht verletzen” (“so that you don’t hurt yourself”). The exact meaning depends on the reflexive verb (sich täuschen = be mistaken, sich sorgen = worry, sich verletzen = hurt yourself).
target_language_example: Bitte beeilen Sie sich nicht.
native_language_example: Please don’t hurry.

additional_notes: "Sie" (capital S) is the formal/polite "you" (to one person or to several people). "uns" means "us" and is an object pronoun. In real sentences, a verb normally comes between them (e.g., "Helfen Sie uns?" = "Can you help us?"). Often used in polite imperatives and requests: "Zeigen Sie uns …" (Show us …), "Helfen Sie uns …" (Help us …), "Geben Sie uns …" (Give us …).
target_language_example: Können Sie uns bitte den Weg zeigen?
native_language_example: Could you please show us the way?

additional_notes: Uses formal/polite **Sie** (“you”). **wollen** expresses a wish/intention: *Wie Sie wollen.* = “As you like.” It also appears in set phrases like **wen Sie wollen** (“whoever you want”) and **ob Sie wollen oder nicht** (“whether you want to or not”).
target_language_example: Kommen Sie heute oder morgen, wie Sie wollen.
native_language_example: Come today or tomorrow—whatever you prefer.

additional_notes: Uses formal "Sie" (you) when speaking politely to someone you don’t know well (e.g., in customer service, at work). Often appears with an infinitive + "zu" after phrases like "schön" or verbs like "sich freuen": "(Es ist) schön, Sie zu sehen" / "Ich freue mich, Sie zu sehen."
target_language_example: Ich freue mich, Sie zu sehen.
native_language_example: I’m happy to see you.

additional_notes: A common philosophical phrase used when talking about big life questions. Often appears with verbs like "über ... nachdenken" (to think about), "sich fragen" (to ask oneself), or "darin liegen" (to lie in). Usually used with the definite article: "der Sinn des Lebens".
target_language_example: Manchmal frage ich mich, was der Sinn des Lebens ist.
native_language_example: Sometimes I ask myself what the meaning of life is.

meaning: to make sense; to be logical/understandable.
additional_notes: Means that something is logical or understandable. Very common with an object: „(einen/keinen) Sinn ergeben“ (often „Das ergibt (keinen) Sinn.“). Also used in the future for reassurance: „Das wird (schon) Sinn ergeben.“
target_language_example: Alles wird dann erst einen Sinn ergeben.
native_language_example: Only then will everything start to make sense.

additional_notes: Used with "haben" (to have) or "keinen ... haben" (to have no). You can describe how strong it is (e.g., "einen großartigen Sinn für Humor") or say you appreciate someone’s humor with "jemandes Sinn für Humor zu schätzen wissen".
target_language_example: Sie hat wirklich einen guten Sinn für Humor.
native_language_example: She really has a good sense of humor.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is logical/understandable. Common variants are: „Das macht (keinen) Sinn.“ and (more formal) „Sinn ergeben“.
target_language_example: Das muss Sinn machen.
native_language_example: That has to make sense.

additional_notes: Usually used with the verb „fahren“ (to ride/go) + „Ski“: „Ich kann Ski fahren.“ In the past, you often say „Ski gefahren“ with „sein“: „Ich bin Ski gefahren.“ You can also use it in comparisons: „lieber Ski fahren als …“, „genauso gut … wie …“, „besser … als …“.
target_language_example: Im Winter gehen wir oft Ski fahren.
native_language_example: In winter, we often go skiing.

additional_notes: Used to show parentage/lineage. Grammar: nominative masculine is usually “der Sohn des + Genitiv” (e.g., des Königs, des Mannes). With names it’s common in titles/introductions (e.g., “Gimli, Sohn des Glóin”).
target_language_example: Er ist der Sohn des Lehrers.
native_language_example: He is the teacher’s son.

additional_notes: On its own, "Sonne geht" sounds incomplete. In everyday German you normally say: "Die Sonne geht auf" = the sun rises, and "Die Sonne geht unter" = the sun sets. These come from the separable verbs "aufgehen" and "untergehen", so in the present tense you split them: "geht ... auf/unter".
target_language_example: Die Sonne geht gleich unter.
native_language_example: The sun is setting soon.

meaning: worried (past tense phrasing; literally “made worries”); typically used as part of „sich Sorgen machen“.
additional_notes: Most commonly used with a reflexive pronoun: „Er hat sich Sorgen gemacht.“ / „Ich habe mir Sorgen gemacht.“ You can intensify it with „große“: „Sie hat sich große Sorgen gemacht.“ Often followed by „um + Akkusativ“ to say what you’re worried about: „Ich habe mir Sorgen um dich gemacht.“
target_language_example: Ich habe mir auch Sorgen gemacht.
native_language_example: I was worried too.

additional_notes: Used to say you are worried about something. Often with a reason: „Ich habe Sorgen wegen …“ / „Ich mache mir Sorgen um …“ (very common alternative). You can also say „Keine Sorge!“ meaning “Don’t worry!”
target_language_example: Ich werde wegen der Prüfung Sorgen haben.
native_language_example: I’ll be worried about the exam.

meaning: to worry (to be concerned); to cause someone worry.
additional_notes: Most commonly used in the reflexive construction **sich Sorgen machen** = “to worry”: **ich fange an, mir Sorgen zu machen** (I’m starting to worry), **mach dir keine Sorgen** (don’t worry). Often with **um + Akkusativ** to say what you’re worried about: **sich um Geld Sorgen machen** (worry about money). Non‑reflexive use is also possible in the sense “to cause worry”: **Das scheint ihm Sorgen zu machen** (That seems to worry him).
target_language_example: Ich fing langsam an, mir Sorgen zu machen.
native_language_example: I slowly began to worry.

additional_notes: Usually used in the past with "haben": "(Etwas) hat (jemandem) Spaß gemacht" = "(Something) was fun (for someone)". The person who enjoyed it is in the dative: "mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/ihnen". Often used with "wirklich", "sehr" etc.: "Es hat wirklich Spaß gemacht."
target_language_example: Der Ausflug hat mir sehr Spaß gemacht.
native_language_example: I really enjoyed the trip.

meaning: to have fun; to enjoy oneself.
additional_notes: Common everyday phrase. Often used with adverbs like „viel“ (a lot) or „richtig“ (really): „Wir hatten viel Spaß.“ You can also say „Spaß haben an + dative“ to mean enjoying something in general: „Ich habe Spaß am Lernen.“
target_language_example: Tom will einfach nur Spaß haben.
native_language_example: Tom just wants to have fun.

meaning: to be fun; to be enjoyable (for someone).
additional_notes: Often used with a dative person to say who enjoys it: „Das macht mir Spaß.“ (= I enjoy it / It’s fun for me). In conditional/subjunctive contexts you may see „würde ... Spaß machen“ (= would be fun).
target_language_example: Ja, das wird Spaß machen.
native_language_example: Yes, that will be fun.

meaning: to be fun (for someone); to enjoy doing something.
additional_notes: Typically used with a person in the dative (mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/ihnen) to express that something is fun for them: „Es scheint dir Spaß zu machen.“ Often appears with verbs like „scheinen“ or „anfangen/aufhören“ in a zu-infinitive construction, and can be followed by a more specific activity clause: „Es schien Tom Spaß zu machen, …“ (= It seemed Tom enjoyed …).
target_language_example: Es scheint dir Spaß zu machen, Deutsch zu lernen.
native_language_example: It seems you enjoy learning German.

meaning: the Philosopher’s Stone (a legendary magical object).
additional_notes: Usually refers to the famous mythical/alchemical object said to turn base metals into gold and/or grant immortality. Often used as a fixed cultural reference (e.g., in stories like Harry Potter). In sentences it’s commonly used with the definite article: „der Stein der Weisen“ (nominative) / „den Stein der Weisen“ (accusative) / „vom Stein der Weisen“ (= von dem, dative).
target_language_example: Alle suchen nach dem Stein der Weisen.
native_language_example: Everyone is looking for the Philosopher’s Stone.

additional_notes: A common descriptive phrase for what you can see in the night sky. "am" is a contraction of "an dem" (literally “at the”), used with places like "am Himmel" (“in the sky”). Often used with verbs like "sehen" (to see) or "zu sehen sein" (to be visible): "Sterne am Himmel sehen" / "Sterne am Himmel zu sehen".
target_language_example: Heute Nacht sind viele Sterne am Himmel zu sehen.
native_language_example: Tonight, many stars can be seen in the sky.

meaning: to take hours; to last for hours.
additional_notes: Used with an amount of time + "dauern" to say how long something takes/lasts. Common patterns: "Es könnte Stunden dauern" (It could take hours), "Das wird mindestens acht Stunden dauern" (That will take at least eight hours). "Stunden" can be replaced with other time units (Minuten, Tage, Wochen).
target_language_example: Warte nicht auf mich — das kann Stunden dauern.
native_language_example: Don’t wait for me — this can take hours.

additional_notes: Used to say how long something lasts or continues. It typically follows a time expression: „ein paar Stunden lang“ (for a few hours), „mehrere Stunden lang“ (for several hours), „sechs Stunden lang“ (for six hours). Often also written as one word („stundenlang“) with the same meaning, but here the two-word form is used.
target_language_example: Ich kann dir heute ein paar Stunden lang helfen.
native_language_example: I can help you for a few hours today.

additional_notes: Used with quantities: "ein/zwei/drei Stück Kreide" = "one/two/three pieces of chalk". In this counting expression, "Stück" often stays the same in the plural ("drei Stück", not *"drei Stücke"*).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir ein Stück Kreide geben?
native_language_example: Can you give me a piece of chalk?

meaning: “piece of shit” (a very insulting way to call someone worthless).
additional_notes: Extremely vulgar and aggressive insult. Often used as a direct form of address: “Du Stück Scheiße!” and frequently intensified with adjectives like “mieses / fettes / verdammtes / verficktes Stück Scheiße”. Can also be used with “ein” to describe someone: “Er ist ein Stück Scheiße.” Avoid in polite/company situations; can escalate conflicts.
target_language_example: Ich rede nicht mit dir, du Stück Scheiße.
native_language_example: I’m not talking to you, you piece of shit.

meaning: "little by little" / "piece by piece" (gradually, in small steps).
additional_notes: Used to describe a gradual change or process over time. Often with verbs like „gehen/verloren gehen“, „besser werden“, „lernen“, „aufbauen“, or „sich verändern“. It can describe improvement, loss, or transformation happening step by step.
target_language_example: Stück für Stück habe ich mehr Selbstvertrauen bekommen.
native_language_example: Little by little, I gained more self-confidence.

additional_notes: A very common noun for this clothing item (borrowed from English). Neuter: das T-Shirt; plural: die T-Shirts. Often used with colors/adjectives (ein rotes/sauberes/altes T-Shirt). With the verb anziehen (to put on): sich ein T-Shirt anziehen; with ausziehen (to take off): sein T-Shirt ausziehen.
target_language_example: Ich ziehe ein blaues T-Shirt an.
native_language_example: I’m putting on a blue T-shirt.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something happens continuously or regularly over many days (often implying a long time or monotony). Can be placed at the beginning for emphasis ("Tag für Tag, ...") or inside the sentence. Similar to "Tag für Tag" = "day for day" in a literal sense, but the natural meaning is "day after day".
target_language_example: Tag für Tag fahre ich mit dem Fahrrad zur Arbeit.
native_language_example: Day after day, I ride my bike to work.

meaning: "(the) day of my life" (used for the best/worst/most important day).
additional_notes: Usually used with a superlative to emphasize how special a day was: „der schönste/beste/glücklichste/schlimmste Tag meines Lebens“. „meines Lebens“ is the genitive form meaning “of my life.” You can use present („Das ist …“) for today, or past („Das war …“) for a past day.
target_language_example: Das war der aufregendste Tag meines Lebens.
native_language_example: That was the most exciting day of my life.

meaning: day and night; all the time (constantly).
additional_notes: Literally “day and night.” Used for doing something continuously (often stressing it’s exhausting or nonstop): „Tag und Nacht arbeiten/lernen/wach bleiben“. Also used to contrast two things as completely different: „verschieden wie Tag und Nacht“ (“as different as day and night”).
target_language_example: Er hat Tag und Nacht an dem Projekt gearbeitet.
native_language_example: He worked on the project day and night.

meaning: "day by day" / "from one day to the next".
additional_notes: Usually used as part of the phrase "von Tag zu Tag" (from day to day) to describe something changing or continuing gradually over time. It’s similar to "Tag für Tag" (day after day), but "von Tag zu Tag" often emphasizes change from one day to the next.
target_language_example: Von Tag zu Tag wird es wärmer.
native_language_example: Day by day, it’s getting warmer.

additional_notes: Used to talk about spending a day at home (not going out). Common with verbs like „einen Tag zu Hause verbringen“ (to spend a day at home) or „einen Tag zu Hause bleiben“ (to stay home for a day). Often you’ll also hear the more specific „einen Tag zu Hause“ (accusative) in sentences.
target_language_example: Am Sonntag mache ich einen Tag zu Hause.
native_language_example: On Sunday I’m having a day at home.

additional_notes: Used with a number to say how long something lasts: „zwei/vier/sieben Tage lang“. It often goes with time expressions and verbs like „sein“, „dauern“, or weather/event descriptions: „Es schneite vier Tage lang.“ Similar patterns: „Wochen lang“, „Monate lang“.
target_language_example: Wir waren drei Tage lang in Berlin.
native_language_example: We were in Berlin for three days.

additional_notes: Often used with an indefinite article: „eine Tasse Kaffee“ = “a cup of coffee.” In invitations and suggestions you’ll often hear patterns like: „Was sagst du zu …?“ / „Was sagen Sie zu …?“ (“How about …?”) and „Wie wäre es mit …?“ (“How about …?”). It can also describe doing something while having coffee: „bei einer Tasse Kaffee“ (“over a cup of coffee”).
target_language_example: Wie wäre es mit einer Tasse Kaffee nach dem Essen?
native_language_example: How about a cup of coffee after the meal?

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to express a very large number (often not exact). It’s the plural of the noun "Tausend" used like a quantity: "Tausende von + [plural noun]". In writing you may also see the adjective form without "von" (e.g., "tausende Bilder"), but "Tausende von" is very common and clear.
target_language_example: In der Stadt gibt es Tausende von Möglichkeiten.
native_language_example: In the city there are thousands of possibilities.

additional_notes: A very common choice question (oder = “or”), often used by hosts, in cafés, or on planes. With a verb like möchten/wünschen/trinken, it means you’re offering or asking which drink someone prefers. You can answer with just one word: „Tee, bitte.“ / „Kaffee, bitte.“
target_language_example: Zum Frühstück nehme ich Tee oder Kaffee, je nachdem, wie müde ich bin.
native_language_example: For breakfast I have tea or coffee, depending on how tired I am.

additional_notes: Used to say that something belongs to a larger whole or group. Often with a quantifier like ein Teil der (a part of), ein großer Teil der (a large part of), der größte Teil der (the largest part of). Also used without an article in fixed phrases like Teil der Gesellschaft sein (“to be part of society”).
target_language_example: Ich will Teil der Gruppe sein.
native_language_example: I want to be part of the group.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a specific area or neighborhood within a city. Very common with adjectives (e.g., alter/ältester Teil, feiner Teil) and with prepositions like „in diesem Teil der Stadt“, „im alten Teil der Stadt“.
target_language_example: In welchem Teil der Stadt wohnst du?
native_language_example: Which part of the city do you live in?

additional_notes: Used to say that something belongs to a larger whole. It’s usually followed by a genitive noun phrase (often with “des” for masculine/neuter singular), e.g., „Teil des Körpers“, „Teil des Problems“. In everyday German you may also hear „Teil von + Dativ“ (e.g., „Teil von dem Team“).
target_language_example: Das ist nur ein Teil des Plans.
native_language_example: That’s only part of the plan.

meaning: to use a phone (to make a call).
additional_notes: "benutzen" means "to use". "das Telefon benutzen" is a polite way to ask to borrow someone’s phone for a moment, often with modal verbs like "darf ich...?") / "dürfte ich...?" (more polite) / "könnte ich bitte...?". You can also say "Ihr Telefon" (your phone, formal) or "dein Telefon" (your phone, informal).
target_language_example: Kann ich kurz dein Telefon benutzen?
native_language_example: Can I use your phone for a moment?

additional_notes: Used with the verb "haben" in the Perfekt to talk about a completed activity in the past: "Ich habe Tennis gespielt." The past participle "gespielt" goes at the end of the clause.
target_language_example: Wir haben am Wochenende Tennis gespielt.
native_language_example: We played tennis on the weekend.

additional_notes: Uses the verb „spielen“ (to play) with the sport name: „Tennis spielen“. Common with modal verbs like „können“ (can), „wollen“ (want), „müssen“ (must), and with people: „mit jemandem Tennis spielen“ (to play tennis with someone). You can also use it as a noun phrase: „Tennis spielen ist leicht“ (Playing tennis is easy).
target_language_example: Ich kann Tennis spielen.
native_language_example: I can play tennis.

meaning: to play tennis (as an infinitive: “to play tennis”).
additional_notes: Used with other verbs that take an infinitive with **zu** (e.g., *Lust haben*, *genießen*, *pflegen*, *ausnutzen, um ...*, *daran hindern*). The **zu** normally goes right before the verb at the end: *Tennis zu spielen*.
target_language_example: Ich habe keine Zeit, heute Tennis zu spielen.
native_language_example: I don’t have time to play tennis today.

additional_notes: „Typen“ is an informal way to say „guys“ (often a bit dismissive: “those guys”). „die“ introduces a relative clause describing them (like “who/that” in English): „Typen, die rumsitzen…“ = “guys who are sitting around…”. You’ll also see other forms depending on the noun: „Typen, die…“ (plural), but e.g. „ein Typ, der…“ (singular masculine).
target_language_example: Da draußen stehen Typen, die ständig laut telefonieren.
native_language_example: There are guys out there who are constantly talking loudly on the phone.

additional_notes: Often used as a short, direct command: „Tür auf!“ = „Open the door!“ You’ll also see it with separable verbs like aufmachen/aufgehen: „Mach die Tür auf.“ / „Die Tür geht auf.“ (The door opens.) Note: Sentence 3 uses a different verb: „auftauchen“ = „to show up/appear“ („an der Tür“ = at the door).
target_language_example: Tür auf, bitte!
native_language_example: Open the door, please!

additional_notes: Usually used with the verb phrase **an die/der Tür klopfen** (to knock on/at the door). In the past, you’ll often see **hat ... an die Tür geklopft** (Perfekt). **an die Tür** emphasizes the direction (onto the door); **an der Tür** is also common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Ich habe an die Tür geklopft, aber niemand hat aufgemacht.
native_language_example: I knocked on the door, but nobody opened up.

additional_notes: Short for „Untergrundbahn“. Used for city train systems that run mostly underground. Common with the verb „fahren“ (to take/ride) and with lines/directions: „Welche U-Bahn fährt …?“
target_language_example: Wir nehmen die U-Bahn zum Hauptbahnhof.
native_language_example: We’re taking the subway to the main train station.

additional_notes: Short for **Unterseeboot** (“undersea boat”). It’s a **neuter** noun: **das U-Boot**. Plural: **die U-Boote**. In English, “U-boat” is also used, especially for German submarines (e.g., in WWII contexts).
target_language_example: Das U-Boot taucht ab.
native_language_example: The submarine dives down.

meaning: (for a clock/watch) to be running/working; to keep time.
additional_notes: Used with the clock/watch as the subject: „Die Uhr geht.“ = it’s running. Common in negatives („Meine Uhr geht nicht.“) and with time-accuracy phrases: „Die Uhr geht falsch.“ (keeps the wrong time), „Die Uhr geht vor.“ (is fast), „Die Uhr geht nach.“ (is slow). Also: „Geht die Uhr?“ = Is the clock/watch working?
target_language_example: Die Uhr geht nicht mehr.
native_language_example: The clock doesn’t work anymore.

additional_notes: Used to say someone’s opinion/claim is incorrect. Commonly said as "Du hast Unrecht" (You’re wrong). The opposite is "Recht haben" (to be right). You can use it in different tenses: "Ich hatte Unrecht" (I was wrong), "Du wirst Unrecht haben" (you’ll be wrong).
target_language_example: Du wirst Unrecht haben.
native_language_example: You will be wrong.

additional_notes: Literally means “father is.” Often used with an article or possessive: „Der Vater ist …“ (the father is …), „Mein Vater ist …“ (my father is …). In some contexts, „Vater“ can be used like a title/name (especially in family talk), so it may appear without an article. In „Vater ist mir zornig“, „mir“ is dative (= “with me/at me”), meaning “Dad is angry at me.”
target_language_example: Mein Vater ist heute sehr müde.
native_language_example: My dad is very tired today.

additional_notes: Uses the simple past (Präteritum) of **sterben** (“to die”): **starb** = “died.” Often appears after **als** (“when”): *Als ihr Vater starb, …* You’ll also commonly see it with a possessive or article: **mein/dein/sein/ihr Vater starb** or **der Vater starb**. Note: **starb** can look like English “starve,” but it does **not** mean that.
target_language_example: Als mein Vater starb, war ich noch in der Schule.
native_language_example: When my father died, I was still in school.

additional_notes: A formal, legal-sounding expression used for extremely serious acts that violate basic human rights (e.g., slavery, forced disappearances, mass violence). Often used in news, history, politics, and law. In German it’s commonly used with the article: „ein Verbrechen gegen die Menschlichkeit“.
target_language_example: Viele halten Folter für ein Verbrechen gegen die Menschlichkeit.
native_language_example: Many consider torture a crime against humanity.

additional_notes: Used with a person, group, or thing you believe is reliable or will do something well. Common patterns: „(großes) Vertrauen in + Akkusativ haben“ (to have (great) trust/confidence in), „Vertrauen in + Akk. verlieren“ (to lose trust in), „Vertrauen in + Akk. steigt/sinkt“ (trust increases/decreases), „jmds. Vertrauen in mich zu schätzen wissen“ (to appreciate someone’s trust in me).
target_language_example: Ich habe Vertrauen in dich, aber ich brauche mehr Zeit.
native_language_example: I trust you, but I need more time.

meaning: pros and cons; advantages and disadvantages.
additional_notes: Used to talk about the positive and negative sides of an option or situation, often when comparing choices or making a decision. Common patterns: „Vor- und Nachteile haben“ (to have pros and cons), „über Vor- und Nachteile nachdenken“ (to think about the pros and cons), „die Vor- und Nachteile von + Dativ“ (the pros and cons of ...).
target_language_example: Lass uns die Vor- und Nachteile abwägen, bevor wir buchen.
native_language_example: Let’s weigh the pros and cons before we book.

additional_notes: Used with the auxiliary verb **haben** in the **Perfekt** (present perfect/simple past in spoken German): **(ich/du/er …) habe/hast/hat … Wasser getrunken**. **getrunken** is the past participle of **trinken** (“to drink”). You can add amounts or time: **ein Glas**, **viel**, **heute**, **drei Liter**.
target_language_example: Ich habe nach dem Sport viel Wasser getrunken.
native_language_example: I drank a lot of water after exercising.

meaning: "Water is" (used to say what water is like or what it means).
additional_notes: Used with the verb **ist** ("is", 3rd person singular of **sein** = "to be") to make statements/definitions about water: **Wasser ist flüssig.** It can also appear in questions when **ist** comes before the subject: **Wie viel Wasser ist ...?** ("How much water is ...?").
target_language_example: Wasser ist wichtig für unsere Gesundheit.
native_language_example: Water is important for our health.

meaning: the way to the train station
additional_notes: Used when asking for or talking about directions to the train station. "der Weg" means "path/way" and "zum" = "zu dem" ("to the"). Common in questions like "Ist das der (richtige) Weg zum Bahnhof?".
target_language_example: Können Sie mir bitte den Weg zum Bahnhof zeigen?
native_language_example: Could you please show me the way to the train station?

meaning: to become reality; to come true.
additional_notes: Used for plans, hopes, wishes, or ideas when they actually happen. Often with a subject like „ein Traum / ein Wunsch / ein Plan“: „Mein Traum wird Wirklichkeit.“ You can also use it with „lassen“ (make something come true): „Sie hat ihren Traum Wirklichkeit werden lassen.“
target_language_example: Endlich wird unser Plan Wirklichkeit werden.
native_language_example: Finally our plan will become reality / will come true.

meaning: to keep your word (to do what you promised).
additional_notes: Often appears with a possessive pronoun: „sein/ihr Wort halten“ (to keep one’s word). Refers to a promise or commitment. Verb forms: halten – hielt – gehalten.
target_language_example: Khan, werden Sie Ihr Wort halten?
native_language_example: Khan, will you keep your word?

meaning: 'time to' / 'time in order to' (used before an action).
additional_notes: Usually followed by an infinitive clause: „Zeit, um … zu + Infinitiv“ (often with a comma). Common with verbs like „Zeit haben“ (to have time) or „Zeit geben“ (to give time): „Ich habe keine Zeit, um zu warten.“ / „Geben Sie mir Zeit, um …“.
target_language_example: Ich brauche Zeit, um das zu verstehen.
native_language_example: I need time to understand that.

meaning: to need time; to take time.
additional_notes: Used to say that something takes a certain amount of time or that someone needs time. Often with a time expression ("Ich brauche zwei Stunden") or with "um ... zu" + infinitive ("Ich brauche Zeit, um das zu lernen"). Also common in the sense "I need some time" (e.g., to think or decide).
target_language_example: Ich werde Zeit brauchen, um mich zu entscheiden.
native_language_example: I will need time to decide.

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone has time available, or to say whether something is a good/bad moment for an activity. It’s followed by a noun phrase: Zeit für + accusative (e.g., Zeit für einen Besuch / ein Frühstück). Common in questions like „Haben Sie Zeit für …?“ and statements like „Ich habe (keine) Zeit für …“.
target_language_example: Hast du heute Abend Zeit für einen kurzen Spaziergang?
native_language_example: Do you have time for a short walk this evening?

meaning: time for me; time to myself.
additional_notes: Often used when asking someone to spend time with you ("Hast du Zeit für mich?") or when talking about personal time/space ("Ich brauche Zeit für mich"). It can also mean a difficult period in your life ("eine dunkle Zeit für mich" = a dark time for me), where "Zeit" means "period/time in life" rather than free time.
target_language_example: Heute Abend brauche ich Zeit für mich, aber morgen habe ich Zeit für dich.
native_language_example: Tonight I need time to myself, but tomorrow I have time for you.

meaning: to give (someone) time; to allow time.
additional_notes: Used when asking someone to wait or to allow more time before you decide, answer, or finish something. Very common with a person in the dative: „Gib mir Zeit.“ It can also be used in the fixed saying „Man muss der Zeit Zeit geben“ (= you have to let time do its work / give it time).
target_language_example: Können Sie mir ein bisschen mehr Zeit geben?
native_language_example: Could you give me a little more time?

additional_notes: Used to say you are available (or not) to do something. Common in questions and polite requests (e.g., "Hast du Zeit?", "wenn Sie Zeit haben"). Often followed by "um ... zu" (in order to ...) or an infinitive clause.
target_language_example: Ich sollte doch die ganze Nacht Zeit haben, um das hier zu knacken.
native_language_example: I should have time all night to crack this.

meaning: to take your time; not to rush.
additional_notes: Most common as the reflexive phrase „sich Zeit lassen“ (e.g., „Lass dir Zeit!“ = “Take your time!”). Used to tell someone to go slowly, or to say you won’t hurry. Often paired with „mit“ + dative: „Lass dir Zeit mit der Entscheidung.“
target_language_example: Du kannst dir ruhig Zeit lassen.
native_language_example: You can take your time.

meaning: “time with (someone)” (usually in: Zeit mit jemandem verbringen = to spend time with someone).
additional_notes:
Most commonly used with the verb **verbringen**: **Zeit mit + Dativ** (jemandem) **verbringen**.
- ich verbringe Zeit mit **dir**
- wir verbringen Zeit mit **Tom**
- Zeit mit **meiner Familie**
It’s about being together/doing things together. In sentence 7, a different expression is used: **die Zeit totschlagen** = “to kill time.”
target_language_example: Am Wochenende verbringe ich viel Zeit mit meinen Freunden.
native_language_example: On the weekend I spend a lot of time with my friends.

additional_notes: Common everyday phrase meaning to do something more efficiently so you need less time. Used with the person who saves time: „Ich spare Zeit“, „Wir sparen Zeit“. Often with „indem“ (by doing): „Wir sparen Zeit, indem wir online bestellen.“
target_language_example: Wenn wir den Bus nehmen, können wir Zeit sparen.
native_language_example: If we take the bus, we can save time.

meaning: to kill time; to pass the time (until something happens).
additional_notes: Used when you’re waiting and want to do something to make time go by faster. Often used with an activity: „Ich schlage die Zeit mit Lesen tot.“ In a full sentence, the verb is commonly split: „Ich schlage die Zeit tot.“
target_language_example: Wir schlagen die Zeit totschlagen, bis der Zug kommt.
native_language_example: We’re killing time until the train arrives.

meaning: to spend time (doing something / with someone).
additional_notes: Used to say how you occupy your time, often with **mit + Dativ** (with someone) or with a place/activity: **Zeit mit Freunden verbringen**, **Zeit im Park verbringen**. Common forms: present **ich verbringe Zeit**, past **ich habe Zeit verbracht**.
target_language_example: Am Wochenende verbringe ich gern Zeit mit meiner Familie — wir können richtig Zeit verbringen.
native_language_example: On the weekend I like to spend time with my family — we can really spend time together.

meaning: to waste time; to lose time (by delaying).
additional_notes: Often used with "keine": "keine Zeit verlieren" = "don’t waste any time / don’t delay" (a sense of urgency). It can mean you’re wasting time in general, or that waiting/delaying will make you miss a deadline or opportunity.
target_language_example: Lass uns keine Zeit verlieren und sofort losgehen.
native_language_example: Let’s not waste any time and leave right away.
