additional_notes: Common everyday phrase. Often used with "mit" + dative to say what you’re wasting time on: "Zeit mit etwas verschwenden". You can also say "meine/deine Zeit verschwenden" (waste my/your time).
target_language_example: Ich möchte keine Zeit verschwenden.
native_language_example: I don't want to waste time.

meaning: time to read / time for reading.
additional_notes: Used with (haben) to say you have (little/no/rarely) time to read: „Ich habe (kaum/keine/selten) Zeit zum Lesen.“ „zum“ = „zu dem“ and is used here to mean “for” doing an activity (reading). You can also say „Zeit zum + infinitive“ for other activities (e.g., „Zeit zum Kochen“).
target_language_example: Heute Abend habe ich endlich Zeit zum Lesen.
native_language_example: This evening I finally have time to read.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone has successfully reached a goal (personal, work, travel, etc.). Often appears with haben + Ziel erreicht (e.g., Wir haben unser Ziel erreicht) or as a short status/message: Ziel erreicht!
target_language_example: Nach vielen Wochen Training habe ich mein Ziel erreicht.
native_language_example: After many weeks of training, I achieved my goal.

additional_notes: Usually used with the verb "haben" in the present perfect: "Ich habe mein Zimmer aufgeräumt" = "I tidied up my room / I have tidied up my room." The verb is "aufräumen" (separable: "räumen" + "auf"); the past participle is "aufgeräumt". Possessives change: mein/dein/ihr/sein/unser Zimmer.
target_language_example: Ich habe mein Zimmer aufgeräumt.
native_language_example: I tidied up my room.

additional_notes: A common everyday phrase meaning to put things away and make your room neat. Usually used with a possessive: „mein/dein/unser/euer Zimmer aufräumen“. Note that „aufräumen“ is a separable verb, so in main clauses it often appears split (e.g., „Ich räume mein Zimmer auf.“), but the infinitive phrase is „Zimmer aufräumen“.
target_language_example: Ich muss mein Zimmer aufräumen.
native_language_example: I have to tidy my room.

meaning: to tidy/clean up (a) room (to put it in order).
additional_notes: From the verb phrase „(ein) Zimmer aufräumen“ = to tidy up a room. In your sentences it appears as „… das Zimmer aufzuräumen“ (zu + infinitive), used after phrases like „beschäftigt sein“, „brauchen“, or „helfen“: „Ich war damit beschäftigt, das Zimmer aufzuräumen.“ Word order: in main clauses you often say „Ich räume mein Zimmer auf.“ (separable verb: auf + räumen).
target_language_example: Ich brauche eine Stunde, um mein Zimmer aufzuräumen.
native_language_example: I need an hour to tidy up my room.

meaning: (to) keep the room clean / (to) clean the room.
additional_notes:
Usually used with a verb, especially: 
- „das Zimmer sauber machen“ = to clean/tidy the room (do the cleaning)
- „das Zimmer sauber halten“ = to keep the room clean (maintain cleanliness)
Used in commands and questions: „Halt dein Zimmer sauber!“ / „Ist dein Zimmer sauber?“
target_language_example: Ich muss mein Zimmer sauber machen.
native_language_example: I have to clean my room.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone can enter/reach a place or use a service/thing. "zur" = "zu der" and is used with feminine nouns (e.g., "zur Bibliothek"). With masculine/neuter nouns you usually use "zum" (= "zu dem"), e.g., "Zugang zum Internet".
target_language_example: Haben Sie Zugang zur Bibliothek?
native_language_example: Do you have access to the library?

additional_notes: Used to say something begins today and continues into the future. Often followed by a present or future meaning: „Ab heute“ + verb (e.g., „Ab heute schlafe ich hier.“). Similar to „von heute an“.
target_language_example: Ab heute arbeite ich jeden Tag bis 18 Uhr.
native_language_example: From today on, I work every day until 6 p.m.

meaning: from here (on); starting at this point/place.
additional_notes: Used to mark a starting point in space or time: from this location onward or from this moment onward (often with rules, responsibility, or what happens next). Common on signs/instructions and in speech (e.g., handing something over: „Ich übernehme ab hier.“).
target_language_example: Ab hier gilt Tempo 30.
native_language_example: From here on, the speed limit is 30.

additional_notes: Used to mark a new starting point in time (often a decision, rule, or change). Common at the beginning of a sentence, but it can also appear mid-sentence. Similar in meaning to "von jetzt an".
target_language_example: Ab jetzt spreche ich nur noch Deutsch im Unterricht.
native_language_example: From now on, I’m only speaking German in class.

additional_notes: Used to say that something begins tomorrow and continues from that point. Often followed by present tense or future meaning (e.g., "Ab morgen ist...", "Ab morgen wird...").
target_language_example: Ab morgen arbeite ich wieder im Büro.
native_language_example: Starting tomorrow, I’m working in the office again.

additional_notes: Used to announce a change that starts right away (often for new rules, decisions, or behavior). It can come at the beginning of the sentence or before the thing that changes: „Ab sofort arbeite ich …“ / „Ich habe beschlossen, ab sofort …“.
target_language_example: Ab sofort sind Handys im Unterricht verboten.
native_language_example: From now on, phones are forbidden in class.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens sometimes, but not regularly or often. Often placed with the verb (e.g., "Das passiert ab und an.") or before what it describes (e.g., "ab und an Geld"). Similar to "manchmal" but usually suggests a bit less frequent.
target_language_example: Ich sehe ihn ab und an in der Stadt.
native_language_example: I see him every now and then in town.

meaning: every now and then; from time to time (occasionally).
additional_notes: Used to say something happens sometimes, but not regularly. Very common in everyday German; it can appear at the beginning of a sentence ("Ab und zu …") or later ("… passiert ab und zu"). You’ll also often hear "ab und zu mal" = "every now and then."
target_language_example: Ab und zu gehe ich nach der Arbeit noch spazieren.
native_language_example: Every now and then I go for a walk after work.

additional_notes: In many verbs, **ab-** is a separable prefix that often suggests doing something **off/away** or **completing** an action (e.g., *abschließen* = to lock, *abkochen* = to boil, *abnehmen* = to take off/remove, *abhauen* = to get away). In a main clause, the **ab** part usually goes to the end: *Schließe die Tür **ab***. **Bevor** introduces a subordinate clause meaning **before**, and the verb goes to the end of that clause: *..., bevor du **gehst***.
target_language_example: Schalte das Licht ab, bevor du gehst.
native_language_example: Turn off the light before you go.

meaning: "every now and then; occasionally" (ab und zu / ab und an).
additional_notes: On its own, "ab und" is usually incomplete; the fixed expressions are "ab und zu" and "ab und an" (= occasionally). In other sentences you may see "ab" as a separable verb prefix (e.g., "Er nahm die Brille ab und ..." = "He took his glasses off and ..."), where "ab" means "off/away" and is not the same as the time expression.
target_language_example: Wir gehen ab und zu ins Kino.
native_language_example: We go to the cinema every now and then.

meaning: “but not / however not” (used to contrast or as a warning).
additional_notes: Used to contrast with what was just said: “X, but not Y” (often after the subject, e.g. „Tiere aber nicht“). It can also add emphasis in a warning/command: „Aber nicht …!“ = “Just don’t … / Make sure you don’t …”.
target_language_example: Du kannst heute ausgehen, aber nicht zu spät nach Hause kommen.
native_language_example: You can go out today, but don’t come home too late.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrast or consequence after what was just said. In dialogues it often means “OK, but then (on that condition) …” and can sound like setting a rule or warning.
target_language_example: Du kannst kommen, aber dann musst du pünktlich sein.
native_language_example: You can come, but then you have to be on time.

additional_notes: Used at the start of a clause to push back against what was just said or to add a limitation: "But that doesn't...", "But that is...". Often followed by a verb in 2nd position in statements (e.g., "aber das ist...", "aber das erklärt..."). Can also soften a refusal or negative statement ("Sorry, but that...", "I regret, but that...").
target_language_example: Ich würde gern helfen, aber das geht heute nicht.
native_language_example: I'd like to help, but that doesn't work today.

meaning: 'but that is…' (to add a contrast or correction).
additional_notes: Used to introduce information that contrasts with what was just said or expected. Very common in conversation and writing. Often followed by an adjective or noun phrase (e.g., „aber das ist nicht wichtig / nicht nötig / meine Kündigung“) or by an evaluation („aber das ist Selbstmord!“). In spoken German you may also hear it starting a new sentence to push back: „Aber das ist doch…“.
target_language_example: Ich verstehe dich, aber das ist nicht mein Problem.
native_language_example: I understand you, but that's not my problem.

additional_notes: Used to react to a statement or situation and push back or emphasize your point. **doch** adds the idea of “after all / really / you know,” often implying that something is obvious, surprising, or contrary to what someone suggested. Common before an adjective or noun phrase (e.g., *unmöglich, zu viel, ein Haufen Arbeit*).
target_language_example: Aber das ist doch viel zu teuer!
native_language_example: But that’s really way too expensive!

additional_notes: Used at the start of a sentence to push back against what was just said and then deny or correct something: “Aber das ist nicht das Problem / der richtige Ort / ungefährlich.” Often followed by a noun phrase (“… das Problem”), an adjective (“… ungefährlich”), or expanded with “sondern …” (“but rather …”).
target_language_example: Aber das ist nicht meine Frage.
native_language_example: But that’s not my question.

meaning: "but that was…" (introduces a contrast about something in the past).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a clause to correct, limit, or add an opposing point to what was just said. It’s typically followed by more information (often with negation: „…war es nicht“, „…war nicht…“) or by a time/condition („…war, bevor…“).
target_language_example: Ich wollte helfen, aber das war nicht möglich.
native_language_example: I wanted to help, but that wasn’t possible.

meaning: 'but you are …' (introduces a contrast or objection).
additional_notes: Used to push back against what was just said, or to point out a surprising/important fact about the other person. Often followed by an adjective, age, role, or group membership (e.g., "Aber du bist erst elf."). In speech, stress on "du" can add emphasis ("But YOU are...").
target_language_example: Ich dachte, du kommst nicht — aber du bist ja doch hier.
native_language_example: I thought you weren’t coming — but you’re actually here after all.

additional_notes: Used to object or correct someone by pointing out a fact about what they did or what has happened. Often followed by a past action (Perfekt with "hast" + past participle) or a state/result ("hast" + object). In English it’s usually "But you did..." or "But you have...", depending on context.
target_language_example: Aber du hast mir doch gesagt, dass du Zeit hast.
native_language_example: But you told me you had time.

meaning: "but you have" / "but you do have" (introduces a contrast).
additional_notes: Used to point out something the other person possesses or a fact about them that changes the situation: "Aber du hast …" is often followed by a noun (eine Familie), or something more abstract (Integrität, andere Prioritäten). In spoken German it can sound like a mild objection or reminder, similar to "But you *do* have…" in English.
target_language_example: Aber du hast doch genug Zeit, um kurz anzurufen.
native_language_example: But you do have enough time to call briefly.

meaning: 'but you can …' (introduces a contrast: you’re able/allowed to do something).
additional_notes: Used to contrast two statements: something is true, but you still have the ability/option/permission to do something else. Often followed by an infinitive at the end of the clause (e.g., „Aber du kannst es morgen machen.“). It can also soften suggestions/offers (e.g., „…, aber du kannst mich Bill nennen.“).
target_language_example: Es ist spät, aber du kannst morgen anrufen.
native_language_example: It’s late, but you can call tomorrow.

meaning: "but you have to / but you must".
additional_notes: Used to add a contrast or correction ("aber" = "but") and then state a necessity/obligation for "you". "Du musst" is 2nd-person singular of "müssen". Often followed by an infinitive later in the clause (e.g., "aber du musst gehen"). Important: "du musst nicht" usually means "you don’t have to" (no obligation), not "you must not" (prohibition).
target_language_example: Ich verstehe dich, aber du musst jetzt losgehen.
native_language_example: I understand you, but you have to leave now.

additional_notes: Used when contrasting what “he” does/is with what you expect or with another fact. “Aber” is a coordinating conjunction (like “but”), so it doesn’t change word order in the clause: after “aber,” you can start a normal main clause with “er” + verb (e.g., “aber er kommt…”).
target_language_example: Ich wollte gehen, aber er blieb noch ein bisschen.
native_language_example: I wanted to leave, but he stayed a little longer.

additional_notes: Used to contrast with what was said before: "aber" = "but" + "er" = "he" + "hat" = "has" (present) or auxiliary for the past (Perfekt), depending on the rest of the sentence. Often followed by a past participle (e.g., „... aber er hat es vergessen.“ = "... but he forgot.").
target_language_example: Ich habe ihn gefragt, aber er hat nichts gesagt.
native_language_example: I asked him, but he didn't say anything.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrast about a man/boy ("er"). Often follows a statement about him and adds a surprising or opposite detail: "Er sieht aus wie …, aber er ist …". In writing, a comma is typically used before "aber" when it connects two main clauses.
target_language_example: Er wirkt sehr freundlich, aber er ist sehr streng.
native_language_example: He seems very friendly, but he is very strict.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrast or limitation: "..., aber es ..." = "..., but it ...". Often starts a new sentence after something was said before ("Aber es hat Spaß gemacht."). Word order stays normal after "aber" (it does NOT push the verb to the end).
target_language_example: Ich war müde, aber es ging trotzdem.
native_language_example: I was tired, but it still worked out / I managed anyway.

meaning: “but there is / but there are” (introduces an exception, limitation, or new point).
additional_notes: Used when you want to add a contrasting fact after what was just said. You’ll often see it followed by a noun phrase: “aber es gibt ein Problem” (but there’s a problem), “aber es gibt keine Wahl” (but there’s no choice). Word order stays the same as normal “es gibt …” (there is/are …); “aber” just connects the contrast.
target_language_example: Ich verstehe deine Idee, aber es gibt ein Risiko.
native_language_example: I understand your idea, but there’s a risk.

additional_notes: Used to contrast two statements: X, aber es ist Y. Often followed by an adjective or noun phrase (e.g., „aber es ist interessant“, „aber es ist die Wahrheit“). In writing, you usually put a comma before „aber“ when it connects two clauses.
target_language_example: Ich habe keine Zeit, aber es ist wichtig.
native_language_example: I don’t have time, but it’s important.

meaning: 'but it was …' (introduces a contrast about a past situation).
additional_notes: Used to add a contrasting fact after a previous statement. Very common pattern: "..., aber es war + Adjektiv/Adverb" ("..., but it was too late/occupied/over quickly"). Note that "war" is the simple past of "sein" ("to be").
target_language_example: Ich wollte dir helfen, aber es war schon zu spät.
native_language_example: I wanted to help you, but it was already too late.

additional_notes: A simple, non-idiomatic combination of aber + ich. It is used to contrast what the speaker says or does with what was said before: “..., but I ...”. Often starts a new clause after a comma, but it can also begin a sentence for emphasis.
target_language_example: Du gehst nach Hause, aber ich bleibe noch hier.
native_language_example: You're going home, but I'm staying here a bit longer.

meaning: “but I am …” / “but I’m …” (used to contrast with what was just said).
additional_notes: Often comes after someone’s statement or an assumption to correct it or add a contrasting fact. Very common in conversation: “..., aber ich bin …” + adjective/noun/prepositional phrase (e.g., „unschuldig“, „der Auserwählte“, „noch nicht da“).
target_language_example: Ich verstehe dich, aber ich bin heute zu müde.
native_language_example: I understand you, but I’m too tired today.

meaning: “but I am not …” (used to disagree or correct).
additional_notes: Used to push back, clarify, or correct what someone thinks about you. Typically followed by a noun/adjective/phrase (e.g., „…der Dieb“, „…wie du“, „…begeistert“). In speech it often contrasts with what was said or implied before: „…, aber ich bin nicht …“.
target_language_example: Ich verstehe deinen Punkt, aber ich bin nicht damit einverstanden.
native_language_example: I understand your point, but I don't agree with it.

additional_notes: Used to contrast what was just said with a necessity or requirement. After "brauche" you typically put the thing you need in the accusative (e.g., "ich brauche ihn / sie / es"), or use "für" + accusative to say what it’s needed for (e.g., "ich brauche es für die Arbeit").
target_language_example: Ich würde gern kommen, aber ich brauche heute Ruhe.
native_language_example: I’d like to come, but I need some peace and quiet today.

meaning: “but I think …” / “but I believe …” (polite, slightly unsure disagreement or correction).
additional_notes: Used to soften a contradiction or to correct someone: you add a polite “but” (aber) and then your opinion/assumption (ich glaube). Often followed by a full clause ("…, aber ich glaube, dass …") or directly by a statement ("…, aber ich glaube, das ist …"). You can add words like "schon" or "eigentlich" to nuance it ("aber ich glaube schon" = “but I do think so”).
target_language_example: Ich verstehe, aber ich glaube, das ist nicht richtig.
native_language_example: I understand, but I think that’s not correct.

meaning: "but I have..." (used to contrast with what was just said).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrasting point from the speaker’s perspective. "Ich habe" can mean (1) "I have" (possession): "Ich habe Zeit." or (2) "I have" as the auxiliary for the Perfekt (past): "Ich habe viel nachgedacht." After "aber", German keeps normal word order here: "aber ich habe ..."
target_language_example: Aber ich habe keine Zeit, heute zu kommen.
native_language_example: But I don’t have time to come today.

meaning: "but I have" (used to contrast with what was just said).
additional_notes: Use this after a statement (yours or someone else’s) to introduce a contrasting point or exception. "aber" = "but" and "ich habe" = "I have" (present tense of "haben"). Often followed by a noun: "Aber ich habe keine Zeit."
target_language_example: Aber ich habe heute keine Zeit.
native_language_example: But I don’t have time today.

meaning: 'but I can …' (contrast: something is true, but you’re able to do something).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrast or limitation after what was just said: “but I can/can’t …”. Often followed by an infinitive or phrase like helfen (help), bleiben (stay), zustimmen (agree). With a direct object, you may see it as: „aber ich kann es nicht tun“ (but I can’t do it).
target_language_example: Ich bin müde, aber ich kann noch ein bisschen arbeiten.
native_language_example: I’m tired, but I can still work a little.

additional_notes: Used to add a constraint or obligation after saying yes, agreeing, or stating a preference. Often used to politely decline or explain why you can’t do something: "Gerne, aber ich muss …". In everyday speech, German often uses "müssen" where English would say "have to".
target_language_example: Ich würde gern länger bleiben, aber ich muss morgen früh arbeiten.
native_language_example: I’d like to stay longer, but I have to work early tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to contrast with what was just said or expected ("but..."). It’s often followed by a clause with "dass ..." or by an object like "es" (e.g., "aber ich weiß es nicht" = "but I don’t know"). Word order is flexible in spoken German, but this phrase typically starts a new thought.
target_language_example: Ich bin nicht sicher, aber ich weiß, dass er heute kommt.
native_language_example: I’m not sure, but I do know that he’s coming today.

additional_notes: Used to contrast with what was just said and then state your intention or future action. "werde" is the 1st-person singular form of "werden" and is often used with an infinitive at the end (future/intent): „Aber ich werde es tun.“ / „Aber ich werde nicht warten.“ It can also be used on its own with an object: „Aber ich werde es herausfinden.“
target_language_example: Ich bin müde, aber ich werde trotzdem weiterarbeiten.
native_language_example: I'm tired, but I'll keep working anyway.

meaning: “but I want …” / “but I do want …” (to object, correct, or insist).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a sentence to push back against what someone else said (“But I want…/But I don’t want…”). Very often followed by a direct object or an infinitive phrase: “Aber ich will euch helfen …” (But I want to help you …). Note: German “will” means “want,” not the English future tense “will” (which is usually “werde”).
target_language_example: Aber ich will das nicht machen.
native_language_example: But I don’t want to do that.

additional_notes: Used to correct or contrast what someone thinks/claims/what seems true with what is really true. Often comes after a statement or assumption: "X, aber in Wirklichkeit Y." You can also say "in Wirklichkeit" without "aber" if no strong contrast is needed.
target_language_example: Sie wirkt sehr selbstbewusst, aber in Wirklichkeit ist sie ziemlich nervös.
native_language_example: She seems very confident, but in reality she’s pretty nervous.

additional_notes: Used to contrast a previous situation with the current one ("before..., but now..."). It can also mean "but right now" when talking about the present moment (often followed by a reason like "keine Zeit"). Usually starts the second part of a sentence after something like "früher/einmal" (before/once).
target_language_example: Früher hatte ich Angst, aber jetzt fühle ich mich sicher.
native_language_example: I used to be scared, but now I feel safe.

additional_notes: Used to contrast two parts of a statement: something is true/possible, but a particular thing is not. In German word order, it often appears after the verb ("..., können ..., sich aber nicht ..."), so the two words don’t always stay right next to each other (e.g., "aber" can come earlier and "nicht" later).
target_language_example: Ich kann heute kommen, aber nicht lange bleiben.
native_language_example: I can come today, but I can’t stay long.

additional_notes: Used to show a contrast: something happened or you expected a response, but no person did it (often after a comma). "Niemand" is singular, so the verb is singular: "aber niemand öffnete" / "aber niemand machte auf".
target_language_example: Ich habe dreimal angerufen, aber niemand ist rangegangen.
native_language_example: I called three times, but nobody picked up.

additional_notes: Often used as an emphatic, friendly answer meaning “definitely/you bet!” (e.g., “Aber sicher doch!”). You’ll also see it in the fixed phrase “langsam aber sicher” = “slowly but surely/gradually but surely.”
target_language_example: Kommst du morgen mit? – Aber sicher!
native_language_example: Are you coming along tomorrow? – Of course!

additional_notes: Used as a strong, often friendly-sounding way to confirm or agree with something. Common in spoken German; the tone can range from enthusiastic reassurance (“yes, absolutely”) to slightly sarcastic depending on context and intonation.
target_language_example: Kommst du morgen mit? – Aber sicher doch!
native_language_example: Are you coming along tomorrow? – Of course!

additional_notes: "aber" = "but". "sie" can mean "she" (singular), "they" (plural), or the formal "you" (Sie). In the middle of a sentence, "sie" is usually "she/they" (lowercase); "Sie" (capitalized) is formal "you".
target_language_example: Ich wollte helfen, aber sie hatte keine Zeit.
native_language_example: I wanted to help, but she didn’t have time.

meaning: "but she is" / "but it is" (introduces a contrast).
additional_notes: Used to correct or add contrasting information after a statement. "sie" can mean "she" (a female person) or "it" when referring to a feminine noun (e.g., "die Verbindung"), and "ist" is the 3rd-person singular of "sein" (to be).
target_language_example: Der Plan klingt gut, aber sie ist zu teuer.
native_language_example: The plan sounds good, but it’s too expensive.

additional_notes: Used to express contrast: something is true or happens despite what was just said. Often follows a comma after the first clause (…, aber trotzdem …). In speech it can also stand in the middle of a sentence for emphasis (Ich habe mich aber trotzdem verspätet = “I was late anyway, even so”).
target_language_example: Ich war müde, aber trotzdem bin ich mitgekommen.
native_language_example: I was tired, but I still came along.

additional_notes: Used to contrast what "we" do/are with what was just said before. Often connects two clauses: "..., aber wir ..." (= "..., but we ..."). Word order after "aber" stays the same as in a normal main clause (the verb is still in position 2).
target_language_example: Es ist schwierig, aber wir schaffen das.
native_language_example: It’s difficult, but we can do it.

meaning: "but we have..." (introduces a contrast and then says what 'we have').
additional_notes: Used to contrast a problem or negative point with something positive or useful that you possess or can rely on. Often used for reassurance: „Aber wir haben uns.“ = “But we have each other.” You typically continue with an object: „Aber wir haben einen Plan / die Schlüssel / genug Zeit.“
target_language_example: Es ist schwierig, aber wir haben genug Zeit.
native_language_example: It’s difficult, but we have enough time.

meaning: 'but we have to / but we must'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrast or objection ("but") and then state a necessity/obligation ("we must"). Typically followed by an infinitive at the end of the clause: "Aber wir müssen gehen." / "Aber wir müssen schnell handeln."
target_language_example: Aber wir müssen jetzt los.
native_language_example: But we have to leave now.

meaning: “but we are …” (to contrast what comes next with what was just said).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrasting point about “us/we” ("wir"). Often followed by an adjective or noun phrase (e.g., „alt“, „keine Kinder mehr“, „eine Familie“) or another comment that corrects/limits the previous statement.
target_language_example: Aber wir sind bereit, es zu versuchen.
native_language_example: But we are ready to try.

meaning: did it on purpose; did it intentionally.
additional_notes: Used to say an action wasn’t an accident. Common pattern: **Das habe(n) ... absichtlich gemacht** (subject changes: ich habe, du hast, ihr habt, sie/Sie haben). You can also use **es** instead of **das** when referring to something already known: **Sie hat es absichtlich gemacht.**
target_language_example: Ich habe das nicht absichtlich gemacht.
native_language_example: I didn’t do that on purpose.

meaning: “oh, you…” — used to show surprise, disbelief, or annoyance.
additional_notes: A very common spoken opener before you react to what someone said or did. Often followed by more words (e.g., “Ach, du meine Güte!” = “Oh my goodness!”) or by a comment addressing the person (“Ach, du machst Witze.” / “Ach, du verarschst uns doch.”). The tone depends on context: it can be amused, shocked, or irritated.
target_language_example: Ach, du machst doch nur Spaß!
native_language_example: Oh, you’re just kidding!

meaning: "Oh, I..." (a reaction before saying something about yourself).
additional_notes: "Ach" is a very common interjection used to show a feeling like surprise, realization, disappointment, impatience, or relief. It often comes at the start of a sentence; adding "ich" means you’re about to say something about yourself ("Ach, ich..." → "Oh, I..."). In writing, it’s usually followed by a comma: "Ach, ich ..."
target_language_example: Ach, ich habe es vergessen.
native_language_example: Oh, I forgot it.

additional_notes: Used to react emotionally (admiration, annoyance, irony, nostalgia, self-criticism). Often followed by an adjective (Ach, wie schön!) or a full sentence with inverted word order (Ach, wie vermisse ich dich!).
target_language_example: Ach, wie schön, dich wiederzusehen!
native_language_example: Oh, how nice to see you again!

meaning: "Oh right!" / "Oh yeah" (sudden remembering, realization, or an afterthought).
additional_notes: Used as an interjection when you suddenly remember something or add something you almost forgot: "Ach ja, ..." It can also react to something someone said. As a question ("Ach ja?") it often means "Oh really?" / "Is that so?" and can sound skeptical depending on tone.
target_language_example: Ach ja, ich muss noch einkaufen gehen.
native_language_example: Oh right, I still need to go shopping.

meaning: “Oh, I see / oh, right.” (shows you’ve just understood or remembered something).
additional_notes: Used as a quick reaction when something becomes clear after an explanation or when you suddenly remember a detail. Often stands alone (“Ach so!”) or comes at the start of a sentence (“Ach so, die Auktion.”). Tone depends on context: neutral to mildly surprised; can sometimes sound a bit dismissive if said flatly.
target_language_example: Ach so, jetzt verstehe ich dich.
native_language_example: Oh, I see—now I understand you.

additional_notes: Used to state a time. With context it can mean 8:00 in the morning or in the evening; you can clarify with „morgens“ (in the morning) or „abends“ (in the evening). After „um“ (at) it becomes „um acht Uhr“.
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns um acht Uhr vor dem Kino.
native_language_example: We’re meeting at eight o’clock in front of the cinema.

additional_notes: Refers back to things already known from the conversation or context. Often used to sum up a situation (“all that”) and can sound emotional or emphatic: Warum all das? = “Why all this/that?”
target_language_example: Ich kann all das nicht vergessen.
native_language_example: I can’t forget all that.

additional_notes: Used when referring back to a whole set of things/situations already mentioned or understood from context. It’s the dative form of "all das" and is common after prepositions that take the dative (e.g., "von all dem" = "of all that", "zu all dem" = "to all that"), or with verbs that require the dative (e.g., "all dem widerstehen" = "resist all that").
target_language_example: Nach all dem brauche ich erst mal eine Pause.
native_language_example: After all that, I need a break first.

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to emphasize the whole group of nearby/mentioned things or people: all these roses/letters/people/questions/things. It’s a common combination of **all** (all) + **diese** (these). Often appears with a noun right after it: **all diese + Nomen (Plural)**.
target_language_example: Ich verstehe all diese Regeln nicht.
native_language_example: I don’t understand all these rules.

meaning: very rarely; once in a blue moon.
additional_notes: Used (often with "nur" and sometimes with "(ein)mal") to say something happens extremely infrequently. Literally refers to a "jubilee year" (a rare, special year), but in everyday German it’s just an idiom for "hardly ever."
target_language_example: Wir sehen uns leider nur alle Jubeljahre.
native_language_example: Unfortunately, we only see each other once in a blue moon.

additional_notes: Used to make a general statement about people as a whole. It often starts a sentence (e.g., „Alle Menschen sind …“). With an added phrase it can be more specific: „Alle Menschen dieser Erde“ = all people on Earth. In comparisons/generalizations you may see „Wie alle Menschen …“ = like everyone (else) / as most people do.
target_language_example: Alle Menschen brauchen Liebe und Respekt.
native_language_example: All people need love and respect.

meaning: all (the) students / every student (in a group).
additional_notes: Used to refer to the entire group of students being talked about (e.g., at a school or in a class). Often followed by extra information like a place or group: „alle Schüler in der Klasse“, „alle Schüler an unserer Schule“. With negation, it means “not all students”: „Nicht alle Schüler …“.
target_language_example: Alle Schüler müssen pünktlich sein.
native_language_example: All students have to be on time.

additional_notes: "Alle" means "all" and "Türen" is the plural of "Tür" (door). It’s used literally for actual doors (e.g., in a house) and figuratively in phrases like "(etwas) öffnet alle Türen" = "(something) opens all doors" meaning it creates many opportunities or makes everything possible.
target_language_example: Ein gutes Netzwerk kann dir alle Türen öffnen.
native_language_example: A good network can open all doors for you.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a large, unspecified group of people—often meaning “it feels like everyone” rather than literally the entire world. Sometimes it can also mean “the whole world” in a more literal sense, but very commonly it means “everyone”.
target_language_example: Auf einmal kennt alle Welt diese Geschichte.
native_language_example: Suddenly everyone knows this story.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the rest of a group (people or things), excluding the one(s) you’re talking about. Very common in comparisons with "als" (e.g., "größer als alle anderen" = "taller than all the others"). You can use it with nouns ("alle anderen Plätze") or on its own ("alle anderen").
target_language_example: Ich nehme den roten Stift; alle anderen brauche ich nicht.
native_language_example: I’ll take the red pen; I don’t need the others.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the rest of a group besides the person/people already mentioned (often meaning “everyone else”). It can stand alone (“Dann alle anderen!”) or follow a noun list (“Mama, Papa und alle anderen …”). It also appears in comparisons: “als alle anderen” = “than all the others.”
target_language_example: Ich habe keine Zeit, aber alle anderen können kommen.
native_language_example: I don't have time, but everyone else can come.

additional_notes: Used to compare one person/thing with the rest of a group. Often appears with comparisons: "besser/schlechter/schneller … als alle anderen" (better/worse/faster than everyone else). Can also be used with prepositions like "über" (above) in phrases like "über alle anderen hinaus" (above all others).
target_language_example: Ich will nicht auffallen; ich möchte einfach sein wie alle anderen.
native_language_example: I don’t want to stand out; I just want to be like everyone else.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that a statement applies to the two people/things being talked about. It often comes after the subject or pronoun (e.g., „Sie sind alle beide …“, „Tom und Maria sind alle beide …“). Common with people, but it can also be used for things.
target_language_example: Wir haben alle beide keine Zeit.
native_language_example: Both of us don’t have time.

additional_notes: Used when you mean exactly three people or things together. Often follows the noun/pronoun it refers to ("Tom, Maria und Johannes sind alle drei da"), but it can also appear at the beginning of the sentence ("Alle drei sahen Tom an"). It inflects for case: nominative/accusative "alle drei", dative "allen drei".
target_language_example: Tom, Maria und Johannes sind alle drei da.
native_language_example: Tom, Maria, and Johannes are all three here.

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to mean you include every one of your things/people: „alle meine Geschwister“ (all my siblings), „alle meine Lehrer“ (all my teachers). The forms can change with case: e.g. nominative/accusative plural „alle meine …“, dative plural „mit allen meinen …“. For singular, German often uses „mein ganzes / meine ganze / mein ganzer …“ (my whole …) instead of *alle meine*.
target_language_example: Alle meine Freunde sind schon da.
native_language_example: All my friends are already here.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your entire group of friends. Often placed at the beginning of the sentence for emphasis (Alle meine Freunde …). In a longer sentence it can also come after the verb: Ich habe alle meine Freunde eingeladen. (accusative object).
target_language_example: Alle meine Freunde kommen heute Abend zu mir.
native_language_example: All my friends are coming to my place tonight.

meaning: all sorts of; all kinds of; all manner of.
additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to mean “a wide variety of” things, often implying “many different types” (not literally every possible one). It commonly appears with rumors, names, ideas, books, insults, etc.: „alle möglichen Gerüchte / Bücher / Schimpfwörter“.
target_language_example: Im Internet findet man alle möglichen Tipps zum Deutschlernen.
native_language_example: On the internet you can find all kinds of tips for learning German.

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to say that every one of the things/people belonging to a man or boy is included: "alle seine Freunde" (all his friends), "alle seine Romane" (all his novels). The noun must be plural; for a singular noun you’d use "sein ganzer / seine ganze / sein ganzes" (his whole). It declines by case (e.g., nominative/accusative "alle seine ...", dative "allen seinen ...").
target_language_example: Sie kennt alle seine Geschichten.
native_language_example: She knows all his stories.

meaning: every two (e.g., every two days); sometimes: both (of them).
additional_notes: Most commonly used with a time word: „alle zwei Tage/Wochen/Monate“ = “every two days/weeks/months” (= every other day/week/month). In some contexts, especially in speech, „alle zwei“ can also mean “both” (similar to „beide“), but „beide/alle beide“ is clearer and more common for “both.”
target_language_example: Ich gehe alle zwei Tage ins Fitnessstudio.
native_language_example: I go to the gym every two days (every other day).

additional_notes: Used to refer to a whole group of people or things that share a condition, followed by a relative clause with verb at the end (e.g., „alle, die … leben/sehen/müssen“). It can refer to people („all who…“) or, depending on context, to things („all the ones that…“). Often used without a noun: „Alle, die kommen, …“ = „Everyone who comes …“.
target_language_example: Alle, die heute Zeit haben, können mitkommen.
native_language_example: Everyone who has time today can come along.

additional_notes: Used to say that a whole group is identical/similar in some way (often with verbs like „sein“ or „aussehen“) or that everyone has the same status/rights (e.g., „Vor dem Gesetz sind wir alle gleich.“ = equal before the law). In statements like „Frauen sind alle gleich“, it can sound like a sweeping generalization.
target_language_example: Für mich sehen sie alle gleich aus.
native_language_example: To me they all look the same.

meaning: all of you / all together (everyone as a group).
additional_notes: Used to address a group or to refer to everyone doing something together. Often set off by commas when speaking to a group (like “everyone”): „Hallo, alle miteinander!“ It can also mean “together as a group” in a sentence: „Wir essen alle miteinander.“
target_language_example: Kommt rein, alle miteinander!
native_language_example: Come in, all of you!

additional_notes: Used to say that a whole group has a state/feeling: **Alle sind aufgeregt/nervös.** Grammatically, **alle** is plural, so it goes with **sind** (3rd person plural of **sein**, “to be”). In the Perfekt tense, **sind** can also be the helping verb with movement/change verbs: **Alle sind auf die Party gegangen.**
target_language_example: Alle sind schon hier.
native_language_example: Everyone is already here.

additional_notes: “Alle” means “everyone” or “all (of them)”. “Waren” is the simple past (Präteritum) of “sein” (“to be”) for wir/sie/Sie: “we/they/you (formal) were”. Used to describe a past state of a whole group (often followed by an adjective or phrase): “Alle waren müde.”
target_language_example: Alle waren froh, als der Test vorbei war.
native_language_example: Everyone was happy when the test was over.

additional_notes: Used to say something is common knowledge. It’s typically followed by a subordinate clause introduced by **dass** (“that”). In German you usually write a comma before **dass**, and the verb in the **dass**-clause goes to the end: **Alle wissen, dass er heute kommt.**
target_language_example: Alle wissen, dass wir morgen eine Prüfung haben.
native_language_example: Everyone knows that we have an exam tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say that all people in a group want something. Often followed by a direct object (e.g., „Alle wollen das.“) or a „dass“-clause (e.g., „Wir alle wollen, dass …“). „Alle“ = everyone/all (people), „wollen“ = want.
target_language_example: Alle wollen endlich Urlaub.
native_language_example: Everyone wants a vacation at last.

meaning: all together; everyone (here), as a group.
additional_notes: Used to address or refer to a whole group at once (like “everyone” or “all of you together”). Common in greetings (“Guten Morgen, alle zusammen!”) and when giving a group instruction (“Los, alle zusammen!”).
target_language_example: Kommt alle zusammen nach vorne!
native_language_example: Everyone, come up to the front together!

meaning: to leave (someone) alone; to let (someone) be alone.
additional_notes: Used when you ask or tell someone not to leave you by yourself, or when you ask people to give you privacy (e.g., “Could you leave us alone for a moment?”). Common with pronouns: jemanden allein lassen (mich/dich/ihn/sie/uns/euch). In the examples it often appears with polite requests (Könnten/Würden Sie … bitte …?).
target_language_example: Kannst du mich bitte kurz allein lassen?
native_language_example: Can you please leave me alone for a moment?

additional_notes: Means being without other people present (physically). Often used when asking for privacy: „Könnten wir kurz allein sein?“ = “Could we be alone for a moment?” Not the same as „einsam sein“ (to feel lonely).
target_language_example: Ich möchte heute Abend allein sein.
native_language_example: I want to be alone tonight.

additional_notes: An infinitive phrase with "zu" used after many verbs (e.g., "sich entschließen", "die Absicht haben", "zu jung sein, um … zu …"). "dorthin" means “to there” (to that place), and "allein" emphasizes you go without anyone else.
target_language_example: Ich traue mich nicht, allein dorthin zu gehen.
native_language_example: I don’t dare to go there alone.

meaning: to stand alone; to be able to stand by itself.
additional_notes: Used both literally (a person/thing stands without support) and figuratively (a word, sentence, or idea can be used independently and still make sense). In everyday speech about relationship status, German more often uses the adjective "alleinstehend" (single) rather than the verb phrase "allein stehen".
target_language_example: Dieser Satz kann allein stehen.
native_language_example: This sentence can stand on its own.

additional_notes: Describes being at home with no other people there. Commonly used with verbs like „sein“ (to be) and „bleiben“ (to stay). Word order can vary: „allein zu Hause“ and „zu Hause allein“ both work, but „allein zu Hause“ is very common.
target_language_example: Ich bin heute Abend allein zu Hause.
native_language_example: I’m home alone tonight.

additional_notes: Used to talk about being by yourself (without other people). Often used with phrases like „Ich mag es …“ (I like it…), „Ich wünsche …“ (I wish…), or „Macht es dir/Ihnen nichts aus …?“ (Do you mind…?).
target_language_example: Heute Abend möchte ich gern allein zu sein.
native_language_example: This evening I’d like to be alone.

meaning: to leave (someone) alone; to leave (someone) by themselves; to stop bothering someone (context-dependent).
additional_notes: Takes a direct object in the accusative: jemanden alleine lassen. Can mean (1) physically leaving someone without company/help/supervision (e.g., a child) or (2) leaving someone in peace ("stop bothering me"). Common in polite requests: „Würden Sie uns kurz alleine lassen?“ = “Would you leave us alone for a moment?”
target_language_example: Würden Sie uns ein paar Minuten alleine lassen?
native_language_example: Would you leave us alone for a few minutes?

additional_notes: Used with reporting verbs like **sagen** or **erzählen**: **jemandem (Dat.) sagen/erzählen, dass …**. **allen** is dative plural (“to everyone”), followed by a **dass**-clause. Word order: the verb in the **dass**-clause goes to the end (e.g., **dass er morgen keine Zeit hat**).
target_language_example: Maria sagte allen, dass es ihr gut gehe.
native_language_example: Maria told everyone that she was doing well.

meaning: “of all time” / “ever” (used to emphasize a superlative).
additional_notes: Usually comes after a superlative: "die beste/größte/schlimmste … aller Zeiten" = “the best/biggest/worst … of all time.” Grammatically it’s genitive plural of "alle Zeiten" (“all times”), meaning across all eras/periods.
target_language_example: Das ist mein Lieblingsfilm aller Zeiten.
native_language_example: That’s my favorite movie of all time.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has an allergy. Usually with a noun: „Ich bin allergisch gegen Milch.“ You can add contrasts with „aber nicht gegen …“ (but not to …). In everyday speech, people also say „allergisch auf“ with a similar meaning.
target_language_example: Bist du allergisch gegen Katzen?
native_language_example: Are you allergic to cats?

additional_notes: A common, friendly way to wish someone well—often when saying goodbye, for birthdays, or before an important event. You can say it on its own as a greeting/farewell (“Alles Gute, Anna!”) or use it with wünschen: “Ich wünsche dir/Ihnen alles Gute.” (to a friend vs. formal).
target_language_example: Alles Gute zum Geburtstag!
native_language_example: All the best for your birthday!

additional_notes: Used to say the exact thing isn’t known or doesn’t matter—there are many possibilities. Often appears after an indefinite pronoun like "etwas"/"nichts"/"alles" (e.g., "etwas alles Mögliche") or on its own ("Das kann alles Mögliche sein"). In "sich alles Mögliche einfallen lassen", it means thinking up all kinds of ideas.
target_language_example: Im Urlaub kann alles Mögliche passieren.
native_language_example: All sorts of things can happen on vacation.

additional_notes: Used to wish someone well, often as a short closing in messages/cards or when saying goodbye. Common with verbs like wünschen: „Ich/Wir wünschen dir/Ihnen alles Gute.“ Also used alone as „Alles Gute!“. In other contexts it can literally mean “everything good” (e.g., „Alles Gute passiert…“).
target_language_example: Alles Gute zum Geburtstag!
native_language_example: All the best for your birthday!

additional_notes: Used before a relative clause to mean “everything that/which …”. In German it’s written with a comma before the relative clause: „alles, was …“.
target_language_example: Alles, was du gesagt hast, stimmt.
native_language_example: Everything that you said is true.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause: **alles, was Sie + verb** = “everything (that) you + verb.” **Sie** is the formal “you” (for strangers, customers, etc.); with friends you’d usually say **alles, was du …**. Often appears in warnings, questions, and customer-service contexts.
target_language_example: Alles, was Sie hier unterschreiben, ist verbindlich.
native_language_example: Everything you sign here is binding.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause referring to “everything” someone knows/has/does, etc. After "was du", the verb goes to the end of the clause (e.g., "alles, was du weißt"). Often followed by a prepositional phrase like "darüber" (about it) or "über ihn" (about him).
target_language_example: Erzähl mir alles, was du gehört hast.
native_language_example: Tell me everything that you heard.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause referring to “everything” (alles). The comma is required: „alles, was ich …“. After „was ich“, you usually continue with a verb at/near the end of the clause (e.g., „alles, was ich brauche“ = everything I need).
target_language_example: Das ist alles, was ich heute brauche.
native_language_example: That’s everything I need today.

additional_notes: Used to say you have (or don’t have) all necessary things. "alles, was ..." introduces a relative clause meaning "everything that ...". Often appears with verbs like "haben" (to have): "Ich habe alles, was ich brauche."
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, ich habe alles, was ich brauche.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I have everything I need.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause with **ihr** (= “you” plural/informal, or “you” formal in some dialects). **Alles** refers to a general set of things, and **was** links to what follows: *alles, was ihr gesehen habt* = “everything that you saw.” Often used to ask if something is the total amount: *Ist das alles, was ihr …?*
target_language_example: Erzähl mir alles, was ihr heute gemacht habt.
native_language_example: Tell me everything you (all) did today.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause with an indefinite subject (man = “one/you/people in general”). It refers to the total of things in a general sense: Alles, was man + VERB, … (“Everything that you eat/need/know/lose …”). Often followed by a verb at the end of the clause.
target_language_example: Alles, was man braucht, ist ein bisschen Geduld.
native_language_example: Everything you need is a bit of patience.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause (comma + "was") referring back to "alles" (“everything”): "Alles, was sie sagt" = “Everything (that) she says.” The pronoun "sie" here can mean “she” or formal “you” (singular/plural), depending on context. The verb in the relative clause usually comes at the end: "Alles, was sie braucht, ist Zeit."
target_language_example: Ich glaube alles, was sie mir erzählt.
native_language_example: I believe everything she tells me.

additional_notes: Used to say/check that you have all necessary items or requirements. Often appears in questions (Hast du/Habt ihr …? Ist das …?) and can be used on its own as a short statement (e.g., on a checklist).
target_language_example: Okay, wir haben alles, was wir brauchen.
native_language_example: Okay, we have everything we need.

additional_notes: Used to contrast one thing with the rest: "X ist wichtig, alles andere ..." It can be the subject or object of a sentence. Often means "everything besides that" (everything else). In questions/negatives it can also mean "anything else" (e.g., "Hast du alles andere?" = "Do you have everything else?").
target_language_example: Ich habe keine Zeit; alles andere muss warten.
native_language_example: I have no time; everything else has to wait.

additional_notes: Used to express strong willingness to do a lot for someone, or that you did/made sacrifices for them. Common with verbs like tun (to do), aufgeben (to give up), opfern (to sacrifice), vorbereiten (to prepare). Depending on context it can sound loving, dramatic, or even threatening/manipulative.
target_language_example: Ich würde alles für dich tun, aber das geht zu weit.
native_language_example: I’d do anything for you, but that goes too far.

meaning: “did everything that …” (i.e., did all they could / did all that was necessary).
additional_notes: Used with a relative clause introduced by **was** to explain what “everything” refers to: **Ich habe alles getan, was ich konnte** = “I did everything I could.” Often followed by **um … zu** to give a goal/purpose: **… um jemanden zu retten** (“… to save someone”).
target_language_example: Ich habe alles getan, was ich konnte, um dir zu helfen.
native_language_example: I did everything I could to help you.

additional_notes: Common, casual reassurance. Used as an exclamation (“Alles gut!” = “It’s okay!”), as a check-in question (“Alles gut?” = “You okay?”), or to say a problem is solved (“Dann ist alles gut.” = “Then everything will be fine.”). Often used to tell someone not to worry or that there’s no harm done.
target_language_example: Alles gut, ich hab’s schon erledigt.
native_language_example: All good, I’ve already taken care of it.

additional_notes: Common phrase to ask if someone is okay or if there’s a problem: „Alles in Ordnung?“ = “Everything okay?” It can also be used to reassure someone: „Es ist alles in Ordnung.“ = “It’s all fine.” Often used in situations like checking on someone, after a mistake, or when something seems wrong.
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, alles in Ordnung.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, everything is okay.

additional_notes: Very common in spoken German. As a question (often with a friendly tone): “Alles klar?” = “You OK?” / “Everything clear?” As a response/confirmation: “Alles klar.” = “OK.” / “Alright.” / “Got it.” With words like “Alter”, “Mann”, “Kleiner” it sounds quite casual and can be slangy depending on context.
target_language_example: Alles klar, ich komme gleich.
native_language_example: OK, I’ll be right there.

additional_notes: Used to check if someone is fine, especially if they look worried, hurt, or something seems wrong. Often used as a short question (sometimes without “Ist”). You can also answer with “Alles ok.” (= Everything’s fine.)
target_language_example: Alles ok bei dir?
native_language_example: Everything OK with you?

additional_notes: Common, friendly check-in about how someone is doing or whether a situation is fine. Often used as a question ("Alles okay?" / "Alles okay mit dir/Ihnen?") or as reassurance ("Ja, alles okay."). Also spelled "Alles OK?". With "Ihnen" it’s formal; with "dir/deiner" it’s informal.
target_language_example: Alles okay bei dir, oder brauchst du Hilfe?
native_language_example: Everything okay with you, or do you need help?

meaning: to do everything that … / to do whatever …
additional_notes: Used with a relative clause introduced by **was** to express doing everything possible/necessary to achieve something: **Ich werde alles tun, was in meiner Macht steht** (“I’ll do everything in my power”). Often followed by an infinitive clause with **um … zu …**. Also appears in imperatives like **Lass/Lasst … alles tun, was er/sie will** (“Let … do whatever he/she wants”).
target_language_example: Ich werde alles tun, was in meiner Macht steht, um dir zu helfen.
native_language_example: I’ll do everything in my power to help you.

meaning: 'everything is under control' / 'I've got everything under control'.
additional_notes: Used to reassure someone that a situation is handled and there’s no need to worry. You can say it alone as a short statement ("Alles unter Kontrolle."), or with a subject to emphasize who is managing things ("Ich habe alles unter Kontrolle.", "Hier ist alles unter Kontrolle.").
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, ich habe alles unter Kontrolle.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ve got everything under control.

meaning: 'everything is OK again' / 'all is well again'.
additional_notes: Used after a problem or difficult moment to say things have returned to normal or been resolved. Often used reassuringly. You can also say it about the future: "Alles wird wieder gut" (Everything will be OK again).
target_language_example: Keine Sorge—morgen ist alles wieder gut.
native_language_example: Don’t worry—tomorrow everything will be OK again.

additional_notes: A common reassuring phrase said to comfort someone or express optimism. Often used on its own ("Alles wird gut.") or with additions like "... sein/werden" to emphasize the future, or with conditions like "..., solange ..." ("... as long as ...").
target_language_example: Mach dir keine Sorgen—alles wird gut.
native_language_example: Don’t worry—everything will be okay.

additional_notes: Used with a noun or pronoun to say someone knows/tells/reports all details about a topic/person/thing: alles über den Plan, alles über mich. Common with verbs like wissen (to know), erzählen/berichten (to tell/report), erfahren (to find out).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir alles über die Stadt erzählen?
native_language_example: Can you tell me everything about the city?

meaning: first (the first one to do something).
additional_notes: Used to say someone (masculine singular) was the first to arrive/do something, often with verbs like kommen/ankommen/sein/überqueren/vorstellen. It answers “in what order?” and agrees in gender/case: als Erster (masc. nom.), als Erste (fem. nom.), als Erstes (neuter / “first of all”), plural: als Erste; with dative: als Erstem/Erster/Erstem, etc.
target_language_example: Tom überquerte die Ziellinie als Erster.
native_language_example: Tom crossed the finish line first.

additional_notes: Used with an ordinal after "als" to say someone does something before anyone else (order in a sequence). It changes with gender/case: als Erste (female), als Erster (male), als Erstes (neuter/"the first thing"), als Erste (plural).
target_language_example: Ich gehe als Erster rein.
native_language_example: I’ll go in first.

additional_notes: Used to say what should be done or checked first, often in instructions, plans, or investigations. It can appear at the start of a sentence ("Als Erstes musst du …") or later for emphasis ("… gehen wir immer als Erstes nach"). Similar to "zuerst" but often highlights “the very first step/priority.”
target_language_example: Als Erstes rufe ich meine Mutter an.
native_language_example: First, I’ll call my mother.

additional_notes: Used with „als“ to describe the role/function of an animal (or even something unusual) in a situation: someone keeps/chooses something „als Haustier“ (= in the role of a pet). Often used with verbs like „halten“ (to keep), „sich halten“ (to keep for oneself), „sich (etw.) erwählen“ (to choose for oneself).
target_language_example: Ich möchte eine Katze als Haustier.
native_language_example: I want a cat as a pet.

meaning: as a teenager; when (someone) was a teenager.
additional_notes: Used with "als" + a life stage (here: "Jugendliche") to say what someone did/was during that time. Usually refers to your/another person’s past, and often appears with the simple past (Präteritum) in writing or with Perfekt in speech. "als Jugendliche" is feminine/plural; for a male singular you’d say "als Jugendlicher".
target_language_example: Als Jugendliche wollte sie unbedingt Musikerin werden.
native_language_example: As a teenager, she really wanted to become a musician.

meaning: as a child; when (I/you/etc.) was a child.
additional_notes: Used to talk about something that was true or happened during someone’s childhood. Often followed by a verb in the past: "Als Kind war ich …" / "Als Kind habe ich …". You can also specify whose childhood with a possessive: "als mein Kind" is wrong—say "als Kind" (me) or "als Kind" + context, or "als Kind meines Bruders" (as my brother’s child) / "als Kind von …" (as the child of …).
target_language_example: Als Kind hatte ich Angst vor Hunden.
native_language_example: As a child, I was afraid of dogs.

meaning: "When I was a child, I ..." / "As a child, I ..."
additional_notes: Used to talk about things you regularly did or that happened to you in childhood. Often followed by the past tense (e.g., Perfekt: „bin ich … gegangen/geschwommen“ or passive: „bin ich … gestochen worden“). You can also use it with other persons: „Als Kind war er …“, „Als Kind habe ich …“.
target_language_example: Als Kind bin ich jeden Samstag zu meiner Oma gefahren.
native_language_example: When I was a child, I went to my grandma’s every Saturday.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the next thing in a sequence or plan. Very common in questions like „Was kommt als Nächstes?“ (= What’s next?) and after verbs like „kommen“, „passieren“, or „zu tun sein“: „Ich frage mich, was als Nächstes passiert.“
target_language_example: Okay, und was machen wir als Nächstes?
native_language_example: Okay, and what are we doing next?

meaning: as the only one; the only person (who).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that one person (or thing) is the only one in a group with a certain situation or quality. It often comes right after the subject: „Tom war als einziger dort.“ For other genders/numbers it changes: „als einzige“ (female), „als einziges“ (neuter), „als einzige“ (plural = the only ones).
target_language_example: Tom war als einziger dort.
native_language_example: Tom was the only one there.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is the first to do something. It changes to match the person’s gender/number/case: **als Erster** (male), **als Erste** (female), **als Erstes** (neuter/impersonal: “first of all”), **als Erste/Erste** (plural). Often followed by what happened (e.g., *als erster gehen/ankommen/gratulieren/erfahren*).
target_language_example: Ich möchte dir als Erster gratulieren.
native_language_example: I’d like to be the first to congratulate you.

additional_notes: Used to say what happens first in a sequence or priority. Often placed in the middle of the sentence (e.g., "Ich wasche mir als erstes die Hände") or at the beginning for emphasis ("Als erstes ..."). Can also be used in questions/offers to choose who goes first or what to start with ("Wer will als erstes?").
target_language_example: Als erstes machen wir die Hausaufgaben, dann schauen wir einen Film.
native_language_example: First we do the homework, then we watch a movie.

additional_notes: Used to indicate the final step in a sequence or the last item in a list. Often appears in instructions or when describing the order of actions: "Erst ..., dann ..., und als Letztes ...".
target_language_example: Und als Letztes schalten wir das Licht aus.
native_language_example: And lastly, we switch off the light.

meaning: next; next up; the next thing.
additional_notes: Used to talk about what happens next in a sequence (who goes next, what you do next, what stop comes next). Often appears in questions: „Was machen wir als nächstes?“ or „Bin ich als nächstes dran?“ It refers to the next item/action/person after the current one.
target_language_example: Ich bin als nächstes dran.
native_language_example: I’m next (it’s my turn next).

meaning: to do next; what to do next.
additional_notes: Used when planning the next step in a process. Very common in questions with "Was" (e.g., "Was soll ich als nächstes tun?") and after verbs like "wissen", "entscheiden" or "sagen" (e.g., "Ich weiß nicht, was ich als nächstes tun soll.").
target_language_example: Ich weiß nicht, was ich als nächstes tun soll.
native_language_example: I don't know what I should do next.

additional_notes: Used with a comparative (Komparativ) to emphasize that something is stronger/more/less now than at any time in the past: e.g., besser/schlimmer/schneller/größer als je zuvor. Similar to “mehr denn je” (“more than ever”).
target_language_example: Ich bin motivierter als je zuvor.
native_language_example: I’m more motivated than ever before.

meaning: "as well as" / part of "sowohl … als auch" = "both … and".
additional_notes: Most commonly used with "sowohl" to pair two (or more) items: "sowohl X als auch Y" = "both X and Y". It can link nouns, adjectives, or verbs (activities). Usually the same grammatical form follows on both sides (e.g., two nouns, two adjectives).
target_language_example: Wir haben sowohl Zeit als auch Lust.
native_language_example: We have both time and desire (we feel like it).

meaning: “when the phone rang” (at that moment in the past).
additional_notes: Uses **als** to introduce a time clause for a **single, specific event in the past**. Often used with another past action that was in progress or had just (barely) happened (e.g., **gerade**, **kaum**, **mitten**). Word order: **Als das Telefon klingelte, ...** or **..., als das Telefon klingelte.**
target_language_example: Ich war gerade eingeschlafen, als das Telefon klingelte.
native_language_example: I had just fallen asleep when the phone rang.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a subordinate clause (verb goes to the end). Common with preferences/comparisons, especially with „lieber …, als dass …“ (= “I’d rather … than …”). It’s also used after „zu“ to express that something is so much/so [adjective/adverb] that the result is impossible: „zu …, als dass …“ (= “too … for … to …”), often with Konjunktiv II in the clause (e.g., „hätte … können“).
target_language_example: Es war zu laut, als dass wir hätten schlafen können.
native_language_example: It was too loud for us to have been able to sleep.

additional_notes:
“als du” is “als” + “du” and is used in two very common ways:
1) Time: “als du …” = “when you …” (talking about a single point or period in the past). In this use, “als” introduces a subordinate clause, so the conjugated verb goes to the end: “als du gekommen bist …”.
2) Comparison: “…, als du (bist)” = “…, than you (are)”. The verb is often left out because it’s understood: “größer als du (bist)”.
target_language_example: Ich war überrascht, als du so früh angerufen hast.
native_language_example: I was surprised when you called so early.

additional_notes: Used after a comparative (e.g., besser, größer, klüger, reicher) to say someone/something is more/less X than the listener expects. Often follows a comma: „…, als du denkst.“
target_language_example: Das ist schwieriger, als du denkst.
native_language_example: That is harder than you think.

additional_notes: Compositional phrase: als + er. It often means "when he" when introducing a past event or situation, and "than he" after a comparative expression such as mehr, älter, jünger, or besser. In the subordinate clause, the conjugated verb goes to the end.
target_language_example: Als er nach Hause kam, schliefen alle schon.
native_language_example: When he came home, everyone was already asleep.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a specific moment in the past. "als" introduces a one-time past event; "er" = he; "starb" is the simple past of "sterben" (to die). You can swap the pronoun: "als sie starb" (when she died), or use a name: "als Tom starb".
target_language_example: Er war bei seiner Mutter, als er starb.
native_language_example: He was with his mother when he died.

additional_notes: Used after a comparative (e.g., mehr, weniger, stärker, eher, früher/später) to say something is different from what you expected. It often implies the result surprised you.
target_language_example: Der Test war schwieriger als erwartet.
native_language_example: The test was harder than expected.

additional_notes: Uses **als** for a single event in the past. **es** is a dummy pronoun meaning "it" (the event/situation), and **passierte** is past tense of *passieren* (to happen). Common after statements or questions about where/with whom you were at that moment: *Ich war ..., als es passierte.* / *Warst du da, als es passierte?*
target_language_example: Ich war im Zug, als es passierte.
native_language_example: I was on the train when it happened.

meaning: “as if you had …” / “like you had …” (talking to one person).
additional_notes: Used to compare reality with an imagined situation, often in a guess, impression, or exaggeration. It introduces a clause in the subjunctive (Konjunktiv II) with hättest (from haben) + past participle (e.g., verloren, genossen, gehabt). Common after expressions like du wirkst/klangst/siehst aus, mir war, als … .
target_language_example: Du siehst aus, als hättest du die ganze Nacht nicht geschlafen.
native_language_example: You look as if you hadn’t slept all night.

additional_notes: Usually introduces a subordinate clause. For a specific situation or time in the past, als ich means 'when I', and the verb goes to the end of the clause: als ich ankam. After a comparative, it means 'than I' or 'than me': besser als ich. For repeated events or future situations, German usually uses wenn instead of als.
target_language_example: Als ich gestern nach Hause kam, war niemand da.
native_language_example: When I came home yesterday, nobody was there.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a single event in the past: **Als ich ankam, ...** = “When I arrived, ...”. Often sets the time for what happened next. In an **als**-clause, the verb goes to the end (**ankam**). Compare: **als** (one-time past) vs **wenn** (whenever / if, repeated or general).
target_language_example: Als ich ankam, war das Konzert schon vorbei.
native_language_example: When I arrived, the concert was already over.

additional_notes: Used after a comparison (often with words like einfacher/schwieriger, weniger/mehr, länger/kürzer, besser/schlechter) to say reality is different from your expectation. Common pattern: "(mehr/weniger/…)-er, als ich dachte."
target_language_example: Die Reise war teurer, als ich dachte.
native_language_example: The trip was more expensive than I thought.

meaning: “when I … you” (talking about a specific moment in the past).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a past-time clause with **als** (one particular time/occasion). **ich** = “I” (subject), **dich** = “you” (direct object, informal singular). You’ll usually need a verb to complete it (e.g., *als ich dich sah / gesehen habe / besucht habe / gerufen habe*). Word order: the verb goes to the end of the *als*-clause in German (e.g., *als ich dich gestern gerufen habe*).
target_language_example: Ich war erleichtert, als ich dich endlich gesehen habe.
native_language_example: I was relieved when I finally saw you.

additional_notes: Used after a comparative (mehr, weniger, besser, leichter, teurer, etc.) to compare reality with what you expected in the past. In these sentences, als means “than” (not “when”). Often paired with “(nicht) so …, wie ich erwartet hatte” (= “(not) as … as I had expected”).
target_language_example: Der Test war schwieriger, als ich erwartet hatte.
native_language_example: The test was harder than I had expected.

meaning: "when I" / "than I" + "it" (referring back to something already mentioned).
additional_notes: This is a common chunk inside a longer clause. **Als** can mean **"when"** (for a one-time past event) or **"than"** (in comparisons). **Es** usually points back to a previously mentioned thing/idea, and in comparisons it often stands for an implied verb phrase: *geduldiger, als ich es bin* = “more patient than I am (patient)”; *besser ausgedrückt, als ich es könnte* = “better expressed than I could (express it).” Word order: the verb typically comes at the end of the *als*-clause (e.g., *als ich es bemerkte / als ich es bin / als ich es könnte*).
target_language_example: Das ist schwieriger, als ich es gedacht habe.
native_language_example: That is harder than I thought.

meaning: “when I … this morning” (talking about a past moment).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a time clause in the past with als (“when” for a one-time past situation). You typically add a verb at the end of the clause: als ich heute Morgen aufgewacht bin / als ich heute Morgen angerufen habe. The main clause and als-clause often describe what was happening at that time.
target_language_example: Ich war noch müde, als ich heute Morgen das Haus verlassen habe.
native_language_example: I was still tired when I left the house this morning.

meaning: "when I (… ) him" (talking about a past moment).
additional_notes: Used to start a time clause about the past. **als** is used for a single time period/event in the past (“when”), not for repeated events (then you often use **wenn**). **ich** = “I”. **ihn** is the accusative form of “he” and means “him” (the direct object). The verb usually comes at the end of the **als**-clause: *Als ich ihn sah, …*
target_language_example: Als ich ihn gestern getroffen habe, war er sehr freundlich.
native_language_example: When I met him yesterday, he was very friendly.

meaning: "when I was in …" / "when I lived in …" (introduces a time in the past).
additional_notes: Used to start a subordinate clause with **als** for a single time period/event in the past. Word order: **Als ich in + place + verb …,** then the main clause follows (often with the verb in position 2). Common with **war** (was), **wohnte/lebte** (lived). Not used for repeated situations in the past (that’s usually **wenn**).
target_language_example: Als ich in Berlin war, habe ich jeden Tag Museen besucht.
native_language_example: When I was in Berlin, I visited museums every day.

meaning: “when I was young” / “back when I was young.”
additional_notes: Used to talk about a past period in your life. It’s a time clause introduced by **als** (for a single time/period in the past), often paired with the simple past (**war**) or past tense in the main clause (**habe … gespielt**, **lebte**, **konnte**). You can put it at the start of the sentence (then the verb comes second in the main clause) or later in the sentence.
target_language_example: Als ich jung war, wollte ich Feuerwehrmann werden.
native_language_example: When I was young, I wanted to be a firefighter.

meaning: when I was little / when I was young.
additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened regularly or at a specific time in your childhood. It often introduces a past situation (“Als ich klein war, …”) and commonly goes with past tense verbs (Perfekt or Präteritum). Word order can vary: “Als ich klein war, …” or “…, als ich klein war.”
target_language_example: Als ich klein war, wollte ich jeden Tag ein Eis essen.
native_language_example: When I was little, I wanted to eat ice cream every day.

additional_notes: Used with **als** to talk about a **single event in the past** (“when…”). It often starts a time clause, and the verb goes to the end in that clause: **Als ich nach Hause kam, …**. In the main clause, the verb comes right after this clause: **…, bemerkte ich / sah er / lernte Tom …**.
target_language_example: Als ich nach Hause kam, war niemand da.
native_language_example: When I got home, nobody was there.

meaning: “when I still …” / “back when I still …” (talking about a past time that continued up to that point).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a time clause in the past: *als* = “when” (one-time/past period), *ich* = “I”, *noch* = “still”. It’s usually followed by a verb at the end of the clause (e.g., **als ich noch klein war** = “when I was still little”). Often used for childhood memories or earlier stages of life.
target_language_example: Als ich noch Student war, hatte ich kaum Geld.
native_language_example: When I was still a student, I hardly had any money.

additional_notes: Used with comparatives ("-er" forms or "mehr/weniger") to emphasize that something is stronger/more intense now than at any time in the past: "schöner/stärker/mehr … als je zuvor". It can also appear as a short headline-style phrase (e.g., "Lebendiger als je zuvor.").
target_language_example: Wir sind heute besser vorbereitet als je zuvor.
native_language_example: Today we’re better prepared than ever before.

additional_notes: Used in comparisons with "mehr/besser/schneller … als" to say someone does something more/better/etc. than all others in a group. "jeder" = everyone/anyone; "andere" = other. It can refer to people in general or in a specific group (e.g., "hier", "in der Klasse").
target_language_example: Sie arbeitet härter als jeder andere im Team.
native_language_example: She works harder than anyone else on the team.

additional_notes: Means “as if / as though” and introduces a comparison to something unreal or only imagined. Often used with Konjunktiv II (subjunctive) to show it’s not really true: „als ob er das wüsste“ (“as if he knew that”). It can also be used sarcastically/exclaiming disbelief: „Als ob!“ / „Als ob dir jemand glauben würde!“ (“Yeah, right! / As if anyone would believe you!”).
target_language_example: Er tut so, als ob er mich nicht kennen würde.
native_language_example: He acts as if he didn’t know me.

additional_notes: Used to compare reality with an (often unlikely) impression or hypothetical situation: "It looks/sounds as if you..." It can also be used sarcastically to express disbelief: "Yeah, as if you had a choice." The verb typically goes to the end of the clause (e.g., „als ob du es nicht mehr willst“). In more formal German you may see Konjunktiv II (e.g., „als ob du es nicht mehr wolltest“).
target_language_example: Du redest, als ob du alles besser wüsstest.
native_language_example: You talk as if you knew everything better.

additional_notes: Used to compare something to an imagined situation: “He talks as if he knew everything.” Very often followed by Konjunktiv II (subjunctive) to show it’s not (necessarily) true: wäre/wär’ (were), hätte (had), wüsste (knew). In everyday speech you may hear contractions like “wär’”.
target_language_example: Er schaut mich an, als ob er mich nicht kennen würde.
native_language_example: He looks at me as if he didn’t know me.

additional_notes: Used to say that something seems a certain way, or that someone behaves/speaks in a way that isn’t really true. Very often followed by Konjunktiv II to show it’s unreal: „als ob ich verrückt wäre“ (not really crazy). You’ll also see it after feelings/perceptions like „Mir war, als ob …“ (“It felt as if …”).
target_language_example: Er tut so, als ob ich ihn beleidigt hätte.
native_language_example: He acts as if I had insulted him.

additional_notes: Used to compare reality with an appearance, impression, or imagined situation. It’s often followed by Konjunktiv II (e.g., wäre/hätte) to show something is not real or is just assumed: "als ob sie reich wäre" = as if she were rich. In speech you may also hear "als wenn sie" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Er tut so, als ob sie ihn nicht kennen würde.
native_language_example: He acts as if she didn’t know him.

additional_notes: Lowercase sie can mean 'she' or 'they', so the exact meaning depends on context. With als, it commonly means 'when she/they' for a specific past event, or 'than she/her/them' after a comparison. In German, als is used for one-time events in the past; beginners often confuse this with wenn. In phrases like 'als sie auszuführen', sie can refer back to a plural noun, so English may translate it as 'them'.
target_language_example: Ich war froh, als sie endlich ankam.
