native_language_example: I was glad when she finally arrived.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a past event (often a one-time event) with **als** (“when” for past situations). The verb goes to the end of the **als**-clause: **als sie die Nachricht hörte**. Often sets the scene for an emotional reaction in the main clause.
target_language_example: Als sie die Nachricht hörte, konnte sie zuerst nichts sagen.
native_language_example: When she heard the news, she couldn’t say anything at first.

additional_notes: Used after a comparative ("-er" forms or "mehr/weniger") to compare something to what is normal or typical: "länger als sonst", "voller als sonst", "später als sonst". You can also hear "nicht mehr als sonst (auch)" = "no more than usual".
target_language_example: Heute bin ich früher als sonst aufgestanden.
native_language_example: Today I got up earlier than usual.

additional_notes:
"als wir" most often means "when we" and is used for a single event in the past (often like English "when"). Example: "Als wir ankamen, ..." = "When we arrived, ..." 
It can also appear in comparisons after a comparative word (besser, größer, schneller, etc.): "Besser Sie als wir." = "Better you than us."
target_language_example: Als wir zu Hause ankamen, war es schon spät.
native_language_example: When we got home, it was already late.

additional_notes: Used after a comparative (länger, näher, schlimmer, ernster, reicher, etc.) to say reality is different from what you expected. Pattern: [comparative] + als wir dachten. In everyday speech you can also say: „als gedacht“ (“than expected”).
target_language_example: Der Weg war kürzer, als wir dachten.
native_language_example: The route was shorter than we thought.

additional_notes: Used to start a time clause in the past: **als** = “when (at that time)”. **wir** = “we”. **uns** is a reflexive pronoun that often means “each other” with plural subjects (e.g., **als wir uns kennenlernten** = “when we met / got to know each other”, **als wir uns den Film angesehen haben** = “when we watched the movie”). The verb usually comes at the end of the clause after **als wir uns …**.
target_language_example: Als wir uns das erste Mal trafen, waren wir beide nervös.
native_language_example: When we met for the first time, we were both nervous.

additional_notes: Used to make an unreal/imaginary comparison (often implying it’s not true). It uses Konjunktiv II (wäre = subjunctive of „sein“) and typically comes after a comma: „…, als wäre er …“ You can replace „er“ with other subjects: „als wäre ich/du/sie/wir/ihr/sie“.
target_language_example: Sie redet mit mir, als wäre er nicht im Raum.
native_language_example: She talks to me as if he weren’t in the room.

meaning: “as if it were/was” (as though it were).
additional_notes: Used to describe something that seems unreal, hypothetical, or only appears true. Very common in comparisons and impressions (e.g., “It feels as if…”). The verb is in Konjunktiv II (subjunctive), so you’ll often see it with time words like „gestern“ or „erst“ to mean “as if it were only yesterday.”
target_language_example: Er tut so, als wäre es ganz einfach.
native_language_example: He acts as if it were really easy.

additional_notes: Used to describe how something seems or how someone is treated, not as a real fact. It uses Konjunktiv II (wäre) after als (often also als ob) to show that the situation is hypothetical or contrary to reality: "Sie behandelt mich, als wäre ich ..." = "She treats me as if I were ...".
target_language_example: Er schaut mich an, als wäre ich verrückt.
native_language_example: He looks at me as if I were crazy.

meaning: "Well, I…" (a spoken filler to start or soften what you’re about to say).
additional_notes: Common in conversation when beginning an explanation, confession, or uncertain statement. It often signals hesitation, a transition, or that you’re organizing your thoughts. Not the same as English “also” (= “too/as well”); German “also” can mean “so/well/anyway” depending on context.
target_language_example: Also, ich bin mir nicht sicher, ob das stimmt.
native_language_example: Well, I’m not sure if that’s true.

additional_notes: Used to open a question, often to move the conversation along or get to the point. Depending on tone, it can sound neutral (“So, what are we doing?”) or a bit impatient/expecting an explanation (“So, what’s this all about?”). Note: German „also“ usually means “so/well/therefore,” not English “also.”
target_language_example: Also, was machen wir jetzt?
native_language_example: So, what are we doing now?

meaning: "all right then" / "okay, fine" (accepting a plan or moving on).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a sentence as a conversational marker to signal a decision, agreement, or reluctant acceptance, often followed by "dann" (then). It can also introduce a conclusion or lesson ("Also gut, was lernen wir daraus?").
target_language_example: Also gut, dann machen wir das so.
native_language_example: All right then, we'll do it like that.

meaning: to grow old; to get old.
additional_notes: Literally “to become old.” Used to talk about aging in general or about wanting to spend your life with someone (“Mit dir möchte ich alt werden” = “I want to grow old with you”). Often appears with adverbs/phrases like „in Würde“ (with dignity).
target_language_example: Ich will gesund alt werden.
native_language_example: I want to grow old in good health.

additional_notes: This is the accusative form of **(ein) alter Mann**. After verbs like **helfen** (to help), German often uses the **dative** (e.g., *hilf einem alten Mann*), but in other contexts you may see *einen alten Mann* as the direct object.
target_language_example: Ich sehe einen alten Mann im Park.
native_language_example: I see an old man in the park.

meaning: old man; (also) “old man” as a form of address (often teasing or annoyed).
additional_notes: Literally refers to an elderly male person: "ein alter Mann" = "an old man". It can also be used when speaking directly to someone (often with a comma: "alter Mann,") similar to English "old man"—this can sound informal and can be friendly/teasing or insulting depending on tone and context (and the person may not actually be old).
target_language_example: Da drüben steht ein alter Mann.
native_language_example: An old man is standing over there.

meaning: “old house”; also (as a friendly greeting) “old pal/old friend”.
additional_notes: Literally, it means an old building/house: „unser altes Haus“. But in the greeting „Na, altes Haus!“ it’s a casual, friendly way to address someone you know well (similar to “Hey, old friend!”). In that idiomatic use, it doesn’t refer to a building.
target_language_example: Na, altes Haus, wie geht’s dir?
native_language_example: Hey, old pal, how are you?

additional_notes: Used to give a recommendation or say what the best option is. Often appears in sentences like “Am besten + verb …” (= “It’s best to …”) or “X ist am besten” (= “X is best”).
target_language_example: Am besten rufst du morgen früh an.
native_language_example: It’s best if you call tomorrow morning.

additional_notes: "Am besten" is the adverbial superlative of "gut" and is used to say what works best or what you recommend (often like “it’s best to … / you’d better …”). Use "am besten" for actions/methods (Wie macht man das am besten?), but use "der/die/das beste" before a noun (z.B. "der beste Plan").
target_language_example: Am besten gehst du früher los, dann bist du pünktlich.
native_language_example: It’s best to leave earlier so you’ll be on time.

meaning: most of all; preferably (the option you like best).
additional_notes: Used to say your strongest preference among choices (superlative of "gern"). Common with verbs like "mögen" (like), "hören" (listen to), and with questions: "Was/Wen/Welchen … am liebsten?" It can also appear with "würde(n)" to ask what someone would prefer in a hypothetical situation.
target_language_example: Ich würde am liebsten zu Hause bleiben.
native_language_example: I’d prefer to stay at home (most of all).

additional_notes: Used to form the superlative with verbs and in many set phrases: "am" + adjective/adverb + "-sten" (or "-esten"). It often answers questions like "What do you like most?" and can also mean "the most" in comparisons (e.g., who/what does something the most). Not the same as English "at most" (= "höchstens").
target_language_example: Ich mag den Sommer am meisten.
native_language_example: I like summer the most.

additional_notes: Superlative form of "schnell" (fast). Used to say someone/something is the fastest, or which route/method is the quickest: "am schnellsten" = "fastest" (literally "at the fastest"). Often appears with questions like "Wie komme ich am schnellsten ...?" (What’s the fastest way for me to get ...?).
target_language_example: Wie komme ich am schnellsten ins Stadtzentrum?
native_language_example: What’s the fastest way to get to the city center?

additional_notes: Used to form the superlative of the adjective/adverb "schön" (beautiful, nice), often with seasons or places: "im Frühling am schönsten" = "most beautiful in spring." Common in the pattern "[Place] ist ... am schönsten" and the set phrase "Zu Hause ist’s am schönsten" (Home is nicest/best).
target_language_example: Die Stadt ist nachts am schönsten.
native_language_example: The city is most beautiful at night.

additional_notes: Superlative form of "wenig" (little). Used to compare three or more things: "am wenigsten interessant" = "the least interesting". Often appears with "von den ..." (of the ...): "von den dreien am wenigsten". With verbs/likes: "das mag ich am wenigsten" = "I like that the least". Also in the common phrase "wenn man es am wenigsten erwartet" = "when you least expect it".
target_language_example: Ich bin am Wochenende am wenigsten gestresst.
native_language_example: I’m least stressed on the weekend.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happens in the evening (a general time of day or a regular routine). Literally "an dem Abend"; commonly used with habits (e.g., "am Abend sind wir zu Hause"). For a specific evening you can also say "an diesem Abend" or simply "abends" for "in the evenings."
target_language_example: Am Abend rufe ich meine Eltern an.
native_language_example: In the evening, I call my parents.

meaning: at the beginning; in the beginning (at first).
additional_notes: Used to talk about the first stage of something (a time period, a process, an event, a story). Often contrasts with what happened later (e.g., “Am Anfang …, aber später …”). Can refer to time (“am Anfang des Jahres”) or to a position/order (“am Anfang stehen” = to be at the start of a line/sequence).
target_language_example: Am Anfang war alles schwierig, aber dann wurde es besser.
native_language_example: At the beginning everything was difficult, but then it got better.

additional_notes: Used in phone calls to say that you/your name/your organization is the one speaking on the line. Common in more formal/old-fashioned telephone style: "Ja, am Apparat" (= "Yes, speaking") or "X am Apparat" (= "This is X speaking"). Also used in questions like "Wer ist (bitte) am Apparat?" (= "Who’s speaking?").
target_language_example: Guten Tag, Müller am Apparat.
native_language_example: Good day, this is Müller speaking.

meaning: (vulgar) screwed / in deep trouble; also: broken/ruined.
additional_notes:
Very informal and vulgar (literally “at the ass”), used in several common expressions:
- „am Arsch sein“ = to be screwed / done for / exhausted.
- „Das geht mir/dir am Arsch vorbei.“ = I/you don’t care at all.
- „Jemanden am Arsch kriegen“ = to catch/get someone (often in a threatening sense).
Often expresses frustration: „Am Arsch!“ ≈ “Oh crap!” / “We’re screwed!”
target_language_example: Wenn wir den Zug verpassen, sind wir am Arsch.
native_language_example: If we miss the train, we’re screwed.

additional_notes: "am" = "an dem" and is used for locations (where something happens). Common with verbs like ankommen (arrive), abfahren (depart), treffen/begegnen (meet/run into).
target_language_example: Wir sehen uns morgen am Bahnhof um acht Uhr.
native_language_example: We’ll see each other tomorrow at the train station at eight o’clock.

meaning: on the ground / on the floor; (figurative) devastated.
additional_notes: Literally means being located on the ground/floor (liegen/schlafen/sitzen am Boden). It’s also common in the fixed phrase „am Boden zerstört“, meaning emotionally crushed/devastated. Often used with movement or position: „am Boden rennen“ (run along the ground), „bewusstlos am Boden liegen“ (lie unconscious on the ground).
target_language_example: Nach der Nachricht war sie völlig am Boden zerstört.
native_language_example: After the news, she was completely devastated.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone feeling extremely upset after bad news, a breakup, disappointment, etc. Often used with "sein" (e.g., "Ich bin am Boden zerstört"). "Am Boden" literally means "on the ground" and emphasizes being knocked down emotionally.
target_language_example: Als ich die Nachricht hörte, war ich am Boden zerstört.
native_language_example: When I heard the news, I was devastated.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone feeling extremely upset after bad news or a major disappointment. It’s an idiom; literally it looks like “to be destroyed on the ground,” but the meaning is emotional devastation. Conjugate *sein* as needed: ich bin / du bist / er/sie ist / wir sind / ihr seid / sie sind **am Boden zerstört**.
target_language_example: Als sie die Nachricht hörte, wollte sie einfach nur am Boden zerstört sein.
native_language_example: When she heard the news, she just wanted to be devastated.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens on Tuesday. "am" is a contraction of "an dem" and is used with days of the week (and dates) to mean "on". You can use it in statements and questions about schedules/appointments.
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns am Dienstag um zehn Uhr.
native_language_example: We’re meeting on Tuesday at ten o’clock.

additional_notes: Often used to mean “in the end / ultimately” when talking about the final result (Am Ende werden sie nicht durchkommen.). It can also mean literally “at the end” (of a process, story, line, etc.). In the fixed expression “Ich bin am Ende.” it means “I’m at my limit / I’m exhausted / I can’t go on (anymore).”
target_language_example: Am Ende hat er doch recht gehabt.
native_language_example: In the end, he turned out to be right.

meaning: at the end of the (feminine genitive: der).
additional_notes: Used to indicate position at the far end of something (e.g., hallway, line) or something written at the bottom/end of a page. It’s the contraction of "an dem" → "am" + "Ende" + the genitive article "der" (because the next noun is feminine, e.g. "die Seite" → "der Seite"). With masculine/neuter nouns you’ll see "am Ende des" (e.g. "am Ende des Tages").
target_language_example: Am Ende der Straße gibt es einen Supermarkt.
native_language_example: At the end of the street there is a supermarket.

meaning: at the end of the sentence.
additional_notes: Used when talking about where something should be placed in a sentence (especially punctuation like a period) or about word order in grammar. Literally: “at the end of the sentence.”
target_language_example: Setz bitte ein Ausrufezeichen am Ende des Satzes.
native_language_example: Please put an exclamation mark at the end of the sentence.

additional_notes: “am” = “an dem” (at the). Used to say someone or something is located right next to the window (often in a room, e.g., a seat in a café/restaurant or someone standing there).
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, ist der Platz am Fenster noch frei?
native_language_example: Excuse me, is the seat by the window still free?

additional_notes: "am" = "an dem" (dative), used for a specific place. You use it to say something happens at the airport (meeting someone there, being there, etc.). With location questions like "Wo?" it typically takes dative: "am Flughafen".
target_language_example: Wir sehen uns morgen am Flughafen.
native_language_example: We’ll see each other tomorrow at the airport.

meaning: by/on the river; at the river.
additional_notes: "am" = "an dem" and is used for a location right next to something (here: the river). With movement you’ll often hear related phrases like "am Fluss entlang" (along the river).
target_language_example: Das Café ist am Fluss.
native_language_example: The café is by the river.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens on a specific day (Friday). It’s the contraction of "an dem Freitag" and is used with days of the week: am Montag, am Dienstag, etc.
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns am Freitag um 18 Uhr.
native_language_example: We’re meeting on Friday at 6 p.m.

meaning: on/at the neck; (idiom) on your back / to have to deal with.
additional_notes: “am” = “an dem”. Literal uses talk about something located at the neck (“Der Pullover kratzt am Hals.”). In the common idiom “jdn/etw am Hals haben” it means someone/something is bothering you or you’re stuck dealing with them/it (e.g., “die Polizei am Hals haben” = the police are after you / on your case; “jemanden am Hals haben” can be like “to have someone on your hands”).
target_language_example: Wenn wir zu spät kommen, haben wir den Chef am Hals.
native_language_example: If we’re late, we’ll have the boss on our back.

additional_notes: Used to say something is located or happening up in the sky. Very common with verbs like sein (to be), fliegen (to fly), funkeln (to sparkle), and with things like stars, clouds, planes, birds. Literally "at the sky" (an + dem), but in English you usually say "in the sky."
target_language_example: Heute ist kein einziges Wölkchen am Himmel.
native_language_example: There isn’t a single cloud in the sky today.

additional_notes: Used to say something is visible far away where the sky seems to meet the الأرض/land/sea. Often with verbs like erscheinen (appear), sehen (see), versinken (sink), or to describe the sun at sunrise/sunset. "am" = "an dem" (dative).
target_language_example: Am Horizont ziehen dunkle Wolken auf.
native_language_example: Dark clouds are gathering on the horizon.

meaning: at the piano; (playing) on the piano.
additional_notes: "am" = "an dem" and is used here for being positioned at an instrument or doing something using it. With verbs like "üben" or "spielen", it means practicing/playing the piano; with "begleiten", it means accompanying someone on the piano.
target_language_example: Er sitzt am Klavier und spielt leise.
native_language_example: He’s sitting at the piano and playing quietly.

additional_notes: Means “alive” (not dead). Common with verbs like sein/bleiben (“to be/stay alive”) and jemanden am Leben lassen/halten/erhalten (“to let/keep someone alive”).
target_language_example: Zum Glück ist das Kind noch am Leben.
native_language_example: Luckily, the child is still alive.

additional_notes: Used for literally surviving (not dying), often in urgent or life-or-death situations. Common with modal verbs like wollen/müssen/sollen/dürfen: „am Leben bleiben wollen/müssen/sollen/dürfen“.
target_language_example: Wenn wir Hilfe bekommen, können wir am Leben bleiben.
native_language_example: If we get help, we can stay alive.

additional_notes: Used to describe being alive (often with feelings like grateful, happy, or lucky), especially after danger or as a general appreciation of life. Common with adjectives like „froh/ glücklich/ dankbar“: „Ich bin froh/dankbar, am Leben zu sein.“
target_language_example: Nach der Operation war sie einfach nur dankbar, am Leben zu sein.
native_language_example: After the operation, she was simply grateful to be alive.

meaning: by the sea; at the seaside.
additional_notes: “am” = “an dem” (at/on the). “am Meer” is used for being located next to the sea (a town, a house, spending holidays there). Often contrasts with “im Meer” (= in the sea/water).
target_language_example: Im Sommer fahren viele Leute ans Meer und verbringen ein paar Tage am Meer.
native_language_example: In summer many people go to the sea and spend a few days at the seaside.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens on a specific Monday. "am" = "an dem" and is used for days of the week and specific dates (am Montag, am 3. Mai).
target_language_example: Am Montag habe ich frei.
native_language_example: On Monday I have the day off.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happens during the morning. It can refer to a specific morning (often with past/future context: "Am Morgen war...") or to a regular habit ("am Morgen" = in the mornings). It’s a contraction of "an dem Morgen" ("am" = "an dem").
target_language_example: Am Morgen habe ich oft keine Zeit für ein großes Frühstück.
native_language_example: In the morning, I often don’t have time for a big breakfast.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happens or is planned during the afternoon. "am" = "an dem" (on/in the), so it often translates as "in the afternoon" in English.
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns am Nachmittag im Park.
native_language_example: We’re meeting in the park in the afternoon.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens on a specific Saturday. "am" = "an dem" and is used with days of the week (am Montag, am Dienstag, etc.).
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns am Samstag um 10 Uhr.
native_language_example: We’re meeting on Saturday at 10 o’clock.

additional_notes: Used for the end of a process, story, or time period ("In the end, ..."), and also for the physical end of something ("at the back/end of the train"). Often similar to "zum Schluss"; "am Schluss" can sound a bit more like "at the end (of it all)".
target_language_example: Am Schluss hat alles doch noch funktioniert.
native_language_example: In the end, everything worked out after all.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens on Sunday (a specific day of the week). It often answers the question "Wann?" (When?). Note: "am" = "an dem" and is used with days and dates (am Montag, am 3. Mai).
target_language_example: Am Sonntag haben wir Zeit.
native_language_example: On Sunday we have time.

meaning: at the wheel; in control (of something).
additional_notes: Used literally for driving a vehicle: „am Steuer sitzen“ = to be driving / to be behind the wheel. It can also be used figuratively to mean being in charge, especially with „das Steuer“ (e.g., „am Steuer des Landes“ = in control of the country).
target_language_example: Ich bin heute am Steuer, du kannst dich entspannen.
native_language_example: I’m driving today; you can relax.

meaning: to go for a walk on the beach.
additional_notes: Used with the verb „spazieren gehen“ (= to go for a walk). „am Strand“ means “at/on the beach” (literally: at the beach). Common in relaxed, leisure contexts; can be used in different tenses (e.g., „gingen“, „bin … gegangen“).
target_language_example: Wir gehen abends am Strand spazieren.
native_language_example: We go for a walk on the beach in the evening.

additional_notes: Contraction of "an dem". Often used (1) to mean "during the day" (opposite of "in der Nacht"), and (2) to express frequency: "einmal/zweimal/mehrmals am Tag" = "once/twice/multiple times a day". You can also specify a particular day with a following noun phrase: "am Tag der Hochzeit" = "on the day of the wedding".
target_language_example: Ich trinke dreimal am Tag Kaffee.
native_language_example: I drink coffee three times a day.

meaning: at the scene of the crime (at the location where it happened).
additional_notes: "Tatort" is the place where a crime happened; "am" = "an dem". Often used in police/news reports: "am Tatort gesehen" (seen at the crime scene), "am Tatort gestorben/verstorben" (died at the scene).
target_language_example: Die Polizei fand die Waffe am Tatort.
native_language_example: The police found the weapon at the crime scene.

meaning: on the phone; talking on the phone.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is currently on a phone call or to describe how someone sounds/what happens during a call. Common with verbs like sein (to be), klingen (to sound), sprechen (to talk), and phrases like Zeit am Telefon verbringen (to spend time on the phone).
target_language_example: Kannst du später anrufen? Ich bin gerade am Telefon.
native_language_example: Can you call later? I’m on the phone right now.

meaning: at the table (sitting/being at a table).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is seated at a table or an activity happens there (eating, playing cards, talking). It’s a contraction of "an dem Tisch" ("an" + dative for location). Often with verbs like "sitzen", "essen", "spielen", "reden".
target_language_example: Wir sitzen am Tisch und trinken Kaffee.
native_language_example: We’re sitting at the table and drinking coffee.

meaning: on the weekend; at the weekend.
additional_notes: Used to talk about something happening during the weekend in general, often as a repeated habit ("am Wochenende") or about plans for the upcoming weekend. "am" = "an dem" (at/on the).
target_language_example: Am Wochenende schlafe ich oft länger.
native_language_example: On the weekend, I often sleep in longer.

meaning: at the destination; at the goal (finished/achieved).
additional_notes: Used for reaching a physical destination (arriving somewhere) or a figurative goal (being finished or successful). Often appears with verbs like sein (Ich bin am Ziel), ankommen (am Ziel ankommen), and with bald/fast/schon to say you're nearly there. Also used in comparisons like knapp am Ziel vorbei (“just missed the target/goal”).
target_language_example: Wir sind endlich am Ziel und können uns ausruhen.
native_language_example: We’re finally at our destination and can rest.

additional_notes: Used to give advice or suggest the best option. Common patterns: “Am besten + Verb …” (Am besten nimmst du … = You’d better take …), “Am besten wäre es, wenn …” (It would be best if …), and “Am besten, wir …” (Best if we … / We’d better …).
target_language_example: Am besten gehst du jetzt nach Hause und ruhst dich aus.
native_language_example: You’d better go home now and rest.

additional_notes: Used as the superlative of "gut" in an adverbial sense, especially in questions asking for the best method: "Wie kann man das am besten machen?" It can also mean "preferably" when choosing between options: "Am besten rufst du morgen an."
target_language_example: Am besten machst du gleich einen Termin aus.
native_language_example: It’s best if you make an appointment right away.

meaning: all over the body; on the whole body.
additional_notes: Used to say something (itching, shaking, spots, bruises, pain, etc.) affects your body everywhere, not just one part. Often appears with verbs like „jucken“ (itch), „zittern“ (shiver), or with symptoms like „Flecken“ (spots) and „blaue Flecken“ (bruises).
target_language_example: Nach dem Insektenstich hatte ich am ganzen Körper Ausschlag.
native_language_example: After the insect bite, I had a rash all over my body.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened on the most recent weekend (Saturday/Sunday). It’s a time phrase: "am" = "an dem" (on the), "letzten" = last (dative). You can also say "letztes Wochenende" (without "am") depending on the sentence.
target_language_example: Am letzten Wochenende habe ich meine Freunde besucht.
native_language_example: Last weekend I visited my friends.

meaning: most of all; preferably; (I/you/etc.) would most like to.
additional_notes: Used to express a strong preference. Often with verbs like "möchte" or "würde" to say what you’d most like to do: "Am liebsten würde ich ..." It can also modify a verb to mean "preferably/most often": "Ich trinke am liebsten ..."
target_language_example: Am liebsten würde ich heute einfach zu Hause bleiben.
native_language_example: Most of all, I’d like to just stay at home today.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a preference or favorite. Often with verbs like mögen (to like) or schlafen (to sleep): „Am liebsten mag ich …“ / „Ich mag … am liebsten.“ It can also mean “preferably” in the sense of “if I can choose”: „Ich würde am liebsten zu Hause bleiben.“
target_language_example: Ich trinke am liebsten Kaffee am Morgen.
native_language_example: I like drinking coffee best in the morning.

additional_notes: Used with verbs or adjectives to say something is liked, wanted, or affects you more than anything else (superlative). Often appears in questions like "Was ... am meisten?" = "What ... the most?" It’s the superlative of "viel" (more: "mehr", most: "am meisten").
target_language_example: Ich mag Schokolade am meisten.
native_language_example: I like chocolate the most.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happens on the morning of the next day (after what was just mentioned). Often starts a sentence as a time expression (position 1), but it can also appear later: „Ich rief Tom am nächsten Morgen an.“
target_language_example: Am nächsten Morgen gingen wir früh los.
native_language_example: The next morning we left early.

meaning: the next day; on the following day.
additional_notes: Used to say something happened one day after a time/event that was just mentioned. Very common for telling stories or describing sequences of events. Often appears at the start of a sentence: "Am nächsten Tag …"
target_language_example: Am nächsten Tag sind wir früh losgefahren.
native_language_example: The next day we set off early.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happens (or is done) again on the following day. Common in stories and when describing routines. Word order can vary depending on emphasis (e.g., „wieder am nächsten Tag“).
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns am nächsten Tag wieder um zehn Uhr.
native_language_example: We’ll meet again the next day at ten o’clock.

additional_notes: Used to say two events happen on the same calendar day as each other, or on the exact day already mentioned. Often refers back to a previous time expression (e.g., "he arrived on Monday" → "am selben Tag" = on that same Monday).
target_language_example: Wir haben uns getroffen und am selben Tag zusammen gegessen.
native_language_example: We met and ate together on the same day.

additional_notes: Used mainly for things like lights, devices, engines, etc. In real sentences the separable part usually goes to the end: „Das Licht ist an.“ The opposite is „aus sein“ (to be off).
target_language_example: Kannst du prüfen, ob das Licht an sein soll?
native_language_example: Can you check whether the light is supposed to be on?

meaning: on board (on/into a ship, plane, train, etc.).
additional_notes: Used for being on a vehicle (on board) or getting onto it (come on board/go on board). Common with verbs like „kommen/gehen“ (to come/go aboard) and in announcements like „Alle an Bord!“ (“All aboard!”).
target_language_example: Sind alle Passagiere an Bord?
native_language_example: Are all passengers on board?

additional_notes: Used to give advice by imagining yourself in the other person’s situation (“in your place”). Very common in spoken German. It’s usually followed by an infinitive at the end of the clause: „An deiner Stelle würde ich … machen/gehen/sagen.“ You can change the pronoun: „an Ihrer Stelle“ (formal), „an seiner/ihrer Stelle“ (his/her), „an eurer Stelle“ (you plural).
target_language_example: An deiner Stelle würde ich früher ins Bett gehen.
native_language_example: If I were you, I would go to bed earlier.

additional_notes: "An dem" is the dative form used after the preposition "an" when the noun is masculine or neuter ("dem"). It often answers where something is (at/on something) or what something is connected to (e.g., "Interesse an dem", "teilnehmen an dem"). In everyday speech it’s very often shortened to "am" (e.g., "am Turm", "am Wettbewerb"). With verbs like "teilnehmen an", "Vergnügen haben an", "Interesse haben an" it links the verb to what it’s about/connected to.
target_language_example: Ich nehme an dem Kurs teil.
native_language_example: I'm taking part in the course.

additional_notes: Refers to a specific evening (often one already mentioned or important in the story). Commonly used when looking back at an event: "an dem Abend damals" = "that evening back then". Often followed by a relative clause with "als" to describe what happened: "an dem Abend, als ..." = "on the evening when ...".
target_language_example: An dem Abend habe ich ihn zum letzten Mal gesehen.
native_language_example: I saw him for the last time that evening.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific day that’s already known from context or has been mentioned before. Often shortened to the contraction "am Tag"; with "dem" it points to a particular day (that day). Common in story-telling and when asking what happened on a certain day.
target_language_example: An dem Tag hatte ich meine erste Deutschstunde.
native_language_example: On that day, I had my first German lesson.

additional_notes: Used in relative clauses to refer back to a masculine or neuter noun (der/das) that is the object of the preposition "an". Often appears as the contracted form "am" (e.g., "der Tag, am dem..." is usually "der Tag, an dem..." or "der Tag, an dem..."; in simple phrases like "am Montag" = "an dem Montag").
target_language_example: Das ist der Tisch, an dem wir immer essen.
native_language_example: That’s the table at which we always eat.

additional_notes: “an” usually means “at/on (the edge of)” or “to (up to)” and is a two-way preposition: with dative for location (where?) and accusative for movement/direction (where to?). “den” is “the” in dative plural (all genders) and also accusative masculine plural. Common with things like doors/walls/flowers: „an den Türen“ = at/on the doors; „an den Blumen riechen“ = smell/sniff the flowers; „bis an den Horizont“ = (all the way) to the horizon.
target_language_example: Die Schilder hängen an den Wänden.
native_language_example: The signs are hanging on the walls.

meaning: to/at the head; (idiom) to someone’s face (as an insult).
additional_notes: Literally means “to the head” and is used for something directed at a person’s head (e.g., hold a gun to someone’s head, get kicked in the head). With verbs like werfen/schleudern/sagen + jemandem + etwas + an den Kopf, it’s an idiom meaning to say/throw something (often insults) at someone—i.e., right to their face.
target_language_example: Er hat mir eine Beleidigung an den Kopf geworfen.
native_language_example: He hurled an insult at me (right to my face).

additional_notes: Used with motion verbs (e.g., gehen, fahren) to express going toward a specific beach area. Uses accusative (den Strand) because it answers “where to?” (wohin?). For being at the beach (no movement), German often uses “am Strand” (wo?).
target_language_example: Morgen gehen wir an den Strand, wenn das Wetter gut ist.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we're going to the beach if the weather is good.

meaning: to/at the table (movement to a seated position).
additional_notes: Used with verbs of motion or change of position (especially "sich setzen") to mean going to the table and sitting down there. Often appears as "sich an den Tisch setzen" = "to sit down at the table." Contrast: "am Tisch" usually describes already being at the table (location).
target_language_example: Setz dich bitte an den Tisch.
native_language_example: Please sit down at the table.

meaning: to Santa Claus; in Santa Claus (believe in Santa).
additional_notes: A common phrase used with different verbs. With schreiben: „einen Brief an den Weihnachtsmann schreiben“ = to write a letter to Santa. With glauben: „an den Weihnachtsmann glauben“ = to believe in Santa. (The preposition „an“ changes case depending on the verb: movement/target → accusative „an den“, belief/attachment → dative „an dem“.)
target_language_example: Die Kinder glauben noch an den Weihnachtsmann.
native_language_example: The kids still believe in Santa Claus.

additional_notes: Combination of an + der. It is often used with a feminine noun in the dative case, especially for location or for identifying something by a feature: an der Ecke = at the corner, an der Tankstelle = at the gas station, an der Stimme = by the voice. In some fixed expressions, the English translation is less literal, for example an der Sache vorbei = beside the point.
target_language_example: Wir warten an der Bushaltestelle.
native_language_example: We're waiting at the bus stop.

meaning: at work; working (on the job / on a task).
additional_notes: Often used with verbs and nouns that take the preposition "an" + dative to express a connection to work: e.g. "Freude an der Arbeit" (enjoyment of the work), "an der Arbeit interessiert" (interested in the work). It can also describe being affected by work: "an der Arbeit kaputtgehen" = to be worn out/burned out from work.
target_language_example: Ich bin gerade an der Arbeit und kann nicht telefonieren.
native_language_example: I’m at work right now and can’t talk on the phone.

meaning: at the bar (bar counter / in the bar area).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is located at the bar counter or in the bar area (e.g., waiting, sitting, ordering). Often with verbs like warten, sitzen, bestellen. In German, "an" + dative often means "at/next to" a place or object; here: "an der" because "die Bar" is feminine.
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns an der Bar und bestellen etwas zu trinken.
native_language_example: We'll meet at the bar and order something to drink.

additional_notes: Used to say where something is located. With location (not movement), German often uses "an" + dative: "an der Decke" (literally "at/on the ceiling"), especially for something attached to or touching the ceiling (e.g., a fly, a lamp).
target_language_example: Die Lampe hängt an der Decke.
native_language_example: The lamp is hanging from the ceiling.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a street corner or a place located right at the corner. Often appears in directions with verbs like „abbiegen“ (to turn): „An der Ecke links/rechts abbiegen.“ Can also describe a building’s location: „das Haus an der Ecke“ = “the house on the corner.”
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns an der Ecke bei der Bäckerei.
native_language_example: We’ll meet at the corner by the bakery.

meaning: on the hand; by the hand (holding someone’s hand).
additional_notes: Used (1) literally for something located on your hand or an injury there: „Ich habe mich an der Hand verletzt.“ / „Was hast du an der Hand?“ and (2) with verbs like „führen/halten/nehmen“ to mean holding someone by the hand: „Sie führte das Kind an der Hand.“
target_language_example: Kannst du mich bitte an der Hand nehmen?
native_language_example: Can you take my hand, please?

meaning: at/on the nose; also used in the idiom „jdn. an der Nase herumführen“ = to trick/lead someone on.
additional_notes: Literally describes where something happens: „Du blutest an der Nase.“ (= you’re bleeding from the nose). Very commonly appears as part of the fixed expression „jemanden an der Nase herumführen“, meaning to deceive someone, string them along, or lead them by the nose (often implying the person didn’t notice at first).
target_language_example: Er hat mich an der Nase herumgeführt.
native_language_example: He tricked me / led me on.

meaning: to be next / to be your turn.
additional_notes: Used when people take turns or wait in a line or sequence (e.g., at a counter, in a game, in class). Common with "sein": "Ich bin an der Reihe" (It’s my turn), "Wer ist als Nächster an der Reihe?" (Who’s next?).
target_language_example: Du bist jetzt an der Reihe.
native_language_example: It’s your turn now.

meaning: at the school (often: at/near the school building).
additional_notes: "An" + dative ("der Schule") commonly describes being at a place/location, often emphasizing the school as a site or meeting point (e.g., dropping someone off, working there, waiting outside). Often overlaps with "in der Schule" (in the school), but "an der Schule" can sound more like "at/near the school" rather than inside a classroom.
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns an der Schule um acht Uhr.
native_language_example: We’ll meet at the school at eight o’clock.

meaning: at the door; on the door.
additional_notes: Used with the dative (der Tür) after "an". It can mean a location next to the door (standing/waiting at the door, someone is at the door) or something attached to the door (a sign/lock on the door). You often see it with sounds/actions like "klingeln/läuten/klopfen an der Tür" (to ring/knock at the door).
target_language_example: Bitte warte an der Tür.
native_language_example: Please wait at the door.

additional_notes: Used to say someone studies, learns, works, or is physically located at a university. Often with verbs like „studieren“, „lernen“, „arbeiten“, or „sein“. „an der“ = „at the“ (dative feminine: die Universität → der Universität).
target_language_example: Ich studiere Informatik an der Universität.
native_language_example: I study computer science at the university.

meaning: on the wall; on the surface of the wall.
additional_notes: Used to say that something is located on/at the wall (e.g., hanging, painted, written, a spot/stain). With verbs like hängen/stehen/schreiben it often means something is displayed or written on the wall. Note: "an" is used where English often uses "on" because it expresses contact/attachment to a vertical surface.
target_language_example: Neben der Tür hängt ein Spiegel an der Wand.
native_language_example: Next to the door, there’s a mirror hanging on the wall.

additional_notes: Usually used in the fixed pattern „Es ist/war (wieder/langsam/allmählich) an der Zeit, …“ + infinitive (e.g., „zu handeln“). It means something should happen now because the right moment has come; it can sound a bit urgent or like a suggestion/decision.
target_language_example: Es ist an der Zeit, nach Hause zu gehen.
native_language_example: It’s time to go home.

additional_notes: Used for public transport (bus, tram, subway, train) to say where you want to get off or where someone should stop. Often used with verbs like aussteigen (get off), halten/stoppen (stop), and with requests like „Bitte …“.
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, ich möchte an der nächsten Haltestelle aussteigen.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I’d like to get off at the next stop.

additional_notes: Commonly means “to you” when talking about giving/sending something to someone (e.g., ein Geschenk/eine Nachricht an dich). It’s also used with certain verbs that take "an" + accusative, especially: an dich denken = to think about you; sich an dich erinnern = to remember you. "dich" is the accusative form of “you” (informal, singular).
target_language_example: Ich schicke dir später ein Foto an dich.
native_language_example: I’ll send you a photo later.

meaning: to think of you; to have you on my mind.
additional_notes: Uses the verb "denken" with the preposition "an" + accusative (an + dich). It often means keeping someone in your thoughts (often personal/emotional), rather than thinking about a topic analytically. In contexts like "nur an dich denken," it can also mean being selfish/only thinking of yourself.
target_language_example: Wenn ich dieses Lied nur höre, muss ich an dich denken.
native_language_example: Whenever I hear this song, I have to think of you.

meaning: "in/at/to the" (feminine singular or plural after "an"), often "to" when "an" is used with verbs.
additional_notes: "An" is a preposition that can take either accusative (movement/direction, “to”) or dative (location, “at/on”). "An die" is accusative and is used with feminine singular nouns (die Tür) and plural nouns (die Touristen). Common with verbs like glauben an (believe in), sich anpassen an (adapt to), sich gewöhnen an (get used to), sich halten an (stick to/follow), klopfen an (knock on), herantreten an (approach). Contrast: "an der" (dative) = at/on the (feminine), e.g., "an der Tür" = at the door.
target_language_example: Ich muss mich an die neuen Regeln gewöhnen.
native_language_example: I have to get used to the new rules.

meaning: "Get to work!" / "Back to work!" (a firm command to start working).
additional_notes: Used as a (often strict) call to begin working immediately. Very common in the pattern „Sich an die Arbeit machen“ = “to get down to work” (e.g., „Mach dich an die Arbeit!“). Can sound like an order, depending on tone.
target_language_example: So, jetzt an die Arbeit — wir haben nicht viel Zeit.
native_language_example: Alright, back to work—we don’t have much time.

meaning: (come) to power; into power (especially political power).
additional_notes: Most often used with verbs like **kommen** or **gelangen**: **an die Macht kommen/gelangen** = “to come to power” (e.g., a party/leader takes control of a government). Literally it’s “to the power,” but in English you usually say “to power / into power.” Not to be confused with **an die Macht glauben**—that’s usually **an die Macht (von …) glauben** = “to believe in the power (of …)” (e.g., *die Macht der Liebe*).
target_language_example: Die neue Partei kam nach der Wahl an die Macht.
native_language_example: The new party came to power after the election.

additional_notes: Used with movement/placing something or someone to the side (often with verbs like „gehen“, „stellen“, „legen“). Common in the phrase „jemanden an die Seite nehmen“ = to take someone aside (for a private talk).
target_language_example: Können wir kurz an die Seite gehen?
native_language_example: Can we step aside for a moment?

additional_notes: Used with verbs of writing/drawing/putting something onto a classroom board. The accusative "die" is used because it implies movement/direction (putting something onto the board). Often with: "(etwas) an die Tafel schreiben".
target_language_example: Die Lehrerin schreibt die Hausaufgaben an die Tafel.
native_language_example: The teacher writes the homework on the board.

additional_notes: Usually used with verbs of movement or contact directed at a door, e.g. klopfen an die Tür (knock on the door), klingeln an der/an die Tür (ring the doorbell), gehen an die Tür (go to the door to answer/open it). With location (no movement) you more often see an der Tür (“at the door”).
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte an die Tür gehen?
native_language_example: Can you please go to the door?

meaning: 'against the wall' / 'to the wall' (placing something so it touches the wall).
additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement/placement (stellen, lehnen, bringen, malen, hängen) to say something is put/leaned/painted onto the wall. Grammar note: "an" + accusative (an die Wand) = motion/direction; compare "an der Wand" (dative) = already located on/at the wall.
target_language_example: Kannst du das Regal an die Wand stellen?
native_language_example: Can you put the shelf against the wall?

additional_notes: "An diesem" is "an" + "diesem" (dative masculine/neuter), used before a noun: z.B. "an diesem Gerücht" (about this rumor), "an diesem Gebäude" (about/on this building). You often see it in patterns like "etwas dran an + Dativ" (there’s something to it) and "(jemandem) gefällt etwas an + Dativ" (someone likes something about…).
target_language_example: An diesem Plan gefällt mir, dass er so einfach ist.
native_language_example: What I like about this plan is that it’s so simple.

meaning: at this place; in this location.
additional_notes: Used to point to a specific place (often one you’re in, looking at, or talking about). Common with events happening there: „An diesem Ort werden Gebete gesprochen.“ / „Es fing an diesem Ort an.“ With verbs like „hängen“ it can mean someone is hanging out or spending time there (context decides).
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns an diesem Ort um 18 Uhr.
native_language_example: We'll meet at this place at 6 p.m.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific day already known from context (often a particular date or occasion). With days/dates, German commonly uses "an" + dative: "an diesem Tag", "an dem Tag" (often shortened to "an dem" → "am").
target_language_example: An diesem Tag hat es den ganzen Tag geregnet.
native_language_example: It rained all day on that day.

meaning: this weekend (at some point during it).
additional_notes: Used to talk about plans, availability, or events happening at any time during the upcoming/current weekend. Often in questions like „Hast du an diesem Wochenende Zeit?“
target_language_example: Ich kann an diesem Wochenende leider nicht, ich bin unterwegs.
native_language_example: Unfortunately I can't this weekend; I'm traveling.

additional_notes: Used before a noun (usually feminine singular in the dative) with the preposition „an“ to mean being located at/on something: „an dieser Maschine“ = at/on this machine, „an dieser Tür“ = at/on this door. With „an“ + dative it often answers „wo?“ (where?).
target_language_example: An dieser Haltestelle müssen wir aussteigen.
native_language_example: We have to get off at this stop.

meaning: at this point; at this spot/place.
additional_notes: Used for either (1) a specific physical location (a particular spot along a river/road, etc.) or (2) a point in a text, conversation, or process (“at this point”). Often describes what changes or happens there: „Der Weg gabelt sich an dieser Stelle.“
target_language_example: An dieser Stelle müssen wir kurz anhalten.
native_language_example: We need to stop briefly at this point.

additional_notes: "an" + "einem" (dative of "ein") is used with masculine/neuter singular nouns. Common uses: (1) time: "an einem Mittwoch" = "on a Wednesday"; (2) location/position: "an einem kühlen Ort" = "in/at a cool place"; (3) contact/attachment: "an einem heißen Bügeleisen" = "on/against a hot iron". Often implies being right at something (close to/touching) rather than just generally "in" it.
target_language_example: An einem Sonntag ist die Stadt ganz ruhig.
native_language_example: On a Sunday, the city is very quiet.

meaning: in one day; within a single day.
additional_notes: Used to say something is done in the time span of one day (often emphasizing speed or that it can/can’t be finished in a day). Contrast: "an einem Tag" = within one day vs. "an einem Tag" in the sense of "on a certain day" (less common without more context). Often interchangeable with "innerhalb eines Tages" in many contexts.
target_language_example: Ich muss das bis morgen schaffen, aber nicht an einem Tag.
native_language_example: I have to get it done by tomorrow, but not in one day.

meaning: at a table; seated together at the same table.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like sitzen/essen/reden to describe where someone is seated. It can mean simply physically at a table, or (with zusammen/mit jemandem) being together in a group. In phrases like „mit jemandem an einem Tisch sitzen“, it can also imply being associated with or willing to deal with someone (e.g., politically or morally).
target_language_example: Wir saßen an einem Tisch und haben noch lange geredet.
native_language_example: We sat at a table and talked for a long time.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition „an“ to say you are studying/working/doing something at an institution or place, especially with feminine nouns like „die Universität“, „die Schule“. Here „einer“ is the dative form of „eine“ (because „an“ often takes dative when it means location: where?).
target_language_example: Sie arbeitet an einer Schule in Berlin.
native_language_example: She works at a school in Berlin.

additional_notes: "an" + "ihrem" is used with the dative to express being at/located at, sitting at, or attached to something that belongs to her or to them. "ihrem" is the dative form of "ihr" and is used with masculine or neuter nouns (e.g., an ihrem Platz/Schreibtisch/Telefon/Verstand). It can also occur in expressions like "Schuld an ihrem Versagen" where "an" marks what something relates to (blame for/regarding their failure).
target_language_example: Maria saß an ihrem Schreibtisch und schrieb eine E-Mail.
native_language_example: Maria sat at her desk and wrote an email.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition **an** + **dative** to mean that something happens/exists on each occasion or at each item in a set. Common with time expressions like **an jedem Freitag** (“every Friday”) and with parts/places like **an jedem Finger** (“on each finger”). The form **jedem** is the dative masculine/neuter form of **jeder**.
target_language_example: An jedem Montag gehe ich ins Fitnessstudio.
native_language_example: Every Monday I go to the gym.

meaning: on that day (a specific day in the past).
additional_notes: Used to refer back to a particular day that’s already known from the story/context, often in narration. "jenem" is a demonstrative form of "jener" (“that”), and it sounds a bit more literary/dramatic than the everyday "an dem Tag" or "an diesem Tag".
target_language_example: An jenem Tag habe ich zum ersten Mal Deutsch gesprochen.
native_language_example: On that day I spoke German for the first time.

meaning: on that day (back then; referring to a specific past day).
additional_notes: Points to a particular day in the past that’s known from the story/context (often a dramatic or important day). Very common in written/storytelling style; in everyday German you’ll more often hear: „an jenem Tag“ or simply „an dem Tag“/„an diesem Tag“ depending on meaning.
target_language_example: An jenem Tage begann für sie ein neues Leben.
native_language_example: On that day, a new life began for her.

additional_notes: Combination of the preposition **an** + **meinem** (dative masculine/neuter of *mein*). Used for position near or touching something (*an meinem Arbeitsplatz* = at my workplace/desk), or in the common pattern **liegen an + Dativ** meaning “to be due to / to be because of” (*Es lag an meinem Zauber* = It was because of my magic). With people, it can also mean “by my side” (*an meinem Totenbett* = by my deathbed).
target_language_example: Das liegt an meinem Plan.
native_language_example: That’s because of my plan.

additional_notes: "an" is a preposition; "meiner" is the dative feminine form of "mein". You use "an meiner" before a feminine noun in the dative case, e.g. for a location/point you pass ("an meiner Station vorbei" = past my stop) or with certain verbs/prepositions like "an etwas arbeiten" (to work on something). For masculine/neuter you’d say "an meinem"; for plural "an meinen".
target_language_example: Ich arbeite heute Abend noch an meiner Hausaufgabe.
native_language_example: I’m going to work on my homework again this evening.

meaning: by my side; next to me (physically or in support).
additional_notes: Literally “at my side.” It can mean someone is standing/sitting next to you, or (more often) that they stay with you and support you, especially in difficult moments. Common with verbs like sein (to be), bleiben (to stay), and haben/wollen … an meiner Seite haben (to have/want someone by your side). You can change the possessive: an deiner Seite, an seiner/ihrer Seite, an unserer/eurer Seite.
target_language_example: Danke, dass du in dieser schweren Zeit an meiner Seite bist.
native_language_example: Thank you for being by my side during this difficult time.

additional_notes: Used to ask what someone would do if they were in your situation (often with the conditional/subjunctive: „würdest … tun“, „hättest … getan“, „wärst“). You can swap the pronoun: „an deiner Stelle“ (in your place), „an Ihrer Stelle“ (formal), „an seiner/ihrer Stelle“ (in his/her place), „an unserer/eurer Stelle“.
target_language_example: Was würdest du an meiner Stelle tun?
native_language_example: What would you do in my place?

additional_notes:
Literally “an” + “mich” (“me”), but the meaning depends on the verb:
- denken an mich = think about me
- glauben an mich = believe in me
- sich an mich erinnern = remember me
- sich an mich wenden = turn to me / address me
- (an mich) heran- = up to me / towards me (movement)
Uses “mich” (accusative).
target_language_example: Bitte denk an mich, wenn du dort bist.
native_language_example: Please think of me when you’re there.

additional_notes: "an" + dative is used with masculine/neuter "sein-" forms: seinem (e.g., seinem Akzent, seinem Haus, seinem Kaffee). It can mean (1) "by/from" as the basis for recognizing something ("an seinem Akzent" = by his accent), (2) physical location/contact (at/on his house/arm), or (3) with some verbs, a point you are drinking/smoking from ("an seinem Kaffee schlürfen" = sip at/from his coffee).
target_language_example: An seinem Gesichtsausdruck sehe ich, dass er müde ist.
native_language_example: I can tell by his facial expression that he’s tired.

additional_notes: Describes someone’s location: being seated/working/eating at their desk. Often used with verbs like sitzen (to sit), essen (to eat), arbeiten (to work), or sein (to be). The preposition "an" + dative shows being at a place (not moving toward it). You can swap the possessive: an meinem/deinem/ihrem Schreibtisch = at my/your/her desk.
target_language_example: Egal wann du zu ihm gehst, er sitzt immer an seinem Schreibtisch.
native_language_example: No matter when you go to him, he’s always sitting at his desk.

meaning: on/at his …; in some phrases also “from/of his …” (e.g., dying from injuries).
additional_notes: “an” + “seinen” is usually “on/at his” with a following noun (often plural: an seinen Türen/Nägeln/Wunden = on/at his doors/nails/wounds). With certain verbs—especially health-related ones like “an … sterben/versterben”—“an” means “from” (cause): “an seinen Verletzungen” = from his injuries.
target_language_example: Die Bilder hängen an seinen Wänden.
native_language_example: The pictures are hanging on his walls.

meaning: in his place; if you were him.
additional_notes: Used to express what someone would do in another person’s situation (often in hypotheticals, frequently with Konjunktiv II): „Was hättest du an seiner Stelle getan?“ You can swap the possessive pronoun depending on whose situation you mean: an meiner/deiner/ihrer/unserer/eurer Stelle = in my/your/her/our/your (pl.) place.
target_language_example: Was hättest du an seiner Stelle getan?
native_language_example: What would you have done in his place?

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens or exists at your school. Here, "an" means "at" (location/association), and "unserer Schule" is dative feminine ("die Schule" → "unserer Schule"). Common with institutions like schools/universities: "an der Schule", "an unserer Schule".
target_language_example: An unserer Schule gibt es eine große Bibliothek.
native_language_example: At our school there is a big library.

additional_notes: Used when a verb or situation requires the preposition "an" before a person. Very common with verbs like "sich erinnern an" (to remember) and "schicken an" (to send to). With "erinnern an" it takes the accusative: "An wen erinnerst du dich?"
target_language_example: An wen soll ich die E-Mail schicken?
native_language_example: Who should I send the email to?

meaning: ..., when he ... (talking about a specific past time).
additional_notes: This pattern often appears with separable-prefix verbs that end in **an** (e.g. **anrufen**, **anfangen**, **anlächeln**, **sich anfreunden**): the **an** moves to the end of the clause, then a comma introduces a time clause with **als er**. **Als er** is used for a single event/time in the past (= “when he ...”), not for repeated events (use **wenn er** for that). Note: **als** looks like English “as”, but here it usually means “when”.
target_language_example: Ich fing an, als er ankam.
native_language_example: I started when he arrived.

meaning: Used with certain verbs to introduce a 'that…' clause (e.g., "Ich nehme an, dass…" = "I assume that…").
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself. It’s the pattern you see when a separable-prefix verb with **an-** is split: the verb stem stays in position 2 and **an** goes to the end of the clause, right before a comma + **dass**-clause. Common ones: **annehmen, dass…** (to assume/think that), **jdm etw. ansehen, dass…** (to be able to tell/see from someone that), **damit angeben, dass…** (to brag that). The comma before **dass** is required.
target_language_example: Ich nehme an, dass wir morgen früher losfahren.
native_language_example: I assume that we’ll leave earlier tomorrow.

additional_notes: Reflexive verb phrase: „anfangen“ + „sich langweilen“. Commonly used with time expressions (e.g., „nach ein paar Minuten“, „nach einer Viertelstunde“) to say boredom begins after some time. In the past tense you’ll often see „fing … an“; in the present tense „fängt … an“.
target_language_example: Maria fing nach ein paar Minuten an, sich zu langweilen.
native_language_example: Maria started getting bored after a few minutes.

additional_notes: Most often seen as the pattern **anrufen / bei … anrufen, um … zu + infinitive** to say why you’re calling or contacting someone. **um … zu** expresses purpose (“in order to”). The comma is standard: *Er rief an, um …*
target_language_example: Ich rufe bei der Praxis an, um einen Termin zu vereinbaren.
native_language_example: I’m calling the doctor’s office to make an appointment.

additional_notes: Common with the separable verb **anrufen** (“to call”). In main clauses, the prefix **an** goes to the end: **Ruf mich an.** The **wenn du…** clause (“when you…”) often comes after it: **Ruf mich an, wenn du zu Hause bist.** If the **wenn** clause comes first, word order flips in the main clause: **Wenn du zu Hause bist, ruf mich an.**
target_language_example: Ruf mich an, wenn du Zeit hast.
native_language_example: Call me when you have time.

meaning: Used when a separable verb with the prefix **an-** is split: the **an** goes to the end, often right before **und** (“and”).
additional_notes: In German main clauses, many verbs with **an-** are *separable*: the main verb stays in position 2 and the prefix **an** moves to the end. When you add another action with **und**, the **an** often appears immediately before **und**: **Ich rufe Tom an und erzähle …** (= *I call Tom and tell …*). Common verbs: **anrufen** (rufen … an = to call), **ankommen** (kommen … an = to arrive), **anziehen** (ziehen … an = to put on), **anlegen** (legen … an = to put on/put on equipment). In subordinate clauses, it usually stays together: **…, weil ich Tom anrufe.**
target_language_example: Ich mache das Licht an und lese noch ein bisschen.
native_language_example: I turn on the light and read a little more.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like „anfangen“/„beginnen“: „anfangen + an zu + infinitive“ (e.g., „Er fing an zu weinen.“). In modern German you’ll also often hear „anfangen zu weinen“ without the extra „an“.
target_language_example: Als sie die Nachricht hörte, fing sie an zu weinen.
native_language_example: When she heard the news, she started to cry.

additional_notes: Used with the adjective "anders" (other/different) + "Mädchen" (girl). The form "anderen" is a declined ending (here: dative). It often appears after prepositions like "mit" (with) or after certain verbs. "Mädchen" is grammatically neuter (das Mädchen), and its singular and plural form are the same; context shows whether it means one girl or multiple girls.
target_language_example: Er hat mit einem anderen Mädchen getanzt.
native_language_example: He danced with another girl.

meaning: of a different kind/type; different in nature.
additional_notes: Used with a noun (often after it) to say something is a different kind from what was expected or previously mentioned: e.g., „Probleme anderer Art“ = “problems of a different kind.” Note: „Art“ here means “kind/type,” not “art” (painting, music, etc.).
target_language_example: Wir brauchen Hilfe anderer Art.
native_language_example: We need a different kind of help.

additional_notes: Usually used with the verb "sein": "anderer Meinung sein" = to think differently / not share the same opinion. Common patterns: "Ich bin (da) anderer Meinung." (I disagree.), "Ich bin anderer Meinung als du." (I have a different opinion than you.), "Zu diesem Thema bin ich anderer Meinung." (On this topic, I disagree.).
target_language_example: Ich bin da anderer Meinung – ich finde, das ist keine gute Idee.
native_language_example: I disagree—I don't think that's a good idea.

meaning: the other shore/bank (of a river or lake).
additional_notes: Often used with a preposition and inflected: ans andere Ufer (to the other bank), am anderen Ufer (on the other bank). Note: It can also appear in the dated euphemism vom anderen Ufer sein (“to be gay/lesbian”); this can sound old-fashioned or awkward today.
target_language_example: Wir rudern ans anderes Ufer.
native_language_example: We’re rowing to the other bank.

additional_notes: Used to compare two people/things and say they are not the same. Often follows a description of how something is done/seen ("anders") and then names what it’s compared to ("als" + noun/pronoun): "anders als Männer" (differently than men), "anders als diese" (different from these).
target_language_example: Das ist anders als gestern.
native_language_example: That’s different from yesterday.

additional_notes: Used with the fixed reflexive phrase **es sich anders überlegen** = “to change one’s mind / decide differently.” The **sich** changes with the person: **ich überlege es mir anders**, **du überlegst es dir anders**, **er/sie überlegt es sich anders**, **wir überlegen es uns anders**, **ihr überlegt es euch anders**, **Sie überlegen es sich anders**. Often appears with **wieder** (“again”) or **plötzlich** (“suddenly”).
target_language_example: Ich habe es mir anders überlegt und komme doch mit.
native_language_example: I changed my mind and I’m coming along after all.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "anfangen" (= to start/begin) + a comma + an infinitive phrase ("... zu lernen" = to learn). Very common pattern: "anfangen, etwas zu tun" (to start doing something). Often said in the past with "haben" ("Ich habe angefangen, ...").
target_language_example: Ich habe letztes Jahr angefangen, Französisch zu lernen.
native_language_example: I started learning French last year.

additional_notes: Past form of the phrase "angeln gehen" (“to go fishing”). In the Perfekt, German uses **sein**: "Ich bin angeln gegangen" / "Wir sind angeln gegangen". Often used with time words like "letztes Wochenende" and with "nicht" to say you didn’t go: "Wir sind nicht angeln gegangen."
target_language_example: Wir sind gestern früh angeln gegangen.
native_language_example: We went fishing early yesterday.

additional_notes: Common past-time sequence to show that by the time someone arrived, another state/situation was already true. Typically used with **als** (= when, for one-time past events). **ankam** is Präteritum of *ankommen* (to arrive), and **war** is Präteritum of *sein* (to be). Frequently paired with **schon/bereits** (= already). Pattern: **Als** + (subject) + … + **ankam**, **war** + …
target_language_example: Als ich am Bahnhof ankam, war der Zug schon abgefahren.
native_language_example: When I arrived at the train station, the train had already left.

meaning: to come to light; to be revealed.
additional_notes: Used when hidden information (often the truth, facts, or a secret) becomes known or is uncovered. Common with nouns like "die Wahrheit" (the truth) and in contexts like investigations, journalism, or court ("Vor Gericht wird noch mehr ans Licht kommen").
target_language_example: Früher oder später wird die Wahrheit ans Licht kommen.
native_language_example: Sooner or later, the truth will come to light.

meaning: to the sea; to the seaside.
additional_notes: "Ans" = "an das" (to/at the) and is used with neuter nouns like "das Meer". It usually describes going to the sea/seaside (a destination): "Ich fahre ans Meer." For being already there, you often use "am Meer" ("at the sea").
target_language_example: Wir fahren am Wochenende ans Meer.
native_language_example: We’re going to the seaside this weekend.

meaning: to the phone; to answer/pick up the phone.
additional_notes: Used especially with verbs like „gehen/kommen“ to mean you go to the phone and answer it. „ans“ is a contraction of „an das“ (accusative, movement toward something): „ans Telefon gehen“ = to go to the phone / to pick up the phone.
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte ans Telefon gehen?
native_language_example: Can you please answer the phone?

additional_notes: Imperative form of „antworten“ (to answer) addressed to one person („du“). „mir“ is dative = “to me.” Often sounds demanding or impatient; in polite situations you’d say „Antworten Sie mir“ or „Bitte antworten Sie mir.“
target_language_example: Antworte mir bitte, wenn du Zeit hast.
native_language_example: Please answer me when you have time.

additional_notes: Used with **Sie** (capital S) to speak politely to one person or to address people formally. Often appears in questions like **Arbeiten Sie hier?** (“Do you work here?”) or with details: **Wo/Für wen/Wie viele Stunden arbeiten Sie?**.
target_language_example: Arbeiten Sie heute im Büro oder zu Hause?
native_language_example: Are you working in the office today or at home?

meaning: to go to work; to go and work.
additional_notes: Uses "gehen" + infinitive to express going somewhere in order to do an activity. Very common for everyday routines (similar patterns: "einkaufen gehen" = go shopping, "schwimmen gehen" = go swimming). Often used with a time word: "morgens/gleich/heute arbeiten gehen".
target_language_example: Ich muss morgen früh arbeiten gehen.
native_language_example: I have to go to work tomorrow morning.

meaning: "do you work" (asking someone about their job/work).
additional_notes: This is the verb-first word order used for yes/no questions: **Arbeitest du ...?** = “Do you work ...?” / “Are you working ...?”. **du** is the informal "you" (used with friends, family, classmates); with **Sie** it becomes **Arbeiten Sie ...?**.
target_language_example: Arbeitest du heute?
native_language_example: Are you working today?

additional_notes: Used to say someone’s profession/role: [Person] arbeitet als + job title (often feminine/masculine forms, e.g., Übersetzerin/Übersetzer). You can add where they work afterwards (e.g., in einem Büro).
target_language_example: Mein Bruder arbeitet als Lehrer in Berlin.
native_language_example: My brother works as a teacher in Berlin.

meaning: “works in the” (for places/organizations with feminine nouns).
additional_notes: Used with the verb *arbeiten* + *in* to say where someone works. After *in* (location, not movement), German usually uses the dative case: *in der* is dative feminine (e.g., *in der Fabrik*, *in der Personalabteilung*, *in der Stadt*). For masculine/neuter nouns you often see *in dem* → *im* (e.g., *im Büro*).
target_language_example: Er arbeitet in der Schule.
native_language_example: He works at/in the school.

additional_notes: Used to say someone’s workplace. "arbeitet" is the verb "to work". "in" + dative often expresses location; "einem" is the dative form of "ein" used here (often before a neuter noun like "Krankenhaus" or "Restaurant"). You’ll also see other forms depending on the noun: e.g., "arbeitet in einer Klinik" (feminine) or "arbeitet in einem Büro" (neuter).
target_language_example: Sie arbeitet in einem Büro in Berlin.
native_language_example: She works in an office in Berlin.

meaning: “works in a …” (a workplace in the dative case).
additional_notes: Used to say where someone works. It’s typically followed by a feminine noun for a place of work (e.g., Bäckerei, Fabrik, Bibliothek, Pizzeria). Because of the preposition "in" (location), "eine" becomes "einer" (dative feminine). For masculine/neuter places you’d use "in einem" (e.g., in einem Büro).
target_language_example: Sie arbeitet in einer Schule.
native_language_example: She works in a school.

meaning: as poor as a church mouse; extremely poor.
additional_notes: An idiom used to emphasize that someone has very little or no money. Often used with „sein“ (e.g., „Er ist/war arm wie eine Kirchenmaus.“).
target_language_example: Nach der Miete bin ich arm wie eine Kirchenmaus.
native_language_example: After paying the rent, I'm as poor as a church mouse.

additional_notes: Used when a main clause is followed by a "dass"-clause, and "auch" shows that this information is in addition to something else ("I also think/know/feel that …"). The comma comes before "dass". In English you usually translate it as "also" or "too" (not literally as "also, that").
target_language_example: Ich hoffe auch, dass du Zeit hast.
native_language_example: I also hope that you have time.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine or neuter noun with the indefinite article (ein) to say someone/something is an additional example or has an additional role/quality: "He is also a ..." / "It can be dangerous too." Word order can vary with emphasis: "Ich bin auch ein Deutscher" (I’m also German) vs. "Ich bin ein Deutscher auch" (more emphasis on also; less common). In questions it often means "Do you also ...?": "Spielst du auch ein Instrument?"
target_language_example: Er ist auch ein guter Lehrer.
native_language_example: He is also a good teacher.

meaning: also good; that’s fine too / okay as well.
additional_notes: Used to say something is fine in addition to (or as an alternative to) something else. Often appears as a short reaction meaning “fine/okay then.” With "auch gut so" it means “that’s a good thing too / that’s fine the way it is.” In questions, it can mean “also” in the sense of “as well” (e.g., "Geht es dir auch gut?" = “Are you well too?”).
target_language_example: Wir können heute nicht ins Kino gehen? Auch gut, dann bleiben wir zu Hause.
native_language_example: We can’t go to the movies today? That’s fine; then we’ll stay home.

meaning: "always, too"; or (with question words) "whatever / whichever" (emphasis: no matter which).
additional_notes:
1) With time expressions like "immer": "... und wird es auch immer geben" = "... and it will always exist too" (adds "also/too" to "immer").
2) Often used after a question word to mean “no matter which/what”: "was auch immer" (whatever), "welches auch immer" (whichever), "wer auch immer" (whoever), etc. It adds emphasis: any choice is fine.
target_language_example: Nimm, was auch immer du brauchst.
native_language_example: Take whatever you need.

meaning: “too / as well (sometime),” often with “for once” nuance.
additional_notes: Combines **auch** (“also/too”) + **mal** (a common spoken particle that makes requests/questions sound more casual or means “once/sometime”). In statements it can express wanting to do something too (sometimes with impatience: “I want to as well, for once!”). In questions it can mean “ever/sometime” in the sense of “Will you come by sometime?”
target_language_example: Ich möchte das auch mal ausprobieren.
native_language_example: I’d like to try that too (sometime/for once).

additional_notes: combines auch and nicht. It is used to add another negative statement: if something is not true for one thing, it is also not true for another. In English, it is often translated as 'not ... either' rather than word-for-word.
target_language_example: Ich kann morgen auch nicht kommen.
native_language_example: I can't come tomorrow either.

additional_notes: Used to add emphasis that something is no longer true, often in addition to another negative statement ("me neither" / "not anymore"). It can stand alone as a short reply ("Auch nicht mehr.") or appear in longer sentences to show a change over time: "Es ist hier auch nicht mehr so ...". In some contexts it implies "if X happens, then you won’t be able to Y anymore" (e.g., "kommst du auch nicht mehr heraus" = "you won’t get out again").
target_language_example: Ich habe dafür auch nicht mehr die Zeit.
native_language_example: I don’t have the time for that anymore either.

additional_notes: In negative sentences, **auch** often means **“either”** (not “also”). So **auch nichts** is used to add emphasis like “nothing either” or “doesn’t help either.” Common patterns: **Das bringt/nutzt/taugt auch nichts.** = “That doesn’t help either / That’s no good either.” It can also mean “also nothing” in a simple listing: **Und das ist auch nichts.** = “And that is also nothing (special).”
target_language_example: Wenn wir uns beeilen, hilft das auch nichts.
native_language_example: Even if we hurry, that won’t help either.

meaning: also; as well; on top of that (an additional thing).
additional_notes: Used to add one more item/person/action to what’s already the case. Often implies “in addition to everything else” and can sound slightly emphatic or annoyed depending on context (e.g., "Du hast ihm auch noch geholfen!" = "You even helped him, too!").
target_language_example: Ich muss heute auch noch einkaufen.
native_language_example: I also have to go shopping today (on top of everything else).

meaning: “already” (often with extra emphasis: “as well / even / anyway”).
additional_notes: Combines **auch** (“also/even/anyway”) + **schon** (“already”). It often means **“already”** with a tone of surprise, impatience, or emphasis: *Auch schon kapiert?* ≈ “Got it yet?” / “Finally got it?” In other contexts it can mean “also already” (= someone has done something before, too): *Er hat auch schon Kindern geholfen.* In questions like *Was soll sich auch schon verändert haben?* it can sound like **“anyway” / “really”** (“What could have changed anyway?”).
target_language_example: Bist du auch schon fertig?
native_language_example: Are you finished already?

meaning: also like that; the same way too.
additional_notes: Used to say something is true in the same way for someone/something else (a comparison): "bei deiner Mutter auch so" = "it was the same with your mother". It can also add emphasis with adjectives/adverbs, often meaning "anyway / all the same": "Ist ja auch so egal" = "It’s (all) the same anyway."
target_language_example: Bei mir war das früher auch so.
native_language_example: It used to be the same for me too.

additional_notes: Introduces a contrast: something is true or happens despite another condition or fact. Use it at the start of a clause, often followed by a comma: "Auch wenn ..., ...". With the verb in the "auch wenn" clause typically at the end (subordinate clause).
target_language_example: Auch wenn ich müde bin, gehe ich heute noch spazieren.
native_language_example: Even though I'm tired, I'm still going for a walk today.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a concessive clause: something is true or will happen despite a difficult condition. It’s often followed by strong consequences ("even if it kills me"). Grammar tip: in the full clause after "auch wenn", the verb typically goes to the end (e.g., "Auch wenn es nur fünf Minuten dauert, ...").
target_language_example: Ich komme, auch wenn es regnet.
native_language_example: I'll come even if it rains.

meaning: right away; immediately; on the first try.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens instantly/without difficulty (e.g., verstehen, mögen, gelingen). Often implies “without needing a second attempt” or “from the very start.”
target_language_example: Ich habe die Aufgabe nicht auf Anhieb gelöst.
native_language_example: I didn’t solve the task on the first try.
