additional_notes: Used to give a strong positive opinion. "echt" works like an intensifier meaning "really" (similar to "wirklich"), and is common in everyday spoken German. It can stand alone as a short reaction: "Echt gut!"
target_language_example: Dein Deutsch ist echt gut!
native_language_example: Your German is really good!

additional_notes: Informal phrase used to show surprise, disbelief, or to challenge what someone just said. It can be a question (“Echt jetzt?”) or used for emphasis (“Aber echt jetzt.” = “No, seriously.”). Often said with an incredulous tone.
target_language_example: Echt jetzt, du hast das schon fertig?
native_language_example: Seriously, you already finished that?

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause meaning something will be true or happen in every case. Often followed by a verb at the end: „Egal, was du machst, …“. You may also see emphasis with „auch“: „egal, was du auch sagst“.
target_language_example: Egal, was du heute isst, trink bitte genug Wasser.
native_language_example: No matter what you eat today, please drink enough water.

additional_notes: A rather literary/old-fashioned fixed expression meaning that something has been the case for a very long time (basically “always”). Very often used in the phrase "wie eh und je" (“as always / just like ever”).
target_language_example: In diesem Dorf war es eh und je ruhig.
native_language_example: In this village, it has always been quiet.

additional_notes: Used with "sein" (to be): "Sei/Sind/Seid ehrlich zu mir" = “be honest with me.” "zu" + person (mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/ihnen) shows who you’re being honest with.
target_language_example: Bitte sei ehrlich zu mir und sag mir die Wahrheit.
native_language_example: Please be honest with me and tell me the truth.

additional_notes: Used with other verbs (e.g., scheinen/versuchen) to describe someone’s honesty: „Er scheint ehrlich zu sein“ = “He seems to be honest.” You can also use it about yourself: „Ich versuche immer, ehrlich zu sein“ = “I always try to be honest.”
target_language_example: Um ehrlich zu sein, habe ich keine Zeit.
native_language_example: To be honest, I don’t have time.

additional_notes: Used as a discourse marker to introduce a candid opinion, admission, or correction. It often comes at the start of a sentence ("Ehrlich gesagt, …") or inserted after the verb ("Ich fand es ehrlich gesagt …").
target_language_example: Ehrlich gesagt, habe ich keine Lust, heute auszugehen.
native_language_example: To be honest, I don’t feel like going out today.

additional_notes: Often used literally (e.g., losing an eye, opening one eye, only one eye being affected). It also appears in the common expression „ein Auge für etwas haben“ = “to have an eye for something” (to notice/appreciate it).
target_language_example: Ich habe nur ein Auge geöffnet, weil ich noch müde war.
native_language_example: I opened only one eye because I was still tired.

meaning: “an eye on” / “keep an eye on” (to watch or monitor; also: to be interested in).
additional_notes: Usually used with a verb like **haben** or **werfen**: **ein Auge auf etwas/jemanden haben** (keep an eye on / have your eye on) or **ein Auge auf etwas/jemanden werfen** (cast an eye on). It takes an accusative object (**auf + Akk.**). Depending on context it can mean supervising/monitoring or showing interest (sometimes romantic).
target_language_example: Kannst du ein Auge auf meine Tasche haben, während ich kurz weg bin?
native_language_example: Can you keep an eye on my bag while I’m gone for a moment?

additional_notes: "ein" is the masculine nominative/accusative indefinite article. Use "ein Auto" when you mean a non-specific car (e.g., you need a car / he won a car). In questions and with verbs like "brauchen" (to need) and "mieten" (to rent), it often stays in the accusative: "ein Auto".
target_language_example: Wir haben noch kein Auto, aber wir wollen ein Auto kaufen.
native_language_example: We don't have a car yet, but we want to buy a car.

additional_notes: Past participle phrase used with the verb "kaufen" in the present perfect: "Ich habe ein Auto gekauft" = "I bought/I have bought a car." Often includes a time/place: "gestern/in Boston". With an indirect object it means buying for someone: "Sie hat ihm ein Auto gekauft" (She bought him a car). With "sich" it means buying for yourself: "Er hat sich ein Auto gekauft" (He bought himself a car).
target_language_example: Wir haben letztes Jahr ein Auto gekauft.
native_language_example: We bought a car last year.

additional_notes: Means “to buy a car.” Often used after another verb (e.g., beabsichtigen/vorhaben/entschlossen sein, um …) where the verb “kaufen” stays in the infinitive with “zu.” You may also see it with a dative pronoun: „dir/euch ein Auto zu kaufen“ = “to buy yourself a car.”
target_language_example: Nächstes Jahr plane ich, mir ein Auto zu kaufen.
native_language_example: Next year I’m planning to buy myself a car.

additional_notes: Used when asking a celebrity/public figure for their signature. Common patterns: „ein Autogramm haben/kriegen/bekommen“ (to get an autograph) and „ein Autogramm geben“ (to give an autograph). You can also add „von …“ to say whose autograph it is: „ein Autogramm von Taylor Swift“.
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, könnte ich bitte ein Autogramm von Ihnen bekommen?
native_language_example: Excuse me, could I please get an autograph from you?

additional_notes: Used with the indefinite article (ein) to mean “a baby” (a very young child). Common with verbs like haben (to have), bekommen/kriegen (to have/get, as in having a baby), and sein (to be). In comparisons like „wie ein Baby“, it can mean someone is acting very childish or needy.
target_language_example: Wir haben seit drei Wochen ein Baby.
native_language_example: We’ve had a baby for three weeks.

additional_notes: Often used with the verb „nehmen“: „ein Bad nehmen“ = to take a bath. With „einlassen“ it means to run/fill a bath: „ein Bad einlassen“ (fill the bathtub with water). It’s a countable noun: „ein Bad“ (a bath).
target_language_example: Ich nehme heute Abend ein Bad.
native_language_example: I'm taking a bath this evening.

additional_notes: Used when giving or asking for an instance that illustrates something. Common patterns: „ein Beispiel nennen/geben“ (to name/give an example), „ein Beispiel für …“ (an example of …).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir ein Beispiel geben?
native_language_example: Can you give me an example?

additional_notes: Used when ordering or asking for a single beer. "Ein" is the indefinite article meaning "a/one" for neuter nouns like "Bier" (das Bier).
target_language_example: Ich hätte gern ein Bier, bitte.
native_language_example: I’d like a beer, please.

meaning: a picture; an image (photo or drawing).
additional_notes: Used for a physical picture or an image in general (photo, drawing, etc.). Common patterns: „ein Bild von + Dativ“ = “a picture of …” (often a photo), and „ein Bild der/des + Genitiv“ = “a picture of the …” (more formal/written). You can also say „ein Bild zeichnen“ (to draw a picture) and „ein Bild schicken“ (to send a picture).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir ein Bild von deiner Katze schicken?
native_language_example: Can you send me a picture of your cat?

additional_notes: Used to say what (or who) is shown in a picture: "ein Bild von + noun/name". Often used with verbs like haben (to have), machen (to take), zeigen (to show), hochladen (to upload), malen (to paint).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir ein Bild von deinem Hund zeigen?
native_language_example: Can you show me a picture of your dog?

additional_notes:
Used when someone sends, shows, or shares a picture of themselves. The reflexive pronoun changes with the subject: 
- er schickt … ein Bild von sich = he sends a picture of himself
- sie schickt … ein Bild von sich = she sends a picture of herself
- ich schicke … ein Bild von mir = I send a picture of myself
- du schickst … ein Bild von dir = you send a picture of yourself
Also common as: „ein Foto von sich“.
target_language_example: Er hat mir ein Bild von sich geschickt.
native_language_example: He sent me a picture of himself.

additional_notes: "Blatt" literally means "leaf" but is commonly used as a counting word for paper (like "sheet"): ein Blatt Papier, zwei Blätter Papier. Used in polite requests with "bitte" and either informal "Bring mir …" or formal "Bringen Sie mir …".
target_language_example: Kannst du mir bitte ein Blatt Papier geben?
native_language_example: Can you please give me a sheet of paper?

additional_notes: An indefinite noun phrase: "ein" = "a" (or "one") + "Boot" = "boat". Used when introducing a boat that hasn’t been specified yet. "ein" changes with gender/case (e.g., "ein Boot", "ein Boot mieten"; plural: "Boote").
target_language_example: Wir wollen am Wochenende ein Boot mieten.
native_language_example: We want to rent a boat this weekend.

additional_notes: Used to identify the sender. Put the person after "von" (typically dative with articles/pronouns, e.g. "von meiner Mutter", "von ihm/ihr").
target_language_example: Das ist ein Brief von meiner ehemaligen Lehrerin.
native_language_example: That is a letter from my former teacher.

additional_notes: Used to say what the subject of a book is. "über" is followed by the accusative case (e.g., über Sterne, über China, über das Thema). Often used with verbs like "schreiben" (to write) and "leihen" (to lend).
target_language_example: Ich suche ein Buch über die Geschichte Berlins.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a book about the history of Berlin.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a quantity of 12 items. Common when ordering or counting things (e.g., eggs, rolls, donuts). With nouns: "ein Dutzend Eier" = "a dozen eggs". If the noun is plural, it often appears without an extra article: "ein Dutzend Katzen".
target_language_example: Ich nehme ein Dutzend Eier, bitte.
native_language_example: I’ll take a dozen eggs, please.

additional_notes: Used when buying or talking about quantities in shops/markets. "Ein Dutzend" = twelve (often used for eggs). You can swap the noun: "ein Dutzend Brötchen" (a dozen rolls).
target_language_example: Ich brauche ein Dutzend Eier für den Kuchen.
native_language_example: I need a dozen eggs for the cake.

additional_notes: "ein" is the indefinite article meaning "a/an". "Ei" is a neuter noun (das Ei). Use it when talking about a single egg, often with cooking/eating verbs like "ein Ei kochen" (boil an egg), "ein Ei braten" (fry an egg), or "ein Ei essen" (eat an egg).
target_language_example: Zum Frühstück esse ich ein Ei.
native_language_example: For breakfast I eat an egg.

additional_notes: Used when you mean one ice cream as a treat (e.g., a cone or a scoop/cup). In German, "Eis" can also mean "ice" in other contexts, but with "ein" and verbs like "kaufen" or "möchten," it usually means ice cream.
target_language_example: Nach dem Essen holen wir uns ein Eis.
native_language_example: After the meal, we’ll get an ice cream.

meaning: an end; (hat ein Ende) “comes to an end / is over.”
additional_notes: Common in set phrases: **etw. hat ein Ende** = “something is over/comes to an end.” Also **jdm./etw. ein Ende machen** = “to put an end to someone/something” (often used with **machen**: *Wir haben geschworen, diesem Unfug ein Ende zu machen.*).
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, das Warten hat bald ein Ende.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, the waiting will be over soon.

meaning: “an angel” (literally), or “a sweetheart/an incredibly good person” (figuratively).
additional_notes: Used literally for an angel (religious/mythical being). Very often used figuratively as a compliment for someone who is kind, helpful, or well-behaved (especially about a child: “Ihr Sohn ist ein Engel.”). You can also use it as a surprised reaction: “Ein Engel?” = “An angel?”
target_language_example: Danke für deine Hilfe — du bist ein Engel.
native_language_example: Thanks for your help—you’re an angel.

additional_notes: "ein" is the indefinite article (“a/an”) for neuter nouns. "Fahrrad" is neuter: das Fahrrad. In the accusative it stays the same: Ich habe ein Fahrrad. For emphasis/comparison you can say: genau so ein Fahrrad wie … (“exactly such a bike as …”).
target_language_example: Ich habe mir ein Fahrrad gekauft.
native_language_example: I bought myself a bike.

additional_notes: Means something done wrong or incorrect. Common patterns: "Das ist ein Fehler" (That’s a mistake), "Das war ein Fehler" (That was a mistake), and "einen Fehler machen" (to make a mistake).
target_language_example: Es war ein Fehler, das so spät zu sagen.
native_language_example: It was a mistake to say that so late.

additional_notes: A noun for a person who is not brave. Use with the verb "sein" (to be): "Du bist ein Feigling." / "Er ist kein Feigling." The feminine form is "eine Feiglingin" (less common) or more commonly "eine feige Person".
target_language_example: Ich will kein Feigling sein.
native_language_example: I don’t want to be a coward.

additional_notes: Used for asking someone to open a window, often to get fresh air. In requests, German commonly uses polite modal verbs like „können“ (Kannst du/Könnten Sie…?) or the very polite „Hätten Sie etwas dagegen, wenn…?“ (“Would you mind if…?”).
target_language_example: Es ist stickig hier—kannst du bitte ein Fenster öffnen?
native_language_example: It’s stuffy in here—can you please open a window?

additional_notes: "Foto" is short for "Fotografie" and is commonly used. With "von" or "vom" it means "a photo of" someone/something: "ein Foto von dir" (a photo of you), "ein Foto vom Flughafen" (a photo of the airport). With "machen" it means "to take a photo": "ein Foto machen".
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte ein Foto von uns machen?
native_language_example: Can you please take a photo of us?

additional_notes: Used to say what or who is in the photo. The noun after von is usually in the dative: von meiner Familie, von dem Haus (often shortened to: vom Haus).
target_language_example: Kannst du ein Foto von uns machen?
native_language_example: Can you take a photo of us?

meaning: a stranger; an outsider (someone unknown or unfamiliar).
additional_notes: Often refers to an unknown person (e.g., someone you don’t know in a room). It can also be used more generally/figuratively for someone who doesn’t belong or isn’t familiar with a place or situation: „Tom ist hier ein Fremder.“ (Tom is an outsider here). Noun: der Fremde (masc.); a woman would be „eine Fremde“.
target_language_example: Da steht ein Fremder vor der Tür.
native_language_example: There’s a stranger standing at the door.

additional_notes: Usually means “a friend” (male person). With “von” it means “a friend of …” (e.g., „ein Freund von dir“ = “a friend of yours”). It can also mean “a fan/lover of” something: „ein Freund klassischer Musik“ = “a fan of classical music.”
target_language_example: Er ist ein Freund von meiner Schwester, aber kein Freund von Fußball.
native_language_example: He’s a friend of my sister, but not a fan of soccer.

additional_notes: Used to refer to one (unspecified) male friend you have. Often used when introducing someone or mentioning a friend in a story. For a female friend, say: „eine Freundin von mir“. You can also use it after „sein“: „Er ist ein Freund von mir.“
target_language_example: Ein Freund von mir wohnt in Berlin.
native_language_example: A friend of mine lives in Berlin.

additional_notes: A neuter noun: das Gedicht (plural: die Gedichte). Common with verbs like schreiben (to write), lesen (to read), lernen (to memorize/learn), aufsagen (to recite), and vorlesen (to read aloud).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir ein Gedicht empfehlen?
native_language_example: Can you recommend a poem to me?

additional_notes: Used to refer to information that should not be told to other people. Often used with verbs like „ein Geheimnis haben“ (to have a secret), „ein Geheimnis hüten/bewahren“ (to keep a secret), or „ein Geheimnis verraten“ (to reveal a secret).
target_language_example: Bitte erzähl niemandem davon — es ist ein Geheimnis.
native_language_example: Please don’t tell anyone about it — it’s a secret.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is very intelligent or exceptionally talented; it can be meant literally or as praise. Often appears in patterns like „jemanden für ein Genie halten“ (to consider someone a genius) or „weit davon entfernt, ein Genie zu sein“ (far from being a genius). „Genie“ is neuter: „ein Genie“ (a genius), „das Genie“ (the genius).
target_language_example: Alle dachten, sie sei ein Genie, aber sie hatte einfach viel geübt.
native_language_example: Everyone thought she was a genius, but she had simply practiced a lot.

meaning: a noise; a sound (usually something you hear).
additional_notes: Used with hearing verbs like „hören“ (to hear) and „vernehmen“ (to perceive/hear). It often means an unspecified sound/noise, sometimes implying something suspicious or unexpected (like a noise in the house). Plural: „Geräusche“.
target_language_example: Ich habe im Flur ein Geräusch gehört.
native_language_example: I heard a noise in the hallway.

additional_notes: Means something you give to someone (or to yourself) for a special occasion or as a nice gesture. Often used with "für" (for) to say who it is for, and with "jemandem" (dative) to say who receives it: "Ich kaufe Maria ein Geschenk" / "Ich kaufe ein Geschenk für Maria."
target_language_example: Ich habe ein Geschenk für dich.
native_language_example: I have a gift for you.

additional_notes: Used to say who will receive the gift. The receiver comes after **für** in the accusative (e.g., **für meinen Mann**, **für meine Freundin**, **für Maria**). Often used with verbs like **kaufen** (to buy), **besorgen** (to get), **aussuchen** (to pick out).
target_language_example: Ich habe ein Geschenk für meine Mutter gekauft.
native_language_example: I bought a gift for my mother.

additional_notes: Used to say who gave the gift. The giver comes after von (dative): von mir (from me), von dir, von ihm/ihr/uns/euch/ihnen; with names it stays the same: von Alice, von Dracos Vater.
target_language_example: Das ist ein Geschenk von meiner Schwester.
native_language_example: This is a gift from my sister.

additional_notes: Used to say you had or are having a (usually somewhat formal or serious) talk with a person. Common verbs: ein Gespräch mit jemandem haben (to have a talk with someone) and ein Gespräch mit jemandem führen (to conduct/hold a talk with someone). The person after „mit“ is in the dative case (e.g., mit Tom, mit meiner Lehrerin).
target_language_example: Ich hatte gestern ein Gespräch mit meiner Chefin.
native_language_example: I had a talk with my boss yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to order or ask for a serving of milk. "ein" changes depending on case (e.g., accusative: "ein Glas Milch" after "bringen/geben/bekommen"; dative: "mit einem Glas Milch". In restaurants you might also hear "ein Glas Milch, bitte".)
target_language_example: Ich hätte gern ein Glas Milch, bitte.
native_language_example: I’d like a glass of milk, please.

additional_notes: A very common polite request in cafés/restaurants and at home. Use with polite phrases like „bitte“ or verbs like „möchten“ (would like), „können“ (can/could), and „bringen“ (to bring).
target_language_example: Könnte ich bitte ein Glas Wasser bekommen?
native_language_example: Could I please get a glass of water?

additional_notes: Used when ordering, offering, or talking about having a single serving of wine. Note: **Glas** is neuter (**das Glas**), so with **ein** it stays **ein Glas** (not *einen*).
target_language_example: Ich hätte gern ein Glas Wein.
native_language_example: I’d like a glass of wine.

additional_notes: Used to express relief that something happened (or didn’t happen). Often comes at the start of a sentence: "Ein Glück, dass …" or "So ein Glück, dass …". The verb goes to the end in the "dass" clause.
target_language_example: Ein Glück, dass du heute Zeit hast.
native_language_example: Luckily, you have time today.

additional_notes: Used when asking for or offering a towel, or saying you have/need one. The noun is "das Handtuch" (neuter), so in the nominative/accusative singular it’s "ein Handtuch". Common places: im Badezimmer (in the bathroom), am Strand (at the beach).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir bitte ein Handtuch geben?
native_language_example: Can you please give me a towel?

meaning: a lot of; a bunch of (literally: a heap/pile).
additional_notes: Common in spoken German to mean “many/much,” especially with plural nouns: ein Haufen Briefe/Leute/Typen. It can also be used literally for a physical pile (ein Haufen Sand). Depending on context, it can sound casual or insulting (“ein Haufen Idioten/Verlierer”). With “ein Haufen + plural noun,” the verb is often singular (Ein Haufen Leute ist da), though plural is also heard.
target_language_example: Auf dich warten ein Haufen Briefe.
native_language_example: A bunch of letters are waiting for you.

additional_notes: "ein" is the indefinite article (“a/an”) for neuter nouns in the nominative and accusative case. "ein Haus" is very literal: it usually means a (single) house/building; depending on context it can also mean “a home.” In phrases like "in ein Haus" it often just means “into a house” (a building).
target_language_example: Wir suchen ein Haus mit Garten.
native_language_example: We’re looking for a house with a garden.

meaning: “a house in …” (a house located in a place).
additional_notes: Used to say where a house is located: „ein Haus in Berlin / Italien / London“. With „in“ meaning location (not movement), the place is usually in the dative: „in Italien“, „in London“, „in der Schweiz“, „in den USA“. Often appears with verbs like „haben“ (to have) or „sich ein Haus kaufen“ (to buy oneself a house).
target_language_example: Sie haben ein Haus in der Schweiz.
native_language_example: They have a house in Switzerland.

additional_notes: Uses "zu" + infinitive to express a purpose or plan (often with verbs like "vorhaben" or phrases like "darüber nachdenken"). Commonly appears after "um ... zu" for "in order to": "Er spart, um ein Haus zu kaufen." With "mir/uns" it means buying a house for myself/ourselves: "mir ein Haus kaufen" / "uns ein Haus kaufen".
target_language_example: Wir hoffen, nächstes Jahr ein Haus zu kaufen.
native_language_example: We hope to buy a house next year.

additional_notes: Means a (male) hero. With famous people, it often refers to someone admired for brave or outstanding actions. In everyday speech it can be used more generally or playfully (e.g., someone did something helpful). Plural: Helden. Feminine form: eine Heldin.
target_language_example: Für meine kleine Schwester bist du ein Held.
native_language_example: To my little sister, you’re a hero.

additional_notes: "Hund" means "dog"; "ein" is the indefinite article ("a/an"). In questions like "Was für ein Hund ist das?", it means "What kind of dog is that?".
target_language_example: Ich sehe draußen ein Hund.
native_language_example: I see a dog outside.

additional_notes: Used to insult someone or call them very stupid. Often appears in exclamations like "Was für ein Idiot!" (= "What an idiot!"). Not polite—avoid in formal situations.
target_language_example: Ich war ein Idiot und habe den Termin vergessen.
native_language_example: I was an idiot and forgot the appointment.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the length of time (duration) or a unit in the calendar. As a direct object, it often changes to accusative: "ein Jahr" → "ein Jahr" (or "eins" as a pronoun), but with masculine/neuter article it becomes "ein Jahr" / "ein" stays the same; however in some contexts you’ll see "ein(en)" with masculine nouns—here "Jahr" is neuter, so "ein Jahr" and "ein Jahr Pause" are common. After prepositions it can change: "in einem Jahr" (in a year), "seit einem Jahr" (for a year/since a year ago).
target_language_example: Ich war ein Jahr in Deutschland.
native_language_example: I was in Germany for a year.

meaning: a boy; a male child (sometimes: a baby boy).
additional_notes: "Junge" is a masculine noun meaning “boy.” With the indefinite article it’s "ein Junge" (nominative: “a boy”). In contexts about pregnancy/birth or a baby, it can mean “a boy” in the sense of “a baby boy” (e.g., "Ihnen wurde ein Junge geboren" = “They had a baby boy”). Often contrasted with "ein Mädchen" (“a girl”).
target_language_example: Ist das Baby ein Junge oder ein Mädchen?
native_language_example: Is the baby a boy or a girl?

additional_notes:
Indefinite article + noun: used when talking about one child in general (not a specific one). Common in set phrases like:
- „Als ich ein Kind war …“ = “When I was a child …”
- „ein Kind haben“ = “to have a child”
- „ein Kind erwarten“ = “to be expecting a baby.”
Note: German „Kind“ is a false friend with English “kind” (it means “child,” not “type”).
target_language_example: Als ich ein Kind war, wollte ich Astronaut werden.
native_language_example: When I was a child, I wanted to become an astronaut.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like singen (to sing) and hören/anhören (to listen to). In German, Lied is neuter: das Lied; plural: Lieder.
target_language_example: Kannst du mir ein Lied vorsingen?
native_language_example: Can you sing me a song?

additional_notes: Used for a physical opening or gap in something (a sock, pants), a hole in the ground (dug or fallen into), or a cavity in a tooth (ein Loch im Zahn). In German it’s neuter: das Loch; accusative with indefinite article: ein Loch; with locations often: in + dative (im Socken, im Zahn).
target_language_example: Pass auf, da ist ein Loch im Boden!
native_language_example: Watch out, there’s a hole in the ground!

meaning: “a hole in” / “to make a hole in”.
additional_notes: Used with the accusative (in + Akk.) to say that something causes or creates a hole in something: ein Loch in meine Jeans / in die Wand. Very common with verbs like reißen (tear) and schlagen (hit/punch). Can also be used in exaggeration or figuratively (e.g., ein Loch in die Luft schlagen).
target_language_example: Ich habe aus Versehen ein Loch in mein T-Shirt gemacht.
native_language_example: I accidentally made a hole in my T-shirt.

meaning: a liar (a man); someone who lies.
additional_notes: "Lügner" is a noun for a male person; for a woman you’d usually say "eine Lügnerin". Often used as an accusation or judgment (can sound harsh), e.g. "Du bist so ein Lügner!". With "sein" (to be): "Er ist ein Lügner."
target_language_example: Ich glaube dir nicht — du bist ein Lügner.
native_language_example: I don't believe you — you're a liar.

additional_notes: Indefinite article + noun: used to introduce an unknown/unspecified man ("a man") in a story or situation. It can also mean "one man" when you’re emphasizing a single person (context decides). Often appears in different cases depending on the sentence (e.g., "Ich sehe einen Mann" = "I see a man").
target_language_example: Vor der Tür steht ein Mann und wartet.
native_language_example: There’s a man standing at the door waiting.

meaning: “a man who …” (introduces a relative clause describing a man).
additional_notes: Used to describe what kind of man someone is by adding more information in a relative clause. After "der" the verb goes to the end of that clause (e.g., "der zu seinem Wort steht"). You can change it for case/number: "ein Mann, den …" (whom), "ein Mann, dem …" (to/for whom), "eine Frau, die …", "Menschen, die …".
target_language_example: Er ist ein Mann, der immer die Wahrheit sagt.
native_language_example: He is a man who always tells the truth.

additional_notes: Uses the indefinite article: "ein Mensch" = "a person / a human being" (one individual). Often used in general statements about humans (like "A person can...") or to mean "just a person" ("Nur ein Mensch.").
target_language_example: Ein Mensch braucht Schlaf und Wasser.
native_language_example: A person needs sleep and water.

additional_notes: Used with the indefinite article ein (“a/an”): Ich brauche ein Messer. In everyday contexts it means a kitchen knife (e.g., for butter), but in crime/violence contexts it can mean a weapon (e.g., jemandem ein Messer an den Hals / an die Kehle halten = to hold a knife to someone’s throat).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir bitte ein Messer geben?
native_language_example: Can you please give me a knife?

additional_notes: Means “a girl”; can also refer to a young woman depending on context. “Mädchen” is neuter in German, so you often see “das Mädchen” and pronouns like “es,” even when talking about a female person (e.g., “Es ist ein Mädchen.”).
target_language_example: Das ist ein Mädchen aus meiner Klasse.
native_language_example: That’s a girl from my class.

additional_notes: Used as an insult (“Du bist ein Narr!”) or self-criticism (“Ich war ein Narr ...”). It can also be used more generally for someone who behaves very foolishly. Feminine form: „eine Närrin“.
target_language_example: Sei kein Narr und hör auf ihn!
native_language_example: Don’t be a fool and listen to him!

meaning: a nap; a short sleep (usually during the day).
additional_notes: Commonly used with the verb „machen“: „ein Nickerchen machen“ = to take/have a nap. Typically refers to a brief rest/sleep, often in the afternoon.
target_language_example: Nach dem Mittagessen mache ich oft ein Nickerchen.
native_language_example: After lunch I often take a nap.

additional_notes: Used with nouns to mean “a pair of” things that belong together (often two items, e.g., Schuhe, Handschuhe, Augen). It can also mean “a couple” in the relationship sense (ein Paar sein). Note the difference to lowercase „ein paar“ = “a few / a couple of” (number, not necessarily exactly two).
target_language_example: Wir sind seit drei Jahren ein Paar.
native_language_example: We’ve been a couple for three years.

additional_notes: "ein" is the indefinite article (“a/an”) used with masculine/neuter nouns in the nominative case. You’ll see "ein Pferd" as the subject or object of a sentence (e.g., owning, wanting, or seeing a horse). It also appears in the common exclamation "Ich glaub’, mich tritt ein Pferd!" meaning “I can’t believe it!” / “You’ve got to be kidding!” (colloquial).
target_language_example: Wir sehen draußen ein Pferd.
native_language_example: We see a horse outside.

additional_notes: "ein" is the masculine indefinite article (“a/an”). "Polizist" is a masculine noun for a male police officer; the feminine form is "Polizistin". In the plural you say "Polizisten" (“police officers”). Often you’ll also hear the gender-neutral "Polizeibeamter/Polizeibeamtin".
target_language_example: Da drüben steht ein Polizist.
native_language_example: A police officer is standing over there.

additional_notes: Means a difficulty, trouble, or something that needs to be solved. Common with „haben“: „Ich/Wir habe(n) ein Problem.“ You can also ask „Gibt es (hier) ein Problem?“ = “Is there a problem (here)?”
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, ich habe ein Problem mit meiner Rechnung.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have a problem with my bill.

meaning: a riddle; a mystery (something hard to understand).
additional_notes: Used with "sein" to say something is puzzling or unexplained: "(Das) ist mir ein Rätsel" = "It’s a mystery to me / I can’t figure it out." Also common: "Es ist mir ein Rätsel, warum ..." (I have no idea why ...). Can refer to a literal puzzle/riddle or a real-life mystery (e.g., a case, someone’s plans).
target_language_example: Es ist mir ein Rätsel, warum er nie pünktlich ist.
native_language_example: It’s a mystery to me why he’s never on time.

additional_notes: Used with the indefinite article for a single, unspecified sandwich. In sentences it’s often the direct object: etwas essen/machen (to eat/make something). In questions, “Was für ein Sandwich …?” means “What kind of sandwich …?”.
target_language_example: Ich nehme ein Sandwich, bitte.
native_language_example: I’ll have a sandwich, please.

meaning: a joke; something said/done as a joke.
additional_notes: Used to say that something isn’t serious or to ask if someone is joking. Common with "Das ist ein Scherz" ("That’s a joke" / "You must be kidding") and "nur/bloß ein Scherz" ("just a joke").
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, das war nur ein Scherz.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, that was just a joke.

additional_notes: "Schiff" is a neuter noun (das Schiff). With the indefinite article it becomes "ein Schiff". Often used when pointing something out ("Das ist ein Schiff.") or when seeing one at a distance, e.g. on the horizon ("am Horizont", "in der Ferne").
target_language_example: Da draußen ist ein Schiff auf dem Meer.
native_language_example: Out there is a ship on the sea.

meaning: a pig; (also) a very dirty/unpleasant person (insult).
additional_notes: Literally an animal (“a pig”). Often appears in comparisons with wie: essen/fressen wie ein Schwein = “to eat like a pig” (very messily), bluten wie ein Schwein = “to bleed like a pig” (a lot). Calling someone ein Schwein is an insult (roughly “you pig”).
target_language_example: Er benimmt sich manchmal wie ein Schwein.
native_language_example: Sometimes he behaves like a pig.

meaning: "a game" (sometimes: "a joke" / "a trick" in a figurative sense).
additional_notes: Literally means a game (something you play). In questions like "Was ist das für ein Spiel?", it can also mean "What kind of game is this?" or (depending on context/intonation) "What is this supposed to be?" / "What kind of trick is this?". You’ll also see it used metaphorically: "Das ist (doch) ein Spiel" = "This is (just) a game".
target_language_example: Glaubst du, das ist nur ein Spiel?
native_language_example: Do you think this is just a game?

additional_notes: Used with the indefinite article "ein" to mean "a spy". The noun is masculine: der Spion. Common patterns: "ein Spion sein" (to be a spy), "als Spion arbeiten" (to work as a spy), "beschuldigt werden, ein Spion zu sein" (to be accused of being a spy).
target_language_example: Ich glaube, er ist ein Spion.
native_language_example: I think he’s a spy.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a portion or section of something: food (ein Stück Brot/Fleisch), materials (ein Stück Holz), or even land (ein Stück Land). Often used when asking for some of something: „Kann ich ein Stück davon haben?“ In a shop or at the table, „Ein Stück!“ can be a short request meaning “(I’ll have) a piece!”
target_language_example: Kannst du mir ein Stück Kuchen geben?
native_language_example: Can you give me a piece of cake?

additional_notes: Used to offer, request, or talk about eating one portion of cake. "ein Stück" means "a piece" and is commonly used with food (e.g., ein Stück Brot, ein Stück Pizza). In questions/offers you’ll often hear it after verbs like "möchtest du/willst du" or with "Appetit auf" (appetite for).
target_language_example: Kann ich bitte ein Stück Kuchen haben?
native_language_example: Can I please have a piece of cake?

additional_notes: Used when you need some paper (e.g., to write on) or when talking about a small piece or single sheet. Often said as a request: „ein Stück Papier, bitte“.
target_language_example: Hast du ein Stück Papier für mich?
native_language_example: Do you have a piece of paper for me?

meaning: a taxi; a cab (one taxi ride).
additional_notes: "ein" is the indefinite article (like "a") and the noun is "Taxi" (neutral: das Taxi). Common verbs with it: "ein Taxi nehmen" (to take a taxi), "ein Taxi rufen" (to call a taxi), "ein Taxi bestellen" (to order/book a taxi).
target_language_example: Können Sie mir bitte ein Taxi rufen?
native_language_example: Could you please call me a taxi?

additional_notes: Used to say you choose a taxi as your means of transport, often because it’s faster or there’s no bus/train. You’ll also often hear it with a reflexive pronoun: „sich ein Taxi nehmen“ (same meaning, slightly emphasizing that you get yourself a taxi). In the past, it’s commonly „musste ein Taxi nehmen“ = “had to take a taxi.”
target_language_example: Da ich es eilig hatte, musste ich ein Taxi nehmen.
native_language_example: Since I was in a hurry, I had to take a taxi.

meaning: a part; a piece (one item of a whole).
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something belongs to a bigger group or thing: „ein Teil davon“ = “a part of it.” It can also mean one individual piece/item (often something that can break) or a component/part (e.g., of a machine).
target_language_example: Ich möchte ein Teil von dem Kuchen.
native_language_example: I’d like a piece of the cake.

additional_notes: Used with the genitive case to show that something belongs to a larger whole. "ein Teil der" is used before feminine singular nouns and plural nouns in the genitive (e.g., "ein Teil der Stadt" = part of the city; "ein Teil der Kosten" = part of the costs). With masculine/neuter singular nouns you usually say "ein Teil des ..." (e.g., "ein Teil des Plans"). In everyday speech you may also hear "ein Teil von ..." + dative.
target_language_example: Das ist ein Teil der Geschichte.
native_language_example: That is a part of the story.

meaning: a ticket (e.g., for travel or an event).
additional_notes: Used with transport (train/plane/bus) or events. Often followed by details like destination ("ein Ticket nach Paris"), type/class ("erster Klasse"), or price ("Wie viel kostet ...?"). The word "Ticket" is commonly used in German, alongside "Fahrkarte" (more specifically for public transport).
target_language_example: Ich brauche ein Ticket nach Berlin, bitte.
native_language_example: I need a ticket to Berlin, please.

meaning: an animal; (about a person, colloquial) a beast / an animal.
additional_notes: Literal meaning: a living animal (often with "sein": "X ist ein Tier"). Said to a person ("Du bist ein Tier"), it’s usually a strong, informal expression meaning someone is acting wild, rough, or extremely intense (sometimes as a compliment, sometimes as criticism—depends on context and tone). "… oder so was?" means "…or something like that?"
target_language_example: In dem Spiel war er ein Tier und hat alles gewonnen.
native_language_example: In that game he was a beast and won everything.

meaning: a dream; (figuratively) something you really wish for or something wonderful.
additional_notes: Used literally for a dream you have while sleeping: „Es war alles ein Traum.“ It’s also used figuratively to mean an unreal/imagined goal („eine Reise zum Mond ist nicht länger ein Traum“) or, in a positive sense, that something is amazing/ideal („Das ist (ja) ein Traum!“).
target_language_example: Für mich war dieser Urlaub ein Traum.
native_language_example: For me, this vacation was a dream.

additional_notes: A noun meaning something illegal punishable by law. Often used with verbs like „ein Verbrechen begehen“ (to commit a crime) and in questions like „Ist das ein Verbrechen?“ (Is that a crime?).
target_language_example: Er hat ein Verbrechen begangen und wurde verurteilt.
native_language_example: He committed a crime and was convicted.

meaning: a fortune; a lot of money.
additional_notes: Often used to emphasize that something is (too) expensive: "Das kostet ein Vermögen" (“That costs a fortune”). It can also mean actual wealth someone has or leaves behind: "ein Vermögen hinterlassen" (“to leave a fortune behind”). Grammar note: "Vermögen" is neuter (das Vermögen); with the indefinite article it’s "ein Vermögen".
target_language_example: Die neue Küche hat ein Vermögen gekostet.
native_language_example: The new kitchen cost a fortune.

additional_notes: Means a commitment to do (or not do) something. Common with: „ein Versprechen geben“ (to make a promise), „ein Versprechen brechen“ (to break a promise). Often used in the saying „Ein Versprechen ist ein Versprechen.“ (= a promise is a promise).
target_language_example: Ich kann nicht kommen, aber ich gebe dir ein Versprechen: Ich rufe dich morgen an.
native_language_example: I can’t come, but I promise you: I’ll call you tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an unspecified bird (indefinite article „ein“ + noun „Vogel“). Common in questions like „Ist das ein Vogel?“ (“Is that a bird?”) and „Was für ein Vogel ist das?“ (“What kind of bird is that?”). Note: without the article, „(Du) Vogel!“ can be an insult meaning “idiot” (informal).
target_language_example: Ich sehe draußen ein Vogel.
native_language_example: I see a bird outside.

meaning: “a joke”; also “you’ve got to be kidding” (showing disbelief/annoyance).
additional_notes: Literally “a joke.” In questions like „Ist das ein Witz?“ or „War das ein Witz?“ it often means you think something can’t be serious. With „Das ist doch wohl ein Witz.“ it’s usually sarcastic and means “This is ridiculous / This can’t be serious.” You can soften it with „bloß/nur“: „Es ist bloß/nur ein Witz.“ = “It’s just a joke.”
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, das war nur ein Witz.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, that was just a joke.

meaning: 'a word' (also: 'a single word' / 'anything at all' in negatives).
additional_notes: Literally means “a word,” but very often used in fixed phrases to mean “(even) a single word.” Common patterns: „ein Wort mit jemandem“ = “a word with someone” (a quick talk); „kein/nicht ein Wort“ = “not a word / nothing at all” (e.g., not saying or revealing anything); „ohne ein Wort (zu sagen/zu wechseln)“ = “without saying a word.”
target_language_example: Kann ich kurz ein Wort mit dir reden?
native_language_example: Can I have a quick word with you?

meaning: a miracle; something amazing and unexpected.
additional_notes: Used for something that seems impossible or extremely unlikely. Common in phrases like "Das wäre ein Wunder" (That would be a miracle) and "wie durch ein Wunder" (as if by a miracle / miraculously).
target_language_example: Es ist ein Wunder, dass der Zug heute pünktlich ist.
native_language_example: It’s a miracle that the train is on time today.

additional_notes: "Wörterbuch" is a neuter noun (das Wörterbuch). You use "ein Wörterbuch" when it’s an indefinite/unspecified dictionary (e.g., buying one, needing one, using one for an exam). In the plural: "Wörterbücher".
target_language_example: Kann ich mir kurz ein Wörterbuch ausleihen?
native_language_example: Can I borrow a dictionary for a moment?

meaning: a sign; a signal; an omen (a meaningful sign).
additional_notes: Used for something that is taken as meaning something else (often fate/God/the universe giving you a hint): „Das muss ein Zeichen sein.“ It can also mean a concrete signal or gesture: „Gib uns ein Zeichen!“ Common patterns: „ein Zeichen sein“ (to be a sign), „ein Zeichen geben“ (to give a sign), „ein Zeichen von …“ (a sign from …), „als ein Zeichen“ (as a sign), „ein Zeichen der Hoffnung“ (a sign of hope).
target_language_example: Ich sehe das als ein Zeichen, dass wir weitermachen sollen.
native_language_example: I see that as a sign that we should keep going.

additional_notes: Used when you need or talk about a single room. Common with verbs like mieten (to rent) and with hotel-style requests: ein Zimmer für vier Nächte (a room for four nights), ein Zimmer mit Aussicht (a room with a view). Also used in the phrase Nehmt euch ein Zimmer! (“Get a room!”), a humorous/annoyed way to tell two people (often a couple) to stop being so affectionate in public.
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, ich hätte gern ein Zimmer für zwei Nächte.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I’d like a room for two nights.

meaning: a coincidence; chance (something that happens by accident).
additional_notes: Used to say something happened without planning or intention. Often appears in questions like „Ist das nur ein Zufall?“ (= Is that just a coincidence?) and as an exclamation: „So ein Zufall!“ (= What a coincidence!).
target_language_example: Es war kein Plan — es war einfach ein Zufall.
native_language_example: It wasn’t a plan — it was just a coincidence.

additional_notes: Common, literal noun phrase for an elderly male person; can also be used figuratively/teasingly (e.g., someone behaves like an old man). Grammar note: nominative is "ein alter Mann"; accusative "einen alten Mann"; dative "einem alten Mann"—the adjective ending changes with the case.
target_language_example: Ein alter Mann saß neben mir im Bus.
native_language_example: An old man sat next to me on the bus.

additional_notes: Used before a neuter noun (das-words), e.g. ein altes Auto / ein altes Fahrrad. It’s the indefinite article "ein" + the adjective "alt" with the ending -es. The noun often follows; by itself ("ein altes") can sound incomplete unless the noun is understood from context.
target_language_example: Ich habe ein altes Buch gefunden.
native_language_example: I found an old book.

additional_notes: A simple noun phrase: **ein** (a) + **altes** (old) + **Auto** (car). Notice the adjective ending **-es** in **altes** because **Auto** is neuter (**das Auto**) and it follows **ein** in the nominative case.
target_language_example: Ich habe ein altes Auto, aber es fährt noch gut.
native_language_example: I have an old car, but it still drives well.

additional_notes: Used with a neuter singular noun after ein, as in ein anderes Bier or ein anderes Wort. It can also stand alone when the noun is understood from context: Ich nehme ein anderes = I'll take another one. The form changes with gender and number, for example ein anderer, eine andere, andere.
target_language_example: Kann ich ein anderes Zimmer haben?
native_language_example: Can I have another room?

additional_notes: Used to postpone something to a different occasion (often meaning “not now”). Common with verbs like treffen (meet), sprechen (talk), machen (do), mitnehmen (take along).
target_language_example: Heute habe ich keine Zeit—wir können ein anderes Mal darüber reden.
native_language_example: I don’t have time today—we can talk about it another time.

additional_notes: Used to suggest doing something later or to postpone: "not now, but another time." Often stands alone as a short reply ("Ein andermal.").
target_language_example: Lass uns ein andermal darüber reden.
native_language_example: Let's talk about it another time.

meaning: “a famous …” (masculine noun phrase in the nominative case).
additional_notes: Used before a masculine noun to describe someone as famous: ein berühmter Sänger/Autor/Architekt. The ending -er appears with masculine nominative after ein. In other cases it changes: acc. einen berühmten Sänger; dat. einem berühmten Sänger. For feminine/neuter/plural: eine berühmte Schauspielerin, ein berühmtes Buch, berühmte Leute.
target_language_example: Er ist ein berühmter Schauspieler.
native_language_example: He is a famous actor.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine noun (often "Mensch") or with an implied noun: "ein besserer (Mensch)" = "a better (person)". This is the declined comparative form of "gut" → "besser". The ending changes with gender/case: e.g., "eine bessere Freundin" (feminine), "ein besseres Leben" (neuter).
target_language_example: Ich will ein besserer Vater sein.
native_language_example: I want to be a better father.

additional_notes: Used for a small amount or degree. With nouns, it usually means a small quantity (especially with uncountable things: ein bisschen Wasser = a little water). With adjectives, adverbs, or verbs, it often means 'slightly' or 'a bit'.
target_language_example: Ich bin ein bisschen müde.
native_language_example: I'm a little tired.

additional_notes: Used to soften statements or requests and to mean a small amount or degree. Very common with adjectives/adverbs ("ein bisschen krank/müde/komisch" = "a bit ill/tired/weird") and with comparisons/changes ("ein bisschen mehr" = "a little more"). In casual speech it’s often shortened to "’n bisschen".
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte ein bisschen leiser sprechen?
native_language_example: Could you speak a little more quietly, please?

additional_notes: Used to express a small amount or degree. Often comes before a noun (ein bisschen Zeit) or as an adverb with adjectives/verbs (ein bisschen müde, warte ein bisschen). Also common in softening statements: ein bisschen Wut = a bit of anger.
target_language_example: Kannst du ein bisschen leiser sprechen?
native_language_example: Can you speak a little more quietly?

additional_notes: Used to soften a statement or request, or to mean a small amount/degree. It can refer to time (ein bisschen bleiben = stay a little while) or feelings/intensity (ein bisschen verliebt = a little in love). Often interchangeable with "ein wenig" (a bit more formal).
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte ein bisschen langsamer sprechen?
native_language_example: Can you please speak a little more slowly?

additional_notes: Used to soften statements or requests (often like “kind of” / “a little”). It can modify adjectives/adverbs ("ein bißchen gestresst" = "a bit stressed") or verbs ("ein bißchen rücken" = "move a little"). Very common in spoken German. Modern spelling is usually "ein bisschen".
target_language_example: Ich brauche ein bißchen Zeit.
native_language_example: I need a little time.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine noun (e.g., ein echter Freund, ein echter Diamant) to say someone/something is real/authentic (not fake) or a true example of a type (“a true gentleman”, “a real friend”). For feminine nouns: eine echte …; for neuter nouns: ein echtes ….
target_language_example: Das ist ein echter Klassiker.
native_language_example: That’s a real classic.

meaning: "a real / genuine" (used before a neuter noun).
additional_notes: Used with a neuter noun (das-Wort) in nominative or accusative: ein echtes + Noun (e.g., ein echtes Problem, ein echtes Pferd). It contrasts something authentic/true with something fake, imaginary, or not the “real thing,” and can be used literally or figuratively.
target_language_example: Das ist ein echtes Problem.
native_language_example: That’s a real problem.

additional_notes: Used with a neuter noun (das) to mean something that belongs to one person/family or is separate for each unit: ein eigenes Bankkonto, ein eigenes Bad. It can also stand alone when the noun is understood: lieber ein Kind adoptieren als ein eigenes (Kind) bekommen = “rather adopt a child than have one of their own.” The adjective changes endings with gender/case (e.g., ein eigener Garten, eine eigene Wohnung).
target_language_example: Ich möchte irgendwann ein eigenes Auto haben.
native_language_example: I’d like to have my own car someday.

meaning: a room of one’s own (a private bedroom).
additional_notes: Used to say someone has their own separate room, not shared with siblings/roommates. Often with verbs like haben/bekommen/wollen: „ein eigenes Zimmer haben/bekommen/wollen“.
target_language_example: In der neuen Wohnung hat jedes Kind ein eigenes Zimmer.
native_language_example: In the new apartment, each child has their own room.

additional_notes: Used to stress that something happens only once, or to emphasize that it never happened at all (often with negation: „nicht ein einziges Mal“ = “not even once”). It can also sound like a warning or threat in contexts like „noch ein einziges Mal“ (“one more time”).
target_language_example: Ich habe ihn nicht ein einziges Mal angerufen.
native_language_example: I didn’t call him even once.

meaning: once and for all; for good (finally).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is settled or should be done definitively, so it won’t be discussed or repeated again. Often said firmly on its own ("Ein für alle Mal!") or with verbs like "beilegen" (settle), "klarstellen" (make clear), "sagen" / "wiederholen" (say/repeat).
target_language_example: Klär das bitte ein für alle Mal mit ihm.
native_language_example: Please sort that out with him once and for all.

additional_notes: Used before an adjective to intensify it: „ein ganz kleines Mädchen“ = “a very small girl”, „ein ganz tolles Spiel“ = “a really great game”. It’s common in spoken German. Don’t confuse this with „ein ganzes …“ (with an -es ending), which means “a whole …” (e.g., „ein ganzes Jahr“ = “a whole year”).
target_language_example: Das ist ein ganz guter Vorschlag.
native_language_example: That’s a really good suggestion.

meaning: “a born …” / “a natural …” (someone who is naturally suited to or good at something).
additional_notes: Used before a noun to describe an inborn talent, tendency, or character type: „ein geborener Gewinner“ = a born winner. The ending changes with gender and case: „ein geborener …“ (masc. nom.), „eine geborene …“ (fem. nom.), „ein geborenes …“ (neut. nom.), plural „geborene …“. Common with roles/types of people (Gewinner, Redner, Abenteurer, Kavalier, etc.).
target_language_example: Er war ein geborener Abenteurer.
native_language_example: He was a born adventurer.

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s overall life being happy/satisfying. Very often with the verb „(ein) Leben führen“ (to lead/live a life): „ein glückliches Leben führen“. You can also use it in wishes: „Ich wünsche dir ein glückliches Leben.“
target_language_example: Nach all den Jahren möchte ich einfach ein glückliches Leben führen.
native_language_example: After all these years, I just want to live a happy life.

meaning: a great / wonderful (masculine form before a noun).
additional_notes: Used to praise someone or something. This is the masculine nominative form ("ein großartiger Mann/Tag/Abend/Vater"). The ending changes with gender/case: "ein großartiges" (neuter), "eine großartige" (feminine), plural "großartige".
target_language_example: Das war ein großartiger Moment.
native_language_example: That was a great moment.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine noun to describe it as big/important/special (e.g., ein großer Tag = a great day). It’s the masculine nominative form of the adjective: ein großer + Noun. (Neuter: ein großes; feminine: eine große.)
target_language_example: Das ist ein großer Moment für uns.
native_language_example: This is a big moment for us.

meaning: a tall/big man (sometimes: a great/important man).
additional_notes: Most often describes physical height/size: "groß" = tall/big. Depending on context, it can also mean "great" in the sense of important or admirable (e.g., a "great man" in history). Adjective endings change with the article/case (e.g., "ein großer Mann", "der große Mann", "einen großen Mann").
target_language_example: Er war ein großer Mann.
native_language_example: He was a tall man.

additional_notes: Used before a singular neuter noun in the nominative or accusative, e.g. ein großes Auto, ein großes Problem. Depending on the noun, it can also mean "a great" in English, as in ein großes Vergnügen ("a great pleasure").
target_language_example: Wir brauchen ein großes Auto.
native_language_example: We need a big car.

additional_notes: "Ein" means "a" (indefinite article). "Großes" is the adjective "groß" (big/large) with the ending -es because "Haus" is neuter (das Haus) in the nominative or accusative: "ein großes Haus". In other cases the ending changes (e.g., "in einem großen Haus" = in a big house).
target_language_example: Da ist ein großes Haus auf dem Hügel.
native_language_example: There is a big house on the hill.

additional_notes: Used to say a situation is serious or could become serious. Often appears with verbs like haben (to have), sein (to be), or werden (to become): Ich habe ein großes Problem. / Es kann ein großes Problem werden. You can add hier to stress that the problem is right here/with this situation: Ich habe hier ein großes Problem.
target_language_example: Wenn wir das jetzt nicht lösen, wird es ein großes Problem.
native_language_example: If we don’t solve this now, it will become a big problem.

meaning: a large fortune; a lot of wealth.
additional_notes: Used to talk about someone having, building up, inheriting (erben), or leaving behind (hinterlassen) a lot of money and valuable property. Often appears with verbs like besitzen (to own), ansammeln (to accumulate), erben (to inherit), and hinterlassen (to leave behind).
target_language_example: Sie hat ein großes Vermögen geerbt.
native_language_example: She inherited a large fortune.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine noun: *ein guter Student / ein guter Arzt*. It’s the indefinite article *ein* + the adjective *gut* with the ending *-er* because the noun is masculine and in the nominative case (often the subject or after *sein/werden*). The ending changes in other cases/genders (e.g., *einen guten Student*).
target_language_example: Er ist ein guter Freund.
native_language_example: He is a good friend.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone as being a skilled, trustworthy doctor. Often appears with “sein” (to be): „Er ist ein guter Arzt.“ and with “werden” (to become / will be): „Aus ihm wird einmal ein guter Arzt.“
target_language_example: Sie ist ein guter Arzt und nimmt sich viel Zeit für ihre Patienten.
native_language_example: She is a good doctor and takes a lot of time for her patients.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone as a good teacher (often with "sein/werden": "Er ist/wird ein guter Lehrer"). After forms of "sein/werden", the noun usually has no ending: "ein guter Lehrer" (not *einen guten Lehrer*).
target_language_example: Er wird bestimmt ein guter Lehrer.
native_language_example: He will definitely be a good teacher.

meaning: a good person; a kind person.
additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s character or moral qualities (often as a compliment). It can be said directly to someone (Du bist …) or about someone (Er ist …). In the nominative with “sein” (to be): „Er ist ein guter Mensch.“
target_language_example: Sie ist wirklich ein guter Mensch und hilft immer anderen.
native_language_example: She’s really a good person and always helps others.

additional_notes: Describes a male student (Schüler). For a female student, say: „eine gute Schülerin“. In the plural: „gute Schüler“ (mixed/all male) or „gute Schülerinnen“ (all female). Used with „sein/war“ to describe someone’s school performance or behavior.
target_language_example: Mein Bruder war in Mathe ein guter Schüler.
native_language_example: My brother was a good student in math.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone as being a good dad, or to talk about the goal/ideal of being a good father. The noun changes with case: nominative/accusative: „ein guter Vater“ (Er ist ein guter Vater. / Ich möchte ein guter Vater sein.), dative: „einem guten Vater“ (mit einem guten Vater).
target_language_example: Er will ein guter Vater sein.
native_language_example: He wants to be a good father.

additional_notes: Used before a singular neuter noun, as in ein gutes Buch, ein gutes Team, or ein gutes Restaurant. Here gutes is the form of gut that matches a neuter noun after ein in the nominative or accusative.
target_language_example: Ich suche ein gutes Hotel in der Stadt.
native_language_example: I'm looking for a good hotel in the city.

additional_notes: Used with "haben" (to have) to describe someone who remembers things well: "Ich habe/du hast/er hat … ein gutes Gedächtnis." It’s a normal, neutral compliment; the opposite is "ein schlechtes Gedächtnis" (a bad memory).
target_language_example: Meine Schwester hat ein gutes Gedächtnis und merkt sich immer Namen.
native_language_example: My sister has a good memory and always remembers names.

meaning: a good feeling; a good gut feeling (a hunch).
additional_notes: Used to express that you feel positive or confident about a situation, often based on intuition rather than facts. Very common with "ich habe/hatte" (I have/had): "Ich habe ein gutes Gefühl (bei der Sache)". You can also say it to reassure someone: "Hab ein gutes Gefühl!" = "Have a good feeling (about it)!".
target_language_example: Ich habe ein gutes Gefühl bei dem Vorstellungsgespräch.
native_language_example: I have a good feeling about the job interview.

additional_notes: “hübsch” means “pretty” or “good-looking” (often about a person). “Mädchen” is “girl” (a young female). Because “Mädchen” is neuter in German (das Mädchen), you say “ein hübsches Mädchen” (not *eine*). With “ein” (indefinite article), it often means “a/one (pretty) girl” rather than a specific person.
target_language_example: Auf der Party habe ich ein hübsches Mädchen gesehen.
native_language_example: At the party I saw a pretty girl.

additional_notes: Somewhat formal/old-fashioned and often found in written or literary German. It emphasizes that it applies to every single person. It can be followed by a relative clause (e.g., „Ein jeder, der …“). In everyday speech, people usually say „jeder“ or „alle“ instead.
target_language_example: Ein jeder, der hier arbeitet, kennt die Regeln.
native_language_example: Everyone who works here knows the rules.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine noun in the nominative with the indefinite article: ein + kleiner + Noun (e.g., ein kleiner Teich, ein kleiner Mann). The adjective ending changes with gender/case: e.g., eine kleine Frau (feminine), ein kleines Kind (neuter). In phrases like „ein kleiner Junge“, it means “a little boy/when he was a little boy.”
target_language_example: In unserem Garten steht ein kleiner Baum.
native_language_example: There is a small tree in our garden.

meaning: a little boy; a young boy.
additional_notes: Used to describe a male child (roughly kindergarten/early elementary age). Often appears after the verb "sein" (to be): "Er war/ist ein kleiner Junge". With "seit" (since), German typically uses the present tense even for something that started in the past and continues: "seit er ein kleiner Junge ist" (= since he was/has been a little boy).
target_language_example: Als ich ein kleiner Junge war, wollte ich Pilot werden.
native_language_example: When I was a little boy, I wanted to become a pilot.

additional_notes: "kleines" is the adjective "klein" (small) with the ending -es because "Haus" is neuter (das Haus) and follows "ein". Used to describe the size of a house; in plural: "kleine Häuser".
target_language_example: Wir suchen ein kleines Haus auf dem Land.
native_language_example: We’re looking for a small house in the countryside.

additional_notes: Refers to a female child. Often used with „sein“ (Sie ist ein kleines Mädchen.) or to talk about the past: „als ich ein kleines Mädchen war“ = “when I was a little girl.” „klein“ here means “young/small,” and „Mädchen“ is grammatically neuter in German (das Mädchen), so you may see pronouns like „es“ referring to a girl.
target_language_example: Als ich ein kleines Mädchen war, wollte ich Tierärztin werden.
native_language_example: When I was a little girl, I wanted to become a veterinarian.

meaning: a small/minor problem; a slight issue.
additional_notes: Often used to introduce a complication in a situation, sometimes as a polite or understated way to say there is a problem. Common patterns: „Es gibt ein kleines Problem.“ (There’s a small problem.) and „Wir haben ein kleines Problem.“ (We have a small problem.)
target_language_example: Ich kann heute kommen, aber es gibt ein kleines Problem: Ich bin erst um acht da.
native_language_example: I can come today, but there’s a small problem: I won’t be there until eight.

additional_notes: This is the masculine nominative form of the adjective "klug" after the indefinite article "ein". It typically comes directly before a masculine noun (e.g., "ein kluger Junge", "ein kluger Kerl", "ein kluger Mensch"). On its own, "ein kluger" usually sounds incomplete unless the noun is clearly understood from context (similar to “a clever one/guy”).
target_language_example: Er ist ein kluger Junge.
native_language_example: He is a clever boy.

meaning: a long way; a long journey (also: a long road/path).
additional_notes: Used literally for a physically long route (by foot, car, etc.) and figuratively for a long process still ahead (often with verbs like „vor uns liegen“ = “to lie ahead of us”). You can also say „Das ist ein langer Weg“ to comment that something will take a lot of time/effort.
target_language_example: Bis zum Bahnhof ist es ein langer Weg.
native_language_example: It’s a long way to the train station.

meaning: one last time; for the last time.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens one final time (often with emotion: goodbye, regret, a final warning). Common with verbs like sehen (see), sagen (say), umarmen (hug), halten (hold). In statements like „Ich sage das ein letztes Mal“, it can mean “for the last time” as a firm warning.
target_language_example: Ich rufe dich ein letztes Mal an, dann lasse ich es.
native_language_example: I'll call you one last time, then I'll drop it.

additional_notes: This is the adjective **nett** (“nice/pleasant/kind”) with the ending **-es** after **ein** when the noun is **neuter** (das-words), e.g. **ein nettes Haus**, **ein nettes Lächeln**, **ein nettes Gespräch**. It’s a common way to give a friendly, mild compliment.
target_language_example: Das ist ein nettes Geschenk.
native_language_example: That’s a nice gift.

meaning: “a new …” (masculine nominative singular), e.g. “a new customer” / “a new one.”
additional_notes: Used before a masculine noun in the nominative case: ein neuer Kunde (a new customer). It can also stand on its own to mean “a new one” when the noun is understood from context.
target_language_example: Ist das ein neuer Kollege?
native_language_example: Is that a new colleague?

additional_notes: Used before a singular neuter noun, usually in the nominative or accusative: e.g. ein neues Buch, ein neues Telefon, ein neues Museum. It is ein + neu with the adjective ending -es.
target_language_example: Ich brauche ein neues Auto.
native_language_example: I need a new car.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase: "ein" (a) + "neues" (new; adjective ending for neuter "Auto") + "Auto" (car). Used with verbs like "haben" (to have), "kaufen" (to buy), "wollen" (to want), "brauchen" (to need). In the accusative after many verbs, it stays "ein neues Auto".
target_language_example: Ich will mir ein neues Auto kaufen.
native_language_example: I want to buy myself a new car.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "kaufen" (to buy) in the Perfekt past tense: "(hat/habe/hast) ... gekauft". The object is "ein neues Auto" (a new car). You may also see a dative/recipient: "Ich habe ihr ein neues Auto gekauft" (I bought her a new car), or a reflexive pronoun to mean buying it for yourself: "Sie hat sich ein neues Auto gekauft" (She bought herself a new car). Word order: the past participle "gekauft" usually goes at the end of the clause.
target_language_example: Wir haben uns ein neues Auto gekauft.
native_language_example: We bought ourselves a new car.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase: „ein“ (a) + „neues“ (new, neuter form) + „Fahrrad“ (bicycle). Used as a direct object with verbs like „kaufen“ (to buy) and „haben“ (to have). In the accusative, it stays the same: „ein neues Fahrrad“.
target_language_example: Zu meinem Geburtstag wünsche ich mir ein neues Fahrrad.
native_language_example: For my birthday, I’m wishing for a new bicycle.

additional_notes: Used when talking about buying, ordering, making, sewing, or having a dress made. Note the accusative form: "ein neues Kleid" (neuter noun "das Kleid"; adjective ending "-es" after "ein"). Often appears with verbs like "kaufen" (buy), "bestellen" (order), "nähen" (sew), "machen" (make), or "anfertigen lassen" (have made).
target_language_example: Ich brauche ein neues Kleid für die Feier.
native_language_example: I need a new dress for the party.

meaning: a new life; a fresh start.
additional_notes: Used when someone starts over in a major way (new place, job, relationships, identity, routine) after a big change. Often used with verbs like „beginnen“, „anfangen“, „aufbauen“, „sich an … gewöhnen“, or with movement like „in ein neues Leben gehen/ziehen“.
target_language_example: Nach der Trennung wollte sie in einer anderen Stadt ein neues Leben anfangen.
native_language_example: After the breakup, she wanted to start a new life in another city.

additional_notes: Means a small number/amount (more than one). Used with plural nouns: ein paar Freunde, ein paar Fragen. It’s often similar to “some” in English when you mean “a few,” but it suggests a limited number. Not necessarily exactly two, even though it can be translated as “a couple of.”
target_language_example: Ich brauche noch ein paar Minuten.
native_language_example: I need a few more minutes.

additional_notes: A polite, common way to say you want to ask some questions. "ein paar" means "a few" (usually a small number). "Fragen stellen" is the standard verb phrase for "to ask questions" (literally: "to pose questions"). Often used with polite openings like "Dürfte ich …?" or "Hätten Sie etwas dagegen, wenn …?".
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, dürfte ich Ihnen ein paar Fragen stellen?
native_language_example: Excuse me, may I ask you a few questions?

meaning: a few times; a couple of times.
additional_notes: Used to talk about frequency (how often something happens). Often placed at the end of the sentence or near the verb: „Ich habe das ein paar Mal gemacht.“ You can also use it in questions: „Warst du schon ein paar Mal dort?“
target_language_example: Ich war schon ein paar Mal in Berlin.
native_language_example: I’ve already been to Berlin a few times.

additional_notes: Means a small, not exact amount of time. Often used with "in" to mean "in a few minutes" (something will happen soon), or without "in" to mean "for a few minutes" (how long something lasts).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir ein paar Minuten helfen?
native_language_example: Can you help me for a few minutes?

additional_notes: Means an imprecise small number of hours (often 2–4, depending on context). It’s used to talk about duration (seit ein paar Stunden = for a few hours) or time from now/from another event (ein paar Stunden später = a few hours later).
target_language_example: Kannst du noch ein paar Stunden bleiben?
native_language_example: Can you stay a few more hours?

additional_notes: Means a small, indefinite number of days (usually around 2–5). Common with time expressions: „nur noch ein paar Tage“ = “only a few days left”, „in ein paar Tagen“ = “in a few days”, „für ein paar Tage“ = “for a few days”. In speech, „ein paar“ often implies slightly more than „einige“ (“some”), but both are used similarly.
target_language_example: Ich bin in ein paar Tagen wieder da.
native_language_example: I'll be back in a few days.

meaning: a few weeks; a couple of weeks.
additional_notes: Used to talk about an approximate period of time (usually more than one week, often around 2–4 weeks). Common in everyday planning with verbs like „bleiben“ (stay), „warten“ (wait), „dauern“ (last), or „in“ + time: „in ein paar Wochen“ = “in a few weeks.”
target_language_example: Ich bin in ein paar Wochen wieder da.
native_language_example: I’ll be back in a few weeks.

meaning: "a few words" (a short statement or just a little bit of language).
additional_notes: Common when someone is invited to say something briefly (e.g., at an event): „ein paar Worte sagen“. It can also mean knowing only a small amount of a language: „ein paar Worte auf Englisch/Französisch“. Often used with polite „Sie“ in formal situations.
target_language_example: Ich möchte dazu nur ein paar Worte sagen.
native_language_example: I just want to say a few words about that.

additional_notes: Used for a small number of things or people. It usually goes with plural nouns, or can stand alone as in "ein paar von ihnen". In everyday German, it often does not mean exactly two. Compare with capitalized "ein Paar", which means "a pair" or "a couple".
target_language_example: Ich brauche nur ein paar Minuten.
native_language_example: I only need a few minutes.

additional_notes: Means a small number/amount of something (more than one, not many). Often used with plural nouns: „ein paar Übungen“ = “a few exercises.” It can also stand alone when the noun is understood: „Ein paar.“ = “A few.” In „ein paar Sekunden“ it means “a few seconds.” Don’t confuse with „ein Paar“ (capital P) = “a pair/couple” (exactly two, as a set).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir ein paar Minuten geben?
native_language_example: Can you give me a few minutes?

additional_notes: Means a small, not exact amount of time (usually more than 1–2 minutes, but not long). Often used with "nur" to stress it’s short ("nur noch ein paar Minuten" = just a few more minutes). With "vor" it means "a few minutes ago" ("vor ein paar Minuten").
target_language_example: Ich bin in ein paar Minuten zurück.
native_language_example: I’ll be back in a few minutes.

meaning: a few hours (some hours; not many).
additional_notes: Used to describe an approximate, small number of hours. Very common with time expressions (e.g., staying/working/sleeping for a few hours). It can refer to a duration ("für ein paar Stunden" = for a few hours) or to a point in the future ("in ein paar Stunden" = in a few hours).
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte noch ein paar Stunden warten?
native_language_example: Can you please wait a few more hours?

additional_notes: Means an imprecise small number of days (often around 2–5). Used with requests or time spans: „Gib mir ein paar Tage“ (give me a few days), „ein paar Tage bleiben“ (stay a few days).
target_language_example: Ich brauche noch ein paar Tage, um alles zu organisieren.
native_language_example: I need a few more days to organize everything.

additional_notes: Means an imprecise small number of weeks (usually 2–4). Used with time expressions for the near future (in ein paar Wochen = in a few weeks) or to refer to the recent past (vor ein paar Wochen = a few weeks ago).
target_language_example: Ich bin in ein paar Wochen wieder in Berlin.
native_language_example: I'll be back in Berlin in a few weeks.

meaning: “a real/true; a proper” (a genuine or typical example of something).
additional_notes: Used before a noun to emphasize that someone/something really fits the description (e.g., “a true friend,” “a real coward,” “a proper gentleman”). The adjective ending changes with gender and case: ein richtiger Mann, eine richtige Freundin, ein richtiges Problem; also in other cases (e.g., mit einem richtigen Freund). Can also be used ironically depending on tone.
target_language_example: Ein richtiger Freund wird dir die Wahrheit sagen.
native_language_example: A true friend will tell you the truth.

additional_notes: "ein" is the indefinite article ("a/an"). "rotes" is the adjective "rot" (red) with the ending -es because it comes after "ein" and "Auto" is neuter (das Auto). In other cases you may see different endings (e.g., "mit einem roten Auto").
target_language_example: Sie fährt ein rotes Auto.
native_language_example: She drives a red car.

additional_notes: Used to judge someone’s character/morality (yourself or someone else). Often appears with verbs like „sein“ (to be) or „wirken/ scheinen“ (to seem), or in the phrase „sich wie ein schlechter Mensch vorkommen“ = to feel like a bad person.
target_language_example: Ich will kein schlechter Mensch sein.
native_language_example: I don't want to be a bad person.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like "haben" (to have) and "bekommen/kriegen" (to get) to say you feel guilty, often because you think you did something wrong. Related: "Ich habe ein schlechtes Gewissen, weil …" (I feel guilty because …).
target_language_example: Ich habe ein schlechtes Gewissen, weil ich sie angelogen habe.
native_language_example: I feel guilty because I lied to her.

additional_notes: Used with a masculine noun in the nominative case (often after “sein”): ein schrecklicher Fehler / ein schrecklicher Film. The adjective ending changes with gender and case (e.g., eine schreckliche Idee, ein schreckliches Problem).
target_language_example: Das ist ein schrecklicher Tag.
native_language_example: This is a terrible day.

additional_notes: "Schwarzes" is the adjective "schwarz" (black) with the ending -es after "ein" when it describes a neuter noun (das-words), e.g. "ein schwarzes Hemd/Auto/Fahrrad". It usually needs the noun after it; by itself it sounds incomplete.
target_language_example: Ich kaufe ein schwarzes Kleid.
native_language_example: I'm buying a black dress.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine noun in the nominative case: ein schöner Tag, ein schöner Baum. The adjective ending changes with gender/case (e.g., eine schöne Blume, ein schönes Haus). In exclamations like “Das wird ein schöner Sommer!”, it can be sincere or (depending on tone/context) sarcastic.
target_language_example: Das ist ein schöner Tag für einen Spaziergang.
native_language_example: That’s a beautiful day for a walk.

additional_notes: Used to describe pleasant weather or a good day in general. Often appears with „Es ist/war …“ (It is/was …) or as an exclamation: „Was für ein schöner Tag!“ / „Welch ein schöner Tag!“ (= What a beautiful day!). You can also add a purpose with „für“: „ein schöner Tag für ein Picknick“.
target_language_example: Es ist heute ein schöner Tag, also gehen wir spazieren.
native_language_example: It’s a nice day today, so we’re going for a walk.

additional_notes: Used before a singular neuter noun, as in ein schönes Bild or ein schönes Gefühl. schön can mean "beautiful," "nice," or "lovely" depending on context. The ending changes with gender and case: compare ein schöner..., eine schöne..., ein schönes....
target_language_example: Das ist ein schönes Geschenk.
native_language_example: That's a lovely gift.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone how their weekend was (past) or to wish them a pleasant weekend (often when saying goodbye on Friday). With verbs like **haben** (to have): *Hattest du …?* / *Ich hoffe, dass du … hattest.* With **wünschen** (to wish): *Ich wünsche dir/Ihnen …* Use **du/dir** for friends and family, and **Sie/Ihnen** for formal situations.
target_language_example: Ich wünsche dir ein schönes Wochenende!
native_language_example: Have a nice weekend!

additional_notes: Not a fixed expression on its own; it is simply ein + sehr, used before an adjective and a singular noun: ein sehr guter Lehrer = "a very good teacher." The form of the article can change depending on gender and case, for example eine sehr nette Frau or einen sehr alten Hund.
target_language_example: Das ist ein sehr gutes Buch.
native_language_example: That is a very good book.

meaning: a very big/large (one) / a very large (noun).
additional_notes: Used before a neuter noun (das Wort) in the nominative or accusative, e.g., „ein sehr großes Tier/Land/Feld“. It’s the indefinite article „ein“ + intensifier „sehr“ + adjective „groß“ with the ending „-es“ (for neuter). For masculine/feminine nouns, the ending changes: „ein sehr großer Hund“, „eine sehr große Stadt“.
target_language_example: Das ist ein sehr großes Problem.
native_language_example: That is a very big problem.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun to describe someone/something as very good: ein sehr guter Arzt / Boden / Fahrer. It can also stand alone when the noun is implied: „Tom ist Rechtsanwalt, noch dazu ein sehr guter.“ = “Tom is a lawyer—what’s more, a very good one.” Changes with gender/case: ein sehr guter (m.), eine sehr gute (f.), ein sehr gutes (n.).
target_language_example: Das ist ein sehr guter Plan.
