target_language_example: Willst du einen Keks zum Kaffee?
native_language_example: Do you want a cookie with your coffee?

additional_notes: Used when you need emergency medical transport. "einen" is the accusative form of "ein" (because it’s the direct object), e.g. "Rufen Sie einen Krankenwagen" (“Call an ambulance”). The base word is "der Krankenwagen" (nominative).
target_language_example: Können Sie bitte sofort einen Krankenwagen rufen?
native_language_example: Can you please call an ambulance immediately?

additional_notes: Used when a cake is the direct object of the verb (e.g., backen/machen): Ich backe/mache einen Kuchen. After masculine words like Kuchen, the indefinite article changes from "ein" (nominative) to "einen" (accusative).
target_language_example: Ich backe heute einen Kuchen.
native_language_example: I’m baking a cake today.

additional_notes: Most often used with the verb „geben“: „jemandem einen Kuss geben“ = to give someone a kiss. Also common with „von“ to say who it’s from: „Gib deiner Mutter einen Kuss von mir“ (“Give your mom a kiss from me”). You may also see fixed contexts like „zum Abschied“ (“as a goodbye kiss”).
target_language_example: Kann ich dir einen Kuss geben?
native_language_example: Can I give you a kiss?

additional_notes: Used when “man” is the direct object (accusative) of the verb (e.g., lieben, sehen, heiraten, jagen) or after many prepositions that take the accusative (e.g., für: Was für einen Mann?). Compare: nominative “ein Mann” (subject) vs. accusative “einen Mann” (object).
target_language_example: Ich kenne einen Mann aus Berlin.
native_language_example: I know a man from Berlin.

additional_notes: Used for a very short time span. Common in polite requests meaning “please wait a moment” (e.g., „Warten Sie bitte einen Moment.“ / „Einen Moment!“). It can also mean “for a moment” with actions: „einen Moment nicht aufpassen“ (not pay attention for a moment), „einen Moment aufhören“ (stop for a moment). Often used without a preposition even though it refers to time.
target_language_example: Einen Moment, ich komme gleich.
native_language_example: One moment, I’ll be right there.

additional_notes: Used with time expressions to say how long something lasts, how long ago something happened, or how long someone is/was somewhere. Often appears with words like „erst“ (only/just), „nicht einmal“ (not even), „mehr als“ (more than), „länger als“ (longer than), and „lang“ (for).
target_language_example: Ich war einen Monat in Deutschland.
native_language_example: I was in Germany for one month.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like „haben“ (to have), „brauchen“ (to need), „geben“ (to give), „aussuchen“ (to choose): „einen Namen haben/brauchen/geben/aussuchen“. Very common when naming a person, thing, project, or even a dish. In questions you’ll often see „Was für einen Namen …?“ = “What kind of name …?”
target_language_example: Wir brauchen noch einen Namen für das Baby.
native_language_example: We still need a name for the baby.

additional_notes: Used when "Plan" is the direct object, often with verbs like "haben" (to have), "machen" (to make), or "brauchen" (to need): "Ich habe einen Plan." Note the case change: "ein Plan" (nominative) → "einen Plan" (accusative, masculine).
target_language_example: Ich habe einen Plan für morgen.
native_language_example: I have a plan for tomorrow.

meaning: to have a plan; to know what you’re going to do.
additional_notes: Used to say you’ve thought something through or have a clear idea of the next steps. Often used with a context word: „einen Plan für + Akk.“ (a plan for something) or „einen Plan, wie …“ (a plan for how to …). In speech you may also hear the opposite: „keinen Plan haben“ = to have no idea.
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, ich werde einen Plan haben, bevor wir losfahren.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ll have a plan before we set off.

meaning: a place / a spot / a seat.
additional_notes: Accusative form of "ein Platz" (masculine). Used when "a place" is the direct object, often with verbs like: "einen Platz suchen" (look for a seat/spot), "einen Platz haben" (have a place/seat), "einen Platz finden" (find a place), and "(für jdn.) einen Platz frei machen" / "Platz machen" (make room). Depending on context it can mean a physical seat, an empty spot, or a figurative “place” (e.g., in a group or in your life).
target_language_example: Kann ich hier einen Platz nehmen?
native_language_example: Can I take a seat here?

meaning: "a sweater / a jumper" (accusative: something you put on or make).
additional_notes: "Pullover" is a masculine noun (der Pullover). You’ll often see it as "einen Pullover" after verbs that take the accusative, especially with clothing (e.g., "einen Pullover anziehen" = to put on a sweater). It can also be the direct object of verbs like "stricken" (to knit).
target_language_example: Ich ziehe mir einen Pullover an, weil es draußen kalt ist.
native_language_example: I’m putting on a sweater because it’s cold outside.

meaning: (to give/need) a piece of advice; a tip.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like „einen Rat geben“ (to give advice) and „einen Rat brauchen/gebrauchen“ (to need advice). „Rat“ is masculine (der Rat), so in the accusative it becomes „einen Rat“. In polite/formal speech you may see „Ihnen“ and refer back to it with „ihn“ (masculine).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir einen Rat geben?
native_language_example: Can you give me some advice?

additional_notes: "Regenschirm" means "umbrella" (literally "rain shield"). "Einen" is the masculine accusative form of "ein" and is used after many verbs like "haben" (to have) and "brauchen" (to need): "Hast du einen Regenschirm?" / "Er braucht einen Regenschirm."
target_language_example: Ich habe keinen Regenschirm dabei.
native_language_example: I don’t have an umbrella with me.

meaning: "a novel" (accusative: the direct object form of "ein Roman").
additional_notes: Used with many verbs like lesen (to read), schreiben (to write), veröffentlichen (to publish). Because "Roman" is masculine (der Roman), the accusative singular is "einen Roman". The base form is "ein Roman"; plural: "Romane".
target_language_example: Ich habe gestern Abend einen Roman angefangen.
native_language_example: I started a novel yesterday evening.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like „nehmen“ (to take/have), „trinken“ (to drink), or „möchten“ (would like) to mean taking a small amount of a drink. You can add what it’s a sip of with „von“: „einen Schluck von …“. In phrases like „einen Schluck nötig haben“, it means someone could use a drink (often implying alcohol, depending on context).
target_language_example: Ich brauche nur einen Schluck.
native_language_example: I just need a sip.

additional_notes: Used when "key" is the direct object (something you need, have, give, or take out). Common with verbs like brauchen (need), haben (have), geben (give), holen (fetch/take out). The accusative masculine article is "einen" (not "ein").
target_language_example: Kannst du mir einen Schlüssel geben?
native_language_example: Can you give me a key?

additional_notes: Used with verbs like gehen or machen to describe taking a step, often with a direction (e.g., „einen Schritt nach vorn/zurück“). It’s also common in the phrase „einen Schritt weitergehen“ = “to go one step further” (literally: to go one step farther).
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte einen Schritt zur Seite gehen?
native_language_example: Could you please take one step to the side?

meaning: a shot (e.g., a gunshot); also a splash/dash of alcohol added to a drink.
additional_notes: With hören (“to hear”), it usually means a gunshot or loud bang: „Ich habe einen Schuss gehört.“ In food/drink contexts with geben/tun (“to add/put”), it means a small added amount, often alcohol: „einen Schuss Brandy/Rum in den Tee“. (Related but different: „einen Schuss haben“ = to be a bit crazy.)
target_language_example: Kannst du mir einen Schuss Rum in den Kakao geben?
native_language_example: Can you add a shot of rum to my cocoa?

additional_notes: This is the accusative form of “ein Sohn” (a son). You use it after many verbs like haben (“to have”): „Er hat einen Sohn.“ After some prepositions you also need accusative, e.g. „für einen Sohn“ (“for a son”).
target_language_example: Wir haben einen Sohn und eine Tochter.
native_language_example: We have a son and a daughter.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like „machen“ or „unternehmen“: „einen Spaziergang machen/unternehmen“ = to go for a walk. It’s an accusative phrase (einen Spaziergang), so it often follows the verb directly, and you can add details with „im Park“, „am Morgen“, „entlang des Flusses“, etc.
target_language_example: Nach dem Abendessen machen wir einen Spaziergang.
native_language_example: After dinner we go for a walk.

additional_notes: "Stein" is a masculine noun (der Stein). You use "einen" when it’s the direct object in the accusative case: Ich sehe **einen Stein**. In the nominative (subject) it’s "ein Stein": **Ein Stein** liegt da. Watch out: German "Stein" can look like English "stein" (a beer mug), but it usually means "stone/rock".
target_language_example: Ich habe einen Stein im Garten gefunden.
native_language_example: I found a stone in the garden.

meaning: a prank; a trick (often in „jemandem einen Streich spielen“ = to play a trick on someone / to deceive someone).
additional_notes: Most often used with „spielen“: „jemandem einen Streich spielen“ (to prank someone). It can also be used when something misleads you, especially your imagination or senses: „Die Phantasie/Augen spielen mir einen Streich“ = “My imagination/eyes are playing tricks on me” (something isn’t actually as it seems).
target_language_example: Ich glaube, meine Ohren spielen mir einen Streich – ich dachte, ich hätte meinen Namen gehört.
native_language_example: I think my ears are playing tricks on me—I thought I heard my name.

meaning: "a chair" (accusative: a chair as the object of the sentence).
additional_notes: Used after many verbs when the chair is what you get, need, move, or interact with (e.g., holen, brauchen, nehmen, werfen). It’s the accusative form of the masculine noun "der Stuhl"; in the nominative you say "ein Stuhl" (a chair).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir bitte einen Stuhl geben?
native_language_example: Can you please give me a chair?

meaning: one day (for one day; one more day).
additional_notes: Accusative form of "ein Tag" used with durations of time ("for a day") and with "noch" to mean "one more day." Often appears with verbs like bleiben (stay) or nehmen (take) and with Urlaub: "einen Tag Urlaub nehmen" = "take a day off."
target_language_example: Können wir einen Tag länger bleiben?
native_language_example: Can we stay one day longer?

additional_notes: Used with verbs like **haben** (to have) and **(sich) nehmen** (to take): **einen Tag frei haben** = to have a day off; **(sich) einen Tag frei nehmen** = to take a day off (e.g., from work/school). Often appears as **einen Tag frei nehmen** or **sich einen Tag frei nehmen**.
target_language_example: Ich nehme morgen einen Tag frei.
native_language_example: I’m taking a day off tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like „haben“ (to have) or „machen/vereinbaren“ (to make/arrange), especially for a doctor, office, or official meeting. „Haben Sie einen Termin?“ often means “Do you have an appointment (scheduled)?”
target_language_example: Ich habe morgen um zehn Uhr einen Termin beim Arzt.
native_language_example: I have an appointment at the doctor’s tomorrow at ten o’clock.

meaning: to have an appointment (a scheduled time).
additional_notes: Used for scheduled meetings or time slots (e.g., with a doctor, at an office, with a client). Often used with a time or place: „Ich habe um 10 Uhr einen Termin.“ You can also say who/where the appointment is with: „Ich habe einen Termin beim Arzt / bei der Bank.“
target_language_example: Ich werde morgen einen Termin haben.
native_language_example: I will have an appointment tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "haben" ("einen Unfall haben" = "to have an accident"). In questions like "Handelte es sich um einen Unfall?", it means "Was it an accident?" (i.e., not intentional). "Unfall" is masculine: der Unfall; accusative: einen Unfall.
target_language_example: Ich hatte gestern auf dem Weg zur Arbeit einen Unfall.
native_language_example: I had an accident yesterday on the way to work.

additional_notes: "Wagen" often means "car" in everyday German, and "einen" shows it’s masculine accusative (the direct object), used after verbs like "kaufen" (buy), "mieten" (rent), "leihen" (borrow), and "finden" (find). You’ll also see "Auto" as a very common word for "car".
target_language_example: Kann ich hier irgendwo einen Wagen mieten?
native_language_example: Can I rent a car somewhere here?

additional_notes: Accusative form of "ein Weg". It can be literal (a physical route) or figurative (a solution or method). Very common in phrases like "einen Weg finden" (to find a way) and "es gibt einen Weg" (there is a way). Often followed by an infinitive with "zu": "einen Weg finden, ... zu ...".
target_language_example: Wir finden einen Weg, das Problem zu lösen.
native_language_example: We’ll find a way to solve the problem.

meaning: a joke (as the object: to tell/make/crack a joke).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like „einen Witz erzählen“ (to tell a joke), „einen Witz machen“ (to make a joke / be joking), and more informal options like „einen Witz reißen“ or „einen Witz vom Stapel lassen“ (to crack a joke). The full base form is „der Witz“; here it appears in the accusative with „einen“.
target_language_example: Kannst du mir einen Witz erzählen?
native_language_example: Can you tell me a joke?

additional_notes: Used before a masculine noun in the accusative case, usually as the direct object: einen alten Wagen / Film / Brief / Schuhkarton. The adjective ending (-en) comes from this grammar pattern (ein + masculine accusative). It normally needs a noun after it: "einen alten ...".
target_language_example: Ich habe einen alten Mantel gefunden.
native_language_example: I found an old coat.

additional_notes: Used when the noun is masculine and in the accusative case (often after verbs like haben, brauchen, nehmen, sehen, küssen). It can stand alone if the noun is understood from context (e.g., „Ich brauche einen anderen.“ = I need a different one/another one). For feminine/neutral/plural you use other forms: „eine andere“, „ein anderes“, „andere“.
target_language_example: Kann ich einen anderen Stuhl bekommen?
native_language_example: Can I get a different chair?

additional_notes: Used when you’re looking for or suggesting an alternative way to do something. Often appears with verbs like „geben“ (there must be another way), „finden“ (to find another way), or „wissen“ (to know another way). Here, „Weg“ is usually figurative (a solution/method), not a physical road.
target_language_example: Wir brauchen einen anderen Weg, um das Problem zu lösen.
native_language_example: We need another way to solve the problem.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine noun in the accusative case after verbs like haben/bekommen or in questions like „Gibt es …?“. Pattern: „einen besseren + [masculine noun]“ (e.g., „einen besseren Vorschlag“, „einen besseren Preis“). Other forms: „ein besseres“ (neuter), „eine bessere“ (feminine), „bessere“ (plural).
target_language_example: Ich brauche einen besseren Plan.
native_language_example: I need a better plan.

meaning: "a big/large/great" (before a masculine noun in the accusative).
additional_notes: This is the accusative masculine form of the adjective "groß" used with the indefinite article: "einen" + "großen" + masculine noun (e.g., "einen großen Fehler", "einen großen Park"). You’ll see it after many verbs that take the accusative (like "haben", "sehen", "machen"). Note: German "groß" looks like English "gross" but does NOT mean "gross" (disgusting).
target_language_example: Ich habe einen großen Hund.
native_language_example: I have a big dog.

additional_notes: Used with the verb „machen“ (to make) or after phrases like „Ich halte das für …“ (I consider that …). The noun „Fehler“ is masculine: „ein großer Fehler“ (nominative), but often „einen großen Fehler“ (accusative) after verbs like „machen“.
target_language_example: Wenn du jetzt gehst, machst du einen großen Fehler.
native_language_example: If you leave now, you’re making a big mistake.

additional_notes: Used with masculine nouns in the accusative case: "einen guten + Noun" (e.g., einen guten Gedanken = a good idea/thought, einen guten Dienst = a good service/favor, einen guten Lebenslauf = a good CV). It’s not usually used alone; a noun follows. Contrast: nominative masculine "ein guter ..." and accusative feminine "eine gute ...".
target_language_example: Ich brauche einen guten Arzt.
native_language_example: I need a good doctor.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like „machen“ (to make) and „hinterlassen“ (to leave) to talk about how someone/something seems to others, especially at first (e.g., at a job interview, meeting new people). You often say: „einen guten Eindruck machen“ / „einen guten Eindruck hinterlassen“.
target_language_example: Beim Vorstellungsgespräch will ich einen guten Eindruck machen.
native_language_example: At the job interview, I want to make a good impression.

additional_notes: Used when you want to justify an action or decision, or when you demand a convincing explanation. Often appears with: „einen guten Grund dafür“ (a good reason for it/that), „einen guten Grund nennen“ (to name/state a good reason), or „Gib mir einen guten Grund, …“ (Give me a good reason to …). The noun „Grund“ is masculine; in the accusative singular it becomes „einen Grund“.
target_language_example: Ich brauche einen guten Grund, um das zu machen.
native_language_example: I need a good reason to do that.

meaning: a good job (a good position); also: doing a good job.
additional_notes: Used either literally for employment ("Ich brauche/fand/habe einen guten Job") or as praise for performance ("einen guten Job machen" = to do a good job). In sentence 2, it appears in the fixed phrase "einen guten Job gemacht" (past of "einen guten Job machen"). "Job" is a common loanword in German; "Arbeit" is also used, but "Job" often sounds more like a position/employment.
target_language_example: Du machst einen guten Job!
native_language_example: You're doing a good job!

additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase by itself—it normally comes right before a masculine noun in the accusative case: einen kleinen Unterschied (a small difference), einen kleinen Spaziergang (a little walk). The -en ending on kleinen is the adjective ending used after the indefinite article einen. (With a neuter noun you’d use: ein kleines …)
target_language_example: Ich brauche einen kleinen Moment.
native_language_example: I need a little moment.

additional_notes: This is the accusative masculine form of **ein + kurzer**. You use it before a masculine noun that is the direct object (or after certain prepositions/expressions that take accusative), e.g. **einen kurzen Schwanz / Kuss / Bericht / Urlaub**. The adjective ending **-en** is typical for masculine accusative after **ein-**.
target_language_example: Ich schreibe einen kurzen Brief.
native_language_example: I’m writing a short letter.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine noun when it’s the direct object (accusative): **einen langen + noun** (e.g., *einen langen Brief, einen langen Spaziergang, einen langen Tunnel*). The **-en** ending on *langen* is the normal adjective ending after *einen* in this case.
target_language_example: Ich habe heute einen langen Brief geschrieben.
native_language_example: Today I wrote a long letter.

additional_notes: This is the adjective phrase used before a masculine noun in the accusative case (after verbs like haben/machen): einen leichten + Noun. Meaning depends on the noun: einen leichten Schlaf = “a light sleep,” einen leichten Akzent = “a slight accent,” einen leichten Herzinfarkt = “a mild heart attack,” einen leichten Bogen = “a slight curve.”
target_language_example: Ich habe nur einen leichten Schnupfen.
native_language_example: I just have a slight cold.

additional_notes: "Rechner" often means "computer" (especially in the sense of a PC) in everyday German. In this phrase, "einen" shows the accusative case (used after many verbs like "brauchen" = to need, or in phrases like "sich einen neuen Rechner zulegen" = to get/buy oneself a new computer).
target_language_example: Ich habe mir einen neuen Rechner gekauft, weil der alte zu langsam war.
native_language_example: I bought myself a new computer because the old one was too slow.

additional_notes: Used when the noun is understood from context and left out. It refers to a masculine thing in the accusative case (often after verbs like haben/kaufen/tragen): e.g., (Badeanzug/Wagen) → „einen roten“. The adjective ending -en matches masculine accusative.
target_language_example: Ich nehme den blauen, und du nimmst einen roten.
native_language_example: I’ll take the blue one, and you take a red one.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine noun in the accusative case (direct object): einen schlechten Tag, einen schlechten Traum, einen schlechten Ruf. It’s the declined form of schlecht (“bad”) and needs a noun after it.
target_language_example: Ich hatte einen schlechten Tag.
native_language_example: I had a bad day.

meaning: "a black one" (masculine accusative), or "a black [noun]" when the noun is understood.
additional_notes: Used when talking about a masculine noun in the accusative case (often after verbs like "haben" or "tragen"). It can either come before a masculine noun (e.g., "einen schwarzen Anzug" = "a black suit") or stand alone with the noun left out because it’s obvious from context (e.g., "Ich habe einen schwarzen und einen weißen." = "I have a black one and a white one.").
target_language_example: Ich nehme einen schwarzen.
native_language_example: I'll take a black one.

meaning: "a nice/beautiful" (masculine accusative), or in wishes: "have a nice …!"
additional_notes: This is the masculine accusative form of "ein schöner" and is used before a masculine noun in the accusative case (often after verbs like "haben": "Du hast einen schönen Hund."). It’s also very common as a shortened wish where the noun is understood or added, e.g. "Einen schönen Tag!" = "Have a nice day!" You’ll change the ending depending on gender/case (e.g. "eine schöne …", "ein schönes …").
target_language_example: Einen schönen Abend noch!
native_language_example: Have a nice evening!

additional_notes: Used as a friendly wish or greeting, often on its own: "Einen schönen Tag!" You also commonly hear it with "wünschen": "Ich wünsche dir/euch/Ihnen einen schönen Tag" (= I wish you a nice day). In questions it means "a nice day" in the sense of how your day went: "Hattest du einen schönen Tag?"
target_language_example: Einen schönen Tag noch, und bis morgen!
native_language_example: Have a nice rest of your day, and see you tomorrow!

additional_notes: Used before a masculine noun after “einen” (accusative of “ein”): e.g., „einen sehr guten Eindruck/Lehrer/Job/Start“. The adjective ending „-en“ comes from the masculine accusative form. You’ll also see other forms depending on gender/case (e.g., „eine sehr gute …“, „ein sehr gutes …“).
target_language_example: Ich habe einen sehr guten Eindruck von ihr.
native_language_example: I have a very good impression of her.

meaning: "a strange/weird dream" (accusative: a dream as the object of the sentence).
additional_notes: Used after verbs like "haben" (to have) and "träumen"/"einen Traum träumen" (to dream / to have a dream). The adjective changes with the case: nominative "ein seltsamer Traum" (a strange dream), accusative "einen seltsamen Traum" (I had a strange dream). Common time phrases: "letzte Nacht" (last night).
target_language_example: Ich hatte letzte Nacht einen seltsamen Traum über die Schule.
native_language_example: I had a strange dream about school last night.

meaning: 'a strong' (masculine, accusative), used before a noun.
additional_notes: This is the accusative masculine form of the adjective "stark" after "einen". It must be followed by a masculine noun (e.g., "einen starken Willen" = "a strong will", "einen starken Menschen" = "a strong person"). Note: German "stark" looks like English "stark" but usually means "strong" (not "stark" in English).
target_language_example: Er hat einen starken Akzent.
native_language_example: He has a strong accent.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine noun when that noun is the direct object (accusative), e.g. after verbs like haben, kennen, backen, machen, verbringen. The adjective changes with gender/case: ein toller Mann (nom.), einen tollen Mann (acc.), eine tolle Idee, ein tolles Hotel. Note: German toll means “great/awesome” (or sometimes “crazy”), not the English “toll” (road fee).
target_language_example: Ich habe einen tollen Film gesehen.
native_language_example: I saw a great movie.

meaning: “of a woman” / “a woman’s” (genitive) or “to/for a woman” (dative).
additional_notes:
"einer" is the feminine form used for two cases:
- Genitive singular: shows possession/association ("das Leben einer Frau" = "a woman’s life").
- Dative singular: after many prepositions/verbs that take dative (e.g., "mit einer Frau" = "with a woman", "einer Frau helfen" = "help a woman").
Which meaning it has depends on the sentence.
target_language_example: Er hat einer Frau geholfen, die ihre Tasche verloren hatte.
native_language_example: He helped a woman who had lost her bag.

additional_notes: Used with "sein" to say you (don’t) share the same opinion: "(nicht) einer Meinung sein". Common patterns: "mit jemandem (völlig) einer Meinung sein" (= agree with someone) and "in solchen Dingen einer Meinung sein" (= agree on such matters). Often refers to viewpoints rather than concrete facts.
target_language_example: Ich bin nicht deiner Meinung, aber wir können ruhig darüber reden.
native_language_example: I don't agree with you, but we can talk about it calmly.

meaning: 'one hour' (in/within/for an hour; an hour ago).
additional_notes: This is the dative form of **eine Stunde** (“one hour”). It’s very common in time expressions with prepositions: **in einer Stunde** = in one hour; **vor einer Stunde** = an hour ago; **seit einer Stunde** = for/since an hour; **innerhalb einer Stunde** = within an hour. Often used with approximations like **etwa** (about) or **mindestens** (at least).
target_language_example: Ich bin in etwa einer Stunde wieder da.
native_language_example: I'll be back in about an hour.

meaning: a cup of coffee (dative: “(with/over) a cup of coffee”; often used in invitations like “How about a cup of coffee?”).
additional_notes: "einer Tasse Kaffee" is the dative form of "eine Tasse Kaffee" (feminine noun "Tasse"). It commonly appears after prepositions that take the dative (e.g., "mit", "bei") and in suggestion/invitation frames like "Was sagen Sie/du zu ...?".
target_language_example: Was sagen Sie zu einer Tasse Kaffee?
native_language_example: How about a cup of coffee?

meaning: 'a cup of tea' (often used when offering/inviting).
additional_notes: Literally means “(of/to) a cup of tea.” In these examples it appears in the dative case after phrases like “Was halten Sie von …?” / “Was sagen Sie zu …?” meaning “What do you think about …?” It’s a polite way to suggest having tea.
target_language_example: Hättest du Lust auf einer Tasse Tee?
native_language_example: Would you like a cup of tea?

additional_notes: This is the declined form of **ein anderer / eine andere / ein anderes** (“another/different”). **Einer anderen** is used when the noun is **feminine** and in the **dative case**, often after prepositions like **mit** (with), **in** (in/into), **von** (from/of), **zu** (to): *mit einer anderen Frau*, *in einer anderen Stadt*, *von einer anderen Welt*. The noun may be stated (*einer anderen Stadt*) or sometimes understood from context.
target_language_example: Ich spreche lieber mit einer anderen Person.
native_language_example: I’d rather talk to another person.

additional_notes: Used with time expressions like "in" (in half an hour), "vor" (half an hour ago), and "seit" (for half an hour). It’s dative feminine because of "(die) Stunde": "in/vor/seit einer halben Stunde".
target_language_example: Ich bin in einer halben Stunde zu Hause.
native_language_example: I’ll be home in half an hour.

additional_notes: Refers to an (often unspecified) male person and then adds a relative clause: „einer, der …“. Used in statements and exclamations; can sound emphatic or slightly ironic/annoyed depending on context (e.g., „Schon wieder einer, der …!“). For other genders: „eine, die …“ (female) and „eins/eines, das …“ (neuter), with case changing as needed (e.g., „einen, der …“ in the accusative).
target_language_example: Endlich einer, der uns versteht.
native_language_example: Finally someone who understands us.

additional_notes: Used to pick out one person/thing from a group: "one of the + plural noun". The following clause often describes the group: "einer der Männer, die ...". Changes with gender and case: e.g., "eine der" (feminine), "eines der" (neuter), "einen der" (accusative masculine).
target_language_example: Er ist einer der besten Freunde meines Bruders.
native_language_example: He is one of my brother’s best friends.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone/something is one member of a group that belongs to you: e.g., one of my brothers/sons/neighbors/suitcases. It’s the masculine/neuter form (einer) + the possessive in the genitive plural (meiner). For feminine nouns, use "eine meiner" (e.g., eine meiner Schwestern). For plural-only groups without a singular member word, you usually say "eins von meinen …" (e.g., eins von meinen Büchern).
target_language_example: Einer meiner Freunde kommt aus Kanada.
native_language_example: One of my friends is from Canada.

additional_notes: Used to refer to an unspecified person from your group of friends. This is a genitive construction: "meiner Freunde" = "of my friends". The form of "einer" changes with gender/case (e.g., "eine meiner Freundinnen" = one of my (female) friends; "einen meiner Freunde" = one of my friends (accusative)).
target_language_example: Einer meiner Freunde wohnt in Berlin.
native_language_example: One of my friends lives in Berlin.

meaning: one after another; one by one.
additional_notes: Used to describe people or things doing the same action in sequence (not all at once). It can change for gender/number, e.g. "eine nach der anderen" (all feminine) or "eines nach dem anderen" (neuter).
target_language_example: Bitte kommt einer nach dem anderen nach vorne.
native_language_example: Please come to the front one by one.

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something belongs to a group of several people/things. It’s a common spoken variant of the more standard “einer von den/der + plural noun” (e.g., “einer von den Leuten”) and can also be used with things (“Einer von den Koffern …”). Often you’ll also hear/see “einer von den” instead of the more formal “einer der …” / “einer von denjenigen, die …”. Case and gender change as needed: e.g., “eine von den …”, “eines von den …”.
target_language_example: Ich bin einer von den neuen Mitarbeitern.
native_language_example: I’m one of the new employees.

meaning: "one of you" (one person from your group).
additional_notes: Used when speaking to two or more people you address with informal plural "ihr/euch" (“you all”). It often appears in questions like "Hat/Kann/Kennt einer von euch ...?" = “Does/Can/Does anyone (among you) …?”. For mixed-gender or unspecified gender groups, you may also hear "eine von euch" (female) or "einer/eine von Ihnen" with formal "Sie".
target_language_example: Kann einer von euch mir kurz helfen?
native_language_example: Can one of you help me for a moment?

meaning: 'one of them' (referring to a male person, or a person of unknown gender).
additional_notes:
Used to single out one person from a group previously mentioned. It changes with gender/case: 
- masculine nominative: einer von ihnen (one of them)
- feminine nominative: eine von ihnen
- neuter nominative: eines von ihnen
Also commonly appears with other pronouns: einer von uns (one of us), einer von euch (one of you all).
target_language_example: Ich glaube, einer von ihnen kennt dich.
native_language_example: I think one of them knows you.

meaning: 'one of us' (a person from our group).
additional_notes: Used when choosing or pointing out a single person from a group that includes the speaker ("uns" = "us"). Can be replaced depending on gender/number: "eine von uns" (female), "eines von uns" (neuter/child), "einer/eine von euch" (one of you all). Often used in situations where someone has to volunteer or take responsibility.
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, einer von uns kann dir helfen.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, one of us can help you.

meaning: "of a man" (genitive: belonging to/connected with a man).
additional_notes: This is the genitive form of "ein Mann". It’s used to show possession or relationship, often after a noun: "das Gesicht eines Mannes" = "the face of a man." In the genitive, masculine/neuter "ein" becomes "eines," and "Mann" commonly takes the ending "-es" → "Mannes."
target_language_example: Ich kenne den Namen eines Mannes, der hier wohnt.
native_language_example: I know the name of a man who lives here.

meaning: one night (once, on a particular night).
additional_notes: Used to set the scene for a past event, often in stories. It means “one night” in the sense of “on a certain night” (not necessarily the following night). The genitive form “eines” is fixed in this phrase.
target_language_example: Eines Nachts hörten wir ein seltsames Geräusch.
native_language_example: One night we heard a strange noise.

additional_notes: Used for an unspecified time in the future. It often appears at the start of a sentence to mean that something will happen eventually.
target_language_example: Eines Tages möchte ich am Meer wohnen.
native_language_example: One day I'd like to live by the sea.

meaning: “one day (will) …” (saying something will happen in the future).
additional_notes: Used to express a hope, prediction, or warning about the future. Often placed at the beginning of the sentence for emphasis. It’s commonly followed by the future auxiliary verb "wird" (from "werden") plus an infinitive at the end of the clause (e.g., "Eines Tages wird er verstehen.").
target_language_example: Eines Tages wird sie nach Berlin ziehen.
native_language_example: One day she will move to Berlin.

meaning: one of the (used with plural nouns).
additional_notes: Common pattern: **eines der + plural noun (Genitive)**, e.g. *eines der Fenster* (“one of the windows”), *eines der Teams* (“one of the teams”). Often used with superlatives: *eines der schönsten …* (“one of the most beautiful …”).
target_language_example: Das ist eines der besten Restaurants in der Stadt.
native_language_example: That’s one of the best restaurants in the city.

meaning: “just/simply not” (emphatic: “not at all / not no matter what”).
additional_notes: Used to stress that something is not true or not happening, often with a tone of frustration, surprise, or emphasis. Common with verbs to show that someone/something won’t do something (e.g., „Er kommt einfach nicht.“ = “He just won’t come.”). Word order: typically after the verb or after the statement element you’re emphasizing.
target_language_example: Ich verstehe das einfach nicht.
native_language_example: I just don’t understand that.

additional_notes: Used to downplay or narrow something to ‘nothing more than’ that one thing. Often expresses ‘all I want is…’, ‘he just wants to…’, or ‘maybe it’s just…’. Word order: it usually sits near what it limits (e.g., before a verb/infinitive: „will … einfach nur …“; before a noun: „nicht einfach nur Köche“).
target_language_example: Ich will einfach nur schlafen.
native_language_example: I just want to sleep.

meaning: just like that; simply (without a reason/without doing anything about it).
additional_notes: Used to say something happens or is done without a special reason, explanation, or effort (“for no particular reason”), or that someone lets something happen without intervening (“just let it happen”). Often expresses surprise, criticism, or disbelief: "einfach so stehen/liegen lassen" (just leave it there), "einfach so gehen" (just leave).
target_language_example: Du kannst nicht einfach so gehen, ohne dich zu verabschieden.
native_language_example: You can’t just leave like that without saying goodbye.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone broke into a place (home, shop, bank), usually when the person is unknown or not mentioned. Commonly appears in the impersonal passive: "Es ist ... eingebrochen worden" or with the place first: "Bei uns / In die Bank ist ... eingebrochen worden." This is the perfect passive: "sein" + Partizip II (eingebrochen) + "worden".
target_language_example: In unsere Wohnung ist letzte Nacht eingebrochen worden.
native_language_example: Our apartment was broken into last night.

additional_notes: Used to refer to an unspecified number of people (not everyone, not a specific group). Often introduces a general opinion or observation. For a few specific individuals you can also say "ein paar Leute"; for more emphasis on “many,” use "viele Leute".
target_language_example: Einige Leute mögen Kaffee, andere lieber Tee.
native_language_example: Some people like coffee; others prefer tea.

additional_notes: Used to refer to an unspecified small number of days (often around 2–5), in the past or future. It’s less specific than „zwei/drei Tage“ and often implies a short period. Common in phrases like „für einige Tage“ (for a few days) or with verbs like „bleiben“ (to stay).
target_language_example: Gib mir einige Tage.
native_language_example: Give me a few days.

additional_notes: Refers to an unspecified (often not very long) period of time. Common with verbs like dauern (to take time) and with für: für einige Zeit = for a while. Can also be used without für when it clearly refers to a time span (e.g., Einige Zeit lebten sie… = They lived… for some time).
target_language_example: Warte bitte noch einige Zeit, dann bin ich fertig.
native_language_example: Please wait a little while longer, then I’ll be finished.

additional_notes: Used with "sein" + "gegangen" to say someone went shopping: "Ich bin einkaufen gegangen." You can also ask it as a question: "Bist du einkaufen gegangen?" Often refers to grocery shopping or running shopping errands.
target_language_example: Ich bin nach der Arbeit noch schnell einkaufen gegangen.
native_language_example: After work, I quickly went shopping.

additional_notes: Used to talk about frequency (how often something happens). Often placed after the verb or at the end of the sentence: „Ich mache das einmal am Tag.“ You may also see the more formal synonym „einmal täglich“. In spoken German it can appear as a short, unfinished phrase when the verb is understood from context (like in sentence 3).
target_language_example: Ich trinke einmal am Tag Kaffee.
native_language_example: I drink coffee once a day.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens one time per year (frequency). Often used with verbs like kommen/fahren/besuchen. You can add emphasis with words like „wenigstens“ (at least): „wenigstens einmal im Jahr“.
target_language_example: Ich gehe einmal im Jahr zum Zahnarzt.
native_language_example: I go to the dentist once a year.

additional_notes: Used to talk about how often something happens (frequency). Often goes near the verb or at the beginning/end of the sentence: "Ich gehe einmal im Monat ins Kino." / "Einmal im Monat gehe ich ins Kino."
target_language_example: Einmal im Monat rufe ich meine Großeltern an.
native_language_example: Once a month I call my grandparents.

additional_notes: Used to talk about frequency (how often something happens). It often answers the question „Wie oft?“ (How often?). You can swap in other time units: „einmal am Tag“ (once a day), „einmal im Monat“ (once a month).
target_language_example: Ich rufe meine Oma einmal in der Woche an.
native_language_example: I call my grandma once a week.

additional_notes: Used to say how often something happens. Often placed near the verb: „Ich schwimme einmal pro Woche.“ You can swap the time unit: „einmal pro Tag“ (once a day), „einmal pro Monat“ (once a month).
target_language_example: Wir telefonieren einmal pro Woche.
native_language_example: We talk on the phone once a week.

meaning: “finally … up” — used with separable verbs ending in **auf** (e.g. *aufhören, aufmachen, aufwachen, aufgehen, aufgeben*) to mean “finally” + that action.
additional_notes: **Endlich** means “finally / at last.” **Auf** here is usually the separated prefix of a **separable verb**, and it moves to the end of the clause: *Die Sonne geht auf.* → *Die Sonne ging endlich auf.* Common patterns from the examples: **hör … auf** = stop, **mach … auf** = open (a door/window), **wach … auf** = wake up, **geh … auf** = rise (sun), **gib … auf** = give up. In commands, **endlich** often adds impatience: *Hör endlich auf!* = “Stop it already!”
target_language_example: Hör endlich auf, so laut zu sein!
native_language_example: Stop being so loud already!

additional_notes: Describes a strong, personal friendship (people you trust and are close to). Often used with verbs like „sein“ (Tom und Maria sind enge Freunde) or „werden“ (Sie wurden enge Freunde = they became close friends). You can also strengthen it with words like „richtig“ or „sehr“: „richtig enge Freunde“, „sehr enge Freunde“.
target_language_example: Wir sind enge Freunde und erzählen uns alles.
native_language_example: We’re close friends and tell each other everything.

meaning: to be fired (from a job); to be dismissed/released.
additional_notes: Passive form: *werden* + past participle *entlassen*. Most commonly used for losing your job (*aus der Firma entlassen werden*). It can also mean being released/discharged (e.g., from the hospital or the army), depending on context.
target_language_example: Wenn du zu spät kommst, kannst du entlassen werden.
native_language_example: If you come late, you can be fired.

meaning: “to have been discharged/released” (often from a hospital) or “to have been fired” (from a job).
additional_notes: This is the passive form (Perfekt) of **entlassen**: *jemanden entlassen* = to discharge/release/fire someone. **entlassen worden** focuses on what happened to the person (not who did it). Very common with **aus dem Krankenhaus entlassen werden** (“to be discharged from the hospital”). In a work context, it usually means “to be fired/laid off.”
target_language_example: Er ist gestern aus dem Krankenhaus entlassen worden.
native_language_example: He was discharged from the hospital yesterday.

additional_notes: Past tense of the reflexive verb „sich entscheiden“ (to decide). Common patterns: „sich für + Akk.“ = decide on/choose something (e.g., „für den roten Mantel“), and „sich (dafür) entscheiden, zu + Infinitiv“ = decide to do something (e.g., „Sie entschied sich, Tom zu heiraten.“). Often used with adverbs like „schließlich“ (finally) or „stattdessen“ (instead).
target_language_example: Er entschied sich dafür, heute zu Hause zu bleiben.
native_language_example: He decided to stay home today.

additional_notes: Used to start a sentence with an apology, often to soften what you’re about to say (a mistake, misunderstanding, interruption, or awkward situation). Common with verbs like dachte (thought), wollte (wanted), weiß nicht (don’t know). Also appears as the more formal Sie-form: „Entschuldigen Sie, ich …“.
target_language_example: Entschuldige, ich habe dich falsch verstanden.
native_language_example: Sorry, I misunderstood you.

additional_notes: Used when addressing someone with „Sie“ (formal “you”), e.g., to apologize, to interrupt politely, or to get someone’s attention. Often used on its own („Entschuldigen Sie!“) or with more information: „Entschuldigen Sie (bitte) …“ / „Entschuldigen Sie mich …“ / „Entschuldigen Sie wegen …“.
target_language_example: Entschuldigen Sie bitte, wo ist der Bahnhof?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where is the train station?

additional_notes: A very polite, formal phrase used with **Sie** when speaking to strangers, customers, officials, etc. It can be used to apologize (often followed by a noun or **dass**-clause: *Entschuldigen Sie bitte, dass …*) or to politely get someone’s attention (*Entschuldigen Sie bitte!*).
target_language_example: Entschuldigen Sie bitte, können Sie mir helfen?
native_language_example: Excuse me, could you help me?

additional_notes: Polite, formal phrase used to apologize and/or to politely get someone’s attention, often before asking something or when you need to leave. Used with "Sie" (formal "you"), so it’s common with strangers, customers, officials, or in professional settings. You can add "bitte" or "kurz" to soften it: "Bitte entschuldigen Sie mich" / "Entschuldigen Sie mich kurz".
target_language_example: Entschuldigen Sie mich, könnten Sie mir bitte helfen?
native_language_example: Excuse me, could you please help me?

additional_notes: Präteritum (simple past) of **sich für etwas entschuldigen** = to apologize for something. Used with **für + accusative**: *sich für den Fehler / das Verhalten entschuldigen*. Common in writing and narration; in everyday speech you often hear **hat sich für … entschuldigt** (Perfekt).
target_language_example: Er entschuldigte sich für seinen Fehler.
native_language_example: He apologized for his mistake.

meaning: Relax! / Calm down! (said to one person).
additional_notes: An informal imperative meaning “(you) relax.” Used when telling one person (du-form) to calm down or not worry. For more than one person: „Entspannt euch!“; formal: „Entspannen Sie sich!“
target_language_example: Hey, entspann dich — wir haben noch genug Zeit.
native_language_example: Hey, relax—we still have enough time.

additional_notes: "Er" = "he" and "arbeitet" is the 3rd-person singular present tense of "arbeiten" (to work). It can describe a general fact (He works here.) or what he is doing right now (He’s working right now.), depending on context. Often followed by details like place (hier), time (nachts, jeden Tag), or purpose/employer (für eine Universität).
target_language_example: Er arbeitet heute bis spät.
native_language_example: He’s working until late today.

meaning: "he works as" (he has the job of).
additional_notes: Used to say someone’s profession or role: "arbeiten als + [job]". You can change the subject and verb (e.g., "Ich arbeite als…", "Sie arbeitet als…"). Often followed by a noun for a job, sometimes with more info ("als Lehrer an einer Schule").
target_language_example: Mein Bruder arbeitet als Koch in einem Restaurant.
native_language_example: My brother works as a cook in a restaurant.

additional_notes: „arbeitete“ is the Präteritum (simple past) of „arbeiten“ (to work). It’s common in writing and storytelling; in everyday speech people often use the perfect instead: „Er hat gearbeitet.“ You can add time/amount phrases like „den ganzen Tag“ (all day) or „bis spät in die Nacht“ (until late at night).
target_language_example: Er arbeitete bis spät in die Nacht.
native_language_example: He worked until late into the night.

additional_notes: Past tense (Präteritum) of **bitten**: **er bat** = “he asked/requested,” and **mich** = “me.” Very often followed by **zu + infinitive** (e.g., *Er bat mich aufzustehen.*) or by a clause with a comma (e.g., *Er bat mich, ihm zu helfen.*). Slightly more formal than **er hat mich gebeten** in everyday speech, but common in writing and storytelling.
target_language_example: Er bat mich, die Tür zuzumachen.
native_language_example: He asked me to close the door.

additional_notes: Past tense (Präteritum) of the reflexive verb **sich benehmen** (“to behave”). Often used with an adverb: **Er benahm sich sehr sonderbar.** = “He behaved very strangely.” Said on its own (**Er benahm sich.**), it often implies “He behaved well / properly” (as in a reminder to behave).
target_language_example: Er benahm sich sehr sonderbar.
native_language_example: He behaved very strangely.

additional_notes: "Er blieb" is the simple past (Präteritum) of "er bleibt" (present) from the verb "bleiben" (to stay/remain). It’s often used in writing and storytelling. Common expression: "bei seiner Meinung bleiben" = to stick to your opinion (not change your mind).
target_language_example: Er blieb den ganzen Abend zu Hause.
native_language_example: He stayed at home the whole evening.

additional_notes: *Er brachte* is the **simple past (Präteritum)** of *er bringt* (“he brings”). It often means “he brought” (carried/delivered): *Er brachte seinen Gästen Getränke.* In many common patterns it means “he managed to / got something to happen”: **zu Ende bringen** (finish), **zum Ausdruck bringen** (express), **zu Papier bringen** (put down on paper), **jdn. zum Weinen bringen** (make someone cry), **jdn. zur Arbeit bringen** (take/bring someone to work).
target_language_example: Er brachte das Paket zur Post.
native_language_example: He brought the package to the post office.

additional_notes: "Er" = "he" and "braucht" is the 3rd-person singular of "brauchen" (to need). It’s usually followed by the thing needed in the accusative (e.g., "Er braucht Zeit" = He needs time). With "kein/keine" it means "doesn’t need" ("Er braucht keine Hilfe" = He doesn’t need any help). In sentences like "Was er braucht, ist ..." it means "What he needs is ...".
target_language_example: Er braucht heute deine Hilfe.
native_language_example: He needs your help today.

additional_notes: From the verb **denken** (to think). Common patterns: **er denkt, dass ...** / **er denkt, ...** (he thinks that ...), **er denkt an + Akk.** (he thinks about/of someone/something), **er denkt daran, ... zu + infinitive** (he’s thinking of doing something). Word order changes in the **dass**-clause: *Er denkt, dass es hilft.*
target_language_example: Er denkt, dass das eine gute Idee ist.
native_language_example: He thinks that’s a good idea.

additional_notes: Often used after verbs like „sehen“ or „man sah“ with „wie“: „Ich sah, wie er die Straße überquerte.“ Here „überquerte“ is Präteritum (simple past) of „überqueren“ (“to cross”).
target_language_example: Ich merkte, wie er die Straße überquerte und dann verschwand.
native_language_example: I noticed how he crossed the street and then disappeared.

additional_notes: From the verb **anfangen** (“to start/to begin”). In the past tense, **anfangen** splits: **Er fing ... an.** Often used with **zu + infinitive**: **Er fing an, Englisch zu sprechen.** (He started to speak English.)
target_language_example: Er fing an, lauter zu reden.
native_language_example: He started to speak louder.

meaning: 'he asked me whether/if I …' (reported yes/no question).
additional_notes: Used to report a yes/no question in the past. "ob" = whether/if. The verb usually goes to the end of the clause (e.g., "ob ich beschäftigt bin/war", "ob ich ihm helfen wolle"). In reported speech, German often shifts tense/mood (e.g., "sei", "wolle", "hätte") even if the original question was in the present or past.
target_language_example: Er fragte mich, ob ich morgen Zeit habe.
native_language_example: He asked me if I have time tomorrow.

meaning: 'he drove' / 'he went (by vehicle)' (simple past of fahren).
additional_notes: "Fuhr" is the simple past (Präteritum) of "fahren". It’s common in writing and storytelling, and can mean traveling by car/bus/train, etc.: "Er fuhr nach Berlin." It can also take an object meaning 'to drive someone': "Er fuhr mich zum Bahnhof." In the fixed expression "(vor Schreck) zusammenfahren", it means 'to flinch/jump' (from shock), not driving.
target_language_example: Er fuhr gestern mit dem Zug nach Hamburg.
native_language_example: He went to Hamburg by train yesterday.

additional_notes: "Fahren" is used for traveling in or on a vehicle (car, bus, train, bike, etc.): *Er fährt los.* = he sets off/leaves; *Er fährt zu schnell.* = he’s driving too fast. It’s also used with some activities like skiing: *Ski fahren* = to ski.
target_language_example: Er fährt heute mit dem Zug nach Berlin.
native_language_example: He’s going to Berlin by train today.

meaning: "he felt" (describing his physical condition or emotional state).
additional_notes: "sich fühlen" is a reflexive verb meaning "to feel" in the sense of one’s condition or mood (e.g., besser/schuldig/müde/wohl). It’s commonly followed by an adjective or adverb: "Er fühlte sich besser." It can also be used with "wie" for comparisons: "Er fühlte sich wie in einem Traum."
target_language_example: Er fühlte sich ein wenig schuldig.
native_language_example: He felt a little guilty.

additional_notes: Simple past (Präteritum) of **geben** used with **er** (“he”). Common in writing and storytelling; in everyday speech you often hear **er hat (mir) gegeben** instead.
target_language_example: Er gab mir seine Telefonnummer.
native_language_example: He gave me his phone number.

additional_notes: *Er* = “he”. *gab* is the simple past (Präteritum) of *geben* (“to give”), used often in writing and storytelling; in everyday speech you’ll often hear the perfect tense instead: *Er hat mir … gegeben.* The dative pronoun *mir* means “to me.” The phrase can be used literally (*Er gab mir ein Buch.*) and also in common expressions like *jemandem die Schuld geben* (“to blame someone”) and *jemandem sein Wort geben* (“to give someone one’s word”).
target_language_example: Er gab mir die Schuld.
native_language_example: He blamed me.

additional_notes: Past tense (Präteritum) of the separable verb **zugeben** (“to admit”). In a main clause, the verb splits: **gab** comes early, and **zu** goes to the end. Often followed by a **dass**-clause: *Er gab zu, dass …*
target_language_example: Er gab zu, dass er einen Fehler gemacht hatte.
native_language_example: He admitted that he had made a mistake.

meaning: 'he goes' / 'he walks'; also: 'he's going (to ...)' (present tense depending on context).
additional_notes: Commonly used with an adverb or direction ("Er geht einfach weiter." = he simply keeps going), with a destination using **zu/nach/in** ("Er geht nach Hause." = he goes home), or with an activity in the infinitive ("Er geht laufen." = he goes running). As an exclamation, **zu Boden gehen** means to fall to the ground ("Er geht zu Boden!").
target_language_example: Er geht einfach weiter.
native_language_example: He just keeps going.

additional_notes: "Er ging" is the simple past (Präteritum) of "gehen" for "he". In everyday spoken German, people often use the perfect tense instead: "er ist gegangen" (he went/has gone). "Ging" also appears in common expressions, e.g. "Er ging fremd" (he cheated), "Er ging in die Luft" (he blew up / got very angry), and "Er ging so weit, ..." (he went so far as to ...).
target_language_example: Er ging nach der Arbeit nach Hause.
native_language_example: He went home after work.

additional_notes: Used to say someone traveled to a destination. With places you usually use **nach** for **cities** and **most countries** (especially without an article): *nach Paris*, *nach Italien*. For countries with an article or for specific places/buildings, German often uses **in** + accusative instead (e.g., *in die USA*, *in die Schweiz*). The verb is **gehen** (to go): *er ging* = he went (simple past).
target_language_example: Er ging nach Berlin, um seine Freunde zu besuchen.
native_language_example: He went to Berlin to visit his friends.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a subordinate clause with the idea or opinion he has. The verb in the clause introduced by "dass" goes to the end (e.g., "dass es stimmt"). Often implies a belief or assumption (sometimes mistaken), depending on context.
target_language_example: Er glaubt, dass morgen alles besser wird.
native_language_example: He believes/thinks that everything will be better tomorrow.

additional_notes: Literally "he has." In sentences like these, "hat" is often used with a past participle to form the German perfect tense: "Er hat gut gekämpft," "Er hat vorgeschlagen ..." In English, this is often translated with the simple past: "he fought," "he suggested." It can also mean possession in other contexts, as in "he has."
target_language_example: Er hat gestern angerufen.
native_language_example: He called yesterday.

meaning: “he has …” (used with a neuter direct object: “the/that …”, often in the Perfekt).
additional_notes: This is the start of a common Perfekt sentence pattern: **Er hat das + noun + past participle at the end** (e.g., *Er hat das Fenster offen gelassen.*). Here **hat** is the helping verb “has”, and **das** is “the/that” for a neuter noun (accusative). It can also appear with other verbs (*Er ist …* for some intransitive verbs) and with other articles (*den/die/einen…*) depending on the noun’s gender.
target_language_example: Er hat das Buch schon gelesen.
native_language_example: He has already read the book.

additional_notes: This is the start of a sentence in the Perfekt (present perfect) tense: **er hat** (he has) + a **past participle** at/near the end of the clause (e.g., *auserwählt, gehen lassen, geliebt, gewarnt, vermisst*). **dich** means "you" (singular, informal, accusative). So it often translates as "he [did something] to you" / "he [verb]-ed you" rather than literally "he has you."
target_language_example: Er hat dich gesehen.
native_language_example: He saw you.

meaning: “he has the …” (often used to form the German past tense/Perfekt: “he … the …”).
additional_notes: This is the start of a very common past tense pattern: **Er hat + die + (object) + past participle**. Here **hat** is the helping verb (“has”), and **die** is the accusative article for **feminine singular** or **plural** nouns (“the”). In natural English you usually translate the whole sentence with the **simple past**: “He dropped out of high school,” “He broke the clothespin,” etc.
target_language_example: Er hat die Tür zugemacht.
native_language_example: He closed the door.

meaning: “he has a …” / “he’s got a …” (with a masculine noun in the accusative).
additional_notes: Used either with **haben** as the main verb (“to have”) or as the auxiliary in the **Perfekt** past tense: **Er hat einen + noun + past participle** (e.g., *gegessen, erhalten*). **Einen** is the accusative form of **ein** for **masculine** nouns (e.g., *einen Bagel, einen Fahrschein*).
target_language_example: Er hat einen Termin um drei Uhr.
native_language_example: He has an appointment at three o’clock.

additional_notes: Literally means “he has it,” but very often it’s the start of the Perfekt (present perfect) when a past participle comes at the end of the sentence: “Er hat es erklärt/gesagt/erzählt …” = “He explained it / He told it …”. “es” means “it” and refers to something already known from context. In main clauses, the participle typically goes to the end.
target_language_example: Er hat es mir gestern erklärt.
native_language_example: He explained it to me yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to report what a man said, followed by a subordinate clause with **dass** (“that”). In written German you often see **dass** (new spelling) instead of **daß**. The verb in the reported clause may be in the indicative (**…dass er gerne hier ist**) or in the subjunctive for reported speech (**Konjunktiv I/II**, e.g. **…dass er gerne hier sei / Angst habe**).
target_language_example: Er hat gesagt, daß er morgen keine Zeit hat.
native_language_example: He said that he doesn’t have time tomorrow.

meaning: “he said that he …” (reporting what he said).
additional_notes: Used to introduce indirect/reported speech. Very often followed by the subjunctive (Konjunktiv): Konjunktiv I (e.g., „er habe“, „er könne“) in formal reporting, or Konjunktiv II (e.g., „er hätte“) when Konjunktiv I sounds the same as the indicative or to show doubt. In everyday speech, many people also use „…, dass er …“ with normal verb forms.
target_language_example: Er hat gesagt, er komme später.
native_language_example: He said that he would come later.

additional_notes: This is a very common German structure: **er** = “he”, **hat** = “has” (auxiliary verb in the **Perfekt**), **ihn** = “him” (accusative object). The main action is usually in a **past participle** later in the sentence (e.g., *Er hat ihn gesehen.* = “He saw him.”). In English you often translate it as **simple past** (“he …ed him”), not literally “he has him.”
target_language_example: Er hat ihn nicht erkannt.
native_language_example: He didn’t recognize him.

additional_notes: Used at the start of many Perfekt (conversational past) sentences: "Er hat ..." + a dative pronoun "ihr" (= to her). The main verb usually comes as a past participle at the end: "Er hat ihr geholfen" (He helped her). "ihr" here means "to her" (indirect object), not "her" as a direct object. Word order: Er hat ihr + [thing/person] + past participle.
target_language_example: Er hat ihr heute beim Umzug geholfen.
native_language_example: He helped her with the move today.

meaning: he ... me (Perfekt: he has ... me / he ...ed me)
additional_notes: Common start of a sentence in the Perfekt past tense: "er" (he) + "hat" (has) + "mich" (me, accusative). It’s normally followed by a past participle at/near the end of the clause (e.g., "getäuscht", "gebracht", "eingeladen"). In English this is often translated as simple past ("he tricked me", "he took me"), even though German uses "hat".
target_language_example: Er hat mich gestern angerufen.
native_language_example: He called me yesterday.

additional_notes: Used with the dative pronoun "mir" (= to me / for me) to show the indirect object (the recipient/beneficiary). Often followed by a past participle in the Perfekt (present perfect) tense: "Er hat mir Kaffee gebracht" (He brought me coffee). You can also end the sentence after it if the verb idea is understood from context: "Er hat mir geschrieben" (He wrote to me). Word order tip: "mir" usually comes before a direct object noun (e.g., "mir das Buch").
target_language_example: Er hat mir heute geholfen.
native_language_example: He helped me today.

er hat mir gesagt, daß er

target_language_multi_word_term: er hat mir gesagt, daß er
meaning: “he told me that he …” (introduces what he said).
additional_notes: Used to report what a man/boy said. It’s followed by a „daß/dass“-clause; in standard modern spelling you’ll usually see „dass“, while „daß“ is the older spelling. The verb in the subordinate clause typically goes to the end: „… daß er morgen kommt.“ In reported speech you may also see Konjunktiv I (e.g. „sei“) to signal it’s reported, not necessarily the speaker’s own statement.
target_language_example: Er hat mir gesagt, daß er zu Fuß nach Hause gegangen ist.
native_language_example: He told me that he walked home.

additional_notes: This is the start of a very common German sentence pattern: **Er hat + sein- (his) + object + past participle** (often with the participle at the end). It can mean simply “he has his …” (possession), but very often it’s part of the **Perfekt** tense to say he **has done/finished/achieved** something with *his* thing (e.g., *Er hat sein Bier ausgetrunken* = “He finished his beer”). *sein* changes with the noun: *sein* (masc./neut.), *seine* (fem./plural).
target_language_example: Er hat sein Handy verloren.
native_language_example: He lost his phone.

meaning: “he has his …” / “he has (done) his …” (with feminine singular or plural nouns).
additional_notes: This is the start of a very common pattern: **Er hat …** (present perfect: “he has …”) + **seine** (“his”) + a noun. **seine** is used with **feminine singular** nouns (e.g., *seine Entscheidung, seine Energie*) and with **plural** nouns (e.g., *seine Antworten, seine Pflichten, seine Taschen*). With **masculine/neuter singular** nouns you usually see **seinen/sein** instead (e.g., *Er hat seinen Schlüssel verloren.*).
target_language_example: Er hat seine Entscheidung schon erklärt.
native_language_example: He has already explained his decision.

additional_notes: Common start of a sentence in the Perfekt (present perfect): **er hat** + past participle (often later in the sentence). **seinen** is the possessive "his" used with a **masculine accusative** noun (e.g., *seinen Fehler, seinen Kopf, seinen Traum, seinen Wagen*). For a neuter noun it’s also **sein** in accusative (*sein Auto*), and for feminine/plural it changes (*seine Tasche / seine Freunde*).
target_language_example: Er hat seinen Schlüssel verloren.
native_language_example: He lost his key.

additional_notes: Used with reflexive verbs in the Perfekt (past): **Er hat sich + Partizip II**. The **sich** refers back to *er* (“himself”), but in English it’s often not translated literally (e.g., *Er hat sich beklagt.* = “He complained.”). Some verbs take an extra object after **sich** (e.g., *Er hat sich den Arm gebrochen.* = “He broke his arm.”).
target_language_example: Er hat sich gestern geduscht.
native_language_example: He showered yesterday.

meaning: “he has her/them” (often the start of a past/perfect sentence: “he … her/them”).
additional_notes: Common pattern in the Perfekt (conversational past): **Er hat sie + past participle** (e.g., *geliebt, bedroht, verachtet*). **sie** can mean **“her”** (singular, feminine) or **“them”** (plural)—context tells you which. By itself, **er hat sie** sounds incomplete; it usually needs the main verb at the end.
target_language_example: Er hat sie gestern angerufen.
native_language_example: He called her/them yesterday.

additional_notes: Common sentence start in the German Perfekt (spoken past). Pattern: "Er hat uns" + past participle / infinitive phrase. Examples: "Er hat uns gefunden" = he found us; "Er hat uns geholfen" = he helped us (note: with "helfen", "uns" is dative = to us); "Er hat uns arbeiten lassen" = he made/let us work ("lassen" + infinitive). Not the same as English "he has us" (possession).
target_language_example: Er hat uns gestern angerufen.
native_language_example: He called us yesterday.

additional_notes: "Er" means "he," and "hat" is the 3rd-person singular form of "haben". It usually means "he has," but it can also be part of the present perfect tense, as in "Er hat gearbeitet" = "He has worked / He worked."
target_language_example: Er hat einen Hund.
native_language_example: He has a dog.

additional_notes: literally 'he has a/an.' In many common sentences, though, hat is also the auxiliary used to form the present perfect, so a full sentence like Er hat ein Fenster kaputtgemacht usually means 'he broke a window' or 'he has broken a window,' not 'he has a window.' ein means 'a/an' and changes form depending on gender and case.
target_language_example: Er hat ein Buch gelesen.
native_language_example: He read a book.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "haben" (to have) + the accusative feminine indefinite article "eine". It introduces something he possesses or has (an object like "eine Eintrittskarte"), but also qualities/conditions or abstract things (e.g., "eine Neigung", "eine Meinung", "eine schwache Blase"). For masculine/neuter nouns you use "er hat einen / er hat ein" instead.
target_language_example: Er hat eine Schwester.
native_language_example: He has a sister.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **haben** (“to have”) and the masculine accusative article **einen**. It introduces something he possesses or has/experiences: **Er hat einen Hund** (possession), **Er hat einen Kater** (condition). The noun that follows is masculine in the accusative case.
target_language_example: Er hat einen Hund, aber keine Katze.
native_language_example: He has a dog, but no cat.

meaning: “he has no / he doesn’t have any …” (used before a neuter noun).
additional_notes: Used to say that a man/boy (er) does not have something. The negative article **kein** changes like *ein* depending on the noun: **kein** (neuter: *kein Geld*), **keine** (feminine/plural: *keine Zeit / keine Freunde*), **keinen** (masculine accusative: *keinen Job*). Often followed by a noun, sometimes with an extra phrase like **um … zu …** (“in order to …”) or a relative clause (**…, in dem …**).
target_language_example: Er hat kein Auto, also fährt er mit dem Bus.
native_language_example: He doesn’t have a car, so he takes the bus.

additional_notes: Used to say that a man/boy doesn’t have something. "keine" is the negation used with nouns ("no / not any") and is used here with feminine singular nouns (e.g., keine Kraft, keine Fantasie) or plural nouns (e.g., keine Geschwister, keine Einwände). With masculine/neuter singular nouns you use "keinen/kein" instead (e.g., er hat keinen Bruder; er hat kein Geld).
target_language_example: Er hat keine Zeit für ein Treffen.
native_language_example: He has no time to meet.

meaning: “he has no…” / “he doesn’t have any…” (with a masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used with a noun after "haben" to say someone doesn’t have something. "keinen" is the accusative form for masculine nouns (e.g., keinen Freund, keinen Hut, keinen Sinn). With other genders it changes: "er hat keine Zeit" (feminine), "er hat kein Geld" (neuter/plural as a mass noun), "er hat keine Freunde" (plural).
target_language_example: Er hat keinen Schlüssel dabei.
native_language_example: He doesn’t have a key with him.

additional_notes: Used to say that a man/boy possesses or has a large number of things (or abstract things like talents or debts). It’s typically followed by a plural noun: „Er hat viele Bilder.“ = “He has many pictures.” (With an uncountable noun, you’d usually use „viel“ instead of „viele“.)
target_language_example: Er hat viele Freunde in Berlin.
native_language_example: He has many friends in Berlin.

additional_notes: "Er" = "he" + "hatte" = simple past (Präteritum) of "haben" (to have). Very common in written stories and descriptions; in spoken German you often hear the perfect tense instead ("er hat ... gehabt"). In sentences like "Er hatte doch recht", "doch" adds emphasis, like "actually/after all".
target_language_example: Er hatte keine Zeit, also blieb er zu Hause.
native_language_example: He had no time, so he stayed at home.

additional_notes: "Angst haben" means "to be afraid." "Er hatte Angst" is past tense (Präteritum) and is common in writing and storytelling; in everyday speech you often hear "Er hat Angst" (present/perfect). It’s frequently followed by a clause with "zu" + infinitive (e.g., "allein dorthin zu gehen") or by "vor" + dative to say what someone is afraid of (e.g., "Er hatte Angst vor Hunden").
target_language_example: Er hatte Angst, im Dunkeln nach Hause zu gehen.
native_language_example: He was afraid to walk home in the dark.

meaning: "he had a" (used before a feminine noun).
additional_notes: This is the simple past (Präteritum) of "er hat" ("he has"). It’s followed by a feminine noun in the accusative case: "Er hatte eine + [feminine noun]". In context, it can be literal (e.g., having/holding something) or part of fixed expressions like "eine Operation haben" (= to have/undergo an operation) or "eine Fahne haben" (= to have a hangover / smell of alcohol).
target_language_example: Er hatte eine Idee.
native_language_example: He had an idea.

meaning: he had no / he didn’t have any.
additional_notes: Used to say that a man lacked something (often a noun in the accusative), e.g. "keine Erfahrung" (no experience), "keine Familie" (no family), "keine Schmerzen" (no pain). The feminine plural form "keine" matches nouns like "die Erfahrung" and plural nouns like "die Schmerzen"; with masculine/neuter nouns you’ll see "keinen/kein" instead (e.g. "Er hatte keinen Hunger.").
target_language_example: Er hatte keine Zeit für ein Treffen.
native_language_example: He didn’t have any time to meet.

additional_notes:
Past tense (Präteritum) of **halten**. Very common in writing and storytelling. Meaning depends on the construction:
- **etwas halten** = to hold/carry: *Er hielt die Hände hoch.*
- **eine Rede halten** = to give a speech: *Er hielt eine Rede.*
- **etwas für + Akk. halten** = to consider/think something (to be): *Er hielt das für eine schlechte Idee.*
- **etwas geheim halten** = to keep something secret.
- **Schritt halten (mit)** = to keep up (with).
- **sich für + Akk. halten** = to think you are (mistakenly): *Er hielt sich für eine Katze.*
- **sich an + Akk. halten** = to stick to/follow: *Er hielt sich nicht an die Regeln.*
target_language_example: Er hielt den Brief fest in der Hand.
native_language_example: He held the letter tightly in his hand.

meaning: "he would have" / "he was supposed to" (Konjunktiv II, past).
additional_notes: Used with a past participle to talk about an unreal/imagined past or a regret: „Er hätte … kaufen sollen“ = he should have bought…. It’s also common in reported speech to show it’s someone’s claim or thought: „Er denkt, er hätte …“ ≈ he thinks he has/had…. „Er hätte es so gewollt“ means “he would have wanted it that way.”
target_language_example: Er hätte dir helfen können, aber er hatte keine Zeit.
native_language_example: He could have helped you, but he didn’t have time.

additional_notes: "Er" means "he" and "isst" is the 3rd-person singular present of "essen" (to eat). Used to say what a man/boy eats or when/where he eats; it can also appear before a subordinate clause (e.g., "Er isst, bevor...").
target_language_example: Er isst heute keine Süßigkeiten.
native_language_example: He isn't eating any sweets today.

additional_notes: The subject pronoun + verb form of sein. It is used to talk about a male person’s identity, qualities, condition, or location: Er ist müde. / Er ist in der Küche. It can also be part of the perfect tense with certain intransitive verbs, especially verbs of movement or change of state, as in Er ist gekommen or Er ist taub geworden, where English may use 'he has ...' instead.
target_language_example: Er ist heute sehr müde.
native_language_example: He is very tired today.

meaning: “he is on/at …” (used before a place, activity, trip, or condition).
additional_notes: This is not usually a complete sentence by itself—you add what he is “auf”: e.g. auf Dienstreise/auf Geschäftsreise (“on a business trip”), auf Drogen (“on drugs”), auf dem Baum (“up in the tree”), auf eigenen Wunsch (“at his own request”). With locations, it’s often **auf + dative** (auf dem Baum). Some uses are set phrases (auf Dienstreise, auf eigenen Wunsch).
target_language_example: Er ist auf dem Weg nach Hause.
native_language_example: He’s on his way home.

additional_notes: A basic, fully compositional phrase used before a singular noun to identify or describe a male person: profession, role, nationality, or type of person. In sentences like these, 'ein' is the indefinite article 'a/an'.
target_language_example: Er ist ein guter Lehrer.
native_language_example: He is a good teacher.

meaning: “he is a good …” (before a masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used as a starter phrase with a masculine noun in the nominative: **Er ist ein guter + Nomen** (e.g., *Esser, Koch, Zuhörer*). **guter** is the adjective ending for **ein guter** + masculine noun. For feminine nouns, you’d say **Sie ist eine gute …**; for plural: **Sie sind gute …**.
target_language_example: Er ist ein guter Lehrer.
native_language_example: He is a good teacher.

meaning: "he is a very ..." (used before an adjective + noun).
additional_notes: This is the start of a common description pattern: "Er ist ein sehr + adjective + noun" (e.g., Mann/Junge). After "ein" in the nominative masculine, the adjective usually ends in -er: "ein sehr netter Mann", "ein sehr kluger Junge". You can swap in many adjectives (attraktiv, gefährlich, intelligent, nett, freundlich, etc.).
target_language_example: Er ist ein sehr netter Mann.
native_language_example: He is a very nice man.

meaning: "he has just" / "he just" (something happened very recently).
additional_notes: Used with "gerade" to say something happened moments ago. Common with movement/arrival/departure verbs: "Er ist gerade gekommen" (He just arrived), "... rausgegangen" (just went out), "... hineingegangen" (just went in). "Er ist gerade weg" usually means "He just left / he’s just gone (not here now)."
target_language_example: Er ist gerade nach Hause gegangen.
native_language_example: He just went home.

additional_notes: "im" is a contraction of "in dem" and is used with masculine/neuter nouns in the dative case. It often means being located in something ("im See" = in the lake) or being in a state/phase ("im Alpha-Schlaf" = in alpha sleep; "im ersten Studienjahr" = in the first year of studies).
target_language_example: Er ist im Büro.
native_language_example: He is in the office.

additional_notes: Used to describe a habitual, constant, or repeated situation about a man/boy. It’s commonly followed by an adjective ("Er ist immer ehrlich."), a state ("beschäftigt"), or a phrase with a preposition ("an meiner Seite", "mit ... unterwegs"). For other people: "sie ist immer" (she), "du bist immer" (you), "ich bin immer" (I).
target_language_example: Er ist immer pünktlich.
native_language_example: He is always on time.

meaning: 'he is in …' / 'he is at …' (location); also in fixed phrases like 'in jemanden verknallt sein' = 'to have a crush on someone'.
additional_notes: Used with a place or country to say where he is ("Er ist in Tokyo.") or where something happened: "in Australien groß geworden" = grew up in Australia; "in Osaka geboren" = born in Osaka. With feelings it can appear in set expressions: "in dieses Mädchen verknallt" means he has a crush on this girl (not a physical location).
target_language_example: Er ist in Berlin, aber er ist in niemanden verknallt.
native_language_example: He is in Berlin, but he doesn't have a crush on anyone.

additional_notes: Used to say that a male person does not belong to a category (nationality, job, role, type). "kein" is the negative form of "ein" (a/an) and agrees with the noun’s gender/case (e.g., "Er ist kein Student"; with feminine nouns: "Sie ist keine Lehrerin"). Often contrasted with "sondern" to correct a statement: "Er ist kein X, sondern Y."
target_language_example: Er ist kein Arzt, sondern Krankenpfleger.
native_language_example: He isn't a doctor; he's a nurse.

meaning: "he is my" (used to say who a male person is to you, or what he is for you).
additional_notes: Use this to introduce or identify a man/boy by his relationship/role: a family member ("Er ist mein Ehemann."), a work connection ("Er ist mein Kollege."), or someone you’re dating/into ("Er ist mein Typ!" is more colloquial). It’s followed by a masculine noun in the nominative case. For feminine nouns, you need "Sie ist meine …"; for neuter nouns, "Er ist mein …" is still possible if you’re talking about a male person and the noun is neuter (e.g., "Er ist mein Kind.").
target_language_example: Er ist mein Bruder.
native_language_example: He is my brother.

additional_notes: Basic negation with „nicht“ after the (conjugated) verb „ist“: „Er ist nicht …“ (= He isn’t … / He is not …).
