additional_notes: Used with the Perfekt tense: **hat** (3rd person singular of *haben*) + past participle later in the clause, with **letztes Jahr** (“last year”) specifying time. In English this is typically rendered with the **simple past** (“did … last year”), not present perfect.
target_language_example: Tom hat letztes Jahr die Schule gewechselt.
native_language_example: Tom changed schools last year.

additional_notes: Usually not a fixed expression on its own. In many sentences, hat is the perfect-tense form of haben for er/sie/es, and mich means me. The main action word often comes later: Sie hat mich vergessen = She forgot / has forgotten me. Don't confuse hat here with the English noun hat.
target_language_example: Das hat mich überrascht.
native_language_example: That surprised me.

additional_notes: Past tense (Perfekt) of **bitten** = “to ask/request”: **jemand hat mich gebeten, ...** is usually followed by an infinitive clause (often with **zu**) that says what you were asked to do. Word order: *Er/Sie hat mich gebeten, zu kommen.*
target_language_example: Meine Kollegin hat mich gebeten, ihr bei der Präsentation zu helfen.
native_language_example: My colleague asked me to help her with the presentation.

additional_notes: This is a common word order with the Perfekt (present perfect) in German: subject + hat + direct object (mich) + time adverb (nie) + past participle at the end. It’s usually part of a larger sentence, e.g., „Er hat mich nie **angerufen**.“ = “He never called me.”
target_language_example: Sie hat mich nie eingeladen.
native_language_example: She never invited me.

additional_notes: Past tense (Perfekt) of *überraschen*: used to say that something surprised you. Structure: [subject] + hat + mich + überrascht. You can replace "mich" with another object pronoun: hat dich/ihn/sie/uns/euch/sie überrascht.
target_language_example: Sein Schweigen hat mich überrascht.
native_language_example: His silence surprised me.

meaning: “has … to me … it/that” (Perfect tense with “mir” = to me, “das” = it/that).
additional_notes: Used in the Perfekt (present perfect) to say someone did something to/for you involving “it/that.” It usually appears with a past participle at the end: “Er hat mir das geschickt.” Word order: subject + hat + mir (to me) + das (it/that) + past participle. “mir” is dative; “das” is accusative.
target_language_example: Sie hat mir das gestern erklärt.
native_language_example: She explained that to me yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to say you liked something. The thing you liked is the subject: *Das Buch hat mir gefallen.* = “I liked the book.” The person who liked it is in the dative (*mir* = “to me”). You’ll also see: *hat dir gefallen* (you liked), *hat ihm/ihr gefallen* (he/she liked), *hat uns/euch gefallen* (we/you all liked).
target_language_example: Der Film hat mir gefallen.
native_language_example: I liked the movie.

additional_notes: Perfect tense of **helfen** (“to help”): **hat geholfen**. The person receiving help is in the **dative** case: **mir** = “to me.” Used to say that someone helped you (in the past, or with present relevance).
target_language_example: Der Arzt hat mir geholfen.
native_language_example: The doctor helped me.

additional_notes: Used to report what a woman/girl said. After „daß“ (older spelling; modern: „dass“) you often see Subjunctive I (e.g., „habe“, „sei“, „trinke“) to show you’re repeating someone else’s words. You can swap pronouns and cases: „hat dir gesagt“ (told you), „hat ihm/ihr gesagt“ (told him/her), etc., and change „sie“ to „er“ (he) or another subject as needed.
target_language_example: Maria hat mir gesagt, daß sie lieber Rotwein trinke.
native_language_example: Maria told me that she prefers red wine.

additional_notes: Used with the present perfect (hat + past participle) to say something has not happened at any time up to now. Often implies “never before”/“not yet ever” (but it could happen in the future). Can also be used for emphasis in comparisons: “So hat noch nie jemand …” = “No one has ever … like that.”
target_language_example: Tom hat noch nie Sushi gegessen.
native_language_example: Tom has never eaten sushi.

meaning: “has (already) again / yet again” — something happened again (often annoyingly).
additional_notes: Used with a subject in the 3rd person singular (er/sie/es) in the present perfect: **hat + Partizip II**. **schon wieder** means “again” with a feeling of repetition (often impatience/annoyance): *Er hat schon wieder verschlafen.* For other subjects: **habe/hast/hat/haben/habt** (e.g., *Ich habe schon wieder…*, *Wir haben schon wieder…*).
target_language_example: Er hat schon wieder seine Schlüssel verloren.
native_language_example: He’s lost his keys again (yet again).

additional_notes: Not a fixed expression. Here, hat is the 3rd-person singular form of haben and often serves as the auxiliary in the German present perfect, while sein is the possessive word meaning "his/its"—not the verb sein ("to be"). In natural English, sentences with hat ... often translate with the simple past: for example, Sie hat sein Tagebuch gelesen. = "She read his diary."
target_language_example: Er hat sein Auto verkauft.
native_language_example: He sold his car.

meaning: "has his" (used with a past participle to form the present perfect).
additional_notes: "hat" is the 3rd person singular form of "haben" (to have). "seine" means "his" (or "its") and changes depending on the gender/case of the noun: e.g., "seine Firma" (his company), "seine Kleidung" (his clothes). In German perfect tense, the past participle often comes at the end: "Er hat seine Firma verkauft."
target_language_example: Er hat seine Hausaufgaben gemacht.
native_language_example: He has done his homework.

meaning: “has his” (with a masculine noun in the accusative).
additional_notes: Often appears in the Perfekt (present perfect) where **hat** is the auxiliary (“has”) and **seinen** is the possessive determiner “his” in **accusative masculine** (e.g., *seinen Pass, seinen Schlüssel*). The form changes with gender/case: *sein* (neuter acc.), *seine* (feminine acc./nom.), *seinen* (masc. acc.), *seinem* (dat.).
target_language_example: Er hat seinen Termin vergessen.
native_language_example: He forgot his appointment.

additional_notes: A common perfect-tense pattern: hat + sich for a third-person singular subject (er/sie/es or a singular noun). It is used with reflexive verbs and also when someone does something to/for themselves. In English, the reflexive may be translated directly ("built himself") or may disappear in natural English ("was delayed").
target_language_example: Lisa hat sich einen Tee gemacht.
native_language_example: Lisa made herself a tea.

additional_notes: This is the perfect tense of a reflexive pattern: **sich als + noun**. It usually appears with a verb that explains *how*: **sich als … erweisen** (turn out to be), **sich als … verkleiden** (dress up as), **sich als … ausgeben** (pose/pretend to be). By itself, **hat sich als** is incomplete—you need the role/identity after **als** and typically a verb/participle later in the sentence.
target_language_example: Sie hat sich als Expertin erwiesen.
native_language_example: She turned out to be an expert.

additional_notes: Common pattern: **[Person] hat sich beim + (activity) + verletzt**. **beim** = **bei dem** and is usually followed by a noun or a **nominalized verb** (often written with a capital letter), e.g. **beim Skifahren** = “while skiing”. Often used with injuries: **sich verletzen** (to get injured), **sich das Bein/den Arm brechen** (to break one’s leg/arm).
target_language_example: Er hat sich beim Fußballspielen verletzt.
native_language_example: He hurt himself while playing soccer.

meaning: “(he/she) hit their head” or “(he/she) racked their brains” (depending on the verb that follows).
additional_notes:
This is the start of two very common patterns:
- **sich den Kopf stoßen** = to bump/hit your head (literal, physical).
- **sich den Kopf zerbrechen** (often with **über** + noun) = to think very hard about something; to rack your brains (idiomatic).
Grammar: **sich** is the reflexive pronoun (hat **sich** …), and **den Kopf** is the object (“the head”). Often appears with a following participle: **hat sich den Kopf gestoßen/zerbrochen**.
target_language_example: Tom hat sich den Kopf über eine Lösung des Problems zerbrochen.
native_language_example: Tom racked his brains over a solution to the problem.

meaning: “(he/she) washed/dyed their hair …” (literally: “has [done something] themself the hair”).
additional_notes: Used with reflexive constructions to talk about doing something to your own hair. German typically uses a reflexive pronoun and often the dative for the person: ich habe mir die Haare gewaschen; du hast dir …; er/sie hat sich … . Common verbs: waschen (wash), färben (dye), schneiden lassen (have cut). The ellipsis (…) stands for the verb phrase or extra details (e.g., blau gefärbt).
target_language_example: Tom hat sich die Haare blau gefärbt.
native_language_example: Tom dyed his hair blue.

additional_notes: This isn’t a fixed phrase by itself. It’s usually a combination of **hat sich** (perfect tense of a reflexive verb) + **ein** (the indefinite article “a/an”). Very common pattern: **sich (etwas) kaufen** = “to buy oneself something” (often said with dative: **Er hat sich/mir ein Auto gekauft**). It can also appear with other verbs where **ein** just belongs to the noun: **Ein Knopf hat sich gelöst** (“a button came loose”).
target_language_example: Er hat sich ein neues Handy gekauft.
native_language_example: He bought himself a new phone.

additional_notes: Perfect tense of the reflexive verb "sich entscheiden" (to decide). Very often followed by "zu" + infinitive ("Er hat sich entschieden zu gehen") or by a comma and infinitive clause ("… entschieden, Jura zu studieren"). You can also decide for/against something: "sich für/gegen etwas entscheiden".
target_language_example: Sie hat sich entschieden, morgen früher aufzustehen.
native_language_example: She decided to get up earlier tomorrow.

meaning: has decided; has made up (his/her) mind.
additional_notes: Perfect tense (3rd person singular) of the reflexive verb „sich entschließen“ (= to decide). It’s commonly followed by „zu“ + infinitive: „Er hat sich entschlossen, morgen abzufahren.“ For other persons: „ich habe mich entschlossen“, „wir haben uns entschlossen“, etc.
target_language_example: Tom hat sich entschlossen, das nicht zu tun.
native_language_example: Tom has decided not to do that.

additional_notes: Perfect tense of the reflexive verb „sich ändern“ (to change). Used when a person, opinion, situation, address, phone number, etc. is different now than before. Structure: „[Something] hat sich geändert.“ (present perfect with „haben“ + past participle „geändert“).
target_language_example: Meine Meinung darüber hat sich geändert.
native_language_example: My opinion about it has changed.

meaning: “has [done something] in/into …” (perfect tense with a reflexive verb + “in”).
additional_notes: This isn’t a fixed idiom by itself; it’s a common grammar pattern: **hat** (perfect tense of *haben*) + **sich** (reflexive “himself/herself/itself”) + **in**. The exact meaning depends on the verb that follows/has already appeared (e.g. **sich verlieben in** = “to fall in love with”, **sich einschließen in** = “to lock oneself in”, **sich in Luft auflösen** = “to vanish into thin air”). Often **in** takes accusative here (movement/into), but some verbs use set phrases.
target_language_example: Er hat sich in die Arbeit vertieft.
native_language_example: He immersed himself in the work.

meaning: “has … with” (Perfekt form of a reflexive verb used with **sich mit + dative**).
additional_notes:
This isn’t a fixed phrase by itself; it’s the **past tense pattern** of many reflexive verbs that take **mit**. It often marks:
- the **person/thing you interact with**: *sich mit Maria streiten / verloben / anfreunden / verstehen* (argue/get engaged/make friends/get along with Maria)
- sometimes the **means/instrument**: *sich mit Gift umbringen* (kill oneself with poison)
Form: **haben + sich + (Verb) + mit + Dativ**. Pronoun changes: *ich habe mich…, du hast dich…, er/sie hat sich…, wir haben uns…*
target_language_example: Er hat sich mit seinem Nachbarn gestritten.
native_language_example: He argued with his neighbor.

additional_notes: Perfect tense of the reflexive verb "sich verändern" = "to change" (the subject changes itself/its state, not something else). Formed with "hat" + "sich" + past participle "verändert": "etwas/jemand hat sich verändert". Often used with "seit" to indicate change since a point in time: "... hat sich verändert, seit ...".
target_language_example: Die Welt hat sich verändert.
native_language_example: The world has changed.

additional_notes: "hat" is the present-tense form of "haben" (to have) used as an auxiliary to form the present perfect (e.g., "hat ... gegessen" = "has eaten"). Word order changes with sentence type: in statements you often see "... hat sie ..." (verb in 2nd position), and in yes/no questions you get inversion: "Hat sie ...?" = "Has she ...?" Not to be confused with English "hat" (the clothing item).
target_language_example: Hat sie das schon gemacht?
native_language_example: Has she already done that?

additional_notes: This is a very common German pattern: **hat** (auxiliary verb for the Perfekt/past) + **sie** (“she”) + **sich** (reflexive pronoun, “herself”). It appears with reflexive verbs like **sich wehren** (to defend oneself/resist), **sich melden** (to get in touch/report), **sich verwandeln** (to transform), **sich in die Luft jagen lassen** (to let herself be blown up), **sich ins Zeug legen** (to really make an effort), **sich geben** (to present/behave oneself). In questions, German often inverts word order, so you can get **Hat sie sich ...?** = “Did she ...?” / “Has she ...?”
target_language_example: Hat sie sich schon bei dir gemeldet?
native_language_example: Has she gotten in touch with you yet?

additional_notes: "hat" is the 3rd-person singular form of "haben" used in the Perfekt (present perfect) with a past participle (e.g., "hat … gezeigt/gegeben/erzählt"). "uns" means "us" and is often the dative object (roughly "to us"), especially with verbs like "geben" (to give), "zeigen" (to show), "erzählen" (to tell). In sentences like "Das Schwimmen hat uns Spaß gemacht", "uns" is still dative and the idea is "Swimming was fun for us."
target_language_example: Der Lehrer hat uns die Hausaufgaben erklärt.
native_language_example: The teacher explained the homework to us.

meaning: "tried" / "has tried" (present perfect of "versuchen"; often translates as simple past "tried").
additional_notes: Used with a 3rd-person singular subject (er/sie/es or a singular noun/name) to say someone attempted to do something. Commonly followed by an infinitive with "zu": "hat versucht, ... zu + Verb" (e.g., "Er hat versucht, mir zu helfen"). In spoken German, the Perfekt often corresponds to English simple past.
target_language_example: Tom hat versucht, das Tor selbst zu reparieren.
native_language_example: Tom tried to repair the gate himself.

meaning: is afraid of (that); is scared to (do something).
additional_notes: Used with **haben + Angst** plus **davor** to refer back to what someone fears (often something already mentioned or an action). Commonly followed by **zu + infinitive**: *Er hat Angst davor, zu fliegen.* If you name the object directly, you typically use **Angst vor + dative** instead: *Er hat Angst vor Spinnen.*
target_language_example: Tom hat Angst davor, nachts nach draußen zu gehen.
native_language_example: Tom is afraid to go outside at night.

meaning: is afraid of; is scared of.
additional_notes: From the phrase "Angst haben vor" (to be afraid of). You conjugate "haben": ich habe Angst vor…, du hast Angst vor…, er/sie/es hat Angst vor…, wir haben Angst vor…, ihr habt Angst vor…, sie/Sie haben Angst vor…. The noun or pronoun after "vor" is in the dative case (e.g., vor dem Hund, vor der Katze, vor ihm/ihr).
target_language_example: Er hat Angst vor Spinnen.
native_language_example: He is afraid of spiders.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone/something has three of something. "hat" is the 3rd-person singular present of "haben" (to have): "er/sie/es hat". The number comes before the noun: "hat drei Hunde" = "has three dogs".
target_language_example: Das Haus hat drei Zimmer.
native_language_example: The house has three rooms.

additional_notes: Usually means that someone or something possesses something. "hat" is the 3rd-person singular form of "haben" ("to have"), and "ein" is the indefinite article used with masculine or neuter singular nouns. In questions, the word order can change: "Hat ein Hai ...?" means "Does a shark have ...?"
target_language_example: Er hat ein neues Fahrrad.
native_language_example: He has a new bike.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something has a good quality, feature, or thing. It must be followed by a neuter noun (das-word) in the accusative, so the adjective takes the ending -es: ein gutes Herz, ein gutes Ende, ein gutes Argument, ein gutes Gedächtnis/Erinnerungsvermögen. For non-neuter nouns you change the ending (e.g., ein guter Freund, eine gute Idee).
target_language_example: Der Plan hat ein gutes Ergebnis.
native_language_example: The plan has a good result.

additional_notes: Common pattern: **[Person/thing] hat ein sehr + adjective + noun** to describe a quality, feature, or ability (e.g., *ein sehr hübsches Gesicht* = “a very pretty face”, *ein sehr freundliches Lächeln* = “a very friendly smile”). The adjective ending changes with the noun’s gender/case: *ein sehr hübsches Gesicht* (neuter), *eine sehr gute Idee* (feminine), *einen sehr guten Freund* (masculine accusative).
target_language_example: Er hat ein sehr gutes Gedächtnis.
native_language_example: He has a very good memory.

additional_notes: “hat” is the 3rd-person singular present tense of “haben” (to have): he/she/it has. “eine” is the feminine form of “ein” (a/an) used with feminine nouns (e.g., eine Struktur, eine Schwester). Used for possession/availability (“Das Geschäft hat eine große Auswahl”) and in common expressions like “eine Ahnung haben” = “to have an idea/clue.”
target_language_example: Sie hat eine Frage.
native_language_example: She has a question.

additional_notes: Used with a noun to say someone has many/much of something: „hat eine Menge + Nomen“ (e.g., „eine Menge Bücher“ = “a lot of books”). In the plural it often means “many,” and with uncountable nouns it means “a lot of.” Similar to „hat viele“ (many) / „hat viel“ (a lot).
target_language_example: Sie hat eine Menge Arbeit heute.
native_language_example: She has a lot of work today.

meaning: 'has a good …' (used before a feminine noun).
additional_notes: This is a common pattern: **(er/sie/es) hat** + **eine gute** + feminine noun (e.g. *Qualität, Stelle, Handschrift, Gitarre*). The adjective ending **-e** in *gute* matches the feminine noun after *eine*.
target_language_example: Sie hat eine gute Idee.
native_language_example: She has a good idea.

meaning: "has a very …" (followed by an adjective + noun).
additional_notes: Used with a singular feminine noun: hat (from haben = to have) + eine ("a" for feminine nouns) + sehr ("very"). Typically followed by an adjective and then the noun: "hat eine sehr interessante Geschichte". Note: "hat" here is a verb form ("has"), not the English noun "hat".
target_language_example: Sie hat eine sehr gute Idee.
native_language_example: She has a very good idea.

additional_notes: "hat" is the 3rd-person singular of "haben" (to have). "einen" is the accusative form of the indefinite article for a masculine singular noun, so you use it when the thing being had is masculine: "Er hat einen Hund." For feminine it’s "eine" ("Sie hat eine Katze."), and for neuter it’s "ein" ("Er hat ein Auto."). Note: "hat" looks like the English noun "hat" but here it’s a verb (“has”)—a common confusion.
target_language_example: Er hat einen neuen Job.
native_language_example: He has a new job.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone owns/keeps a dog. Conjugation changes with the subject: ich habe einen Hund, du hast einen Hund, er/sie/es hat einen Hund, wir haben einen Hund, ihr habt einen Hund, sie/Sie haben einen Hund.
target_language_example: Meine Nachbarin hat einen Hund.
native_language_example: My neighbor has a dog.

meaning: "has a big/large …" (with a masculine noun in the accusative).
additional_notes: Used with the verb **haben** to say someone/something has a big/large thing: **Er hat einen großen Hund.** The word **großen** is the adjective ending for **masculine accusative** after **einen** (e.g., *einen großen Hund / Schnurrbart*). With *Wert* it often means "has great value": **Das hat einen großen Wert.** Note: German **groß** means "big/large" and is a false friend with English **gross**.
target_language_example: Dieses Haus hat einen großen Garten.
native_language_example: This house has a big garden.

additional_notes: Used with masculine nouns in the accusative after **haben**: **einen guten + Noun** (e.g., *Charakter, Freund, Geschmack, Sinn*). The adjective ending **-en** is typical here. With other genders it changes: *hat eine gute Freundin*, *hat ein gutes Gefühl*.
target_language_example: Er hat einen guten Plan.
native_language_example: He has a good plan.

additional_notes: "hat" is the 3rd-person singular form of "haben" (to have), and "er" means "he." In questions, German often puts the verb first: "Hat er …?" = "Does he have …?" / "Has he …?" In short answers, you can also hear "Hat er nicht." meaning "He doesn’t." (short for "Er hat nicht …").
target_language_example: Hat er Zeit?
native_language_example: Does he have time?

additional_notes: "hat" is the 3rd-person singular present of "haben" (to have): er/sie/es hat = he/she/it has. "immer" means "always" and often comes right after the verb in simple sentences: "Sie hat immer ...". Note: in fixed phrases like "(Der Kunde) hat immer Recht" the word "Recht" is a noun and is usually capitalized; "recht" (lowercase) is an adverb meaning "quite/pretty" (e.g., "recht gut" = "pretty good").
target_language_example: Sie hat immer so viel zu tun.
native_language_example: She always has so much to do.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "haben" to say a situation continues up to now (often unexpectedly or despite time passing). Common in negatives: "hat immer noch keine ..." = "still has no ...". Word order: subject + hat + immer noch + noun (or "keine" + noun).
target_language_example: Sie hat immer noch keine Antwort bekommen.
native_language_example: She still hasn’t gotten an answer.

additional_notes: Used to negate possession or existence with the verb **haben** in 3rd person singular (he/she/it). **kein** changes like **ein** depending on the noun: **kein** (masc./neut. nominative/accusative: *kein Geld*), **keine** (feminine/plural: *keine Zeit*), **keinen** (masc. accusative: *keinen Hund*), etc. Other persons use different forms of **haben**: *ich habe kein…*, *du hast kein…*, *wir haben kein…*.
target_language_example: Er hat kein Geld.
native_language_example: He has no money.

additional_notes: Used with a feminine singular noun (or a plural noun) after "haben" to say someone/something has none of it: "Sie hat keine Schwester" / "Sie hat keine Freunde". For masculine/neuter singular nouns, use "hat keinen" (m.) or "hat kein" (n.). Word order is usually: subject + hat + keine + noun.
target_language_example: Er hat keine Zeit.
native_language_example: He has no time.

meaning: "has no" / "doesn't have a" (negates a masculine noun in the accusative).
additional_notes: Used with the verb "haben" to say someone/something does not have a specific thing. "Keinen" is the form of "kein" used for masculine nouns in the accusative (direct object): "Er hat keinen Pass." For neuter accusative it’s usually "kein" ("Es hat kein Dach."), and for feminine accusative "keine" ("Sie hat keine Zeit."). Note: with neuter nouns you’d say "hat kein ..." (e.g., "Die Statue hat kein Gesicht."), not "hat keinen".
target_language_example: Der Fremde hat keinen italienischen Namen.
native_language_example: The stranger has no Italian name.

additional_notes: Used to compare how much money someone has: **[Person] hat mehr Geld als [comparison]**. The word after **als** can be another person (**als du/ich/Maria**) or something else for emphasis/idioms, e.g. **mehr Geld als Verstand** (“more money than sense”) or **mehr Geld als notwendig** (“more money than necessary”).
target_language_example: Sie hat mehr Geld als ihr Bruder.
native_language_example: She has more money than her brother.

additional_notes: Used to state that someone is correct: "X hat recht" = "X is right." Common variations include: "Du hast recht" (you're right), "Er hatte recht" (he was right), and "Er hat recht gehabt" (he has/had been right).
target_language_example: Er hat recht, das ist keine gute Idee.
native_language_example: He is right, that's not a good idea.

meaning: "has its own" (referring to a masculine/neuter owner + a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to say that someone/something possesses a unique thing of its own. In this pattern, "seine" refers back to the owner (e.g., a country: "Schweden"), while "eigene" matches the gender/number of the thing owned. Here, "eigene" is feminine singular (often before nouns like "Sprache", "Flagge", "Nationalhymne"). Other forms: "hat seinen eigenen" (masc.), "hat sein eigenes" (neut.), "hat seine eigenen" (plural).
target_language_example: Die Firma hat seine eigene Website.
native_language_example: The company has its own website.

additional_notes: Used with a third-person singular subject (er/sie/es or a singular noun). It is followed by a plural noun: hat viele Einwohner, hat viele Röcke.
target_language_example: Das Hotel hat viele Zimmer.
native_language_example: The hotel has many rooms.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **haben** (to have) to say someone has a lot of friends. **viele** = “many/a lot of”, and **Freunde** is the plural of **Freund** (friend). You can add a place: **Er hat viele Freunde in Berlin.**
target_language_example: Sie hat viele Freunde in der Schule.
native_language_example: She has many friends at school.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive clause: „jemand hat vor, … zu + Infinitiv“. It expresses an intention/plan (not a fixed arrangement). The full verb is „vorhaben“ (separable): „Ich habe vor, …“, „Er/Sie hat vor, …“, „Wir haben vor, …“.
target_language_example: Tom hat vor, nächstes Jahr im Ausland zu studieren.
native_language_example: Tom plans to study abroad next year.

additional_notes: Past perfect of "hoffen" (to hope): "ich/er/sie/es hatte gehofft". Often used to talk about a past hope or expectation—frequently one that didn’t happen or turned out differently than expected.
target_language_example: Ich hatte gehofft, dass du heute Zeit hast.
native_language_example: I had hoped you would have time today.

additional_notes: Used with the simple past of **haben** (**hatte**) plus **noch nie** to say that something had *never happened before* a certain moment in the past (often a story background / before another past event). The verb itself usually comes at the end in German (e.g., *hatte noch nie … gemacht/geküsst/gearbeitet*). You can also use **noch nie** with other tenses (e.g., *Ich habe noch nie…* = “I have never…”).
target_language_example: Ich hatte noch nie so ein gutes Essen gegessen.
native_language_example: I had never eaten such good food.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a fear or worry about what might happen. "hatte" is the past tense of "haben" (ich hatte, du hattest, er/sie hatte, wir hatten, ihr hattet, sie/Sie hatten). After "dass", German often uses Konjunktiv II in more formal writing to express an unlikely/imagined outcome (e.g., "würde verlieren", "käme", "erführe"), but in everyday speech you’ll also hear simple past or "würde" forms.
target_language_example: Ich hatte Angst, dass ich den Zug verpassen würde.
native_language_example: I was afraid that I would miss the train.

meaning: was afraid of it / was scared to (do it).
additional_notes: Uses "haben" + "Angst" + "davor" to say you fear something, often followed by an infinitive clause: "Angst davor, (etwas) zu tun" (fear doing something) or passive: "Angst davor, ausgelacht zu werden" (fear being laughed at). "hatte" is past tense (ich/er/sie hatte). In present tense: "hat Angst davor".
target_language_example: Ich hatte Angst davor, ihn anzurufen.
native_language_example: I was afraid to call him.

additional_notes: "hatte" is the simple past (Präteritum) of "haben" (= to have). It’s common in writing and storytelling; in conversation you’ll often hear the perfect tense: "hat ... gehabt". "ein" is the indefinite article and changes with gender/case (e.g., "hatte einen Hund", "hatte eine Idee", "hatte ein Problem").
target_language_example: Ich hatte ein Problem, aber jetzt ist alles gut.
native_language_example: I had a problem, but now everything is fine.

meaning: “had a” (past tense of *haben*, used with a feminine noun).
additional_notes: *Hatte* is the simple past (Präteritum) of *haben* (“to have”). *Eine* is the indefinite article for feminine nouns in the accusative (direct object), e.g., *eine Idee, eine Tasche, eine Arbeit, eine Pistole*. In everyday spoken German, people often use the perfect instead: *Er hat eine gute Idee gehabt.*
target_language_example: Ich hatte eine Frage, aber jetzt nicht mehr.
native_language_example: I had a question, but not anymore.

meaning: 'had a' (past tense), used with masculine nouns in the accusative.
additional_notes: "hatte" is the simple past of "haben" (to have). "einen" is the accusative form of "ein" for masculine nouns (e.g., "einen Flügel", "einen Traum", "einen Grund"). With feminine nouns you use "hatte eine", and with neuter nouns "hatte ein". You’ll also see "Es hatte ..." meaning "It had ..." (e.g., a taste or smell).
target_language_example: Ich hatte einen Termin beim Arzt.
native_language_example: I had a doctor’s appointment.

additional_notes: Simple past (Präteritum) of "einen Unfall haben". Used for accidents in general (often traffic or workplace accidents). In everyday spoken German, the Perfekt is also common: "hat einen Unfall gehabt".
target_language_example: Tom hatte einen Unfall und brach sich das Bein.
native_language_example: Tom had an accident and broke his leg.

additional_notes: Präteritum (simple past) of „recht haben“ (to be right). Used after the subject: „Ich hatte recht.“ The opposite is „hatte unrecht“ (was wrong). Present tense: „hat recht“ (is right).
target_language_example: Tom hatte recht, und Maria hatte unrecht.
native_language_example: Tom was right, and Maria was wrong.

additional_notes: "Hatten" is the simple past of "haben" (to have), used with "Sie" (formal "you"). It’s common in polite questions about past experiences or whether someone had something (e.g., a good day, problems, a cold). Depending on context, English may use simple past ("Did you have…?") or present perfect ("Have you ever had…?").
target_language_example: Hatten Sie heute Morgen Zeit?
native_language_example: Did you have time this morning?

meaning: “had a” (past tense of *haben* with a masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used when the subject is plural (*wir/ihr/sie* or several people/things) or formal *Sie*: *Sie hatten einen …*. It takes the accusative masculine article *einen* before a masculine noun (e.g., *einen Garten, einen Streit, einen Aufenthalt*). For feminine nouns you’d use *hatten eine …*; for neuter *hatten ein …*.
target_language_example: Wir hatten einen Termin um zehn Uhr.
native_language_example: We had an appointment at ten o’clock.

additional_notes: "Hatten" is the Präteritum (simple past) form of "haben" for "wir". It’s common in written German and storytelling; in everyday speech, many people often use Perfekt instead ("wir haben gehabt" / usually just "wir haben ..."). Word order can change: after another element you often get inversion, e.g. "Am Anfang hatten wir ..." (= "At the beginning, we had ...").
target_language_example: Gestern hatten wir keine Zeit.
native_language_example: Yesterday we had no time.

additional_notes: "hattest" is the simple past (Präteritum) of "haben" for "du". It’s very common in spoken questions: "Hattest du ...?" = "Did you have ...?" In statements you usually keep the normal word order: "Du hattest ..." (You had ...). Use it only when speaking to one person you address as "du" (friends, family, kids).
target_language_example: Hattest du Zeit, mir zu helfen?
native_language_example: Did you have time to help me?

additional_notes: "Hattet" is the simple past (Präteritum) of "haben" for "ihr" (you plural). It’s used when talking to more than one person. In speech, German often uses "habt ihr ... gehabt?" instead, but "hattet ihr ...?" is also common—especially with "haben" and in writing. Word order: in questions the verb usually comes first ("Hattet ihr Zeit?"); in statements it comes second ("Ihr hattet Zeit.").
target_language_example: Hattet ihr genug Zeit, um alles zu erledigen?
native_language_example: Did you all have enough time to get everything done?

additional_notes: Very informal and often rude/hostile. It’s the imperative of **(ab)hauen** meaning “to leave/run off.” Common in arguments or when telling someone to go away quickly: **Hau ab!**, **Hau ab, du Idiot!**, **Nimm deine Sachen und hau ab!**
target_language_example: Hau ab, ich will dich nicht mehr sehen!
native_language_example: Get lost, I don’t want to see you anymore!

meaning: 'runs off / leaves quickly' or (as an order) 'get out of here!'
additional_notes: From the separable verb **abhauen**. Used for someone escaping or suddenly leaving (**Er haut ab.** = “He runs off.”). In the imperative it’s a rude/strong way to tell someone to leave (**Haut ab!** = “Get out of here!” / “Beat it!”). Common forms: **ich hau ab, du haust ab, er/sie haut ab; haut ab!** (plural/you all).
target_language_example: Er haut ab.
native_language_example: He runs off.

additional_notes: This is an extremist phrase associated with Nazi Germany and is considered hateful. Using it today is offensive and may be illegal in some places (e.g., Germany, where Nazi symbols/slogans are restricted except in clearly educational, historical, or artistic contexts). You may encounter it in movies, history books, or when reporting/condemning Nazi ideology, but it should not be used as a greeting.
target_language_example: Er wurde angezeigt, weil er „Heil Hitler“ gerufen hat.
native_language_example: He was reported to the police because he shouted “Heil Hitler.”

additional_notes: Used for the drink you order in a café or make at home. Common patterns: „eine heiße Schokolade“ (one hot chocolate) and „Tasse heiße Schokolade“ (a cup of hot chocolate). In questions, you’ll often hear „Möchtest du …?“ (Would you like …?) or „Wer hat … bestellt?“ (Who ordered …?).
target_language_example: Ich hätte gern eine heiße Schokolade, bitte.
native_language_example: I’d like a hot chocolate, please.

additional_notes: Used for water that is hot (often for tea, cooking, washing). It’s the adjective „heiß“ (hot) + „Wasser“ (water). You’ll often see it with amounts/containers: „ein Glas heißes Wasser“, „zwei Liter heißes Wasser“; and with verbs like „kochen“ (boil), „gießen“ (pour), „geben“ (give).
target_language_example: Kann ich bitte ein heißes Wasser haben?
native_language_example: Can I please have a hot water?

additional_notes: Used to check or confirm a conclusion you’re drawing from what someone just said (often with a question mark). In questions it’s commonly followed by a comma and then a full clause: "Heißt das, (dass) ...?" Literally "does that mean" (from "heißen" = to mean + "das" = that).
target_language_example: Heißt das, wir müssen morgen früher los?
native_language_example: Does that mean we have to leave earlier tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used to say someone will help, but only under a condition introduced by **wenn** (“if/when”). In German, you normally put a **comma** before the **wenn**-clause. The verb in the **wenn**-clause goes to the **end**: *…, wenn du mich lässt.* Often used with **kann** (can), **würde** (would), or future meaning with **wird** (will).
target_language_example: Ich kann dir helfen, wenn du mich lässt.
native_language_example: I can help you if you let me.

additional_notes: Polite/formal way to ask one person for help (Sie-form). Used with strangers, customers, or in professional situations. Often followed by an infinitive with „zu“ to say what kind of help you need: „Helfen Sie mir, das zu tragen/zu finden/zu öffnen.“ For friends/family you usually say „Hilf mir.“
target_language_example: Entschuldigen Sie, helfen Sie mir bitte, den Weg zum Bahnhof zu finden.
native_language_example: Excuse me, please help me find the way to the train station.

additional_notes: Used with the modal verb **können** to say someone is able/willing to help. The main verb stays in the infinitive (**helfen**), and **kann** is the conjugated modal. In subordinate clauses, **helfen kann** often comes at the end: *Gibt es jemanden, der mir helfen kann?* You can use **mir** (me) or polite **Ihnen** (you).
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, können Sie mir sagen, wer mir helfen kann?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can you tell me who can help me?

additional_notes: Used when someone has the intention/desire to help. It’s built from the verb *helfen* (to help) + the modal verb *wollen* (to want). As a verb cluster, it commonly appears in the infinitive (e.g., after another modal or in certain constructions), with both verbs at the end: *… helfen wollen*.
target_language_example: Ich würde dir gern helfen wollen.
native_language_example: I would like to want to help you.

additional_notes: Imperative of **helfen** for **ihr** (you plural/informal). Used to ask several people for help, often with an extra action: **Helft mir, … zu …** (“Help me (to) …”). For one person: **Hilf mir!**; formal/plural formal: **Helfen Sie mir!**.
target_language_example: Helft mir bitte, die Kisten zu tragen.
native_language_example: Please help me carry the boxes.

meaning: to find out what (…); to figure out what (…); to discover what (…).
additional_notes: Used when you want to learn or clarify something unknown and it’s followed by an indirect question introduced by **was** (“what”). **herausfinden** is a separable verb: in main clauses it splits (**Ich finde heraus, was…**), but it stays together in subordinate clauses and with modals (**…weil ich herausfinden muss, was…** / **Ich muss herausfinden, was…**).
target_language_example: Wir sollten herausfinden, was als Nächstes zu tun ist.
native_language_example: We should find out what to do next.

additional_notes: Used to greet someone in a friendly, warm way (more warm/formal than just „Willkommen“). Often said when welcoming guests to a place or event: „Herzlich willkommen im …“ or „… heißen“ / „… willkommen heißen“ (“to welcome someone”). Can be intensified as „ganz herzlich willkommen“.
target_language_example: Herzlich willkommen bei uns zu Hause!
native_language_example: A warm welcome to our home!

meaning: "many thanks" / "thank you very much" (warm, heartfelt thanks).
additional_notes: A polite, warm way to thank someone; often used in speaking and writing (emails, letters). Commonly followed by "für" + accusative to say what you’re thanking for (e.g., "Herzlichen Dank für Ihre Hilfe"). Often intensified with words like "vielen", "ganz", or "recht".
target_language_example: Herzlichen Dank für deine Hilfe!
native_language_example: Thank you very much for your help!

additional_notes: Common set phrase used to congratulate someone (e.g., on a promotion, birthday, success). Often followed by a comma and the person/group being addressed ("Herzlichen Glückwunsch, Anna!"). You can also say "Herzlichen Glückwunsch zum Geburtstag!" (for a birthday).
target_language_example: Herzlichen Glückwunsch zum Geburtstag!
native_language_example: Happy birthday! (Congratulations on your birthday!)

additional_notes: Refers to the evening of today. It's commonly used for plans, events, or situations happening later the same day. Depending on context, English may use either "this evening" or "tonight."
target_language_example: Kommst du heute Abend zu mir?
native_language_example: Are you coming over to my place tonight?

additional_notes: Means the morning of today. Often used without a preposition (not *am*): „Ich habe heute Morgen…“. With a specific time you can also say „heute Morgen um 7“.
target_language_example: Ich habe heute Morgen keine Zeit.
native_language_example: I don't have time this morning.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens later today during the afternoon. You can put it at the start or end of a sentence: "Heute Nachmittag komme ich" / "Ich komme heute Nachmittag." Often used to ask about plans or availability.
target_language_example: Heute Nachmittag habe ich einen Termin.
native_language_example: This afternoon I have an appointment.

additional_notes: Means the night connected to today. Depending on context and tense, it can refer to the coming night ("tonight") or to the night that already happened ("last night"). Often used with future plans ("Ich komme heute Nacht.") or to ask where someone was ("Wo warst du heute Nacht?").
target_language_example: Ich kann heute Nacht nicht schlafen.
native_language_example: I can't sleep tonight.

additional_notes: Used to talk about plans or events happening later today (in the evening). Common in questions about plans (Was machst du heute Abend?) and invitations/requests (Kommst du heute Abend?). Also written and said as „heute Abend“; in Switzerland often „heute Abend“/„hüt Abig“ (dialect).
target_language_example: Ich habe heute Abend keine Zeit.
native_language_example: I don’t have time tonight.

additional_notes: Refers to the early part of today, usually in the morning hours. In everyday speech, people often just say „heute Morgen“ for “this morning”; „heute früh“ emphasizes “early.” It can appear at the beginning or in the middle of a sentence: „Heute früh habe ich…“ / „Ich habe heute früh…“.
target_language_example: Heute früh bin ich um sechs Uhr aufgestanden.
native_language_example: Early this morning, I got up at six o’clock.

meaning: “today I have …” (often starting a sentence to emphasize that it happened today).
additional_notes: Common sentence starter with inversion: the time word (Heute) comes first, and the conjugated verb (habe) comes second (German V2 word order). Often used with the Perfekt tense: "Heute habe ich" + past participle (… gelernt/geschafft/geträumt). The past participle usually goes to the end of the clause.
target_language_example: Heute habe ich meine Hausaufgaben gemacht.
native_language_example: Today I did my homework.

additional_notes: Used to start a sentence with a time word (heute = today). In German, when something like "heute" comes first, the verb (habe) comes next, and the subject (ich) comes after it: "Heute habe ich ..." (= "I have ... today"). Often followed by a noun or "keine" + noun (e.g., keine Zeit).
target_language_example: Heute habe ich einen Termin.
native_language_example: Today I have an appointment.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened (or someone was/wasn’t) at school today. Often comes after a verb: „Warst du heute in der Schule?“ / „Ich war heute in der Schule.“
target_language_example: Ich habe heute in der Schule einen Test geschrieben.
native_language_example: I took a test at school today.

additional_notes: Used to say what day/date it is, or to describe today’s situation (often with "es" for weather/conditions: "Heute ist es kalt."). Common pattern: "Heute ist + noun/adjective" ("Heute ist Dienstag." / "Heute ist ein guter Tag.").
target_language_example: Heute ist ein guter Tag, um Deutsch zu lernen.
native_language_example: Today is a good day to learn German.

meaning: "today is a ..." (introduces a masculine noun phrase).
additional_notes: Use it to describe what kind of day today is, or what today represents: Heute ist ein Feiertag. / Heute ist ein schöner Tag. It’s used with masculine nouns (ein Tag, ein Feiertag). With feminine nouns use "heute ist eine ..." (eine gute Idee), and with neuter nouns "heute ist ein ..." as well (ein Problem, ein Fest).
target_language_example: Heute ist ein besonderer Tag.
native_language_example: Today is a special day.

meaning: “today it is …” (used to describe how something is today).
additional_notes: Used to make statements about the current day, often about weather, time, or how a situation feels/compares (e.g., warmer/colder, easier/harder). Typically followed by an adjective or description: „Heute ist es kalt/warm/spät/anders.“
target_language_example: Heute ist es besser als gestern.
native_language_example: Today it is better than yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened in the morning of today. Note: German capitalizes nouns, so "Morgen" is usually capitalized here. Don’t confuse "Morgen" (morning) with "morgen" (tomorrow).
target_language_example: Ich habe heute Morgen keine Zeit gehabt.
native_language_example: I didn’t have time this morning.

additional_notes: Used with movement verbs to say that someone goes/comes home today. Common verbs: „(nach Hause) gehen“ (go home on foot/in general), „(nach Hause) fahren“ (go home by vehicle), „(nach Hause) kommen“ (come home). „nach Hause“ expresses direction (to home), so it’s used without an article (not *nach dem Haus*).
target_language_example: Ich gehe heute nach Hause.
native_language_example: I'm going home today.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something happening later today, in the afternoon. Often used with future plans/appointments (e.g., meeting, shopping, going swimming). You can also say "heute Nachmittag"; capitalization is common because "Nachmittag" is a noun.
target_language_example: Ich habe heute Nachmittag einen Termin.
native_language_example: I have an appointment this afternoon.

additional_notes: Refers to the night connected to “today.” If you’re talking about plans or something that will happen later, it usually means “tonight.” If you’re talking about sleep, dreams, or something that already happened during the night before this morning, it often means “last night.” Often written and said as “heute Nacht” (Nacht is a noun).
target_language_example: Kommst du heute Nacht nach Hause?
native_language_example: Are you coming home tonight?

additional_notes: Used to say someone will/should/must not go out today. "zu Hause bleiben" is the core phrase (“to stay at home”); adding "heute" specifies “today.” Often used with modal verbs like "sollen" (should), "müssen" (must), or "können" (can).
target_language_example: Wir müssen heute zu Hause bleiben, weil es den ganzen Tag regnet.
native_language_example: We have to stay at home today because it’s raining all day.

additional_notes: Used as a casual opener before saying who you are (name/role) or what your current situation is (e.g., here/with you, finished). Very common in informal speech. Note: "ich bin" literally means "I am" and can be followed by a name (Ich bin Ben), a noun with an article/possessive (Ich bin ihre Schwester), or an adjective (Ich bin fertig).
target_language_example: Hey, ich bin neu hier.
native_language_example: Hey, I'm new here.

additional_notes: An informal way to get someone’s attention and ask what something is or what’s happening. Often used with an extra phrase: "Hey, was ist los?" (what’s going on?), "Hey, was ist das?" (what is that?), "Hey, was ist mit dir/dir?" (what’s wrong with you?/what about you?). On its own ("Hey, was ist?") it usually means "Hey, what’s up?/What’s going on?"
target_language_example: Hey, was ist los?
native_language_example: Hey, what’s going on?

additional_notes: Past tense (Präteritum) of **etwas für + adjective/noun halten** = to consider/think something is something. **es** is a dummy “it” that refers to what comes next (often an adjective or a noun phrase). Common patterns: **jdn./etw. für dumm halten** (think someone/something is stupid), **etw. für wichtig halten, dass ...** (think it’s important that ...).
target_language_example: Ich hielt es für keine gute Idee, allein zu gehen.
native_language_example: I thought it wasn’t a good idea to go alone.

additional_notes: Used when handing someone something or telling them to take/pick up something. Often followed by an object ("Hier, nimm das/den Schlüssel/es!"). The comma reflects a pause in speech; you can also hear it as "Hier—nimm!". Adding "mal" ("Hier, nimm mal") makes it softer/more casual, like "here, take this".
target_language_example: Hier, nimm meine Jacke—draußen ist es kalt.
native_language_example: Here, take my jacket—it's cold outside.

additional_notes: Usually used with an infinitive clause: **hier, um ... zu + infinitive**. It explains why someone is here (their goal/purpose). The comma before **um** is standard: *Ich bin hier, um dir zu helfen.*
target_language_example: Ich bin hier, um Ihnen ein paar Fragen zu stellen.
native_language_example: I’m here to ask you a few questions.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is physically present next to you (often with verbs like bleiben/sein: "Bleib hier bei mir" = stay here with me). It can also express a wish about someone’s presence: "Ich wünschte, du wärst hier bei mir" (I wish you were here with me).
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte hier bei mir bleiben?
native_language_example: Can you please stay here with me?

additional_notes: Used to announce your presence or arrival (often as an exclamation: „Hier bin ich!“). It can also be used in longer sentences to describe your situation in a place: „Hier bin ich in Sicherheit.“ (“Here I’m safe.”).
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, hier bin ich!
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’m here!

additional_notes: Used to say someone remains in the current place (and doesn’t leave). Often used in questions about how long someone will stay ("Wie lange wirst du hier bleiben?") or to ask permission ("Darf ich hier bleiben?"). "bleiben" changes with the subject: ich bleibe, du bleibst, er/sie/es bleibt, wir bleiben, ihr bleibt, sie/Sie bleiben.
target_language_example: Ich kann heute Nacht hier bleiben.
native_language_example: I can stay here tonight.

additional_notes: Used to point to a place that is outside or away from where the speaker considers “inside” or “in here” (often contrasted with „drinnen“ = inside). It can mean literally outside a building (“out here in the yard”) or more generally “out here in this area/part of town.”
target_language_example: Es ist kalt hier draußen, komm lieber rein.
native_language_example: It’s cold out here—come inside instead.

additional_notes: Used to say you are inside a specific place (a room, building, shop, etc.), often contrasted with being outside. Common in spoken German; you may also hear the longer form "hier drinnen" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Ich war noch nie hier drin, obwohl ich oft vorbeigekommen bin.
native_language_example: I’ve never been in here, even though I’ve often passed by.

meaning: “this way” / “along here” (used to show the way).
additional_notes: Often said while guiding someone or pointing in a direction. Common with imperatives like „Kommen Sie hier entlang“ (formal) or „Komm hier entlang“ (informal). Can also describe movement along a route: „hier entlang gehen“ = “walk along here / go this way.”
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, zur Toilette? — Ja, hier entlang.
native_language_example: Excuse me, where’s the bathroom? — Yes, this way.

additional_notes: Used to say that something exists or is available in this place. It’s the phrase “es gibt” (there is/are) with “hier” (here) added. Word order can change in questions, e.g. “Gibt es hier …?”
target_language_example: Hier gibt es kostenloses WLAN.
native_language_example: There is free Wi‑Fi here.

meaning: “There are no … here.” / “There isn’t any … here.”
additional_notes: Used to say something does not exist or is not available in this place. It’s usually followed by a noun with **keine** (negation of *ein/eine*): **keine + plural noun** (keine Blumen) or **keine + uncountable noun** (keine Zeit). Word order stays: **Hier gibt es keine …**
target_language_example: Tut mir leid, hier gibt es keine Parkplätze.
native_language_example: Sorry, there are no parking spaces here.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the local area near where you are now. Very common with questions about places (restaurants, shops) and with verbs like wohnen (to live) and aufwachsen (to grow up).
target_language_example: Gibt es hier in der Gegend einen Supermarkt?
native_language_example: Is there a supermarket around here?

additional_notes: Used to ask about or describe something close to your current location. Often placed at the end of the sentence. Similar alternatives: „in der Nähe“ (nearby) or „ganz in der Nähe“ (very close by).
target_language_example: Gibt es hier in der Nähe eine Apotheke?
native_language_example: Is there a pharmacy near here?

additional_notes: Used when you don’t know the exact place, but mean a location in this general area. Often appears in questions and requests: “Gibt es hier irgendwo …?” (“Is there … somewhere around here?”). You can also add extra detail like “hier irgendwo in der Nähe” (“somewhere nearby”).
target_language_example: Gibt es hier irgendwo eine Apotheke?
native_language_example: Is there a pharmacy somewhere around here?

additional_notes: Used to point out something’s location or presence: „Hier ist der Schlüssel.“ = “Here’s the key.” In introductions (especially on the phone), it can mean “This is …”: „Hallo, hier ist Anna.“ Also appears in sentences like „Hier ist es …“ (“It’s … here”) and „… hier ist …“ to emphasize “here” in the middle of a sentence: „Der Baum hier ist älter.“
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, hier ist mein Ticket.
native_language_example: Excuse me, here is my ticket.

additional_notes: Used when pointing something out or presenting something/someone nearby. "Der" is the masculine form of "the" (nominative), so it’s followed by a masculine noun (e.g., "der Ausgang") or a masculine person/thing being identified ("der, der ..."). For other genders you’d use "hier ist die" (feminine) or "hier ist das" (neuter).
target_language_example: Hier ist der Schlüssel, den du gesucht hast.
native_language_example: Here is the key you were looking for.

additional_notes: Used when you point to or hand someone something, or when you introduce something you’re about to show/play/read. It must be followed by a feminine noun (die + noun), e.g. „hier ist die Bäckerei“ (the bakery), „hier ist die Akte“ (the file). For masculine/neuter use „hier ist der/das …“, and for plural „hier sind die …“. You may also hear it in recorded messages like „Hier ist die Mailbox von …“ (“This is the voicemail of …”).
target_language_example: Hier ist die Rechnung.
native_language_example: Here is the bill.

meaning: 'here is a' (presenting or pointing out something).
additional_notes: Used when you hand someone something or point to something nearby. Very common in speech. Often followed by a noun (with "ein/eine"): "Hier ist ein Brief" / "Hier ist eine Karte". You can also use it to introduce an item in a description/list: "Hier ist ein Zelt ...".
target_language_example: Hier ist ein Stift für dich.
native_language_example: Here is a pen for you.

additional_notes: Used to describe how things are in a place: *Hier ist es kalt/schön/voll/toll.* The **es** is often a “dummy subject” (especially with weather/conditions). As a question (**Hier ist es?**), it can mean “Is it here?” (often with surprise/confirming location).
target_language_example: Hier ist es viel ruhiger als in der Stadt.
native_language_example: It’s much quieter here than in the city.

meaning: “There is no … here” / “This isn’t a …” (with masculine/neuter nouns).
additional_notes: Used to say that something is not present in this place, or to correct what something is. Grammar: “kein” is used with masculine/neuter singular nouns in the nominative (e.g., hier ist kein Bahnhof / kein Problem). For feminine or plural nouns, use “hier ist keine …” / “hier sind keine …”.
target_language_example: Tut mir leid, hier ist kein WLAN.
native_language_example: Sorry, there’s no Wi‑Fi here.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is not possible/allowed in this place. Often comes after the verb to emphasize the location: „Wir können das hier nicht …“ = “We can’t … here.”
target_language_example: Das geht hier nicht.
native_language_example: That’s not possible here.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone/something has stopped being here (at this place). Built from **hier** (“here”) + **nicht mehr** (“no longer”). Often appears with common verbs like **wohnen**, **sein**, **brauchen**: *Er ist hier nicht mehr.* / *Sie wohnt hier nicht mehr.* Word order can vary, but the meaning stays “no longer here.”
target_language_example: Tut mir leid, aber die Ärztin ist hier nicht mehr.
native_language_example: Sorry, but the doctor isn’t here anymore.

meaning: up here (in this higher place/upper floor).
additional_notes: Used to point out your location or something’s location at a higher level than the speaker’s reference point (e.g., upstairs, on a hill, higher up in a building). Often contrasted with „hier unten“ (down here). Common with „von hier oben“ = “from up here.”
target_language_example: Komm hier oben hoch, ich warte vor der Tür.
native_language_example: Come up here, I’m waiting by the door.

additional_notes: Means leaving this place or getting someone/something out of this place. Common with verbs like wollen/müssen: „Ich will hier raus!“ = “I want to get out of here!” It can also mean being released/allowed to leave (e.g., a hospital, prison): „Du bist in zehn Tagen hier raus.“ = “You’ll be out of here in ten days.”
target_language_example: Lass uns hier rausgehen, es ist schon spät.
native_language_example: Let’s get out of here; it’s already late.

additional_notes: Usually used to talk about leaving a place or moving something from inside to outside: "Wir müssen hier raus." = "We have to get out of here." Often with verbs like "gehen/kommen/müssen". "raus" is the common spoken form of "heraus" (more formal).
target_language_example: Komm, wir gehen hier raus.
native_language_example: Come on, let’s get out of here.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement (especially "komm") to tell someone to come toward the speaker. "rüber" emphasizes moving from there to here/across to this side. Can sound very direct; adding swear words like "verdammt noch mal" makes it rude/angry.
target_language_example: Komm bitte hier rüber und setz dich neben mich.
native_language_example: Please come over here and sit next to me.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone is in this place or will be present here. With time expressions, it often means that someone needs to arrive or be present by a certain time, as in um fünf hier sein ('be here at five').
target_language_example: Ich werde morgen den ganzen Tag hier sein.
native_language_example: I will be here all day tomorrow.

meaning: to be here; to be present (in this place).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is (or should be) in this location. It commonly appears with modal verbs to express possibility/necessity/permission (e.g., „kann hier sein“ = might be here, „sollte hier sein“ = should be here, „darf hier sein“ = am allowed to be here, „muss hier sein“ = has to be here).
target_language_example: Bist du schon hier, oder wirst du später hier sein?
native_language_example: Are you here already, or will you be here later?

meaning: "here are" (used to point out or hand over multiple things).
additional_notes: Used with plural nouns (or polite/plural "Sie") to indicate that things are here/present, often when showing where they are or giving them to someone: "Hier sind deine Sachen." For singular, you usually say "Hier ist ...". Word order can vary depending on what comes first (e.g., "Deine Sachen sind hier.").
target_language_example: Hier sind die Tickets für das Konzert.
native_language_example: Here are the tickets for the concert.

additional_notes: Used with plural nouns to (1) hand/present things: “Hier sind die Eintrittskarten.” = “Here are the tickets.” or (2) talk about what something/someone is like in this place: “Hier sind die Häuser alt.” = “Here, the houses are old.” In (2), you often add an adjective or other description after the noun. Can also be used for dramatic announcements: “Hier sind die Samurai!”
target_language_example: Hier sind die Schlüssel, die du gesucht hast.
native_language_example: Here are the keys you were looking for.

meaning: down here; down below (in this place).
additional_notes: Used to point out a location that is lower than where the speaker imagines the listener to be (e.g., downstairs, underground, down in a basement/valley), or to emphasize being in a specific area: "down here (where we are)". Often contrasts with "da oben" (up there).
target_language_example: Komm hier unten her, ich brauche deine Hilfe.
native_language_example: Come down here, I need your help.

meaning: 'to be here' (to be present at this place).
additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s presence at the current location, often with a time (e.g., um fünf hier zu sein = to be here at five). Can also be used to question or deny someone’s right/permission to be somewhere (kein Recht, hier zu sein = no right to be here).
target_language_example: Ich bin froh, heute hier zu sein.
native_language_example: I’m glad to be here today.

meaning: to search/look for (something) here; in the accusatory question pattern: “to have business here / to belong here”.
additional_notes: Literal meaning: searching in this place (“It’s pointless to search here.”). Very common in confrontational/accusatory phrasing, especially **Was hast du hier zu suchen?** meaning “What are you doing here?/What business do you have here?/You don’t belong here.” The verb **suchen** often takes an object (e.g., *den Schlüssel*), but the phrase can be used without one when the context is clear.
target_language_example: Was hast du hier zu suchen?
native_language_example: What business do you have here? / What are you doing here?

additional_notes: Perfect tense of "(hierher) kommen" (to come here), usually formed with "sein": "Ich bin hierher gekommen." "Hierher" emphasizes movement toward the speaker or the place you are talking from (similar to "to here").
target_language_example: Warum bist du so spät hierher gekommen?
native_language_example: Why did you come here so late?

meaning: to come here (toward the speaker/this place)
additional_notes: Used when someone moves to the place where the speaker is (or the place being referred to as “here”). Common with modal and future constructions: „Du darfst/kannst/sollst nicht hierher kommen“, „Er wird hierher kommen“. Often contrasts with „dorthin gehen“/„dahin gehen“ (to go there).
target_language_example: Du kannst nicht hierher kommen.
native_language_example: You can’t come here.

additional_notes: Used to say you came to this place with a purpose. It’s often used as: „Ich bin hierhergekommen, um …“ + infinitive (e.g., „zu reden“, „zu finden“). In reported speech or hypotheticals you may see: „ich wäre … hierhergekommen, um …“ (Konjunktiv II).
target_language_example: Ich bin hierhergekommen, um dir zu helfen.
native_language_example: I came here to help you.

additional_notes: Imperative (command/request) using the informal "du" form of "helfen". Often softened with "bitte". Common patterns: "Hilf mir bei + Dativ" (help me with …) and "Hilf mir, … zu + Infinitiv" (help me to …).
target_language_example: Hilf mir bitte, das Auto zu reparieren.
native_language_example: Please help me fix the car.

meaning: “will you help me?” / “can you help me?”
additional_notes: Uses the verb „helfen“ (to help). „Du“ = you (informal singular), „mir“ = me (dative). Often used as a polite request, especially with „bitte“ or „mal“ (softens the request). Common patterns: „Hilfst du mir (bitte)?“; „Hilfst du mir in der Küche?“ (with a place); „Hilfst du mir bei …?“ (with a task/noun); „Hilfst du mir (dabei), … zu …?“ or „Hilfst du mir, … zu …?“ (to do something).
target_language_example: Hilfst du mir bitte, das zu tragen?
native_language_example: Can you help me carry that, please?

meaning: back and forth; to and fro.
additional_notes: Used for repeated movement between two directions/places: "Die Lampe schwang hin und her." It’s also used figuratively for an exchange that goes back and forth (messages, emails, arguments): "Wir haben hin und her geschrieben." Often used with verbs like schwingen, gehen, laufen, laufen, schreiben, diskutieren.
target_language_example: Die Kinder rannten im Garten hin und her.
native_language_example: The kids ran back and forth in the garden.

meaning: now and then; from time to time.
additional_notes: Means something happens occasionally (not regularly). Often placed at the beginning of the sentence for emphasis, but it can also appear in the middle: „Ich reite hin und wieder gern.“
target_language_example: Hin und wieder gehe ich nach der Arbeit noch spazieren.
native_language_example: Now and then I go for a walk after work.

meaning: '(go/come) there/to it in order to' (expresses purpose).
additional_notes: Used when someone moves to a place/position (hin = “to there / away from the speaker”) and does something with a goal. Very often you’ll see it as a verb + hin + , um … zu + infinitive: „Ich gehe hin, um …“ / „Er setzt sich hin, um …“ / „Sie kniet sich hin, um …“. The purpose part is the „um … zu“ clause; „hin“ emphasizes the movement (go over there, sit down, kneel down) before doing the action.
target_language_example: Ich gehe hin, um dir zu helfen.
native_language_example: I’m going over there to help you.

additional_notes: Used to mean that someone is (or should be) put in prison. Often appears with verbs like „bringen“/„gebracht werden“ (to put in jail / be put in jail) or with „gehören/müssen“ to express that someone deserves to go to jail (e.g., „Er gehört hinter Gitter.“).
target_language_example: Wenn er das nochmal macht, kommt er hinter Gitter.
native_language_example: If he does that again, he'll go to jail.

meaning: 'behind the' (with masculine or neuter nouns in the dative).
additional_notes: Used to say something is located behind something else (a position, not usually movement toward/into). It’s the contraction of "hinter" + "dem" (dative "the" for masculine/neuter). With movement/direction, German often uses "hinter den" (accusative) instead.
target_language_example: Die Toilette ist hinter dem Restaurant.
native_language_example: The restroom is behind the restaurant.

meaning: beyond the horizon; out of sight (often: unknown).
additional_notes: Literally describes something disappearing past the visible line where sky and earth/sea meet (ships, the sun). It’s also used figuratively for things that are not yet visible or understandable—something unknown, far away, or in the future. Uses dative: hinter + dem (when describing a location).
target_language_example: Unsere Sorgen waren nicht weg, nur hinter dem Horizont.
native_language_example: Our worries weren’t gone—just beyond the horizon.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is on the other side of a curtain (often hidden). Common with verbs like (sich) verstecken (to hide) and hervorkommen / hervortreten / hervorkommen (to come out from behind).
target_language_example: Die Kinder haben sich hinter dem Vorhang versteckt.
native_language_example: The children hid behind the curtain.

additional_notes: "hinter" is a two-way preposition. With "der" it’s dative feminine/neuter (e.g., hinter der Hecke = behind the hedge). It can describe location (staying behind something) and can also be used with accusative for direction/movement (e.g., hinter die Hecke = to behind the hedge). Often used for physical position, sometimes for being out of sight (like behind a barn).
target_language_example: Der Hund sitzt hinter der Tür.
native_language_example: The dog is sitting behind the door.

additional_notes: Used to describe a location (not movement): someone/something is positioned behind the door, often to hide or to be out of sight. Grammar tip: because it’s a fixed location, it uses dative (der Tür). For movement to that position, you’d usually say hinter die Tür (accusative).
target_language_example: Ich habe mich hinter der Tür versteckt.
native_language_example: I hid behind the door.

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is located behind the person you’re talking to. "Hinter" (behind) takes the dative here because it describes a position (Where?). With movement (to where?), you’d often use accusative instead: "Geh hinter mich!" (Go behind me!).
target_language_example: Pass auf, ein Fahrrad ist hinter dir!
native_language_example: Watch out, a bicycle is behind you!

meaning: 'behind me' (literally); also 'over/behind me' = in the past, done with.
additional_notes: Most often it means physical position: something/someone is behind you ("Er stand hinter mir."). With verbs like "lassen" it commonly means leaving something behind ("das hinter mir lassen" = put it behind you, move on). With "haben" it often means you’ve been through something and it’s now in the past ("eine Beziehung / einen schlimmen Tag hinter mir haben" = to have just gotten through it). "Hinter jemandem stehen" can mean to support someone ("Meine Eltern standen ... hinter mir" = they stood by me).
target_language_example: Zum Glück habe ich die Prüfung jetzt hinter mir.
native_language_example: Luckily, I’ve got the exam behind me now.

meaning: behind us; (figuratively) over / in the past.
additional_notes: Used for physical location (something is behind us) and also figuratively to say something is finished or already in the past. Common patterns: „liegen hinter uns“ = to be behind us (already done), „Bringen wir es hinter uns“ = let’s get it over with.
target_language_example: Zum Glück liegt das Schlimmste jetzt hinter uns.
native_language_example: Luckily the worst is behind us now.

additional_notes: Past tense (Präteritum) of **die Hand heben** (“to raise your hand”), often used in school/class to show you want to speak or ask a question. **hob** is used with **ich/er/sie** (e.g., *Sie hob die Hand.*). With other subjects: *wir hoben*, *sie/Sie hoben*.
target_language_example: Sie hob die Hand, weil sie etwas sagen wollte.
native_language_example: She raised her hand because she wanted to say something.

additional_notes: Used as an imperative to tell someone to raise something or to get up (often in a rough, impatient, or insulting tone). Common with body parts or people: „Hoch mit den Armen!“ = “Hands up!”, „Hoch mit dir/euch!“ = “Get up!/Up you get!” The object is in the dative after „mit“: „mit dir“, „mit euch“, „mit dem Hintern“.
target_language_example: Na los, hoch mit den Händen!
native_language_example: Come on, hands up!

additional_notes: Used to introduce what you are hoping will happen. The verb is often followed by a clause with "dass" (“that”). Word order: after "dass", the verb in the clause goes to the end (e.g., „Ich hoffe, dass er kommt.“). Common with „nur“: „Ich kann nur hoffen, dass …“ = “I can only hope that …”.
target_language_example: Ich kann nur hoffen, dass Ihnen klar ist, wie viel Glück Sie hatten.
native_language_example: I can only hope that you realize how lucky you were.

meaning: 'hopes that' (introduces a clause about something you want to happen).
additional_notes: Used with the verb "hoffen" (3rd person singular: "er/sie/es hofft") + a "dass"-clause to express hope about an outcome. In the "dass"-clause, the conjugated verb typically goes to the end: "Er hofft, dass er gewinnen kann." Other persons use forms like "ich hoffe, dass...", "wir hoffen, dass...".
target_language_example: Er hofft, dass er gewinnen kann.
native_language_example: He hopes that he can win.

additional_notes: "hoffte" is the simple past of "hoffen" (to hope). It’s commonly followed by a "dass"-clause to express a hope about a situation or outcome. The "dass"-clause usually sends the conjugated verb to the end: "Er hoffte, dass sie gewinnt."
target_language_example: Ich hoffte, dass du heute Zeit hast.
native_language_example: I hoped that you have time today.

additional_notes: “Holen Sie …” is the formal imperative (to one person: “you” = Sie). It can mean to fetch something/someone and bring them (often to the speaker), or to pick someone up (“abholen”). It’s very common with separable prefixes that specify direction: **herholen** (bring here), **rausholen** (take/get out), **abholen** (pick up). The object is usually in the accusative: “Holen Sie **die Bücher** raus.”
target_language_example: Holen Sie bitte den Schlüssel.
native_language_example: Please get the key.

additional_notes: This is the question form of **du holst** (2nd person singular, present) from **holen** = “to get/fetch/bring.” It’s used when you go and retrieve something (keys, a wheelchair, a beer) and often implies bringing it back. With a person, it can mean “to pick up,” often with **abholen**: **Um wie viel Uhr holst du Tom ab?** (“What time are you picking Tom up?”). You’ll often see a dative pronoun for “for me”: **Holst du mir ein Bier?** (“Can you get me a beer?”).
target_language_example: Holst du mir bitte die Jacke aus dem Auto?
native_language_example: Can you please get me the jacket from the car?

additional_notes: Used to state someone’s or something’s age. Often used with „sein“ (to be): „Er ist hundert Jahre alt.“ You can also use it with „werden“ (to turn/reach): „Sie wird hundert Jahre alt (werden).“ Related phrasing: „über hundert Jahre alt“ = over 100 years old.
target_language_example: Mein Urgroßvater ist hundert Jahre alt.
native_language_example: My great-grandfather is 100 years old.

additional_notes: Used with a reflexive pronoun (sich) + für + noun/role: "sich für + Akkusativ". It often suggests the person has an exaggerated opinion of themselves (similar to "He thinks he’s...").
target_language_example: Sie hält sich für etwas Besseres.
native_language_example: She thinks she’s better than everyone else.

meaning: "do you think I am / do you take me for" (…?).
additional_notes: From "jemanden für + Akkusativ halten" = to consider someone (as) something. It’s often used as a confrontational question when you feel insulted or misunderstood: "Hältst du mich für blöd?" = "Do you think I’m stupid?" Also: "Ich halte dich für nett." = "I think you’re nice."
target_language_example: Hältst du mich für einen Idioten?
native_language_example: Do you think I’m an idiot?

meaning: to let someone down; to abandon (someone).
additional_notes: Often used with an object or pronoun: „jemanden hängen lassen“ = to not support someone when they need you. Common fixed phrase: „den Kopf hängen lassen“ = to feel discouraged. It can also be used literally as „to let (something) hang“ depending on context.
target_language_example: Bitte häng mich nicht hängen lassen.
native_language_example: Please don't let me down.

additional_notes: "Hätte" is Konjunktiv II of "haben" (to have). With "es" it often appears in unreal or imagined situations in the past, especially in: (1) wishes/regrets: "Ich wünschte, er hätte es getan." = "I wish he had done it." (2) conditional sentences: "Ohne dich hätte es nicht geklappt." = "Without you, it wouldn’t have worked." (3) comparisons with "als ob/als": "als hätte es nie existiert" = "as if it had never existed." Here, "es" is a pronoun that usually refers to an action/thing already understood from context ("it").
target_language_example: Wenn du mir geholfen hättest, hätte es schneller geklappt.
native_language_example: If you had helped me, it would have worked faster.

meaning: 'almost' / 'nearly (would have …)' (a near miss in the past).
additional_notes: Used with Konjunktiv II past forms to say something nearly happened but didn’t. Common patterns: "Ich hätte fast …" + past participle (e.g., "… verloren", "… geöffnet") or "hätte fast angefangen zu …". Note: German "fast" means "almost", not "fast/quick" in English.
target_language_example: Ich hätte fast meinen Zug verpasst.
native_language_example: I almost missed my train.

additional_notes: Konjunktiv II of „haben“ with „ich“. Used for unreal/hypothetical situations and regrets. Often appears at the start of a sentence with inverted word order to express a wish/regret: „Hätte ich doch …!“ (= “If only I had …!”). Also used with modals like „können/sollen“: „Das hätte ich machen sollen“ (= “I should have done that”). In conditional sentences it often pairs with „wenn“: „Wenn ich … hätte, hätte ich …“ (= “If I had …, I would have …”).
target_language_example: Hätte ich mehr Zeit gehabt, hätte ich dir geholfen.
native_language_example: If I had had more time, I would have helped you.

additional_notes: This is a common Konjunktiv II pattern used to talk about unreal past situations: regret (“Hätte ich das nur vorher gewusst!” = “If only I had known that earlier!”) or to question what you were supposed to do (“Hätte ich das erzählen müssen?” = “Was I supposed to tell that?”). It’s usually followed by an infinitive/participle or understood from context (e.g., wissen/tun/erzählen/erfahren). Often used with question words: “Woher hätte ich das wissen sollen?” = “How was I supposed to know that?”
target_language_example: Hätte ich das früher gewusst, hätte ich anders entschieden.
native_language_example: If I had known that earlier, I would have decided differently.

additional_notes: This is Konjunktiv II with „hätte“ (subjunctive past), used to talk about an unreal/imagined situation in the past—often with a „wenn“-clause. It’s usually completed by a past participle or modal + infinitive: „hätte ich es getan/gemacht“ (I would have done it), „hätte ich es kaufen können“ (I could/would have been able to buy it). Word order can change with the clause (e.g., after „wenn“: „… hätte ich es …“).
target_language_example: Wenn ich mehr Zeit gehabt hätte, hätte ich es gestern erledigt.
native_language_example: If I had had more time, I would have finished it yesterday.

meaning: “If I had …, I would …” (hypothetical / unreal condition).
additional_notes: This is the common German pattern for unreal wishes or imagined situations in the present/future: **Wenn ich + hätte/wäre/könnte …, würde ich + infinitive …**. **hätte** is Konjunktiv II of *haben* (“had”), and **würde ich** is used like “I would” (often followed by a verb in the infinitive at the end of the clause).
target_language_example: Wenn ich ein Auto hätte, würde ich dich abholen.
native_language_example: If I had a car, I would pick you up.

additional_notes: “Hätten Sie” is the Subjunctive II of “haben” with the formal pronoun “Sie.” It’s used for hypothetical or unreal situations, often about the past: “Was hätten Sie getan?” = “What would you have done?” It can also sound more polite/indirect than a simple past or present form, especially in questions and suggestions.
target_language_example: Hätten Sie das anders gemacht?
