additional_notes: Used to promise that you will always do something. Often followed by an infinitive at the end of the sentence (future): "Ich werde immer … bleiben/kommen/helfen." It can also express a firm intention, similar to "I’ll always …" in English.
target_language_example: Ich werde immer für dich da sein.
native_language_example: I will always be there for you.

meaning: “I will … (myself …)” — start of a future tense sentence with a reflexive verb.
additional_notes: Used with **werden + infinitive** to talk about the future: **Ich werde …** = “I will …”. The **mich** shows the verb is **reflexive** (the action refers back to the speaker), e.g. **mich bemühen** (to make an effort), **mich treffen** (to meet up), **mich umbringen** (to kill myself). You normally need an infinitive at the end: **Ich werde mich morgen mit einem Freund treffen.**
target_language_example: Ich werde mich später bei dir melden.
native_language_example: I’ll get back to you later.

additional_notes: Used with **werden + infinitive** to talk about a future action: *Ich werde morgen kommen.* (“I’ll come tomorrow.”) The word **morgen** can also be used with other forms, e.g. the **passive** with *werden + past participle*: *Ich werde morgen bezahlt.* (“I get paid tomorrow.” / “I’ll be paid tomorrow.”) In speech, German often uses the present tense with *morgen* instead of *werden* (e.g. *Ich komme morgen.*).
target_language_example: Ich werde morgen zu Hause bleiben.
native_language_example: I’ll stay at home tomorrow.

meaning: “I will not / I’m not going to …”
additional_notes: Used with **werden** to make a future statement or express intention, negated with **nicht**. It’s usually followed by an **infinitive** at the end (e.g., *ich werde nicht gehen*) or a **past participle** in the passive (e.g., *ich werde nicht zum Narren gehalten* = “I will not be made a fool”).
target_language_example: Ich werde nicht warten, wenn du zu spät kommst.
native_language_example: I won’t wait if you come too late.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what you intend to do in the future: **ich werde** + **infinitive at the end**. **sie** can mean **her** (formal *you* is also *Sie*, but that’s capitalized). Context tells you whether **sie** = her or them. Example pattern: *Ich werde sie morgen anrufen.*
target_language_example: Ich werde sie morgen besuchen.
native_language_example: I will visit her/them tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to express a strong guess or confidence about something. Very common in spoken German: "Ich wette, (dass) …"; the "dass" is often omitted ("Ich wette, du weißt das."). It can also be used more literally with a stake: "Ich wette mein letztes Hemd darauf, dass …" (= I’d bet my last shirt that …).
target_language_example: Ich wette, es regnet gleich.
native_language_example: I bet it’ll rain in a moment.

additional_notes: Means the speaker wants or intends something. It is the present-tense form of wollen with ich. Often followed by an infinitive verb (Ich will gehen. = I want to go.) or by a thing/object (Ich will Kaffee. = I want coffee.). It can sound quite direct; for more polite wording, German often uses ich möchte.
target_language_example: Ich will heute zu Hause bleiben.
native_language_example: I want to stay home today.

additional_notes: Used before another verb (often with an infinitive like sagen/zeigen/berichten) to express what the speaker intends to tell/show/report to someone they address formally. “Ihnen” is the dative form of formal “Sie” (= to you). Note: “ich will …” can sound quite strong; in polite situations you often hear “ich möchte Ihnen …” (“I’d like to …”).
target_language_example: Ich will Ihnen kurz erklären, wie das funktioniert.
native_language_example: I want to briefly explain to you how this works.

meaning: "I don't want to (you)…" / "I don't mean to…" (formal "you").
additional_notes: Used with a verb after it (e.g., verletzen, stören, belästigen) to say you don’t want to do something to someone. With "Sie" it’s polite/formal and is often used to soften what you’re about to say ("I don’t want to bother you, but…"). Word order: "Ich will Sie nicht + VERB" (infinitive at the end).
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, ich will Sie nicht unterbrechen, aber ich habe eine Frage.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t want to interrupt you, but I have a question.

additional_notes: Used to add that you want the same thing as someone else, or you want something in addition. Often followed by a noun (Ich will auch ein Geschenk.) or an action with an infinitive/verb of motion (Ich will auch mit! / Ich will auch mitgehen!). With "gar nicht / überhaupt nicht" it can mean "I also don’t want to…" or "I don’t want to… at all" while still linking to the previous context.
target_language_example: Du gehst ins Kino? Ich will auch mit!
native_language_example: You’re going to the movies? I want to come too!

meaning: "I don't want that" / "I don't want to."
additional_notes: Used to refuse or express strong unwillingness. Often followed by an infinitive to say what you don’t want to do/hear/see: „Ich will das nicht hören/sehen/wiederholen.“ In conversation it can sound firm or even rude, depending on tone; for a softer version you can say „Ich möchte das nicht“ (more polite).
target_language_example: Tut mir leid, ich will das nicht machen.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t want to do that.

additional_notes: "Ich" = I, "will" (from "wollen") = want, and "dich" = you (informal singular, accusative). Very often it’s followed by another verb to mean “I want you to …” (e.g., "Ich will dich hier nie wieder sehen" = “I never want to see you here again”; "Ich will dich hier raus haben" = “I want you out of here”). Note: German "will" means "want"—not the English future "will".
target_language_example: Ich will dich heute Abend sehen.
native_language_example: I want to see you tonight.

additional_notes: Used as the start of a sentence to say you don’t want to do something that affects the other person, usually followed by an infinitive: “Ich will dich nicht + Infinitiv” (e.g., nerven/stören/verlieren/sehen). Note: German “will” means “want,” not the English future “will.”
target_language_example: Ich will dich nicht enttäuschen.
native_language_example: I don’t want to disappoint you.

meaning: "I want to (do something) for you / to you."
additional_notes: This is the start of a sentence: **ich** = I, **will** = want, **dir** = to you (dative). It’s usually followed by an infinitive or a verb phrase, e.g. *ich will dir helfen* (I want to help you), *ich will dir etwas sagen* (I want to tell you something). Note the difference: **ich will dich** = I want you (accusative), but **ich will dir ...** introduces what you want to do *to/for* someone.
target_language_example: Ich will dir etwas zeigen.
native_language_example: I want to show you something.

additional_notes: Used to stress that your wish/goal is simple and nothing more. Often followed by an infinitive phrase ("… geliebt werden", "… wissen") or a destination ("… nach Hause"). Note: "ich will" usually means "I want" (not the English future "I will").
target_language_example: Ich will einfach nur schlafen.
native_language_example: I just want to sleep.

additional_notes: Used to express a strong desire or intention. “Es” can refer to a specific thing (“I want it back”) or act as a placeholder for an action/idea when the details follow or are understood (e.g., “Ich will es wissen” = “I want to know (it)”). Often followed by an infinitive or a phrase that explains what “es” refers to.
target_language_example: Ich will es heute noch erledigen.
native_language_example: I want to get it done today.

additional_notes: "Ich will" is used to express a wish/plan/intent. "Euch" refers to more than one person (you all). It can be the direct object (accusative) or indirect object (dative), depending on the verb: e.g., "Ich will euch besuchen" (accusative: I want to visit you all) vs. "Ich will euch eine Frage stellen" (dative: I want to ask you all a question). Note: German "will" often means "want" and can be confused with English "will" (future).
target_language_example: Ich will euch helfen, wenn ihr Zeit habt.
native_language_example: I want to help you all, if you have time.

additional_notes: Used to say what you want to do in this place/situation. It’s typically followed by an infinitive or another phrase: Ich will hier bleiben. / Ich will hier weg. Note: German "will" (from "wollen") means "want"—not the English future "will".
target_language_example: Ich will hier nicht warten.
native_language_example: I don't want to wait here.

meaning: "I want him" / "I want to (do something with) him".
additional_notes: "Ich" = I, "will" = want (from "wollen"), "ihn" = him (accusative). Usually followed by an infinitive verb to say what you want to do with him: "Ich will ihn sehen" (I want to see him), "Ich will ihn wiederfinden" (I want to find him again). Word order: "Ich will ihn" + infinitive at the end.
target_language_example: Ich will ihn heute noch sehen.
native_language_example: I want to see him today.

meaning: "I don’t want any / I don’t want (a/an)" (with a feminine or plural noun).
additional_notes: Used to refuse or say you don’t want something. "keine" is the negative form of "eine" and is used with feminine singular nouns (keine Spritze) and plural nouns (keine Übungen). Often the noun comes right after: "Ich will keine Hilfe." You can also leave the noun unstated if it’s clear from context.
target_language_example: Nein danke, ich will keine Milch.
native_language_example: No thanks, I don’t want any milk.

meaning: "I want to …" (before a reflexive verb: "I want to [do something]" / "I want to [myself]").
additional_notes: Used when the verb is reflexive (with "mich"), e.g. "sich ausruhen" (to rest), "sich beschweren" (to complain), "sich entschuldigen" (to apologize), "sich bemühen" (to make an effort), "sich an etw. gewöhnen" (to get used to something). Note: German "will" usually means "want" (not future tense like English "will").
target_language_example: Ich will mich heute früh ins Bett legen.
native_language_example: I want to go to bed early today.

meaning: “I want to … with …” / “I want to talk to …”.
additional_notes: Used when you want to do something together with someone (mit + dative): Ich will mit dir/euch/ihm/ihr … . With sprechen, German commonly uses mit where English often says “to”: Ich will mit Ihrem Vorgesetzten sprechen. Also appears in the pattern mit + etwas + aufhören = “to stop/quit something” (e.g., mit der Schule aufhören).
target_language_example: Ich will mit dir darüber sprechen.
native_language_example: I want to talk to you about it.

additional_notes: Used to refuse or say you don’t want to do something. Often followed by an infinitive (verb in the basic form), e.g. „Ich will nicht kommen.“ You can also say it alone as a strong refusal (“I don’t want to”).
target_language_example: Ich will nicht ins Kino gehen.
native_language_example: I don't want to go to the movies.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone you don’t want them to do something. It’s followed by a dependent clause with **dass** + a verb at the end (e.g., „… dass du **rauchst**.“). Often expresses a request or rule; it can sound firm/strict depending on tone.
target_language_example: Ich will nicht, dass du so spät nach Hause kommst.
native_language_example: I don’t want you to come home so late.

meaning: "I don't want to anymore" / "I don't want to do this any longer."
additional_notes: Used to say you want to stop doing something or that you’ve had enough. Often followed by an infinitive (e.g., "Ich will nicht mehr + spielen/denken/leben") or used with "mit" ("Ich will nicht mehr mit dir ..."). "nicht mehr" means "no longer / not anymore" and can also be used with other subjects (e.g., "Er will nicht mehr"). Can sound very strong depending on context (e.g., "Ich will nicht mehr leben").
target_language_example: Ich will nicht mehr warten; lass uns jetzt gehen.
native_language_example: I don't want to wait anymore; let's go now.

additional_notes: Used to soften what you’re saying (“just”), to emphasize that your request/goal is limited, or to reassure someone you don’t want more than that. Often followed by an infinitive (Ich will nur sagen/sehen/wissen …) or a noun phrase (Ich will nur eine …). Word order: Ich will nur + VERB (infinitive) … / Ich will nur + NOUN … .
target_language_example: Ich will nur kurz fragen, ob du morgen Zeit hast.
native_language_example: I just want to quickly ask if you have time tomorrow.

meaning: “I want to know how …” / “I want to find out how …”
additional_notes: Used to introduce an indirect question starting with **wie** (“how”). It’s often followed by a verb at the end of the clause (e.g., *… wie du das gemacht hast*). In polite situations you can use **Ich möchte wissen, wie …** (softer/more polite). Note: **will** in German usually means “want,” not English “will” (future).
target_language_example: Ich will wissen, wie ich zum Bahnhof komme.
native_language_example: I want to know how to get to the train station.

additional_notes: From the verb "wollen." It expresses a strong wish, desire, or intention. With a noun, it means "I want ..." ("Ich will mehr Geld"). With another verb, it means "I want to ..." ("Ich will gehen"). It can sound stronger or more demanding than English "I want," so for polite requests German often uses "ich möchte" instead.
target_language_example: Ich will heute zu Hause bleiben.
native_language_example: I want to stay home today.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone (addressed as Sie) what you want them to do. Grammatically it’s „Ich will, dass …“ + a clause with the verb at the end (e.g., „… dass Sie warten.“). Often sounds strong/commanding; for polite requests, learners will also often use „Ich möchte, dass Sie …“ or „Könnten Sie …?“
target_language_example: Ich will, dass Sie mir zuhören.
native_language_example: I want you to listen to me.

additional_notes: Used to express what you want someone else to do. It’s followed by a full clause with the verb at the end (subordinate clause): Ich will, dass du hierbleibst. In conversation it can sound like a strong demand; for a more polite request you can use: Ich möchte, dass du … / Ich hätte gern, dass du …
target_language_example: Ich will, dass du mir hilfst.
native_language_example: I want you to help me.

additional_notes: Used to state a strong desire or demand. "dass" introduces a subordinate clause; the verb in that clause goes to the end (e.g., "… dass ihr wartet"). "ihr" is the informal plural "you" (you all), used with friends, family, children, or a group you address with "ihr".
target_language_example: Ich will, dass ihr mir zuhört.
native_language_example: I want you all to listen to me.

additional_notes: Used to express a strong wish or demand directed at someone you address as **Sie** (formal “you”). It’s followed by a **dass**-clause (often written **daß** in older spelling): **Ich will, daß Sie …**. Word order: the conjugated verb goes to the end of the clause (**… daß Sie ehrlich sind**). Note: **will** here means “want,” not the English future auxiliary “will.”
target_language_example: Ich will, daß Sie ehrlich zu mir sind.
native_language_example: I want you to be honest with me.

additional_notes: Used to state what you want someone else to do; it introduces a full subordinate clause with the verb at the end (e.g., „… daß du ihm hilfst“). It can sound like a strong demand; for a more polite request, use „Ich möchte, dass du …“ or „Kannst du …?“. Note on spelling: modern German typically uses „dass“; „daß“ is the older spelling, kept here to match the term exactly.
target_language_example: Ich will, daß du ihm hilfst.
native_language_example: I want you to help him.

meaning: “I want you (all) to …” (addressing more than one person).
additional_notes: Used to express a strong wish or demand, followed by a subordinate clause. The spelling **„daß“** is the older/pre-1996 form; modern spelling is **„dass“**. Word order: after **daß** the verb goes to the end of the clause (e.g., **… daß ihr bis Montag bleibt / daß ihr ehrlich zu mir seid**). This can sound quite direct/commanding; **„Ich möchte, daß ihr …“** is softer.
target_language_example: Ich will, daß ihr bis nächsten Montag in Boston bleibt.
native_language_example: I want you to stay in Boston until next Monday.

meaning: "I don't want to anymore" / "I don't want any more."
additional_notes: Used to express that you want to stop doing something or you’re fed up and don’t want to continue. Often said emotionally (frustrated, exhausted). Commonly followed by an infinitive with "(zu)": "Ich will nicht mehr warten."
target_language_example: Ich will nicht mehr warten.
native_language_example: I don't want to wait anymore.

additional_notes: Used to downplay a request or emphasize that you want *only* one thing (and nothing more). It’s often followed by a noun/pronoun ("…nur dich") or by a clause: "Ich will nur, dass …" (= “I just want you to … / I just want that …”). Note: German "wollen" means “to want,” not the English future "will."
target_language_example: Ich will nur kurz sagen, dass ich später komme.
native_language_example: I just want to quickly say that I’ll come later.

additional_notes: From the verb "wohnen" (to live somewhere / reside). Very commonly used with a place: "Ich wohne in Berlin" (in + city/country), "Ich wohne allein" (alone), "Ich wohne gegenüber" (opposite/across the street), "Ich wohne über einem Geschäft" (above a shop). Often contrasts with "leben" when you mean the general fact of being alive or “life” in a broader sense.
target_language_example: Ich wohne seit einem Jahr in dieser Stadt.
native_language_example: I’ve been living in this city for a year.

additional_notes: Use this to say where you live. It’s followed by a location (country/city/neighborhood). With countries, the preposition can change depending on the article: usually **in** (e.g., *in Deutschland*), but **in der** with feminine countries/regions (e.g., *in der Schweiz*) and **in den** with plural names (e.g., *in den USA*). For cities, it’s usually just **in** (e.g., *in Berlin*).
target_language_example: Ich wohne in Berlin, aber ich arbeite in Potsdam.
native_language_example: I live in Berlin, but I work in Potsdam.

additional_notes: First-person singular past form of wollen. It expresses a past wish, intention, or plan. It can be followed by a noun (Ich wollte das Haus) or by an infinitive verb without zu (Ich wollte anfangen).
target_language_example: Ich wollte dich anrufen.
native_language_example: I wanted to call you.

meaning: "I wanted to" / "I was hoping to" (polite, to you).
additional_notes: Used to politely introduce what you want to say to someone you address as Sie/Ihnen (formal "you"). Often sounds softer/more courteous than a direct present tense: Ich wollte Ihnen danken/mitteilen/gratulieren… It can refer to a plan or intention, and in conversation it’s frequently used as a polite lead-in, not necessarily past time.
target_language_example: Ich wollte Ihnen kurz Bescheid geben, dass ich mich verspäte.
native_language_example: I just wanted to let you know that I’m running late.

meaning: “I wanted to (tell you / do something for you).”
additional_notes: Used to introduce something you intended to say or do for someone (“dir” = “to you,” dative). Very common as a polite, soft opener: Ich wollte dir danken / schreiben / sagen … Often implies you’re bringing something up gently (thanks, apology, explanation) or that you intended to do it earlier.
target_language_example: Ich wollte dir noch sagen, dass ich morgen keine Zeit habe.
native_language_example: I wanted to tell you that I don’t have time tomorrow.

meaning: "I wanted to (you all)" / often: "I just wanted to..." (said to a group).
additional_notes: "Euch" is the accusative/dative form of "ihr" and refers to multiple people ("you" plural). "Wollte" is the past form of "wollen"; in this pattern ("Ich wollte euch ...") it’s very commonly used to sound polite/less direct, similar to English "I just wanted to tell you..." or "I was going to...".
target_language_example: Ich wollte euch kurz fragen, ob ihr morgen Zeit habt.
native_language_example: I just wanted to ask you quickly if you have time tomorrow.

meaning: “I was just about to …” / “I was just going to …”.
additional_notes: Used to say you were on the point of doing something (often right before something else happened or someone interrupted). It uses the past form of **wollen** (*wollte*) plus **gerade** (“just/right now”) to express “just about to,” not a literal “I wanted just now.” Common with an event in the past: **Ich wollte gerade gehen, als …** (“I was just about to leave when …”).
target_language_example: Ich wollte gerade ins Bett gehen, aber dann kam noch eine E-Mail.
native_language_example: I was just about to go to bed, but then another email came in.

meaning: “I wanted to … (to him)” / “I meant to … (to him)” (talking about a male person).
additional_notes: "Wollte" is the past tense of "wollen" (to want/to intend). "Ihn" means "him" and is accusative (direct object). This phrase is usually followed by an infinitive at the end of the clause: "Ich wollte ihn umarmen" (I wanted to hug him). In context it often explains your intention (sometimes as an excuse): "Ich wollte ihn doch nur erschrecken" (I only wanted to scare him).
target_language_example: Tut mir leid — ich wollte ihn nicht verletzen.
native_language_example: Sorry — I didn’t mean to hurt him.

meaning: “I wanted to …” (often used to politely introduce what you’re about to say, with a reflexive verb).
additional_notes: Common opener to soften a message or make it sound polite/less direct. It’s typically followed by a reflexive verb in the infinitive, e.g. mich bedanken (thank you), mich entschuldigen (apologize), mich vergewissern (make sure), mich erinnern (remember), mich umsetzen (move seats). Often used with "nur" (“just”): "Ich wollte mich nur vergewissern, ob …".
target_language_example: Ich wollte mich nur entschuldigen.
native_language_example: I just wanted to apologize.

additional_notes: Used to say you didn’t want something to happen, or didn’t want someone to do/think something. It introduces a dependent clause with **dass** (“that”), and the **verb goes to the end** of the dass-clause: *Ich wollte nicht, dass du dir Sorgen machst.* In English, this is often translated with an infinitive: “I didn’t want you to worry.”
target_language_example: Ich wollte nicht, dass du allein nach Hause gehst.
native_language_example: I didn’t want you to go home alone.

meaning: “I just wanted to …” / “I only meant to …” (often to soften what you’re saying).
additional_notes: Literally past tense (“I wanted”), but very commonly used to sound polite, less direct, or to downplay a request/visit/question: ich wollte nur fragen/schauen/sicher sein. Often used when explaining your intention (“I didn’t mean anything bad, I just wanted…”). You’ll also see it with mal: ich wollte nur mal … (“I just wanted to quickly…”).
target_language_example: Ich wollte nur fragen, ob alles in Ordnung ist.
native_language_example: I just wanted to ask if everything is okay.

meaning: "I’ve always wanted to" / "I’ve long wanted to."
additional_notes: Used to say you’ve had a wish or goal for a long time (often since childhood). Typically followed by an infinitive (e.g., haben/sein/wissen/leben) or a noun phrase (e.g., einen Hund). In speech, it often sets up something personal: Ich wollte schon immer + (… machen/… haben/… sein/… wissen).
target_language_example: Ich wollte schon immer nach Japan reisen.
native_language_example: I’ve always wanted to travel to Japan.

additional_notes: “wollte” is the simple past of *wollen* (“to want”). It’s commonly followed by an infinitive at the end of the clause: *Ich wollte sie küssen.* = “I wanted to kiss her.” **sie** can mean “her” or “them” (and sometimes formal “you”), so you use context to know which. In some contexts, *ich wollte …* can also imply an intention/plan (“I was going to …”).
target_language_example: Ich wollte sie anrufen, aber ich hatte keine Zeit.
native_language_example: I wanted to call her/them, but I didn’t have time.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what you wanted in the past. In conversation, *Ich wollte …* is also often used to sound a bit softer/more polite when making a request or bringing something up (similar to “I wanted to…” / “I was hoping to…”).
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, ich wollte nur kurz fragen, ob das noch verfügbar ist.
native_language_example: Sorry, I just wanted to ask if that’s still available.

meaning: "I wanted (that)…" / "I wanted … to …" (introduces what you wanted to happen).
additional_notes: Used to say what you wanted someone to do or what you wanted to happen. Very common with a subclause starting with dass + verb at the end (Ich wollte, dass du kommst.) In everyday English, it’s often translated as "I wanted you to…" or "I wanted him/her to…".
target_language_example: Ich wollte, dass du heute mitkommst.
native_language_example: I wanted you to come along today.

additional_notes: Past tense of „ich werde“ (from „werden“). Often used in the passive voice with a past participle: „Ich wurde gekündigt/ausgeraubt/geschlagen“ = “I was fired/robbed/beaten.” It can also mean “I became” with an adjective/noun: „Ich wurde sehr wütend“ = “I got very angry.”
target_language_example: Ich wurde gestern im Zug bestohlen.
native_language_example: I was robbed on the train yesterday.

additional_notes: "Ich wurde …" is the past passive of "werden" and is commonly used with "geboren" to say where you were born: "Ich wurde in [place] geboren." Use "in" with cities/countries/buildings; with countries, you’ll often see "in" (e.g., "in Brasilien").
target_language_example: Ich wurde in Berlin geboren.
native_language_example: I was born in Berlin.

additional_notes: "Ich wusste" is the simple past form of "ich weiß" (to know). It’s used for knowledge you had at a point in the past, often followed by a clause with "dass"/a comma: "Ich wusste, (dass) ...".
target_language_example: Ich wusste nicht, dass du heute kommst.
native_language_example: I didn’t know you were coming today.

additional_notes: Uses the simple past of **wissen** (*ich wusste*) to introduce a **dass**-clause (a “that”-clause). The verb in the **dass**-clause goes to the end: *Ich wusste, dass er kommt.* In stories or reported thoughts, you may also see **Konjunktiv II** to express “would” in the past: *Ich wusste, dass du kommen würdest.*
target_language_example: Ich wusste, dass du recht hattest.
native_language_example: I knew that you were right.

additional_notes: Used to say you already knew something about the other person. "wusste" is the simple past of "wissen" (to know). It introduces a "dass" (that) clause, where the verb usually goes to the end: "Ich wusste, dass du Recht hast." In conversation, it can sound confident or slightly reproachful depending on tone.
target_language_example: Ich wusste, dass du heute keine Zeit hast.
native_language_example: I knew that you didn’t have time today.

additional_notes: A common sentence starter used to introduce something you already knew or realized in the past. It’s followed by a subordinate clause (introduced by „dass“), where the verb goes to the end of that clause: „Ich wusste, dass ich es schaffen würde.“
target_language_example: Ich wusste, dass ich heute zu spät kommen würde.
native_language_example: I knew that I would be late today.

additional_notes: Used to say you didn’t have certain information before. The verb is in the past (wusste = knew), and it introduces a subordinate clause with „dass“ (“that”). In the „dass“-clause, the verb usually goes to the end: „Ich wusste nicht, dass du schon zu Hause bist.“ Often used as an apology or to show surprise: „Tut mir leid, ich wusste nicht, dass …“.
target_language_example: Ich wusste nicht, dass der Laden heute geschlossen ist.
native_language_example: I didn’t know that the shop is closed today.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a subordinate clause with **dass/daß** (“that”). **wußte** is the older spelling of **wusste**, and **daß** is the older spelling of **dass**. It’s the simple past of **wissen** (“to know”) and is common in storytelling and written German; in conversation you also often hear **Ich habe gewusst, dass …**.
target_language_example: Ich wußte, daß du Recht hattest.
native_language_example: I knew that you were right.

additional_notes: Used to offer good wishes to one person (Sie) or a group addressed formally. Typically followed by a noun phrase: alles Gute (all the best), ein schönes Wochenende (a nice weekend), frohe Weihnachten (Merry Christmas), viel Glück (good luck). With a group, you may hear: „Ich wünsche Ihnen allen …“ (“I wish you all …”).
target_language_example: Ich wünsche Ihnen einen schönen Tag.
native_language_example: I wish you a nice day.

additional_notes: Used to express good wishes to someone, often followed by what you’re wishing them (e.g., "alles Gute", "viel Glück", "einen schönen Tag", "eine schöne Zeit"). Common in cards, greetings, and polite conversation. Grammar note: "dir" is informal singular (“to you”); for formal use say "Ich wünsche Ihnen …", and for plural "Ich wünsche euch/Ihnen …".
target_language_example: Ich wünsche dir viel Erfolg bei der Prüfung.
native_language_example: I wish you lots of success on the exam.

additional_notes: Used to express good wishes to more than one person. "euch" is the informal/plural "you" (to friends, family, a group). Common with nouns like "viel Glück" (good luck), "Erfolg" (success), or with "einen schönen …" (a nice …): "Abend" (evening), "Tag" (day), "Urlaub" (vacation).
target_language_example: Ich wünsche euch eine gute Reise!
native_language_example: I wish you a good trip!

additional_notes: Used to express a desire or hope. Often followed by a noun/pronoun (Ich wünsche mir was.) or by a clause with „dass“ (Ich wünsche mir, dass …). You can also use it with the subjunctive to express an unreal wish: „Ich wünsche mir, ich wäre …“ (“I wish I were …”).
target_language_example: Ich wünsche mir, dass wir uns bald wiedersehen.
native_language_example: I hope/wish that we see each other again soon.

additional_notes: Used to express a wish about something unreal, unlikely, or contrary to fact. It is typically followed by Konjunktiv II forms (e.g., Sie wären…, Sie könnten…, Sie hätten…). Often implies regret about the past (Sie hätten… = “I wish you had…”) or a wish about the present (Sie wären/könnten… = “I wish you were/could…”). Formal/polite because of “Sie”.
target_language_example: Ich wünschte, Sie könnten heute länger bleiben.
native_language_example: I wish you could stay longer today.

meaning: "I wish you had …" (regret about the past).
additional_notes: Used to express a wish/regret about something that did not happen in the past. It’s followed by a verb in the past participle (Perfekt) with the Konjunktiv II form of the auxiliary: du hättest/du wärst (e.g., „Ich wünschte, du hättest mich angerufen.“ / „Ich wünschte, du wärst gekommen.“).
target_language_example: Ich wünschte, du hättest mir früher Bescheid gesagt.
native_language_example: I wish you had told me earlier.

meaning: “I wish there were …” (expressing an unreal/imagined situation).
additional_notes: Used to express a wish about something that is not true right now. It’s the subjunctive (Konjunktiv II): ich wünschte (“I wish”) + es gäbe (from geben → es gibt / “there is/are”). You normally follow it with a noun phrase: „… es gäbe mehr Zeit / eine bessere Lösung / mehr Leute wie dich“.
target_language_example: Ich wünschte, es gäbe heute keine Hausaufgaben.
native_language_example: I wish there were no homework today.

meaning: "I wish it were…" (expressing an unreal wish).
additional_notes: Used to say you wish something were different from reality. It’s followed by the subjunctive form of "sein" (wäre). Common with adjectives or situations: "…anders", "…wahr", "…so wie früher". Often implies regret or longing.
target_language_example: Ich wünschte, es wäre schon Freitag.
native_language_example: I wish it were already Friday.

meaning: "I wish I had ..." (regret about the past).
additional_notes: Used to express regret or a missed opportunity about something in the past. It’s followed by the subjunctive II form of "haben" ("hätte") plus a past participle (Perfekt), e.g. "Ich wünschte, ich hätte gelernt/gehört/gekauft." Often implies “but I didn’t.”
target_language_example: Ich wünschte, ich hätte früher Bescheid gesagt.
native_language_example: I wish I had told you earlier.

meaning: “I wish I had …” (wishing for something you don’t have).
additional_notes: Used to express an unreal/imaginary wish about the present: you want something to be true now, but it isn’t. Grammar pattern: „Ich wünschte, ich hätte + noun …“ (subjunctive II of „haben“). You can add a purpose with „…, um … zu …“ (e.g., „genug Geld, um … zu kaufen“).
target_language_example: Ich wünschte, ich hätte mehr Zeit.
native_language_example: I wish I had more time.

additional_notes: Used to express a wish about an unreal/possible situation—usually something you would like to do but can’t right now. Often followed by an infinitive at the end of the clause (e.g., „helfen“, „mitkommen“, „aufhören“). The verb form „wünschte“ is the subjunctive (Konjunktiv II) of „wünschen“ to show it’s not reality.
target_language_example: Ich wünschte, ich könnte länger bleiben, aber ich muss arbeiten.
native_language_example: I wish I could stay longer, but I have to work.

meaning: "I wish I were …" (expressing an unreal wish).
additional_notes: Used to express a wish about something that is not true (now or in general). It’s the subjunctive form: „ich wäre“ = “I were / I would be”. Often followed by a comparison („… wie …“ = “like/as …”) or an adjective/noun phrase. For past regrets, German often uses „… gewesen“ (e.g., „Ich wünschte, ich wäre früher gegangen.“ = “I wish I had left earlier.”).
target_language_example: Ich wünschte, ich wäre zu Hause.
native_language_example: I wish I were at home.

additional_notes: Used to express a wish/regret about something that isn’t possible or isn’t happening (often a polite or realistic limitation). It’s followed by an infinitive at the end of the clause (e.g., „… kommen“, „… helfen“). Grammar note: „wünschte“ + „könnten“ is Konjunktiv II (subjunctive) to talk about hypothetical/desired situations.
target_language_example: Ich wünschte, wir könnten dir heute helfen.
native_language_example: I wish we could help you today.

additional_notes: Used to talk about hypothetical/imagined situations, wishes, or to sound more polite. Very often used as the Konjunktiv II form of "werden" in the pattern "ich würde + infinitive" (e.g., "ich würde helfen" = "I would help"). Can also be used on its own when the main verb is understood from context.
target_language_example: Ich würde gern einen Kaffee trinken.
native_language_example: I would like to drink a coffee.

meaning: “I would … you” (I’d … you) — used for hypothetical or polite/soft statements.
additional_notes: This is the start of a sentence with the conditional/subjunctive II form “würde”. It usually needs an infinitive later: “Ich würde dich gern sehen” = “I’d like to see you.” It can express (1) a hypothetical situation (“I thought I would find you there”), (2) a wish (“I’d really like to see you”), or (3) something you would/wouldn’t do (“I would never kiss/hurt you”).
target_language_example: Ich würde dich sofort anrufen, wenn ich Zeit hätte.
native_language_example: I would call you right away if I had time.

additional_notes: Used with Konjunktiv II (würde + infinitive) to talk about what you would do in a situation, or to sound more cautious/polite. The "es" often refers to a previously mentioned action or idea (like “do it”, “say it”, “prefer it”). Typical patterns: „Ich würde es (nicht) tun/sagen.“ / „Ich würde es vorziehen, …“ / „Ich würde es gern …“
target_language_example: Ich würde es nicht machen, wenn ich du wäre.
native_language_example: I wouldn’t do it if I were you.

additional_notes: Used to express a polite wish or request, often followed by an infinitive verb: „Ich würde gern + Verb …“ (e.g., „Ich würde gern zahlen.“). It’s a common, soft-sounding alternative to „Ich möchte …“.
target_language_example: Ich würde gern einen Kaffee bestellen.
native_language_example: I would like to order a coffee.

meaning: "I would like (to)" (polite way to say what you want).
additional_notes: Used to express a wish or preference in a friendly, polite way. Often followed by an infinitive verb (Ich würde gerne schlafen.) or by a noun with a verb like haben/möchten implied (Ich würde gerne einen Kaffee. = I’d like a coffee.). In formal situations you can add "mit Ihnen" (with you) or make it a question: "Würden Sie gerne …?"
target_language_example: Ich würde gerne einen Termin vereinbaren.
native_language_example: I would like to make an appointment.

additional_notes: Used to express a preference in a polite, hypothetical way (Konjunktiv II of "werden"). Often followed by an infinitive: "Ich würde lieber bleiben." You can compare two options with "als": "Ich würde lieber A (machen) als B (machen)" (= rather A than B). For negation, use "lieber nicht": "Ich würde lieber nicht ...".
target_language_example: Ich würde lieber heute zu Hause bleiben, als spät auszugehen.
native_language_example: I’d rather stay at home today than go out late.

meaning: "I would" (used with a reflexive verb: "I would ... myself").
additional_notes: This is the Konjunktiv II form of "ich" + "werden" ("würde") plus the reflexive pronoun "mich". It’s used before a reflexive verb to talk about a hypothetical situation or to sound more polite/less direct: e.g. "Ich würde mich gern ..." = "I’d like to ...". The exact English translation depends on the reflexive verb that follows (e.g. "mich unterhalten" = have a conversation, "mich verlaufen" = get lost, "mich begeben" = go/put myself into).
target_language_example: Ich würde mich gern entschuldigen.
native_language_example: I would like to apologize.

meaning: “I’d say …” (a polite/soft way to give your opinion).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a guess, assessment, or recommendation without sounding too direct. Often followed by a comma and then your statement ("Ich würde sagen, …"). It can also imply “in my view / if you ask me.”
target_language_example: Ich würde sagen, wir treffen uns um sieben.
native_language_example: I’d say we’ll meet at seven.

meaning: “I’d like to know” / “I’d like to find out.”
additional_notes: Polite way to ask for information. Uses Konjunktiv II of *wissen* (“wüsste”) to sound softer/more indirect than *ich möchte wissen* or *ich will wissen*. Often followed by an indirect question with *ob/was/wie/wann/wer*, etc.
target_language_example: Ich wüsste gern, ob der Zug heute pünktlich ist.
native_language_example: I’d like to know if the train is on time today.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask for an explanation or reason. Literally “I would know gladly why…”. It’s more formal/soft than "Warum...?" and is often followed by a clause (subject + verb), e.g., "..., warum er so spät ist."
target_language_example: Ich wüsste gerne, warum du heute nicht kommen kannst.
native_language_example: I’d like to know why you can’t come today.

additional_notes: Used when speaking politely to one person (or a group) with Sie. Ihnen is the dative form meaning “to you.” Often followed by what you’re showing (usually in the accusative): Ich zeige Ihnen den Weg / den Campus / ein Foto.
target_language_example: Warten Sie kurz, ich zeige Ihnen das Zimmer.
native_language_example: Wait a moment, I’ll show you the room.

additional_notes: Used when you’re about to demonstrate something or explain how to do something. Often followed by a comma + a clause (e.g., “wie …” = “how …”, “was …” = “what …”), or by a noun/pronoun (“welche” = “which ones”). You can add a time word like “jetzt” (now) or “gleich” (in a moment).
target_language_example: Warte kurz, ich zeige dir, wie das geht.
native_language_example: Wait a second, I’ll show you how it works.

meaning: "I pull / I draw" (forms many common verbs like "put on", "take off", "move house", "tease").
additional_notes: "Ich ziehe" is the 1st-person singular of *ziehen* (present tense). On its own it most literally means "I pull" or "I draw" (e.g., draw a card), but in everyday German it very often appears with prefixes/particles that change the meaning: **anziehen** = put on clothes, **ausziehen** = take off clothes / move out, **umziehen** = move house / change clothes, **durchziehen** = carry through/finish, **(jemanden) aufziehen** = tease someone. Watch for separable parts that may appear later in the sentence (e.g., *Ich ziehe ... an/aus/um/durch*).
target_language_example: Ich ziehe nächsten Monat um.
native_language_example: I’m moving house next month.

meaning: “I’m getting dressed / changing (clothes)” (with an added particle like an/um) or “I’m withdrawing” (with zurück).
additional_notes:
This is the reflexive verb "sich ziehen" (“to pull oneself”), but in everyday German it’s mostly used with separable particles: 
- sich anziehen → to get dressed: "Ich ziehe mich an." 
- sich umziehen → to change clothes: "Ich ziehe mich um." 
- sich zurückziehen → to withdraw / retreat: "Ich ziehe mich zurück." 
Without the particle (an/um/zurück), "Ich ziehe mich" sounds incomplete in these common meanings.
target_language_example: Warte kurz, ich ziehe mich schnell um.
native_language_example: Wait a second, I’m going to change quickly.

additional_notes: Used when you mean being honest with a male person (ihm = “to him” in the dative case). You can also change the person: ihr die Wahrheit sagen (tell her the truth), ihnen die Wahrheit sagen (tell them the truth). Common with modal verbs like sollen: Du solltest ihm die Wahrheit sagen. (“You should tell him the truth.”).
target_language_example: Ich werde ihm die Wahrheit sagen, auch wenn es schwer ist.
native_language_example: I will tell him the truth, even if it’s hard.

meaning: "(to) him a…" (dative: marking the male recipient of something).
additional_notes: Used when a man/boy is the indirect object (recipient) of a feminine noun: jemandem (Dativ) + eine (Akkusativ). Common with verbs like schenken (to give as a present) and schicken (to send). In English you usually say “give him a …” (without “to”), but in German the dative pronoun shows the “to him” idea.
target_language_example: Ich gebe ihm eine Nachricht.
native_language_example: I’m sending him a message.

additional_notes: Past participle phrase from "jemandem helfen" (to help someone), which takes the dative; "ihm" is the dative pronoun meaning "to him". Commonly used in the Perfekt tense with "haben" + "geholfen" (e.g., "Ich habe ihm geholfen"). Word order changes in questions: "Hast du ihm geholfen?"
target_language_example: Gestern habe ich ihm geholfen.
native_language_example: Yesterday I helped him.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like **sagen** (“to say/tell”) and the dative pronoun **ihm** (“to him”). You’ll often see it in the **Perfekt/Plusquamperfekt**: **(ich) habe ihm gesagt …** / **(ich) hatte ihm gesagt …**. It can be followed by a clause (**…, dass …**) or a question word (**was/wie/warum …**).
target_language_example: Ich habe ihm gesagt, dass wir später kommen.
native_language_example: I told him that we’re coming later.

additional_notes: "Ihm" is the dative form of "er" (he) and means "to him". Many verbs (including "helfen") take the dative, so you say "jemandem helfen" (to help someone).
target_language_example: Du kannst ihm helfen.
native_language_example: You can help him.

additional_notes: "ihm" is the dative form of "er" (= him), used because helfen takes the dative: "jemandem helfen". "zu helfen" is the infinitive with "zu" (often after verbs like anbieten, vorhaben, bereit sein, bitten), meaning "to help" as an action/plan.
target_language_example: Ich versuche, ihm zu helfen.
native_language_example: I'm trying to help him.

additional_notes: Used in the common pattern **jemanden als + (noun/role) + verb**: *choose/see/consider/call/use someone as…* The noun after **als** is often **without an article** (e.g., *als Vorsitzenden*), but can also take one (e.g., *als den besten Arzt*). Note: **als** can also mean **“than”** in comparisons (*größer als…*), but here it means **“as.”**
target_language_example: Alle sehen ihn als guten Freund.
native_language_example: Everyone sees him as a good friend.

meaning: him … (with separable verbs: „… an“ goes at the end)
additional_notes: Not a fixed phrase by itself. It’s the accusative pronoun „ihn“ (usually “him”, sometimes “it” for a masculine noun) plus the separable prefix „an“ placed at the end of the clause. The exact English translation depends on the verb: „ruf ihn an“ = call him, „sieh ihn an“ = look at him, „lächle ihn an“ = smile at him, „nimm ihn an“ = accept it/him.
target_language_example: Tom errötete, denn Maria sah ihn an.
native_language_example: Tom blushed because Maria looked at him.

meaning: “him with a …” (using something as the tool/means).
additional_notes: This is the pattern **jemanden + mit + einem/einer/einem + noun** to say what you use to do something to someone (instrument/means): *Sie überraschte ihn mit einem Geschenk.* It’s a fragment that depends on a verb (e.g., wecken, erschießen, überraschen). Case: **ihn** = accusative (direct object); **mit** always takes **dative** → *mit einem Eimer, mit einem Gewehr, mit einem Kissen, mit einem Trick*.
target_language_example: Er öffnete die Dose und fütterte ihn mit einem Löffel.
native_language_example: He opened the can and fed him with a spoon.

additional_notes: This is the accusative pronoun ihn (“him”) combined with nie (“never”). It’s used to say you never do/did something to him: Ich habe ihn nie gesehen. In normal word order, ihn often comes before nie (pronoun before adverb), but the exact position can vary depending on what’s emphasized.
target_language_example: Ich werde ihn nie vergessen.
native_language_example: I will never forget him.

additional_notes:
This is not a fixed phrase by itself. It shows the common German pattern with **separable verbs**, where the object pronoun (**ihn** = “him/it”) comes in the middle and the separable prefix (**um**) goes to the end: 
- **umdrehen** → *Tom drehte ihn um.* = “Tom turned it over/around.” 
- **umbringen** → *Ihr bringt ihn um.* = “You’re killing him.” 
- **umlegen** (in some contexts) → *Siehst du ihn, legst du ihn um.* can mean “If you see him, you take him down/kill him.” 
So the exact meaning depends on the full verb (the part before *ihn* plus *um* together).
target_language_example: Dreh ihn um, ich will die Rückseite sehen.
native_language_example: Turn it over; I want to see the back.

additional_notes: „umbringen“ means “to kill” (often in the sense of murdering). „ihn“ is the accusative pronoun “him.” The word order can change for emphasis (e.g., „Ihn umbringen würde sie“ = “She would kill him”). In questions you’ll often see: „Willst/Wirst du ihn umbringen?“
target_language_example: Sie will ihn umbringen, aber er kann fliehen.
native_language_example: She wants to kill him, but he can escape.

additional_notes: "heiraten" means "to marry". "ihn" = "him" (accusative object). The "zu" + infinitive form is used after many verbs to express an action someone decides, promises, tries, or manages to do (e.g., "beschließen", "versprechen", "bitten", "überzeugen"). You can swap "ihn" for other pronouns/nouns: "sie zu heiraten" (to marry her), "dich zu heiraten" (to marry you), "Tom zu heiraten" (to marry Tom).
target_language_example: Ich kann mir vorstellen, ihn zu heiraten.
native_language_example: I can imagine marrying him.

additional_notes: A common German structure is **zu + infinitive** (“to + verb”), often used after verbs like *versuchen* (to try), *erlauben* (to allow), or in statements like *Ihn zu töten ist …* (“To kill him is …”). **ihn** is the accusative form of “he/him” (referring to a male person or animal). Putting **ihn** before **zu töten** can sound more emphatic, like “him, to kill (him)”.
target_language_example: Sie wollten ihn zu töten, aber die Polizei kam rechtzeitig.
native_language_example: They wanted to kill him, but the police arrived in time.

additional_notes: Used to address a group directly (“ihr” = you plural) in an angry, insulting way—often like shouting at people. Extremely offensive; avoid in polite or normal conversation.
target_language_example: Lasst mich in Ruhe, ihr Arschlöcher!
native_language_example: Leave me alone, you assholes!

meaning: her car; also: their car / your (formal) car (depending on context).
additional_notes:
"ihr" is a possessive determiner. It can mean:
- her (referring to "sie" = she)
- their (referring to "sie" = they)
- your (formal) (referring to "Sie" = you)
Which meaning is intended depends on the surrounding sentence and who is being talked about.
target_language_example: Ich sehe ihr Auto vor dem Haus.
native_language_example: I see her car in front of the house.

meaning: her money; their money (depending on context).
additional_notes: "ihr" is a possessive determiner meaning "her" (singular feminine) or "their" (plural). It changes with the case: e.g., nominative/accusative "ihr Geld", dative "ihrem Geld". Don’t confuse with capitalized "Ihr Geld" (= "your money" in formal address).
target_language_example: Sie spart ihr Geld für eine Reise.
native_language_example: She saves her money for a trip.

additional_notes: "ihr" is a possessive pronoun meaning "her" (or "their" depending on context). With "Gesicht" (face), it’s used both literally (a person’s face) and figuratively, e.g. "Die Sonne zeigte ihr Gesicht" = "The sun showed its face" (the sun comes out). Common with descriptions of emotions or appearance: "Ihr Gesicht hellte sich auf" (her face brightened), "Ihr Gesicht war feucht von Tränen" (her face was wet with tears).
target_language_example: Ich konnte ihr Gesicht kaum im Dunkeln erkennen.
native_language_example: I could barely make out her face in the dark.

additional_notes: "ihr" is a possessive determiner meaning "her" (or "their" depending on context). "Haar" is usually used as a mass noun in the singular to mean hair in general (like English "hair"), even though it can also mean a single hair. Often used with verbs like waschen (to wash), tragen (to wear), or werden (to become): e.g., "Ihr Haar wird grau" = "Her hair is turning gray."
target_language_example: Sie hat ihr Haar kurz geschnitten.
native_language_example: She cut her hair short.

meaning: her house; their house; your (formal) house.
additional_notes: "ihr" is a possessive word and its meaning depends on context: (1) her (3rd person singular feminine: "Sie" = she), (2) their (3rd person plural: "sie" = they), or (3) your (formal "Sie"). In the examples with "Sie" meaning "she" (e.g., "Sie verkaufte ..."), it means "her house". The form "ihr" agrees with the noun "Haus" (neuter), so it stays "ihr" in the nominative/accusative: "ihr Haus".
target_language_example: Sie möchte ihr Haus nächstes Jahr verkaufen.
native_language_example: She wants to sell her house next year.

meaning: her heart (literal or figurative: feelings, love, courage, character).
additional_notes:
Most literally it means the physical heart. Very often it’s used figuratively: 
- emotions/inner feelings (jemandem ihr Herz öffnen = to open her heart to someone)
- sadness (ihr Herz brach = her heart broke)
- personality/character (ein schwarzes Herz = a black heart)
- inner voice/instinct (auf ihr Herz hören = listen to her heart)
Also common in physical expressions like an ihr Herz drücken (= hold/press someone to her chest).
target_language_example: Sie nahm ihren Mut zusammen und öffnete ihm ihr Herz.
native_language_example: She gathered her courage and opened her heart to him.

additional_notes: "ihr" is a possessive meaning "her" or "their" (and also "your" in the formal form "Ihr"). Context tells you whose child it is. Note that German "Kind" means "child" (not English "kind").
target_language_example: Sie sucht ihr Kind im Park.
native_language_example: She’s looking for her child in the park.

additional_notes: “ihr” is the possessive pronoun “her” (also can mean “their,” depending on context). Common in set phrases like “jemandem ihr Leben anvertrauen” (to trust someone with her life) and “um ihr Leben kommen” (literally “to come around her life,” meaning “to die”).
target_language_example: Sie hat Angst um ihr Leben.
native_language_example: She is afraid for her life.

additional_notes: “ihr” is a possessive that usually means “her” (referring to a woman). So “ihr Mann” commonly means “her husband.” Depending on context/capitalization, it can also mean “their husband” (rare) or “your husband” in the formal “Sie” form (“Ihr Mann”). “Mann” can mean “man,” but in phrases like this it often specifically means “husband.”
target_language_example: Sie ist traurig, weil ihr Mann im Krankenhaus ist.
native_language_example: She is sad because her husband is in the hospital.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a woman’s husband and then describe him (job/nationality/where he is, etc.). Note: lowercase **ihr** usually means “her” (or “their” in other contexts). Capital **Ihr** would be the formal “your,” but with **Mann** it most often means “your husband.”
target_language_example: Ihr Mann ist heute im Büro.
native_language_example: Her husband is at the office today.

additional_notes: "ihr" can mean "her" (referring to a woman) or "your" in the formal form "Sie". So "ihr Name" can mean either "her name" or "your name" (formal), depending on context. In questions, you often hear: "Wie ist Ihr Name?" / "Ihr Name?" (formal; "Ihr" is usually capitalized when it means "your" formal).
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, wie ist Ihr Name?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what is your name? (formal)

meaning: “her name is” (sometimes: “their name is” / “your name is” formal).
additional_notes: “ihr” can mean **her**, **their**, or **your** (formal, to one person). In many everyday introductions, “Ihr Name ist …” is understood as **her name is …** from context (talking about a woman). In sentence 3 (“Ihr Name ist immer noch auf der Liste.”), it means the person’s name is still on the list.
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, ich glaube, ihr Name ist Anna.
native_language_example: Sorry, I think her name is Anna.

meaning: her son; their son (sometimes: your son, formal).
additional_notes: "ihr" is a possessive word that can mean "her", "their", or (with polite address) "your". Which one it is depends on context (and polite "your" is often written "Ihr" in formal writing). "ihr Sohn" is nominative (subject). Other common forms: "ihren Sohn" (accusative), "ihrem Sohn" (dative).
target_language_example: Ihr Sohn geht noch zur Schule.
native_language_example: Her son is still in school.

additional_notes: Means “her father” when referring to a female person (e.g., “sie”, “Maria”). Note the difference between "ihr" = her (possessive) and "Ihr" = your (formal). In some contexts, "ihr" can also mean “their,” so it depends on who is being talked about.
target_language_example: Ihr Vater kommt heute Abend nach Hause.
native_language_example: Her father is coming home this evening.

additional_notes: "ihr" can mean "her" (to/for her) or "their" depending on context; "Vater" is a masculine noun (capitalized). Used to identify who someone’s father is or to state his nationality, job, or status. In questions you’ll often see: "Wer ist ihr Vater?" (Who is her/their father?)
target_language_example: Ihr Vater ist Arzt.
native_language_example: Her father is a doctor.

additional_notes: "ihr" is a possessive that can mean **her**, **their**, or **your** (to more than one person, or formal "your" = *Ihr*). In writing, **Ihr** (capital I) usually signals formal "your". "war" is the past tense of *sein* (to be), used to describe what someone/something **was** (job, state, opinion, etc.).
target_language_example: Sie sagte, ihr Vater war sehr streng.
native_language_example: She said her father was very strict.

additional_notes: "ihr" is a possessive word meaning "her" or "their" depending on context. In sentences with "sie" (she), it usually means "her": "Sie ging in ihr Zimmer." With "sie" meaning "they", it means "their": "Sie sind in ihr Zimmer gegangen." "Zimmer" means a room (often a bedroom in this context).
target_language_example: Nach dem Essen ging sie in ihr Zimmer.
native_language_example: After dinner she went to her room.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that you mean the whole group of people you’re addressing. "ihr" is the 2nd-person plural form used for people you address with "du" (not the formal "Sie"). Often placed right after "ihr" or at the end for emphasis (e.g., "Ihr habt mir gefehlt, ihr alle").
target_language_example: Kommt bitte her, ihr alle!
native_language_example: Please come here, all of you!

additional_notes: Used when speaking directly to exactly two people. It uses the plural “ihr” (2nd person plural), so the verb is conjugated in the ihr-form: “ihr beide seid…”, “ihr beide habt…”. Similar to “ihr zwei”.
target_language_example: Ihr beide seid heute sehr pünktlich.
native_language_example: You both are very punctual today.

additional_notes: Used when speaking to exactly two people, often for emphasis. It’s made from the plural pronoun “ihr” (you all) + “beiden” (the two of you). You’ll also see other forms depending on case: “euch beide(n)” (you two, accusative/dative), “ihr zwei” (more casual), and similar patterns like “wir beide” (we two) or “sie beide” (those/they two).
target_language_example: Kommt ihr beiden morgen mit?
native_language_example: Are you two coming along tomorrow?

additional_notes: "Ihr" is the informal plural "you" (addressing more than one person). "brauchen" means "to need" (often + a noun: "Ihr braucht einen Schlüssel.") or + "zu" + infinitive: "Ihr braucht euch nicht zu verstecken." In everyday speech, "ihr braucht nicht …" can mean "you don’t have to …"; with emphasis like "gar nicht" it means "really don’t need to".
target_language_example: Ihr braucht einen Schlüssel.
native_language_example: You (all) need a key.

additional_notes: A compositional combination of ihr (“you” when speaking to more than one person informally) and das (“it/that”). In German these words can appear next to each other before or after the verb, but in natural English you usually translate them with the verb in between, e.g. ihr das tun = “do it/that”, ihr das getan habt = “you did it/that”.
target_language_example: Ich frage mich, ob ihr das schon wisst.
native_language_example: I wonder whether you already know that.

meaning: “you (all) think” / “you think” (to more than one person).
additional_notes: "Ihr" is the informal plural form of "you" (addressing two or more people). "Denkt" is the verb "denken" (to think) in the present tense: "ihr denkt". Often used in comparisons like "..., als ihr denkt" (“...than you think”) or to ask for opinions: "Was denkt ihr?" / "Sagt mir, was ihr denkt."
target_language_example: Es ist einfacher, als ihr denkt.
native_language_example: It’s easier than you think.

additional_notes: Uses the modal verb **dürfen** with **ihr** (2nd person plural). It’s used to give permission or say what is allowed (often to a group, friends, family, children). With **nicht** it means **must not / are not allowed to**: *Ihr dürft hier nicht rauchen.* (You’re not allowed to smoke here.) Not used for the formal “you” (**Sie dürfen**).
target_language_example: Ihr dürft jetzt reinkommen.
native_language_example: You (all) may come in now.

additional_notes: A combination of pronouns: ihr is informal plural subject ('you all') and euch is the object/reflexive form. Together they often appear with reflexive verbs, where English may say 'yourselves', or with reciprocal meaning, where English says 'each other'. The exact translation depends on the verb and context.
target_language_example: Versteht ihr euch gut?
native_language_example: Do you get along well?

additional_notes: Used when speaking to more than one person with the informal "ihr" (like "you all"). "Eure" is the possessive "your" that matches the noun it describes (usually plural or feminine nominative/accusative): eure Kinder (your children), eure Medikamente (your medications), eure Freizeit (your free time). Other common forms are euer (masc./neut.), euren (masc. acc./dat. pl.), eurem (dat. masc./neut.), eurer (dat./gen. fem.).
target_language_example: Habt ihr eure Hausaufgaben schon gemacht?
native_language_example: Have you (all) already done your homework?

additional_notes: Used when talking to more than one person (plural "you"). This is the Perfekt of **tun** (to do): **ihr** (you-plural) + **habt** (have) + **getan** (done). In subordinate clauses with words like **was** (“what”) the conjugated verb **habt** often goes to the end: **… was ihr getan habt** (“… what you have done”).
target_language_example: Danke für alles, was ihr getan habt.
native_language_example: Thank you for everything you’ve done.

additional_notes: The informal plural form of haben, used when speaking to more than one person. It can mean possession, but very often it is also the helping verb in the present perfect: ihr habt gemacht = 'you have done' or simply 'you did'.
target_language_example: Ihr habt heute viel gelernt.
native_language_example: You all learned a lot today.

additional_notes: "Ihr" addresses more than one person (you all). "Habt" is the 2nd-person plural form of "haben" and is often used to form the Perfekt (past tense): "ihr habt" + past participle (e.g., "geschafft", "erklärt", "versprochen"). "Es" usually refers to something already known from context (it/that), and can be a placeholder object ("Ihr habt es geschafft" = you managed to do it).
target_language_example: Ihr habt es schon gehört, oder?
native_language_example: You’ve already heard it, right?

meaning: "you (all) have ..." (perfect tense with the reflexive pronoun "euch").
additional_notes: Used with reflexive or reciprocal verbs in the Perfekt (present perfect). "Ihr" = you (plural, informal), "habt" = have, and "euch" = yourselves/each other. It must be followed by a past participle (e.g., "ihr habt euch geirrt" = you were mistaken; "ihr habt euch Zeit gelassen" = you took your time).
target_language_example: Ihr habt euch verlaufen.
native_language_example: You (all) got lost.

additional_notes: "ihr" = you (plural/informal). "habt" is the 2nd person plural form of "haben" (to have). "eure" means "your" and is used with feminine singular nouns (e.g., "eure Arbeit") and with plural nouns (e.g., "eure Ziele", "eure Regenschirme"). For masculine/neuter singular, use "euer" (e.g., "euer Handy"). Often followed by a noun, and sometimes by a past participle to form the present perfect (e.g., "ihr habt eure Regenschirme vergessen").
target_language_example: Ihr habt eure Hausaufgaben schon gemacht.
native_language_example: You all have already done your homework.

meaning: “you (all) have … me” / “you guys have … me” (addressing more than one person).
additional_notes: Used with **ihr** (2nd person plural) when talking to a group you address informally. **habt** is the plural form of **haben** and often forms the **Perfekt** (present perfect) with a past participle: *Ihr habt mich gesehen/found/überrascht.* You usually add the participle or another object to complete the meaning.
target_language_example: Ihr habt mich total falsch verstanden.
native_language_example: You guys completely misunderstood me.

meaning: “you (all) have … (to/for me)” (plural informal ‘you’ + Perfekt with haben).
additional_notes: Used when talking to more than one person (plural informal: ihr). “habt” is the present tense of “haben” used to form the Perfekt (present perfect/past) with a past participle at the end: “Ihr habt mir geholfen.” “mir” is the dative pronoun meaning “to me / for me,” common with verbs like fehlen (miss), leid tun (feel sorry for), versprechen (promise), geben (give), verderben (ruin).
target_language_example: Ihr habt mir wirklich geholfen.
native_language_example: You all really helped me.

additional_notes: Present tense of "haben" with "ihr" = you (plural, informal). Used when speaking to two or more people you address as "ihr" (friends, family, kids, etc.). Contrast: "Sie haben" (formal you), "du hast" (one person).
target_language_example: Ihr habt heute viel zu tun.
native_language_example: You all have a lot to do today.

additional_notes: *Ihr* is the informal plural “you” (talking to more than one person). *Hattet* is the simple past (Präteritum) of *haben* (“to have”). Common in storytelling and in set phrases like *Ihr hattet Glück/Pech/Recht* (“You were lucky/unlucky/right”). In questions it often implies “had” in the sense of “were you going to / did you have”: *Ihr hattet mir etwas zu sagen?* = “Did you have something to tell me?” (literally “You had something to tell me?”).
target_language_example: Ihr hattet gestern keine Zeit.
native_language_example: You (all) didn’t have time yesterday.

additional_notes: "Ihr" is the informal plural "you" (to more than one person). "Hättet" is Konjunktiv II (subjunctive) of "haben" for "ihr". It’s commonly used with a past participle to talk about unreal/imagined past situations or to express criticism/advice about the past: "Ihr hättet … (nicht) sollen" = "You (guys) should (not) have …" It can also appear in reported speech where English often uses simple past: "Ich dachte, ihr hättet …" = "I thought you had …".
target_language_example: Ihr hättet mich vorher anrufen sollen.
native_language_example: You (guys) should have called me earlier.

additional_notes: "ihr" is the informal/familiar "you" for more than one person (friends, family, kids). "könnt" is the "ihr" form of the verb "können" (can/to be able to). It’s usually followed by another verb in the infinitive, which often goes to the end of the clause: "Ihr könnt uns helfen." (You can help us.) For formal "you" (one or more people), use "Sie können".
target_language_example: Ihr könnt später anrufen, wenn ihr Zeit habt.
native_language_example: You (all) can call later when you have time.

meaning: "you (plural) can ..." (often used with a reflexive verb: "you can ... yourselves").
additional_notes: "Ihr" is "you" when talking to more than one person. "Könnt" is the present-tense form of "können" (can/to be able to). "Euch" is the reflexive object for "ihr" (yourselves/you all). It’s very common before reflexive verbs like "euch ausruhen" (to rest), "euch freuen" (to be happy), or expressions like "ihr könnt euch sicher sein" (you can be sure). Word order: Ihr könnt euch + infinitive at the end (e.g., "Ihr könnt euch heute freinehmen.").
target_language_example: Ihr könnt euch später bei mir melden.
native_language_example: You (all) can get back to me later.

meaning: "you (all) can … me" (you are able to … / you’re allowed to …).
additional_notes: Used with a following verb to say what a group of people can do to/with you: Ihr könnt mich anrufen. = You can call me. On its own (often with "alle mal": "Ihr könnt mich alle mal!") it’s an insulting way to dismiss people (roughly: “You can all get lost / screw you”).
target_language_example: Ihr könnt mich jederzeit anrufen.
native_language_example: You can call me anytime.

additional_notes: "Ihr" is the informal 2nd-person plural pronoun ("you all"). "Könntet" is Konjunktiv II of "können" and is often used to make suggestions more polite/less direct (like "you could...") or to talk about possibilities in an imagined situation ("you might..."). In conditional warnings it can mean "could end up" (e.g., "ihr könntet entlassen werden" = "you could be fired").
target_language_example: Ihr könntet später vorbeikommen, wenn ihr Zeit habt.
native_language_example: You could come by later if you have time.

meaning: "you (plural)" + "me" (used when talking to several people: you … me).
additional_notes: "ihr" is the subject pronoun for addressing multiple people informally (like "you all" / "you guys"). "mich" is the direct-object form of "ich" ("me"). You’ll usually see them with a verb in between or nearby (e.g., "ihr habt mich…", "ignoriert ihr mich?", "dass ihr mich…"). For polite/formal address to one or more people, German uses "Sie" instead of "ihr" ("Sie mich" in similar patterns).
target_language_example: Habt ihr mich verstanden?
native_language_example: Did you (all) understand me?

additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom; it’s simply two pronouns that often appear together in a sentence. **ihr** is the 2nd-person plural pronoun (“you all”), used for addressing more than one person (informal plural and also identical in form to the formal singular/plural **Sie**’s possessive, but here it’s the pronoun **ihr**). **mir** is 1st-person singular dative (“to/for me”), used with many verbs that take a dative object (e.g., *helfen*, *geben*, *bringen*). In typical word order, a dative pronoun like **mir** often comes before an accusative noun: *ihr gebt mir das Buch*.
target_language_example: Vielen Dank, dass ihr mir geholfen habt!
native_language_example: Thank you very much for helping me!

additional_notes: "Ihr" is the informal "you" for talking to more than one person (friends, kids, family). "Müsst" is the verb "müssen" (to have to / must) conjugated for "ihr". Often used to give instructions or express strong necessity; in phrases like "Ihr müsst verrückt sein" it can also mean "you must be..." (a strong guess/opinion).
target_language_example: Ihr müsst jetzt leise sein.
native_language_example: You (all) have to be quiet now.

additional_notes: Used when speaking to a group in the informal “ihr” form, and it’s followed by a reflexive verb (a verb that takes “sich”, here “euch”): z.B. euch fragen, euch umdrehen, euch an etwas halten, euch helfen lassen. The formal version is “Sie müssen sich …”.
target_language_example: Ihr müsst euch beeilen, sonst verpassen wir den Zug.
native_language_example: You (all) have to hurry, otherwise we’ll miss the train.

additional_notes: Addressing more than one person (2nd person plural). Expresses obligation/necessity. Note: In modern German spelling, this is usually written „ihr müsst“ (with -ss); „ihr müßt“ is the older spelling. Often followed by an infinitive: „ihr müßt mehr üben“.
target_language_example: Ihr müßt diesen Bericht noch einmal neu schreiben.
native_language_example: You (all) have to rewrite this report once again.

meaning: 'you (plural) have to / must' (often used with a reflexive verb: 'you must … yourselves').
additional_notes: "Ihr" is "you" addressing a group (friends, kids, students). "müßt" (also spelled "müsst" in modern German) is from "müssen" = "must / have to". "euch" is the reflexive pronoun for "you (plural)" and is used with reflexive verbs like "sich beeilen" (to hurry), "sich anstrengen" (to make an effort), "sich an etwas halten" (to stick to something), and "sich verhalten" (to behave). This phrase is common in instructions and rules.
target_language_example: Ihr müßt euch jetzt entscheiden.
native_language_example: You (all) have to decide now.

additional_notes: Used mostly in questions, especially with the present perfect: „Habt ihr schon einmal …?“ It addresses a group of people with „ihr“ (plural ‘you’). „schon einmal“ literally means ‘already once’, but in this pattern it usually means ‘ever/before’ (asking about life experience).
target_language_example: Habt ihr schon einmal in Deutschland gelebt?
native_language_example: Have you ever lived in Germany?

additional_notes: "Ihr" is the informal "you" for more than one person (talking to friends, family, kids). "Seht" is the 2nd-person plural form of "sehen" (to see). Very often you’ll hear it with "aussehen": "Ihr seht müde aus" = "You look tired." (Compare: "du siehst" = you (one person), informal; "Sie sehen" = you, formal.)
target_language_example: Ihr seht heute wirklich gut aus.
native_language_example: You all look really good today.

additional_notes: Used to address two or more people informally. It is the present-tense form of sein with ihr. For formal 'you are', German uses Sie sind.
target_language_example: Ihr seid heute sehr ruhig.
native_language_example: You are very quiet today.

additional_notes: Used with **ihr** (2nd person plural) when speaking to several people you know well, such as friends, family, classmates, or children. **alle** emphasizes that it’s true for everyone in the group. Common in statements like *Ihr seid alle müde / fertig / hier / verrückt!*
target_language_example: Kommt rein, ihr seid alle willkommen!
native_language_example: Come in, you’re all welcome!

meaning: "You (all) are ... (you know / after all / surely)" — an emphatic "you are" (plural).
additional_notes: "Ihr seid" is the 2nd-person plural form of "sein" (you all/you guys are). Adding "doch" makes it more emphatic and often expresses correction, disbelief, or reminding someone of what should be obvious (similar to "come on, you are..." / "but you are..."). The tone depends on context and can sound accusing or emotional: "Ihr seid doch keine Tiere!" = "You’re not animals!"
target_language_example: Ihr seid doch meine Freunde!
native_language_example: But you’re my friends (after all)!

additional_notes: Used to negate a statement about a group you address with "ihr" (informal plural = "you all"). It’s the present tense of "sein" (to be): ihr seid (you are) + nicht (not). Often followed by an adjective or phrase: "ihr seid nicht allein" (you’re not alone).
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, ihr seid nicht zu spät.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, you’re not late.

additional_notes: "Ihr" addresses more than one person ("you all"). "Sollt" is the 2nd person plural form of "sollen". It’s used to give instructions or express obligation/expectation (sometimes like a firm command: "Ihr sollt hierbleiben!"). In general it’s less absolute than "ihr müsst" ("you must"), but in context it can still be very strict.
target_language_example: Ihr sollt pünktlich sein.
native_language_example: You’re supposed to be on time.

additional_notes: Used to give advice or a strong suggestion to a group of people ("ihr" = you plural). "solltet" is the subjunctive form of "sollen" and often sounds a bit softer/more polite than "ihr sollt".
target_language_example: Ihr solltet früher ins Bett gehen, wenn ihr morgen fit sein wollt.
native_language_example: You (all) should go to bed earlier if you want to feel fit tomorrow.

meaning: you (all) should do that / you should (plural)
additional_notes: Used to give advice or a recommendation to a group ("ihr" = you all). "solltet" is the subjunctive II form of "sollen" and often sounds a bit softer/more polite than a direct command. "das" refers to a specific thing or action already known from context, and is usually followed by an infinitive or clause (e.g., "...mit Tom besprechen", "...einrahmen lassen").
target_language_example: Ihr solltet das heute noch mit eurer Lehrerin klären.
native_language_example: You all should clear that up with your teacher today.

meaning: “you (all) should …” (giving advice; often with a reflexive verb).
additional_notes: Used when speaking to a group (“ihr”) to recommend or advise something. “solltet” is the subjunctive of “sollen,” which makes it sound like advice rather than a strict order. “euch” is the reflexive pronoun for “you all” and is needed with many common verbs (e.g., euch ausruhen = rest, euch entschuldigen = apologize, euch bemühen = make an effort, euch ansehen = look at, euch kümmern = take care of, euch untersuchen lassen = get examined, euch fernhalten = keep away).
target_language_example: Ihr solltet euch warm anziehen, es ist kalt draußen.
native_language_example: You all should dress warmly; it’s cold outside.

additional_notes: Second-person plural, simple past of **sein** (“to be”). Used when speaking to more than one person (like “you all / you guys were …”). Often interchangeable with **ihr seid gewesen** in meaning, but **ihr wart** is the simple past form.
target_language_example: Ihr wart gestern sehr müde.
native_language_example: You were very tired yesterday.

meaning: "you (all) will" (future tense) / sometimes "you (all) are going to".
additional_notes: Used with "ihr" (plural "you") plus the verb "werden" to talk about the future. It’s often followed by an infinitive at the end of the clause (e.g., "ihr werdet lernen"). It can also be used alone meaning "you’ll see" / "you’ll find out" (often as a warning or promise: "Ihr werdet sehen!").
target_language_example: Keine Sorge—ihr werdet das schaffen.
native_language_example: Don’t worry—you’ll manage it.

additional_notes: "Ihr" is the informal plural form of "you" (used for more than one person, like friends, family, kids). "Wisst" is the 2nd-person plural form of "wissen" (to know). Often used to introduce what the speaker assumes the group already knows (e.g., "Wie ihr wisst, ..." = "As you know, ...") or with a clause: "Ihr wisst, dass/was/wo ...".
target_language_example: Ihr wisst doch, dass wir heute keine Zeit haben.
native_language_example: You all know that we don’t have time today.

additional_notes: "Ihr" is the informal 2nd-person plural pronoun (addressing more than one person). "Wollt" is the present-tense form of "wollen" for "ihr". It can be used in statements or (often) in surprised/critical questions: "Ihr wollt …?" For the formal/plural "you," use "Sie wollen …".
target_language_example: Wenn ihr wollt, können wir heute früher gehen.
native_language_example: If you want, we can leave earlier today.

additional_notes: Second-person plural form of **wollen** (“to want”). Used when talking to a group (friends, family, classmates). Often appears in flexible phrases like **so viel … wie ihr wollt** (“as much as you want”), **macht, was (auch immer) ihr wollt** (“do whatever you want”), or with question words: **worüber ihr wollt** (“about whatever you want”). Note: it can look like English **will**, but it usually means **want** (not the future tense).
target_language_example: Ihr wollt heute Abend Pizza essen.
native_language_example: You (all) want to eat pizza tonight.

additional_notes: Used when speaking directly to exactly two people. "ihr" is the informal 2nd-person plural pronoun, so it’s typically for friends, family, kids, etc. For a more formal version you can say "Sie zwei". Word order can also be "ihr beiden" (very common) or "ihr zwei".
target_language_example: Kommt ihr zwei bitte kurz her?
native_language_example: Can you two please come here for a moment?

additional_notes: "helfen" takes the dative case, so "ihr" is the dative pronoun meaning "to her" (often translated simply as "her"). It can also mean "to them" (dative plural) depending on context, but in these examples it’s "her." Often used with "können" (can) or "wollen" (want): "Ich will ihr helfen."
target_language_example: Kannst du ihr helfen?
native_language_example: Can you help her?

additional_notes: "ihr" is the dative pronoun meaning “to her” (because "helfen" takes the dative in German: jemandem helfen = to help someone).
