additional_notes: Used with the modal verb "können" (can/to be able to) plus "nicht" (not). It can be a statement ("können wir nicht …" = we can’t …) or a question ("Können wir nicht …?" = Can’t we …?/Couldn’t we …?). In statements, it often appears before the main verb at the end: "Das können wir nicht tun."
target_language_example: Können wir nicht morgen darüber sprechen?
native_language_example: Can’t we talk about it tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used to ask if something is possible/okay for “us” to do, often with a reflexive meaning (“each other”), e.g. treffen (meet), umarmen (hug), unterhalten (talk). In German, the main action often comes as an infinitive at the end: „Können wir uns morgen treffen?“ Also used with reflexive verbs like „sich kümmern“ (to take care of): „… können wir uns später kümmern.“
target_language_example: Können wir uns morgen um 10 Uhr treffen?
native_language_example: Can we meet tomorrow at 10 o’clock?

meaning: "can we" (to meet/see each other, talk, etc.).
additional_notes: Used to suggest or ask about doing something together. With many verbs (e.g., sehen, treffen, unterhalten), German uses the reflexive pronoun "uns" (= each other). In a question with a modal verb, the main verb often goes to the end: "Können wir uns morgen sehen?"
target_language_example: Können wir uns morgen treffen?
native_language_example: Can we meet tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used to ask several people informally whether they are able to do something, or to make a request. "ihr" is the informal plural "you". In a normal statement, the order is "ihr könnt" ("you can"). The formal version is usually "können Sie ...?"
target_language_example: Könnt ihr mir bitte helfen?
native_language_example: Can you help me, please?

meaning: 'can you (all) … that?' / 'are you (all) able to do that?'
additional_notes: Used when speaking to two or more people (ihr). It’s often followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., erklären, tun): „Könnt ihr das erklären?“ = „Can you explain that?“ In statements, it can appear in the middle of the sentence: „… könnt ihr das gerne tun.“
target_language_example: Könnt ihr das bitte wiederholen?
native_language_example: Can you (all) repeat that, please?

meaning: "can you (all) ..." (addressing a group, with a reflexive verb).
additional_notes: Used with reflexive verbs where the subject (ihr = you plural) also has a reflexive pronoun (euch = yourselves). Common patterns include: „Könnt ihr euch erinnern …?“ (Can you remember …?), „Könnt ihr euch vorstellen …?“ (Can you imagine …?), and „Auf mich könnt ihr euch verlassen.“ (You can rely on me.). Word order changes depending on whether it’s a question or statement, but the core idea is „you (plural) can/could …“ with a reflexive verb.
target_language_example: Könnt ihr euch bitte kurz vorstellen?
native_language_example: Can you all please introduce yourselves briefly?

meaning: "can you (plural) ... for me?" / "could you (plural) ... for me?"
additional_notes: Used to ask two or more people (or one person informally as "you all") to do something for you. It’s a polite request starter: "Könnt ihr mir ...?" + verb or object (e.g., "helfen", "ein Glas Wasser bringen"). "mir" is the dative pronoun "to/for me." In formal situations use "Können Sie mir ...?" (to one or more people).
target_language_example: Könnt ihr mir kurz sagen, wie ich zum Bahnhof komme?
native_language_example: Can you (all) quickly tell me how to get to the train station?

additional_notes: Uses Konjunktiv II of können ("could") + "ich" ("I"). Common in polite requests/questions ("Könnte ich …?" = "Could I …?/Could I have …?") and in hypothetical/conditional statements (often with "wenn" or implied conditions), e.g. "Ohne … könnte ich … nicht" = "Without … I couldn’t …". In strong emotional statements, it can express what you feel like doing (not necessarily what you will do).
target_language_example: Könnte ich bitte mit dem Chef sprechen?
native_language_example: Could I speak with the boss, please?

additional_notes: Used to ask for something politely. Literally it’s “could I, please…”, with the verb in conditional form (könnte) to sound softer and more formal. Typically followed by an infinitive (benutzen, sprechen) or by what you want (ein Glas Wasser, eine Quittung) plus a verb like bekommen/haben.
target_language_example: Könnte ich bitte die Speisekarte bekommen?
native_language_example: Could I please get the menu?

meaning: "might be able to" / "could be able to".
additional_notes: Used to express a possibility (not a certainty) that someone has the ability or opportunity to do something. Often followed by an infinitive with "zu": "... in der Lage sein, etwas zu tun". Example pattern: "Er könnte in der Lage sein, dir zu helfen." = "He might be able to help you."
target_language_example: Ich könnte in der Lage sein, morgen früher zu kommen.
native_language_example: I might be able to come earlier tomorrow.

meaning: “one could / you could” (a possibility, suggestion, or hypothetical).
additional_notes: Uses the subjunctive form of können (könnte) with the impersonal pronoun man (“one/you/people”) to talk generally and politely about what would be possible or what someone might say/do. Common for soft suggestions (Das könnte man so machen.), cautious opinions (Das könnte man so sagen.), and hypothetical situations (Für das Geld könnte man …).
target_language_example: Mit ein bisschen mehr Zeit könnte man das Problem leicht lösen.
native_language_example: With a bit more time, you could easily solve the problem.

additional_notes: Polite/formal way to make a request or ask for help, used with "Sie" (formal "you")—common with "bitte". Literally it’s the subjunctive of "können" ("can") and is softer than "Können Sie ...?".
target_language_example: Könnten Sie mir bitte sagen, wo der Bahnhof ist?
native_language_example: Could you please tell me where the train station is?

additional_notes: Used to make very polite requests, especially to strangers, customers, or in formal situations. It uses the subjunctive form "könnten" (from "können" = can) plus the formal "Sie". You can place the verb at the end of the sentence: "Könnten Sie bitte mir helfen?" / "Könnten Sie mir bitte helfen?"
target_language_example: Könnten Sie bitte langsamer sprechen?
native_language_example: Could you please speak more slowly?

additional_notes: Used to make a formal, polite request to someone you address as Sie (e.g., staff, strangers, officials). It’s commonly followed by an infinitive phrase (tun, erklären, wiederholen) or a short object + verb. Often shortened to “Könnten Sie bitte …?”
target_language_example: Könnten Sie das bitte wiederholen?
native_language_example: Could you please repeat that?

meaning: “could you … me” (polite way to ask someone to take/call/drive you).
additional_notes: A very polite request in the formal "Sie" form. It’s usually followed by an infinitive phrase like "mitnehmen" (give me a ride/take me along), "zurückrufen" (call me back), "nach Hause fahren" (drive me home), or "zum Bahnhof bringen" (take me to the station). Often used when asking a stranger or in service situations.
target_language_example: Könnten Sie mich bitte zum Flughafen bringen?
native_language_example: Could you please take me to the airport?

meaning: Could you (please) … for me? / Could you … me?
additional_notes: A very polite/formal way to start a request. It uses the subjunctive form "könnten" (from "können") plus formal "Sie". Typically followed by an infinitive at the end of the clause (e.g., "helfen", "zeigen", "leihen") and often includes "bitte". Use with strangers, staff, or in professional situations.
target_language_example: Könnten Sie mir bitte sagen, wo der Bahnhof ist?
native_language_example: Could you please tell me where the train station is?

additional_notes: Used with **Sie** (formal “you”) to make a very polite request, often with strangers, customers, or in professional situations. It’s the subjunctive form of *können* (“can”) to sound softer than *Können Sie…?*. Typically followed by an infinitive at the end of the clause (e.g., *…sagen*, *…helfen*).
target_language_example: Könnten Sie mir bitte helfen, den Weg zum Bahnhof zu finden?
native_language_example: Could you please help me find the way to the train station?

additional_notes: Uses Konjunktiv II of „können“ („könnten“) to sound more polite/less direct than „können wir“. Often followed by „bitte“ and an infinitive or request: „Könnten wir bitte kurz allein sein?“ You can also use it for hypothetical situations: „Könnten wir zum Mond fliegen, wenn …?“
target_language_example: Könnten wir bitte die Rechnung bekommen?
native_language_example: Could we get the bill, please?

additional_notes: Polite way to ask someone to do something. It’s the subjunctive form of „können“ (literally like “could you”), often used with „bitte“. Common pattern: „Könntest du mir (bitte) + infinitive …?“
target_language_example: Könntest du mir bitte kurz helfen?
native_language_example: Could you please help me for a moment?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone informally (du) to do something in a very polite way. It uses the Konjunktiv II form of „können“ (könntest) to sound softer than „Kannst du …?“. Typically followed by an infinitive verb at the end: „Könntest du bitte das Fenster öffnen?“
target_language_example: Könntest du bitte mir kurz helfen?
native_language_example: Could you please help me for a moment?

additional_notes: A very polite way to ask someone to do something. Uses the subjunctive form "könntest" (from "können") to soften the request. Often followed by an infinitive verb, e.g., "geben", "buchstabieren", "erklären", "noch mal machen". You can replace "das" with something else: "Könntest du bitte die Tür schließen?"
target_language_example: Könntest du das bitte wiederholen?
native_language_example: Could you please repeat that?

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to do something for you. It uses **Konjunktiv II** (*könntest*) to sound softer/more polite than *Kannst du mich …?*. It’s usually followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., *abholen, wecken, zurückrufen, fahren*). Word order: **Könntest du mich + infinitive?**
target_language_example: Könntest du mich vom Bahnhof abholen?
native_language_example: Could you pick me up from the station?

additional_notes: A polite way to ask someone (informal singular 'du') to do something for you or help you. It uses the subjunctive form 'könntest' to soften the request (more polite than 'kannst du mir ...?'). Typically followed by an infinitive: 'Könntest du mir helfen / sagen / zeigen ...?'. Often includes particles like 'mal' or 'wohl' to sound even softer.
target_language_example: Könntest du mir bitte kurz helfen?
native_language_example: Could you please help me for a moment?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone politely to do something. It’s the subjunctive form of "können" ("könntest"), which makes the request softer than "Kannst du …?". Often followed by an infinitive: "… helfen", "… sagen", "… einen Gefallen tun". "mir" means "to me/for me" and can be omitted if you don’t need it ("Könntest du bitte …?").
target_language_example: Könntest du mir bitte kurz erklären, wie das funktioniert?
native_language_example: Could you please quickly explain to me how that works?

additional_notes: Uses the subjunctive II form of "können" with "ihr" (you plural) to make a request sound more polite/less direct than "Könnt ihr …?". Commonly followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., helfen, warten, bringen) and often used with "bitte".
target_language_example: Könntet ihr bitte die Tür schließen?
native_language_example: Could you please close the door?

additional_notes: A very polite way to ask two or more people to do something. It uses the subjunctive form (könntet) to sound softer than “könnt ihr”. Typically followed by an infinitive verb at the end of the clause (e.g., „… warten?“, „… öffnen?“). Used with friends, strangers, or in service situations when you want to be especially polite.
target_language_example: Könntet ihr bitte leiser sprechen?
native_language_example: Could you please speak more quietly?

additional_notes: Uses the subjunctive form ("könntet") to sound more polite/indirect than "könnt ihr". "ihr" is addressed to two or more people (or informal plural "you"). Often followed by an infinitive at the end of the clause: "Könntet ihr mir helfen?" / "… etwas erklären?"
target_language_example: Könntet ihr mir kurz sagen, wo der Bahnhof ist?
native_language_example: Could you (all) quickly tell me where the train station is?

meaning: “take care of” / “look after” / “deal with” (informal singular command).
additional_notes: From “sich um etwas/jemanden kümmern” = to take care of / look after / handle. “Kümmere dich um …” is the imperative for “du” (one person you know well). It can be caring (looking after someone) or more admonishing (“Mind your own business!” → “Kümmere dich um deine eigenen Angelegenheiten!”).
target_language_example: Ich bin gleich zurück — kümmere dich um die Gäste.
native_language_example: I’ll be right back — take care of the guests.

additional_notes: Formal (Sie) imperative of "sich um etwas/jemanden kümmern". Used to tell someone to take responsibility for a person/thing/task. With people it often means 'look after' (care for); with things/tasks it can mean 'handle it' or 'take care of it'.
target_language_example: Kümmern Sie sich um Ihre Gesundheit.
native_language_example: Take care of your health.

meaning: takes care of; looks after; deals with.
additional_notes: 3rd person singular present tense of the reflexive verb phrase „sich um (etw./jdn.) kümmern“. Conjugation pattern: „ich kümmere mich um…“, „du kümmerst dich um…“, „er/sie kümmert sich um…“. Used both for caring for people (children, parents) and for handling tasks, responsibilities, or problems.
target_language_example: Der Manager kümmert sich um viele Probleme.
native_language_example: The manager deals with many problems.

additional_notes: A common, mostly formal/neutral term for computer systems that can “think” or learn in ways similar to humans. Often used in discussions about technology, jobs, and the future. Usually shortened in German to „KI“ (pronounced like the English letters “K” “I”). The adjective changes with case: „künstliche Intelligenz“ (nom.), „die künstliche Intelligenz“ (acc.), „der künstlichen Intelligenz“ (dat.).
target_language_example: Viele Firmen nutzen künstliche Intelligenz, um Daten zu analysieren.
native_language_example: Many companies use artificial intelligence to analyze data.

additional_notes: Simple past (Präteritum) form of the reciprocal/reflexive verb „sich küssen“ (to kiss). Used mostly in written narratives; in everyday speech you often hear the perfect: „Sie haben sich geküsst.“ The verb agrees with the subject („sie“ = they), and „sich“ shows the action is mutual/reciprocal.
target_language_example: Sie küssten sich im Regen.
native_language_example: They kissed each other in the rain.

meaning: "Long live …!" (a cheer wishing someone/something a long life).
additional_notes: Used in slogans, toasts, and ceremonial or patriotic contexts: “Lang lebe + noun/name” (e.g., Lang lebe der König!). The word order is a set, old-fashioned/subjunctive-style formula: “lebe” refers to “(may) … live”.
target_language_example: Lang lebe die Freiheit!
native_language_example: Long live freedom!

additional_notes: Common noun phrase describing hair length. Often used with the verb "haben" (to have): "Ich habe lange Haare." You can intensify with "zu" to mean "too": "zu lange Haare" = "hair that’s too long". "Haare" is plural in German (literally “hairs”), but in English you usually say “hair” (uncountable).
target_language_example: Ich will wieder lange Haare haben.
native_language_example: I want to have long hair again.

meaning: a long time (for a long period).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a long duration. Often placed at the beginning of a sentence as a time expression ("Lange Zeit ..."), or after the verb/object ("... lange Zeit"). You can also intensify it with "sehr" ("sehr lange Zeit" = a very long time).
target_language_example: Ich habe lange Zeit in Berlin gelebt.
native_language_example: I lived in Berlin for a long time.

meaning: “how long are you / have you been …” (part of a question about duration).
additional_notes: Usually used with **wie**: **Wie lange bist du …?** You often add **schon** to mean “for how long (already)”: **Wie lange bist du schon hier?** In English this is often translated with the present perfect (“How long have you been …?”).
target_language_example: Wie lange bist du schon in Berlin?
native_language_example: How long have you been in Berlin?

meaning: 'how long do you need?' (as in: how much time will it take you?)
additional_notes: Usually used with the question word "wie": "Wie lange brauchst du?" You can add "noch" to mean "how much longer": "Wie lange brauchst du noch?" Common contexts: finishing a task, getting ready, or traveling (often with "bis" + place: "Wie lange brauchst du bis zum Bahnhof?").
target_language_example: Wie lange brauchst du noch, bis du fertig bist?
native_language_example: How much longer do you need until you're finished?

meaning: to take a long time until / before (something happens)
additional_notes: Used to say that something will take a long time before a later event happens. Very common frame: „Es wird (nicht) lange dauern, bis …“ = “It won’t (will) take long before …” / “It will be a while before …”. After „bis“ you typically have a full clause with the verb at the end.
target_language_example: Es könnte lange dauern, bis wir uns wieder treffen.
native_language_example: It could take a long time before we meet again.

meaning: “how long have you (all) …” (used to ask about duration).
additional_notes: Usually appears in a question with "Wie": "Wie lange habt ihr …?". "ihr" is the informal plural "you" (talking to more than one person). The verb often comes at the end: "Wie lange habt ihr hier gewohnt?"
target_language_example: Wie lange habt ihr schon Deutsch gelernt?
native_language_example: How long have you (all) been learning German?

meaning: “how long have you…?” / “how long do you have…?” (question word order).
additional_notes: Usually used with **wie**: **Wie lange hast du …?** It’s a question structure where the verb (**hast**) comes before the subject (**du**). Common with **Zeit** (“time”) or with a past participle: **Wie lange hast du hier gewohnt?** (“How long have you lived here?”). On its own, **lange hast du** sounds incomplete without what comes next.
target_language_example: Wie lange hast du Zeit?
native_language_example: How much time do you have?

meaning: a long time ago; a long time since (then).
additional_notes: Used with "es ist ... her" to say how much time has passed since something happened: "Es ist lange her" (It was a long time ago / It’s been a long time). Often intensified: "zu lange her" (too long ago), "viel zu lange her" (far too long ago). In exclamations you can also say: "Ist das lange her!"
target_language_example: Es ist schon lange her, dass wir uns gesehen haben.
native_language_example: It’s been a long time since we’ve seen each other.

meaning: “Long time no see!” / “Haven’t seen you in a long time.”
additional_notes: Used as a friendly greeting when you meet someone again after a long time. You can say it on its own (“Lange nicht gesehen!”) or add a name (“Lange nicht gesehen, mein Freund.”). In a normal sentence you often use it with “sich sehen”: “Wir haben uns lange nicht gesehen.”
target_language_example: Hey, lange nicht gesehen! Wie geht's dir?
native_language_example: Hey, long time no see! How are you?

additional_notes: Usually used in questions as **wie lange seid ihr …?** (“how long have you been …?”). **seid** is the 2nd person plural form of **sein** (to be) in the present tense, often used with **schon** (“already”) to ask about duration: *Wie lange seid ihr schon hier?*
target_language_example: Wie lange seid ihr schon in Berlin?
native_language_example: How long have you been in Berlin?

additional_notes: Used to talk about having to wait for a long period. Common in questions like „Muss ich lange warten?“ (= Will I have to wait long?). You can also use it with „lassen“: „jemanden lange warten lassen“ = to keep someone waiting for a long time.
target_language_example: Wir mussten am Bahnhof lange warten.
native_language_example: We had to wait a long time at the train station.

additional_notes: Usually used with the preposition **vor**: **vor langer Zeit** = “a long time ago.” You can modify it: **vor nicht allzu langer Zeit** = “not too long ago,” **vor sehr langer Zeit** = “a very long time ago.” With **vor**, **Zeit** is in the dative: **vor langer Zeit** (not *vor lange Zeit*).
target_language_example: Vor langer Zeit habe ich hier gewohnt.
native_language_example: A long time ago, I lived here.

additional_notes: Means hair length in general (not a single strand). Often used with the verb „haben“ (to have): „Er/Sie hat langes Haar.“ In German, „Haar“ can be singular when talking about someone’s hair overall; for one individual hair you’d typically say „ein Haar“.
target_language_example: Sie hat langes Haar und trägt es oft offen.
native_language_example: She has long hair and often wears it down.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to slow down their speech (common when you’re learning German). Often appears in questions like „Kannst du/Können Sie … langsamer sprechen?“ You can soften it with „ein bisschen“ (a bit) or „etwas“ (somewhat).
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, könnten Sie bitte langsamer sprechen?
native_language_example: Excuse me, could you please speak more slowly?

additional_notes: "Lass" is the informal (du) imperative of "lassen" + "dich" (you, accusative). Often used with another verb to mean "don’t let yourself ..." / "let yourself ..." (e.g., "Lass dich nicht abschießen" = don’t let them shoot you down / knock you out). With "in Ruhe" it means "leave you alone" ("Ich lass dich in Ruhe."). In "Lass dich gehen!" it means "let yourself go" (stop controlling yourself / relax your behavior).
target_language_example: Lass dich nicht stressen.
native_language_example: Don’t let yourself get stressed.

additional_notes: Imperative (command) with du: "Lass es …" = "Let it … / Leave it …". Often followed by an infinitive ("Lass es Tom tragen" = let Tom carry it). As a standalone phrase ("Lass es!" / "Lass es bleiben!") it commonly means "Stop it" or "Don’t do it". For other people you’ll hear: "Lass(t) es" (ihr), "Lassen Sie es" (formal).
target_language_example: Lass es einfach so, wie es ist.
native_language_example: Just leave it the way it is.

additional_notes: A friendly phrase said to someone who is about to eat or is eating. Literally “let it taste good to you,” but used like “Enjoy!” or “Bon appétit.” Common in informal, everyday situations (at home, with friends, in casual settings).
target_language_example: Hier ist dein Essen—lass es dir schmecken!
native_language_example: Here’s your food—enjoy your meal!

additional_notes: Common request meaning “please tell me when you know” or “keep me informed.” Often followed by a clause with „wenn …“ (“if/when …”), e.g., „Lass es mich wissen, wenn du Zeit hast.“ You can also use the polite form: „Lassen Sie es mich wissen.“
target_language_example: Lass es mich wissen, sobald du angekommen bist.
native_language_example: Let me know as soon as you arrive.

additional_notes: Imperative (du-form) of **lassen** + **ihn** (him). Common patterns: **Lass ihn + infinitive** ("Let him do ...": *Lass ihn mal Luft holen.*), **Lass ihn los!** ("Let him go!"), **Lass ihn in Ruhe!** ("Leave him alone!"). Often used to tell someone to stop interfering or to allow a man/boy to do something.
target_language_example: Lass ihn in Ruhe, er ist müde.
native_language_example: Leave him alone, he's tired.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to allow you to do something or to stop interfering. Often followed by an infinitive (e.g., „… zuerst sprechen“, „… etwas sagen“). With „in Ruhe/in Frieden“ it means “please leave me alone” (e.g., „Lass mich bitte in Frieden/ in Ruhe essen!“).
target_language_example: Lass mich bitte kurz erklären, was passiert ist.
native_language_example: Please let me briefly explain what happened.

meaning: "let me (do something) to/for you" (talking to one person).
additional_notes: Used with a verb right after it: "Lass mich dich + VERB" (e.g., fragen, fahren, umarmen, einladen). "Lass" is the informal imperative (du). For a formal version (Sie), you’d say: "Lassen Sie mich Sie …".
target_language_example: Lass mich dich kurz anrufen.
native_language_example: Let me call you briefly.

additional_notes: Uses the informal imperative of **lassen** (“lass…”, with **du**) + **mich** (“me”) + **dir** (“to you”). It’s typically followed by an infinitive phrase: **Lass mich dir etwas zeigen/geben/erklären**. In English you usually just say “Let me show/tell you …” (the “to you” is implied).
target_language_example: Lass mich dir kurz erklären, wie das funktioniert.
native_language_example: Let me quickly explain to you how that works.

additional_notes: An imperative (command) meaning you want someone to stop bothering you and go away. Often sounds annoyed or angry depending on tone; you can soften it with “bitte” or “Entschuldigung” (e.g., “Bitte, lass mich in Ruhe.”). Grammatically it’s “lass” = (du) imperative of “lassen” + “mich” (me) + “in Ruhe” (in peace/quiet).
target_language_example: Lass mich in Ruhe, ich muss arbeiten.
native_language_example: Leave me alone, I have to work.

additional_notes: Imperative of "lassen" + "mich" + "los". Used when someone is holding you (physically or figuratively) and you want them to release you. Can be polite with "bitte" or very rude with insults (e.g., "du Hund"). Also appears as "Lass mich in Ruhe" (“leave me alone”) with a slightly different meaning.
target_language_example: Hey, lass mich los! Das tut weh.
native_language_example: Hey, let go of me! That hurts.

additional_notes: Used to ask for a moment to do something yourself (look, check, try, etc.). The particle "mal" doesn’t mean "once" here; it softens the request and makes it sound casual and friendly (often like “just/quickly”). Common in spoken German.
target_language_example: Lass mich mal kurz nachsehen, ob das stimmt.
native_language_example: Let me quickly check if that’s correct.

additional_notes: Imperative form of **lassen** + **sie**. Used to tell someone to allow something to happen (**Lass sie sagen, was sie wollen.** = Let them say what they want) or to not hold on / to release or leave someone/something somewhere (**Lass sie los!** = Let her/them go; **Lass sie hier.** = Leave her/them here; **Lass sie raus.** = Let her/them out). **sie** can mean **her** or **them**, depending on context.
target_language_example: Lass sie in Ruhe, sie ist müde.
native_language_example: Leave her alone, she's tired.

additional_notes: Used to make a suggestion for doing something together. It’s the imperative form of "lassen" + "uns" and is usually followed by an infinitive: "Lass uns gehen." (= Let’s go.) In more formal contexts, "Lassen Sie uns …" is used instead.
target_language_example: Lass uns später telefonieren.
native_language_example: Let’s talk on the phone later.

additional_notes: Used to suggest leaving or starting to go somewhere. It’s a common, casual-sounding imperative: "lass" (let) + "uns" (us) + "gehen" (go). Often said with "komm" (“come on”) or "dann" (“then”).
target_language_example: Es wird spät—lass uns gehen.
native_language_example: It’s getting late—let’s go.

additional_notes: Formal (polite) command with "Sie". Often used as an imperative meaning "allow/let" + infinitive (e.g., "Lassen Sie ihn gehen" = "Let him go") or "leave" something in a state/place ("Lassen Sie das Fenster offen" = "Leave the window open"). In phrases like "Lassen Sie … los!", it means "Let go of …!".
target_language_example: Lassen Sie mich bitte kurz erklären.
native_language_example: Please let me explain briefly.

additional_notes: Used with a following infinitive to politely offer to do something or ask permission: „Lassen Sie es mich + Verb“ (e.g., erklären, wissen, holen). Very common in formal situations (with „Sie“). In the sense of “tell me,” it often appears as „Lassen Sie es mich wissen“ (“Let me know”).
target_language_example: Lassen Sie es mich kurz zusammenfassen.
native_language_example: Let me summarize it briefly.

additional_notes: Formal command (to one person) using **Sie**. With another verb it means **let him + verb** (e.g., *lassen Sie ihn leben* = let him live). On its own (*Lassen Sie ihn!*) it often means **leave him alone / stop it / don’t touch him**. Uses **ihn** (accusative = “him”).
target_language_example: Lassen Sie ihn in Ruhe!
native_language_example: Leave him alone!

additional_notes: Used with **Sie** (formal “you”) to ask permission or insist on being allowed to do something: **Lassen Sie mich + infinitive** (often with *nur* = “just” for emphasis). It can also be used as a request to stop bothering you: **Lassen Sie mich (in Ruhe)!** (“Leave me alone!”).
target_language_example: Lassen Sie mich bitte kurz erklären, was passiert ist.
native_language_example: Please let me briefly explain what happened.

additional_notes: Used in polite/formal situations ("Sie") to offer help, introduce someone, share information, congratulate, etc. It’s usually followed by an infinitive clause: "Lassen Sie mich Ihnen helfen / etwas zeigen / gratulieren / berichten". Often translates naturally as "Let me help you / Let me introduce…" rather than word-for-word.
target_language_example: Lassen Sie mich Ihnen den Weg zeigen.
native_language_example: Let me show you the way.

additional_notes: Used with "Sie" to make a formal, polite request for permission or access. Often followed by an infinitive (e.g., "sehen", "hinein", "durch"). In everyday speech you also hear the informal version "Lass mich bitte…" (to one person) or "Lasst mich bitte…" (to a group).
target_language_example: Lassen Sie mich bitte kurz erklären, was passiert ist.
native_language_example: Please let me briefly explain what happened.

additional_notes: A strong, direct request (often a complaint) telling someone to stop bothering you. Uses formal "Sie" (to a stranger, customer/service situations, or someone you address politely). The verb "lassen" + object means "to let/leave"; "in Ruhe" means "in peace/alone". Tone depends on context but is often irritated.
target_language_example: Entschuldigen Sie, aber lassen Sie mich in Ruhe.
native_language_example: Excuse me, but leave me alone.

meaning: formal: “take/get (something done/for yourself)” or, with *Zeit*, “take your time.”
additional_notes: This is the polite imperative of **sich lassen**. It often introduces a reflexive construction where *Sie* is the person affected: **Lassen Sie sich Zeit.** = “Take your time.” With a verb in the infinitive, it can mean “have/get something done”: **Lassen Sie sich die Haare schneiden.** It can also be used to urge someone to come up with an idea: **Lassen Sie sich etwas einfallen!** (“Think of something!”).
target_language_example: Lassen Sie sich ruhig Zeit, ich warte hier.
native_language_example: Take your time, I’ll wait here.

additional_notes: Formal/polite phrase used when speaking to one person or a group with „Sie“. Common uses: (1) requests like „Lassen Sie uns wissen, …“ = “Let us know …”; (2) asking for permission or release: „Lassen Sie uns raus!“ = “Let us out!”; (3) asking someone to leave you alone: „Lassen Sie uns allein.“ = “Leave us alone.”
target_language_example: Lassen Sie uns kurz darüber sprechen.
native_language_example: Let’s talk about it briefly.

meaning: to have something done (by someone); to let someone do something.
additional_notes:
More idiomatic patterns are usually „etwas machen lassen“ or „jemanden etwas machen lassen“; the fixed phrase „lassen machen“ can occur when „machen“ stands in for a more specific action (like „reparieren“, „schneiden“, etc.).
- „lassen“ is the verb you conjugate: Ich lasse…, du lässt…, er/sie lässt…
- Meaning often equals English “have (something) done”: „Ich lasse mein Auto reparieren.“ = “I’m having my car repaired.”
- The other verb in the infinitive goes to the end of the clause.
target_language_example: Ich lasse das machen.
native_language_example: I’ll have that done.

meaning: let us / allow us; also (with reflexive use) “have something done for us” or “let ourselves …” depending on structure
additional_notes:
"lassen" + "uns" can express different meanings depending on the construction:
- "Sie lassen uns singen" = "They let/allow us to sing" (lassen + infinitive).
- "Wir lassen uns ein Zimmer geben" = "We have/get a room given to us" (arrange for something to be done for us).
- Reflexive feel: "Wir lassen uns treiben" = "We let ourselves drift".
- Fixed phrase: "sich scheiden lassen" = "to get divorced" ("Wir lassen uns scheiden").
target_language_example: Sie lassen uns singen, tanzen und lächeln.
native_language_example: They let us sing, dance, and smile.

additional_notes: This corresponds to the verb phrase *lassen* + *uns* + infinitive (*gehen*) and can be translated literally as “let us go.” In everyday German, the idiomatic/informal version is usually **„Lass uns gehen.“** (to someone you address as *du*). **„Lassen uns gehen“** without **„Sie“** is uncommon as a standalone sentence in standard German, but it can appear as a quoted or intentionally stylized phrase.
target_language_example: Es ist spät; lassen uns gehen.
native_language_example: It’s late; let’s go.

additional_notes: Imperative of **lassen** for **ihr** (talking to several people): **Lasst + ihn + (verb)**. Often used to tell others to allow him to do something (**Lasst ihn ausreden!** = let him finish speaking) or to stop holding/bugging him (**Lasst ihn los!** = let him go).
target_language_example: Lasst ihn in Ruhe!
native_language_example: Leave him alone!

additional_notes: Imperative of **lassen** addressed to **more than one person** (ihr-form): *Lasst mich …* = “(you all) let me …”. Often followed by an infinitive (*Lasst mich euch helfen.*). It can also mean “leave me (alone)” in fixed phrases like **Lasst mich in Ruhe!** (“Leave me alone!”). Related forms: **Lass mich …** (to one person), **Lassen Sie mich …** (formal).
target_language_example: Lasst mich das kurz erklären.
native_language_example: Let me explain that briefly.

additional_notes: "Lasst" is the imperative (command/request form) of "lassen" for "ihr" (you plural). It’s used to suggest doing something together (like English “let’s”), or to ask someone to allow “us” to do something ("Lasst uns rein" = “Let us in”). More formal/neutral alternatives are "Lassen wir …" (let’s …) or "Lassen Sie uns …" (formal “let’s/let us …”).
target_language_example: Lasst uns eine Pause machen.
native_language_example: Let’s take a break.

meaning: to let something/someone continue; to leave something running; to let someone go (free).
additional_notes: Literally “to let run,” but usage is broader. Common uses: (1) not intervening / letting a situation continue: „Ich werde das laufen lassen.“ (2) letting someone go/releasing them: „Ich werde dich laufen lassen.“ (3) making someone run (e.g., drills/training): „Er hat uns die Hügel rauf und runter laufen lassen.“ Also used for leaving machines/programs running: „den Motor/Computer laufen lassen.“
target_language_example: Willst du die Sache einfach so weiter laufen lassen?
native_language_example: Do you just want to let the matter continue like this?

additional_notes: Means music played at a high volume. "laut" changes its ending to match the noun: "laute Musik" (with no article) / "die laute Musik" (with an article). Often used when complaining about noise (e.g., "Laute Musik geht mir auf den Geist" = loud music annoys me).
target_language_example: Kannst du die laute Musik bitte leiser machen?
native_language_example: Can you please turn the loud music down?

additional_notes: Imperative of "lassen" + "mich". Used to ask for permission or to insist you should be allowed to do something (often followed by an infinitive: „Laß mich … machen/helfen/zusammenfassen“). Spelling: „Lass mich“ is the common modern spelling; „Laß mich“ is older.
target_language_example: Laß mich kurz zusammenfassen, was passiert ist!
native_language_example: Let me briefly sum up what happened!

additional_notes: Used when you may not see the person again, or to sound serious/poetic. It can also be used sarcastically/insultingly depending on tone (e.g., “Leb wohl, Loser.”). Literally means “live well.”
target_language_example: Leb wohl, und pass gut auf dich auf.
native_language_example: Farewell, and take good care of yourself.

additional_notes: Used with the formal pronoun **Sie** when speaking politely to strangers, customers, etc. It’s often a yes/no question: **Leben Sie in Berlin?** = “Do you live in Berlin?” You can also use it in other question patterns, e.g. **Seit wann leben Sie in …?** = “Since when have you lived in …?”
target_language_example: Leben Sie in Deutschland oder in Österreich?
native_language_example: Do you live in Germany or in Austria?

additional_notes: Used to say where someone (or an animal) lives. Often interchangeable with "wohnen in" for people ("leben" can sound a bit more general). With a place (location), "in" is usually followed by the dative: "in Berlin", "in der Ukraine".
target_language_example: Wir leben in Hamburg.
native_language_example: We live in Hamburg.

meaning: 'do you live' / 'are you living' (addressing one person as 'du').
additional_notes: Used to ask about someone’s place or way of living. Common in questions like "Lebst du in …?" (Do you live in …?), "Lebst du allein?" (Do you live alone?), or "Lebst du hier gerne?" (Do you like living here?). Because it uses "du", it’s for informal situations (friends, family, kids).
target_language_example: Lebst du schon lange in Berlin?
native_language_example: Have you lived in Berlin for a long time?

additional_notes: Used with a place (city/country/village) to say where someone lives. You can also use it figuratively: „in ihrer eigenen Welt“ = 'in her own world' (not paying attention to reality). Grammar note: „lebt“ is 3rd-person singular of „leben“ (to live). The preposition „in“ takes dative for location: in Bagdad / in England / in dem Dorf (often shortened to „im Dorf“), in einer kleinen Stadt.
target_language_example: Meine Schwester lebt in Berlin.
native_language_example: My sister lives in Berlin.

additional_notes: Used to say where someone lives, followed by a noun phrase in the dative case: "in einem + (dative)". With masculine/neuter nouns you often hear the contraction "im" (= "in dem") for a specific place (e.g., "Er lebt im Haus" = in the house), while "in einem" is more like "in a" (one of many).
target_language_example: Sie lebt in einem kleinen Dorf.
native_language_example: She lives in a small village.

additional_notes: Literally “live well,” used as a formal or dramatic farewell. Grammatically it’s the imperative for plural “ihr” (speaking to more than one person); the singular form is “Leb wohl!” (to one person). In modern everyday speech, people more often say “Tschüss” or “Auf Wiedersehen.”
target_language_example: Lebt wohl, meine Freunde, und passt auf euch auf.
native_language_example: Farewell, my friends, and take care of yourselves.

meaning: “Kiss my ass!” (a very rude way to say “fuck off”).
additional_notes: A highly vulgar insult/exclamation used to express anger, contempt, or refusal. Often said as a standalone outburst, or directed at someone (e.g., with “du …”). Avoid in polite situations; it can easily escalate conflict.
target_language_example: Leck mich am Arsch, ich mache das sicher nicht!
native_language_example: Kiss my ass—I'm definitely not doing that!

additional_notes: "Legen Sie" is the formal (Sie) imperative of "legen" and is used when speaking politely to one person (or to a group). It often takes an object: "Legen Sie das Telefon weg" = “Put the phone away,” "Legen Sie es auf den Tisch" = “Put it on the table.” Common fixed phrases: "Legen Sie los" = “Get started,” and reflexive "Legen Sie sich hin" = “Lie down.”
target_language_example: Legen Sie bitte Ihre Tasche auf den Stuhl.
native_language_example: Please put your bag on the chair.

additional_notes: Formal command using **Sie**. Often used with the separable particle **hin**: **Legen Sie sich (hin)!** = “Lie down!” You can add where/how with **auf + accusative**: **auf den Bauch** (on your stomach), **auf die linke Seite** (on your left side), **auf die Liege** (onto the examination table).
target_language_example: Bitte legen Sie sich (hin) und entspannen Sie sich.
native_language_example: Please lie down and relax.

additional_notes: Past tense (Präteritum) of **es ablehnen** = “to refuse/decline.” **es** refers to the offer/request/idea (like “it” in English). Often followed by **zu + infinitive**: *Er lehnte es ab, ...* = “He refused to ...”.
target_language_example: Ich lehnte es ab, noch länger zu warten.
native_language_example: I refused to wait any longer.

additional_notes: "leichter" is the comparative form of "leicht". Use it with "als" to compare two things: X ist leichter als Y. It can mean physical weight ("lighter") or difficulty ("easier"), depending on context. Often used with intensifiers like "viel": "viel leichter als ...".
target_language_example: Deutsch ist für mich leichter als Französisch.
native_language_example: German is easier for me than French.

meaning: to like someone; to be fond of someone.
additional_notes: Used mainly in the pattern **jemanden leiden mögen** (= to like someone as a person). It’s a fairly common, slightly old-fashioned/colloquial way to say you like someone (not romantic). The person you like is in the accusative: **Er mag sie leiden.** Don’t translate it word-for-word from **leiden** (“to suffer”)—together it has a different meaning.
target_language_example: Ich habe dir ja gesagt, dass er dich leiden mag.
native_language_example: I told you that he likes you.

additional_notes: Used to give a polite, regretful “no” or to say that something isn’t possible/true. Often answers a question on its own (“Leider nicht.”). You can also insert it before the verb/phrase you’re negating: “Ich kann leider nicht kommen.”
target_language_example: Hast du heute Zeit? Leider nicht, ich muss arbeiten.
native_language_example: Do you have time today? Unfortunately not, I have to work.

additional_notes: Used with problems, illnesses, shortages, or bad conditions (often a noun). Can describe both people and things/places. Basic pattern: jemand/etwas leidet unter + Dativ (e.g., unter Wassermangel, unter Zahnschmerzen, unter Gedächtnisverlust). Note: the dictionary form is "(jemand/etwas) leidet unter"; other conjugations include "leide/leiden/litt/hat gelitten".
target_language_example: Dieses Gebiet leidet unter Wassermangel.
native_language_example: This area suffers from a water shortage.

meaning: "Will you lend me …?" / "Can you lend me …?"
additional_notes: A common way to ask someone informally (du) to lend you something. It uses the verb "leihen" (to lend/borrow); here it means "lend" because the speaker is receiving the item. Structure: "Leihst du mir + thing (+ for how long)?" You can add "mal" to sound more casual: "Leihst du mir mal …?"
target_language_example: Leihst du mir dein Handy für einen Moment?
native_language_example: Can you lend me your phone for a moment?

additional_notes: Question form of the verb **lernen** (“to learn/study”) with **du** (“you”, informal singular). Used to ask what someone is learning or whether they are currently studying. Often followed by what is being learned (e.g., **Englisch**) or a time expression (e.g., **gerade**, **wann**).
target_language_example: Lernst du gerade für die Prüfung?
native_language_example: Are you studying for the exam right now?

meaning: "you learn / one learns" (general statement with man).
additional_notes: Used with the impersonal pronoun **man** to talk about what people generally learn or how something is learned (similar to English generic “you”). Common in explanations and questions: **Wie lernt man ...?** = “How do you/does one learn ...?” In subordinate clauses it becomes **..., lernt man ...** or **..., dass man ... lernt** depending on the sentence.
target_language_example: Eine Sprache lernt man am besten, wenn man jeden Tag ein bisschen übt.
native_language_example: You learn a language best if you practice a little every day.

additional_notes: "Lesen" is the verb “to read.” "Sie" is the formal/polite “you” used with strangers, customers, or in official contexts. With an exclamation mark or context, it’s usually a request/command: "Lesen Sie …!" (= “Please read …!”). With a question mark, it’s a question: "Lesen Sie …?" (= “Do you read …?”).
target_language_example: Lesen Sie bitte diese E-Mail.
native_language_example: Please read this email.

additional_notes: Commonly used with "lernen" (to learn) and "können" (to be able to), often to say someone is literate or can read/write a particular language: "Deutsch/Japanisch/Französisch lesen und schreiben". In some contexts it can also simply mean the activities of reading and writing (e.g., poems, emails).
target_language_example: Ich kann Deutsch lesen und schreiben, aber ich spreche es nicht so gut.
native_language_example: I can read and write German, but I don’t speak it that well.

additional_notes: Used when it’s the final time something can happen or be done successfully. Often appears with possessives (meine/deine/unsere/ihre letzte Chance) or with "noch eine letzte Chance geben" (= to give someone one last chance).
target_language_example: Wenn wir den Zug verpassen, ist das unsere letzte Chance heute.
native_language_example: If we miss the train, that’s our last chance today.

additional_notes: Means the night before today. Often used without a preposition: „letzte Nacht“ (= last night), like other time expressions (e.g., „letzte Woche“). It can be placed early or later in the sentence.
target_language_example: Ich habe letzte Nacht kaum geschlafen.
native_language_example: I hardly slept last night.

additional_notes: Means the week before the current one. Very common time expression; it can go at the beginning or later in the sentence: „Letzte Woche habe ich …“ / „Ich habe letzte Woche …“. Usually no preposition is needed.
target_language_example: Letzte Woche war ich krank und bin zu Hause geblieben.
native_language_example: Last week I was sick and stayed at home.

meaning: “last week in” (talking about something that happened in a place last week).
additional_notes: Used to combine a past time expression (letzte Woche) with a place introduced by in. With a location (being/occurring there), in usually takes the dative: in Boston, in Potsdam, in Kyōto. (If it meant motion “into”, it would typically use accusative.) Often appears in sentences about travel or events: „Was ist letzte Woche in … passiert?“
target_language_example: Was ist letzte Woche in Berlin passiert?
native_language_example: What happened last week in Berlin?

additional_notes: Used to talk about the final outcome after everything has happened (often after delays, difficulties, or uncertainty). Commonly placed at the beginning of a sentence for emphasis: "Letzten Endes ...".
target_language_example: Letzten Endes war es die richtige Entscheidung.
native_language_example: In the end, it was the right decision.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened in the previous month. It’s the accusative form of the time phrase (like "letzte Woche", "letztes Jahr"). Common word order: "Ich war letzten Monat in Berlin" or "Letzten Monat war ich in Berlin."
target_language_example: Letzten Monat habe ich einen neuen Job angefangen.
native_language_example: Last month I started a new job.

additional_notes: Common way to say a specific day in the recent past. Uses the adjective ending: letzter → letzten before masculine days like Montag (accusative/time expression: "letzten Montag"). Similar: letzten Dienstag, letzten Freitag, etc. Not the same as "am Montag" (on Monday, could be past or future depending on context).
target_language_example: Letzten Montag hatte ich frei.
native_language_example: Last Monday I had the day off.

additional_notes: A common time expression meaning the summer of the previous year/season. Usually used without an article (not *im letzten Sommer*). You can use it as an adverbial of time: *Ich war letzten Sommer in Berlin.*
target_language_example: Letzten Sommer habe ich Deutsch gelernt.
native_language_example: Last summer I learned German.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the Sunday of the previous week. Often used without a preposition at the start of a sentence as a time expression (accusative): „Letzten Sonntag …“. You can also say „am letzten Sonntag“ (more like “on the last Sunday / this past Sunday,” depending on context).
target_language_example: Letzten Sonntag habe ich meine Großeltern besucht.
native_language_example: Last Sunday I visited my grandparents.

additional_notes: Refers to the year before the current one. Often used without an article: „letztes Jahr“ (= last year). With a preposition you usually use an article and adjective ending: „im letzten Jahr“ (= in the last year / last year).
target_language_example: Letztes Jahr bin ich nach Berlin gezogen.
native_language_example: Last year I moved to Berlin.

meaning: "last year in" (referring to being in a place during the previous year).
additional_notes: Used to indicate where someone was last year. Commonly used with a form of "sein" (war/warst/waren) and followed by a city/country: "Ich war letztes Jahr in …". The phrase is compositional: "letztes Jahr" (last year) + "in" (in/at) + place.
target_language_example: Ich war letztes Jahr in Boston.
native_language_example: I was in Boston last year.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the previous occasion something happened: "letztes Mal" = last time (before now). Often appears without an article: "Ich hatte letztes Mal ein Problem." You can also say "ein letztes Mal" = one last time / for the last time (often with "noch": "noch ein letztes Mal" = one last time, again).
target_language_example: Können wir das wie letztes Mal machen?
native_language_example: Can we do it like last time?

additional_notes: Used to talk about the most recent weekend in the past. Often placed at the beginning of the sentence for emphasis (then the verb comes second): "Letztes Wochenende habe ich..." It can also appear later in the sentence: "Ich war letztes Wochenende..."
target_language_example: Letztes Wochenende haben wir einen Film gesehen.
native_language_example: Last weekend we watched a movie.

meaning: to love; to be fond of (someone).
additional_notes: Used mostly for people, pets, or things you feel affection for. Often sounds a bit more gentle/childlike than "lieben" (which can sound stronger or more romantic). Frequently appears in the conjugated pattern "jdn. lieb haben" (e.g., "Ich hab dich lieb"), but the infinitive is "lieb haben".
target_language_example: Ich werde dich immer lieb haben.
native_language_example: I will always love you.

additional_notes: Used to compare two things and say you like or prefer the first one more. Common with verbs like **mögen** (to like): **Ich mag A lieber als B.** You can also use it with **haben**/**essen**/**trinken** etc. when expressing preference.
target_language_example: Ich esse Pizza lieber als Pasta.
native_language_example: I prefer pizza to pasta.

additional_notes: "Liebst du ...?" is the 2nd-person singular present-tense question form of "lieben" (to love). It’s used with a direct object in the accusative (often a name or pronoun: "Liebst du ihn/sie?"). It can be about people (romantic love) and also about things/activities in the sense of really liking or loving them (e.g., "Liebst du schwarzen Humor?").
target_language_example: Liebst du Musik oder hörst du sie nur nebenbei?
native_language_example: Do you love music, or do you just listen to it in the background?

additional_notes: A direct question using the verb **lieben** (to love). **du** is informal singular "you" (used with friends/partners, not in formal situations). You’ll often hear it with adverbs like **auch** (too), **wirklich** (really), or **noch** (still): *Liebst du mich noch?* = "Do you still love me?"
target_language_example: Liebst du mich noch?
native_language_example: Do you still love me?

additional_notes: Present-tense verb phrase: "liebt" is the 3rd-person singular of "lieben" (to love). "dich" means "you" (accusative, used as the direct object). Used when talking about someone else’s feelings toward the person you’re speaking to.
target_language_example: Sie liebt dich wirklich.
native_language_example: She really loves you.

additional_notes: "liebt" is the 3rd-person singular form of "lieben" (to love). "mich" means "me" (accusative). Used to say someone/something loves you; can be romantic (a person) or affectionate (a pet).
target_language_example: Ich glaube, er liebt mich.
native_language_example: I think he loves me.

meaning: to be due to; to be because of.
additional_notes: Used with a thing or reason in the dative: „an + Dativ“. Often with „es“ as the subject: „Es liegt an …“ (= It’s because of …). You can also use it for causes in general: „Das liegt am Wetter.“
target_language_example: Es kann an der schlechten Verbindung liegen, dass es so lange dauert.
native_language_example: It may be because of the bad connection that it’s taking so long.

meaning: to stay lying down; to remain in bed; to stay down (not get up).
additional_notes: Often used as an instruction (imperative): „Liegen bleiben!“ = “Stay down / Don’t get up,” for example when someone is injured, sick, or should not move. It can also be used more generally for something that remains lying where it is (e.g., an object left on the ground).
target_language_example: Du bist verletzt — liegen bleiben!
native_language_example: You’re injured—stay down!

meaning: to leave something behind; to leave something lying (and not take/pick it up).
additional_notes: Used when someone forgets an object somewhere (often accidentally): „Ich habe meinen Ausweis im Hotel liegen lassen.“ It can also mean leaving someone/something where it is and not helping or moving it: „Wir können ihn nicht einfach so liegen lassen.“ Grammar: usually with an object in the accusative (etw. liegen lassen).
target_language_example: Ich habe mein Handy im Café liegen lassen.
native_language_example: I left my phone behind at the café.

meaning: "is lying on the table" / "is on the table" (for an object).
additional_notes: Used with the verb **liegen** to describe where something is (its position). **liegen** is for things that are lying/placed flat (book, newspaper, wallet). Change the verb for other positions: **steht auf dem Tisch** (standing/upright), **sitzt auf dem Tisch** (a person/animal sitting).
target_language_example: Mein Handy liegt auf dem Tisch.
native_language_example: My phone is on the table.

meaning: is dying; is close to death.
additional_notes: Used with a person or animal to say they are currently in the process of dying (often a serious/urgent situation). It can also be used figuratively for something that is failing and about to stop working (e.g., a device, a system). Grammar: "liegen" is conjugated (ich liege, du liegst, er/sie/es liegt, wir liegen, ihr liegt, sie liegen) + "im Sterben".
target_language_example: Der alte Hund liegt im Sterben, wir müssen sofort zum Tierarzt.
native_language_example: The old dog is dying; we need to go to the vet immediately.

additional_notes: Form of the verb "liegen" (to lie, to be located). Common patterns: 1) "etw. liegt in + Dativ" = something is found/contained in something (often abstract: "in der Natur von ..."). 2) "etw. liegt in jmds. Händen" = something is in someone’s hands / depends on them (often about fate, decisions, responsibility).
target_language_example: Die Lösung liegt in den Details.
native_language_example: The solution lies in the details.

additional_notes: Used when someone gets something temporarily and plans to give it back. Common patterns: **sich (Akk.) von + Dativ leihen** = to borrow (something) from (someone): *Sie lieh sich von ihm einen Bleistift.* With money you also hear **Geld bei + Dativ**: *Er lieh sich Geld bei seiner Familie.*
target_language_example: Er lieh sich Geld bei seiner Familie.
native_language_example: He borrowed money from his family.

meaning: "do you read" / "are you reading" (addressing one person).
additional_notes: Question form with verb first: "Liest du ...?" = "Do you read ...?" / "Are you reading ...?" It uses the present tense and can ask about a general habit ("Do you read...") or what someone is reading right now (often with words like "gerade"). Related forms: "du liest" = "you read/you are reading" (statement).
target_language_example: Liest du gerade ein interessantes Buch?
native_language_example: Are you reading an interesting book right now?

meaning: "(he/she/it) is reading a book" / "reads a book".
additional_notes: "liest" is the 3rd-person singular present tense of "lesen" (to read): er/sie/es liest. It can describe what someone is doing right now (present continuous in English) or a general habit, depending on context. Often followed by details like frequency ("ein Buch pro Woche") or topic ("ein Buch über ...").
target_language_example: Sie sitzt im Zug und liest ein Buch.
native_language_example: She’s sitting on the train reading a book.

additional_notes: "gerne" means "gladly/with pleasure" and is commonly used to say you like doing something: "Ich lese gerne" (I like reading). "liest" is the 3rd-person singular present tense of "lesen" (to read), used with er/sie/es (and names like Tom).
target_language_example: Meine Schwester liest gerne Krimis.
native_language_example: My sister likes reading crime novels.

additional_notes: Past tense (Präteritum) of "ich lasse ihn". Often used with an infinitive: "Ich ließ ihn + Verb" = I let him / made him / had him do something. It can mean permission (let) or instruction/arranging (had/made), and sometimes a cause: "Etwas ließ ihn ..." = something made him ... .
target_language_example: Ich ließ ihn die Rechnung bezahlen.
native_language_example: I made him pay the bill. / I had him pay the bill.

meaning: “let me / made me / left me” (simple past of "mich lassen").
additional_notes: "ließ" is the simple past of **lassen** (“to let; to make; to leave”). With **mich** (“me”), it often appears in patterns like: **jdn. + Infinitiv lassen** = “to let/make someone do something” (e.g., *ließ mich warten* = “made me wait”); **jdn. im Stich lassen** = “to abandon/let someone down” (e.g., *ließ mich im Stich*). It can also be used with **es** as the subject: **Es ließ mich ...** = “It made me ... / It caused me to ...” (e.g., *Es ließ mich an Tom denken*).
target_language_example: Der Chef ließ mich eine Stunde länger arbeiten.
native_language_example: The boss made me work an hour longer.

meaning: “could be / was possible (to do)” (often like a passive: “could be opened/answered”).
additional_notes: Past tense of the pattern **sich lassen + infinitive**. It’s used to say something is (not) doable/possible: **Die Tür ließ sich nicht öffnen.** = “The door couldn’t be opened.” With an object, it can also mean **to have something done for oneself**: **Sie ließ sich ein Kleid anfertigen.** = “She had a dress made (for herself).”
target_language_example: Der Fleck ließ sich nicht entfernen.
native_language_example: The stain couldn’t be removed.

additional_notes: Usually appears with articles and case endings: **am linken Arm** = “on/at the left arm” (an + dem, dative), **den linken Arm** = “the left arm” (accusative). Also used in the common exaggeration **(seinen) linken Arm geben/tauschen** (“to give/trade one’s left arm”) meaning you’d do almost anything for something.
target_language_example: Ich habe Schmerzen im linken Arm.
native_language_example: I have pain in my left arm.

additional_notes: Used when giving directions. Often appears with the verb "abbiegen" (to turn off): "links abbiegen" / "links ab". Common in imperative form: "Biegen Sie links ab!" (formal) or "Bieg links ab!" (informal).
target_language_example: Am Kreisverkehr bitte links ab.
native_language_example: At the roundabout, please turn left.

additional_notes: Used for giving directions while walking or driving. "links" = left, "abbiegen" = to turn (onto another street). Often used with places like "an der Ecke" (at the corner), "an der Ampel" (at the traffic light), or "an der ersten/nächsten" (at the first/next). In spoken directions, "bitte" makes it polite.
target_language_example: An der nächsten Ampel links abbiegen!
native_language_example: Turn left at the next traffic light!

meaning: 'is going on' / 'is happening' (what the matter is)
additional_notes: Most often appears in embedded clauses after "was" (and the verb comes last): "... was los ist" = "... what's going on" / "... what's wrong". Also common with "mit + Dativ": "... was mit ihm los ist" = "... what's wrong with him".
target_language_example: Ich will nur wissen, was los ist.
native_language_example: I just want to know what's going on.

meaning: to be going on; to be happening; (with people) to be wrong / the matter
additional_notes: Typically used with an impersonal or generic subject to ask what is happening or what the problem is: „Was ist los?“ / „Was ist mit dir los?“ Also used to describe how much activity there is: „Hier ist viel los.“ The core idea is that something is going on (often implying something unusual).
target_language_example: Was könnte hier los sein? Es ist ungewöhnlich still.
native_language_example: What could be going on here? It’s unusually quiet.

meaning: "Come on, come!" (urging someone to come or to hurry up).
additional_notes: Used to push someone to move/act, often with impatience or encouragement. You’ll often hear it as "Los, komm!" or "Los, komm schon!". "Los" is a very common spoken prompt meaning "Come on! / Let’s go!"; "komm" can mean "come here" or simply "come on" depending on context and tone.
target_language_example: Los, komm schon, wir sind spät!
native_language_example: Come on, hurry up—we're late!

additional_notes: "Los!" is a very common shout to urge someone to start moving or to do something faster. Repeating it ("los, los, los!") adds urgency or impatience, similar to "come on!" or "hurry up!" in English.
target_language_example: Los, los, los — wir müssen jetzt zum Bus!
native_language_example: Go, go, go — we have to get to the bus now!

additional_notes: Used to push/encourage someone to answer or say something now. Often followed by an object like „mir“ (me) and a question or statement: „Los, sag mir, was du siehst!“ Similar to „Komm schon, sag ...“. Common in spoken, casual German; can sound impatient depending on tone.
target_language_example: Los, sag mir endlich die Wahrheit!
native_language_example: Come on, tell me the truth already!

meaning: Come on, let's … / Come on, we …
additional_notes: Used to urge a group to act quickly or get moving. Very common in spoken German, often with an exclamation mark. You can replace "wir" with another subject (e.g., "Los, du!"), or follow "Los!" directly with an imperative ("Los, geh!").
target_language_example: Los, wir müssen jetzt los!
native_language_example: Come on, we have to go now!

meaning: to make fun of (someone); to mock.
additional_notes: Usually used as **sich über jemanden lustig machen** (reflexive). It takes **über + Akkusativ**: *über ihn / sie / mich / dich / uns / euch*. Word order can split the verb phrase in main clauses (e.g., *macht … lustig*), but the fixed expression is **lustig machen**.
target_language_example: Du solltest dich nicht über ihn lustig machen.
native_language_example: You shouldn’t make fun of him.

meaning: "will you let me …?" / "are you letting me …?"
additional_notes: Used with a following verb or phrase to ask for permission or to demand access/space. Common patterns: "Lässt du mich rein?" (let me in), "Lässt du mich auch mal?" (let me have a turn / let me do it too), "Lässt du mich sehen, was passiert." (let me see what happens). Word order: "Lässt du mich …?" = question; "Lass mich …" is the more direct imperative ("Let me …"). Not the same as "Du lässt mich" meaning "you leave me" in the sense of abandoning someone.
target_language_example: Lässt du mich kurz vorbei?
native_language_example: Will you let me pass for a moment?

meaning: “can be / can be done” (often: “is easy to”).
additional_notes: Used in the pattern **sich lassen + infinitive** to express possibility in a passive-like way: **Das lässt sich machen.** = “That can be done.” Often combined with adverbs like **einfach/leicht/schwer**: **Das lässt sich leicht erklären.** = “That’s easy to explain.” Note: **sich etwas entgehen lassen** is a separate idiom meaning “to miss out on something” (e.g., **Tom lässt sich den Spaß entgehen** = “Tom misses out on the fun”).
target_language_example: Das Problem lässt sich schnell lösen.
native_language_example: The problem can be solved quickly.

additional_notes: Used with “sich lassen” to express that something is possible or doable without much effort. Often followed by an infinitive at the end of the clause (e.g., vermeiden, herausfinden, beantworten, schneiden). With people, it can mean “is easily + past participle/adjective” (e.g., sich leicht ablenken lassen = to get distracted easily).
target_language_example: Das Problem lässt sich leicht lösen.
native_language_example: The problem can be solved easily.

meaning: "can’t be" / "won’t" (something is not possible or won’t work).
additional_notes: Used with **sich lassen** to express an impersonal, passive-like meaning: **X lässt sich nicht + infinitive** = “X can’t be + past participle / it’s not possible to + verb.” Common with things like **öffnen, machen, übersetzen**. Example: **Die Tür lässt sich nicht öffnen** = “The door won’t open / can’t be opened.” Note: it can also be used about people meaning “doesn’t like to be told” (e.g., **Er lässt sich nicht gern sagen...**).
target_language_example: Die Datei lässt sich nicht speichern.
native_language_example: The file can’t be saved.

meaning: 'are you running?' / 'do you run?' (to walk/run; 2nd person singular).
additional_notes: From the verb "laufen" (to run; also often used for walking). "Läufst du ...?" can ask about what someone is doing right now ("Are you running?"), or about a general preference/habit ("Do you run?"). With "herum/rum" it often means "to walk/run around": "Warum läufst du da allein herum?" = "Why are you walking around there alone?"
target_language_example: Läufst du jeden Morgen zur Arbeit?
native_language_example: Do you run to work every morning?

additional_notes: Imperative of the separable verb **aufmachen** (“to open”). Commonly used to tell someone to open a **door** (or window, etc.), often meaning “open up (the door)!” You can add **bitte** to make it more polite: *Bitte mach auf.*
target_language_example: Bitte mach auf, ich habe den Schlüssel vergessen.
native_language_example: Please open up, I forgot my key.

meaning: "get yourself …" / "start …" (imperative, usually followed by something like bereit, an die Arbeit, auf etw. gefasst).
additional_notes: Used as an imperative with „du“ (informal singular): „Mach dich + adjective/phrase“ = get yourself into a state / get ready. Very common patterns: „Mach dich bereit!“ (Get ready!), „Mach dich (wieder) an die Arbeit!“ (Get back to work!), „Mach dich auf etwas gefasst“ (Brace yourself for something). Note: In „Ich mach dich fertig!“ the „dich“ is a direct object (not reflexive) and means „I’ll finish you / I’ll mess you up“ (threatening/hostile).
target_language_example: Mach dich auf eine lange Nacht gefasst.
native_language_example: Brace yourself for a long night.

meaning: “(you) make yourself …” — used in fixed phrases like “don’t worry / don’t bother / don’t get your hopes up.”
additional_notes: “Mach dir …” is the informal (du) imperative of the reflexive verb construction “sich (etwas) machen”. It’s usually followed by a noun: “Mach dir (keine) Sorgen” (don’t worry), “Mach dir keine Mühe” (don’t bother / don’t go to the trouble), “Mach dir nicht zu viele Hoffnungen” (don’t get your hopes up), “Mach dir keinen Kopf” (don’t stress). Often used with “nicht/keine” to tell someone not to do something.
target_language_example: Mach dir keine Sorgen, ich melde mich später.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ll get in touch later.

additional_notes: Common reassuring phrase. Literally “make yourself no worries.” Often said alone, or followed by a short explanation (e.g., that something is okay or you can wait). Can also be used with extra details: „Mach dir keine Sorgen, ich kümmere mich darum.“
target_language_example: Mach dir keine Sorgen, das kriegen wir hin.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, we’ll manage it.

meaning: “Come on, do it already!” / “Just do it!” (urging someone to act).
additional_notes: Used to impatiently encourage someone to start or hurry up. Often said on its own, or with names: „Mach schon, …“. You’ll also hear it with „Los“ or „Jetzt“: „Los, mach schon!“ / „Jetzt mach schon!“
target_language_example: Mach schon, wir haben keine Zeit!
native_language_example: Come on, hurry up—we don’t have time!

additional_notes: Very common, friendly farewell in spoken German. "mach's" is short for "mach es" (imperative of "machen"). Often used at the end of a conversation, similar to "take care" or "all the best".
target_language_example: Ich muss los—mach's gut, bis morgen!
native_language_example: I have to go—take care, see you tomorrow!

additional_notes: Present-tense form of machen with ich. It often appears as mache ich when another element comes first (Das mache ich. / Morgen mache ich das.) or in questions like Was mache ich...? Depending on context, it can also express a planned future action. In some common expressions, it is better translated idiomatically, e.g. einen Spaziergang machen = take a walk.
target_language_example: Nach der Arbeit mache ich einen Spaziergang.
native_language_example: After work I take a walk.

meaning: to do whatever / to do what (someone wants).
additional_notes: Used with a comma before the relative clause introduced by **was** ("what/whatever"). Common pattern: **(etwas) machen, was + subject + verb** (e.g., **Du kannst machen, was du willst**). In the **was**-clause, the conjugated verb goes to the end: **was du willst**.
target_language_example: Du kannst machen, was du willst.
native_language_example: You can do whatever you want.

additional_notes: Used as a common sentence pattern: (Was) willst du machen, wenn du ...? = “What do you want to do when/if you …?” With future situations (wenn du erwachsen/groß bist) it usually means “when”. With hypothetical situations, especially with Konjunktiv II (würdest du ... wenn du ... hättest), it means “if”. In German, machen here often means “to do” (not “to make”).
target_language_example: Was würdest du machen, wenn du heute frei hättest?
native_language_example: What would you do if you had today off?

additional_notes: Formal/polite command using „Sie“ (like “do …, please” or “would you …”). Often appears with a complement: „Machen Sie weiter“ (continue), „Machen Sie die Tür auf“ (open the door), „Machen Sie eine Vorhersage“ (make a prediction), „Machen Sie es möglich“ (make it possible), „Machen Sie, was …“ (do what …). Many verbs with „machen“ are separable, so the prefix goes to the end: „machen … auf“, „machen … weiter“.
target_language_example: Machen Sie bitte das Fenster zu.
native_language_example: Please close the window.

meaning: formal command: “make/get yourself …” (into a certain state).
additional_notes: Used with a reflexive pronoun (sich) plus an adjective or phrase to tell someone what to do or how to be. Common patterns: „Machen Sie sich nützlich“ (make yourself useful), „Machen Sie sich (eine) Liste“ (make yourself a list), „Machen Sie es sich bequem“ / „Machen Sie sich bequem“ (make yourself comfortable), „Machen Sie sich fertig“ (get ready/finish getting dressed).
target_language_example: Machen Sie sich bereit, wir gehen gleich los.
native_language_example: Get ready, we’re leaving soon.

meaning: to have/get something done (by someone); to let someone do something.
additional_notes:
Used to express that you arrange for something to be done (often a service) instead of doing it yourself.
- Ich habe mir die Haare machen lassen. = I had my hair done.
It can also mean allowing someone else to do something:
- Du solltest es einen von uns machen lassen. = You should let one of us do it.
Typical structure: [object] + machen lassen (+ optional: von + person).
target_language_example: Ich habe gestern einen Ölwechsel machen lassen, weil ich das nicht selbst machen wollte.
native_language_example: Yesterday I had an oil change done because I didn’t want to do it myself.

additional_notes: From the verb "machen" (to do/make) + "wir" (we). Common in spoken German to agree on a plan or decide what to do next: "Dann machen wir das so" = “Then we’ll do it that way.” It can also be a short agreement/acceptance: "Ja, machen wir" = “Yes, let’s do it / yes, we will.” In questions it’s used to ask how to proceed: "Wie machen wir das?" = “How do we do that?/How should we do that?”
target_language_example: Okay, machen wir das morgen.
native_language_example: Okay, let’s do that tomorrow.

additional_notes: This is the Konjunktiv II form used to talk about something imagined, uncertain, or conditional: often in sentences with wenn (if) or in reported expectations ("I never thought he would..."). It can also sound more polite/soft in requests: „Hätten Sie etwas dagegen, wenn ich es später machen würde?“ = “Would you mind if I did it later?” In many contexts you can also say „machen würde“ where English uses “would do” rather than “would make,” depending on what „machen“ means in that sentence.
target_language_example: Ich hätte Angst, wenn ich das machen würde.
native_language_example: I would be scared if I did that.

additional_notes: Question form of du machst ("you do/make"). Used when speaking to one person informally. Because machen is very broad, the full sentence can mean do, make, turn on, etc., depending on the rest of the sentence.
target_language_example: Was machst du morgen?
native_language_example: What are you doing tomorrow?

meaning: “are you doing that?” / “do you do that?”
additional_notes: A very common yes/no question using verb-first word order (Machst …?). "du" = you (informal singular). "das" refers to something already known from context (“that/it”). Depending on context words like "morgen" (tomorrow) or "oft" (often), it can ask about the future or a habit. In "Wie machst du das?" it means “How do you do that?”.
target_language_example: Machst du das wirklich allein?
native_language_example: Are you really doing that alone?

meaning: used in common phrases meaning “do you worry (about)…?” or “do you care (about)…?”.
additional_notes:
Usually part of set expressions with a reflexive pronoun (dir = “to yourself”). Most common patterns:
- „(Worüber/Worum) machst du dir Sorgen?“ = “What are you worried about?”
- „Machst du dir was/nichts aus + Dativ?“ = “Do you like/care about …?” / “Do you mind …?” (e.g., „aus Süßigkeiten“).
On its own, „machst du dir“ is incomplete—you need the rest (Sorgen / was aus …, etc.).
target_language_example: Machst du dir Sorgen wegen der Prüfung?
native_language_example: Are you worried about the exam?

additional_notes: Used with a subject (a thing or activity) to say it’s fun: „X macht Spaß.“ Literally “makes fun,” but in natural English it’s “X is fun.” Common with activities in the infinitive: „Tanzen macht Spaß.“ You can also say „Es macht Spaß“ (“It’s fun”).
target_language_example: Mit Freunden zu kochen macht Spaß.
native_language_example: Cooking with friends is fun.

additional_notes: Present tense of "machen" with "das" as a demonstrative pronoun: "er/sie macht das". "das" refers to something already known from context (an action, habit, or task). Common in everyday speech to describe what someone does, often with frequency adverbs like "ständig", "immer wieder", or phrases like "die ganze Zeit".
target_language_example: Er macht das die ganze Zeit.
native_language_example: He does that all the time.

additional_notes: Form of **machen** (3rd person singular *macht* or imperative/plural *macht*) + **es**. Common uses: (1) **to do something**: *Sie macht es selbst.* / *Macht es doch selbst!* (2) **to do something in a certain way**: *Macht es auf diese Weise!* (3) **to make/cause an effect**: *Macht es einen Unterschied?* = “Does it make a difference?” (4) in patterns like **(jdm.) macht es Mühe, ...** = “(Someone) finds it difficult to ...”.
target_language_example: Macht es einen Unterschied?
native_language_example: Does it make a difference?

additional_notes: Present-tense form of "machen" used with "ihr" (you plural, informal). Common in questions to a group of friends/kids/teammates. Often means "do" (an activity): "Macht ihr Yoga?"; "make" (a sound/thing): "Wie macht ihr dieses Geräusch?"; or "make it a topic/issue": "Warum macht ihr das immer wieder zum Thema?" Not used for formal "you" ("Sie").
target_language_example: Was macht ihr heute Abend?
native_language_example: What are you doing tonight (you all)?

meaning: "makes me" (causes me to feel/ become something).
additional_notes: Used with an adjective (or sometimes a verb like verrückt machen) to say something causes a feeling/state: „X macht mich traurig/nervös/glücklich.“ It’s the 3rd-person singular of „machen“ (er/sie/es macht). You can swap the subject: „Das macht mich …“ (That makes me …), „Du machst mich …“ (You make me …).
target_language_example: Das kalte Wetter macht mich müde.
native_language_example: The cold weather makes me tired.

additional_notes: Used to say that something/someone makes you feel happy. Pattern: „(Etwas/Jemand) macht + mich/dich/ihn/sie/uns/euch/sie + glücklich.“ Related expression: „jemanden glücklich machen“ = to make someone happy. Note: „glücklich“ usually means “happy” (not “lucky”).
target_language_example: Zeit mit meiner Familie zu verbringen, macht mich glücklich.
native_language_example: Spending time with my family makes me happy.

additional_notes: Used with things, situations, thoughts, or people that frighten you. Pattern: „[X] macht mir Angst.“ = “X scares me.” You can change the pronoun: „macht dich/ihn/sie/uns/euch Angst“ or use the more common variant „macht mir Angst“ / „macht mir Angst, ...“ (with an infinitive clause). Also possible: „X macht mir Angst, weil ...“ (“because ...”).
target_language_example: Die Vorstellung, allein umzuziehen, macht mir Angst.
native_language_example: The idea of moving alone scares me.

meaning: “No problem / it doesn’t matter / never mind.”
additional_notes: Commonly used as a short response to say something is okay (e.g., after a mistake, an apology, or bad news).
