Common in emotional or emphatic phrases like **"Verschwindet aus meinem Leben!"** (“Get out of my life!”) and **"Willkommen in meinem Leben!"** (“Welcome to my life!”).
target_language_example: Ich möchte mehr aus meinem Leben machen.
native_language_example: I want to make more of my life.

additional_notes: Used when “my uncle” is the indirect object or follows certain prepositions. Common triggers: **gehören** (“to belong to”) → *Das gehört meinem Onkel.* and the preposition **mit** (“with”) → *mit meinem Onkel*. The possessive **mein-** takes the dative masculine/neuter ending **-em**: *meinem*.
target_language_example: Das Geschenk ist von meinem Onkel.
native_language_example: The gift is from my uncle.

additional_notes: "Meinem Sohn" is the dative form of "mein Sohn" and is used when your son is an indirect object (e.g., something belongs to him) or after certain prepositions like "von" (from/of) and expressions like "weg von" (away from). Compare: "mein Sohn" (nominative), "meinen Sohn" (accusative), "meinem Sohn" (dative).
target_language_example: Ich gebe meinem Sohn das Buch.
native_language_example: I give my son the book.

additional_notes: This is the dative case of "mein Vater". You use it after certain prepositions like "von" (from/by) and "bei" (at/with), and often for an indirect object (to/for whom something happens). In the examples: "von meinem Vater" = by my father; "bei meinem Vater" = at/with my father.
target_language_example: Ich helfe meinem Vater im Garten.
native_language_example: I help my father in the garden.

additional_notes: Used when the arm is the direct object of the verb (someone grabs, holds, hurts, or lets go of it). "meinen" is the masculine accusative form of "mein" (my); the nominative form is "mein Arm".
target_language_example: Bitte fass meinen Arm nicht an.
native_language_example: Please don't touch my arm.

additional_notes: Used after prepositions like **mit** (*mit meinen Augen* = “with my eyes”) and with some verbs that take the dative, especially **(jdm.) glauben** and **(jdm.) trauen** in phrases like **Ich kann meinen Augen nicht trauen/glauben** (“I can’t believe my eyes”). The base form is **meine Augen** (“my eyes”); **meinen Augen** is the dative form.
target_language_example: Ich kann meinen Augen nicht trauen.
native_language_example: I can’t believe my eyes.

meaning: "my letter" (in the accusative: something receives/gets "my letter").
additional_notes: "Meinen" is the possessive pronoun "my" with masculine accusative noun "Brief" (the thing being received: jemanden/etwas bekommen, erhalten). Note: German "Brief" usually means a letter (mail), not an English "brief" (short summary) — it’s a common false friend.
target_language_example: Ich habe meinen Brief schon abgeschickt.
native_language_example: I already sent my letter.

additional_notes: Used when "my brother" is the direct object of a verb (e.g., sehen, abholen). The base possessive is "mein" (my), which changes endings by case: "mein Bruder" (nominative), "meinen Bruder" (accusative).
target_language_example: Ich rufe meinen Bruder später an.
native_language_example: I’ll call my brother later.

meaning: to my parents / for my parents (dative plural of „meine Eltern“).
additional_notes: „Eltern“ means „parents“ (plural). „Meinen Eltern“ is the dative form and is used after verbs and prepositions that take the dative (e.g., „jemandem etwas sagen“ = to tell someone something; „jemandem gehorchen“ = to obey someone; „mit jemandem reden“ = to talk with someone). Note: „meine Eltern“ = my parents (nominative/accusative), but „meinen Eltern“ = to/for my parents (dative).
target_language_example: Ich habe meinen Eltern ein Foto geschickt.
native_language_example: I sent my parents a photo.

additional_notes: This is the accusative form of "mein Freund" (used after many verbs and prepositions, e.g., treffen, besuchen, für). In German, "mein Freund" can mean either a male friend or a boyfriend—context usually makes it clear. If you want to emphasize “just a friend,” people may say "ein Freund von mir" (a friend of mine).
target_language_example: Ich sehe meinen Freund heute Abend.
native_language_example: I'm seeing my friend (or my boyfriend) tonight.

meaning: 'my friends' (dative plural: 'to/for/with my friends', depending on the verb or preposition).
additional_notes: Used when the noun phrase is in the dative case. Common after certain verbs like "begegnen" (to meet/encounter someone) and after dative prepositions like "von" (from/by) and "vor" (in front of/before). In English you often still just say "my friends," but German marks the role with dative: "meinen Freunden" (not "meine Freunde").
target_language_example: Ich helfe meinen Freunden oft bei den Hausaufgaben.
native_language_example: I often help my friends with their homework.

additional_notes: Used when “my dog” is the direct object of the sentence (the dog is the one being fed, looked after, found, etc.). The base form is “mein Hund” (subject), but after many verbs and some prepositions you often need the accusative: “meinen Hund”.
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte meinen Hund kurz ausführen?
native_language_example: Can you please take my dog out for a short walk?

additional_notes: Used when "Job" is masculine and in the accusative case (e.g., after verbs like mögen, kündigen, verlieren). In the nominative you’d say "mein Job". "Job" is very common in everyday German; "Beruf" can sound a bit more formal/like a profession.
target_language_example: Ich brauche meinen Job, aber ich will weniger Stress.
native_language_example: I need my job, but I want less stress.

additional_notes: Used when “my children” is the indirect object (e.g., jemanden etwas sagen/geben = to say/give something to someone) or after dative prepositions like “mit” (mit meinen Kindern = with my children). “meinen” is the dative plural form of “mein-”.
target_language_example: Ich lese meinen Kindern jeden Abend eine Geschichte vor.
native_language_example: I read my children a story every evening.

additional_notes: This is the accusative form of "mein Mann" (my husband), used as the object of a verb: e.g., "Ich vermisse meinen Mann" = "I miss my husband." In German, "mein Mann" usually means "my husband" (not just "my boyfriend/partner"). It also appears in the idiom "seinen Mann stehen" (e.g., "Ich steh meinen Mann"), meaning "to hold your own / stand your ground."
target_language_example: Ich vermisse meinen Mann wirklich.
native_language_example: I really miss my husband.

additional_notes: Used when the passport is the direct object (something you show, present, lose, find, renew, etc.). It’s the accusative form of "mein Pass" → "meinen Pass" because "Pass" is masculine (der Pass). Common in travel/border situations: "meinen Pass zeigen/präsentieren", "meinen Pass verlieren", "meinen Pass erneuern lassen".
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, ich kann meinen Pass gerade nicht finden.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t find my passport right now.

additional_notes: Used when talking about advice you give. Common with verbs like „(jemandes) Rat hören“ (listen to someone’s advice), „auf meinen Rat hören“ (follow my advice), and „meinen Rat ignorieren“ (ignore my advice). Note: German „Rat“ means advice/counsel (not the animal “rat”).
target_language_example: Du musst nicht immer auf meinen Rat hören, aber denk wenigstens darüber nach.
native_language_example: You don’t always have to follow my advice, but at least think about it.

additional_notes: "Meinen Sohn" is used when "my son" is the direct object or follows a preposition that takes the accusative (e.g., "für", "auf"). Compare: nominative subject = "mein Sohn" (My son is...), accusative object = "meinen Sohn" (I see my son). For dative you usually say "meinem Sohn" (e.g., "Ich helfe meinem Sohn.").
target_language_example: Ich sehe meinen Sohn heute Abend.
native_language_example: I’m seeing my son this evening.

additional_notes: Used when "my father" is the direct object of the verb (the person being missed, called, brought, reminded of, etc.). Changes with gender/case: nominative "mein Vater" (subject), accusative "meinen Vater" (object). With the same verbs from the examples: "Ich vermisse meinen Vater" (I miss my father), "Können Sie meinen Vater anrufen?" (Can you call my father?).
target_language_example: Ich rufe meinen Vater später an.
native_language_example: I'll call my father later.

meaning: "my car" (accusative: 'my car' as the object of the sentence).
additional_notes: "Wagen" here means a car/vehicle. "meinen" is the accusative form of "mein" used with masculine nouns like "der Wagen" when it’s the direct object (e.g., "Ich nehme meinen Wagen."). In other cases you’ll see other forms: nominative "mein Wagen" (my car), dative "meinem Wagen" (to/with my car).
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte meinen Wagen vor dem Haus parken?
native_language_example: Can you please park my car in front of the house?

additional_notes: From the verb **meinen** (= to mean, to think) with **Sie** (formal “you”). Used to ask for clarification (**Wen meinen Sie?** = “Who do you mean?”), to check what someone is referring to (**Meinen Sie heute Abend?** = “Do you mean tonight?”), or to question someone’s opinion/reasoning (**Warum meinen Sie, dass…?** = “Why do you think that…?”).
target_language_example: Was genau meinen Sie damit?
native_language_example: What exactly do you mean by that?

additional_notes: "Meiner" is the dative form of "mein" used with the feminine noun "Familie". Use it after verbs and prepositions that take the dative, often meaning "to/for my family" (e.g., helfen) or after fixed phrases like "mit ... zu tun haben".
target_language_example: Ich erzähle meiner Familie heute Abend davon.
native_language_example: I’ll tell my family about it this evening.

additional_notes:
"meiner" is the dative or genitive form of "mein" (my). In the examples, it’s dative feminine: 
- after certain prepositions like "zwischen" (here: between me and my wife) 
- as an indirect object: "Sagen Sie meiner Frau ..." = "Tell my wife ..." 
- after "mit" (always dative): "mit meiner Frau" = "with my wife". 
The base form is "meine Frau" (nominative/accusative).
target_language_example: Ich habe meiner Frau Blumen gekauft.
native_language_example: I bought flowers for my wife.

additional_notes: Genitive plural form meaning “of my friends.” Often used after quantity words (die meisten/viele/einige) and in the pattern “einer/einem meiner Freunde” = “one of my friends” (because “einer/einem” is declined for case, while “meiner Freunde” stays genitive).
target_language_example: Einer meiner Freunde wohnt in Berlin.
native_language_example: One of my friends lives in Berlin.

additional_notes: "Meiner Großmutter" is the dative form of "meine Großmutter" (my grandmother). You often see it after prepositions like "von" (from) or when the grandmother is the indirect object (the person something is given/bought for): e.g., "Ich kaufe meiner Großmutter ..." = "I’m buying my grandmother ...".
target_language_example: Ich habe meiner Großmutter heute eine Karte geschrieben.
native_language_example: Today I wrote my grandmother a card.

meaning: "my childhood" (in the time of my childhood).
additional_notes:
Genitive form of "meine Kindheit" used after many common prepositions, especially:
- "seit meiner Kindheit" = since my childhood (from then until now)
- "in meiner Kindheit" = in/during my childhood
- "aus meiner Kindheit" = from my childhood
Also used like "die Helden meiner Kindheit" = the heroes of my childhood (childhood heroes).
target_language_example: Seit meiner Kindheit spiele ich Klavier.
native_language_example: I've played the piano since my childhood.

additional_notes: Used to politely introduce your personal view. Literally “according to my opinion.” It’s common at the start of a sentence, but it can also be placed later: „Das ist meiner Meinung nach falsch.“
target_language_example: Das ist meiner Meinung nach eine gute Idee.
native_language_example: In my opinion, that's a good idea.

meaning: my mother (in the dative or genitive case).
additional_notes: "Meiner Mutter" is the declined form of "meine Mutter" (my mother). It’s often **dative** (= roughly “to/for my mother”) after verbs like **helfen** (to help): "Ich habe meiner Mutter geholfen." It’s also used with expressions like **jdm. ähnlich sehen** (to look like someone): "Meine Schwester sieht meiner Mutter ähnlich." In some contexts it can be **genitive** (= “my mother’s”), though that’s not shown in the examples.
target_language_example: Ich habe meiner Mutter ein Geschenk gekauft.
native_language_example: I bought my mother a present.

additional_notes: German changes the form of "meine" depending on the grammatical case. "Meiner Schwester" is used when "Schwester" is feminine singular in the genitive (often meaning "of my sister": "ein Foto meiner Schwester") or in the dative (often meaning "to/for my sister": "Ich habe meiner Schwester ein Wörterbuch geschenkt").
target_language_example: Ich habe meiner Schwester gestern eine Nachricht geschrieben.
native_language_example: I wrote my sister a message yesterday.

meaning: 'my aunt' (feminine singular in the dative or genitive case).
additional_notes: You’ll most often see "meiner Tante" in the dative case, e.g. after certain prepositions like **bei** (at/with), **zu** (to), or as an indirect object: **Ich kaufe meiner Tante ein Geschenk** (I’m buying my aunt a gift). It can also be genitive in more formal contexts meaning 'of my aunt,' but that’s less common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Ich helfe meiner Tante am Wochenende.
native_language_example: I’m helping my aunt this weekend.

additional_notes: This is the dative form of "meine Tochter". You commonly see it after prepositions that take dative (e.g., mit, von, zu) and as the indirect object: "Ich widme dieses Buch meiner Tochter" (I dedicate this book to my daughter).
target_language_example: Ich habe meiner Tochter ein Geschenk gekauft.
native_language_example: I bought my daughter a present.

meaning: "of my life" (often used to say "the [best/worst/love/light] of my life").
additional_notes: Genitive form of „mein Leben“ meaning something belongs to or is part of your life. Very common after superlatives and emotional nouns: „die besten/schlimmsten Tage meines Lebens“, „die Liebe/Licht/Sonnenschein meines Lebens“. You also see it in fixed phrases like „unter Einsatz meines Lebens“ = "at the risk of my life."
target_language_example: Das war der beste Urlaub meines Lebens.
native_language_example: That was the best vacation of my life.

additional_notes: Used to indicate that something belongs to or is connected with your husband. It’s the genitive form of "mein Mann": masculine/neuter genitive uses "meines" and the noun often adds "-es" (Mann → Mannes). Common in more formal writing and fixed phrases like "im Namen meines Mannes" (in my husband's name).
target_language_example: Das ist der Pass meines Mannes.
native_language_example: That is my husband's passport.

additional_notes: This is the genitive form used to show possession or belonging. It’s masculine (der Vater), so it becomes: meines Vaters. It usually comes after the thing that belongs to him: das Büro meines Vaters = my father's office. (Often you can also say: das Büro von meinem Vater.)
target_language_example: Das ist das Auto meines Vaters.
native_language_example: That is my father's car.

meaning: as far as I know; to the best of my knowledge.
additional_notes: Used to soften a statement and show you’re not 100% sure. Often at the beginning of a sentence ("Meines Wissens ...") but it can also be placed in the middle. Grammatically it’s a genitive phrase (literally “of my knowledge”), and it’s fairly neutral/formal.
target_language_example: Meines Wissens hat das Museum montags geschlossen.
native_language_example: As far as I know, the museum is closed on Mondays.

additional_notes: From the verb **meinen**. Used to ask what someone intends or refers to: **Meinst du diesen?** (“Do you mean this one?”), **Meinst du mich?** (“Do you mean me?”). Can also introduce an opinion/question with a clause: **Meinst du, (dass) …?** (“Do you think (that) …?”). **Meinst du nicht?** often means “don’t you think?” / “right?”.
target_language_example: Meinst du, dass das eine gute Idee ist?
native_language_example: Do you think that’s a good idea?

additional_notes: Used to ask for clarification or to check whether someone is serious. Often appears with "ernst" or "im Ernst" (e.g., "Meinst du das ernst?" = "Are you serious?"). In very neutral contexts it can simply mean "Do you mean that (what you just said)?".
target_language_example: Meinst du das wirklich so?
native_language_example: Do you really mean it that way?

additional_notes: Used as a question to check what someone thinks or to gently push for agreement, often like a tag question: "Das ist unfair, meinst du nicht?" (= "That’s unfair, don’t you think?"). It can also introduce a correction/clarification: "Meinst du nicht June?" (= "Don’t you mean June?"). Depending on context and tone, it can sound surprised or skeptical ("Das meinst du nicht ernsthaft." = "You can’t be serious.").
target_language_example: Wir sollten früher losfahren, meinst du nicht?
native_language_example: We should leave earlier, don’t you think?

additional_notes: From the verb **meinen** (3rd person singular: **er/sie/es meint**). Commonly used to report what someone thinks or claims: **Er/Sie meint, dass …**. Although it resembles English “mean,” it’s usually better translated as “thinks/believes” in this structure. In a **dass**-clause, the other verb typically goes to the end.
target_language_example: Sie meint, dass wir warten sollen.
native_language_example: She thinks we should wait.

additional_notes: "Meint ihr" is the 2nd-person plural form of **meinen** (to mean / to think). It’s used to address **more than one person** ("you all"). In questions it often introduces what someone believes, suggests, or intends: *Meint ihr, dass…?* = “Do you think that…?” It can also mean “Do you really mean that…?” depending on context.
target_language_example: Meint ihr, wir sollten jetzt losfahren?
native_language_example: Do you all think we should leave now?

additional_notes: Used in reported speech with the verb "meinen" in the past tense ("meinte"). It introduces what someone believed, thought, or said as their opinion: "Er meinte, dass …". In everyday German, "dass" is sometimes omitted: "Er meinte, das Haus ist schön."
target_language_example: Sie meinte, dass es heute regnen wird.
native_language_example: She said/thought that it will rain today.

meaning: Please get in touch (with us) / let us know.
additional_notes: Formal imperative with „Sie“ (used with strangers, customers, etc.). „sich melden“ often means to contact someone again (phone/email) or to inform them about something (e.g., a change). It’s also used in other contexts like reporting to an office or registering, but in these examples it means “contact us / let us know.”
target_language_example: Melden Sie sich bitte, wenn Sie Fragen haben.
native_language_example: Please get in touch if you have any questions.

additional_notes: Simple past of "merken" + a "dass" (that) clause. Used to say someone became aware of something (often suddenly or after observing clues). In the present tense you’ll often see: "Ich merke, dass …".
target_language_example: Ich merkte, dass ich meinen Schlüssel verloren hatte.
native_language_example: I realized that I had lost my key.

additional_notes: Not a fixed expression by itself. mich is the accusative form of ich ('me'), and an is often the separated prefix of a verb. So the meaning depends on the full verb: schau mich an = look at me, ruf mich an = call me, geht mich an = concerns me / is my business. It's best to learn the whole verb, not mich an on its own.
target_language_example: Sie schaut mich an.
native_language_example: She's looking at me.

meaning: “me too / me as well” (with *mich* = “me” as the object).
additional_notes: Used when you are (or want to be) included as the object of an action. Often appears in questions with *auch* meaning “also/as well”: *Hörst du mich auch?* = “Can you hear me too/as well?” As a short, standalone echo question (*Mich auch?*), it’s an ellipsis meaning “Me too?” / “Me as well?” (i.e., “Does that apply to me too?”).
target_language_example: Kannst du mich auch mitnehmen?
native_language_example: Can you take me along too?

additional_notes: Used in polite requests when the speaker is the direct object of the verb. "mich" means "me" (accusative of "ich"), and "bitte" means "please." It usually appears after the verb, as in "Bring mich bitte ..." or "Ruf mich bitte ...".
target_language_example: Ruf mich bitte heute Abend an.
native_language_example: please call me this evening.

meaning: made me do it; caused/led me to (do something).
additional_notes: From the verb **bringen**. Commonly used in the **Perfekt** with **haben**: **jemanden dazu bringen, etwas zu tun** = to get someone to do something. The pronoun changes with the person (e.g., *dich/ihn/sie/uns/euch dazu gebracht*). Usually followed by an infinitive clause with **zu**.
target_language_example: Er hat mich dazu gebracht, es zu versuchen.
native_language_example: He made me try it.

additional_notes: Commonly used with requests or commands. Here, „doch“ doesn’t mean “though/yet”; it adds emphasis or a friendly push (like “do …, will you” / “just …”). It can also signal the speaker expects agreement, especially in negative questions like „Sie wollen mich doch nicht …?“ (“You don’t want to …, do you?”). The exact tone depends on context: it can sound inviting („Besuchen Sie mich doch …“), urging („Sieh mich doch …!“), or challenging („Fangt mich doch …“).
target_language_example: Ruf mich doch morgen an.
native_language_example: Give me a call tomorrow, will you?

meaning: "me out of here" / "get me out of here."
additional_notes: Used with verbs like „holen“ or „rausholen“ (e.g., „Hol mich hier raus!“) to ask someone to remove/rescue you from a place or situation. Often sounds urgent. Pronouns and verb endings change with who you’re speaking to: „Hol mich…“ (du), „Holen Sie mich…“ (formal), „Holt mich…“ (ihr).
target_language_example: Kannst du mich hier raus holen? Ich finde den Ausgang nicht.
native_language_example: Can you get me out of here? I can’t find the exit.

meaning: "hear me" (be able to hear my voice).
additional_notes: Uses the accusative pronoun "mich" (me) with "hören" (to hear). Common in phone/video calls and audio checks, often in questions like: "Kannst du mich hören?" If you mean "listen to me" in the sense of paying attention/obeying, German more often uses "mir zuhören".
target_language_example: Kannst du mich hören?
native_language_example: Can you hear me?

additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom—just the object pronoun **mich** (accusative: “me”) plus **immer** (“always”). In German, **immer** often comes after the object or other sentence elements: *Sie kritisieren mich immer* = “They always criticize me.” The English word order is usually “always” before the main verb (“always criticize me”).
target_language_example: Du unterbrichst mich immer, wenn ich telefoniere.
native_language_example: You always interrupt me when I’m on the phone.

additional_notes: This is a common pattern with separable-prefix verbs that end with **-an** (e.g., **anfassen** touch, **anlügen** lie to, **anschreien** yell at). In commands, **an** goes to the end: **Fass mich nicht an!** (= *Don’t touch me!*). Swap **mich** for another person: **Fass ihn/sie nicht an!** (don’t touch him/her), **Fassen Sie mich nicht an!** (formal).
target_language_example: Schrei mich nicht an!
native_language_example: Don’t yell at me!

additional_notes: Used with a verb to say that something doesn’t happen to you anymore (or shouldn’t happen anymore): e.g. "Schlag mich nicht mehr" = "Don’t hit me anymore"; "Das interessiert mich nicht mehr" = "I’m not interested in that anymore"; "Du sollst mich nicht mehr anrufen" = "You shouldn’t call me anymore." Word order: "mich" (object) usually comes before "nicht mehr" in the middle of the sentence.
target_language_example: Bitte ruf mich nicht mehr an.
native_language_example: Please don’t call me anymore.

meaning: 'me' + 'never' (used to say someone never does something to/with me).
additional_notes: "mich" is the accusative form of "ich" (me). "nie" means "never" and usually goes near the verb, but "mich" can come before it depending on word order: "Er grüßt mich nie" = "He never greets me." In questions with "oder?" it often means you expect the answer "no": "Du würdest mich nie anlügen, oder?" = "You’d never lie to me, right?"
target_language_example: Warum antwortest du mir nie? Du ignorierst mich nie sonst.
native_language_example: Why do you never reply to me? Otherwise you never ignore me.

additional_notes: Used with separable verbs that take the prefix **an-** (e.g. **anlügen** = to lie to someone, **ansprechen** = to speak to someone / approach someone, **anrufen** = to call someone). In imperatives the verb splits: **Verb + mich + nie wieder + an**. Often said in anger or to set a strong boundary. Can appear with **du** (Sprich!/Sprecht!) or formal **Sie** (Sprechen Sie!).
target_language_example: Ruf mich nie wieder an!
native_language_example: Don’t ever call me again.

meaning: “at me like that” (as in: “Why are you looking at me like that?”)
additional_notes: Used with separable verbs like **anschauen** (to look at) or **anstarren** (to stare at). In sentences like *Warum schaust du mich so an?*, **mich** = “me” and **an** is the separated prefix that often goes to the end. **so** means “like that/that way” and often suggests the look is strange, rude, or surprised.
target_language_example: Warum schaust du mich so an?
native_language_example: Why are you looking at me like that?

meaning: to kill me (sometimes: “I’m in big trouble / they’ll be furious with me”).
additional_notes: From the separable verb **umbringen** = “to kill”. In context it can be meant literally (“You wanted to kill me”), but it’s also commonly used as an exaggeration, especially with family: **Mein Vater wird mich umbringen** often means “My dad will be furious / I’ll be in big trouble,” not actual killing.
target_language_example: Wenn meine Mutter das erfährt, wird sie mich umbringen.
native_language_example: If my mom finds out, she’ll kill me. (i.e., she’ll be furious.)

additional_notes: "wirklich" means "really/truly" and here it emphasizes that something genuinely affects/concerns "mich" (me). It often appears after the object pronoun ("mich") in normal word order: e.g., "Du magst mich wirklich?" = "Do you really like me?" In questions, it can show surprise or doubt ("Willst du mich wirklich verlassen?" = "Do you really want to leave me?").
target_language_example: Glaubst du mich wirklich?
native_language_example: Do you really believe me?

additional_notes: This is a common word order in German with a zu-infinitive: the object pronoun (mich = me) often comes before "zu" + verb (kontaktieren, nerven, betrügen, etc.). It appears in phrases like "versuchen, mich zu …" (to try to … me), "anfangen, mich zu …" (to start to … me), "jemanden dazu bringen, mich zu …" (to get someone to … me).
target_language_example: Hör bitte auf, mich zu stören.
native_language_example: Please stop bothering me.

additional_notes: "mich" means "me" (accusative). "zu küssen" is the infinitive "to kiss" and is often used after verbs like "versuchen" (to try), "wagen" (to dare), "erlauben" (to allow), etc. The full infinitive phrase is "mich zu küssen" (= to kiss me).
target_language_example: Ich wollte ihn nicht bitten, mich zu küssen.
native_language_example: I didn’t want to ask him to kiss me.

additional_notes: An infinitive phrase with **zu** ("zu" + infinitive), often used after verbs like **(sich) freuen** (to be happy), **scheinen** (to seem), or adjectives like **erfreut** (pleased): *Sie schien nicht erfreut, mich zu sehen.* The pronoun **mich** is the accusative form of **ich** (me) because **sehen** takes a direct object.
target_language_example: Ich freue mich, dich wiederzusehen, aber ich glaube, er freut sich nicht, mich zu sehen.
native_language_example: I’m happy to see you again, but I think he’s not happy to see me.

additional_notes: Usually used with the verb phrase **jemanden zum Lachen bringen** (“to make someone laugh”). The pronoun changes depending on who is laughing: **mich** (me), **dich** (you), **ihn/sie** (him/her), etc. Often used after verbs like **bringen** or **schaffen es**, e.g. **Er schafft es, mich zum Lachen zu bringen** (“He manages to make me laugh”).
target_language_example: Manche Leute bringen mich zum Lachen.
native_language_example: Some people make me laugh.

meaning: “(myself) to/at …” — used with reflexive verbs that take the preposition „an“ (e.g., „sich erinnern an“, „sich gewöhnen an“, „sich festhalten an“).
additional_notes: „mich“ is the reflexive pronoun for „ich“ (me/myself). With many reflexive verbs, „an“ introduces what the action relates to: „Ich erinnere mich an + Akk.“ = “I remember …”, „Ich gewöhne mich an + Akk.“ = “I get used to …”, „Ich halte mich an + Akk.“ / „festhalten an + Dat.“ can mean “hold on to …” (case depends on the specific verb). On its own, „mich an“ is incomplete—you need the verb and the object after „an“.
target_language_example: Ich erinnere mich an deinen Namen.
native_language_example: I remember your name.

meaning: 'not me/myself' (used to negate a verb with 'mich').
additional_notes: This is the combination of the reflexive pronoun "mich" (myself/me) + "nicht" (not). It often appears with reflexive verbs like "sich scheiden lassen" (to get divorced), "sich sehen" (to see oneself), "sich sehnen" (to long for), "sich aufregen" (to get upset). In many sentences, "mich" comes before "nicht": "Ich reg mich nicht auf." = "I’m not getting upset."
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, ich beschwere mich nicht.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’m not complaining.

meaning: “for/about …” in certain reflexive verb phrases (e.g., apply for; take care of).
additional_notes: Not used on its own: it appears with specific reflexive verbs + „um“ + accusative noun/pronoun. Common patterns: „sich um etwas kümmern“ = to take care of / look after something; „sich um etwas bewerben“ = to apply for something (a job, a spot). The reflexive pronoun changes with the subject: ich mich, du dich, er/sie/es sich, wir uns, ihr euch, sie/Sie sich.
target_language_example: Ich kümmere mich um meine kleine Schwester.
native_language_example: I take care of my little sister.

meaning: “me, that I …” — a pattern used when a verb takes “mir” and then a “dass”-clause.
additional_notes: This isn’t a fixed phrase, but a common structure: **[verb] + mir** (to/for me) + **, dass ich ...** (that I ...). You see it with verbs like **(ver)zeihen** (forgive): *Verzeih mir, dass ich ...*; **sich wünschen** (wish): *Ich wünsche mir, dass ich ...*; and with **von mir erwarten** (expect of me): *Sie erwarten von mir, dass ich ...*. The comma before **dass** is normal because **dass ich ...** is a subordinate clause.
target_language_example: Entschuldigen Sie mir, dass ich zu spät gekommen bin.
native_language_example: Forgive me for arriving late.

additional_notes: "mir" is the dative form of "ich" and often means "to me" (indirect object). "alles" means "everything". Together they commonly appear when someone does something (say/tell/explain/show) everything *to* someone: "Er hat mir alles erklärt." In phrases like "Das ist mir alles egal", "mir" marks who feels that way, and the idea is "I don’t care about any of it / it’s all the same to me."
target_language_example: Kannst du mir alles ganz genau erklären?
native_language_example: Can you explain everything to me in detail?

meaning: 'to me too / to me as well' (also me).
additional_notes: Uses the dative pronoun "mir" (= to me) with "auch" (= also). Often means "me too" as a reply (e.g., "Ich komme morgen." – "Mir auch."), but it can also appear inside a longer sentence to mean that something applies to you as well.
target_language_example: Ich möchte mir auch ein Stück Kuchen nehmen.
native_language_example: I'd like to take a piece of cake too.

meaning: out of my way; (also) avoiding me.
additional_notes: Used with gehen (“to go/walk”) in phrases like: Geh/Gehen Sie mir aus dem Weg! = “Get out of my way!” It can also be figurative: Jemand geht mir aus dem Weg = “Someone is avoiding me.” The pronoun changes in the dative: mir (me), dir (you), ihm/ihr (him/her), uns (us), euch (you all), ihnen/Ihnen (them/you formal).
target_language_example: Warum gehst du mir aus dem Weg?
native_language_example: Why are you avoiding me?

additional_notes: Used when you politely ask someone to do something for you, often right after the verb: "Hilf mir bitte" / "Sag mir bitte …". "mir" is dative = 'to me'; "bitte" softens the request. Word order can vary: "Bitte hilf mir" is also common. Often combined with "mal" to sound more casual: "Leih mir bitte mal …".
target_language_example: Schick mir bitte die Adresse.
native_language_example: Please send me the address.

additional_notes: Used to ask or tell someone to assist you with a specific task or situation. "mir" is the dative pronoun "to me," and "dabei" means "with that/with it" (referring back to something already mentioned). You can change the pronoun/person: "dir dabei helfen" (help you), "ihm/ihr dabei helfen" (help him/her), etc. Works with informal "du" or formal "Sie."
target_language_example: Kannst du mir dabei helfen, das Formular auszufüllen?
native_language_example: Can you help me fill out the form?

additional_notes: Used with verbs that take two objects: something is done/sent/taught to you (mir) and 'it/that' is the thing (das). Often translates as “me it/that” or more naturally “it/that to me” / “for me” depending on the verb (e.g., 'Gib mir das' = 'Give it to me'). Word order can vary: 'Kannst du mir das erklären?' / 'Kannst du das mir erklären?' (the first is much more common).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir das bitte erklären?
native_language_example: Can you please explain that to me?

additional_notes: Used when someone does something for you or gives/tells/shows something to you: e.g. „Gib mir das“ (Give me that), „Sag mir das“ (Tell me that), „Könntest du mir das erklären?“ (Could you explain that to me?). Word order can change depending on emphasis, but the pronouns often stay together like this.
target_language_example: Kannst du mir das bitte erklären?
native_language_example: Can you please explain that to me?

meaning: 'my back' (literally: 'me the back', used with a body part).
additional_notes: Used with many verbs that involve touching or doing something to someone’s body (e.g., streicheln, massieren, waschen, kratzen). German often uses the dative pronoun (mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/ihnen) + the definite article (den Rücken) instead of a possessive like “my back”.
target_language_example: Kannst du mir den Rücken massieren?
native_language_example: Can you massage my back?

meaning: (to) me the way to the train station.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like „sagen“ (tell) or „zeigen“ (show) when asking for directions: „Können/Könnten/Würden Sie mir den Weg zum Bahnhof sagen/zeigen?“ Here „mir“ = to me, „den Weg“ = the way, „zum Bahnhof“ = to the train station (zu + dem). You can swap „zum Bahnhof“ for another place (e.g., „zum Hotel“, „zur Apotheke“).
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, können Sie mir den Weg zum Bahnhof zeigen?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can you show me the way to the train station?

additional_notes: Used when someone does something to/for you involving a specific feminine noun (singular) or plural noun: **jemand gibt/zeigt/verkauft/schickt mir die/den/das …**. Here **mir** is the indirect object (= to me), and **die** is the definite article for what is being given/sold/etc. (often the direct object).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir die Adresse schicken?
native_language_example: Can you send me the address?

meaning: “my hair” expressed with the dative pronoun mir in common German constructions with body parts (literally “to me the hair”).
additional_notes: German frequently uses a dative pronoun (mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/ihnen) with body parts when the action affects the person: „Ich wasche mir die Haare“ = literally “I wash myself the hair,” meaning “I wash my hair.” The same structure is also used when someone does it for you: „Schneid mir die Haare“ = “Cut my hair (for me).” It can also appear in idioms, e.g. „Ich hätte mir die Haare raufen können“ (“I could have torn my hair out” in frustration).
target_language_example: Ich wasche mir die Haare.
native_language_example: I’m washing my hair.

additional_notes: Used when asking or insisting that someone be honest with you. "mir" = "to me" (dative), and the verb phrase is "die Wahrheit sagen". Commonly used with modal verbs (e.g., "können", "müssen") or in questions (e.g., "Wird er mir die Wahrheit sagen?").
target_language_example: Du kannst mir die Wahrheit sagen.
native_language_example: You can tell me the truth.

additional_notes: Used when something is done/given/bought *for me* or *to me*. **mir** is the dative pronoun (indirect object: “to/for me”), and **ein** starts a noun phrase (ein Gefühl, ein paar Minuten, ein Motorrad, ein Mineralwasser, ein Stück Kuchen). With some verbs it can be reflexive to mean “for myself,” e.g. *ich könnte mir ein Motorrad kaufen* = “I could buy myself a motorcycle.”
target_language_example: Kannst du mir ein Ticket kaufen?
native_language_example: Can you buy me a ticket?

meaning: “to/for me a …” (indicating you are the recipient).
additional_notes: Used with verbs that involve giving/sending/saying/recommending something to someone. **mir** is the dative pronoun “to me/for me,” and **eine** is “a/an” for feminine nouns (accusative), e.g., *eine Postkarte, eine Unterkunft, eine Bemerkung, eine Freude*. Common in polite requests: *Können Sie mir eine … empfehlen?* / *Schicken Sie mir eine …*
target_language_example: Kannst du mir eine Adresse schicken?
native_language_example: Can you send me an address?

meaning: “me a …” / “to me a …” (masculine accusative object after a verb like give/bring).
additional_notes: Used when something is done or given to you: **mir** = “to me” (dative), **einen** = “a/an” for a masculine noun in the accusative (the thing being given). Common with verbs like **geben** (to give), **bringen** (to bring), **reichen/überreichen** (to hand over). Example pattern: **Gib/Bring mir einen + [masculine noun].**
target_language_example: Kannst du mir einen Kaffee bringen?
native_language_example: Can you bring me a coffee?

additional_notes: A very common pattern: **mir** = “to me” (dative pronoun) and **etwas** = “something”. You’ll see it with many verbs, e.g. **mir etwas erzählen** (tell me something), **mir etwas erklären** (explain something to me), **mir etwas verheimlichen/vorenthalten** (hide/withhold something from me), **mir etwas bedeuten** (mean something to me). Word order changes depending on the sentence, but the idea is always that something is directed to/for you.
target_language_example: Kannst du mir etwas empfehlen?
native_language_example: Can you recommend something to me?

additional_notes: Used when asking someone to get/make/give you food. "mir" is the dative pronoun meaning "to/for me" (often used with verbs like geben, bringen, holen, machen, besorgen). "etwas zu essen" literally means "something to eat" and works like a noun phrase.
target_language_example: Kannst du mir etwas zu essen bringen?
native_language_example: Can you bring me something to eat?

meaning: I remember; it occurs to me.
additional_notes: From the verb "einfallen" (= to come to mind). It’s used when a thought/idea suddenly comes to you. Grammar: the person is in the dative (mir/dir/ihm …) and the thing/idea is the subject: "Mir fällt ein Name ein." Common: "Mir fällt nichts ein."
target_language_example: Mir fällt ein, dass ich noch Milch kaufen muss.
native_language_example: It occurs to me that I still need to buy milk.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **gefallen** to say you like something. The person who likes is in the **dative**: **mir** (to me), **dir** (to you), **ihm/ihr** (to him/her), **uns/euch**, **ihnen**. The thing you like is the grammatical subject, so the verb agrees with it: **Mir gefällt** der Film (singular), **Mir gefallen** die Augen / Fremdsprachen (plural).
target_language_example: Mir gefallen deine Ohrringe.
native_language_example: I like your earrings.

additional_notes: Used to say you like something. Literally it’s like “to me, it pleases/appeals.” The thing you like is the subject: “Mir gefällt der Klang …” (= I like the sound …). With plural things: “Mir gefallen die Schuhe.” You can also use “Mir gefällt es, … zu …” to say you like doing something.
target_language_example: Mir gefällt dieses Lied wirklich gut.
native_language_example: I really like this song.

meaning: “I like your …” / “I don’t like your …” (literally: “your … pleases me”).
additional_notes: Used to say you (don’t) like something about someone else. German uses the verb **gefallen** with the person in the **dative** (**mir** = “to me”) and the thing that is liked as the grammatical subject: **Deine Art gefällt mir.** The word **deine** is the possessive “your” (informal singular), usually before a feminine noun (**deine Art**, **deine Einstellung**) or plural (**deine Augen**).
target_language_example: Mir gefällt deine Stimme sehr.
native_language_example: I really like your voice.

additional_notes: Used to say you don’t like something. German often phrases this with **gefallen**: the thing you like is the grammatical subject. Common pattern: „Mir gefällt X nicht.“ (singular) / „Mir gefallen X nicht.“ (plural). You can also say: „Das gefällt mir nicht.“ = “I don’t like that.”
target_language_example: Der Film, mir gefällt nicht, ist zu lang.
native_language_example: The movie I don't like is too long.

additional_notes: Used to talk about how you are doing, especially health or well-being. Literally it’s like “to me, it goes,” so German uses the dative: mir (to me) + geht es (is going). Common patterns: “Mir geht es gut/schlecht/besser.” You can also add words like „wieder“ (again) or „jetzt“ (now).
target_language_example: Mir geht es heute viel besser.
native_language_example: I feel much better today.

meaning: I’m doing well / I feel good.
additional_notes: Common answer to "Wie geht es dir/Ihnen?" (“How are you?”). Literally it’s like “To me it goes well” (German uses the dative: mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/ihnen). In everyday speech you often hear the shortened form "Mir geht’s gut".
target_language_example: Danke, mir geht es gut, und dir?
native_language_example: Thanks, I’m doing well—how about you?

additional_notes: Used with the verb „helfen“, which takes the dative case: „jemandem helfen“ (to help someone). So „mir“ is the dative form of „ich“ and corresponds to “me” / “to me”. Common in questions like „Kannst du mir helfen?“ (informal) or „Können Sie mir helfen?“ (formal).
target_language_example: Mein Vater wird mir helfen.
native_language_example: My father will help me.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like „sehen/schauen/gucken“ + „jemandem in die Augen“ to mean making eye contact with someone. „mir“ is the dative pronoun “to me” (= “me” here). Often used as an instruction or demand: „Sieh/Sehen Sie mir in die Augen!“
target_language_example: Kannst du mir in die Augen schauen, wenn du mit mir redest?
native_language_example: Can you look me in the eyes when you talk to me?

additional_notes: Used with verbs to indicate that something is directed at the speaker’s face (e.g., someone stares at you; wind blows at you; someone laughs/lies to your face). Common in fixed expressions like „jemandem ins Gesicht lügen“ (to lie to someone’s face) and „jemandem ins Gesicht lachen“ (to laugh in someone’s face). Grammar: „mir“ is dative (= to me) and „ins Gesicht“ is a contraction of „in das Gesicht“ (into the face).
target_language_example: Der Wind bläst mir ins Gesicht.
native_language_example: The wind is blowing in my face.

meaning: "I don't care" / "it doesn't matter to me."
additional_notes: Uses dative mir (“to me”) + ist egal (“is irrelevant/doesn’t matter”). Often followed by a clause with ob/was/wer/warum, etc.: Mir ist egal, ob/was/wer… It can sound blunt; for a softer tone you can say: Das ist mir egal.
target_language_example: Mir ist egal, wo wir essen gehen.
native_language_example: I don't care where we go to eat.

additional_notes: Used to talk about how you feel (temperature). German often uses this pattern: "mir ist + adjective" (literally “to me is ...”), e.g. "mir ist warm" (I’m warm), "mir ist heiß" (I’m hot). You can add a body part with "an den/der ...": "Mir ist kalt an den Händen" (My hands are cold).
target_language_example: Kannst du das Fenster schließen? Mir ist kalt.
native_language_example: Can you close the window? I’m cold.

additional_notes: Used with the dative pronoun mir (“to me/for me”) plus nicht (“not”). It often appears in common patterns like: etwas nicht erzählen/geben/sagen (don’t tell/give/say me), es erscheint mir nicht … (it doesn’t seem … to me), ich kann es mir nicht leisten (I can’t afford it), ich hätte mir nicht träumen lassen (I never would have imagined). In questions, it can also sound like a polite suggestion/request: Wollen Sie mir nicht antworten? (“Won’t you answer me?”).
target_language_example: Das ist mir nicht klar.
native_language_example: That isn’t clear to me.

additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom—it's just the dative pronoun **mir** (“to me”) + **nie** (“never”). You see it with verbs that take the dative, e.g. **jemandem zuhören** (to listen to someone): *Er hört mir nie zu.* It also appears with some reflexive verbs that use a dative pronoun, e.g. *Ich werde mir nie vergeben* (“I’ll never forgive myself”). Word order can vary: **Tom hört mir nie zu** / **Tom hört nie mir zu** (the first is more neutral).
target_language_example: Bitte hör mir nie wieder so zu spät zu.
native_language_example: Please never listen to me that late again.

additional_notes: Not a fixed expression. mir is the dative form of ich and means "to me" or "for me." noch can mean "still/yet" or "another," so the exact English translation depends on context: mir noch Geld schulden = "still owe me money," mir noch eine Chance geben = "give me another chance."
target_language_example: Er schuldet mir noch zehn Euro.
native_language_example: He still owes me ten euros.

additional_notes: Uses the dative pronoun mir (“to me”). Common in questions like „Was wolltest du mir sagen?“ (“What did you want to tell me?”). With „zu mir sagen“ it can also mean “call me” (a name), e.g. „Du kannst Bill zu mir sagen.“
target_language_example: Kannst du mir sagen, wie spät es ist?
native_language_example: Can you tell me what time it is?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to explain the reason for something. Common pattern: „Kannst du/Könnt ihr mir sagen, warum …?“ After „warum“, German usually uses subordinate-clause word order with the verb at the end: „…, warum Tom das tut.“ (not: „warum Tom tut das“).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir sagen, warum du heute so spät bist?
native_language_example: Can you tell me why you’re so late today?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the location of a person/place/thing. Often appears in polite questions with "können/könnten/könntest" (e.g., "Könnten Sie mir sagen, wo …?"). In a subordinate clause after "sagen", the verb goes to the end: "… wo die Post ist".
target_language_example: Könnten Sie mir sagen, wo der Bahnhof ist?
native_language_example: Could you tell me where the train station is?

additional_notes: Uses the dative pronoun mir (= “to me”). With körperliche/gefühlte Schwere: „Der Kopf ist mir schwer.“ / „Mein Herz wird mir schwer.“ With difficulty: „Es fällt mir schwer, …“ (= “I find it hard to …”). You can also say „jemand macht es mir schwer“ (= “someone makes it hard for me”).
target_language_example: Es fällt mir schwer, heute zu konzentrieren.
native_language_example: I find it hard to concentrate today.

additional_notes: Used to say that a specific body part hurts. Pattern: „Mir tut der/die/das + body part + weh.“ (e.g., der Kopf, der Rücken, die Hand, das Knie). You can add „etwas“ (= a little) for mild pain.
target_language_example: Mir tut der Rücken weh.
native_language_example: My back hurts.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **versprechen** (“to promise”) with **mir** = “to me” (dative). Very common in the **Perfekt** (past) form: **(jemand) hat mir … versprochen** / **ihr habt mir … versprochen**. Often followed by **dass ...** (“that ...”) or an infinitive clause: **mir versprochen, nicht wieder ... zu tun** (“promised me not to do ... again”).
target_language_example: Du hast mir versprochen, heute pünktlich zu sein.
native_language_example: You promised me you’d be on time today.

meaning: to help me (as an infinitive clause: “to help me”)
additional_notes: "mir" is the dative form of "ich" (me), because "helfen" takes the dative case (jemandem helfen). "zu helfen" is the infinitive used after verbs like "bitten" (ask), "versuchen" (try), "sich weigern" (refuse), and in purpose clauses with "um ... zu ..." (in order to). The full phrase typically appears as part of a larger sentence (e.g., "jemanden bitten, mir zu helfen").
target_language_example: Ich bat ihn darum, mir zu helfen.
native_language_example: I asked him to help me.

additional_notes: Used to say someone did something deliberately (not by accident). Often used in questions or accusations: "Machst du das mit Absicht?" = "Are you doing that on purpose?" The opposite is "aus Versehen" (by mistake).
target_language_example: Ich habe das nicht mit Absicht gemacht.
native_language_example: I didn’t do that on purpose.

additional_notes: Used to say something wasn’t an accident. Often you’ll also hear just “mit Absicht” (without “gemacht”), or the more formal adverb “absichtlich” (intentionally). Word order is flexible in sentences, e.g. “Er hat das mit Absicht gemacht.”
target_language_example: Ich habe das nicht mit Absicht gemacht.
native_language_example: I didn’t do that on purpose.

meaning: by far; with some distance (figuratively: from a detached perspective).
additional_notes: Most often used with superlatives/comparisons to intensify: "mit Abstand der/die/das Beste" = "by far the best". It can also mean taking a step back mentally: "die Dinge mit Abstand sehen" = "to see things with distance / more objectively".
target_language_example: Er ist mit Abstand der schnellste Läufer in unserem Team.
native_language_example: He is by far the fastest runner on our team.

additional_notes: A literal, compositional phrase meaning that something is done by seeing/looking. Most commonly appears inside longer expressions (e.g., "mit eigenen Augen" = with your own eyes; "mit offenen Augen" = with your eyes open/attentively). On its own, it can sound a bit incomplete and is usually used with an implied modifier.
target_language_example: Man muss mit Augen sehen und mit dem Kopf denken.
native_language_example: You have to see with your eyes and think with your head.

meaning: in view of; with regard to.
additional_notes: A fairly formal prepositional phrase used to introduce the aspect/topic you’re considering. Common in writing and news/business German. Often followed by a noun phrase: „mit Blick auf + Akkusativ“ (e.g., „mit Blick auf die Zukunft“). Similar in meaning to „angesichts“ (in view of) or „hinsichtlich“ (regarding).
target_language_example: Mit Blick auf das Wetter nehmen wir eine Jacke mit.
native_language_example: In view of the weather, we’re bringing a jacket.

meaning: with a kind, caring heart; kind-hearted.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is warm or compassionate despite seeming rough or rude. Often appears in phrases like „(ein) X mit Herz“ (e.g., „ein Arsch mit Herz“), meaning “a jerk with a heart (of gold)”—insulting but humorous/affectionate in context.
target_language_example: Er wirkt manchmal hart, aber er ist ein Kerl mit Herz.
native_language_example: He sometimes seems tough, but he’s a guy with a kind heart.

meaning: with the help of; using (something) as help.
additional_notes: Often used as a prepositional phrase meaning you achieve something by using a tool, resource, or person. Common patterns: "mit Hilfe + Genitive" (more formal: "mit Hilfe dieses Buches") and "mit Hilfe von + Dative" (very common: "mit Hilfe von Wörtern").
target_language_example: Mit Hilfe einer App lerne ich jeden Tag Deutsch.
native_language_example: With the help of an app, I learn German every day.

additional_notes: "Ihnen" is the formal (polite) form of "you" used with strangers, customers, older people, or in professional situations. "mit Ihnen" is used after verbs that take "mit" (e.g., "sprechen/reden mit", "sich unterhalten mit", "Zeit verbringen mit"). It can also mean "to you" in the sense of affecting you (e.g., "Was ist mit Ihnen passiert?" = "What happened to you?").
target_language_example: Ich möchte kurz mit Ihnen sprechen.
native_language_example: I'd like to speak with you briefly.

additional_notes: Used when addressing one person politely with "Sie/Ihnen" (e.g., a stranger, customer, teacher, or someone you don’t know well). "mit" + dative → "mit Ihnen". Often appears with modal verbs: "möchte/will/wollte ... mit Ihnen reden".
target_language_example: Entschuldigen Sie, ich muss kurz mit Ihnen reden.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I need to talk to you for a moment.

additional_notes: "mit" + dative means "with" in the sense of talking to someone. "Ihnen" is the formal/polite "you" (used with strangers, customers, officials, etc.), so this phrase is common in professional or polite situations. In casual situations, you would usually say "mit dir sprechen" (to speak with you, informal).
target_language_example: Könnte ich kurz mit Ihnen sprechen?
native_language_example: Could I speak with you briefly?

additional_notes: A polite/formal way to introduce what you want to talk to someone about. Commonly used with verbs like „reden“ and „sprechen“: „mit Ihnen über + [topic] reden/sprechen“. „Ihnen“ is the formal “you” (used with strangers, customers, officials, etc.).
target_language_example: Könnte ich kurz mit Ihnen über Ihren Termin sprechen?
native_language_example: Could I briefly speak with you about your appointment?

additional_notes: Used with the formal possessive "Ihr-" (for "Sie" = you). "Mit" takes the dative case, so before a masculine/neuter noun you get: mit Ihrem + noun (e.g., mit Ihrem Mann, mit Ihrem Hund). In the common question "Was ist mit ...?", it often means "What about ...?" / "What’s going on with ...?" (e.g., Was ist mit Ihrem Ausflug?).
target_language_example: Kommen Sie bitte mit Ihrem Ausweis zur Rezeption.
native_language_example: Please come to reception with your ID.

meaning: "with your" (formal; used with feminine singular nouns).
additional_notes: Used with the preposition "mit" (which takes the dative case). "Ihrer" is the dative feminine singular form of the formal possessive "Ihr" (= your, addressed as "Sie"). Common patterns include: "mit Ihrer Tochter/Frau" (with your daughter/wife), "mit Ihrer Hilfe" (with your help), and "Was ist mit Ihrer ...?" meaning "What about your ...?".
target_language_example: Kommen Sie mit Ihrer Kollegin zur Besprechung?
native_language_example: Are you coming to the meeting with your colleague?

additional_notes: Used to say something is done effortlessly or with no difficulty. Often with verbs like lernen (learn), lösen (solve), gelingen (succeed), heben (lift), springen (jump). It can emphasize that something is surprisingly easy for someone.
target_language_example: Sie hat die Prüfung mit Leichtigkeit bestanden.
native_language_example: She passed the exam with ease.

additional_notes: Used to say a feeling, statement, or action is justified. Often placed before an adjective/verb phrase ("mit Recht stolz", "mit Recht verärgert"). Can also be used on its own: "Und das mit Recht." = "And rightly so."
target_language_example: Du bist mit Recht wütend.
native_language_example: You’re right to be angry.

additional_notes: Describes something whose surface is covered by snow. Common with sein/war: „Der Berg ist/war mit Schnee bedeckt.“ You can intensify it with words like „ganz/gänzlich“ (completely) or time phrases like „das ganze Jahr (über)“ (all year (round)).
target_language_example: Am Morgen war die ganze Stadt mit Schnee bedeckt.
native_language_example: In the morning, the whole city was covered with snow.

additional_notes: Used to say you are sure about something. Common patterns: „Ich weiß es mit Sicherheit.“ (= I know it for sure), „Ich kann (nicht) mit Sicherheit sagen, …“ (= I can(not) say for certain …), and at the start of a sentence „Mit Sicherheit …“ (= certainly / definitely …).
target_language_example: Mit Sicherheit wird sie heute anrufen.
native_language_example: She will definitely call today.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like "füllen" (to fill) to say what something is filled with. Common patterns: "etw. mit Wasser füllen" / "etw. mit Wasser auffüllen". In these sentences, the container is in the accusative (den Eimer, die Badewanne).
target_language_example: Kannst du die Flasche mit Wasser füllen?
native_language_example: Can you fill the bottle with water?

additional_notes: Uses dative after "mit" ("allem" = dative of "alles"). Common in set phrases like "mit allem ausgestattet" (fully equipped) and "mit allem fertig sein/werden" (to be finished with everything / to get everything done).
target_language_example: Die Wohnung ist mit allem ausgestattet, was du brauchst.
native_language_example: The apartment is equipped with everything you need.

additional_notes: Uses the preposition **mit** (“with”) plus **allen** (dative plural of **alle**). Often refers to being together or interacting **with all people in a group** (*mit allen Familien, mit allen Klassenkameraden*), but it can also mean “with all” in a broader sense like “provided with all information” (*mit allen Informationen*).
target_language_example: Ich habe heute mit allen aus meinem Team gesprochen.
native_language_example: I talked with everyone on my team today.

meaning: "in other words" (to rephrase or sum up).
additional_notes: Used to restate what you just said more clearly, more simply, or as a conclusion. Often placed at the start of a sentence, sometimes followed by a comma: "Mit anderen Worten, ..."
target_language_example: Mit anderen Worten: Wir müssen jetzt gehen.
native_language_example: In other words: We have to leave now.

additional_notes: Used to describe doing something using both hands at the same time (e.g., holding, catching, waving). After "mit" (with), the noun is in the dative: "beiden Händen" (plural).
target_language_example: Bitte nimm die Tasse mit beiden Händen.
native_language_example: Please take the cup with both hands.

meaning: with the naked eye (without any tools like binoculars or a microscope).
additional_notes: Used to say something can (or can’t) be seen without optical aids. Often used with "sichtbar" (visible) or "sehen" (to see): "mit bloßem Auge sichtbar/nicht sichtbar".
target_language_example: Die Details sind nur mit bloßem Auge schwer zu erkennen.
native_language_example: The details are hard to make out with the naked eye alone.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine/neuter noun in the dative case: dein → deinem. Common after the preposition "mit" (with), e.g. "mit deinem Bruder" = "with your brother". Also appears in phrases like "das mit deinem ..." meaning "that thing about/with your ..." (e.g. news or a situation involving them).
target_language_example: Kannst du heute mit deinem Vater sprechen?
native_language_example: Can you talk with your father today?

additional_notes: Uses the preposition "mit" (with) + dative: "deinem Vater" (your father). Common in contexts like doing something together (arbeiten/reden mit deinem Vater) or having a situation/conflict involving him (Ärger mit deinem Vater, das mit deinem Vater…).
target_language_example: Ich möchte heute Abend mit deinem Vater sprechen.
native_language_example: I want to talk with your father this evening.

meaning: “with your …” (used with plural nouns, or masculine/neuter nouns in the dative case).
additional_notes:
Used after the preposition **mit** (“with”), which always takes the **dative**. **deinen** is the dative form of **dein-** (“your”, informal singular). You use **mit deinen** before:
- **plural nouns**: *mit deinen Hausaufgaben* (with your homework)
- **masculine/neuter dative** (less common as a fixed phrase without the noun shown): e.g., *mit deinem Bruder* (with your brother), *mit deinem Kind* (with your child)
Contrast: **mit deiner** (feminine singular) and **mit deinem** (masc./neut. singular).
target_language_example: Spielst du oft mit deinen Freunden Fußball?
native_language_example: Do you often play soccer with your friends?

additional_notes: Used with verbs that take "mit" (which requires the dative case): *mit deinen Eltern*. Common patterns: **mit deinen Eltern sprechen** = talk to your parents; **Schwierigkeiten/Stress mit deinen Eltern haben** = have difficulties/stress with your parents; **mit deinen Eltern zusammenleben** = live together with your parents; **Wie verstehst du dich mit deinen Eltern?** = How do you get along with your parents? Also in **Was ist mit deinen Eltern?** it means “What’s going on with your parents?” / “What about your parents?”
target_language_example: Ich verstehe mich gut mit deinen Eltern.
native_language_example: I get along well with your parents.

additional_notes: Used to say you do something together with your friends. After the preposition **mit** (“with”), German uses the **dative** case, so it’s **deinen Freunden** (plural dative of *deine Freunde*). You can swap *deinen* for other possessives: *mit meinen Freunden* (with my friends), *mit seinen Freunden* (with his friends).
target_language_example: Ich gehe heute mit deinen Freunden ins Kino.
native_language_example: I’m going to the cinema today with your friends.

additional_notes: “Mit” always takes the dative case. “Deiner” is the dative form of “deine” and is used before a feminine singular noun (e.g., mit deiner Vermutung, mit deiner Geschichte). It’s used when speaking to one person informally (du), not formally (Sie).
target_language_example: Ich bin mit deiner Antwort nicht ganz zufrieden.
native_language_example: I’m not completely satisfied with your answer.

meaning: with your work (job/task you are doing).
additional_notes: Used with verbs and expressions that take **mit + dative** to show what you’re dealing with or working on. Common patterns: **fertig sein mit deiner Arbeit** (to be finished with your work), **zufrieden sein mit deiner Arbeit** (to be satisfied with your work), **weitermachen mit deiner Arbeit** (to continue with your work), **aufhören mit deiner Arbeit** (to stop working), **vorankommen mit deiner Arbeit** (to make progress with your work). Here **deiner** is dative feminine (die Arbeit).
target_language_example: Ich bin noch nicht mit deiner Arbeit fertig.
native_language_example: I’m not finished with your work yet.

additional_notes: Used when someone is talking to their mother (mit deiner Mutter reden) or making plans involving her (mit deiner Mutter verabredet sein). Also appears in questions like „Was wird mit deiner Mutter?“ meaning “What about your mother?/What will happen to your mother?” Note: „deiner“ is dative feminine of „dein“ because it follows „mit“ (a dative preposition).
target_language_example: Kannst du später noch mal mit deiner Mutter sprechen?
native_language_example: Can you talk to your mother again later?

additional_notes: A very common combination of mit + dem. mit always takes the dative case, and dem is the dative singular form of the definite article for masculine and neuter nouns. It often translates directly as "with the," but in some expressions English may use a different phrasing, such as mit dem Bus = "by bus" or mit dem Trinken aufhören = "stop drinking."
target_language_example: Ich spreche mit dem Lehrer nach dem Unterricht.
native_language_example: I'm talking with the teacher after class.

meaning: by car; in a car (using the car as transport).
additional_notes: Used with "mit" + dative to say how someone travels or is transported. Often answers "Wie?" (How?/By what means?). You can swap in other transport words: "mit dem Bus", "mit dem Fahrrad", "mit der Bahn".
target_language_example: Wir fahren morgen mit dem Auto nach Berlin.
native_language_example: We’re going to Berlin tomorrow by car.

additional_notes: Used to say you travel to a place by car. Structure: **mit + dative** (*mit dem Auto*) + **nach + place** (*nach Berlin/nach Japan*). **Nach** is commonly used with cities and countries (usually without an article).
target_language_example: Wir fahren morgen mit dem Auto nach Berlin.
native_language_example: We’re driving to Berlin tomorrow.

meaning: to go/commute to work by car.
additional_notes: Used to say how you travel to your workplace. Often with verbs like fahren (to drive/go), zur Arbeit fahren (drive to work), or zur Arbeit kommen (get/come to work). “Mit dem Auto” = by car; “zur Arbeit” = to work (zu + der Arbeit → zur Arbeit).
target_language_example: Morgen fahre ich nicht mit dem Auto zur Arbeit, sondern mit dem Bus.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I’m not going to work by car, but by bus.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement (e.g., fahren, kommen) to say how you travel. It’s the dative form after "mit" (mit + dem = dative): "mit dem Bus". Common in questions about directions: "Wie komme ich mit dem Bus ...?"
target_language_example: Wir fahren morgen mit dem Bus zur Arbeit.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we’re going to work by bus.

additional_notes: Common way to say how you travel to school. Uses dative after "mit" (mit dem Bus). "zur" = "zu der" (= to the). Often used with "fahren" (to go/drive/ride).
target_language_example: Heute fahre ich mit dem Bus zur Schule.
native_language_example: Today I’m going to school by bus.

additional_notes: Used to say how someone travels (their means of transport). Often used with verbs of going/coming/traveling like „fahren“, „kommen“, „hingefahren“, „gefahren“. Literally „with the bicycle“, but in English it’s usually “by bike” or “on a bike.”
target_language_example: Heute fahre ich mit dem Fahrrad zur Arbeit.
native_language_example: Today I’m going to work by bike.

meaning: to go to school by bike.
additional_notes: Used to say how you travel to school. Pattern: „mit dem Fahrrad“ = by bike; „zur Schule“ = to school (zu + der). Often used with fahren/go verbs (fahren, gehen, kommen).
target_language_example: Wir fahren heute mit dem Fahrrad zur Schule.
native_language_example: Today we’re going to school by bike.

additional_notes: Used to say how you travel (means of transportation). You often see it with verbs like reisen (to travel) or fahren (to go/travel), and it contrasts with options like mit dem Zug (by train) or mit dem Auto (by car).
target_language_example: Wir reisen morgen mit dem Flugzeug nach Berlin.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we’re traveling to Berlin by plane.

additional_notes: Used to ask or say what someone did, plans to do, or what happened to a specific sum of money (often implying responsibility or suspicion). Common with verbs like „tun“ (do), „vorhaben“ (plan), and in questions like „Was ist mit dem Geld passiert?“ (What happened to the money?).
target_language_example: Was machst du mit dem Geld?
native_language_example: What are you doing with the money?

additional_notes: Means you are accompanied by the dog, especially when going out (often implying taking the dog for a walk): „mit dem Hund ausgehen / mit dem Hund rausgehen“. Uses dative after „mit“, so it’s „dem Hund“ (not „der Hund“). In questions like „Was ist mit dem Hund?“ it means “What’s wrong/what’s going on with the dog?”
target_language_example: Ich gehe heute Abend mit dem Hund spazieren.
native_language_example: I’m going for a walk with the dog this evening.

additional_notes: Used to describe actions done using the head, especially gestures like **mit dem Kopf schütteln** (to shake your head = ‘no’) and **mit dem Kopf nicken** (to nod your head = ‘yes’/agreement), or physical contact like **mit dem Kopf gegen etwas schlagen** (to hit your head against something). Often the verb makes the meaning clear.
target_language_example: Er schüttelt mit dem Kopf, weil er nicht einverstanden ist.
native_language_example: He shakes his head because he doesn’t agree.

meaning: with the knife; using a knife.
additional_notes: Uses "mit" + dative ("dem Messer") to say you do something using a knife as a tool, or to warn someone to be careful when handling it ("Vorsicht mit ...").
target_language_example: Schneid das Brot bitte mit dem Messer.
native_language_example: Please cut the bread with the knife.

additional_notes: Used to say how you travel (your mode of transport). Often with verbs like fahren/kommen/sein: „mit dem Rad fahren“ (to ride a bike), „mit dem Rad kommen“ (to come by bike). Also appears as „mit dem Fahrrad“ (same meaning).
target_language_example: Heute komme ich mit dem Rad zur Arbeit.
native_language_example: Today I’m coming to work by bike.

additional_notes: Used with the verb „aufhören“ + „mit“ + dative to say you stopped doing an activity: „mit dem Rauchen aufhören“ (to stop/quit smoking). Often appears in the perfect tense: „Ich habe … aufgehört.“ In questions: „Haben Sie … aufgehört?“
target_language_example: Ich habe vor einem Jahr mit dem Rauchen aufgehört.
native_language_example: I quit smoking a year ago.

meaning: to quit smoking; to stop smoking.
additional_notes: Pattern: "mit" + dative + "aufhören" = to stop doing an activity (e.g., "mit dem/der + [noun/gerund-like noun] aufhören"). Here, "das Rauchen" is a nominalized verb meaning "smoking," so "mit dem Rauchen aufhören" literally corresponds to "to stop with the smoking" → "to quit smoking." Common forms: "Hör mit dem Rauchen auf!" (Quit smoking!) and "Ich will mit dem Rauchen aufhören." (I want to quit smoking).
target_language_example: Als Erstes musst du mit dem Rauchen aufhören.
native_language_example: First of all, you have to quit smoking.

additional_notes: Uses the verb phrase „mit etwas aufhören“ = “to stop (doing) something.” Here: „mit dem Rauchen“ (with smoking) + „aufhören“. Often appears after verbs like „versuchen“ (try), „beschließen“ (decide), „raten“ (advise), „gezwungen sein“ (be forced), or „sich bemühen“ (make an effort). In many sentences you’ll see it as „aufzuhören“ (zu + infinitive) at the end: „Ich versuche, mit dem Rauchen aufzuhören.“
target_language_example: Ich versuche gerade, mit dem Rauchen aufzuhören.
native_language_example: I’m trying to quit smoking right now.

meaning: "with this shit" / "with this crap" (used to complain and tell someone to stop).
additional_notes: Very rude/vulgar. Commonly used with commands like „Hör auf mit dem Scheiß!“ (Stop that shit!) or „Schluss mit dem Scheiß!“ (Enough of this shit!). It refers to whatever annoying behavior, talk, or situation is happening.
target_language_example: Hör auf mit dem Scheiß und konzentrier dich.
native_language_example: Stop that shit and focus.

additional_notes: Used to say you use a taxi as your means of transport. It often answers the question „Wie fährst du?“ (How are you going?). You can also say „Wir fahren mit dem Taxi“ (We’re going by taxi).
target_language_example: Weil der letzte Bus schon weg war, musste ich mit dem Taxi fahren.
native_language_example: Because the last bus had already gone, I had to go by taxi.

meaning: by train; on the train (as a means of travel).
additional_notes: Used with verbs of travel/movement like fahren, kommen, ankommen, abfahren to say the mode of transport. Literally “with the train,” but in English it’s usually “by train.” Often contrasts with other options: mit dem Auto, mit dem Bus, etc.
target_language_example: Ich fahre morgen mit dem Zug nach Berlin.
native_language_example: I’m going to Berlin by train tomorrow.

additional_notes: "Mit dem" is the contraction of "mit" + "dem" (dative). It’s used (1) after verbs that take "mit" to mean "with that/this" (often referring back to something already mentioned): "mit dem aufhören" = stop doing that; "mit dem auskommen" = manage with that/what we have; "Was ist los mit dem?" = what’s wrong with him/it. (2) In relative clauses meaning "with whom/which": "ein Freund, mit dem er sprechen konnte" = a friend (that) he could talk to. It can refer to a masculine person (him) or a neuter thing (it), depending on context.
target_language_example: Kannst du mir sagen, was ich mit dem machen soll?
native_language_example: Can you tell me what I should do with it?

additional_notes: Used when you refer back to a specific thing/action/content that’s described by a relative clause with "was" (e.g., "was Tom geschrieben hat" = "what Tom wrote"). "mit" takes the dative case, so you often see "mit dem" before the "was"-clause. Common with verbs like "einverstanden sein" (to agree), "aufhören" (to stop), or "tun" (to do) when you mean "with what someone did/said/wrote."
target_language_example: Ich bin nicht zufrieden mit dem, was er gesagt hat.
native_language_example: I’m not happy with what he said.

meaning: "with which I" / "with that I" (introduces a relative clause).
additional_notes: Used in a relative clause to refer back to a masculine or neuter noun (e.g., der Zug, der Bus, das Auto). The preposition „mit“ always takes the dative case, so you get „mit dem“ (not *mit den* or *mit der*). Often translates as “that/which I (travel) with/on/in,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Das ist der Bus, mit dem ich jeden Tag zur Arbeit fahre.
native_language_example: That’s the bus that I take to work every day.

additional_notes: "mit" takes the dative case. "mit den" is used with plural nouns in the dative (and also with masculine/neuter nouns in the dative plural form). Common in descriptions ("das Mädchen mit den langen Haaren" = "the girl with the long hair"). It can also appear in fixed/emphatic expressions like "Hoch mit den ...!" ("Up with your ...!"), "Zur Hölle mit den ...!" ("To hell with the ...!") or with abstract nouns like "mit den Folgen" ("with the consequences").
target_language_example: Ich kann mit den neuen Regeln noch nicht gut umgehen.
native_language_example: I still can’t handle the new rules well.

additional_notes: Used to describe doing something using your fingers (often with a body movement), e.g. tapping/drumming on a surface (mit den Fingern auf den Tisch), snapping/cracking your fingers, feeling for something in the dark, or running your fingers through your hair. "den" is dative plural after "mit".
target_language_example: Sie klopfte ungeduldig mit den Fingern auf den Tisch.
native_language_example: She tapped her fingers impatiently on the table.

additional_notes: Used with "mit" + dative plural ("den Händen") to say you do something using your hands (instead of a tool), or to specify that something is done by hand. Often used with verbs like essen (eat), machen (do/make), schlagen (hit/beat), fühlen (feel). You can also say "mit der Hand" for one hand.
target_language_example: Ich esse das lieber mit den Händen.
native_language_example: I prefer to eat that with my hands.

additional_notes: Uses the preposition "mit" (with) + dative: "den Kindern" is dative plural of "die Kinder". Often describes doing something together with the children (e.g., Zeit mit den Kindern verbringen). In questions like "Was ist mit den Kindern?", it can mean "What about the children?" or "What’s wrong with the kids?" depending on context.
target_language_example: Am Wochenende gehe ich oft mit den Kindern in den Park.
native_language_example: On the weekend I often go to the park with the kids.

meaning: with the people; with those people.
additional_notes: "Mit" + dative plural "den Leuten". Used to mean being together with a group (going somewhere with them), talking/working with them, or doing something to/with them (often: treating people in a certain way: "Das kann man nicht mit den Leuten tun" = you can’t do that to people/them). Often followed by a clarifier like "vom Theater", "da hinten", "im Keller".
target_language_example: Ich gehe heute Abend mit den Leuten aus dem Kurs etwas trinken.
native_language_example: I’m going out for a drink tonight with the people from the class.

additional_notes: Used with a plural noun to introduce a relative clause: "die Leute, mit denen ich arbeite" = "the people I work with." It’s the dative plural form of the relative pronoun after the preposition "mit". It can also stand alone to mean "with them/those people": "Mit denen habe ich nichts zu tun" = "I have nothing to do with them."
target_language_example: Das sind die Freunde, mit denen ich oft unterwegs bin.
native_language_example: Those are the friends I often go out with.

additional_notes: Usually means 'with the'. After mit, German uses the dative case, so der here is the feminine singular dative form of die. It is used for accompaniment (mit der Familie), means or body parts (mit der rechten Hand, mit der Zunge), and descriptions like der Mann mit der grünen Jacke.
target_language_example: Sie spricht mit der Lehrerin.
native_language_example: She is speaking with the teacher.

additional_notes: Used to state someone’s purpose or planned goal. It’s typically followed by an infinitive with „zu“ (e.g., „mit der Absicht, ... zu ...“) or sometimes by a „dass“-clause. Formal/neutral in tone.
target_language_example: Sie kam mit der Absicht, sich zu entschuldigen.
native_language_example: She came with the intention of apologizing.

additional_notes: Used with **sein** (e.g., *ich bin, wir sind*) to say you’ve completed your work/task. You can add a time (*gegen Mitternacht*) or a limit (*für heute*) and you can also use it with **vorhaben/planen**: *Ich hatte vor, mit der Arbeit fertig zu sein* (“I planned to be done with work”).
target_language_example: Bist du schon mit der Arbeit fertig?
native_language_example: Are you done with work already?

additional_notes: Used to describe doing something using your hand(s), often meaning “manually” (not with a tool or machine): etwas mit der Hand machen. Common in set phrases like „mit der Hand auf etw. zeigen“ (to point at something) or „jdn. mit der Hand erwischen“ (to catch someone in the act / red-handed, e.g. „mit der Hand in der Keksdose“).
target_language_example: Ich habe den Teig mit der Hand geknetet.
native_language_example: I kneaded the dough by hand.

meaning: with the police; to/with the police (when speaking/dealing with them).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like sprechen (talk), Ärger haben/kriegen (get into trouble), or dealing/being involved with police. The case changes with gender/number: mit der Polizei (singular), mit den Polizisten (plural people). Also common: zur Polizei gehen = go to the police/police station; bei der Polizei = at/with the police (as an institution).
