native_language_example: It's a shame that we don't have good weather today.

additional_notes: Colloquial short form of "schaffe ich" (from "schaffen" = to manage, to accomplish). Often used with "es": "Schaff ich (es) nicht" = "I can’t do it." With "schon" it can sound reassuring/confident: "Das schaff ich schon" = "I’ll manage that." In other contexts it can mean "I manage to...": "Ich schaff(e) es nicht, ..." = "I can’t manage to..."
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, das schaff ich heute noch.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ll manage that today.

meaning: "I can't do it / I won't manage (it)."
additional_notes: Spoken, contracted form of "(Das) schaffe ich nicht." You often leave out "das" when it’s clear from context. Used to say you can’t manage a task, don’t have time/energy, or it’s too difficult. In more formal speech/writing: "Das schaffe ich nicht."
target_language_example: Heute schaff ich nicht, den Bericht fertig zu machen.
native_language_example: I can’t manage to finish the report today.

meaning: “can you do it / will you manage (to)?”
additional_notes: From the verb "schaffen" (to manage, to accomplish). "es" is a dummy pronoun meaning “it” (the task/situation). Very often used with an infinitive clause: "Schaffst du es, ... zu ...?" = “Can you manage to …?” In negative form: "Schaffst du es nicht, ..." = “If you don’t manage to …” / “Can’t you manage to …?”
target_language_example: Schaffst du es, morgen früher aufzustehen?
native_language_example: Can you manage to get up earlier tomorrow?

additional_notes: “Schalten Sie …” is the polite/formal imperative with Sie (you). It’s commonly used with particles like **aus** (off) and **an** (on): **Schalten Sie das Licht aus.** / **Schalten Sie es wieder an.** In spoken German it can sound like a firm instruction, especially without **bitte**.
target_language_example: Schalten Sie bitte Ihr Handy aus.
native_language_example: Please turn off your phone.

meaning: "look at" / "take a look at" (du-imperative, used with "... an").
additional_notes: This is part of the separable, reflexive verb phrase "sich etw. ansehen" (= to look at something). In the du-command you typically say: "Schau dir + [thing/person] + an." Example pattern: "Schau dir den Einband an." (More formal: "Schauen Sie sich ... an.")
target_language_example: Schau dir das mal an!
native_language_example: Take a look at that!

additional_notes: Common spoken phrase used to draw attention to something you’re about to show, point out, or comment on. Often used at the start of a sentence, sometimes with an exclamation mark or semicolon, and it can be followed by a noun or a whole clause (e.g., “Schau mal, was …”). Slightly casual but not rude.
target_language_example: Schau mal, wie schön der Sonnenuntergang ist!
native_language_example: Look, how beautiful the sunset is!

additional_notes: Used with **Sie** (formal “you”) as a polite command/request. It’s usually part of the separable verb **sich etwas anschauen**: **Schauen Sie sich … an!** (= “Look at …!”). The **sich** is a reflexive pronoun that goes with this verb pattern and doesn’t translate literally into English.
target_language_example: Schauen Sie sich das bitte einmal an.
native_language_example: Please take a look at that.

additional_notes:
Polite command using **Sie** (formal “you”), used when speaking to strangers, customers, etc. Often followed by:
- **... genauer hin** = “look more closely”
- **... mal her** = “look here (for a moment)”
It can also introduce what you’re about to say: **Schauen Sie, …** = “Look, … / See, …”.
target_language_example: Schauen Sie bitte hier auf den Bildschirm.
native_language_example: Please look here at the screen.

meaning: “look (at …),” said to more than one person (you all).
additional_notes: Used in the plural imperative (command/request) with the reflexive pronoun euch. It’s often followed by a separable verb prefix like in **schaut euch … an** (“look at …”). You can also use it as an excited prompt: **Schaut euch das an!** = “Look at that!”
target_language_example: Schaut euch bitte die Speisekarte an.
native_language_example: Please look at the menu.

meaning: to get divorced; to have a divorce finalized.
additional_notes: Used reflexively with sich: sich scheiden lassen = to get divorced. Often followed by von + dative to say who you divorce: sich von seiner Frau scheiden lassen. In perfect tense it’s commonly hat sich ... scheiden lassen (or hatte ... scheiden lassen in past perfect).
target_language_example: Nach zehn Jahren Ehe haben sie sich scheiden lassen.
native_language_example: After ten years of marriage, they got divorced.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive after „zu“ to express that something appears to be the case (based on impressions, not certainty). Conjugate only „scheinen“: „Ich scheine … zu sein“, „Er/Sie scheint … zu sein“, „Wir scheinen … zu sein“. Often interchangeable with „scheint, als ob …“ ("seems as if …"). Note: „scheinen“ can also mean “to shine” (sun/light), depending on context.
target_language_example: Er muss sehr glücklich scheinen zu sein.
native_language_example: He must seem to be very happy.

additional_notes: Used to describe sunny weather. Word order can change: “Die Sonne scheint.” (most common) and “Heute scheint die Sonne.” Also note the vulgar idiom “Ihm scheint die Sonne aus dem Arsch.” meaning someone has everything going their way / is extremely lucky (very rude).
target_language_example: Heute scheint die Sonne, aber es ist kalt.
native_language_example: The sun is shining today, but it’s cold.

additional_notes: Very vulgar and aggressive. Used to dismiss someone/something or say it doesn’t matter. Usually followed by an accusative object (e.g., „Scheiß auf deinen Boss!“). You’ll also hear „Scheiß drauf!“ (= “Fuck it.”).
target_language_example: Scheiß auf den Stress, wir gehen nach Hause.
native_language_example: Screw the stress, we’re going home.

additional_notes: Very vulgar, angry way to say you don’t care about someone/something or you reject it. Used as an exclamation. It’s short for the pattern „Scheiß auf + Akkusativ“ (e.g. „Scheiß auf den Verein!“, „Scheiß auf das Geld!“, „Scheiß auf die Regeln!“). Here „den“ is masculine accusative (“that guy/that thing”).
target_language_example: Scheiß auf den Plan — wir machen es anders.
native_language_example: Screw the plan—we’re doing it differently.

additional_notes: "Schicken" means "to send"; "Sie" is the formal "you". Used for polite instructions or requests (often with "bitte"). Common patterns: "Schicken Sie + object" (Send/dispatch + something/someone), "Schicken Sie + jemanden + zu mir" (Send someone to me), "Schicken Sie mir + etwas" (Send me something).
target_language_example: Schicken Sie mir bitte die Unterlagen per E-Mail.
native_language_example: Please send me the documents by email.

meaning: to go to sleep; to go to bed.
additional_notes: Common everyday phrase meaning you’re going to bed for the night. Often used with a modal verb (e.g., müssen/wollen/sollen) or with time words: „Ich muss jetzt schlafen gehen.“ You can also say „ins Bett gehen“ (= to go to bed), which focuses more on going to bed physically.
target_language_example: Ich muss wirklich schlafen gehen, ich bin total müde.
native_language_example: I really have to go to sleep; I’m totally tired.

additional_notes: Used with forms of „sein“ (to be) to describe someone’s mood: „Ich bin/sie ist schlecht gelaunt.“ Often strengthened with words like „sehr“, „total“, „recht“, or „so“ (e.g., „recht schlecht gelaunt“ = rather in a bad mood).
target_language_example: Heute bin ich schlecht gelaunt, weil ich kaum geschlafen habe.
native_language_example: Today I’m in a bad mood because I barely slept.

meaning: badly about other people; to speak ill of others.
additional_notes: Usually used with verbs like „reden/sprechen“: „schlecht über andere reden/sprechen“ = criticize others or say negative things about them (often like gossiping, especially „hinter jemandes Rücken“ = behind someone’s back).
target_language_example: Bitte rede nicht schlecht über andere.
native_language_example: Please don’t speak badly about other people.

additional_notes: Used with "haben" (to have) to say someone is in a bad mood: "Ich habe schlechte Laune." You can also say "schlechte Laune haben" (to be in a bad mood). Often with reasons or time words: "Ohne Frühstück...", "heute Morgen...".
target_language_example: Ich habe heute schlechte Laune, weil ich zu wenig geschlafen habe.
native_language_example: I’m in a bad mood today because I didn’t sleep enough.

additional_notes: A common phrase to introduce unpleasant or disappointing information. Often used with "Ich habe ..." (I have ...) or "Das sind ..." (That’s ...), and sometimes paired with "gute Nachrichten" (good news): "Ich habe gute und schlechte Nachrichten."
target_language_example: Leider habe ich schlechte Nachrichten: Der Zug fällt heute aus.
native_language_example: Unfortunately I have bad news: the train is cancelled today.

additional_notes: Usually used with "sein": "(jemand) ist schlechter Laune" = "(someone) is in a bad mood". Often used with intensifiers like "ziemlich" (pretty) or "gerade" (at the moment), and in questions: "Bist du schlechter Laune?" / formal "Sind Sie schlechter Laune?".
target_language_example: Ich bin heute etwas schlechter Laune, weil ich schlecht geschlafen habe.
native_language_example: I’m in a bit of a bad mood today because I slept badly.

meaning: a sore loser (someone who reacts badly to losing).
additional_notes: Used to criticize someone who can’t accept defeat (e.g., gets angry, complains, makes excuses). Often used with “sein” (Tom ist ein schlechter Verlierer) or as a warning/command: “Sei kein schlechter Verlierer.”
target_language_example: Du hast nur ein Spiel verloren—sei kein schlechter Verlierer.
native_language_example: You only lost one game—don’t be a sore loser.

additional_notes: Used with „ein“ or „ohne“ to talk about guilt: „ein schlechtes Gewissen haben“ (to feel guilty) and „jemandem ein schlechtes Gewissen machen“ (to make someone feel guilty, to guilt-trip someone).
target_language_example: Ich kann das nicht tun, ohne ein schlechtes Gewissen zu haben.
native_language_example: I can’t do that without feeling guilty.

additional_notes: Used for comparisons with adjectives/adverbs: "X ist schlimmer als Y" (= X is worse than Y). You can also start a sentence with it for emphasis (often in an incomplete comparison): "Schlimmer als Ungeziefer, ...". "viel schlimmer als" = "much worse than".
target_language_example: Das Wetter ist heute schlimmer als gestern.
native_language_example: The weather is worse today than yesterday.

additional_notes: Narrative phrase used to describe a sequence of actions. **schloss** is simple past of **schließen** (“to close”); **die Augen** = “the eyes”. In English you usually add a possessive (“his/her eyes”), even though German often uses **die** here.
target_language_example: Er schloss die Augen und lächelte leise.
native_language_example: He closed his eyes and smiled softly.

additional_notes: Used to say someone suggested an idea or plan. Very often followed by a comma and an infinitive clause with "zu" (e.g., "schlug vor, eine Pause zu machen") or by a "dass"-clause / indirect suggestion (e.g., "schlug vor, ich solle ...").
target_language_example: Sie schlug vor, früher nach Hause zu gehen.
native_language_example: She suggested going home earlier.

additional_notes: This is the 2nd-person singular (du) present tense of "schlafen" (to sleep), used in questions. It can mean (1) right now: "Are you sleeping (already)?" or (2) in general/habitually: "Do you sleep (well)?" It also appears in phrases like "mit jemandem schlafen" meaning "to sleep with someone" (have sex). Word order in questions: verb first (schläfst) + subject (du).
target_language_example: Hey, schläfst du schon?
native_language_example: Hey, are you asleep already?

additional_notes: Used with the impersonal subject "es" for weather: "Es schneit." In yes/no questions, the verb comes first: "Schneit es (hier)?" You can add time/place words: "Im Januar schneit es" / "Bei uns schneit es oft."
target_language_example: Schneit es morgen in Berlin?
native_language_example: Is it going to snow in Berlin tomorrow?

meaning: "does it snow here?" / "it snows here" (depending on context).
additional_notes: From the verb "schneien" (to snow). With normal word order you often get a statement: "Hier schneit es (oft)." With inverted word order you get a yes/no question: "Schneit es hier (oft)?" You can add time/frequency words like "im Winter" (in winter), "oft" (often), "selten" (rarely), "jemals/je" (ever).
target_language_example: Schneit es hier im Januar oft?
native_language_example: Does it snow here often in January?

meaning: to do (something) quickly; to hurry up (and get it done).
additional_notes: Common in everyday speech. Often used when urging someone to speed up and finish something promptly; also used about doing a task quickly. In imperatives you’ll often hear the separated form: "Mach das schnell" or "Mach schnell", but the full term appears as "schnell machen" in sentences like "Ich muss das schnell machen."
target_language_example: Ich muss das schnell machen, sonst verpassen wir den Zug.
native_language_example: I have to do this quickly, otherwise we’ll miss the train.

additional_notes: Used to describe running at a high speed. In comparisons you’ll often see it with words like „so“ (so fast), „genauso“ (just as fast), and „wie“ (as/like): „so schnell … wie …“.
target_language_example: Ich muss schnell rennen, sonst verpasse ich den Bus.
native_language_example: I have to run fast, otherwise I'll miss the bus.

additional_notes: Used with the comparative form of an adjective/adverb + „als“ to compare two people/things: „X ist schneller als Y.“ After „als“, you often use the nominative (like English subject form): „schneller als ich/du/er wir/sie/Sie“. It can also be used more generally to mean “quicker than” (not only literal running speed).
target_language_example: Ich bin heute schneller als gestern.
native_language_example: I'm faster today than yesterday.

meaning: “faster than” (used to compare speed or how quickly something happens).
additional_notes: Used in comparisons: X ist/geht/rennt/läuft schneller als Y. With pronouns, you’ll often see the dative: schneller als mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch. Also common in the phrase schneller als man denkt (“faster than you think”).
target_language_example: Kannst du das schneller als ich machen?
native_language_example: Can you do that faster than me?

additional_notes: "schon" means "already" and "angefangen" is the past participle of "anfangen" (to start). It’s typically used with "haben" in the present perfect to say something has already begun (often earlier than expected). Common patterns: "Hast du schon angefangen?" (Have you started yet/already?) and "Es hat schon angefangen zu ..." (It has already started to ...).
target_language_example: Ich habe schon angefangen, den Bericht zu schreiben.
native_language_example: I’ve already started writing the report.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something has been happening continuously since earlier today and is still true now. Often placed before what you’re doing/feeling: “Ich suche schon den ganzen Tag …” = “I’ve been looking all day …”.
target_language_example: Ich warte schon den ganzen Tag auf deinen Anruf.
native_language_example: I’ve been waiting for your call all day.

meaning: "all along" / "the whole time" (for a while already).
additional_notes: Used to say something has been true, happening, or intended continuously up to now (often for longer than expected). "schon" adds the sense of "already". Often used with the present perfect or simple past, and with verbs like warten, fragen, wissen, wollen, erwarten.
target_language_example: Ich wusste schon die ganze Zeit, dass du recht hast.
native_language_example: I knew all along that you were right.

additional_notes: Often used in questions about past experience, especially with the perfect tense: Hast du das schon einmal gemacht? = Have you ever done that? Literally it is like “already once,” so in statements it can also mean “once before.”
target_language_example: Hast du dieses Lied schon einmal gehört?
native_language_example: Have you heard this song before?

additional_notes: Used to ask whether someone has seen a person or thing at some point in the past (at least once). Often used in questions with "schon einmal" = "ever/before". Word order: "Haben Sie ... schon einmal gesehen?" (formal) vs. "Habt ihr ... schon einmal gesehen?" (informal plural "you").
target_language_example: Hast du diesen Film schon einmal gesehen?
native_language_example: Have you ever seen this movie before?

additional_notes: Used to ask or state that someone is finished earlier than expected, or to politely check if they’re done (e.g., in a shop, restaurant, at work). “schon” adds the idea of “already/by now,” and “fertig” means “finished/ready.” Often used in questions like “Bist du schon fertig?” or polite “Sind Sie schon fertig?”
target_language_example: Bist du schon fertig, oder brauchst du noch fünf Minuten?
native_language_example: Are you already done, or do you still need five minutes?

additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize a negation, often after a first negative statement: "X nicht, (und) Y schon gar nicht" = "not X, and certainly not Y / let alone Y". It highlights that the second thing is even less likely/less acceptable than the first.
target_language_example: Ich habe heute keine Zeit, und morgen schon gar nicht.
native_language_example: I don't have time today, and certainly not tomorrow (let alone tomorrow).

additional_notes: Used with the Perfekt tense to say someone has eaten earlier than now. Often answers the question of whether the person is still hungry or whether food is still needed. In questions like "Hast du schon gegessen?", it can also mean "Have you eaten yet?" depending on context. Word order is flexible: "Ich habe schon gegessen" / "Ich habe gegessen" (but "schon" adds the idea of 'already').
target_language_example: Ich habe schon gegessen, danke.
native_language_example: I've already eaten, thanks.

additional_notes: Used when you’re reminding someone that you already told them the information that follows. Typical patterns: „Ich habe dir/Ihnen schon gesagt, was …“ (I already told you what …). Often used with „doch“ to sound more emphatic/insistent: „Ich habe doch schon gesagt, was …!“
target_language_example: Ich habe dir schon gesagt, was du jetzt tun sollst.
native_language_example: I already told you what you should do now.

additional_notes: Used with the present perfect (haben + gesehen) to say you’ve already watched/seen/checked something. In questions, it often means “have you seen it yet/already?” depending on context and tone. Word order is flexible in speech (e.g., „Hast du das schon gesehen?“ / „Hast du schon das gesehen?“).
target_language_example: Ich habe den Film schon gesehen, aber ich schaue ihn gern nochmal.
native_language_example: I've already seen the movie, but I like watching it again.

additional_notes: Used to reassure someone, calm them down, or to say “don’t worry about it / never mind.” Often said as a quick response on its own (“Schon gut!”). Depending on tone it can also sound like “Alright, alright” (to stop a discussion).
target_language_example: Schon gut, ich mache das gleich.
native_language_example: It’s okay, I’ll do it in a moment.

meaning: always; ever since (as long as one can remember).
additional_notes: Used to say something has been true for a very long time and still is (a long-standing habit, condition, or dream). It often appears with past tenses or the present to emphasize continuity: „Ich wollte das schon immer.“ = “I’ve always wanted that.”
target_language_example: Ich wollte schon immer nach Berlin fahren.
native_language_example: I’ve always wanted to go to Berlin.

meaning: “always (been) like this/that” (since as long as you can remember).
additional_notes: Used to say something has been the same for a long time (often “all along”). Commonly used in questions about whether someone/ something has always had a certain quality: “War sie schon immer so …?” It can sound accusatory or emphatic depending on tone.
target_language_example: Ich mache das schon immer so.
native_language_example: I’ve always done it like this.

meaning: "for a long time in" (asking how long someone has been in a place).
additional_notes: Used with the present tense to ask about duration up to now. Common in questions like: „Bist du schon lange in …?“ (informal) / „Sind Sie schon lange in …?“ (formal). It can refer to being somewhere temporarily (e.g., traveling) or living there, depending on context.
target_language_example: Bist du schon lange in Berlin?
native_language_example: Have you been in Berlin for a long time?

meaning: “not for a long time anymore” / “haven’t … in a long time.”
additional_notes: Used to say something hasn’t been true or hasn’t happened for a long time up to now. Very common with the present perfect (ich habe … schon lange nicht mehr gemacht) or with the present tense to describe a current state (wir wohnen da schon lange nicht mehr = we don’t live there anymore, and it’s been that way for a long time). Often implies a change happened long ago.
target_language_example: Ich habe schon lange nicht mehr so gut geschlafen.
native_language_example: I haven’t slept this well in a long time.

meaning: "a long time ago / for a long time already" (sooner than expected).
additional_notes: Used to stress that something happened long ago or has been the case for a long time already—often implying “by now” or “it should have happened earlier.” Common in statements like: Ich habe das schon längst gemacht. / Das hätte schon längst passieren müssen.
target_language_example: Wir hätten schon längst losfahren sollen.
native_language_example: We should have left a long time ago (by now).

additional_notes: Used when you do something now a bit earlier than expected, often as preparation or before someone else does something (common with suggestions/imperatives: „Mach das schon mal …“ = go ahead and do it now). In other contexts (especially questions), it can also mean „ever / before“ (e.g., „Warst du schon mal in Berlin?“ = Have you ever been to Berlin?).
target_language_example: Ich rufe schon mal ein Taxi, dann sind wir schneller weg.
native_language_example: I’ll go ahead and call a taxi so we can leave faster.

additional_notes: "schon mal" is a common, slightly colloquial way to say "schon einmal" ("already/once"), and in this phrase it means "at some earlier time" = "before." It’s often used with the present perfect: "Ich habe X schon mal gesehen" ("I’ve seen X before"). As a short question, "Schon mal gesehen?" means "Have you seen it before?"
target_language_example: Ich glaube, wir haben uns schon mal gesehen.
native_language_example: I think we’ve seen each other before.

additional_notes: "Schon" adds the idea of “already / up to now,” and "oft" means “often.” Together, "schon oft" is used to say something has happened many times before now (often with the feel of “this isn’t new” or “I’ve experienced this before”). Common with the present perfect: "Ich habe ... schon oft ...".
target_language_example: Das habe ich schon oft gemacht.
native_language_example: I’ve already done that many times.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize duration up to now. "schon" adds the idea of "already" (it has been that long), and it often comes before the time phrase: "Ich bin schon sehr lange hier." Can be used in statements and questions, and with present tense to describe something that started in the past and is still true now.
target_language_example: Wir kennen uns schon sehr lange.
native_language_example: We've known each other for a very long time.

additional_notes: Used with a time expression to say something started in the past and is still true/continuing now. The word "schon" adds emphasis (often like "already" or "now") and is very common in this pattern: "schon seit drei Jahren" = "for three years now".
target_language_example: Ich kenne sie schon seit 2019.
native_language_example: I’ve known her since 2019 / for her since 2019.

meaning: for years now; already for years.
additional_notes: Used to say something started years ago and is still true/continuing. Common with the present tense (or present perfect) and often placed near the time expression: „Ich wohne schon seit Jahren hier.“
target_language_example: Ich kenne diese Familie schon seit Jahren.
native_language_example: I’ve known this family for years now.

additional_notes: Used to stress that something has been going on for a long time (hours) and is still continuing now. Often expresses impatience or surprise. Typically used with the present tense in German: „Er wartet schon seit Stunden.“
target_language_example: Wir warten schon seit Stunden auf den Bus.
native_language_example: We’ve been waiting for the bus for hours now.

meaning: for three years already (for the past three years).
additional_notes: Used with the present tense to say an action/state started three years ago and is still true now. "seit" = since/for (time duration), and "schon" adds emphasis like “already/as long as”.
target_language_example: Ich lerne schon seit drei Jahren Deutsch.
native_language_example: I've been learning German for three years already.

additional_notes: Used very often with "sein" (e.g., "Er ist schon weg") to say someone/something has already left or is no longer there. It can also mean that something has already been used up/consumed or is missing (e.g., "Die Hälfte ist schon weg"). In questions, it can express surprise that someone is leaving early: "Du willst schon weg?"
target_language_example: Sorry, der letzte Bus ist schon weg.
native_language_example: Sorry, the last bus is already gone.

additional_notes: Used when something happens repeatedly, often with a tone of annoyance, impatience, or surprise (“again?!”). Often placed early in the sentence, and it can stand alone as a reaction: “Schon wieder?” = “Again?”
target_language_example: Musst du schon wieder arbeiten?
native_language_example: Do you have to work again (already)?

additional_notes: “Sie” is the formal “you” (used with strangers, in service situations, or professionally). With “schreiben,” it can be an imperative: “Schreiben Sie …!” (“Write …!”), often softened with “bitte.” It can also be the normal present tense for formal “you”: “Schreiben Sie …?” (“Do you write …?” / “Are you writing …?”).
target_language_example: Schreiben Sie bitte Ihre E-Mail-Adresse hier auf.
native_language_example: Please write your email address down here.

meaning: “do you write…?” / “are you writing…?” (2nd person singular question).
additional_notes: Question form of **du schreibst** (“you write/you’re writing”), with the verb first. Used to ask about a habit (**Schreibst du Kurzgeschichten?** = “Do you write short stories?”) or something happening now, often with **gerade/jetzt** (**Schreibst du gerade einen Brief?** = “Are you writing a letter right now?”). Can take objects or question words: **Was schreibst du? Worüber schreibst du?**
target_language_example: Schreibst du heute Abend noch eine E-Mail?
native_language_example: Are you writing another email tonight?

additional_notes: Used with the verb "sein": "(jemand) ist schuld daran" = someone is responsible for causing something bad. Very often followed by a "dass"-clause: "Du bist schuld daran, dass ...". You can also put the real cause in front: "Schuld daran waren ..." = "... were to blame."
target_language_example: Ich bin nicht schuld daran, dass der Bus zu spät kam.
native_language_example: It’s not my fault that the bus was late.

meaning: to be to blame; to be at fault.
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something caused a problem or is responsible for a bad result. Common patterns: „Wer ist schuld?“ (Who’s to blame?), „X ist schuld.“ (X is to blame.), „an etw. schuld sein“ / „daran schuld sein“ (to be to blame for something), and „schuld sein, dass …“ (to be the reason that …).
target_language_example: Ich will nicht schuld sein, dass wir zu spät sind.
native_language_example: I don’t want to be to blame for us being late.

meaning: to be guilty; to owe (someone something).
additional_notes: Used in two common ways: (1) legal/moral guilt: „Er ist schuldig.“ = „He is guilty.“ (2) owing a person something: „Ich bin dir 10 Euro schuldig.“ = „I owe you 10 euros.“ In the ‘owe’ meaning, it’s often used with a person in the dative (mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/ihnen).
target_language_example: Ich bin dir 10 Euro schuldig sein.
native_language_example: I owe you 10 euros.

meaning: blacklist; a list of people/things that are banned or not trusted.
additional_notes: Used for an official or unofficial list of people, companies, websites, etc. that are excluded, blocked, or considered suspicious. Often appears with verbs like „auf die schwarze Liste setzen“ (to blacklist) or „auf der schwarzen Liste stehen“ (to be blacklisted).
target_language_example: Die Firma steht auf der schwarzen Liste und darf nicht mehr liefern.
native_language_example: The company is on the blacklist and is no longer allowed to deliver.

additional_notes: A noun phrase: "schwarz" (black) + "das Loch" (hole). Used mostly in science/astronomy contexts; can also be used figuratively for something that seems to swallow things up (e.g., money, time), though that’s more context-dependent.
target_language_example: Ein schwarzes Loch hat eine so starke Gravitation, dass nicht einmal Licht entkommen kann.
native_language_example: A black hole has such strong gravity that not even light can escape.

additional_notes: Used to say something is difficult for you, either physically (too heavy) or mentally/emotionally. Often appears as (1) “Es ist schwer für mich, …” + infinitive (to do something), or (2) “zu schwer für mich, um … zu …” (too difficult/heavy for me to…).
target_language_example: Es ist schwer für mich, so früh aufzustehen.
native_language_example: It’s hard for me to get up so early.

additional_notes: Used to describe the severity of an injury (often in accidents or emergencies). It can be used in statements and questions: "Ist er schwer verletzt?" = "Is he seriously injured?" You can intensify it with "sehr" (very): "sehr schwer verletzt".
target_language_example: Nach dem Unfall war der Fahrer schwer verletzt.
native_language_example: After the accident, the driver was seriously injured.

additional_notes: Used to describe a severe injury, often in news or accident contexts. Typically appears with "sein/werden" (e.g., "Er wurde schwer verletzt" = "He was seriously injured").
target_language_example: Bei dem Sturz wurde sie schwer verletzt.
native_language_example: She was seriously injured in the fall.

additional_notes: Common way to talk about the activity of going somewhere (pool, lake, etc.) to swim. Typically used with modal verbs or future context: „Ich will/möchte/kann/werde schwimmen gehen.“ You can add where with „im/am + Dativ“ (e.g., „im See“, „am Strand“) and who with „mit + Dativ“ (e.g., „mit einem Freund“, „mit uns“).
target_language_example: Wollen Tom und Maria nächstes Wochenende mit uns schwimmen gehen?
native_language_example: Do Tom and Maria still want to go swimming with us next weekend?

additional_notes: Uses the modal verb "können" (to be able to/can) with the infinitive "schwimmen" (to swim). In main clauses, the finite form of "können" is in position 2 and "schwimmen" goes to the end (e.g., "Ich kann schwimmen."). With future meaning it often appears as "wird ... schwimmen können" (= "will be able to swim").
target_language_example: Jeder sollte schwimmen können.
native_language_example: Everyone should be able to swim.

meaning: 'nice/beautiful, but …' (a compliment followed by a contrast/criticism).
additional_notes: Used to acknowledge something positive ("schön") and then add a limitation or objection with "aber". Common in evaluations and polite refusals: "Es ist schön, aber …" / "Das ist zwar schön, aber …". In writing, a comma often comes before "aber" when it links two main clauses.
target_language_example: Das ist schön, aber ich habe leider keine Zeit.
native_language_example: That’s nice, but unfortunately I don’t have time.

additional_notes: Used to express pleasure or appreciation about what someone (addressed as Sie) is doing or that they are present. Common with verbs like „da sein“ (be here), „wieder da sein“ (be back), „helfen“ (help), etc. In informal speech with friends you’d usually say „Schön, dass du …“.
target_language_example: Schön, dass Sie heute Zeit haben.
native_language_example: I’m glad you have time today.

additional_notes: Used to express that you’re happy about what the other person did or that they’re present. Typically followed by a verb at the end of the clause: „Schön, dass du gekommen bist!“ (“Glad you came!”), „Schön, dass du wieder da bist!“ (“Nice to have you back!”).
target_language_example: Schön, dass du Zeit hast!
native_language_example: Nice / glad that you have time!

meaning: "Nice to see you." / "Good to see you."
additional_notes: Used as a friendly greeting when you meet someone (again). Often said as a full sentence ("Es ist schön, dich zu sehen!") or shortened ("Schön, dich zu sehen!"). "dich" is informal (to one person you address as "du"); for formal use: "Schön, Sie zu sehen." You can intensify it with words like "so" or "wie" ("So/WIe schön, dich zu sehen!").
target_language_example: Schön, dich zu sehen! Wie geht’s dir?
native_language_example: Nice to see you! How are you?

additional_notes: Used to compliment someone’s eyes; often sounds a bit personal or flirtatious depending on the situation. Usually appears with a form of "haben" (e.g., "Du hast schöne Augen") or in the exclamation "Was für schöne Augen du hast!".
target_language_example: Du hast wirklich schöne Augen.
native_language_example: You have really beautiful eyes.

additional_notes: Used to compare two things/people. It’s the comparative form of schön + als (than). You can strengthen it with words like „noch“ (even) and „sogar noch“ (even more): „noch schöner als …“. Common patterns: „X ist schöner als Y.“ / „schöner als je zuvor“ = "more beautiful than ever before."
target_language_example: Das neue Kleid ist noch schöner als das alte.
native_language_example: The new dress is even nicer than the old one.

additional_notes: Common everyday phrase for pleasant weather (often sunny, warm, and dry). Common with "sein" (Heute ist schönes Wetter), "geben" (Morgen gibt es schönes Wetter), and in forecasts (Es wurde schönes Wetter vorhergesagt). Note the adjective ending changes with grammar: e.g., "schönes Wetter" (nom./acc.), but "bei schönem Wetter" (dat.).
target_language_example: Glaubst du, dass es morgen schönes Wetter gibt?
native_language_example: Do you think there will be nice weather tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used to talk about a length of time (duration) or an age difference. Often used with time expressions like "seit" (for six years), "vor" (six years ago), or with "alt/älter" (six years old/older). In phrases like "Im Mai sind es sechs Jahre", it means "It will have been six years (by May)."
target_language_example: Ich wohne seit sechs Jahren in Berlin.
native_language_example: I’ve been living in Berlin for six years.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a time period (duration) or a deadline/remaining time. Often appears with time expressions like „sechs Monate lang“ (for six months) or with „noch“ to mean “another/only six months left” (e.g., „nur noch sechs Monate“). It can also be used in legal contexts for a sentence or probation period.
target_language_example: Ich bin seit sechs Monaten in Berlin.
native_language_example: I’ve been in Berlin for six months.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration of time ("for six hours") or a time interval/frequency, often with "alle": "alle sechs Stunden" = "every six hours." Can also be used in commands: "Warte/Warten Sie sechs Stunden!" = "Wait six hours!"
target_language_example: Bitte warten Sie sechs Stunden, bevor Sie wieder essen.
native_language_example: Please wait six hours before eating again.

additional_notes: Literally the verb + subject: "sehe" (see) + "ich" (I). In German, verb-first word order is common in questions ("Sehe ich …?") and also after certain words like "da" ("Da sehe ich …"). With "aussehen" (to look), you’ll often get questions like "Sehe ich … aus?" = "Do I look …?" (e.g., "Sehe ich wie dein Dienstmädchen aus?").
target_language_example: Sehe ich das richtig?
native_language_example: Am I seeing that correctly?

additional_notes: This is the formal (Sie) imperative of the reflexive verb **sich ansehen** (“to look at”). In real sentences you usually see the separable prefix **an** at the end: **Sehen Sie sich das an.** You use it to politely ask someone to view or inspect something (a film, photos, a section of a document, etc.).
target_language_example: Sehen Sie sich bitte die Bilder an.
native_language_example: Please take a look at the pictures.

additional_notes: Used with a "dass"-clause to state what someone observes or understands. It can refer to something visually evident ("Everyone can see that …") or to realizing something from the situation ("Tom could see that …"). In the future ("Du wirst sehen, dass …"), it often means "you’ll see / you’ll find that …".
target_language_example: Jeder kann sehen, dass es Lippenstift ist.
native_language_example: Everyone can see that it’s lipstick.

meaning: to see/check whether; to find out if.
additional_notes: Used when you want to check something or find out whether something is true. It’s often used with verbs like „(ich will) sehen“ / „(wir wollten) sehen“ and followed by an „ob“-clause (a yes/no question in indirect form): „… ob er kommt“, „… ob das stimmt“. Common in the fixed phrase „Mal sehen, ob …“ = “Let’s see if …”.
target_language_example: Ich will nur sehen, ob er mich wirklich liebt.
native_language_example: I just want to see whether he really loves me.

meaning: to see what … / to find out what …
additional_notes: Used when you want to look at or discover information about something. It’s typically followed by a subordinate clause introduced by **was** (“what”), so you usually write a **comma** before **was** and the verb often goes to the **end** of the clause: *Ich wollte sehen, was passieren würde.*
target_language_example: Wir werden sehen, was morgen passiert.
native_language_example: We’ll see what happens tomorrow.

meaning: to see how (something turns out / happens).
additional_notes: Common with verbs like wollen/werden: "Ich will sehen, wie …" / "Wir werden sehen, wie …". It introduces an indirect question or subordinate clause with "wie" (“how”), so you typically write a comma before "wie" when it starts that clause.
target_language_example: Wir werden sehen, wie alles läuft.
native_language_example: We’ll see how everything goes.

additional_notes: Used when you want to know or find out the place/location of something (often with a clause: „sehen, wo … ist/war/endete“). Can also mean to make out visually where something is or where something ends.
target_language_example: Komm, wir gehen raus und sehen, wo der Bus hält.
native_language_example: Come on, let’s go outside and see where the bus stops.

additional_notes: Formal ("Sie") form of "sehen" used to address one person politely or a group. Common in questions meaning "Do you see...?" (e.g., "Sehen Sie den Unterschied?"). It can also be used as a parenthetical like "you see," to explain or emphasize a point ("..., sehen Sie, ..."). Often appears with a separable verb: "Sehen Sie sich das an" = "Take a look at that" / "Look at that" (literally "see yourself that" in German word order).
target_language_example: Sehen Sie, ich meine es wirklich ernst.
native_language_example: You see, I really mean it.

additional_notes: This is the formal command form (to one person) of the reflexive verb with “sich”: usually **sich ansehen** (“to look at / view”) as in **Sehen Sie sich das an.** and **sich umsehen** (“to look around”) as in **Sehen Sie sich in Ruhe um!**. It’s often used with separable parts like **… an** or **… um** at the end of the sentence.
target_language_example: Sehen Sie sich bitte diese Fotos an.
native_language_example: Please take a look at these photos.

meaning: to look like; to resemble; to appear to be.
additional_notes: Used to compare appearance to something/someone: "X sieht aus wie Y" (X looks like Y). It can also describe someone’s apparent state: "Du siehst aus wie jemand, der Hilfe braucht" (You look like someone who needs help). Conjugate "sehen" to match the subject: ich sehe aus, du siehst aus, er/sie/es sieht aus, wir sehen aus, ihr seht aus, sie/Sie sehen aus. "wie" is followed by a noun/pronoun or a clause.
target_language_example: Sie sehen aus wie jemand, der Hilfe braucht.
native_language_example: You look like someone who needs help.

meaning: "we’ll see each other" / "see you"; also "shall we take a look…?" (with a separable verb).
additional_notes: From "wir sehen uns" = "we see each other". Common for arranging a meeting or saying goodbye: "Dann sehen wir uns …" / "Sehen wir uns später?". In questions it often starts a separable verb with a reflexive pronoun, e.g. "Sehen wir uns das an?" (ansehen = to look at) or "Zuerst sehen wir uns um" (sich umsehen = to look around).
target_language_example: Alles klar, dann sehen wir uns morgen um zehn.
native_language_example: All right, then I’ll see you tomorrow at ten.

additional_notes: A repeated intensifier used to strongly emphasize an adjective/adverb (similar to “really, really” in English). It’s common in spoken German and informal writing; you can repeat it even more times for extra emphasis ("sehr, sehr, sehr"). In formal writing you’d more often use words like "sehr" once or "äußerst"/"extrem".
target_language_example: Ich bin sehr, sehr müde.
native_language_example: I’m very, very tired.

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is liked by many people. With people, it’s often used with **bei + dative** to show who likes them: *bei ihren Schülern* = “with/among her students.” With things, it can stand alone: *Deutsche Autos sind sehr beliebt.*
target_language_example: Das Café ist bei Touristen sehr beliebt.
native_language_example: The café is very popular with tourists.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has a lot to do or doesn’t have much time. "beschäftigt" can describe a person (busy) and also a phone line (engaged/busy).
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, ich kann gerade nicht telefonieren, ich bin sehr beschäftigt.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t talk on the phone right now—I’m very busy.

additional_notes: Used to describe a strong feeling/state of loneliness. Common with verbs like „sein“ (to be), „sich … vorkommen“ (to feel/seem to oneself), „wirken“ (to seem/appear), and „werden“ (to become).
target_language_example: Seit dem Umzug bin ich oft sehr einsam.
native_language_example: Since the move, I’m often very lonely.

additional_notes: Used to strongly express that someone feels let down or unhappy about an outcome. Often with "sein": "Ich bin sehr enttäuscht" (I’m very disappointed) or in the future/conditional: "wird sehr enttäuscht sein" (will be very disappointed). You can add "muss ... gewesen sein" to guess about the past: "muss sehr enttäuscht gewesen sein" (must have been very disappointed).
target_language_example: Ich war sehr enttäuscht, dass du nicht gekommen bist.
native_language_example: I was very disappointed that you didn’t come.

additional_notes: Used to describe that someone is clearly happy or pleased about something (often in reaction to news, a situation, or another person). "erfreut" can be used on its own; adding "sehr" just strengthens it. Don’t confuse with the greeting phrase "Sehr erfreut" meaning "Pleased to meet you"—for that use it’s often said without "aus" and in a direct introduction context.
target_language_example: Ich war sehr erfreut über deine Nachricht.
native_language_example: I was very pleased about your message.

additional_notes: Use it to describe someone’s personality or behavior ("Er ist sehr freundlich."), including how they treat someone: "sehr freundlich zu + dative" ("zu mir/zu uns"). It can also be used as a polite phrase meaning “That’s very kind of you”: "Es ist sehr freundlich von Ihnen, ...".
target_language_example: Es ist sehr freundlich von dir, mir zu helfen.
native_language_example: That’s very kind of you to help me.

meaning: to like something a lot; to really enjoy something.
additional_notes: Used with the verb *gefallen* (“to please”). The person who likes something is in the dative: *Mir hat … sehr gefallen* = “I really liked …” (literally: “... pleased me a lot”). The thing you like is the grammatical subject, so it can be singular (*hat*) or plural (*haben*): *Mir haben die Geschichten sehr gefallen.*
target_language_example: Mir hat der Film sehr gefallen.
native_language_example: I really liked the movie.

additional_notes: Used to strongly warn about risk or harm. Often used with "sein" (to be) or "werden" (to become): "Es ist sehr gefährlich ..." / "Er wurde sehr gefährlich." You can use it for people, actions, places, or situations.
target_language_example: Es ist sehr gefährlich, bei Glatteis schnell zu fahren.
native_language_example: It’s very dangerous to drive fast on icy roads.

additional_notes: Used to say you enjoy doing something: „Ich mache das sehr gern.“ (= I really like doing that). With people, it often appears as „jemanden sehr gern haben“ (= to like someone a lot / be very fond of someone). It can also be a polite reply meaning “with pleasure / you’re welcome”: „Danke!“ – „Sehr gern.“
target_language_example: Ich helfe dir sehr gern.
native_language_example: I’d be very happy to help you.

additional_notes: Used to express strong enjoyment or willingness. Common with verbs like mögen/lesen/spielen ("Ich lese sehr gerne" = "I really like reading") or with hätte/möchte ("Ich hätte/möchte sehr gerne …" = "I’d really like …").
target_language_example: Ich würde sehr gerne mitkommen.
native_language_example: I’d really like to come along.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that someone feels happy to a high degree. It can describe a general state ("Ich bin sehr glücklich") or a reaction to good news ("Wir sind sehr glücklich, dass …"). Also commonly used with verbs like "sein" (to be), "sich fühlen" (to feel), and "wirken" (to seem/appear).
target_language_example: Ich bin sehr glücklich, dich zu sehen.
native_language_example: I’m very happy to see you.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "aussehen" (or "sehen ... aus") to describe someone’s appearance or mood: "Du siehst sehr glücklich aus." The "aus" here is part of "aussehen" (to look/appear), not the preposition "aus" meaning "out of".
target_language_example: Du siehst heute sehr glücklich aus.
native_language_example: You look very happy today.

additional_notes: "sehr" intensifies the adjective "groß". Use it for size (big) or height (tall), depending on what you’re describing (e.g., a house = big, a person = tall).
target_language_example: Die Tasche ist sehr groß, aber nicht schwer.
native_language_example: The bag is very big, but not heavy.

additional_notes: A common way to praise something or say it is of high quality. It is the straightforward combination of sehr + gut. It can describe things directly (Das war sehr gut.) and also appear in patterns like gut in/bei etwas sein (“to be good at something”), e.g. nicht sehr gut in Französisch = “not very good at French.”
target_language_example: Das Essen hier ist sehr gut.
native_language_example: The food here is very good.

additional_notes: Used to intensify "gut". With verbs it usually means "very well" (ability/understanding): "Ich verstehe sehr gut." With nouns/adjectives it can mean "very good": "ein sehr gutes Buch". With "gefallen" it means "to like (something/someone) a lot": "Er gefällt mir sehr gut." Word order: typically "sehr gut" stays together and comes after what it describes (e.g., "sehr gut sprechen", "sehr gut klettern").
target_language_example: Ich kann heute sehr gut arbeiten.
native_language_example: I can work very well today.

additional_notes: Used to describe something with a high temperature (drinks, water, weather, rooms/vehicles). Often used with "es ist" for general conditions: "Es ist sehr heiß" = "It’s very hot."
target_language_example: Mach das Fenster auf—hier ist es sehr heiß.
native_language_example: Open the window—it's very hot in here.

additional_notes: "Sehr" intensifies the adjective "hungrig" (hungry). Use it to say you’re really hungry. Often used with "sein" (to be) or "sich fühlen" (to feel): "Ich bin sehr hungrig." / "Ich fühle mich sehr hungrig."
target_language_example: Wir sind nach der Wanderung sehr hungrig.
native_language_example: We are very hungry after the hike.

additional_notes: Used to compliment someone’s appearance (more common for women, but can describe anyone). Can also be said on its own as an approving comment: “Sehr hübsch!” = “Very nice/pretty!” Note: "hübsch" is a bit softer/more delicate than "schön" (beautiful).
target_language_example: Dein Kleid ist sehr hübsch.
native_language_example: Your dress is very pretty.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is interesting. Often said about something you saw/heard/learned (Das war … / Es war …). You can swap in other intensifiers like „wirklich interessant“ (really interesting) or make it more polite/neutral with „(sehr) interessant!“ as a short reaction.
target_language_example: Der Vortrag war sehr interessant.
native_language_example: The talk was very interesting.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that someone (or something) is young. Often used with **noch** (“still”): *noch sehr jung* = “still very young.” Can describe people (*Sie war sehr jung.*) or things like plants (*Die Pflanzen sind noch sehr jung.*). Also common with time clauses: *Ich war sehr jung, als ...* (“I was very young when ...”).
target_language_example: Ich war noch sehr jung, als ich nach Deutschland gezogen bin.
native_language_example: I was still very young when I moved to Germany.

additional_notes: Used to describe cold weather, water, rooms, or even an object (often with "es ist/war" = "it is/was"). You can also use it to give a reason with "daher" or "deshalb" ("therefore/that's why").
target_language_example: Zieh deine Jacke an — es ist heute sehr kalt.
native_language_example: Put on your jacket — it’s very cold today.

additional_notes: Used to praise someone’s intelligence. "sehr" = “very” (intensifier) and "klug" = “smart/clever” (adjective). It often comes after a form of "sein" (to be): "Du bist sehr klug."
target_language_example: Das war sehr klug von dir.
native_language_example: That was very smart of you.

additional_notes: Most often used in the fixed apology phrase: „Es tut mir sehr leid.“ (= “I’m very sorry.”). You can change the person: „Es tut uns/ihm/ihr sehr leid.“ Also used to express regret about something: „Mir tat es sehr leid, …“ (= “I really regretted …”).
target_language_example: Es tut mir sehr leid, dass ich zu spät bin.
native_language_example: I’m very sorry that I’m late.

additional_notes: "Sehr" intensifies an adjective (like "very"). "Müde" means tired/sleepy. Common with "sein" (Ich bin sehr müde) and in descriptions (Er wirkt/klingt sehr müde).
target_language_example: Ich bin heute sehr müde und gehe gleich ins Bett.
native_language_example: I’m very tired today and I’m going to bed soon.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s personality/behavior ("He is very nice") or to politely say something would be kind of someone ("That would be very nice of you"). It can also describe how someone treats you ("He treats me very nicely"). "nett" is common and friendly, but a bit general (not as strong as "wunderschön" or "großartig").
target_language_example: Das ist sehr nett von dir, danke!
native_language_example: That’s very kind of you, thanks!

additional_notes: Used to say someone is treating you kindly. Structure: (Person) + ist/sind/war(en) + sehr nett + zu mir. You can swap in other people: „zu dir“ (to you), „zu ihm/ihr“ (to him/her), „zu uns/euch“ (to us/you all). Often used as a polite compliment or thanks: „Das ist sehr nett von dir.“ means “That’s very nice of you.” (note: „von dir“ focuses on the person’s action).
target_language_example: Danke, du bist immer sehr nett zu mir.
native_language_example: Thanks, you’re always very nice to me.

additional_notes: Used to strongly praise something’s usefulness. It commonly appears after forms of "sein" (ist/war/wird) and can describe things, tools, information, or help: "Das ist sehr nützlich." / "Das wird sehr nützlich sein."
target_language_example: Deine Tipps waren sehr nützlich.
native_language_example: Your tips were very useful.

additional_notes: "Sehr" is an intensifier meaning "very". "Reich" here means rich in the sense of having a lot of money (not "the Reich"). Often used with "sein/werden": "Er ist sehr reich" (He is very rich), "Er wurde sehr reich" (He became very rich).
target_language_example: Sie ist sehr reich, aber sie lebt ganz bescheiden.
native_language_example: She is very rich, but she lives very modestly.

additional_notes: Used to intensify "schnell" (fast/quick). "Sehr schnell" can describe how something happens (adverb: "Es ging sehr schnell.") or how someone/something is (adjective: "ein sehr schnelles Auto").
target_language_example: Wir müssen sehr schnell los, sonst verpassen wir den Zug.
native_language_example: We have to leave very quickly, otherwise we’ll miss the train.

additional_notes: Used with both literal and figurative meanings. Literally, it describes weight (e.g., food that feels heavy in your stomach). Figuratively, it describes something emotionally or mentally hard ("Das muss sehr schwer für Sie gewesen sein" = an empathetic way to say something was very difficult for someone).
target_language_example: Der Koffer ist sehr schwer.
native_language_example: The suitcase is very heavy.

additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize that something is hard to do/understand ("Es ist sehr schwierig."). With people, it can mean "very difficult to deal with" or "hard to please" ("Er/Sie ist sehr schwierig").
target_language_example: Die Prüfung war sehr schwierig, aber ich habe es geschafft.
native_language_example: The exam was very difficult, but I managed it.

additional_notes: Used to give a strong positive opinion about people, things, places, sounds, etc. Often translates naturally as “really nice/beautiful.” You can use it with "sein" ("Es ist sehr schön hier") or as an adjective before a noun ("sehr schöne Blumen").
target_language_example: Der Park ist im Frühling sehr schön.
native_language_example: The park is very beautiful in spring.

additional_notes: Used with **sein** (to be): **Ich bin sehr stolz auf ...** The thing/person you’re proud of is introduced with **auf + accusative** (e.g., **auf dich**, **auf meinen Sohn**, **auf deine Kinder**). You can intensify or soften it: **stolz auf** (proud of), **sehr stolz auf** (very proud of), **ganz besonders stolz auf** (especially proud of).
target_language_example: Ich bin sehr stolz auf dich.
native_language_example: I’m very proud of you.

additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize the high price of something. It can describe items, services, or general prices in a place (e.g., "In Berlin sind die Mieten sehr teuer."). Often answers the question "Wie teuer ist es?"
target_language_example: Das Hotel ist sehr teuer, also suchen wir ein anderes.
native_language_example: The hotel is very expensive, so we’re looking for another one.

additional_notes: Used to strongly describe a feeling (or situation) of sadness. Often with "sein" (to be) in present/past/future: "Er ist/war/wird sehr traurig (sein)." Can also describe something that is sad: "Es war sehr traurig."
target_language_example: Ich bin sehr traurig, weil ich meinen Schlüssel verloren habe.
native_language_example: I’m very sad because I lost my key.

additional_notes: Often used with the reflexive verb „sich verändern“ to say that a person or situation has changed a lot over time. Common with time markers like „danach“ (after that) or „seit …“ (since …).
target_language_example: Seit dem Umzug hat sich alles sehr verändert.
native_language_example: Since the move, everything has changed a lot.

additional_notes: Often used to strongly intensify a statement, especially with comparatives: "sehr viel + comparative" = "much/far + comparative" (e.g., "sehr viel schneller" = "much faster"). It can also modify "mehr/weniger": "sehr viel mehr" = "much more". Sometimes it can be translated literally as "very much," but in comparisons English usually prefers "much/far."
target_language_example: Dieses Jahr ist es sehr viel kälter als letztes Jahr.
native_language_example: This year it’s much colder than last year.

meaning: a lot; very much; a great deal.
additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize quantity or amount. Often comes before a noun (sehr viel Geld = a lot of money) or with a verb/feeling (sehr viel Hunger haben = be very hungry). With uncountable nouns it’s typically "sehr viel" (not *viele*). In some contexts it can mean "very many" in the sense of "a large number" (e.g., sehr viele Leute), but that form is "sehr viele".
target_language_example: Wir haben heute sehr viel zu tun.
native_language_example: We have a lot to do today.

additional_notes: Used to strongly increase quantity or degree: „nicht mehr sehr viel“ = “not much anymore.” It can also be a short answer (“Very much.”). In some common expressions, it still keeps the core idea of “a lot,” e.g. „sehr viel von jemandem halten“ = “to think highly of someone,” and „sehr viel um die Ohren haben“ = “to have a lot going on / be very busy.”
target_language_example: Ich habe heute sehr viel zu tun.
native_language_example: I have a lot to do today.

meaning: to be very careful; to be very cautious.
additional_notes: Used to warn someone or to remind yourself to avoid danger, mistakes, or upsetting someone. Common with a modal verb (e.g., "müssen") and often used with "bei + dative" to mean "to be careful around/with someone" (e.g., "Bei ihm musst du sehr vorsichtig sein.").
target_language_example: Bei ihm musst du sehr vorsichtig sein.
native_language_example: You have to be very careful around him.

additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize that something matters a lot. Common patterns: "Das ist mir sehr wichtig" (= It’s very important to me) and "Es ist sehr wichtig (für ...)" (= It’s very important (for ...)).
target_language_example: Es ist sehr wichtig für mich, pünktlich zu sein.
native_language_example: It’s very important for me to be on time.

additional_notes: Often used with "sich wohlfühlen" (to feel comfortable/well): "Ich fühle mich sehr wohl" = “I feel very comfortable here.” In other contexts, "sehr wohl" can also mean “indeed/certainly” (e.g., "Das kann sehr wohl sein" = “That could very well be.”).
target_language_example: In dieser Wohnung fühle ich mich sehr wohl.
native_language_example: I feel very comfortable in this apartment.

additional_notes: "sehr" intensifies the adjective "wütend". Often used with "auf" + accusative to say who you’re angry at: "sehr wütend auf mich/dich/ihn". Common patterns: "Ich bin/war sehr wütend" (I am/was very angry) and "Ich wurde sehr wütend" (I got very angry).
target_language_example: Sie ist sehr wütend auf ihren Bruder.
native_language_example: She is very angry with her brother.

additional_notes: Used to express a strong feeling of satisfaction. Often used with **mit + dative** to say what you’re satisfied with: *Ich bin sehr zufrieden mit …* / *Ich bin mit … sehr zufrieden.* You can also use it without naming the reason: *Ich war sehr zufrieden.*
target_language_example: Wir sind mit dem Service sehr zufrieden.
native_language_example: We’re very satisfied with the service.

additional_notes: Used to compare people, things, ideas, or languages. Often used with a dative comparison: „A ist B sehr ähnlich“ (A is very similar to B), or with reflexive „sich“ in comparisons: „A und B sind sich sehr ähnlich“ (A and B are very similar to each other).
target_language_example: Die beiden Bilder sind sich sehr ähnlich.
native_language_example: The two pictures are very similar.

additional_notes: Used to tell more than one person to look at something. It’s part of the separable verb **sich ansehen** (“to look at”): **Seht euch … an.** = “Look at …”. The **an** goes to the end of the sentence. **mal** is very common and makes it sound more casual/like “just/quickly.”
target_language_example: Seht euch bitte dieses Foto an.
native_language_example: Please look at this photo.

additional_notes: 2nd person plural form of **sehen** (“to see”), used when speaking to a group (friends, a class, etc.). Often used as a question: **Seht ihr …?** (“Do you see …?”). It can also be used on its own as **Seht ihr?** meaning “See?” / “You see?” to check that others understand or noticed something.
target_language_example: Seht ihr das Schild da vorne?
native_language_example: Do you all see the sign up there?

meaning: "Look!" / "Take a look!" (spoken to more than one person).
additional_notes: Imperative of **sehen** for **ihr** (plural "you"): *seht*. **mal** is a very common particle that makes the command sound softer/more casual (like “just” or “for a moment”). Often used to draw attention: *Seht mal, ...!* It can also be used with another verb: *Seht mal nach* = “Have a look / check.”
target_language_example: Seht mal, was ich gefunden habe!
native_language_example: Look what I found!

additional_notes: Imperative (du-form) of "sein" used to tell one person to stop showing a certain attitude or behavior. It’s usually followed by an adjective: "Sei nicht so traurig/angespannt/kindisch". It can also be used alone ("Sei nicht so!") meaning "Don’t be like that". Depending on tone, it can sound blunt or scolding.
target_language_example: Sei nicht so nervös, das klappt schon.
native_language_example: Don’t be so nervous, it’ll work out.

additional_notes:
Imperative (command) addressed to one person (du-form) of "sein" + adjective "vorsichtig". Used as a warning or advice to act carefully. Often followed by:
- "mit" + dative: "Sei vorsichtig mit dem Auto!" (be careful with the car)
- "dass/damit" clause: "Sei vorsichtig, damit du dich nicht verletzt." (so you don’t hurt yourself)
- indirect question: "Sei vorsichtig, was du dir wünschst …" (be careful what you wish for)
Plural/formal: "Seid vorsichtig!" (you all), "Seien Sie vorsichtig!" (formal).
target_language_example: Sei vorsichtig, wenn du die Straße überquerst.
native_language_example: Be careful when you cross the street.

additional_notes: Usually used to introduce one or more possibilities, reasons, or examples, often in patterns like „sei es … oder …“ or „sei es …, sei es …“. It is somewhat formal and common in writing.
target_language_example: Viele Menschen helfen, sei es mit Geld oder mit Zeit.
native_language_example: Many people help, whether with money or with time.

additional_notes: Used to tell one person (du) to treat someone kindly. It’s the imperative of "sein" (to be): "Sei ...!". The person after "zu" is in the dative (e.g., "zu mir", "zu ihr", "zu deinen Eltern"). For formal/polite "you": "Seien Sie nett zu ..."; for plural "you all": "Seid nett zu ...".
target_language_example: Sei nett zu deinem Bruder.
native_language_example: Be nice to your brother.

additional_notes: "Seid" is the 2nd-person plural form of *sein* (to be), and "Ihr" means "you" (plural). Often used in questions with inversion ("Seid Ihr …?"). Capitalized "Ihr" can be used as a respectful/old-fashioned way to address people (common in historical, religious, or fantasy contexts). In modern everyday polite German, people usually use "Sind Sie …?" instead.
target_language_example: Seid Ihr bereit?
native_language_example: Are you (all) ready?

additional_notes: Used when speaking to several people informally. It is the 2nd-person plural form of sein ('to be') and often appears at the start of yes/no questions: Seid ihr ...? Compare with formal plural/singular Sind Sie ...?
target_language_example: Seid ihr schon fertig?
native_language_example: Are you all finished already?

additional_notes: Uses **ihr** (2nd person plural) and **seid** (from *sein*) to address **two or more people** you’re on informal terms with (friends, family, kids). Often followed by **zu + noun** (*zum Essen*, *zum Start*) or an infinitive clause (*bereit, darüber zu sprechen*).
target_language_example: Seid ihr bereit, loszugehen?
native_language_example: Are you (all) ready to go?

additional_notes: "Seid" is the 2nd-person plural form of "sein" (to be) used with "ihr" (= you all / you guys). "Noch" means "still" (the situation continues) or sometimes "yet" depending on context. Used to ask if a state is still true: location ("… hier?"), relationship status ("… zusammen?"), marital status ("… unverheiratet?"), etc. It addresses more than one person and is informal ("ihr", not "Sie").
target_language_example: Seid ihr noch wach?
native_language_example: Are you (all) still awake?

additional_notes: Used to ask whether something has happened by now. "Seid" is the 2nd-person plural form of "sein" (to be) and "ihr" means "you" (plural). "Schon" often means "already", but in questions it can feel like "yet" depending on context (e.g., asking if something is true already).
target_language_example: Seid ihr schon fertig?
native_language_example: Are you (all) finished already / yet?

additional_notes: Used to check or challenge whether a group of people is certain about a fact or decision. It’s the plural (ihr) form; for one person you’d say “bist du sicher, dass …?”. Often followed by a clause with the verb at the end: “..., dass er/sie/es …”.
target_language_example: Seid ihr sicher, dass ihr die Adresse richtig habt?
native_language_example: Are you sure you have the address right?

additional_notes: Used to ask a surprised or doubtful yes/no question to a group of people you address as **ihr** (informal plural “you”). **Seid** is the 2nd-person plural form of **sein** (“to be”), placed first to form a question, and **wirklich** adds “really/actually.” Often followed by an adjective, noun, or past participle phrase: *Seid ihr wirklich allein?* / *Seid ihr wirklich drei Kilometer gelaufen?*
target_language_example: Seid ihr wirklich schon fertig?
native_language_example: Are you (all) really finished already?

additional_notes: Second-person plural informal form of sein, used when speaking to two or more people. As a main verb it means "are you". With a past participle (for example gegangen), it works as an auxiliary in the perfect tense; English often translates this as "have you" or with the simple past. The formal equivalent is "sind Sie".
target_language_example: Seid ihr schon fertig?
native_language_example: Are you finished already?

additional_notes: Used with the formal pronoun “Sie” to give polite instructions or commands. It’s the formal imperative of “sein” (to be) and is usually followed by an adjective or phrase: “Seien Sie vorsichtig.” / “Seien Sie ruhig.”
target_language_example: Seien Sie bitte pünktlich.
native_language_example: Please be on time.

additional_notes: Used to warn someone or advise caution in a polite/formal way. It uses the formal "Sie" and the imperative of "sein" (to be): "Seien Sie …". Often followed by "beim" + noun (e.g., beim Überqueren), "mit" + noun, or a "wenn" clause (when …).
target_language_example: Seien Sie vorsichtig, wenn Sie die Treppe hinuntergehen.
native_language_example: Be careful when you go down the stairs.

meaning: 'may be ..., but ...' (conceding one point, then contrasting it).
additional_notes: Used to admit something about someone/something (often with a modal like „mag“ = “may/might”) and then add a contrasting or more important point with „aber“ (“but”). Very common patterns are „zwar ... aber ...“ (“it’s true that ... but ...”) and „ja ... aber ...“ (“yes/indeed ... but ...”). The first part often contains „sein“ (“to be”): „Er mag (zwar) reich sein, aber ...“.
target_language_example: Ich mag zwar müde sein, aber ich mache noch meine Hausaufgaben.
native_language_example: I may be tired, but I’m still doing my homework.

meaning: to be [adjective] that … / to be [adjective] about the fact that …
additional_notes: Common pattern: **[Adjective/participle] + sein + dass + clause**. The **dass-clause** explains what you’re sure/aware/clear/happy/angry about, etc. Often used with adjectives like **sicher, klar, bewusst, froh, traurig, überrascht**. The verb in the **dass-clause** goes to the end: *Ich will sicher sein, dass er kommt.* Note: in German you may also see **es kann gut sein, dass …** meaning “it may well be that …”.
target_language_example: Ich will ganz sicher sein, dass Tom und Maria das wirklich wollen.
native_language_example: I want to be absolutely sure that Tom and Maria really want that.

meaning: “to be the one who …” (used with a relative clause).
additional_notes: This is the pattern where a form of **sein** (“to be”) is followed by **der/die/das** introducing a relative clause: **… sein, der/die/das + verb**. It identifies who/what did something: *Er war der, der …* (“He was the one who …”). The relative pronoun agrees with the person/thing: **der** (masc.), **die** (fem./plural), **das** (neut.).
target_language_example: Ich werde nicht der Letzte sein, der das Büro verlässt.
native_language_example: I won’t be the last one to leave the office.

meaning: to be (the one) who/that … (followed by a relative clause).
additional_notes: Used in the pattern „[noun/superlative] sein, die …“ to add a relative clause describing the person/thing you just mentioned. The relative pronoun changes with gender/case: „der“ (masc.), „die“ (fem./plural), „das“ (neut.). Common with superlatives/ordinals: „der Erste sein, der …“, „die Einzige sein, die …“.
target_language_example: Ich will die Person sein, die dir hilft.
native_language_example: I want to be the person who helps you.

additional_notes: Used with an adjective or noun + „sein“ and an „um … zu“-clause to say someone has the qualities needed to do something, often as a judgment: „Er muss verrückt sein, um das zu tun“ = “He must be crazy to do that.” In questions it often means meeting a requirement, especially age: „Wie alt muss man sein, um … zu dürfen?“ = “How old do you have to be to be allowed to …?”
target_language_example: Du musst mutig sein, um allein zu reisen.
native_language_example: You have to be brave to travel alone.

additional_notes: Used to connect a state (often an adjective like stinksauer, zufrieden, frei, enttäuscht, hungrig) with a condition or time introduced by wenn. Very common in the future with "wird ... sein, wenn ..." ("will be ... when/if ..."). It can also express a conclusion about someone: "Er muss dumm sein, wenn ..." = "He must be stupid if ...".
target_language_example: Ich werde froh sein, wenn du wieder da bist.
native_language_example: I’ll be happy when you’re back.

meaning: 'to be … when/if you …' (talking about a state/feeling in a certain situation).
additional_notes: This is a common sentence pattern: **[Person] wird/ist … sein, wenn du …**. It links a state (often an emotion or condition) with a condition or time clause introduced by **wenn du** (“when/if you”). With the future **werden … sein**, it often means “will be … when/if you …”.
target_language_example: Ich werde froh sein, wenn du wieder da bist.
native_language_example: I’ll be happy when you’re back.

additional_notes: Used to guess or speculate about what/who something is or where someone is. It’s the Konjunktiv II form ("könnte") and often appears in indirect questions after words like "wissen", "glauben", "eine Idee haben": "Weißt du, wer es sein könnte?"
target_language_example: Ich frage mich, was das sein könnte.
native_language_example: I wonder what that could be.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what something/someone will be like in the future. Very common in sentences with **dass/ob/was** where the conjugated verb (**wird**) often comes at the end: *Ich hoffe, dass es besser sein wird.* (Main clause: *Es wird besser sein.*).
target_language_example: Ich denke, dass es morgen kalt sein wird.
native_language_example: I think it will be cold tomorrow.

meaning: his car (also: its car; or formal: your car).
additional_notes: "sein" is a possessive determiner meaning "his/its" (and sometimes "your" when addressing someone formally: "Ihr Auto" is more common for formal "your"). "Auto" is neuter (das Auto), so you say "sein Auto" in both nominative and accusative (e.g., "Er verkauft sein Auto").
target_language_example: Er parkt sein Auto vor dem Haus.
native_language_example: He parks his car in front of the house.

meaning: “his best”; making the best effort he can.
additional_notes: Commonly used with verbs like „sein Bestes tun“ or „sein Bestes geben“ to express that someone tried as hard as possible. The possessive changes with the person/possessor: „mein Bestes“, „dein Bestes“, „ihr Bestes“, „unser Bestes“, etc. As a fixed phrase, it often means “best effort” rather than literally “his best (thing)”.
target_language_example: Er tat sein Bestes, den Plan auszuführen.
native_language_example: He did his best to carry out the plan.

additional_notes: Means “his brother” (a male sibling belonging to a man/boy mentioned or understood from context). Note: in German, the possessive determiner changes with the grammatical case and gender of the noun. Nominative: „sein Bruder“; Accusative: „seinen Bruder“; Dative: „seinem Bruder“; Genitive: „seines Bruders“. It also changes depending on the owner: „mein Bruder“ (my brother), „dein Bruder“ (your brother), „ihr Bruder“ (her/their brother), „unser Bruder“ (our brother), „euer Bruder“ (your [plural] brother).
target_language_example: Tom sagte mir, Johannes sei sein Bruder.
native_language_example: Tom told me Johannes was his brother.

additional_notes: „sein“ is a possessive pronoun meaning “his” (or “its”). With the neuter noun „das Büro“, you use „sein“ in the nominative/accusative: „sein Büro“ (his office). In other cases it changes (e.g., „in seinem Büro“ = in his office).
target_language_example: Er fand sein Büro ohne Schwierigkeiten.
native_language_example: He found his office without any difficulty.

additional_notes: "sein" is the possessive for "er" (he) and "es" (it). So "sein Geld" usually means "his money" (or "its money" for things/animals). The noun "Geld" is neuter (das Geld), so you get: sein Geld, dein Geld, ihr Geld, unser Geld, etc. It can be the subject or object without changing form: "Sein Geld ist weg." / "Er hat sein Geld verloren."
target_language_example: Er hat sein Geld im Portemonnaie.
native_language_example: He has his money in his wallet.

additional_notes: Literally “his face.” Often appears in sentences describing someone’s facial expression or how it changes (e.g., “sein Gesicht hellte sich auf” = his face/expression brightened) or with reflexive verbs like „sich das Gesicht reiben“ (to rub one’s face). Case changes with the role in the sentence (sein Gesicht = nominative/accusative; seines Gesichts = genitive; seinem Gesicht = dative).
target_language_example: Als er die gute Nachricht hörte, hellte sich sein Gesicht sofort auf.
native_language_example: When he heard the good news, his face (expression) brightened immediately.

additional_notes: Means the hair belonging to a male person (often referring to the hair on his head). In German, "Haar" is often used like a mass noun (similar to "hair" in English), especially when talking about hair length, color, or style. You may also see the plural "seine Haare" when talking about individual hairs or hair in general.
target_language_example: Er wäscht sein Haar jeden Abend.
native_language_example: He washes his hair every evening.

additional_notes: "sein" is the possessive determiner meaning "his" (also "its" for things with neuter grammatical gender). It changes depending on case: nominative/accusative neuter "sein Haus"; dative "seinem Haus" (e.g., "in seinem Haus"). Used to show that the house belongs to a male person (or to refer back to "er").
target_language_example: Er hat sein Haus letztes Jahr verkauft.
native_language_example: He sold his house last year.

additional_notes: A possessive phrase: **sein** = “his” (or “its”) and **Hemd** = “shirt”. The possessive changes with gender/case: e.g. **sein Hemd** (his shirt, nominative/accusative), **seinem Hemd** (to/with his shirt, dative).
target_language_example: Er hat sein Hemd vergessen.
native_language_example: He forgot his shirt.

meaning: his heart (literal or figurative: feelings/inner self).
additional_notes: Literally refers to a male person’s physical heart (often with verbs like „schlagen“ = to beat). Very often it’s used figuratively for emotions, love, courage, or one’s inner self (e.g., „jemandem sein Herz offenbaren“ = to reveal/open up one’s heart). In stories it can also be used literally in a fantasy way („sein Herz stehlen“ = steal his heart).
target_language_example: Als er die Nachricht hörte, schlug sein Herz schneller.
native_language_example: When he heard the news, his heart beat faster.

additional_notes: Uses the possessive pronoun "sein" (= his/its). It changes depending on the person: "mein Leben" (my life), "dein Leben" (your life), "ihr Leben" (her/their life), "unser Leben" (our life). Common with verbs like "riskieren" (to risk), "verlieren" (to lose), and "ändern" (to change).
target_language_example: Er will sein Leben verbessern.
native_language_example: He wants to improve his life.

additional_notes: Used to introduce or identify a male person's name. The possessive "sein" agrees with masculine nouns like "der Name" (so it’s always "sein Name", even when talking about a woman’s name you would say "ihr Name"). Often followed by the person’s name: "Sein Name ist …"
target_language_example: Sein Name ist Tobias.
native_language_example: His name is Tobias.

additional_notes: "sein" is the possessive determiner meaning "his" (and sometimes "its"), used before the masculine noun "Sohn" (son). In the nominative it’s "sein Sohn"; in the accusative it becomes "seinen Sohn" (e.g., "Ich sehe seinen Sohn."). Depending on context, it can emphasize the relationship ("his own son").
target_language_example: Sein Sohn ist acht Jahre alt.
native_language_example: His son is eight years old.

additional_notes: Means “his father” (talking about a male person) or sometimes “its father” (for a masculine noun). This is the nominative form; in other cases it changes (e.g., „Ich sehe seinen Vater.“ = “I see his father.”).
target_language_example: Sein Vater wohnt in Berlin.
native_language_example: His father lives in Berlin.

meaning: his behavior; the way he acts.
additional_notes: "Sein" is the possessive determiner meaning "his" (for a masculine/neuter owner). "Verhalten" means "behavior/conduct" and is often used when judging or describing how someone acted (e.g., polite/rude, surprising, annoying).
