It’s commonly followed by an infinitive at the end of the clause: "Vielleicht sollten wir gehen."
target_language_example: Vielleicht sollten wir morgen früher losfahren.
native_language_example: Maybe we should leave earlier tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to give advice in a soft, non-direct way. It’s formed from "vielleicht" (maybe) + "solltest" (you should, subjunctive of "sollen") + "du" (you). Often followed by an infinitive at the end of the clause: "Vielleicht solltest du mit ihr reden."
target_language_example: Vielleicht solltest du morgen früher ins Bett gehen.
native_language_example: Maybe you should go to bed earlier tomorrow.

meaning: “four eyes”; usually refers to a private one-on-one talk (in the phrase „unter vier Augen“).
additional_notes: Most often used as part of „unter vier Augen“ (= literally “under four eyes”), meaning only two people are present and you speak privately/confidentially. On its own, „vier Augen“ is just the literal “four eyes.”
target_language_example: Können wir das kurz unter vier Augen besprechen?
native_language_example: Can we discuss that briefly in private (just the two of us)?

additional_notes: Used to say a duration (how long something lasts: „dauerte vier Jahre“), a frequency (how often: „alle vier Jahre“ = every four years), or an age (how old someone was: „vier Jahre alt“ = four years old). With time expressions, German often uses the accusative without a preposition for duration (e.g., „Er lebte vier Jahre dort.“).
target_language_example: Ich habe vier Jahre in Berlin gelebt.
native_language_example: I lived in Berlin for four years.

additional_notes: Used with certain time expressions that take the dative plural "Jahren" (from "Jahr"). Common patterns: "mit vier Jahren" = at the age of four; "seit vier Jahren" = for/since four years (still continuing); "vor vier Jahren" = four years ago.
target_language_example: Ich lerne seit vier Jahren Deutsch.
native_language_example: I’ve been learning German for four years.

additional_notes: Used to say a duration or time span. Often appears as an accusative time expression answering “How long?” (e.g., „vier Tage im Bett“, „vier Tage durch/ lang“), or in time clauses like „vier Tage, nachdem …“ (“four days after …”).
target_language_example: Wir bleiben nur vier Tage in Berlin.
native_language_example: We’re only staying four days in Berlin.

meaning: four-leaf clover (a symbol of good luck).
additional_notes: Literally “four-leaf clover.” Used when talking about luck, lucky charms, or something rare and fortunate. Grammar note: it’s an adjective + noun; as a standalone noun phrase you’ll also see it with an article (e.g., „ein vierblättriges Kleeblatt“).
target_language_example: Ich habe ein vierblättriges Kleeblatt gefunden.
native_language_example: I found a four-leaf clover.

meaning: "fourth mistress" / "fourth wife (in rank)" (a form of address).
additional_notes: Used to address a woman who is the fourth-ranked wife/concubine in a household (often in historical or fictional settings with multiple wives). It’s a respectful title + ordinal number (erste/zweite/dritte/vierte Herrin). In modern everyday German, this is unusual; you’ll mostly see it in period dramas, novels, or translations.
target_language_example: Vierte Herrin, der Tee ist fertig.
native_language_example: Fourth Mistress, the tea is ready.

meaning: “fourth sister” (used as a form of address).
additional_notes: Used to address a woman who is considered the “fourth sister” within a group (e.g., sisters in a family or community), where “fourth” reflects her rank/order among the sisters. Often used directly when speaking to her (like a title/name), so you may see it with a comma: „Vierte Schwester, …“.
target_language_example: Vierte Schwester, kannst du kurz hierherkommen?
native_language_example: Fourth sister, can you come here for a moment?

additional_notes: Used with the verb "sein" to describe that something contains a lot of something else: "X ist voll von Y". Often used literally (objects, places) and figuratively (feelings, thoughts). Note: You’ll also hear "voll mit" in everyday speech, but "voll von" is common and correct.
target_language_example: Der Raum ist voll von Menschen.
native_language_example: The room is full of people.

additional_notes: An adverbial phrase used to emphasize total agreement, full dedication, or full availability. Common with verbs like „zustimmen“ (agree) and the expression „jdm. voll und ganz zur Verfügung stehen“ (to be fully at someone’s disposal/available).
target_language_example: Ich unterstütze dich dabei voll und ganz.
native_language_example: I fully support you in that.

additional_notes: Used with forms of "sein" (to be) or "sich fühlen" (to feel) to describe someone’s mood/condition. Grammatically it’s "voll" + genitive: "voller" is the common form before a noun ("voller Energie", "voller Freude").
target_language_example: Nach dem Kaffee bin ich wieder voller Energie.
native_language_example: After the coffee, I’m full of energy again.

additional_notes: "vom" = "von dem" and is used for movement/starting point away from a place. Often used with verbs like "abfahren" (depart), "kommen" (come), "gehen" (go), and in distance/time phrases like "vom Bahnhof zur Schule" (from the station to the school). Also appears in "vom Bahnhof aus" = "starting from the station".
target_language_example: Vom Bahnhof aus sind es nur zehn Minuten zu Fuß bis zum Hotel.
native_language_example: From the train station, it’s only a ten-minute walk to the hotel.

additional_notes: "vom" = "von dem" (from the). Used with movement away from a tree, often when someone/something falls or takes something off it (e.g., apples). Common with verbs like "fallen" (to fall) or "(etwas) stehlen/pflücken" (to steal/pick).
target_language_example: Die Katze sprang vom Baum herunter.
native_language_example: The cat jumped down from the tree.

additional_notes: „vom“ = contraction of „von dem“ (dative). Most often used with movement or action verbs to show someone/something ends up off the roof: „(vom Dach) springen“ (jump off), „(vom Dach) stoßen“ (push off), „sich (vom Dach) stürzen“ (throw oneself off), „jdn. (vom Dach) kriegen“ (get someone off the roof). In some contexts, „vom Dach“ can also mean “about the roof” with verbs like „halten von“ (= think of), e.g. „Was haltet ihr vom Dach?“ = “What do you think of the roof?”
target_language_example: Die Katze ist vom Dach gefallen.
native_language_example: The cat fell off the roof.

additional_notes: "vom" is a common contraction of "von dem" (dative). Use it to talk about a starting point (e.g., traveling from the airport) or where someone/something is picked up ("jemanden vom Flughafen abholen"). It can also mean “of the airport” in contexts like "ein Foto vom Flughafen" (= a photo of the airport).
target_language_example: Wir nehmen ein Taxi vom Flughafen zum Hotel.
native_language_example: We’re taking a taxi from the airport to the hotel.

additional_notes: Contraction of „von dem Himmel“. Used literally with verbs like „fallen“ (to fall) or „kommen“ (to come): „vom Himmel fallen/kommen“ = to fall/come from the sky. Also appears in the common idiom „das Blaue vom Himmel versprechen“ = to promise the impossible / make unrealistic promises.
target_language_example: Plötzlich fielen große Tropfen vom Himmel.
native_language_example: Suddenly big drops fell from the sky.

additional_notes: "vom" is a contraction of "von dem" ("from the"). With food, it’s often used to mean taking some portion of it: "Nimm dir etwas vom Kuchen" = "Help yourself to some cake."
target_language_example: Möchtest du noch ein Stück vom Kuchen?
native_language_example: Would you like another piece of the cake?

meaning: 'off the horse' / 'from the horse' (i.e., from on top of a horse).
additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement or accidents to describe leaving the horse: e.g. fallen/stürzen/geworfen werden (fall off/be thrown off) or steigen (get off). It’s the contraction of „von dem Pferd“ and refers to movement away from the horse’s back.
target_language_example: Nach dem Ausritt stieg sie vom Pferd.
native_language_example: After the ride, she got off the horse.

meaning: from the beginning; right from the start.
additional_notes: Used to say something was true or happened starting at the very beginning and continuously since then (often with verbs like sagen, wissen, verstehen, klar sein). It can also emphasize that there was no change later: it was already like that at the start.
target_language_example: Ich wusste von Anfang an, dass das nicht klappt.
native_language_example: I knew from the beginning that it wouldn’t work.

additional_notes: Used when you mean talking/meeting directly with someone, not by phone, email, etc. Often used with verbs like sprechen (talk) or sich treffen (meet). It can also describe two people standing directly opposite each other ("face to face").
target_language_example: Lass uns das lieber von Angesicht zu Angesicht klären.
native_language_example: Let’s clear this up face to face (in person).

meaning: from scratch; completely/from the ground up.
additional_notes: Used to say something is learned, built, redone, or changed thoroughly and fundamentally (not just small improvements). Common with verbs like lernen, aufbauen, überarbeiten, verändern.
target_language_example: Wir haben die Website von Grund auf neu aufgebaut.
native_language_example: We rebuilt the website from scratch.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s inherent traits or original background/training (what they are “from the start”). Often used with professions or characteristics: "Er ist von Haus aus Ingenieur" (He’s an engineer by training/originally), "Sie ist von Haus aus sehr ruhig" (She’s naturally very calm).
target_language_example: Er ist von Haus aus Informatiker, arbeitet aber jetzt als Lehrer.
native_language_example: He’s a computer scientist by training, but now he works as a teacher.

additional_notes: Used to say something is meant genuinely and with strong feeling (often gratitude, wishes, apologies, or concern). Common with verbs like „danken“ (Ich danke dir/Ihnen von Herzen) or phrases like „Es muss von Herzen kommen“ to emphasize sincerity.
target_language_example: Ich wünsche dir von Herzen alles Gute.
native_language_example: I sincerely wish you all the best.

additional_notes: Polite/formal way to say "from you" when addressing one person formally or more than one person formally. "Von" takes the dative, so the pronoun is "Ihnen".
target_language_example: Ich habe lange nichts von Ihnen gehört.
native_language_example: I haven't heard from you in a long time.

additional_notes: “von” + “Ihrer” is used with the formal “you” (Sie) and typically means “of your” (belonging to you) or “from your.” It’s followed by a feminine noun (e.g., von Ihrer Straße) or can refer to something in a general “about” sense in phrases like “von Ihrer Situation gehört” (“heard about your situation”).
target_language_example: Ich habe von Ihrer Arbeit viel Gutes gehört.
native_language_example: I’ve heard a lot of good things about your work.

meaning: from year to year; year by year (gradually over time).
additional_notes: Used to describe something that changes gradually as time passes, typically increasing or decreasing each year. Often appears with verbs like „steigen“ (rise/increase), „sinken“ (fall/decrease), „sich erhöhen“ (increase), or „sich verbessern“ (improve).
target_language_example: Die Situation wird von Jahr zu Jahr besser.
native_language_example: The situation is getting better year by year.

additional_notes: Used to say a quality is natural/inborn rather than learned or caused by outside influence. Often appears with verbs like „sein“ (to be) or „können“ (can): „Er ist von Natur aus ruhig.“
target_language_example: Ich bin von Natur aus neugierig.
native_language_example: I’m naturally curious.

additional_notes: Means doing something again from the beginning, often after it ended or failed. Common with verbs like beginnen (start), machen (do), anfangen (begin), lesen (read). Often interchangeable with „noch einmal“, but „von Neuem“ emphasizes a fresh restart.
target_language_example: Wir müssen von Neuem anfangen.
native_language_example: We have to start over.

meaning: from day to day; more and more with each passing day.
additional_notes: Used to say something changes gradually over time (often getting better/worse/stronger) as days pass. Common with comparatives like „besser“, „schlimmer“, „kälter“, or verbs like „wachsen“.
target_language_example: Von Tag zu Tag fühle ich mich sicherer auf Deutsch.
native_language_example: Day by day, I feel more confident in German.

meaning: from time to time; now and then; occasionally.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens sometimes, but not regularly. It often goes with the present tense for a general habit (Ich treffe ihn von Zeit zu Zeit …) or with the past to describe repeated actions in the past (Von Zeit zu Zeit blieb er stehen …). You can put it in the middle of the sentence or at the beginning for emphasis.
target_language_example: Von Zeit zu Zeit gehe ich alleine spazieren.
native_language_example: From time to time I go for a walk alone.

meaning: (all) by itself; on its own (without help).
additional_notes: Used to say something happens automatically or independently, without someone doing it or helping. Often with verbs like „gehen“, „fahren“, „fliegen“, „passieren“, „kommen“, „sich entscheiden“. In questions it can imply “without anyone doing anything?” (e.g., „Ging nicht von allein, oder?“).
target_language_example: Keine Sorge — das regelt sich von allein.
native_language_example: Don’t worry — it’ll sort itself out.

additional_notes: Used to compare one person/thing with the whole group: superlatives like der/die/das + -ste often go with it ("der größte von allen" = "the biggest of all"). It can also start the sentence: "Von allen Jungs ..." = "Out of all the boys ...".
target_language_example: Sie ist die schnellste von allen Läuferinnen.
native_language_example: She is the fastest of all the runners.

meaning: from all sides; from every direction.
additional_notes: Used to say something surrounds, comes from, or affects someone/something in every direction (physically or figuratively, e.g., “criticized from all sides”). Often used with verbs like „umgeben sein“ (to be surrounded), „angreifen“ (to attack), and „kritisieren“ (to criticize).
target_language_example: Wir wurden von allen Seiten beobachtet.
native_language_example: We were being watched from all sides.

additional_notes: Used after a superlative to mean “of all (the ones in the group)”: das beste/ billigste/ interessanteste von allen. With passive verbs like „respektiert/geliebt/gehört“, it can mean “by everyone” (agent): „Er wird von allen respektiert.“
target_language_example: Das ist der schönste Park von allen.
native_language_example: That’s the nicest park of all.

additional_notes: Used to describe something seen, done, or affecting something from the outside (often contrasted with „von innen“ = from inside). Common with verbs like „anschauen“ (look at), „verschlossen“ (locked), and in phrases like „Druck von außen“ (outside pressure).
target_language_example: Man kann das Schild von außen gut lesen.
native_language_example: You can read the sign well from outside.

meaning: from then on; from that point onward.
additional_notes: Used to mark a turning point in time: something happens, and after that moment the new situation continues. Often refers back to a specific event or point in a story (similar to "ab dann").
target_language_example: Von da an ging alles viel schneller.
native_language_example: From then on, everything went much faster.

additional_notes: Means leaving a place and going away from it. It’s a fixed, old-fashioned/literary expression (often in stories), commonly used with verbs like „ziehen“ or „(sich) machen“: „von dannen ziehen“, „sich von dannen machen“. In everyday speech you’d more often say „weggehen“, „gehen“, or „davongehen“.
target_language_example: Nach dem Streit ging er schweigend von dannen.
native_language_example: After the argument, he left in silence.

additional_notes: Combination of the preposition "von" + "deinem" (dative, masculine/neuter singular). It’s used for things coming from you/your possession ("ein Schluck von deinem Wein" = a sip of your wine), for talking about something related to you ("etwas von deinem Traum" = something about your dream), and in fixed patterns like "abhängen von" (to depend on) and verbs with "von" (e.g., "absteigen von" = to get off).
target_language_example: Ich möchte gern etwas von deinem Essen probieren.
native_language_example: I'd like to try some of your food.

meaning: “of/from your” (used with a feminine noun in the dative).
additional_notes: Used with the preposition **von** (“from/of”), which takes the **dative** case. **deiner** is the dative form of **dein-** (“your”) for **feminine singular** nouns (e.g., *Straße, Tasche, Wohnung*): *von deiner Straße* = “of/from your street.” It can also appear in other contexts (e.g., genitive), but after **von** it’s dative.
target_language_example: Ich habe ein Foto von deiner Wohnung gesehen.
native_language_example: I saw a photo of your apartment.

additional_notes: "von dem" is the dative form of "von" + "dem" (used with masculine/neuter nouns). Very often it’s contracted to "vom" (e.g., "vom Mädchen" is incorrect because Mädchen is neuter? actually "das Mädchen" → dative "dem Mädchen" → "vom Mädchen" is correct). It’s used for origin/source ("from the"), possession/material/part ("of the"), and for topics/what someone told you ("about the").
target_language_example: Ich habe dir noch nichts von dem Plan erzählt.
native_language_example: I haven’t told you anything about the plan yet.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like **sprechen (von)**, **hören (von)**, **erzählen (von)** to mean “about.” It takes **dative**: **von dem Unfall**. In everyday speech and writing, it’s often contracted to **vom Unfall**.
target_language_example: Tom hat mir eben von dem Unfall erzählt.
native_language_example: Tom just told me about the accident.

meaning: “of whom/which”, “about whom/which”, or “from which” (relative clause connector).
additional_notes: Used to refer back to a masculine or neuter noun (der/das) in a relative clause. It’s the contraction of “von + dem” (dative). Common with verbs like sprechen/reden von (talk about), erzählen von (tell about), and also to express “from which” or “with which” (connection/source). For feminine/plural: von der, von denen.
target_language_example: Das ist der Film, von dem ich dir gestern erzählt habe.
native_language_example: That’s the movie I told you about yesterday.

meaning: “of what” / “of that which” (referring back to a previously mentioned thing/amount, then linking it to a clause).
additional_notes: Used to connect a quantity/portion (e.g., einiges, die Hälfte, ein Teil, kein Wort, das Doppelte) to a relative clause: "[quantity] von dem, was + clause" = "[quantity] of what + clause." Grammatically, "von dem" refers back to a neuter singular idea/amount ("dem" = dative), and "was" introduces the relative clause meaning "what/that which." Common in careful, written, or neutral speech.
target_language_example: Kein Wort von dem, was Tom sagte, war wahr.
native_language_example: Not a word of what Tom said was true.

additional_notes: Used with the dative plural (or dative masculine/neuter in some set phrases) to mean either (1) “of the” when you’re choosing/pointing out some from a larger group (Welche von den…? / Von den vier…), or (2) “from the” when describing origin/source (von den Toten = “from the dead”). In everyday speech it’s often contracted to “von den” → “von den” (no fixed single-word contraction like “zum”).
target_language_example: Von den Gästen sind nur drei gekommen.
native_language_example: Of the guests, only three came.

additional_notes: Used with plural "die" to refer back to a previously mentioned group of people/things. Common uses: (1) comparison: "X unterscheidet sich von denen ..." = "X is different from those ..."; (2) partitive: "einer/eins von denen" = "one (of) those"; (3) in a relative clause: "..., von denen ..." = "..., of whom/which ...".
target_language_example: Ich kenne ein paar Leute, von denen du viel lernen kannst.
native_language_example: I know a few people you can learn a lot from.

additional_notes: Combination of von + the feminine dative article der. Most often it means movement away from or origin/source ('from the'). With some verbs and expressions, it can be closer to 'of the' or 'about the'.
target_language_example: Sie kommt gerade von der Schule nach Hause.
native_language_example: She is just coming home from school.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement to say you’re leaving work or returning home after work (e.g., „von der Arbeit nach Hause“, „von der Arbeit zurückkommen“). „von“ takes the dative case, so it’s „der Arbeit“.
target_language_example: Ich komme heute spät von der Arbeit nach Hause.
native_language_example: I’m coming home late from work today.

meaning: from the bridge / off the bridge.
additional_notes: Used with movement away from a place: **von + dative** (here: *die Brücke* → *von der Brücke*). It can mean being on the bridge as a viewpoint (*Fotos von der Brücke*) or moving/falling/jumping off it (*von der Brücke springen/stürzen*). In contexts like *sich von der Brücke stürzen*, it can refer to suicide.
target_language_example: Wir schauen uns die Stadt von der Brücke aus an.
native_language_example: We’re looking at the city from the bridge.

additional_notes: Used to show distance or origin relative to the coastline. Common with words like "entfernt" (away) and verbs like "liegen": "X liegt ... von der Küste entfernt" = "X is ... away from the coast." It can also describe origin: "Leute von der Küste" = "people from the coast."
target_language_example: Das Hotel liegt nur fünf Minuten von der Küste entfernt.
native_language_example: The hotel is only five minutes away from the coast.

additional_notes: Literally "von" = "from/by" and "der Polizei" = "the police" (dative). Very common in the passive to show who does the action: "wurde von der Polizei festgenommen" = "was arrested by the police". With "sein" it can mean belonging/working there: "Sind Sie von der Polizei?" = "Are you with the police?"
target_language_example: Er wurde von der Polizei kontrolliert.
native_language_example: He was checked by the police.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like "kommen" (to come), "anrufen" (to call), etc. to mean someone/something is coming or contacting you from the school ("ein Anruf von der Schule"). With "abgehen" it means leaving school / dropping out. With nouns like "Abwesenheit" it means being absent from school ("Abwesenheit von der Schule").
target_language_example: Meine Schwester ist heute von der Schule nach Hause gekommen.
native_language_example: My sister came home from school today.

meaning: from the street/road; off the street/road.
additional_notes: Used with movement/change-of-position verbs to show something/someone moving away from the street/road (often with runter: runter von der Straße! = Get off the road!). Also used to show distance/position relative to a road: einige Meter von der Straße entfernt = a few meters away from the road. With picking something up: von der Straße aufheben = pick up from the street.
target_language_example: Runter von der Straße, da kommt ein Auto!
native_language_example: Get off the road, a car is coming!

meaning: from the wall; off the wall.
additional_notes: Used to say something moves/comes away from a wall, or is removed/taken down from a wall. Common with verbs like (ab)prallen (to bounce off), entfernen (to remove), and abnehmen/nehmen (to take down/off).
target_language_example: Kannst du das Bild von der Wand nehmen?
native_language_example: Can you take the picture off the wall?

meaning: of/about the world; from the world.
additional_notes: Literally “from the world.” Often used with verbs like **(etw.) von der Welt tilgen/verbannen** (“to wipe/banish (something) from the world”). It’s also common after nouns/verbs to mean “about the world,” e.g. **eine Vorstellung von der Welt** (“an idea of the world”), **(viel) von der Welt sehen/wissen** (“to see/know (a lot) of the world”).
target_language_example: Sie will mehr von der Welt sehen.
native_language_example: She wants to see more of the world.

meaning: "of this" / "from this" (referring to a masculine/neuter noun).
additional_notes: Used with the preposition "von" + dative to show origin, source, or relation: "von diesem Dokument" = "of/from this document". "Diesem" is the dative form of "dieser" for masculine/neuter nouns; for feminine/plural you’ll see "von dieser" / "von diesen".
target_language_example: Ich brauche eine Kopie von diesem Vertrag.
native_language_example: I need a copy of this contract.

additional_notes: Literally “from you.” Used with the preposition **von** + **dative** (dir). Common uses: (1) talking *about* someone: **von dir erzählen / von dir reden** = “tell/talk about you”; (2) separation/distance: **weg von dir** = “away/far from you”; (3) dependence: **Das hängt von dir ab** = “That depends on you”; (4) what someone wants/expects/needs from you: **Antwort/Hilfe von dir** = “an answer/help from you,” **Wir erwarten von dir ...** = “We expect ... from you.”
target_language_example: Das hängt ganz von dir ab.
native_language_example: That depends entirely on you.

additional_notes: Used to describe the origin or starting point of something (where someone/something comes from, escapes from, speaks from, etc.). Refers to a place that’s already known from context (dort = “there”). Often contrasts with "von hier" (“from here”).
target_language_example: Wir kommen später von dort zurück.
native_language_example: We’ll come back from there later.

additional_notes: von takes the dative case, so ein becomes einem here. It is often used for the doer in passive sentences (for example, 'von einem Hund angegriffen' = 'attacked by a dog'), but depending on context it can also mean 'of a/an' or sometimes 'about a/an'.
target_language_example: Sie wurde von einem Arzt untersucht.
native_language_example: She was examined by a doctor.

meaning: "from a car" (sometimes "by a car" in passive sentences).
additional_notes: "von" + dative ("einem Auto") often means origin/source ("from a car"). In passive constructions it can indicate the agent/cause, similar to English "by": e.g., "Er wurde von einem Auto angefahren" = "He was hit by a car."
target_language_example: Er wurde von einem Auto angefahren.
native_language_example: He was hit by a car.

additional_notes: Used to say the source/origin of something (a letter, help, money, a borrowed item) is a friend. It can also mark the doer in passive sentences: "Sie wurde von einem Freund betrogen" = "She was cheated on/by a friend."
target_language_example: Ich habe das Buch von einem Freund bekommen.
native_language_example: I got the book from a friend.

meaning: "from a" / "by a" (referring to a feminine noun, dative).
additional_notes: Used with feminine singular nouns in the dative case: von + einer + [feminine noun]. Often means "from" (origin/source: von einer Freundin) or "by" in the passive voice (agent: von einer süßen Kellnerin begrüßt). Common feminine nouns: die Freundin, die Universität, die Person, die Brücke, die Kellnerin.
target_language_example: Ich habe den Tipp von einer Kollegin bekommen.
native_language_example: I got the tip from a (female) colleague.

additional_notes: Used in the passive to say someone received a bee sting. Common patterns: „Wurdest du (schon mal) von einer Biene gestochen?“ (Were you ever stung by a bee?) and „Ich bin von einer Biene gestochen worden.“ (I was stung by a bee).
target_language_example: Ich bin gestern im Garten von einer Biene gestochen worden.
native_language_example: I was stung by a bee in the garden yesterday.

additional_notes: Uses the informal plural pronoun euch ('you all'). With von, it often means 'of you' in expressions like einige von euch ('some of you'), after judgments like nett von euch ('nice of you'), or after nouns to show possession, as in Freunde von euch ('friends of yours'). Formal equivalent: von Ihnen.
target_language_example: Einige von euch sprechen schon gut Deutsch.
native_language_example: Some of you already speak German well.

meaning: with all my/your/one’s heart; sincerely, wholeheartedly.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize deep, genuine feelings (thanks, love, wishes, dedication). Often appears with verbs like danken (to thank), lieben (to love), wünschen (to wish), and widmen (to dedicate). The pronoun is usually understood from context (e.g., 'Ich danke dir …' = 'with all my heart').
target_language_example: Wir gratulieren euch von ganzem Herzen.
native_language_example: We congratulate you with all our hearts / wholeheartedly.

additional_notes: Often used after a noun to mean it belongs to yesterday: „die Sendung von gestern“ = “yesterday’s show”, „die Eier von gestern“ = “the eggs from yesterday”. In expressions like „Der/die … von gestern!“ it can mean someone is behind the times (similar to “yesterday’s man/woman”).
target_language_example: Hast du noch das Brot von gestern?
native_language_example: Do you still have yesterday’s bread?

additional_notes: Used to show the starting point of movement or departure (often with verbs like abfahren, gehen, kommen, verschwinden). In everyday speech you may also hear/see the shorter form “hier” when the meaning is clear (e.g., “Ich gehe hier weg.”).
target_language_example: Wir laufen von hier zum Park.
native_language_example: We’re walking from here to the park.

meaning: from here; from where we are (starting from this point).
additional_notes: Used to talk about what you can see/hear/reach starting from your current location. Often with verbs like sehen (see), hören (hear), erkennen (make out), erreichen (reach). It can also be used more generally for “from this standpoint,” but most commonly it’s literally about physical location.
target_language_example: Von hier aus kannst du den Bahnhof in fünf Minuten zu Fuß erreichen.
native_language_example: From here, you can reach the train station on foot in five minutes.

meaning: 'away from here' (at a distance from this place).
additional_notes: Used to say how far something is from where you are now. Very common with distances (e.g., „zwei Kilometer von hier entfernt“) and with „(nicht) weit“: „nicht weit von hier entfernt“ = not far from here. Often appears with „sein“: „X ist … von hier entfernt.“
target_language_example: Die Apotheke ist nur fünf Minuten zu Fuß von hier entfernt.
native_language_example: The pharmacy is only a five-minute walk away from here.

additional_notes: Used to describe movement or an approach coming from behind someone/something (often with verbs like „kommen“, „sich anschleichen“, „sich heranschleichen“). It can also mean doing something starting from the back side. In some contexts (e.g., talking about sex), „von hinten“ can mean “from behind” in a sexual position and may sound suggestive.
target_language_example: Pass auf — jemand kommt von hinten!
native_language_example: Watch out—someone’s coming from behind!

additional_notes: “von” + dative pronoun “ihm” (him). Common uses: (1) source/origin: “einen Brief von ihm” = “a letter from him”; “von ihm erfahren” = “hear/learn it from him”; (2) topic: “von ihm sprechen/erzählen” = “talk about him.” In phrases like “dumm von ihm” it means “stupid of him” (judging his action).
target_language_example: Ich habe das von ihm gehört.
native_language_example: I heard that from him.

additional_notes: Used with a thing you receive: "etwas von ihm bekommen" (e.g., eine Antwort, einen Brief, ein Geschenk). Word order changes in questions: "Hast du ... von ihm bekommen?". "bekommen" here means "receive/get" (not "become").
target_language_example: Ich habe gestern eine Nachricht von ihm bekommen.
native_language_example: I received a message from him yesterday.

meaning: heard from him; heard any news about/from him.
additional_notes: Used with hören + von (+ dative) to ask/report whether you’ve had any contact or information. Very common in the pattern „(etwas) von jemandem hören“ = to hear from someone / to hear something about someone (news, updates). Often used with time expressions like „in letzter Zeit“ (lately).
target_language_example: Ich habe seit Wochen nichts von ihm gehört.
native_language_example: I haven't heard from him in weeks.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition **von** + dative plural pronoun **ihnen** (“them”). It can mean **from them** (source: *Wir hörten es von ihnen.*) or **of them** (belonging/responsibility: *ein Fehler von ihnen* = “a mistake of theirs”). Also appears in polite phrases like **Das war recht von Ihnen!** (“That was very kind of you!”), where **Ihnen** is the formal “you” (capitalized).
target_language_example: Ich habe es von ihnen erfahren.
native_language_example: I found out about it from them.

additional_notes: Used to say that she is the source/giver of something. Very common with objects: „Ich habe das von ihr bekommen.“ = “I got that from her.” In questions: „Hast du was von ihr bekommen?“ = “Did you get anything from her?” Grammar tip: „von“ takes the dative case → „ihr“ (her, dative).
target_language_example: Ich habe die Nachricht von ihr bekommen.
native_language_example: I got the message from her.

meaning: heard from her; heard about her.
additional_notes: Past form of the verb phrase „von jemandem hören“. It can mean (1) getting news/updates from someone (“hear from her”) or (2) hearing information about someone (“hear about her”). Often used with „nichts“: „Ich habe nichts von ihr gehört“ = “I haven’t heard from/about her.”
target_language_example: Ich habe seit Wochen nichts von ihr gehört.
native_language_example: I haven’t heard from her in weeks.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition **von** + **dative**. **ihrem** is the dative form of **ihr** (“her/its”), used with **masculine or neuter nouns** (e.g., *von ihrem Großvater*, *von ihrem Können*). **von + dative** can show (1) where something comes from (*from*), (2) what someone is distracted from, and very often (3) the agent in the passive (*by*): *Sie wurde von ihrem Chef angeschrien.*
target_language_example: Sie war von ihrem Ergebnis überrascht.
native_language_example: She was surprised by her result.

additional_notes: "von" takes the dative case, so "ihrer" is the dative form of "sie" as a possessive meaning "her" or "their" (feminine singular noun or plural noun). It’s used for origin/source ("von ihrer neuen Arbeit erzählen" = talk about her new job), cause/experience ("bewegt von ihrer Freundlichkeit" = moved by her kindness), opinion/assessment ("halten von ihrer Entdeckung" = think of her discovery), and in passive-like meaning with people ("von ihrer Großmutter großgezogen" = raised by her grandmother).
target_language_example: Ich habe das Geschenk von ihrer Schwester bekommen.
native_language_example: I got the gift from her sister.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens/works from the inside of a room, building, object, or body. Very common with doors/locks: "von innen geöffnet/verschlossen/aufschließen" = opened/locked/unlocked from the inside (not from the outside). Also used figuratively: "Schönheit kommt von innen" = beauty comes from within.
target_language_example: Die Fenster lassen sich nur von innen öffnen.
native_language_example: The windows can only be opened from the inside.

additional_notes: Used to mark a change that begins at the present moment and continues into the future. Often followed by a present or future statement (e.g., with "musst", "wirst", or simple present in German).
target_language_example: Von jetzt an gehe ich jeden Tag zu Fuß zur Arbeit.
native_language_example: From now on, I’m walking to work every day.

meaning: from a very young age; since childhood.
additional_notes: Used to say something has been true since someone was little (habits, upbringing, character traits). Often with "schon": "schon von klein auf" = "since I/they were little".
target_language_example: Ich spiele schon von klein auf Klavier.
native_language_example: I’ve played the piano since I was very young.

additional_notes: "von" is used with the dative case. "meinem" is the dative form of "mein" (my) used with masculine or neuter nouns (e.g., von meinem Freund, von meinem Auto). It often means "from my" (origin/possession: something from my friend), but with talking/learning it can mean "about my" (e.g., erzählen von meinem Problem = talk about my problem).
target_language_example: Kann ich mir etwas von meinem Bruder ausleihen?
native_language_example: Can I borrow something from my brother?

additional_notes: Used with the preposition **von** (+ dative) to show a starting point or reference point: distance **from** your house, directions **from** your house, or location relative to it. Often appears with **aus** (e.g., **von meinem Haus aus**) meaning “starting from my house / from where my house is.” (Note: **von dem** is often shortened to **vom**, but with **meinem** you keep **von meinem**.)
target_language_example: Von meinem Haus aus dauert es nur zehn Minuten bis zum Bahnhof.
native_language_example: From my house, it only takes ten minutes to get to the train station.

meaning: by my father; from my father.
additional_notes: Uses **von + dative** (mein Vater → **meinem Vater**). Often means **“by”** to name the doer in the **passive** (Das Haus wurde von meinem Vater gestrichen = “The house was painted by my father”). It can also mean **“from”** to show the source/origin, e.g. a gift or something you received (ein Geschenk von meinem Vater = “a gift from my father”), or authorship (ein Buch von meinem Vater = “a book by my father”).
target_language_example: Der Brief ist von meinem Vater.
native_language_example: The letter is from my father.

additional_notes: "von" takes the dative case, so it becomes "von meiner" before a feminine noun (e.g., "von meiner Mutter", "von meiner Freundin"). It can mean (1) origin/source: "I got it from my…", (2) distance/avoidance with verbs like "sich fernhalten": "Stay away from my…", and (3) “of” in expressions like "überzeugt von": "convinced of my…". In "von ... sprechen", it means “talk about …”.
target_language_example: Ich habe den Rat von meiner Mutter bekommen.
native_language_example: I got the advice from my mother.

meaning: from my mother / by my mother; about my mother.
additional_notes: “von” + dative (“meiner Mutter”) is used in a few common ways: (1) origin/possession: “Fotos von meiner Mutter” = photos of/from my mother; “Briefe von meiner Mutter” = letters from my mother. (2) agent in the passive: “ist von meiner Mutter benutzt worden” = was used by my mother. (3) topic: “so von meiner Mutter reden” = talk about my mother like that. In speech, “Von meiner Mutter, ja.” can be a short confirming answer (“From my mother, yes.”).
target_language_example: Das Geschenk ist von meiner Mutter.
native_language_example: The gift is from my mother.

additional_notes: A common phrase with von + the dative pronoun mir. It usually shows source or origin: something comes from you, was given by you, or was borrowed from you. In some contexts, especially passive-style expressions, it can also mean "by me".
target_language_example: Das Geschenk ist von mir.
native_language_example: The gift is from me.

meaning: “fine by me” / “as far as I’m concerned” (I don’t mind).
additional_notes: Used to give permission or show indifference/acceptance: “Okay, if that’s what you want.” It can also widen an option: “on Monday, or (if you prefer) on Tuesday.” Often sounds slightly reluctant depending on tone (similar to “if you insist”).
target_language_example: Von mir aus können wir auch später anfangen.
native_language_example: Fine by me—we can also start later.

additional_notes: Used to say that something will change and be true or happen beginning at this moment and continuing into the future. Often followed by a present or future idea: "Von nun an mache/werde ich ..." It can appear at the start of the sentence for emphasis.
target_language_example: Von nun an esse ich kein Fleisch mehr.
native_language_example: From now on, I won't eat meat anymore.

meaning: from above; (figuratively) from higher authority (“from the top”).
additional_notes: Used literally for physical position or movement (e.g., looking/hearing from a higher place, ‘von oben nach unten’ = from top to bottom). Figuratively it means an instruction/order coming from superiors (e.g., ‘ein Befehl/eine Anordnung von oben’ = an order from higher up). Often contrasts with ‘von unten’ (from below).
target_language_example: Von oben sieht die Stadt ganz anders aus.
native_language_example: From above, the city looks completely different.

meaning: from above (downwards); condescendingly (“looking down on someone”).
additional_notes: Used as an adverb phrase. Literally describes something moving/falling down from above: „Ein Stein fiel von oben herab.“ Figuratively, it describes an arrogant, patronizing attitude—often with verbs like „jemanden von oben herab behandeln/anschauen“ (“to treat/look at someone condescendingly”).
target_language_example: Er sprach von oben herab mit den neuen Kollegen.
native_language_example: He spoke condescendingly to the new colleagues.

additional_notes: “von” is a very common preposition that takes the dative. “von seinem” is used with masculine/neuter singular nouns (e.g., von seinem Vater, von seinem Auto). Depending on the verb/expression, it can mean literally “from his” (movement/origin: Er stieg von seinem Motorrad.), or more generally “of/about his” (topic/connection: Was hältst du von seinem Vorschlag?; ein Foto von seinem Kätzchen = “a photo of his kitten”).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir mehr von seinem Plan erzählen?
native_language_example: Can you tell me more about his plan?

meaning: from his father; (in passive) by his father.
additional_notes: "von" + dative shows the source/origin of something (e.g., inheriting or taking over something from someone). It can also name the agent in a passive sentence: "Er ist von seinem Vater ..." = "He was ... by his father." (Here: "seinem Vater" is dative masculine; the base form is "sein Vater".)
target_language_example: Er hat das Haus von seinem Vater geerbt.
native_language_example: He inherited the house from his father.

meaning: "from his" / "of his" (used before a plural noun).
additional_notes: "von" is a preposition that usually takes the dative case. "seinen" is the dative plural form of "sein" (his), used with plural nouns (often masculine/neuter in dative plural). Common uses: source/origin ("von seinen Händen" = from his hands), belonging/selection ("eines von seinen Autos" = one of his cars), and fixed patterns like "abhängig von seinen …" (dependent on his …) or "leben von seinen …" (live on/from his …).
target_language_example: Sie bekommt Hilfe von seinen Freunden.
native_language_example: She gets help from his friends.

meaning: "about his" / "of his" (von + dative; refers to something that belongs to him).
additional_notes: Used when a verb or noun takes "von" (with dative). Common patterns: **von seiner Arbeit erzählen** = talk about his job; **ein Bild von seiner Katze** = a picture of his cat. **seiner** is the dative feminine form of **sein** (“his”), used with feminine nouns like **die Arbeit**, **die Katze**, **die Vergangenheit**.
target_language_example: Kannst du mir von seiner Familie erzählen?
native_language_example: Can you tell me about his family?

meaning: from his family; of his family.
additional_notes: Uses the preposition „von“ + dative („seiner Familie“). It can mean (1) source/origin: getting something from his family („Geld von seiner Familie“), (2) belonging to a group: nobody in his family („Niemand von seiner Familie“), or (3) separation: living separated from his family („von seiner Familie getrennt“).
target_language_example: Er bekommt viel Unterstützung von seiner Familie.
native_language_example: He gets a lot of support from his family.

meaning: by itself; on its own (without help).
additional_notes: Used when something happens automatically or without anyone doing it. With people, it can mean they figured something out on their own (without being told). Often used with verbs like gehen (Das Licht ging von selbst aus.), sich schließen (Die Tür schließt sich von selbst.), or kommen (auf etwas von selbst kommen = to figure something out by oneself).
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, das Problem löst sich von selbst.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, the problem will solve itself.

meaning: from oneself; (often) out of one’s mouth / on one’s own initiative.
additional_notes: Common in set phrases. With verbs like „etwas von sich geben“ it means to say/utter something (often: to blurt something out): „Er gab einen Kommentar von sich.“ As a short answer „Von sich aus.“ means “on their own” / “of their own accord” (not because someone told them).
target_language_example: Sie hat von sich aus angerufen.
native_language_example: She called on her own initiative.

additional_notes: Used with "von" + dative pronoun "uns". Common in partitive expressions meaning “some/many/one/few of us” (e.g., "einer von uns", "wie viele von uns"). Also used to show distance: "(zwei Häuser) von uns entfernt" = “(two houses) away from us.” With verbs like "wissen" it often means “know about us”: "Wissen sie von uns?"
target_language_example: Kannst du einen von uns anrufen?
native_language_example: Can you call one of us?

meaning: "from our" / "of our" (with a masculine or neuter noun).
additional_notes: Used with the preposition "von" + dative. "Unserem" is the dative form of "unser" for masculine/neuter nouns (e.g., von unserem Vater, von unserem Haus). "Von" often expresses origin (from), perspective/starting point, or a relation like "of"—and in everyday German it can sometimes be used where English would use "of" or where German could also use the genitive.
target_language_example: Ich habe das von unserem Lehrer gehört.
native_language_example: I heard that from our teacher.

additional_notes: Used for physical position/direction (something comes/is seen/gets pushed from below). Often appears with a direction phrase like „von unten nach oben“ (“from bottom to top”) or with verbs like „kommen“, „stoßen“, „hoch(arbeiten)“. In some contexts it can also mean “from downstairs” (from a lower floor).
target_language_example: Der Lärm kommt von unten.
native_language_example: The noise is coming from downstairs (from below).

meaning: from the beginning; from the front.
additional_notes: Used for starting over (often with verbs like „anfangen/beginnen“: „von vorn anfangen“ = start again from the beginning). It can also mean entering/reading from the front: „von vorn rein“ (come in from the front), „von vorn lesen“ (read from the start). Common fixed phrase: „von vorn bis hinten“ = from start to finish / through and through.
target_language_example: Ich habe mich vertan—wir müssen von vorn anfangen.
native_language_example: I made a mistake—we have to start over from the beginning.

additional_notes: Used to say you start at the beginning again (e.g., after a mistake) or from the front/start of something. Common with verbs like anfangen/beginnen (to begin) and with the pattern “von vorne bis hinten” = “from front to back / from start to finish.” As an answer by itself (“Von vorne.”), it means “Start again from the beginning.”
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, ich habe dich nicht verstanden—kannst du bitte von vorne anfangen?
native_language_example: Sorry, I didn’t understand you—can you please start again from the beginning?

meaning: to start over; to start again from the beginning.
additional_notes: Used when you want to restart a task, conversation, or explanation from the beginning (often because something went wrong or wasn’t understood). Commonly combined with "noch mal / noch einmal" (= again): "Können wir noch mal von vorne anfangen?"
target_language_example: Sorry, ich habe es nicht verstanden—können wir von vorne anfangen?
native_language_example: Sorry, I didn’t understand—can we start over?

meaning: "yeah right" / "as if" (used to reject what was just said or implied).
additional_notes: Very common in spoken German and informal writing. Used to express disbelief, contradiction, or sarcasm. Often comes after the word/idea you’re rejecting (e.g., "Abmachung, von wegen.") or on its own: "Von wegen!"
target_language_example: Du meinst, er kommt pünktlich? Von wegen!
native_language_example: You think he’ll be on time? Yeah right!

meaning: from a distance; from far away.
additional_notes: Used to say something is seen, noticed, or done when you are not close. Often with verbs like aussehen (to look), beobachten (to watch), grüßen (to greet), scheinen (to seem). Common pattern: „Von weitem betrachtet, ...“ = “Seen from a distance, ...”.
target_language_example: Von weitem konnte ich nicht erkennen, wer es war.
native_language_example: From a distance, I couldn't tell who it was.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition **von** to ask about the source, origin, or reference point (e.g., which platform/book/planet). **von** takes the **dative**, so it becomes **von welchem** for **masculine/neuter singular** nouns. For feminine: **von welcher**; for plural: **von welchen**.
target_language_example: Von welchem Land kommst du?
native_language_example: Which country are you from?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the person something comes from or originates with (a gift, an idea, information, etc.). It’s the combination of the preposition "von" (from) + "wem" (whom, dative). Often used alone as a follow-up question: "Von wem?" = "From who(m)?"
target_language_example: Von wem hast du die Nachricht gehört?
native_language_example: Who did you hear the news from?

additional_notes: Used for movement or origin starting at home: leaving home, coming from home, etc. It can also mean something comes from a person's home or family environment, as in habits or behavior learned at home.
target_language_example: Er kommt direkt von zu Hause.
native_language_example: He's coming directly from home.

meaning: from excitement / nervousness (so that you react strongly).
additional_notes: Used to say that excitement or nervousness is the cause of a reaction (e.g., jumping up and down, not being able to sleep, barely being able to control yourself). Often appears with verbs like hüpfen, nicht schlafen können, sich kaum halten können, außer sich sein. Similar: „vor Freude“ (from joy), „vor Angst“ (from fear).
target_language_example: Ich konnte vor Aufregung kaum sprechen.
native_language_example: I could hardly speak from excitement/nervousness.

meaning: with joy; out of joy (because of happiness).
additional_notes: Used to express that someone does something because they feel very happy. Often used with strong reactions like tanzen (dance), springen (jump), lachen (laugh), weinen (cry), schreien (shout). The preposition "vor" can mean "from/out of" with feelings: vor Angst (out of fear), vor Wut (with anger).
target_language_example: Die Kinder sprangen vor Freude, als sie die gute Nachricht hörten.
native_language_example: The children jumped for joy when they heard the good news.

meaning: 'in court' / 'before a court' (in a legal case).
additional_notes: Used in legal contexts for court proceedings (not the food meaning of "Gericht"). Common with verbs like "kommen" (to end up in court), "gehen" (to go to court), and "aussagen" (to testify in court).
target_language_example: Der Zeuge muss morgen vor Gericht erscheinen.
native_language_example: The witness has to appear in court tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened a short time ago (in the recent past). Often placed near the verb, but it can also start a sentence for emphasis: "Vor Kurzem ...". Common in both spoken and written German.
target_language_example: Ich bin vor Kurzem nach Berlin gezogen.
native_language_example: I moved to Berlin recently.

meaning: on site; at the location (there in person).
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is physically at the place where something is happening, or where work is done (e.g., police on site, a video recorded on location). Often contrasts with doing something remotely.
target_language_example: Die Techniker sind schon vor Ort und prüfen die Anlage.
native_language_example: The technicians are already on site and are checking the system.

additional_notes: Used after certain verbs to show the reason or emotion behind a strong reaction, e.g. „zittern vor Wut“ (to tremble with rage), „kochen vor Wut“ (to be boiling with rage), „außer sich vor Wut“ (to be beside oneself with rage). It’s not about physical location; it expresses how strongly someone feels anger.
target_language_example: Sie schrie vor Wut und knallte die Tür zu.
native_language_example: She shouted with rage and slammed the door.

additional_notes: Used to highlight what is most important or the main focus. It can modify a noun phrase (often with a specific example): „Ich mag Obst, vor allem Äpfel.“ It can also be used at the start of a sentence as a discourse marker meaning “above all / first of all” to introduce the main point or a key question.
target_language_example: Vor allem im Winter ist es hier sehr kalt.
native_language_example: Especially in winter, it’s very cold here.

additional_notes: Used with a masculine or neuter noun in the dative case ("dem" = "the" for masculine/neuter dative). Often refers to a physical location ("vor dem Kino" = in front of the cinema) or time ("vor dem Sommer" = before the summer). Also used in more abstract expressions like "vor dem Gesetz" (before the law).
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns vor dem Bahnhof.
native_language_example: We’re meeting in front of the train station.

additional_notes: Used with an action to say it happens earlier than dinner. It’s a time phrase with the preposition "vor" + dative: "vor dem" + noun (here: "Abendessen").
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte vor dem Abendessen den Müll rausbringen?
native_language_example: Can you please take out the trash before dinner?

meaning: in front of the train station.
additional_notes: A location phrase: "vor" + dative means "in front of" (outside, near the entrance). "dem" is the dative form of "der" because "Bahnhof" is masculine (der Bahnhof). Often used for meeting points or where taxis wait.
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns vor dem Bahnhof um acht.
native_language_example: We’ll meet in front of the train station at eight.

meaning: in front of the TV; watching TV.
additional_notes: Literally means “in front of the television.” Often used to describe where someone is sitting/lying (e.g., on the couch) and commonly implies they’re watching TV or spending time watching TV (e.g., Zeit vor dem Fernseher verbringen).
target_language_example: Ich habe gestern Abend zwei Stunden vor dem Fernseher gesessen.
native_language_example: I sat in front of the TV for two hours last night.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens earlier than breakfast (time expression). With the dative: vor + dem + Frühstück (das Frühstück). Often used with daily routines (shower, walk, take medicine, etc.).
target_language_example: Ich trinke vor dem Frühstück ein Glas Wasser.
native_language_example: I drink a glass of water before breakfast.

meaning: 'in front of the house' (outside, by the house).
additional_notes: "vor" + dative (dem Haus) describes a location in front of something. Often used for where someone/something is or stops (e.g., a bus stops in front of the house). Not to be confused with "vor das Haus" (accusative), which means movement to in front of the house.
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte vor dem Haus warten?
native_language_example: Can you please wait in front of the house?

meaning: before going to sleep; before bedtime.
additional_notes: Used to talk about something you do shortly before you go to bed. Often used with a regular habit (e.g., "Ich lese vor dem Schlafengehen") or a suggestion/plan ("Wollen wir ...?").
target_language_example: Ich trinke vor dem Schlafengehen noch einen Tee.
native_language_example: I drink a tea before going to sleep.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is standing/doing something in front of a mirror, often while getting ready (hair, makeup, clothes) or practicing (e.g., speaking, singing, facial expressions). It commonly goes with verbs like stehen (to stand), sich fertig machen (to get ready), üben (to practice).
target_language_example: Ich mache mich vor dem Spiegel fertig.
native_language_example: I’m getting ready in front of the mirror.

meaning: "of death" (e.g., fear of death); also "before death."
additional_notes: Most often used with nouns like Angst/Furcht: **Angst/Furcht vor dem Tod** = “fear of death” (here **vor** + dative expresses what you’re afraid of). It can also be used in a more general sense meaning “before death” or “in the face of death,” e.g. **Vor dem Tod sind alle gleich** (“In the face of death, everyone is equal”).
target_language_example: Viele Menschen haben Angst vor dem Tod.
native_language_example: Many people are afraid of death.

meaning: before going to bed; before bedtime.
additional_notes: Used to talk about something you do as part of your evening routine. Literally “before the going-to-bed” (vor + dem + Zubettgehen). Often pairs with habits like duschen (shower), baden (bathe), lesen (read), Zähne putzen (brush teeth).
target_language_example: Ich trinke vor dem Zubettgehen immer noch einen Tee.
native_language_example: I always drink a tea before going to bed.

meaning: in front of the; before the; from the (to protect/hide/flee).
additional_notes: “Vor” is a two-way preposition. With **Accusative** (like “vor den” = plural masculine/neuter accusative), it often shows **movement/direction** to a position in front of something (e.g., *sich vor den Spiegel stellen*). It’s also used in common patterns meaning **protection or escape from** something/someone (*schützen vor*, *fliehen vor*, *sich verstecken vor*), and it can mean **earlier than** (*vor den anderen ankommen* = arrive before the others) or **in front of others / in the presence of others** (*vor den anderen blamieren*).
target_language_example: Stell dich bitte vor den Spiegel.
native_language_example: Please stand in front of the mirror.

meaning: in front of (someone), in full view (of someone).
additional_notes: Used to say something happens while someone is watching—often emphasizing that it’s public or inappropriate (e.g., “vor den Augen der Kinder” = “in front of the children”). Typically followed by a genitive noun (vor den Augen der Familie/der Nation) or “von” + dative (vor den Augen von Gyges).
target_language_example: Er wurde vor den Augen aller verhaftet.
native_language_example: He was arrested in full view of everyone.

additional_notes: "vor" can describe place ('in front of') or time ('before'). In these examples, "der" is the dative feminine form of 'the', as in "vor der Disko" and "vor der Wahl". After some verbs, especially "warnen vor", English often translates it less literally: "vor der Gefahr warnen" = 'warn about/against the danger'.
target_language_example: Wir warten vor der Schule.
native_language_example: We're waiting in front of the school.

meaning: in front of the door; (figuratively) just around the corner / about to happen.
additional_notes: Literal: the place immediately outside a door (often used with verbs like stehen, warten). Figurative: used with things like events or time periods to mean they’re coming very soon (e.g., Die Ferien stehen vor der Tür). You’ll often also hear it with draußen: draußen vor der Tür.
target_language_example: Ich warte kurz vor der Tür.
native_language_example: I’ll wait outside the door for a moment.

meaning: to be (standing) at the door; (figuratively) to be just around the corner / imminent.
additional_notes: Literal: someone is right outside or in front of the door (often implying they’re about to come in). Figurative: used with events or times to mean they’re coming very soon (e.g., holidays, exams: „Die Prüfung steht vor der Tür.“). Note: In the figurative use, German commonly puts the subject first ("Die Prüfung steht vor der Tür"), but the fixed term is still "vor der Tür stehen".
target_language_example: Die Prüfung wird bald vor der Tür stehen, ich muss lernen.
native_language_example: The exam will soon be just around the corner; I have to study.

meaning: in front of you; ahead of you; (figurative) still to come for you.
additional_notes: Literally describes position: something/someone is directly in front of you (often with movement: laufen vor dir). Figuratively, it can mean your future is still ahead of you: Du hast (noch) viel vor dir. Also used with some verbs to mean “of you,” especially with fear: Angst haben vor dir = “to be afraid of you” (vor + dative).
target_language_example: Keine Sorge — du hast noch alles vor dir.
native_language_example: Don’t worry — you still have everything ahead of you.

additional_notes: Used with a past tense to say something happened three years before now. With "vor" + a time period (dative): vor einem Jahr, vor zwei Wochen, vor drei Monaten, etc. You can often place it at the beginning or end of the sentence.
target_language_example: Vor drei Jahren habe ich angefangen, Deutsch zu lernen.
native_language_example: Three years ago, I started learning German.

additional_notes: Used to say when and where something happened: "vor drei Jahren" = "three years ago" and "in" introduces the place (city/country). Word order is flexible, but this pattern is common: time phrase + in + place.
target_language_example: Ich war vor drei Jahren in Berlin.
native_language_example: I was in Berlin three years ago.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened a certain amount of time before now. Pattern: „vor + time (dative)“ (e.g., vor einem Jahr, vor zwei Wochen, vor drei Monaten). Often used with the simple past (Präteritum) or present perfect (Perfekt).
target_language_example: Wir sind vor drei Monaten umgezogen.
native_language_example: We moved three months ago.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened three hours before now (or before another reference time). Common with the simple past/perfect: „Ich habe … vor drei Stunden …“. You can place it at the start for emphasis: „Vor drei Stunden habe ich …“.
target_language_example: Wir haben vor drei Stunden gegessen.
native_language_example: We ate three hours ago.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happened 3 days before now (or before another reference point in the sentence). With a specific past event, German often uses simple past ("ging") or present perfect ("habe gelesen"). Pattern: "vor + time period" (vor zwei Wochen, vor einem Jahr).
target_language_example: Ich habe ihn vor drei Tagen zum letzten Mal gesehen.
native_language_example: I last saw him three days ago.

additional_notes: Time expression with **vor + dative** to say how long ago something happened. With plural time units like **Wochen**, the form stays the same in dative: **vor drei Wochen** (not *vor drei Wochens*). You can swap the number: **vor zwei Wochen**, **vor vier Wochen**, etc.
target_language_example: Wir sind vor drei Wochen umgezogen.
native_language_example: We moved three weeks ago.

additional_notes: Used to place an event in the past, typically an indefinite time around 2–5 years before now. It often answers “Wann?” (When?) and commonly goes with the simple past (Perfekt/Präteritum). Word order: it can come at the beginning or later in the sentence (e.g., “Vor ein paar Jahren habe ich …” / “Ich habe … vor ein paar Jahren …”).
target_language_example: Vor ein paar Jahren habe ich hier gewohnt.
native_language_example: A few years ago, I lived here.

meaning: a year ago; one year earlier (than now/then).
additional_notes: Used to say that something happened exactly one year before a reference point. Often paired with a time word like heute/gestern (e.g., heute vor einem Jahr = “this day a year ago”). Can also be used more loosely to mean “about a year ago.”
target_language_example: Heute vor einem Jahr habe ich meinen neuen Job angefangen.
native_language_example: This day a year ago, I started my new job.

additional_notes: Used with the dative after "vor" to say how long before now something happened. Often goes with past tense (Perfekt/Präteritum) and can come at the beginning or in the middle of the sentence.
target_language_example: Ich habe ihn vor einer Stunde gesehen.
native_language_example: I saw him an hour ago.

meaning: a week ago (one week before now/then).
additional_notes: Used with a time point in the past to say something happened one week earlier. Often with the simple past (Präteritum) or present perfect (Perfekt): „Ich habe … vor einer Woche …“. Also used with due dates/expected events: „Es war vor einer Woche fällig“ = it was due a week ago.
target_language_example: Wir sind vor einer Woche nach Berlin gezogen.
native_language_example: We moved to Berlin a week ago.

additional_notes: Used with past events to say something happened 30 minutes earlier. Often answers the question "Wann?" (When?) and is placed like a time expression: "Er ist vor einer halben Stunde gegangen." You can change the amount of time: "vor einer Stunde" (an hour ago), "vor zwei Stunden" (two hours ago).
target_language_example: Ich habe ihn vor einer halben Stunde gesehen.
native_language_example: I saw him half an hour ago.

additional_notes: Time expression for something that happened in the past. Uses dative plural after "vor": "vor einigen Jahren" (not *vor einige Jahre*). Often used with past tense (Perfekt or Präteritum).
target_language_example: Vor einigen Jahren habe ich in Berlin gearbeitet.
native_language_example: A few years ago, I worked in Berlin.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened a few days in the past. Often placed at the beginning of the sentence (then the verb comes second: "Vor einigen Tagen habe ich ...") or later in the sentence ("... ist vor einigen Tagen passiert").
target_language_example: Vor einigen Tagen habe ich ihn in der Stadt gesehen.
native_language_example: I saw him in town a few days ago.

additional_notes: Used to say how long before now something happened. Often placed at the beginning of a sentence for emphasis ("Vor fünf Jahren ..."), or after the verb ("... ist vor fünf Jahren ..."). In questions it can show surprise or ask for confirmation ("Vor fünf Jahren?").
target_language_example: Vor fünf Jahren bin ich nach Berlin gezogen.
native_language_example: Five years ago I moved to Berlin.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened in the recent past. Often placed after the verb or at the beginning of the sentence for emphasis (then the verb comes second): „Vor kurzem habe ich …“.
target_language_example: Wir haben uns vor kurzem in Berlin gesehen.
native_language_example: We saw each other in Berlin recently.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened far in the past. Often placed near the beginning of the sentence for emphasis ("Vor langer Zeit ..."), or in the middle after the verb ("... ist vor langer Zeit passiert").
target_language_example: Vor langer Zeit habe ich hier gewohnt.
native_language_example: A long time ago, I lived here.

meaning: because of (so much) …; from nothing but …
additional_notes: Used with a noun to say something happens or is impossible due to an overwhelming amount of something (often emotions or circumstances): vor lauter Wut/Angst/Freude/Lampenfieber. Often implies “so much … that …” (e.g., you can’t speak/see/think).
target_language_example: Er konnte vor lauter Stress nicht einschlafen.
native_language_example: He couldn’t fall asleep because of all the stress.

meaning: 'in front of my house' (outside, on the street side).
additional_notes: Uses the preposition "vor" (in front of) with the dative: "vor" + dative answers "where?" (location), e.g. "vor meinem Haus". For motion to a place, German often uses accusative: "vor mein Haus" (rare in everyday speech here; more common: "vor mein Haus" = to in front of my house). You can swap "meinem" for other possessives: "vor deinem Haus", "vor ihrem Haus".
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns um acht vor meinem Haus.
native_language_example: We’ll meet at eight in front of my house.

meaning: in front of me; ahead of me; (hidden) from me.
additional_notes: Literal meaning is “before me.” Used for physical position (“Tom steht direkt vor mir.” = right in front of me), for things that are coming up in time/tasks (“Ich habe eine lange Fahrt vor mir.” = I have a long drive ahead of me), and with verbs like „verstecken“ to mean keeping something from you (“etwas vor mir verstecken”). Note: „vor“ can look like English “for,” but it means “before/in front of.”
target_language_example: Ich habe heute noch viel Arbeit vor mir.
native_language_example: I still have a lot of work ahead of me today.

meaning: ahead of (oneself); in progress/going on (especially in the phrase „vor sich gehen“ = to happen, to be going on).
additional_notes: Used with reflexive pronouns that match the subject: ich habe … vor mir, du hast … vor dir, er/sie/es hat … vor sich, wir haben … vor uns, ihr habt … vor euch, sie/Sie haben … vor sich. Common patterns: (1) „etw. vor sich haben“ = to have something ahead of you (often about the future): „Er hat eine strahlende Zukunft vor sich.“ (2) „Was geht hier vor sich?“ / „Hier geht etwas Seltsames vor sich.“ = What’s going on here? / Something strange is happening here. In these expressions, „sich“ refers back to the subject.
target_language_example: Er hat eine strahlende Zukunft vor sich.
native_language_example: He has a bright future ahead of him.

meaning: "is going on / is happening" (what’s really happening).
additional_notes: Used mostly with „was … vor sich geht“ to ask or say what is happening, often when it’s unclear or secretive: „Keiner weiß, was hier/da/hinter geschlossenen Türen vor sich geht.“ It can also be used for thoughts/feelings: „was in ihrem Kopf vor sich geht“ = what’s going on in her head. Base verb: „vor sich gehen“; in main clauses it splits: „Was geht hier vor sich?“
target_language_example: Ich weiß nicht, was hier vor sich geht.
native_language_example: I don’t know what’s going on here.

additional_notes: Comes from the verb phrase „vor sich gehen“ (= to happen, to be going on). „vor sich ging“ is the simple past (Präteritum) form used in narration/writing. Very common in sentences like „… um zu sehen, was (da/dort/hier) vor sich ging.“ Often used when someone wants to find out what was happening, especially something unusual.
target_language_example: Ich lief sofort nach unten, um nachzusehen, was da vor sich ging.
native_language_example: I ran downstairs immediately to check what was going on there.

additional_notes: Used as an adverbial phrase, often in the pattern “vor sich hin + verb” to describe an action continuing quietly, absent-mindedly, or without a clear goal. Common with verbs like träumen, starren, murmeln, summen, arbeiten. Depending on the verb, English translations include “to oneself,” “away,” or “into space.”
target_language_example: Er starrte vor sich hin und sagte kein Wort.
native_language_example: He stared into space and didn’t say a word.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like pfeifen (whistle), summen (hum), reden/murmeln (talk/mumble), niesen/husten (sneeze/cough) to show the action happens in a low-key way, often without paying much attention and not directed at other people. It can also suggest something is going on continuously in the background.
target_language_example: Sie murmelte vor sich hin, während sie ihre Sachen suchte.
native_language_example: She was mumbling to herself while she was looking for her things.

meaning: in front of us; ahead of us.
additional_notes: Used for physical position (something is in front of you) and for what is coming in the future (what lies ahead). Also used with verbs like „sich verstecken vor …“ / „fliehen vor …“ meaning “to hide from” / “to flee from” someone (here: from us).
target_language_example: Ich sehe schon das Ziel vor uns.
native_language_example: I can already see the destination ahead of us.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happened ten years before now (or before another reference point in the sentence). Often used for comparisons with the present: „… wie vor zehn Jahren“ = “…than ten years ago.”
target_language_example: Ich habe vor zehn Jahren in Berlin studiert.
native_language_example: I studied in Berlin ten years ago.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened. It’s built with **vor + time period** (e.g., *vor einem Jahr* = a year ago, *vor drei Tagen* = three days ago). The noun is in the dative after **vor** (*vor zwei Jahren*, not *vor zwei Jahre*).
target_language_example: Vor zwei Jahren bin ich nach Berlin gezogen.
native_language_example: Two years ago I moved to Berlin.

additional_notes: Used with the past tense to say something happened two days before now. It can appear at the start of the sentence for emphasis ("Vor zwei Tagen ...") or later in the sentence ("... vor zwei Tagen"). Related patterns: "vor einem Tag" (one day ago), "vor drei Wochen" (three weeks ago).
target_language_example: Vor zwei Tagen habe ich meinen Schlüssel verloren.
native_language_example: Two days ago I lost my key.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened two weeks before now (a point in the past). With other time amounts: vor drei Tagen (three days ago), vor einem Jahr (a year ago).
target_language_example: Wir haben uns vor zwei Wochen zum ersten Mal getroffen.
native_language_example: We met for the first time two weeks ago.

meaning: pros and cons; advantages and disadvantages.
additional_notes: Used when weighing different options or making a decision. Usually appears as a set phrase (often with an article): "die Vor- und Nachteile". Note the hyphen in writing: "Vor- und Nachteile" stands for "Vor- und Nachteile" (= "Vorteile und Nachteile").
target_language_example: Wir sollten die Vor- und Nachteile vergleichen, bevor wir entscheiden.
native_language_example: We should compare the pros and cons before we decide.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive clause: **vorhaben, … zu + Infinitiv**. Typical pattern: **Ich habe vor, … zu + Infinitiv** (present: *habe vor*; past: *hatte vor*). It expresses an intention or plan, often not yet fixed. The *zu*-infinitive usually comes at the end of the clause; a comma is often used before the *zu*-phrase, especially when it’s longer.
target_language_example: Wir haben vorhaben zu reisen, sobald wir Urlaub bekommen.
native_language_example: We intend to travel as soon as we get vacation time.

meaning: to be careful; to be cautious.
additional_notes: Used to warn someone or to remind yourself to avoid danger or mistakes. Often with "bei" + noun (e.g., "beim Autofahren") or with "wenn" (when) / "damit" (so that) clauses. You can also specify what to be careful about with "vorsichtig sein, was ...".
target_language_example: Sie müssen vorsichtig sein, wenn Sie die Treppe hinuntergehen.
native_language_example: You must be careful when you go down the stairs.

meaning: to be more careful; to be more cautious.
additional_notes: Used to advise or warn someone to use more care. Often appears with modal verbs like "sollen" or "müssen": "Du solltest vorsichtiger sein" (You should be more careful), "Er muss vorsichtiger sein" (He has to be more careful). "vorsichtiger" is the comparative of "vorsichtig" (careful).
target_language_example: In Zukunft solltest du wohl etwas vorsichtiger sein.
native_language_example: In the future you should probably be a bit more careful.

additional_notes: Command telling one person to wake up. It’s the imperative of the separable verb „aufwachen“: „wach“ + „auf“. Often used with names or terms of address (e.g., „Mama“, „Schätzchen“). For more than one person, use „Wacht auf!“; formal singular „Wachen Sie auf!“
target_language_example: Wach auf, wir sind schon da!
native_language_example: Wake up, we’re already here!

additional_notes: Used in an infinitive construction with „zu“ + bleiben. Common after verbs like „versuchen“ (to try) or in purpose clauses with „um … zu …“: „Ich trinke Kaffee, um wach zu bleiben.“
target_language_example: Du musst versuchen, wach zu bleiben.
native_language_example: You have to try to stay awake.

additional_notes: Imperative of **aufwachen** (to wake up), addressed to **du** (one person you’re on first-name/"du" terms with). Can be literal (stop sleeping) or figurative ("wake up!" = pay attention/realize what’s happening). For formal or plural: **Wachen Sie auf!** (formal), **Wacht auf!** (you all).
target_language_example: Wach auf, wir sind schon spät dran!
native_language_example: Wake up, we're already running late!

meaning: to be true; to be real (actually the case).
additional_notes: Used to state or question whether something is true. Common with questions or negation: "Kann das wahr sein?" (Can that be true?), "Das kann nicht wahr sein." (That can’t be true.). In exclamations like "Das darf doch nicht wahr sein!" it expresses shock/annoyance: “This can’t be happening/This can’t be true!”
target_language_example: Kann das wahr sein?
native_language_example: Can that be true?

meaning: to come true; to become reality (said of wishes, dreams, hopes, predictions, etc.).
additional_notes: Used for wishes, dreams, hopes, predictions, plans, etc. Grammar: the verb splits in many tenses: present/future often wird ... wahr or wird ... wahr werden; past wurde ... wahr. Common with modals: kann/könnte ... wahr werden = can/could come true. Note: You typically say a wish/dream wird wahr / wird wahr werden (not *macht wahr).
target_language_example: Dein Wunsch könnte wahr werden.
native_language_example: Your wish could come true.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an ideal, deep, genuine kind of love (often in romantic stories). You can use it as a noun phrase ("wahre Liebe") or with "Das nennt man …" (= "That’s what you call …").
target_language_example: Sie glaubt an wahre Liebe.
native_language_example: She believes in true love.

additional_notes: Used with another verb (often in invitations/plans) to say you’re going hiking: z. B. „Hast du vor, …?“ (Do you plan to…?) or „Hättest du Lust, …?“ (Would you like to…?). „wandern“ means hiking (walking in nature), not just wandering around aimlessly.
target_language_example: Hast du Lust, am Samstag wandern zu gehen?
native_language_example: Do you feel like going hiking on Saturday?

additional_notes: Used to mean it doesn’t matter when something happens—at any time. Often introduces a subordinate clause: „Wann auch immer du Zeit hast, …“. It can also stand alone as a short answer meaning “whenever”.
target_language_example: Ruf mich an, wann auch immer du Hilfe brauchst.
native_language_example: Call me whenever you need help.

additional_notes: Used to ask about the starting time/date of an event or period (movie, game, trip, vacation, performance, etc.).
