The verb is "beginnen" (to begin); in a question, the conjugated verb comes second: "Wann beginnt der Film?" You can swap in different subjects (der Film, das Spiel, dein Urlaub, Ihre Reise).
target_language_example: Wann beginnt der Unterricht?
native_language_example: When does the class start?

meaning: “when did you…?” / “when were you…?” (asking about a past time).
additional_notes: Used to ask at what time or on what date something happened, often with the Perfekt (past) tense: "Wann bist du … gewesen/gegangen/gekommen/aufgestanden?". With verbs that use "haben" in the past, you’ll say "Wann hast du …?" instead (e.g., "Wann hast du das gemacht?").
target_language_example: Wann bist du gestern nach Hause gekommen?
native_language_example: When did you come home yesterday?

meaning: 'when do you go / leave' (when are you going to...).
additional_notes: Used to ask at what time/date someone is going somewhere or doing an activity with gehen + a destination or activity (e.g., nach Hause, zur Schule, ins Bett, mit jemandem essen). Very common in everyday planning. For a more formal/polite version (e.g., to strangers), use „Wann gehen Sie ...?“.
target_language_example: Wann gehst du heute nach Hause?
native_language_example: When are you going home today?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the time of a past action in the polite/formal form ("Sie"). It’s typically followed by a past participle (Perfekt), e.g. "Wann haben Sie angefangen?" / "Wann haben Sie es gekauft?" In spoken German this is a very common way to ask "when did you…?"
target_language_example: Wann haben Sie das letzte Mal Ihren Arzt gesehen?
native_language_example: When did you last see your doctor?

wann haben Sie das letzte Mal

target_language_multi_word_term: wann haben Sie das letzte Mal
additional_notes: Used to ask about the most recent time someone did something. It’s a formal/polite question with “Sie” (used with strangers, in service situations, interviews, etc.). The verb usually goes at the end of the clause: „Wann haben Sie das letzte Mal … gemacht/gekauft/gehört?“
target_language_example: Wann haben Sie das letzte Mal Urlaub gemacht?
native_language_example: When was the last time you took a vacation?

meaning: 'when did you (all) ...?' (asking about time in the past).
additional_notes: Used to ask when something happened, addressing a group ("ihr" = you all) or using informal plural "you". Often followed by the Perfekt: "habt" + past participle (e.g., "Wann habt ihr es gemerkt?"). It can also be used with an infinitive phrase after a verb like "anfangen": "Wann habt ihr angefangen, ... zu ...?"
target_language_example: Wann habt ihr die Tickets gekauft?
native_language_example: When did you (all) buy the tickets?

additional_notes: Used to ask when something last happened, addressing two or more people informally ("ihr"). In standard German spelling/capitalization, this is usually written: „Wann habt ihr das letzte Mal …?“ (with „letzte Mal“ as two words and „Wann“ capitalized). The verb phrase typically uses Perfekt, with the past participle at the end: „Wann habt ihr das letzte Mal Spargel gegessen?“
target_language_example: wann habt ihr das letztemal Spargel gegessen?
native_language_example: When was the last time you ate asparagus?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the time/occasion of a past action. It’s often followed by a verb in the past (Perfekt): “Wann hast du das gemacht?” = “When did you do that?” Also appears with reflexive verbs: “Wann hast du dich …?” = “When did you … (yourself)?” In everyday English, this is usually translated as “when did you…?”
target_language_example: Wann hast du das letzte Mal deine Eltern besucht?
native_language_example: When did you last visit your parents?

wann hast du das letzte Mal

target_language_multi_word_term: wann hast du das letzte Mal
additional_notes: Used to ask about the most recent time someone did something. It’s typically followed by a past participle at the end of the sentence (Perfekt), e.g., „… gekauft?“, „… geschlafen?“. You can change „du“ to other people: „Wann haben Sie das letzte Mal …?“ (formal), „Wann hast ihr das letzte Mal …?“ (you plural).
target_language_example: Wann hast du das letzte Mal im Restaurant gegessen?
native_language_example: When was the last time you ate at a restaurant?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the most recent time someone did something. Note: Standard spelling is usually „Wann hast du das letzte Mal …?“ (two words: „letzte Mal“). Your given form „letztemal“ is commonly seen in informal writing, but is nonstandard. It’s typically followed by a past participle at the end of the clause: „… gebadet?“, „… um Hilfe gebeten?“
target_language_example: Wann hast du das letztemal gebadet?
native_language_example: When was the last time you bathed?

additional_notes: Used to ask when someone last did something that takes a reflexive pronoun ("sich" = "yourself"). It’s commonly followed by a past participle in the perfect tense: "Wann hast du dich verlaufen?" (= When did you get lost?). Often appears with time phrases like "das letzte Mal" (the last time) or "zuletzt" (most recently).
target_language_example: Wann hast du dich das letzte Mal bei deinen Eltern gemeldet?
native_language_example: When did you last check in with your parents?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the time something happens. Often followed by the subject and then the rest of the verb phrase. With many movement/change-of-state verbs, German forms the past with "sein" + past participle (e.g. "Wann ist er gegangen/angekommen/geworden?"). It can also be used with a present-time meaning: "Wann ist die Stunde zu Ende?" (= When is the lesson over?).
target_language_example: Wann ist der Zug angekommen?
native_language_example: When did the train arrive?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the time/date of someone’s arrival. "Sie" is the formal “you” (to a stranger, customer, etc.). It’s often followed by a place or phrase like "zurück" (back) and "aus dem Urlaub" (from vacation): "Wann kommen Sie zurück?" / "Wann kommen Sie zurück nach …?" / "Wann kommen Sie aus … zurück?".
target_language_example: Wann kommen Sie zurück nach Deutschland?
native_language_example: When are you coming back to Germany?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the time someone or something arrives. Often followed by a person/thing (Wann kommt Papa?/die Post?) or combined with an adverb like "zurück" (Wann kommt er zurück? = When is he coming back?). In main clauses, the verb stays in 2nd position: "Wann kommt ...?"
target_language_example: Wann kommt der Bus?
native_language_example: When is the bus coming?

meaning: "When are you (plural) coming?" / "When will you (plural) come?"
additional_notes: Used to ask about the time a group of people is arriving/coming back/coming over. "ihr" is the informal plural "you" (talking to two or more people you address with du). Often followed by a destination or direction: "nach Hause" (home), "zurück" (back), "mich besuchen" (visit me). In real sentences, it may appear as "Wann kommt ihr ...?" with extra info at the end.
target_language_example: Wann kommt ihr heute Abend nach Hause?
native_language_example: When are you coming home tonight?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the time something happens or happened. "ihr" is informal plural "you" (talking to more than one person). "seid" is the 2nd-person plural form of "sein" (to be) and is often used with a past participle to form the spoken past (Perfekt) with movement/change-of-state verbs: "Wann seid ihr angekommen?" = "When did you arrive?". Word order is typically: "Wann" + verb ("seid") + subject ("ihr") + ...
target_language_example: Wann seid ihr gestern Abend zurückgekommen?
native_language_example: When did you come back yesterday evening?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the time/date of something involving the listener, using formal "Sie" (you). In questions, the verb comes before the subject: "Wann sind Sie ...?" Often followed by a past participle for the perfect tense (e.g., "angekommen", "gegangen") or an adjective (e.g., "beschäftigt").
target_language_example: Wann sind Sie verfügbar?
native_language_example: When are you available?

meaning: "When should I …?" / "When am I supposed to …?"
additional_notes: Used to ask for the right time to do something, often when someone expects you to do it or you need instructions. Uses the modal verb "sollen" (ich soll), which can mean "should" or "be supposed to". You normally follow it with an infinitive at the end: "Wann soll ich kommen?"
target_language_example: Wann soll ich die Unterlagen mitbringen?
native_language_example: When should I bring the documents?

additional_notes: Used to ask for both the time (wann?) and the place (wo?) of an event, often together in one question: "Wann und wo ...?".
target_language_example: Kannst du mir sagen, wann und wo wir uns treffen?
native_language_example: Can you tell me when and where we're meeting?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the time of a future action in a polite/formal way. "Sie" is the formal "you" (one person or multiple people). The verb comes right after "werden" at the end (e.g., "Wann werden Sie nach Berlin fahren?"). In everyday speech you may also hear "Wann werden Sie ...?" as a slightly formal alternative to "Wann ...?"
target_language_example: Wann werden Sie die Unterlagen schicken?
native_language_example: When will you send the documents?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the timing of a future action when speaking to two or more people informally ("ihr"). "werdet" is the 2nd person plural form of "werden" and is often used to form the future: "Wann werdet ihr kommen?" = “When will you come?” ("werden" can also mean “to become,” but in these questions it usually marks the future.)
target_language_example: Wann werdet ihr wieder zu Hause sein?
native_language_example: When will you be home again?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the time something will happen. Common patterns: (1) future: "Wann wird es beginnen?" = "When will it begin?" (2) passive: "Wann wird der Roman veröffentlicht?" = "When will the novel be published?" In questions, the verb "wird" comes right after "wann" (inversion).
target_language_example: Wann wird der Zug ankommen?
native_language_example: When will the train arrive?

meaning: “When will you …?” (asking about the time when someone will do something).
additional_notes: Used to ask about the timing of a future action. It’s built from: „wann“ = when, „wirst“ = will (2nd person singular of „werden“), „du“ = you. Usually followed by an infinitive (often at the end): „Wann wirst du kommen?“ = When will you come? In casual speech, people also use present tense: „Wann kommst du?“
target_language_example: Wann wirst du ankommen?
native_language_example: When will you arrive?

meaning: 'when was ...?' (asking about a past event/date; often passive).
additional_notes: Used to start questions about when something happened in the past, often in the passive voice: "Wann wurde + noun + Partizip II?" = "When was ... (done/built/founded)?" Example patterns: "Wann wurde das Haus gebaut?" (built), "Wann wurde die Firma gegründet?" (founded). "wurde" is the simple past of "werden" and helps form the passive.
target_language_example: Wann wurde das Museum eröffnet?
native_language_example: When was the museum opened?

meaning: "was, he went" — a snippet of word order often seen when a subordinate clause ends with the verb (… war) and the main clause begins after the comma with the verb first (ging er …), e.g., after "obwohl" (although).
additional_notes: This is not a standalone fixed expression; it’s a grammatical sequence. In an "obwohl" clause, the conjugated verb typically comes at the end (… krank war). After the comma, the main clause often has verb-first order (V1) because the sentence starts with the subordinate clause: "ging er …". The pronoun "er" is part of the main clause subject.
target_language_example: Obwohl er krank war, ging er zur Schule.
native_language_example: Although he was ill, he went to school.

meaning: "was" / "were" + "I have" (used in a past-time clause + the main clause in Perfekt).
additional_notes: This pattern often appears in sentences that start with **als** ("when" for a single time in the past) or **weil/da** ("because"). The clause with **war** is a past state/background (Präteritum of *sein*), and the main clause uses **habe ich** to form the Perfekt tense (e.g., *habe ... bekommen/verbracht/ausgezogen*). Word order: in the first clause the verb goes to the end (*als ich 13 war*), then the main clause starts with the helping verb (*habe ich ...*).
target_language_example: Als ich müde war, habe ich früh geschlafen.
native_language_example: When I was tired, I went to sleep early.

meaning: 'was back then / at that time' (in the past).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a situation, state, age, job, or place at a specific time in the past. It’s usually background info: "X was (like this) back then." It combines the simple past of "sein" (war = was) with "damals" (back then/at the time).
target_language_example: Ich war damals noch Student.
native_language_example: Back then, I was still a student.

additional_notes: Past tense of "sein" (to be): "war" = "was" + "das" = "that/it/the". Used in questions like "War das dein erstes Mal?" (Was that your first time?) and "War das Ramiro?" (Was that Ramiro?). In statements, it can mean "was the": "Der Fluss war das Einzige ..." (The river was the only thing ...). Also common for denying responsibility: "Ich war das nicht" = "That wasn’t me."
target_language_example: War das du, der geklopft hat?
native_language_example: Was that you who knocked?

meaning: "was ... all day" / "was ... the whole day" (past tense).
additional_notes: Uses the simple past of **sein** (**war** = "was") with a time expression **den ganzen Tag** (accusative: "the whole day"). Common with places or situations: **war ... hier/weg/auf seinem Zimmer**, **war ... unruhig**, **war ... unterwegs**, etc. Often you add an adjective or location after it.
target_language_example: Ich war den ganzen Tag zu Hause.
native_language_example: I was at home all day.

additional_notes: "war" is the simple past of "sein" (to be). "der" can be the masculine nominative article (“the”) or a masculine demonstrative/pronoun (“he/that one”). In statements you often see it as "X war der ..." (= “X was the ...”). In yes/no questions, German often inverts word order: "War der Briefträger da?" (= “Was the mailman there?”).
target_language_example: Er war der neue Lehrer.
native_language_example: He was the new teacher.

additional_notes: Used to say a male person was the first to do something or the first in a role/title. It’s the simple past of “ist der Erste” (is the first). Often followed by a relative clause: „Er war der erste, der …“ (He was the first one who …). Variations: feminine „war die Erste“; plural „waren die Ersten“; neuter „war das Erste“ (for a thing). Capitalization: as an adjective it’s often written lowercase („der erste“), but can appear capitalized („der Erste“) when used more like a noun (the first one).
target_language_example: Tom war der erste, der geantwortet hat.
native_language_example: Tom was the first one to reply.

additional_notes: Used to single out/identify the male person responsible for an action, often for emphasis. It’s followed by a relative clause introduced by the relative pronoun „der“. The form changes with gender/number/case: „war diejenige, die …“ (female), „waren diejenigen, die …“ (plural).
target_language_example: Tom war derjenige, der die Polizei gerufen hat.
native_language_example: Tom was the one who called the police.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something was continuously in a certain state or place for the entire relevant period. Often followed by adjectives or location phrases (e.g., "hier", "drinnen", "traurig", "an"). You can change the verb for other persons/tenses (e.g., "ich war die ganze Zeit...", "er ist die ganze Zeit...").
target_language_example: Ich war die ganze Zeit zu Hause.
native_language_example: I was at home the whole time.

additional_notes: Past tense of "sein" (to be) with the indefinite article "ein". Used before a masculine or neuter noun in the nominative (e.g., "Er war ein Lehrer" / "Es war ein Problem"). With feminine nouns you use "war eine".
target_language_example: Mein Opa war ein guter Koch.
native_language_example: My grandpa was a good cook.

meaning: “was a great/big …” (masculine noun), or “there was a big …”.
additional_notes: Past tense of "sein" (to be): "war" = "was". "ein großer" is used before a masculine noun in the nominative case (e.g., "ein großer Mann"). It can describe someone/something ("He was a great …") or introduce something that existed somewhere ("There was a big …"), as in "Hinter dem Haus war ein großer Garten."
target_language_example: Mozart war ein großer Komponist.
native_language_example: Mozart was a great composer.

additional_notes: Used to say an event, show, movie, etc. turned out very successfully. "war" is the simple past of "sein" (to be), common in writing; in speech you’ll also hear "ist ein großer Erfolg gewesen". The adjective changes with case/gender: e.g., "Das Konzert war ein großer Erfolg" (masc.), but "Die Veranstaltung war ein großer Erfolg" (still masc. because "Erfolg" is masculine).
target_language_example: Die Ausstellung war ein großer Erfolg.
native_language_example: The exhibition was a great success.

meaning: "was a good ..." (masculine), or "was a good one."
additional_notes: "war" is the simple past (Präteritum) of "sein" (to be): "he/it was". "ein guter" is the masculine nominative form of "ein" + "gut" and is used before a masculine noun (often with an -er ending: "ein guter König"). Sometimes the noun is implied/left out: "Er war ein guter." = "He was a good one." Note: "war" looks like English "war" but means "was."
target_language_example: Es war ein guter Plan.
native_language_example: It was a good plan.

meaning: “was a” (simple past of *sein* + feminine indefinite article “a”).
additional_notes: Used to state what someone/something was in the past, before a feminine noun: *X war eine …* (e.g., *eine Bibliothek, eine Synagoge, eine Prinzessin*). For masculine/neuter: *war ein …*; for plural: *waren …* (no indefinite article). Note: *war* here means “was” (not English “war”).
target_language_example: Dieses Museum war eine Synagoge.
native_language_example: This museum was a synagogue.

additional_notes: Past tense of **sein** (to be): **ich/er/sie/es war**. Used to talk about something that lasted one week, often with a place or situation: **Ich war eine Woche in Berlin.** You may also see **eine Woche lang** (“for a week”).
target_language_example: Ich war eine Woche in Berlin.
native_language_example: I was in Berlin for a week.

additional_notes: Past tense of "sein" (to be): "war" = "was" + "es" = "it". In statements, German often uses "... war es ..." (e.g., "Im Bus war es sehr heiß" = "On the bus it was very hot"). In yes/no questions, the verb comes first: "War es ...?" = "Was it ...?". Often refers to the situation/weather/condition in general.
target_language_example: Gestern war es den ganzen Tag kalt.
native_language_example: Yesterday it was cold all day.

additional_notes: This is a cleft sentence used to strongly emphasize who (or what) did something: **X war es, der …** = “It was X who …”. The relative pronoun must match the person/thing: **der** (masculine), **die** (feminine/plural), **das** (neuter/thing). In the past, you often see **hat** at the end: *Tom war es, der das Licht ausgemacht hat.*
target_language_example: Mein Bruder war es, der mir geholfen hat.
native_language_example: It was my brother who helped me.

additional_notes: Past tense (Präteritum) of the weather phrase "Es ist kalt" (it is cold). Often used to describe the weather at a past time: "Gestern war es kalt." In questions: "War es kalt?" When talking about a person feeling cold, German often uses dative + "war ... kalt": "Mir/Dir/Ihm war kalt" (I/you/he felt cold).
target_language_example: Gestern Abend war es kalt, also habe ich eine Jacke angezogen.
native_language_example: Yesterday evening it was cold, so I put on a jacket.

additional_notes: Past tense (Präteritum) of "sein" (to be) with negation: "es war nicht" = "it was not". Used (1) in statements to say something was not the case (often with emphasis/contrast: "Einfach war es nicht."), and (2) as a question or rhetorical tag: "War es nicht höchste Zeit?" = "Wasn't it high time?" Word order changes between statement ("… war es nicht") and question ("War es nicht …?").
target_language_example: Ich dachte, er war da, aber er war es nicht.
native_language_example: I thought he was there, but he wasn't.

additional_notes: Past tense of "sein" (to be) + "falsch" (wrong/incorrect). Used to say that something (an answer, address, forecast, sentence, action) was not correct. For plural subjects, use "waren falsch" (they were wrong).
target_language_example: Die Information war falsch.
native_language_example: The information was wrong.

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something was different in the past. It’s the simple past of "sein" (war = was) plus "früher" (earlier/before). Often appears with extra words like "mal" or "einmal" (roughly “at one time”), but the core meaning stays the same.
target_language_example: Ich war früher Lehrerin, aber jetzt arbeite ich im Büro.
native_language_example: I used to be a teacher, but now I work in an office.

meaning: “was (something) to me / for me” (how I experienced or saw it).
additional_notes: Used to express your personal perspective or relationship: *X war für mich ein Rätsel* (“X was a mystery to me”), *wie eine Schwester* (“like a sister to me”), or *war für mich da* (“was there for me”). In the past tense, it’s **war** (from **sein**). In other tenses you’ll see **ist für mich** (present) or **wäre für mich** (would be).
target_language_example: Seine Hilfe war für mich sehr wichtig.
native_language_example: His help was very important to me.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something was in a certain state or place yesterday. *war* is the simple past (Präteritum) of *sein* (“to be”) for *er/sie/es* (and also *ich*). Common with time words like *gestern* (yesterday), *gestern Nachmittag* (yesterday afternoon), etc. Note: *war* looks like English “war” but here it means “was”.
target_language_example: Ich war gestern im Kino.
native_language_example: I was at the cinema yesterday.

meaning: 'was in' (was inside / was in a place, situation, or language).
additional_notes: Simple past of "sein" ("war") + the preposition "in". Used for being in a physical location ("Er war in unserem Haus"), for something being in a language ("Die Nachricht war in Französisch"), or for being in a state/situation (e.g., "in Aufruhr", "in Eile"). With cities/countries, German often uses "in" ("Er war in Berlin/Deutschland").
target_language_example: Der Junge war in unserem Haus.
native_language_example: The boy was in our house.

additional_notes: Simple past of "sein" (to be) + "kein" (no/not a/none). Used to say someone/something was not a certain thing: "Er war kein Arzt." (He wasn’t a doctor.) The form changes with gender/case and singular/plural: "war keine" (feminine), "war kein" (masc./neut. nominative), etc. Often also appears in patterns like "war kein … mehr" = "was no longer …".
target_language_example: Ich war kein guter Schüler.
native_language_example: I was not a good student.

meaning: “was just about to (do something)” / “was close to (doing something)”.
additional_notes: Past tense of the expression „kurz davor sein“, used to say something almost happened or you almost did something. It’s typically followed by „zu“ + infinitive: „Ich war kurz davor, zu gehen.“ (I was about to leave.) You can change the verb for other subjects: „ich war“, „du warst“, „er/sie/es war“, „wir waren“, etc.
target_language_example: Ich war kurz davor, dir zu schreiben, aber dann habe ich es vergessen.
native_language_example: I was just about to text you, but then I forgot.

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something was your first one (first friend, first crush, first thought, etc.). Grammar note: this is past tense of "sein" ("war" = "was"). "mein erster" is masculine; with feminine nouns you say "war meine erste" (z.B. "meine erste Freundin"), and with neuter nouns "war mein erstes" (z.B. "mein erstes Auto").
target_language_example: Das war mein erster Job.
native_language_example: That was my first job.

additional_notes: Used to negate the past state/identity of a single person/thing (3rd person singular): er/sie/es war nicht … = he/she/it was not …. In spoken German, people often use the perfect tense instead: er ist nicht … gewesen.
target_language_example: Es war nicht einfach, aber wir haben es geschafft.
native_language_example: It wasn't easy, but we managed it.

additional_notes: "war" is the simple past of "sein" (to be). "nie" means "never". Together they say that something did not happen at any time in the past. You can swap the subject: "ich war nie…", "sie war nie…", "wir waren nie…" (plural uses "waren").
target_language_example: Ich war nie in Berlin.
native_language_example: I was never in Berlin.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has never visited a place up to now. Common pattern: **[Person] war noch nie in + (Land/Stadt)**. You may also see it with **gewesen** (e.g., *war noch nie in Italien gewesen*), which is a more complete/past form but means the same idea here. **noch nie** = “never (so far)”.
target_language_example: Ich war noch nie in Berlin.
native_language_example: I’ve never been to Berlin.

additional_notes: Literally: past of *sein* (*war* = was) + *schon* (already). With a time/state (*krank*, *tot*, *zu Ende*) it often means “was already” (something had already happened by then / earlier than expected): *Einer war schon tot.* In comments/evaluations, *schon* can act as a soft intensifier (“really / kind of / quite”): *Das war schon irgendwie schade.* Context decides which meaning fits.
target_language_example: Das war schon irgendwie schade.
native_language_example: That was kind of a shame, really.

additional_notes: Used to say that something has been true for a very long time (from the beginning, as long as you can remember). Often used to emphasize that something isn’t new or surprising: "Er war schon immer so" = “He’s always been like that.” The verb is in the past ("war"), so it commonly appears in stories or when describing someone’s long-standing traits.
target_language_example: Diese Straße war schon immer sehr laut.
native_language_example: This street has always been very noisy.

additional_notes: Used with an adjective to describe someone/something in the past (Präteritum of **sein** + **sehr**). Common in writing and storytelling; in spoken German you may also hear **ist sehr … gewesen**. Note: **war** looks like English “war” but means “was.”
target_language_example: Der Film war sehr spannend.
native_language_example: The movie was very exciting.

additional_notes: Past tense (Präteritum) of "sein" + adjective: "(ich/er/sie) war" = "was". Used to describe a strong feeling of surprise in the past, often with "über" + accusative for the reason ("über diese Neuigkeiten") or with an infinitive clause ("überrascht, das zu hören"). You can change the person: "Ich war...", "Sie war...", "Wir waren...".
target_language_example: Ich war sehr überrascht, dich hier zu sehen.
native_language_example: I was very surprised to see you here.

meaning: “was so …” (used to show degree, often with a result: “so … that …”).
additional_notes: “war” is the simple past of “sein” (to be). With “so” + an adjective/adverb, it expresses a strong degree and is very often followed by a “dass …” clause to describe the consequence: “Er war so müde, dass …” = “He was so tired that …”. You’ll also see comparisons like “so … wie …” (“as … as …”).
target_language_example: Ich war so müde, dass ich im Zug eingeschlafen bin.
native_language_example: I was so tired that I fell asleep on the train.

additional_notes: A polite way to say someone did you a favor. It’s the past tense of "(er/sie) ist so nett" and is commonly followed by an infinitive with "zu" (e.g., "...war so nett, mir zu helfen").
target_language_example: Sie war so nett, mir beim Ausfüllen des Formulars zu helfen.
native_language_example: She was kind enough to help me fill out the form.

additional_notes: Used with **sein** in the past tense (**war**) plus **voller** + plural/uncountable noun to say a place/thing/life had a lot of something: **X war voller Y**. It commonly describes rooms, spaces, containers, or even abstract things like life experiences. (Present: **ist voller**.)
target_language_example: Das Zimmer war voller Leute.
native_language_example: The room was full of people.

additional_notes: "war" is the simple past of "sein" (to be). "völlig" means "completely/totally" and is usually used with an adjective: "war völlig + Adjektiv" (e.g., "war völlig müde", "war völlig überrascht").
target_language_example: Ich war völlig überrascht, dich hier zu sehen.
native_language_example: I was completely surprised to see you here.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize a description in the past. "war" is the simple past of "sein" (to be) for ich/er/sie/es: "ich war", "er/sie/es war". "wirklich" often means "really" or "truly" and can strengthen an adjective or statement (e.g., "Er war wirklich müde.").
target_language_example: Ich war wirklich müde nach der Reise.
native_language_example: I was really tired after the trip.

meaning: 'was quite / pretty' (to a fairly strong degree).
additional_notes: Used with an adjective to say someone/something was fairly or noticeably that way. "ziemlich" is a common intensity word like "quite" or "pretty" in English (stronger than "ein bisschen" = "a little").
target_language_example: Der Film war ziemlich spannend.
native_language_example: The movie was quite exciting.

additional_notes: Used with the verb „sein“ in the past: „war“ = “was”. Pattern 1: „X war zu + Adjektiv“ = something was too [adjective]. Pattern 2: „X war zu + Adjektiv, um … zu + Infinitiv“ = X was too [adjective] to [verb] (e.g., too surprised to say anything).
target_language_example: Ich war zu müde, um noch auszugehen.
native_language_example: I was too tired to go out (anymore).

additional_notes: Past tense of "sein" + adjective: "überrascht sein" = "to be surprised." Changes with the subject (ich war, du warst, er/sie/es war, wir waren, ihr wart, sie/Sie waren). Often followed by information about what surprised someone, e.g. "überrascht, das zu hören" (surprised to hear that) or "überrascht, wie ..." (surprised how ...).
target_language_example: Ich war überrascht, wie schnell der Zug kam.
native_language_example: I was surprised how quickly the train arrived.

additional_notes: Used to say someone felt surprise about the fact that follows. "war" is past tense of "sein" (to be), and "überrascht" is an adjective (surprised). After "dass" (that), German usually puts the verb at the end of the clause: "…dass Maria bereits wusste …".
target_language_example: Ich war überrascht, dass er so früh angekommen ist.
native_language_example: I was surprised that he arrived so early.

additional_notes: Polite/formal way to say "were you" in the simple past of sein (to be). Used when speaking to one person you address as Sie (e.g., strangers, customers, officials). Often used in questions: "Waren Sie ...?"
target_language_example: Waren Sie gestern schon hier?
native_language_example: Were you here yesterday already?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone (politely/formally) whether they have visited a place at any time in their life. Uses the formal “Sie”. You can also say “Waren Sie schon einmal in Deutschland?” = “Have you ever been to Germany?”
target_language_example: Waren Sie schon einmal in Deutschland?
native_language_example: Have you ever been to Germany?

additional_notes: "waren" is the simple past of "sein" (to be) for "wir/ihr/sie/Sie". "alle" means "all (of them)" and often refers back to a plural noun mentioned earlier: "Die Äpfel waren alle teuer" = all the apples were expensive. In sentences like the examples, "alle" comes after the verb phrase ("waren") and emphasizes that every single one had that quality.
target_language_example: Die Tickets waren alle schon verkauft.
native_language_example: All the tickets were already sold.

additional_notes: Used with an adjective to describe someone/something in the past. "waren" is the simple past form of "sein" for "wir/sie/Sie" (we/they/you formal): z.B. "Sie waren sehr müde" = "They were very tired."
target_language_example: Wir waren sehr glücklich mit dem Ergebnis.
native_language_example: We were very happy with the result.

additional_notes: Uses the simple past of **sein** (**waren** = “were”) to describe that many people were present somewhere. Often followed by a place: **waren viele Leute im Park / im Zug / da?** Word order can be inverted to form a yes/no question: **Waren viele Leute …?**
target_language_example: Gestern waren viele Leute im Restaurant.
native_language_example: Yesterday there were many people in the restaurant.

additional_notes: Informal (du) form. Past tense of „sein“ (to be) for „du“: „du warst …“. In questions, German often puts the verb first: „Warst du …?“ = “Were you …?”
target_language_example: Warst du schon mal in Berlin?
native_language_example: Have you ever been to Berlin?

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone has visited a place at least once in their life. Literally it’s like “were you already once in …,” but the natural English meaning is “have you ever been to …?”. Use **in** with countries/regions/cities: *Warst du schon einmal in Deutschland / in Berlin?*
target_language_example: Warst du schon einmal in den USA?
native_language_example: Have you ever been to the USA?

additional_notes: Asks if someone has ever visited a place before. Uses informal singular "du" and the past tense of "sein" (warst). "schon mal" is short for "schon einmal" (= ever/before, at some point). Usually followed by a city/country/region: "… in Berlin/Deutschland/Japan".
target_language_example: Warst du schon mal in Berlin?
native_language_example: Have you ever been to Berlin?

additional_notes: Used with "ihr" to ask about a past situation/state involving more than one person (or speaking to one person using "ihr" in some regions). This is Präteritum of "sein" (2nd person plural). For a formal/plural polite version, use "Waren Sie ...?"
target_language_example: Wart ihr gestern Abend zu Hause?
native_language_example: Were you (all) at home last night?

additional_notes: "wart" is the informal past tense of "sein" for "ihr" (you all): "ihr wart" = "you were". "schon mal" is a very common, conversational way to say "ever" or "before" (at some time). It’s often used in questions about past experiences; with places/situations you can translate it as "Have you ever been …?"
target_language_example: Wart ihr schon mal in Berlin?
native_language_example: Have you ever been to Berlin?

meaning: "Wait, I’ll …" (used to interrupt and offer to do something).
additional_notes: Used when you want someone to pause while you do something or step in to help. Often followed by a verb: „Warte, ich helfe dir.“ / „Warte, ich komme mit.“ You can also use „Warte mal“ for a slightly more casual tone.
target_language_example: Warte, ich hole das für dich.
native_language_example: Wait, I’ll get that for you.

additional_notes: Common imperative: "Warte" is the informal singular command (to one person). Use it with "auf" + accusative (auf mich/dich/ihn/sie/uns/euch). For more polite or plural: "Warten Sie auf mich" (formal) / "Wartet auf mich" (to a group). Often followed by where: "Warte auf mich im Büro."
target_language_example: Warte auf mich vor dem Eingang, bitte.
native_language_example: Wait for me in front of the entrance, please.

additional_notes: Often used as an instruction/request to stay in the same place and wait. You’ll also see it as an imperative to one person: „Warte hier!“ or with extra information: „Warte hier auf mich.“ (wait here for me) and „Warte hier, bis …“ (wait here until …). Polite version: „Bitte warte hier …“
target_language_example: Warte hier, bis ich zurück bin.
native_language_example: Wait here until I’m back.

additional_notes: Used with a comma before „bis“ to introduce a clause describing the point in time when you stop waiting (e.g., until it stops, until someone comes). The verb in the „bis“-clause goes to the end: „… bis Tom hier ist/kommt“.
target_language_example: Wir warten, bis der Regen aufhört.
native_language_example: We’ll wait until the rain stops.

additional_notes: Polite/formal imperative of **warten** used when speaking to **Sie** (you). Often appears with **auf** + accusative for “wait for”: **Warten Sie auf mich.** It can also be used on its own to mean “Wait (a moment)!”
target_language_example: Warten Sie bitte einen Moment.
native_language_example: Please wait a moment.

additional_notes: Polite, formal way to tell someone to wait. Uses the formal "Sie" form, so it’s common with strangers, customers, or in official settings. Often followed by a time period or point in time: "einen Moment" (a moment), "fünf Minuten" (five minutes), "bis um fünf" (until 5 o’clock).
target_language_example: Warten Sie bitte hier, ich komme gleich zurück.
native_language_example: Please wait here; I’ll be right back.

additional_notes: Uses the formal/polite command form with Sie, common when speaking to strangers or in customer service. Often appears with bitte (“please”) and can be followed by more information like auf + Akk. (“wait for …”) or bis (“until …”).
target_language_example: Warten Sie hier bitte, bis der Arzt Sie aufruft.
native_language_example: Please wait here until the doctor calls you in.

additional_notes: Used when you are waiting until a person or thing arrives/happens. The person/thing you are waiting for is in the accusative case after auf (e.g., auf mich, auf den Bus, auf eine Antwort).
target_language_example: Meine Eltern warten auf mich.
native_language_example: My parents are waiting for me.

meaning: to make someone wait; to keep someone waiting.
additional_notes: Uses the verb "lassen" + infinitive: "jemanden warten lassen" = cause/allow someone to wait (usually meaning you delay them). The person waiting is in the accusative (mich/dich/ihn/sie/uns/euch/Sie): "Sie haben uns warten lassen." Often used when apologizing or complaining about how long it took.
target_language_example: Tut mir leid, ich habe dich so lange warten lassen.
native_language_example: Sorry, I kept you waiting so long.

additional_notes: Used with the accusative + infinitive pattern: **Ich habe + Person (Akk.) + warten sehen** = “I saw (someone) waiting.” You can add what they were waiting for with **auf + Akk.**: **auf jemanden/etwas warten** (“to wait for someone/something”).
target_language_example: Ich habe ihn am Bahnhof auf den Bus warten sehen.
native_language_example: I saw him waiting for the bus at the train station.

meaning: “are you waiting?” / “do you wait?” (to one person).
additional_notes: Present tense, 2nd person singular of **warten** (“to wait”), used when speaking to one person (**du**). Often used with **auf + Akk.**: *Wartest du auf Tom?* (“Are you waiting for Tom?”). With **darauf, dass ...** it means “waiting for (something to happen)”: *Wartest du darauf, dass ich es tue?* You can also say *Wartest du kurz?* = “Can you wait a moment?”
target_language_example: Wartest du auf mich oder gehst du schon?
native_language_example: Are you waiting for me, or are you leaving already?

additional_notes: From the verb phrase **auf jemanden/etwas warten** = “to wait for someone/something.” It takes the **accusative**: *auf mich / auf den Bus*. **wartet** is 3rd person singular present (“he/she/it waits”), and **Wartet auf …!** is also the **plural imperative** (“Wait for …!”).
target_language_example: Er wartet auf seine Freundin vor dem Kino.
native_language_example: He is waiting for his girlfriend in front of the cinema.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase "auf jemanden warten" (to wait for someone). "wartet" is 3rd person singular present (er/sie/es wartet). For addressing more than one person, use "Wartet auf mich!" (imperative plural: "Wait for me!").
target_language_example: Bitte wartet auf mich vor dem Bahnhof.
native_language_example: Please wait for me in front of the train station.

meaning: “is waiting for (something) to happen / for (someone) to do something.”
additional_notes: Used with a clause introduced by „dass“ to express that someone is waiting until a specific action or event happens. Common pattern: „[Person] wartet darauf, dass + [Nebensatz].“ The verb „warten“ is typically used with „auf“ + accusative (here replaced by the pronominal adverb „darauf“).
target_language_example: Er wartet darauf, dass du etwas sagst.
native_language_example: He is waiting for you to say something.

additional_notes: Past tense of **warten auf** (“to wait for”). When it means “wait for (someone/something)”, **auf** is used with the **accusative**: *auf mich / auf Hilfe*. Word order can change: *Auf mich wartete eine Überraschung* = “A surprise was waiting for me.” (Note: **warten auf + dative** can also describe waiting **on** a place/surface, e.g. *auf der Straßenseite* = “on the side of the street.”)
target_language_example: Ich wartete auf den Bus, aber er kam nicht.
native_language_example: I waited for the bus, but it didn’t come.

wartete sie auf die Resultate der Aufnahmeprüfung

target_language_multi_word_term: wartete sie auf die Resultate der Aufnahmeprüfung
meaning: "she waited for the results of the entrance (admissions) exam."
additional_notes: Common pattern: **warten auf + Akkusativ** (to wait for). Here: **auf die Resultate** (plural). **Aufnahmeprüfung** = entrance/admissions exam (e.g., for a school, university program, or academy). Often used with adverbs like *gespannt* (eagerly/expectantly), *verunsichert* (uncertain), *voller Unruhe* (restlessly).
target_language_example: Gespannt wartete sie auf die Resultate der Aufnahmeprüfung.
native_language_example: Expectantly, she waited for the results of the entrance exam.

additional_notes: Used to ask for the reason. Often followed by an adjective or phrase: "Warum bist du glücklich?" (why are you happy?). With a past participle, it can form the perfect tense with "sein": "Warum bist du dorthin gegangen?" = "Why did you go there?" (literally: "Why are you gone there?").
target_language_example: Warum bist du so spät gekommen?
native_language_example: Why did you come so late?

additional_notes: Used to ask (often with criticism or frustration) why someone consistently behaves in a certain way. It’s usually followed by an adjective: „Warum bist du immer so müde/laut/unfreundlich?“
target_language_example: Warum bist du immer so ungeduldig?
native_language_example: Why are you always so impatient?

additional_notes: Starts a question asking for the reason someone is not somewhere or is not doing something. With another verb at the end (often in the perfect tense), it can mean "Why didn't you …?" e.g., "Warum bist du nicht gekommen?" = "Why didn’t you come?"
target_language_example: Warum bist du nicht mit uns gekommen?
native_language_example: Why didn’t you come with us?

additional_notes: Used to ask the reason for someone’s current state or behavior. You normally complete it with an adjective or adverb: „Warum bist du so müde/nervös/misstrauisch?“ It can sound caring or annoyed depending on tone; with compliments like „süß“ it’s often playful.
target_language_example: Warum bist du so leise heute?
native_language_example: Why are you so quiet today?

additional_notes: Used to ask for a reason, with extra emphasis from "denn". It can sound curious, surprised, or slightly impatient depending on tone. Very common in spoken German; often followed by a noun/phrase ("Warum denn das?", "Warum denn so eilig?") or used alone ("Warum denn?").
target_language_example: Warum denn so plötzlich?
native_language_example: Why so suddenly? / How come all of a sudden?

additional_notes: A direct question asking for the reason behind someone’s question. Often used when you’re surprised or want to know what made the other person ask. In full form it’s usually “Warum fragst du (das)?”
target_language_example: Warum fragst du? Ist etwas passiert?
native_language_example: Why do you ask? Did something happen?

additional_notes: Used to ask for a reason about something the listener did. "Sie" is the formal "you". It’s typically followed by a past participle (Perfekt), e.g., "Warum haben Sie … gesagt/getan/geschrieben?" In speech it often corresponds to English "Why did you …?" even though it literally looks like "Why have you …?"
target_language_example: Warum haben Sie das nicht früher gesagt?
native_language_example: Why didn’t you say that earlier?

meaning: "Why did you ... to me?" / "Why have you ... me?" (formal).
additional_notes: A question starter used with formal "Sie". It’s usually followed by a past participle to ask why someone did something involving you: "Warum haben Sie mich angerufen?" (called me), "... aufgehalten?" (stopped/delayed me), "... geküsst?" (kissed me). In everyday speech, German often uses Perfekt ("haben" + past participle) for past actions.
target_language_example: Warum haben Sie mich nicht informiert?
native_language_example: Why didn't you inform me?

additional_notes: Used to ask for a reason. "Warum" = why, and "habt ihr" is the verb "haben" with "ihr" (you plural), typically in the Perfekt (present perfect) to talk about the past. In main questions, the verb comes before the subject: "habt" + "ihr".
target_language_example: Warum habt ihr so lange gewartet?
native_language_example: Why did you wait so long?

meaning: “Why did you … that?” / “Why have you … that?”
additional_notes: Used to ask why someone did/said something. The verb usually comes at the end: **Warum hast du das gemacht/gesagt/geheimgehalten?** In everyday English it’s often translated with simple past (“Why did you…?”), even though German uses **hast** (present of *haben*) + past participle (Perfekt).
target_language_example: Warum hast du das gemacht?
native_language_example: Why did you do that?

meaning: “why did you …?” (addressing one person, perfect tense; often with a reflexive verb).
additional_notes: Used to ask for a reason about something the other person did. Literally “why have you yourself…”, but in English it’s usually just “Why did you…?”. The “dich” is the reflexive pronoun used with many verbs (e.g., sich verlaufen = get lost, sich zurückziehen = withdraw, sich weigern = refuse, sich bereit erklären = agree/volunteer). You normally continue with a past participle at the end: „Warum hast du dich entschuldigt?“
target_language_example: Warum hast du dich nicht gemeldet?
native_language_example: Why didn’t you get in touch?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the reason behind an action involving a specific thing or action already known from context. Grammatically: "Warum" (why) + "hast du" (have you) + "es" (it). In everyday English, this often translates as "Why did you…?" (past) rather than the literal "Why have you…?".
target_language_example: Warum hast du es mir nicht vorher gesagt?
native_language_example: Why didn’t you tell me earlier?

meaning: "why did you … him?" / "why have you … him?"
additional_notes: Used to ask for the reason for an action involving a male person/thing (ihn = “him” in the accusative). The verb comes at the end as a past participle in the present perfect: "Warum hast du ihn behalten?" (“Why did you keep him?”). In speech, this often refers to a past action.
target_language_example: Warum hast du ihn angerufen?
native_language_example: Why did you call him?

meaning: "Why did you … to me? / Why have you … me?"
additional_notes: Used to ask why someone did something to you, usually in the past. It’s typically followed by a past participle to form the Perfekt tense: "Warum hast du mich + Partizip II?" (e.g., "geweckt", "verlassen"). "mich" is the direct object (accusative) meaning "me".
target_language_example: Warum hast du mich angelogen?
native_language_example: Why did you lie to me?

meaning: “why do you have …?” / “why have you …?” (asking for the reason).
additional_notes: Used to ask why someone has something (possesses it) or why they have a certain state/feeling (e.g., Angst haben = to be afraid). In spoken German it’s often followed by an object or expression: „Warum hast du sein Messer?“ (Why do you have his knife?), „Warum hast du Angst …?“ (Why are you afraid …?), „Warum hast du Handschuhe an?“ (Why are you wearing gloves?).
target_language_example: Warum hast du so viel Stress heute?
native_language_example: Why are you so stressed today?

additional_notes: Used to start a question asking for the reason for a past action or situation. In German questions, the conjugated verb comes second: „Warum hat er …?“ and the past participle often comes at the end (Perfekt), e.g., „Warum hat er das getan?“ = “Why did he do that?”
target_language_example: Warum hat er so spät angerufen?
native_language_example: Why did he call so late?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the reason for a past action. Word order: **Warum** (why) + **hat** (has) + **sie** (she) + past participle later in the sentence (Perfekt), e.g. *Warum hat sie mich unterbrochen?* = “Why did she interrupt me?”
target_language_example: Warum hat sie so spät angerufen?
native_language_example: Why did she call so late?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the reason something is the case. "Ist" is the 3rd-person singular form of "sein" (to be), so this pattern is used with er/sie/es and singular nouns, as in "Warum ist das so?" For plural subjects, use "warum sind".
target_language_example: Warum ist der Zug so spät?
native_language_example: Why is the train so late?

additional_notes: Used to start a question about why a man/boy did something or is in a certain state/place. Word order: in German questions, the verb comes second ("ist") and the subject follows it ("er"). Often continued with a past participle or another phrase: "Warum ist er gegangen?" / "Warum ist er hier?"
target_language_example: Warum ist er so spät gekommen?
native_language_example: Why did he come so late?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the reason something has a certain quality or degree. It’s typically followed by an adjective/adverb (e.g., so dunkel/heiß/leise) or by a longer clause (e.g., so wichtig, dass …). Word order is a normal German question: warum + verb (ist) + subject (es).
target_language_example: Warum ist es so kalt heute?
native_language_example: Why is it so cold today?

meaning: "why do you let" / "why do you leave" (something).
additional_notes: Used to ask why someone allows something to happen or keeps something in a certain state. With **lassen** you often get either **lassen + infinitive** ("let someone do something": *Warum lässt du ihn gehen?*) or **lassen + adjective/participle** ("leave something (open/closed/on)": *Warum lässt du die Tür offen?*). Common pattern: **jemanden davonkommen lassen** = "to let someone get away with it".
target_language_example: Warum lässt du das Licht an?
native_language_example: Why do you leave the light on?

additional_notes: A common question asking for the reason behind someone’s action. It addresses "du" (one person, informal). The verb changes with the person: "Warum machst du das?" (you), "Warum macht er/sie das?" (he/she), "Warum machen wir das?" (we). Often used with extra words like "immer" (always) or "immer noch" (still).
target_language_example: Warum machst du das schon wieder?
native_language_example: Why are you doing that again?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the reason you are required/forced to do something. Follow it with a verb in the infinitive or with a noun phrase (e.g., „Warum muss ich jetzt gehen?“, „Warum muss ich das machen?“). Often sounds frustrated or complaining depending on tone.
target_language_example: Warum muss ich so früh aufstehen?
native_language_example: Why do I have to get up so early?

meaning: "why do we have to …?" / "why must we …?"
additional_notes: Used to question the necessity or obligation to do something. "müssen" is the modal verb for "have to/must"; the main verb usually goes to the end of the clause (e.g., "Warum müssen wir gehen?"). You can replace "wir" with another subject ("ich/du/ihr/Sie").
target_language_example: Warum müssen wir jetzt gehen?
native_language_example: Why do we have to leave now?

meaning: "why do you take ...?" / "why don't you take ...?"
additional_notes: Used to ask why someone is taking/choosing/bringing something or someone. It’s the question form with the verb "nehmen" (to take): "Warum nimmst du ...?" (Why are you taking...?) and often "Warum nimmst du nicht ...?" (Why don’t you take...?). In the set phrase "jemanden in Schutz nehmen" it means "to defend someone" (literally: to take someone into protection).
target_language_example: Warum nimmst du nicht den Bus?
native_language_example: Why don’t you take the bus?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the reason behind what someone is saying. You usually add the rest of the sentence after it (e.g., warum sagst du das?/…auf Wiedersehen?/…mir das?). In speech, it can sound questioning or critical depending on tone.
target_language_example: Warum sagst du so etwas?
native_language_example: Why do you say something like that?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the reason something is the case, addressed to more than one person (ihr = “you all”). Seid is the 2nd-person plural form of sein (to be). Often followed by an adjective/place/state: Warum seid ihr noch hier? (“Why are you still here?”). Not used for the polite/formal “you” (that would be: Warum sind Sie …?).
target_language_example: Warum seid ihr so spät dran?
native_language_example: Why are you running so late?

additional_notes: Used to ask for a reason about someone’s behavior, mood, or a noticeable trait. "ihr seid" is the 2nd-person plural form of "sein" (you all are). After "so" you usually add an adjective/adverb ("so langsam" = so slow) or a fixed phrase like "so schlechter Laune" (= in such a bad mood).
target_language_example: Warum seid ihr so müde heute?
native_language_example: Why are you all so tired today?

meaning: "why are you" / "why were you" (formal or plural).
additional_notes: Used to ask for a reason. "Sie" is the formal "you" (also used for "you" plural). The verb comes before "Sie" in questions: "Warum sind Sie ...?" In context it can refer to the present ("Why are you ...?") or the past (often with a time word like "gestern/damals": "Why were you ...?").
target_language_example: Warum sind Sie so spät gekommen?
native_language_example: Why did you come so late?

additional_notes: A polite/formal way to ask why someone has a certain quality/state. Usually followed by an adjective ("Warum sind Sie so müde?"), but it can also be followed by other descriptions like "in schlechter Laune" (in a bad mood) or "weit weg" (so far away). With friends/family you’d usually use "Warum bist du so ...?".
target_language_example: Warum sind Sie so nervös?
native_language_example: Why are you so nervous?

meaning: "Why should I …?" (questioning why you are supposed to do something).
additional_notes: Used to question a suggestion, instruction, or expectation (often with skepticism or confusion). It’s usually followed by a verb in the infinitive at the end of the clause: "Warum soll ich gehen?" You can also use it when talking about what might happen to you: "Warum soll ich bestraft werden?"
target_language_example: Warum soll ich heute früher kommen?
native_language_example: Why should I come earlier today?

additional_notes: Used to question someone’s reason or motivation, often implying doubt: “What reason would he have?” It uses **sollte** (Konjunktiv II of *sollen*) to sound hypothetical or skeptical. Often followed by an infinitive at the end: *Warum sollte er lügen?*
target_language_example: Warum sollte er dir helfen, wenn er dich gar nicht kennt?
native_language_example: Why would he help you if he doesn’t even know you?

additional_notes: Used to question the reason for doing something, often as a rhetorical question meaning “I don’t see any reason to.” Usually followed by an infinitive clause (e.g., „Warum sollte ich das tun?“). On its own („Warum sollte ich?“) it implies “Why should I (do that)?” based on context.
target_language_example: Warum sollte ich ihm helfen, wenn er nie Danke sagt?
native_language_example: Why should I help him if he never says thank you?

additional_notes: Used to challenge or ask for a good reason to do something. It uses "sollten" (Konjunktiv II of "sollen"), which often sounds a bit softer/more hypothetical than "Warum sollen wir …?" and can imply skepticism: “What reason do we have to…?” Often followed by a verb in the infinitive at the end: "Warum sollten wir das glauben/tun?"
target_language_example: Warum sollten wir jetzt gehen, wenn wir noch Zeit haben?
native_language_example: Why should we leave now if we still have time?

meaning: "why are you wearing" / "why are you carrying" (addressing 'you').
additional_notes: Used to ask the reason for what someone is wearing or carrying. "trägst" is the 2nd-person singular form of "tragen" (to wear/carry), and "du" is informal "you" (used with friends, family, kids). What follows is usually the thing being worn/carried (often with an article: "eine Brille", "meine Schuhe").
target_language_example: Warum trägst du heute einen Hut?
native_language_example: Why are you wearing a hat today?

meaning: “why were you …?” (asking for the reason in the past).
additional_notes: Used with the simple past of **sein** for **du**: **du warst** (“you were”). You typically add a place, time, or description after it: **Warum warst du da?** (there), **… in Boston?**, **… letzte Woche …?**, **… so langsam?**
target_language_example: Warum warst du gestern so spät zu Hause?
native_language_example: Why were you home so late yesterday?

additional_notes: A direct question using informal singular du. „weinen“ = to cry; „weinst“ is the du-form (present tense). Often said to someone close (child, partner, friend). Particles like „denn“ or „dann“ can be added for tone (“so/then”, “(just)”).
target_language_example: Hey, warum weinst du? Kann ich dir helfen?
native_language_example: Hey, why are you crying? Can I help you?

additional_notes: Used to ask for someone’s reason or motivation. It’s followed by the verb in the infinitive at the end of the clause (e.g., „Warum willst du Arzt werden?“). With another verb like „reden“, you often add „mit“ + dative: „Warum willst du mit Tom reden?“
target_language_example: Warum willst du heute so früh gehen?
native_language_example: Why do you want to leave so early today?

additional_notes: Used to ask for someone’s reason or motivation. "Sie" is the formal/polite "you" (to one person or a group). The verb comes first after the question word: "Warum wollen Sie ...?" You usually add another verb at the end: "Warum wollen Sie mich begleiten?" (want + to accompany).
target_language_example: Warum wollen Sie das jetzt machen?
native_language_example: Why do you want to do that now?

additional_notes: Used to ask about someone’s reason in the past. It’s built from: warum (why) + wolltest (wanted; past of "wollen") + du (you). Often followed by an infinitive verb at the end of the clause: „Warum wolltest du gehen?“
target_language_example: Warum wolltest du gestern so früh nach Hause gehen?
native_language_example: Why did you want to go home so early yesterday?

additional_notes: Colloquial short form of **etwas Besseres**. Often used to say you *deserve something better* (**Du hast was Besseres verdient**), *have something better to do/plan* (**Hast du was Besseres vor?**), or *know/have something better* (**Ich weiß da was Besseres / Ich hab was Besseres**). Grammar tip: after **was/etwas**, German commonly uses an adjective with **-es** (e.g., *was Gutes, was Neues, was Schöneres*).
target_language_example: Wenn du willst, suche ich was Besseres für dich.
native_language_example: If you want, I’ll find something better for you.

additional_notes: Common spoken/colloquial way to say "etwas Neues". Used when you want to wear, try, buy, or think of a new thing/idea (e.g., "was Neues anziehen" = to put on something new; "was Neues ausprobieren" = to try something new; "Fällt euch was Neues ein?" = Can you think of something new?).
target_language_example: Ich möchte heute mal was Neues ausprobieren.
native_language_example: I want to try something new today.

meaning: “what do you think … ?” (inserted into a question).
additional_notes: Used as a parenthetical comment inside a question to ask for the other person’s opinion/guess. It’s usually set off by commas: “Was, glaubst du, hat er gemacht?” = “What do you think he did?” You can also use it with other question words (wer/wo/wann/wie), but then the first word changes.
target_language_example: Was, glaubst du, hat er gemacht?
native_language_example: What do you think he did?

additional_notes: Used to raise a possibility—often expressing worry, doubt, or speculation. It’s usually followed by a verb at the end of the clause (e.g., „Was, wenn er kommt?“). You can swap the pronoun: „Was, wenn sie…“, „Was, wenn ich…“, etc.
target_language_example: Was, wenn er zu spät kommt?
native_language_example: What if he comes too late?

additional_notes: Used to ask about a possible situation and its consequences (often expressing worry or considering a different option). Very common in spoken German. Note: without the comma, "was wenn ich" is also possible in casual writing. Sentence order: "Was, wenn ich + verb…?" (e.g., "Was, wenn ich zu spät komme?"). It can also appear as "Macht es dir was, wenn ich …?" = "Do you mind if I …?"
target_language_example: Was, wenn ich heute nicht kommen kann?
native_language_example: What if I can’t come today?

additional_notes: Used to add strong emotion (anger, frustration, surprise) to a question. Often placed right after the question word: "Was, zum Teufel, ...?" It’s rude/impolite in polite situations; softer options include "Was denn...?" or "Was bitte...?"
target_language_example: Was, zum Teufel, hast du getan?
native_language_example: What the hell did you do?

additional_notes: Used with the formal pronoun "Sie" (you) in indirect questions or relative clauses: "..., was Sie ..." = "... what you ...". Often follows verbs like sagen (to say), wissen (to know), zeigen (to show). Word order in the "was" clause is normal German clause order (verb usually later).
target_language_example: Ich verstehe nicht, was Sie meinen.
native_language_example: I don't understand what you mean.

meaning: “what you did / what you have done”.
additional_notes: A relative clause introduced by **was** (“what”) that refers to an action or thing (often something just mentioned or known from context). **Sie** is formal “you.” **getan haben** is the Perfekt of **tun** (“to do”), literally “have done.” Often used after verbs like **sehen**, **wissen**, **sagen**, **zeigen**: *Ich weiß, was Sie getan haben.*
target_language_example: Ich verstehe, was Sie getan haben.
native_language_example: I understand what you did.

meaning: "what you want" (formal, addressing one person as "Sie").
additional_notes: Used in a subordinate clause to refer to the thing(s) someone wants. Common after verbs like sagen/erzählen/lesen/nehmen/essen/denken/tragen: "Sagen Sie mir, was Sie wollen." It can also express freedom of choice/permission: "Sie dürfen ..., was Sie wollen" (= you may ... whatever you want). Word order: the verb goes to the end in the clause ("wollen").
target_language_example: Bestellen Sie, was Sie wollen, ich bezahle heute.
native_language_example: Order what you want; I'm paying today.

additional_notes: Colloquial version of **„etwas anderes“**. Often used when suggesting an alternative (**„Wir könnten was anderes versuchen.“**) or when someone is thinking about something different (**„Du dachtest an was anderes.“**). In more formal speech/writing, use **„etwas anderes“**.
target_language_example: Hast du noch was anderes im Kopf?
native_language_example: Do you have something else on your mind?

additional_notes: Used to say that the exact thing doesn’t matter or isn’t known, often meaning “no matter what it is/what happens.” It can introduce a clause (“Was auch immer daraus wird …” = “Whatever comes of it …”) or refer to an unknown thing (“Was auch immer das hier ist …” = “Whatever this is …”).
target_language_example: Was auch immer du entscheidest, ich unterstütze dich.
native_language_example: Whatever you decide, I’ll support you.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something that must stay true in every possible situation. Often placed at the start of a sentence, followed by a comma: "Was auch passiert, ..." It can also appear after the main clause: "Bleib ruhig, was auch passiert."
target_language_example: Was auch passiert, ruf mich an.
native_language_example: Whatever happens, call me.

additional_notes: Used to ask for the meaning of a word, sign, statement, or situation. Usually followed by the thing you’re asking about: "Was bedeutet das?" (What does that mean?), "Was bedeutet dieses Wort/Schild?". In questions, the verb comes second: "Was bedeutet das jetzt?"
target_language_example: Was bedeutet dieses Wort auf Englisch?
native_language_example: What does this word mean in English?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the meaning or implication of something that was just said, written, or happened. You can add context with “für …” (e.g., “Was bedeutet das für mich?” = “What does that mean for me?”). Often asked as a follow-up question in conversation.
target_language_example: Ich verstehe das Wort nicht—was bedeutet das?
native_language_example: I don’t understand the word—what does that mean?

meaning: An exclamation meaning “how … you are!” / “what a … you are!” (often criticizing).
additional_notes: Used with an adjective or noun to express strong emotion (often annoyance or shock): “Was bist du empfindlich!” = “You’re so sensitive!” With particles like “denn” or “nur” it sounds even more emphatic: “Was bist du denn … geworden?” = “How did you get so …?” / “Why did you become so …?” With a noun it can be insulting: “Was bist du nur für ein Schuft!” = “What a scoundrel you are!” Not the same as the real question “Was bist du?” (“What are you?” e.g., “I’m a student.”).
target_language_example: Was bist du heute ungeduldig!
native_language_example: You’re so impatient today!

additional_notes: Used in indirect questions to ask for the meaning or implications of something previously mentioned. Often follows verbs like wissen, verstehen, lernen, or phrases like die Frage ist … . Can refer to the meaning of a word, a situation, or the consequences (“Do you know what that means?”).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir erklären, was das bedeutet?
native_language_example: Can you explain to me what that means?

additional_notes: Uses the formal “Sie” form, so it’s polite and used with strangers, customers, older people, or in professional situations. Common patterns: “Was denken Sie über …?” = “What do you think about …?”; “Was denken Sie, …?” introduces an opinion/guess (like “What do you think, …?”); “Was denken Sie sich dabei?” is more confrontational: “What were you thinking?”
target_language_example: Was denken Sie über den Plan?
native_language_example: What do you think about the plan?

additional_notes: Used to ask for someone’s opinion or guess. Common patterns: „Was denkst du über …?“ = “What do you think about …?” and „Was denkst du, …?“ = “What do you think (that) …?” Note: „Was denkst du dir?“ is a special case and often sounds like a reproach (“What were you thinking?”).
target_language_example: Was denkst du über den Film?
native_language_example: What do you think about the movie?

meaning: “What do you think about …?” / “What’s your opinion of …?”
additional_notes: Used to ask someone’s opinion about a topic, person, place, or situation. It’s informal because it uses "du"; more formal: "Was denken Sie über …?" Also common: "Was denkst du darüber?" (= about it/that).
target_language_example: Was denkst du über dieses Restaurant?
native_language_example: What do you think about this restaurant?

additional_notes: "Ihr" is the informal plural "you" (talking to a group). Often used to invite people to share their thoughts or guesses, and it can introduce an embedded question: "Was denkt ihr, wer/was/wie ...?" = "Who/what/how do you think ...?".
target_language_example: Was denkt ihr, wann wir losfahren sollten?
native_language_example: When do you think we should leave?

meaning: "what (exactly)?" / "what do you mean?" (often showing surprise or annoyance).
additional_notes: Used in questions to sound more insistent, surprised, or irritated. Very common with „für ein(e) …“ to ask for clarification: „Was denn für ein …?“ = “What kind of … (exactly)?” It can also react to what someone just said: „Was denn?“ = “What?” / “What’s going on?” The tone depends on context and can sound rude if said sharply (e.g., with „verdammt“).
target_language_example: Was denn für ein Problem hast du damit?
native_language_example: What problem exactly do you have with it?

additional_notes: A compositional phrase: was means "what" and du means informal singular "you." It often introduces a subordinate clause about the thing, action, or idea the other person is connected with. In these clauses, the main verb usually comes at the end: was du sagst, was du gekauft hast, was du meinst.
target_language_example: Ich weiß nicht, was du willst.
native_language_example: I don't know what you want.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the things (or qualities) someone needs. Often appears in sentences like „Hast du alles …, was du brauchst?“ or „Nimm mit, was du brauchst.“ It can also refer to something abstract: „Was du brauchst, ist …“ ("What you need is …").
target_language_example: Ich kann dir geben, was du brauchst.
native_language_example: I can give you what you need.

meaning: “what you’re doing/saying there” (what you’re doing right now / in that situation).
additional_notes: Used to point to and often criticize/question what someone is doing, saying, or holding in the current situation. It’s usually followed by a verb like machst/tust/sagst/erzählst/hast, and da adds emphasis like “there/just now/in that context.”
target_language_example: Was du da machst, ist gefährlich.
native_language_example: What you’re doing there is dangerous.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to someone’s earlier words. It’s a clause with the relative pronoun "was" + a verb-at-the-end structure ("gesagt hast"), and it can appear at the beginning or later in the sentence: "Was du gesagt hast, ..." / "..., was du gesagt hast."
target_language_example: Ich habe verstanden, was du gesagt hast.
native_language_example: I understood what you said.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific action someone did in the past. Grammatically, it’s a clause introduced by **was** (“what”) and often works like a noun phrase: **Was du getan hast, war ...** (“What you did was ...”). **getan** is the past participle of **tun** (“to do”) and combines with **hast** (present tense of “have”) to form the German present perfect, which commonly expresses past actions in spoken German.
target_language_example: Ich kann nicht glauben, was du getan hast.
native_language_example: I can’t believe what you did.

additional_notes: Used to refer to someone’s words/content as a thing. It’s a relative clause starting with **was** (“what”), and it often follows a comma: **…, was du sagst.** It can also stand at the beginning as the subject: **Was du sagst, ist wahr.** Word order stays like a normal clause: **du sagst**.
target_language_example: Ich glaube, was du sagst, aber ich brauche dafür ein Beispiel.
native_language_example: I believe what you say, but I need an example for it.

additional_notes: Used to comment on, judge, or react to someone’s statement. It starts a sentence with a relative clause (“was du sagst” = “what you say/are saying”) followed by “ist” (“is”), and then an adjective or phrase: “Was du sagst, ist richtig/falsch/Quatsch/wichtig.” Often written with a comma when something comes before it: “Alles, was du sagst, ist …”.
target_language_example: Was du sagst, ist interessant, aber ich bin nicht sicher.
native_language_example: What you’re saying is interesting, but I’m not sure.

additional_notes: A relative clause referring to your actions/behavior. Often used to contrast actions with words ("Was du tust, ist wichtiger als ...") or as the object of a verb like "wissen" ("Weiß er, was du tust?") and in warnings like "Pass auf, was du tust" (= be careful what you do).
target_language_example: Denk daran: Was du tust, zählt mehr als was du sagst.
native_language_example: Remember: what you do matters more than what you say.

additional_notes: Used as a dependent clause referring to the thing(s) someone wants. Often follows verbs like haben, machen/tun, sagen, spielen, fragen: „Du kannst haben, was du willst.“ In commands like „Mach/Tu, was du willst“, it can simply mean “do what you want,” and depending on tone it can sound dismissive/annoyed (“fine, do whatever you want”).
target_language_example: Bestell, was du willst; ich zahle heute.
native_language_example: Order whatever you want; I'm paying today.

additional_notes: A relative clause meaning “what you want/whatever you want,” often referring to an object or outcome. Used after verbs like sagen/erzählen (to say/tell), bekommen/kriegen (to get), or in set phrases like „Mach, was du willst“ (“Do what you want”). Word order stays: „was“ + subject („du“) + verb at the end („willst“).
target_language_example: Sag mir einfach, was du willst.
native_language_example: Just tell me what you want.

additional_notes: A relative clause: **was** = “what/that which,” **du** = “you,” **wolltest** (Präteritum of *wollen*) = “wanted.” Used after a noun like **das** (“the thing”) or on its own: **Hast du, was du wolltest?** = “Do you have what you wanted?” Often set off by commas in longer sentences.
target_language_example: Ich habe endlich, was du wolltest.
native_language_example: I finally have what you wanted.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause about what a male person says, thinks, does, saw, etc. It often appears in indirect questions or relative-like clauses: for example, was er gesehen hatte = "what he had seen." In German, the verb in this clause usually comes at the end.
target_language_example: Ich weiß nicht, was er meint.
native_language_example: I don't know what he means.

additional_notes: A dependent (subordinate) clause introduced by **was** (“what”) that refers to the content of someone’s words. In this kind of clause, the conjugated verb goes to the end: **… gesagt hat**. Often used after verbs like **verstehen** (understand), **wissen** (know), **sich erinnern** (remember), etc.
target_language_example: Ich weiß nicht, was er gesagt hat.
native_language_example: I don’t know what he said.

meaning: what he did / what he has done.
additional_notes: A relative clause meaning “the thing that he did.” It often appears after verbs like wissen (to know), bereuen (to regret), sagen (to say/tell), or as the subject of a sentence: Was er getan hat, ist ... . Uses the perfect tense of tun: getan hat.
target_language_example: Ich kann nicht glauben, was er getan hat.
native_language_example: I can’t believe what he did.

additional_notes: A clause starting with **was** acts like “what …” in English and refers to the content of what someone says. It often appears at the beginning of a sentence (**Was er sagt, …**) or after a comma (**…, was er sagt**). Note: German **was** here means “what,” not the English verb “was.”
target_language_example: Ich glaube nicht, was er sagt.
native_language_example: I don’t believe what he says.

additional_notes: A noun-like clause (nominalized clause) used to refer to the content of his words. Often used as the subject or object of a sentence: "Was er sagte, stimmt." / "Ich habe verstanden, was er sagte." In this clause, the verb goes at the end: "er sagte".
target_language_example: Ich glaube, was er sagte, war ein Missverständnis.
native_language_example: I think what he said was a misunderstanding.

additional_notes: Used in an indirect question or relative clause to refer to the thing(s) he wants. Word order: in the clause, the verb goes to the end (… was er will).
target_language_example: Ich weiß nicht, was er will.
native_language_example: I don't know what he wants.

meaning: “What brings you …?” (asking why someone has come).
additional_notes: Commonly used with a place or person: „Was führt dich her?“ = “What brings you here?”; „Was führt dich zu mir?“ = “What brings you to me?” Often sounds a bit formal or literary compared with „Warum bist du hier?“ / „Was machst du hier?“
target_language_example: Was führt dich heute zu uns?
native_language_example: What brings you to us today?

additional_notes: Used before a noun to ask about the type or category of something: Was für Musik...? = 'what kind of music...?'. It can also be used in exclamations to show surprise or emphasis: Was für eine interessante Geschichte! = 'what an interesting story!'. In the singular, it is often followed by an indefinite article that changes with case: was für ein / eine / einen ...
target_language_example: Was für Bücher liest du gern?
native_language_example: What kind of books do you like to read?

additional_notes: Used with **was für + noun** to ask about the **type/category** of something (here: books). In questions it often comes first: **Was für Bücher ...?** Depending on context, it can mean either “what kind of books” (genre/type) or “which books” (selection).
target_language_example: Was für Bücher liest du am liebsten?
native_language_example: What kind of books do you like to read most?

meaning: "what kind of movies" / "what type of films".
additional_notes: Used to ask about categories or preferences (e.g., comedy, horror, action). In questions, it’s often followed by a verb like "magst du" (do you like) or "siehst du gern" (do you like to watch). "Film" and "Filme" are common in everyday speech; you can also say "was für Filme" in formal (Sie) and informal (du) situations.
target_language_example: Was für Filme schaust du am Wochenende?
native_language_example: What kind of movies do you watch on the weekend?

additional_notes: Used before a noun to ask about or react to the type/quality of something. Often used as an exclamation: "Was für ein Chaos!" = "What a mess!". The article changes with gender/case: was für ein (masc.), was für eine (fem.), was für ein (neut.); e.g. accusative masc. "was für einen ...". With plural nouns, you usually say "was für" without "ein": "Was für Leute!" = "What (kind of) people!".
target_language_example: Was für ein schönes Wetter!
native_language_example: What beautiful weather!

additional_notes: Used with a noun to express surprise/admiration: "Was für ein schöner Ausblick!" = "What a beautiful view!"
